13541-the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bie:
Ambrose Bierce's collected works, volume one of 1909, gathers Ashes of the Beacon, The Land Beyond the Blow, For the Ahkoond, John Smith Liberator, and Bits of Autobiography. Ashes of the Beacon, an historical monograph written in 4930, imagines a future looking back on America, while fantasy tales carry readers to Ug, Gangewag, Ghargaroo, and Tortirra.

Autobiographical pieces recall Shiloh, Chickamauga, Pickett's Mill, four days in Dixie, Franklin, and a sole survivor's tale, with work for an empress and travel across the plains. Swamp dwellers, pious in their own way, build a temple to a god Bierce will not name. The volume shows Bierce at his sharpest: satirist, soldier, and inventor of strange lands.
15504-mr-edward-arnold-s-new-and-popular:
Edward Arnold's December 1901 catalogue lists his new and popular books from Bedford Street, London, with prices, formats, and press praise for each title. It is a publisher's list, not a single book, and it shows what a London house pushed at Christmas 1901. Short notices quote the Morning Post, the World, and the Times.

Mrs. Charles Bagot's Links with the Past leads the list, praised as a vivid record of social life over much of the last century, drawn from long life in good society. Other titles cover Finland, from its farms and forests to its money, banks, and government, and Sidney Peel's Trooper 8,008, a soldier's frank book with photographs and a map. The catalogue now serves as a window on Edwardian reading taste.
16352-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Rossiter Johnson edited this first volume of a vast history told through famous historians' own words. The plan runs chronologically from the dawn of civilization through Hammurabi's code, Theseus and Athens, the fall of Troy, Solomon's temple, Assyria, and the founding of Rome. Brief introductions by specialists link each narrative.

The volume aims to be readable and fair, neither sectarian nor partisan, with indices, chronologies, and reading courses. Maspero, Plutarch, Grote, and Niebuhr all lend their voices. Readers get world history as a chain of vivid scenes, each told by a master, rather than as a dry summary.
16717-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
This September 1, 1920 number of Punch, volume 159, leads with Charivaria jokes on a Newcastle miner fined for neglecting his children, Mr. Smillie's hobbies and his fine collection of strikes, Amundsen's stay away from civilization, and a poet laureate who never wrote an ode to British weather. A heavy Wolverhampton man and a tactless MP get their turns.

Punch keeps its weekly sting aimed at labor, politics, and home life, with short jokes and cartoons. The miner and Smillie jokes show its edge on strikes and wages in 1920. The issue is a brisk, funny dip into postwar Britain, best taken a page at a time for its jokes and its targets.
2101-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle opens his history of Frederick the Great with Book One on birth and parentage in 1712. It starts not with a date but with a lean old man walking the terraces of Sans-Souci. At home the people called him Vater Fritz, Father Fred. Carlyle begins with the old king at Sans-Souci, a scene he returns to throughout the work.

The proem looks back from that old king to the child he was, and to the parents and court that formed him. Carlyle's vivid, digressive prose sets the scale of the whole work, a life told as the history of Prussia itself. The nickname Vater Fritz shows how Prussians loved a king who lived plainly and worked hard.
21686-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume one of Stevenson's works, in the Swanston Edition of 1911, opens with Andrew Lang's introduction. The set ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand copies for sale. This copy is number sixteen hundred and seventy-eight of the printing.

An Inland Voyage leads the contents, Stevenson's canoe trip from Antwerp toward France. Colvin's memoir tells how illness ordered the young writer south to Mentone. There the born wayfarer wrote on roads for Hamerton's Portfolio. Walter Crane designed the title page of the voyage. The volume shows Stevenson at the start of his road, a traveller before he was a romancer.
23055-the-slanderer-1901:
Anton Chekhov catches a schoolmaster in The Slanderer, his story dated 1901 here. A voice from the adjoining room calls out at a wedding feast. Vankin's cropped head soon appears in the doorway. He is the assistant instructor, and he has heard enough to start trouble. Someone has been kissing in here, Vankin announces, alone with a lady, no less.

A kiss, a witness, and a panic about reputation set Chekhov's little machine running. The slanderer of the title fears gossip so much that he manufactures it himself, begging, explaining, and spreading the story everywhere. Chekhov needs only a few pages to strip a man's dignity with perfect comic timing. The tale is a miniature of his method, funny on the surface, pitiless underneath, and done before the reader wants it to end.
24446-john-corwell-sailor-and-miner-and-:
Louis Becke published this short book with T. Fisher Unwin in 1901, pairing two South Seas tales. The first follows John Corwell, master of the cutter Ceres. He seeks an audience with the governor of the young colony of New South Wales, a colony still struggling with hunger and neglect from the home authorities.

The second piece turns to poisonous fish of the Pacific, a practical danger for sailors and island traders. Becke knew the South Seas at first hand, and he writes with salty detail about ships, governors, and colonial life. Readers get both a brisk colonial yarn and a curious natural-history note from the same pen.
24640-old-mary-1901:
Louis Becke published this South Seas tale with T. Fisher Unwin in 1901. It opens early one morning on an island, as the trade wind lifts the white mist from dark valleys and mountain slopes. Denison, supercargo of the trading schooner Palestine, rows ashore to call on the island's only white trader.

The trader, Handle, a quiet-voiced, white-haired old man, greets him and sends him shooting with Harry and the girls. Becke's tale unfolds in island talk, trade, and old scores. Readers get a vivid, atmospheric story of the Pacific trading world, told by a writer who knew it from the inside.
24641-martin-of-nitendi-and-the-river-of:
Louis Becke published these two South Seas tales with T. Fisher Unwin in 1901. The first opens halfway up a mountain above a little land-locked harbour, where a man lies at full length on jagged rocks, watching a gunboat anchored half a mile away. He wears only a girdle of ti leaves, carries a Snider rifle, and has bleeding, bare feet.

Yet he had once been a white man, and his story explains how he came to Nitendi. The companion tale, The River of Dreams, follows in the same Pacific world. Becke writes with firsthand knowledge of island life. Readers get two vivid, unsentimental stories of the South Seas at the turn of the century.
24642-five-head-creek-and-fish-drugging-:
Louis Becke published these two Australian and Pacific pieces with T. Fisher Unwin in 1901. The first opens after a day's ride through ghostly grey gums and ironbarks. The narrator reaches a slab hut with a corrugated iron roof on Five-Head Creek, twenty-five miles from Townsville in North Queensland.

The hut is to be his home for six months, and he hobbles his horse to feed on lush grass by the creek. The companion piece describes fish drugging in the Pacific, a native method of stunning fish for the catch. Becke's prose gives readers the Queensland bush and island life in sharp, firsthand detail.
24837-the-trader-s-wife-1901:
Louis Becke published The Trader's Wife in 1901, a South Seas novel of marriage and money. John Brabant, master of the schooner Maritana, returns to Levuka harbour in Fiji after five months among the islands. He is still in love with his fair young wife Nell, who watches from a hill house above the port.

Brabant's mate Lester dislikes Nell from the first, calling her selfish for fearing the sun and her skin. At home, Brabant counts the cost: nearly a thousand pounds spent in five months, two hundred a month. Becke writes with his usual island knowledge, and the tale turns on love, pride, and the price of a wife's way of life.
24838-tessa-1901:
Louis Becke published Tessa in 1901, a South Seas tale of trade, fever, and rescue. The trading steamer Motutapu lies off Utiroa village on Drummond's Island, loading copra while her master Carr lies sick with fever on deck. Heat, flies, and the chill of ague rack him as the mate and engineer try to keep the ship working.

Tessa, a young island girl, and her companion Maoni lie in a cabin below, and a rescuer must smash the door with a carpenter's axe to drag them to the quarter-deck. Becke writes with his usual knowledge of island trade and its dangers. The story gives a tense, humid picture of life aboard a copra steamer in the equatorial Pacific.
24873-lucy-maud-montgomery-short-stories:
This volume opens Lucy Maud Montgomery's chronological short stories, gathering twenty tales from 1896 to 1901. Titles run from A Case of Trespass and Detected by the Camera to The Red Room, The Way of Winning Anne, and Young Si, with Christmas stories and kismet along the way.

The first tale finds Dan Phillips trouting a back creek of Carleton pond on a hazy, breathless day, and later stories show girls dousing roof fires with buckets and ladders. Montgomery's Island voice is already sure: warm, funny, and sharp on character. The set lets Anne's readers meet her earliest short fiction, fresh from Prince Edward Island.
24995-the-americans-in-the-south-seas-19:
Louis Becke's 1901 essay, from 'The Tapu of Banderah' and published by C. Arthur Pearson, argues that Americans soon took a hand in South Sea trade and practically monopolized Pacific whaling. His proper title would have been longer, on American enterprise and the maritime development of Australia's first colony. English officials, many veterans of the war of rebellion, gave Cousin Jonathan no warm welcome at Sydney Cove.

The essay recalls the wreck of the Guardian off the Cape of Good Hope, with stores for starving colonists at Cape Town. An American skipper offered to carry them to Sydney, but officers feared chartering a foreign ship, and Lieutenant King wrote to Governor Phillip of a Whitehaven man fitting out a Marblehead schooner. Later passages darken: sealing gangs, cruelties at Cape Barren, and a narrator who ran into the sea to escape torture. Becke writes history with a trader's eye.
24996-the-tapu-of-banderah-1901:
Louis Becke's 1901 novel, published by C. Arthur Pearson, opens with the schooner Starlight bearing down on Mayou, a low, wooded island between the south-east coast of New Guinea and the Solomon Group. The white population is small: missionary Wilfrid Deighton and his wife, German trader Peter Schwartzkoff, English trader Charlie Blount with his half-caste children, and American ex-whaler Nathaniel Burrowes. Some three thousand natives live mostly at the south-west end, near the trading anchorage.

Natives fishing off the island sight the vessel and raise the cry 'Evaka! Evaka!' — a ship — passing it house to house until the village swarms to the beach. Later scenes bring Banderah, a chief demanding an accounting from Bilker, an ex-blackbirder, for men stolen and a brother lost in Fiji. Bilker pleads a man-of-war and ten years in a Sydney calaboose; Banderah answers, flatly, that he lies.
24997-the-beginning-of-the-sea-story-of-:
Louis Becke's 1901 essay, from 'The Tapu of Banderah' and published by C. Arthur Pearson, insists that Australia's first half-century belongs to the ocean. English pictures of the colony run to tented gold-fields, bushrangers, squatters, and sheep runs, never to sea or sailor folk. Yet the British sailor laid the nation's foundation, and the sailorman did the colonizing, and did it well, while whaling once supported Australia and New Zealand.

Exploring seas and surveying coasts opened the ways, and runaway sailors made handier farm labourers, stockmen, and miners than ticket-of-leave men or average free emigrants. The first four governors were all captains in the Navy: Phillip, Hunter, King, and Bligh. Palmerston would have sent men like these when a distant job needed doing well. Becke restores the brine to the national story.
25057-the-adventure-of-elizabeth-morey-o:
Louis Becke's Adventure of Elizabeth Morey of New York, first published in 1901 in his collection The Tapu of Banderah, retells a Pacific sea story from the early 1800s. In October 1804 the American ship Union reached Sydney carrying a young woman rescued from captivity among the people of Tongatabu in the Friendly Islands.

Becke traces how Morey came to be held and how she warned an American mate against a trap laid for his ship. Her warnings saved lives. The tale blends documented shipping history with vivid storytelling. It shows the rough, mixed world of traders, whalers, and island peoples in the early Pacific.
25058-foster-s-letter-of-marque-a-tale-o:
Louis Becke's 1901 tale of old Sydney, from 'The Tapu of Banderah' and published by C. Arthur Pearson, opens on an evening in January 1802, as riding lights are lit aboard store ships and whalers in Sydney Harbour. A bugle peals from the barracks, and boatswains' mates pipe on a frigate in Sydney Cove. The mate of the whaler Policy paces the deck waiting for a captain promised at five and absent at half past seven. The cause, the crusty bachelor mate grumbles, is a pretty girl.

That girl is Dorothy Gilbert, daughter of the Deputy Acting Assistant Commissary General. Captain Charles Foster has fallen very much in love with her, in a settlement where pretty women are scarce and virtue scarcer. Later Dolly produces a letter, mimicking its Dutch accented English as she reads of its writer commanding the privateer Swift. Becke's Sydney is salt and gossip.
25059-in-the-far-north-1901:
Louis Becke's In the Far North, from his 1901 collection The Tapu of Banderah, opens on a drought-stricken cattle station in north Queensland. Jack Barrington, nominal owner of Tinandra Downs on the Gilbert River, rides a sun-baked run. He prays for rain, fears the bank, and faces the loss of everything he has built.

Becke knew the Australian frontier from his own years at sea and on shore. He writes with a sharp eye for heat, dust, debt, and stubborn pride. The story gives readers a compact picture of settler life at the edge of the settled world, where one bad season could undo years of work.
25060-officer-and-man-1901:
Louis Becke's 1901 story, from 'The Tapu of Banderah' and published by C. Arthur Pearson, opens aboard Her Majesty's ship Hannibal at Levuka, as Rear Admiral Garnet finishes farewelling the leading Fijian white residents. Lieutenant Bollard reports a person from shore who desires to see His Excellency on private business. The Admiral, who cannot delay the ship in the passage, sends him to his cabin for five minutes. The stranger is short, fat, and coarse looking, with pig like eyes, scanty black beard, and hair plastered over a bullet head.

Becke paints him as sleek and oleaginous, bowing and smirking, while Garnet guesses at a complaint against the consul, the standing disease of the South Seas. Later, Mr. Carteret lands among friendly islanders to ask whether any white men live there, and is led toward Joajai, a very good man. The story turns on mistaken identity and colonial authority.
25105-pa-kia-1901:
Louis Becke's Pa Kia, from his 1901 collection The Tapu of Banderah, is a short Pacific tale told from a beach at night. The narrator and his friend Temana spread their mats on the sand to catch the sea breeze. Temana, a tall islander, lives with the narrator as a foster brother, away from the village houses.

Talk turns to darker matters, and the story that follows is a grim confession of murder, flight, and a desperate swim to a passing schooner. Becke lived among island peoples. He tells it in the voice of a man who knows the Pacific trade, its loyalties, and its sudden violence, without softening either side.
25106-the-gallant-good-riou-and-jack-ren:
Louis Becke's Gallant, Good Riou and Jack Renton, from his 1901 collection The Tapu of Banderah, pairs two true sea stories from the age of sail. The first honors Lieutenant Edward Riou of the Guardian. In 1789 he carried food and plants to the starving penal colony at Sydney, and showed unselfish heroism after his ship struck an iceberg.

The second follows Jack Renton, a young sailor who deserts a rough American guano ship to settle on a Pacific island with shipmates. Becke tells both tales with a seaman's detail and a storyteller's pace, preserving episodes of courage and restlessness from the early Australian sea frontier.
25107-sarre-o-1901:
Louis Becke's Sarreo, from his 1901 collection The Tapu of Banderah, is a sea yarn told aboard the island-trading barque Reconnaisance. Second mate Thomas Potter, walking the poop with the supercargo Denison, recalls a photograph of the whaling crew of the Fanny Long, taken at Hobart after a lucky sperm-whaling cruise.

Among that crew was Sarreo, a native sailor whom white seamen at first dismissed and then respected. When Sarreo is hurt, the supercargo Warby, once hostile, nurses him like a brother on the long run toward Bougainville. Becke's tale praises island sailors and quietly rebukes the prejudice of the forecastle.
25109-susa-ni-1901:
Louis Becke's Susani, from his 1901 collection The Tapu of Banderah, is a brief, elegiac Pacific story set on Funafala, a palm island in the Funafuti lagoon of the Ellice Group. The narrator recalls watching, with Senior, mate of the Venus, over the last sleep of a dying island child.

Fifty years earlier, he writes, five or six hundred people lived on Funafala in peace and plenty. By the time of the story, gales, sickness, and the pressures of white contact have left almost nothing but bones and a remnant of starving people. Becke's lament for a fading island world is short, plain, and deeply felt.
29211-prevalence-of-imprisonment-in-the-:
Thomas P. Bonczar of the Bureau of Justice Statistics wrote this special report, published by the United States Department of Justice in August 2003. It measures how many American adults had ever done time in state or federal prison, from 1974 through 2001. The report number is NCJ 197976.

At yearend 2001, over 5.6 million adults had ever served time, or 2.7 percent of the adult population. That share had risen from 1.3 percent in 1974 and 1.8 percent in 1991. Tables break the figures down by sex and by race and Hispanic origin. Readers get a concise statistical portrait of imprisonment's reach, useful for anyone studying crime, punishment, and American society.
32862-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, revised by Alexander Leighton, appeared in London and Newcastle in 1887 with a glossary. John Mackay Wilson, a printer turned man of letters, began the series with a tale every week, until overwork broke a delicate constitution and he died.

Leighton carried the work on with Hugh Miller, Professor Thomas Gillespie, Alexander Campbell, the Bethunes, and John Howell. This volume holds The Vacant Chair, The Faa's Revenge, Kate Kennedy, Recollections of Ferguson, and The Disasters of Johnny Armstrong. The preface demands genuine stories, not didactic essays, portraying men and women graphically, with morals parents can trust.
3339-the-wandering-jew-volume-01:
Eugene Sue's great serial opens in this first volume with a note on its author. Sue lived from 1804 to 1857, and his training was double. Physicians and seamen have often made noteworthy novelists, the note observes, but rarely has a man trained in both callings won his greatest fame as a writer. Sue began as a physician and surgeon, then spent six years in the French Navy.

From that experience came the serial that made him famous: a wandering Jew, a scattered family, and a fortune contested in Paris. The first volume sets the machinery moving, with orphans, a soldier guardian, and Jesuit agents already at work. Readers starting Sue here get the novel's premise whole: a family summoned across Europe toward an inheritance and a trap.
3551-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne, Napoleon's private secretary, begins his memoirs in this first volume, edited by Colonel R W Phipps in 1891. The opening chapters run from Bonaparte's youth, including the year 1769, through his early military career to 1797. Bourrienne knew Napoleon from school days, and he writes as a friend turned secretary rather than as a distant historian.

The volume follows the young general's rise in Revolutionary France, with campaigns, politics, and the first taste of power. Bourrienne records conversations, orders, and daily detail that only a man at the desk could know. Readers who want Napoleon from inside his household should start here, then follow the later volumes in order.
3568-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant, Napoleon's first valet, begins his recollections in this first volume, telling how he entered the emperor's household and learned its ways. He describes his first meetings with Napoleon, the duties of a valet, and the strange new world of the Consulate, where a general's home was becoming a court. This volume belongs to the older Project Gutenberg Napoleon series.

Readers meet Napoleon as a young ruler at close range: his habits, his temper, his hours of work, and his kindness to servants he trusted. Constant writes simply and directly, without the polish of a statesman. The volume suits readers starting the series, since it explains the household that later volumes take for granted.
3581-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This first volume of Montaigne's Essays serves as an introduction to the whole work. It contains a preface, a life of Montaigne, and his letters, rather than the essays themselves. The preface presents Montaigne as a great French writer who deserves to rank as a classic in all countries, not only in his own land.

Readers learn how Montaigne retired to his tower to write about himself, and how he took the world into his confidence on every subject. His letters show the man behind the essays: a gentleman, a mayor, and a friend. The volume suits readers who want to meet Montaigne before diving into his famous reflections on custom, fear, and death.
3762-coniston-volume-01:
Winston Churchill opens Coniston as a love story of long ago, set just after Andrew Jackson reached the White House and the era of the first six presidents closed. A new era dawns, which Churchill calls the Boss Era, as clever gentlemen find chinks in the constitution and steal the people's chestnuts. After the boss come soulless things of many parts, the corporations, and the novel watches a New Hampshire village learn their weight.

Young Cynthia Ware, fetching buttons for a coat, overhears store talk about selectmen and plots, and the village of Coniston takes shape around her. The volume pairs a child's view with a hard political moral, drawn from a Lowell text on democracy's dangers. Readers who like American chronicles will find a strong first book, rich in dialect and local color.
3901-the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rou:
Jean Jacques Rousseau's first book opens with an introduction that places the Confessions among the notable books of all time. The editor sets Rousseau against absolutism and feudalism rallying for a last struggle with the modern spirit, represented by Voltaire, the Encyclopedists, and Rousseau himself. Readers are pointed to John Morley's review for the author's paradoxes and errors in logic, since factions have disputed them exhaustively.

Rousseau's own narrative begins in childhood, with a boy who runs after and stones any cock, cow, or dog he sees tormenting another, simply because it is conscious of superior strength. The first injustice he suffered stayed too long and powerfully in memory not to shape him. Readers who start the Confessions here will meet a child of fierce pity and fiercer pride.
3914-serge-panine-volume-01:
Georges Ohnet opens Serge Panine with the Desvarennes household and the young men who circle it. A youth with fair curls plastered on a low forehead shakes his little head in disdain, like an Atlas carrying the world. He complains that his aunt is jealous of him because he is a man of ideas. She wishes to bind him to besotting work, he says, while he wants independence of thought and a wide field for his discoveries.

A fixed rule and common law he cannot submit to, he declares, bent instead on the solution of great problems. The volume sets up the clash between practical business and youthful ambition that drives the novel. Readers who like Ohnet's popular romances will find a household of strong wills and a hero whose charm masks his designs.
3919-the-red-lily-volume-01:
Anatole France opens The Red Lily with the family history behind his heroine Therese. Her husband's line, the Martins, rose from Jacobin origins through the Bellemes, advocates under Louis the Fifteenth, to three ministers of the moderate monarchy. One Count Martin felt forever on his shoulder the hand of the Corsican, died a senator of Napoleon the Third, and left a son agitated by the same fear.

That son married Mademoiselle Belleme, daughter of the first president of the court of Bourges, and took his seat in the Chamber of Deputies without trouble. He then married Therese Montessuy, whose dowry supported his position. Readers who like France's ironic Paris will find a first volume of pedigree, marriage, and money before passion enters.
3923-monsieur-madame-and-be-be-volume-01:
Gustave Droz opens Monsieur, Madame and Bebe with comic sketches of married and family life in Paris. A church scene sets the tone, as Madame de P. sticks for hours in the confessional, and the narrator, foot numb, suspects she confesses her friends' sins along with her own. When she emerges red as a turkey cock, four ladies rush forward with pious ardor to take her place.

Pushing, apologies, and reproaches about respect for a hallowed spot follow in quick succession. Droz, a painter turned author, writes as a sharp observer of intimate domestic comedy. Readers who like light French humor will find a first volume of small humiliations, social jostling, and married wit.
5242-tales-from-the-arabic-volume-01:
John Payne's Tales from the Arabic, first volume, translates stories from the Breslau and Calcutta editions of the Thousand Nights and One Night that do not appear in other printed texts. Its contents include Asleep and Awake, the story of the Lackpenny and the Cook, and the Khalif Omar and the poets. Haroun Er Reshid and the woman of the Barmecides appear too, with the long cycle of the Ten Viziers.

Within that cycle, tales of unlucky merchants, patient men, and kings and their viziers unfold story inside story. The volume holds only the first part of Payne's collection. It offers readers Arabian Nights material rarely found in the familiar versions.
5266-travels-in-the-interior-of-africa-v:
Mungo Park's Travels in the Interior of Africa, first volume, tells of his first journey into West Africa. Born in 1771, the son of a farmer near Selkirk, Park studied medicine in Edinburgh, sailed as a ship's surgeon. He volunteered for the African Association, sailing on May 22, 1795, to take the place of the explorer Major Houghton.

This volume follows Park's early travels inland, through the kingdoms and peoples of the Niger region, as he sought the great river. The book became a classic of exploration literature, and it offers readers a first-hand account of African geography, trade. Hospitality completes the account, told with modesty and plain good sense.
5275-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
The first volume of Jean de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels opens with the author's life and preface, followed by Joconde, the tale that heads the collection. A full table of the tales follows in the front matter. It lists the cudgelled cuckold, the husband confessor, the cobbler, the peasant and his angry lord, and many more to come.

Readers beginning La Fontaine's tales here get the author's own introduction and the first story, in English verse translation. The volume serves as the doorway to the collection, setting out La Fontaine's ironic, gallant manner before the later volumes carry the tales forward.
5307-the-letters-of-wolfgang-amadeus-moz:
The Letters of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, first volume, translated from Ludwig Nohl's collection by Lady Wallace, was published in 1866. It covers the years 1769 to 1791 in two volumes, of which this is the first. Its four parts follow Italy, Vienna, and Munich in 1770 to 1776, then Munich, Augsburg, and Mannheim, Paris, and Munich again for Idomeneo.

Mozart's letters show the composer as a son, a traveller, and a working musician, writing home about courts, operas, and money. Readers get a vivid, personal Mozart, far from the marble statue, in letters that trace a short life of extraordinary music and constant movement.
5353-guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-vol:
Sir Walter Scott's Guy Mannering opens in its first volume with an epigraph from The Lay of the Last Minstrel on words and signs that have power over sprites in planetary hour. Scott's introduction recalls how Waverley made its way slowly, then with accumulating popularity, encouraging him to try again. He cast about for a name and a subject.

This volume holds only the opening portion of the novel of astrology, smuggling, and a stolen heir, set in the Scottish border country. Readers following the novel in order will meet the astrologer, the smugglers. The child whose horoscope foretells danger appears, before later volumes carry the mystery forward.
5356-the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-01:
Winston Churchill's Inside of the Cup opens in its first volume with four chapters: The Waring Problems, Mr Langmaid's Mission, The Primrose Path, and Some Riddles of the Twentieth Century. The novel follows John Hodder, rector of St John's, as he confronts the wealth, power, and fashionable religion of his city parish.

This volume holds only the opening portion of Churchill's novel of faith and social conscience, before later volumes carry Hodder through divine discontent and reconstruction. Readers get the foundation of a story that asks what a church should do when its richest members set its course.
5365-richard-carvel-volume-01:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel opens in its first volume with chapters one through seven: Lionel Carvel of Carvel Hall, Some Memories of Childhood, Caught by the Tide. Grafton Would Heal an Old Breach, If Ladies Be but Young and Fair, I First Suffer for the Cause, and Grafton Has His Chance complete the opening volume. The novel follows Richard, heir of Carvel Hall in Maryland, from childhood into the stirrings of revolution.

This volume holds only the opening portion of the romance, before later volumes carry Richard over the wall, under false colours, and to London. Readers get the foundation of a story of family, love, and the American cause, told in Richard's own voice.
5374-a-modern-chronicle-volume-01:
Winston Churchill's Modern Chronicle opens in its first volume with Book One, chapters one through six: What's in Heredity. Perdita Recalled, Concerning Providence, Of Temperament, In Which Providence Keeps Faith, and Honora Has a Glimpse of the World complete the first book. The novel follows Honora, a young woman whose heredity, temperament, and providence shape a modern life.

This volume holds only the opening portion of Churchill's chronicle of marriage and society, before later volumes carry Honora through the Olympian order and beyond. Readers get the foundation of a story about a woman learning what the world offers and what it costs.
5383-the-celebrity-volume-01:
Winston Churchill's Celebrity opens in its first volume with a narrator who was about to say he had known the Celebrity since he wore kilts. He then amends himself, since the man was not a celebrity then, nor achieved fame until after the narrator had gone west years before. In the old days, to a commonplace mind, the future author gave no evidence of genius.

He never read the narrator any manuscripts, which he surely would have done had he written any then. The failure to detect his promise may be pardoned. This volume holds only the opening portion of Churchill's comedy of fame, introducing the celebrated author before Asquith claims him.
5388-the-crisis-volume-01:
Winston Churchill's Crisis opens in its first volume with Book One, chapters one through seven. They are Which Deals With Origins, The Mole, The Unattainable Simplicity, Black Cattle, The First Spark Passes, Silas Whipple, and Callers. The novel is set in St Louis on the eve of the Civil War, where Stephen Brice grows up among divided loyalties.

This volume holds only the opening portion of Churchill's Civil War novel, before later volumes carry Stephen through Lincoln, Sumter, and the armies of the West. Readers get the foundation of a story about a border city, a young lawyer, and a nation breaking apart.
5409-the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volum:
Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont, edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott, opens in its first volume with a biographical sketch of Hamilton. Later chapters follow Grammont's arrival at the siege of Trino, his education and adventures before Trino, and his arrival at the court of Turin.

Later chapters in this volume follow Grammont back to the court of France. His adventures at the siege of Arras, his reply to Cardinal Mazarin, and his banishment from court follow. Readers get the opening of a classic memoir of seventeenth-century courts, witty, scandalous, and told by a man who lived among kings.
5439-uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-vo:
Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Clara Bell, opens his historical romance Uarda with a dedication and preface. The dedication speaks of suffering eased by a fostering hand, with a rose blooming among thorns, while the preface sets the story in ancient Egypt. Ebers, a scholar of Egypt, built the novel on historical research rather than pure invention.

This first volume introduces the world of the romance: temples, courts, and daily life along the Nile in pharaonic times. Readers meet the setting and the people who will carry the story forward. It suits anyone who likes historical fiction grounded in a real ancient culture.
5450-an-egyptian-princess-volume-01:
Georg Ebers opens his historical romance An Egyptian Princess in this first volume, translated from the German by Eleanor Grove. The preface to the second German edition quotes Horace on poetry that aims both to please and to profit. Ebers explains why he would not let a new edition go out without a few words to readers. Four years had passed since the book first appeared.

The romance is set in ancient Egypt, drawing on its history and court life as Ebers understood them. This opening volume establishes the Egyptian world and its royal household. Readers get the start of a scholarly historical novel, written by an Egyptologist for a general audience.
5473-cleopatra-volume-01:
Georg Ebers's Cleopatra, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, opens with a preface defending love in the pagan world. If anyone doubts that such feeling existed then, Ebers says, Antony and Cleopatra answer the doubt. The Roman general's will asked to be buried beside the woman he loved to his latest hour. His wish was fulfilled.

The romance that follows sets that famous love within Alexandria's courts, families, and politics, introducing Barine and her circle alongside the queen. Ebers writes as an Egyptologist with a storyteller's sense. Readers get the first volume of a tragic historical romance, grounded in the ancient city.
5483-the-emperor-volume-01:
Georg Ebers planned The Emperor fourteen years before writing it. The story grew from lectures on Roman rule in Egypt, and Clara Bell translated it here. Scientific labors delayed the invention. When leisure returned, he took up the story with greater power, turning first to Hadrian's age and then to the early monastic period treated in Homo Sum. This first volume opens the Roman Egyptian romance.

The novel follows Emperor Hadrian's visit to Alexandria, with architects, stewards, artists, and citizens drawn into imperial business. Ebers writes from historical study, grounding court and workshop alike. Readers get the start of a large historical romance about empire meeting a proud old city.
5494-homo-sum-volume-01:
Georg Ebers's Homo Sum, translated from the German by Clara Bell, grows from the author's study of the first centuries of Christianity. While preparing a history of the Sinaitic peninsula, Ebers worked through martyrology, ascetic writings, and histories of saints and monks, and came upon a narrative in Cotelerius that sparked this romance. The title, Latin for I am a man, signals its theme.

The novel follows hermits and monks in the early Christian desert, where faith, temptation, and human weakness meet. Ebers writes as a historian of the period. Readers get the opening volume of a serious, atmospheric romance about the desert fathers and their struggles.
5501-serapis-volume-01:
The busy turmoil of Alexandria has hushed for some hours in the first volume of Georg Ebers's Serapis, translated from the German by Clara Bell. Moon and stars keep silent watch, many inhabitants already dream, and the night feels fresh and gracious. Yet even in this pause for rest, something lacks the soothing calm a peaceful city should offer.

The novel opens in late Roman Alexandria, where pagan temples and a rising Christian world face each other. Performers, priests, and citizens move through streets that hide tension beneath quiet. Readers get the first volume of a historical romance about faith, spectacle, and a city on the edge of change.
5508-arachne-volume-01:
Deep silence broods over water and green islands in the first volume of Georg Ebers's Arachne, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford. Palms, silver poplars, and sycamores on the largest island cast long shadows as the sun touches their crowns, while light falls on shore bushes and papyrus reeds in brackish water. Waterfowl fly past under flecked clouds.

The novel follows artists and lovers in ancient Alexandria, where the weaver Arachne's myth shadows a story of art, pride, and rivalry. Ebers opens with landscape before people, letting place set the mood. Readers get the first volume of a graceful historical romance about makers and their passions.
5517-the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-01:
Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile, translated from the German by Clara Bell, opens with a preface that needs no apology. For professional students, Ebers notes his reliance on de Goeje. That scholar held Mukaukas to be a title, not a name, since Arab writers apply it to responsible representatives of the Byzantine Empire. Scholarship frames the romance from the start.

The novel itself is set in Egypt during the Arab conquest period, among governors, bishops, and families caught between empires. Ebers writes as a historian of the age. Readers get the first volume of a romance where Byzantine and Arab worlds meet on the Nile.
5530-a-thorny-path-volume-01:
A green screen slowly rises over the lower part of a broad studio window in the first volume of Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path. Heron the gem-cutter works inside, while his daughter Melissa pulls the screen up with bent knees and outstretched arms, panting for breath. Her father's impatient voice calls that it is enough, as blinding Alexandrine sunlight floods the room.

The novel opens in an artist's workshop, with a father, a daughter, and the hard light of Alexandria. Ebers builds the story from craft, family, and city life. Readers get the first volume of a historical romance set among gem-cutters, Christians, and imperial power.
5552-margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nurember:
Georg Ebers's Margery, a tale of old Nuremberg, opens with a translator's note on its fifteenth-century language. The book presents itself as a transcript into modern German of Nuremberg speech from that century, and the translator avoids imitating period English, aiming only to avoid essentially modern words and forms. An introduction then begins Margery's own story.

The tale follows a Nuremberg girl's life among council families, kin, and suitors, told in her own voice. Ebers writes old Germany through a young woman's eyes. Readers get the first volume of a charming historical tale, intimate, old-fashioned, and rich in civic detail.
5561-barbara-blomberg-volume-01:
Sunlight sometimes shines on the little round panes of the Golden Cross in Ratisbon in the first volume of Georg Ebers's Barbara Blomberg, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford. The ancient building stands on the northern side of the square people call on the moor, sometimes veiled by gray clouds. A party of nobles, churchmen, and knights from the emperor's train comes out as a spring breeze bangs behind them.

The novel introduces Barbara, a singer in the emperor's world, through Ratisbon's streets and squares. Ebers writes the imperial court on the move. Readers get the first volume of a romance about a woman whose voice draws an emperor's eye.
5572-a-word-only-a-word-volume-01:
A fresh, boyish voice cries, A word, only a word, in the first volume of Georg Ebers's A Word, Only a Word, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford. Two hands clap loudly, a gay laugh echoes through the forest, and silence under pines and beeches breaks. A wood pigeon joins the lad's laugh, while a startled jay spreads brown wings flecked with delicate color.

The novel opens in a forest, with a boy's voice breaking quiet and nature answering. Ebers builds a sixteenth-century romance from that bright start. Readers get the first volume of a story about words, honor, and young lives, told with warmth.
5578-the-burgomaster-s-wife-volume-01:
Georg Ebers dedicates The Burgomaster's Wife to Baroness Sophie von Brandenstein, his father's only sister, in this first volume, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford. He recalls her faithful friendship from early childhood, and his industrious labor as her guest seventeen years earlier. The dedication sets a personal tone for a public story.

The novel follows the wife of Burgomaster Van der Werff during the Spanish siege of Leyden, when a city fights for freedom and survival. Ebers writes Dutch history through a household. Readers get the first volume of a siege romance, grounded in civic courage.
5584-in-the-blue-pike-volume-01:
May a thunderbolt strike you, cries a rough fellow in the first volume of Georg Ebers's In the Blue Pike, translated from the German by Mary T. Safford. The curse suits its speaker, who points out of doors as he speaks, scarcely lowering his strange voice. Of all the rabble around him, only two understand his meaning. One is a fading, sickly girl, and the other is the red-haired woman, a few years older, who leads the swearing man by a chain like a tame bear.

The novel opens among outcasts, magistrates, and street crowds in old Germany. Ebers writes the scene with rough humor. Readers get the first volume of a tale about singers, wanderers, and justice, starting in noise and chains.
5593-the-story-of-my-life-volume-01:
Georg Ebers begins his autobiography, The Story of My Life, from childhood to manhood, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, with a verse address to his sons. He urges himself to record incidents treasured in his soul's depths, so his portrait may remain for his sons, and his errors may guide his loved ones aright. The chapters then glance backward to earliest childhood, festal days, a journey to Holland for a golden wedding, and the Lennestrasse.

The volume follows a Berlin boy's early impressions, art, and family life before revolution. Ebers writes memory as a father's gift. Readers get the first volume of a warm, detailed autobiography, where childhood scenes lead toward a scholar's life.
5612-the-arabian-nights-entertainments-v:
The Arabian Nights Entertainments, in this 1813 first volume, presents one thousand and one stories told by the Sultaness of the Indies to divert the sultan from a bloody vow. He had sworn to marry a lady every day and have her cut off next morning, to avenge the disloyalty of his first sultaness. The Sultaness tells stories to stay alive, night after night.

Contents include the genius and the lady shut in a glass box, plus the fable of the ass, the ox, and the labourer. Other Eastern tales follow, with an account of Eastern customs, manners, and religion. Readers get the classic frame tale in early English dress, rich in wonder and cunning.
5645-sketches-by-seymour-volume-01:
Sketches by Seymour, part one, opens with an editor's introduction to a book published in various versions about 1836. The editor's copy has no date and was published by Thomas Fry in London, with ninety plates including title pages. Some plates note only Seymour's name, while many read engravings by Wallis from sketches by Seymour.

The editor believes the book compiled five smaller volumes, though the separate volumes are not apparent, and suspects the printer thoroughly mixed up the chapters' order. This digital edition splits the complete set into five smaller volumes. Readers get the first part of a classic comic collection.
5664-the-arabian-nights-entertainments-v:
The Aldine Edition of The Arabian Nights Entertainments, illustrated by S. L. Wood from the text of Dr. Jonathan Scott, presents its first volume in a small paper edition limited to five hundred copies for America, this copy number 217, published by Pickering and Chatto in London in 1890. The publishers' preface explains the series: artistic reprints of standard English fiction, well illustrated, with texts carefully chosen from approved editions.

The volume opens the frame tale of the Sultaness telling stories night after night to stay alive. Readers get a handsome late Victorian Arabian Nights, beginning the four-volume Aldine set.
567-the-complete-works-of-brann-the-icon:
William Cowper Brann, the Waco editor called the Iconoclast, opens his collected works with the first of twelve volumes. Brann's newspaper pieces attacked clergy, politicians, and pretence with a pen that spared no one. Brann edited the Iconoclast in Waco, Texas, where his attacks drew lawsuits and threats.

The volume gathers early editorials, satires, and stories, including a lush tale of a lad singing in an Egyptian garden. Readers meet Brann at his most combative, and the book explains why his name still draws both praise and anger in Texas. The twelve-volume set, issued after his death, preserves a journalist who feared no foe.
5688-the-innocents-abroad-volume-01:
Mark Twain opens his account of a grand pleasure excursion to Europe and the Holy Land with the talk, tickets, and grand plans that sent a party of American pilgrims to sea. This first part covers the preparations, the assembling of the passengers, and life aboard ship, where Twain sorts his fellow travellers, notes their habits, and turns sea routine into comedy. The chapter titles promise dignitaries, staterooms, and the slow domestication of pilgrims at sea.

The humor comes from Twain's eye for pretense: celebrated names drop away, comforts prove small, and the grand tour begins in very ordinary seasickness and shipboard gossip. Readers get both a travel record and a satire of American tourists abroad, told in the voice that made Twain famous. This part sets the voyage in motion and introduces the party whose judgments will be tested at every port.
5782-a-tramp-abroad-volume-01:
Volume one of Mark Twain's A Tramp Abroad opens with a tramp over Europe, aboard the Holsatia through Hamburg and Frankfort. Chapters treat Heidelberg, the portier, a great stir at a hotel, Baker's blue-jay yarn, student life, the five corps, the Beet King, and the students' dueling ground. Twain mixes travel notes with tall tales, political economy lessons, and Rhine legends like the Knave of Bergen.

Readers meet Twain as a walking tourist and comic lecturer, turning German student customs into satire. The dueling scenes, blue-jay language, and hotel comedy show his gift for making foreign habits funny without losing observation. This first volume sets the tramp in motion and introduces the voice that will carry readers across Europe, one absurd encounter at a time.
5903-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Part one of Cervantes's History of Don Quixote, in the Ormsby translation, covers chapters one through three, the knight's beginning. Chapter one treats the character and pursuits of the famous gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha. Chapter two covers his first sally from home. Chapter three tells the droll way he had himself dubbed a knight. From a gentleman reader of romances, a knight-errant is born.

Readers meet Quixote and the book's great joke at its source: a sane man made mad by chivalry, setting out to right wrongs that exist mostly in books. The chapters favor comedy and character over action, letting Quixote's delusions announce themselves. This part suits first-time readers perfectly, since it contains the whole premise in miniature, and it rewards rereading for its wit.
6046-works-of-john-bunyan-volume-01:
The first volume of John Bunyan's works, edited by George Offor, opens with a memoir of a man descended from ignoble parents and born in poverty. Bunyan followed his father's trade as a brazier, enlisted as a soldier, returned from war, and gained an amiable, religious wife whose dower included godly books.

The volume then gives Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, his imprisonment, and The Jerusalem Sinner Saved. It adds The Greatness of the Soul, Christ a Complete Saviour, and treatises on prayer, fear of God, law and grace, and the strait gate.
6195-cumner-s-son-and-other-south-sea-fo:
Cumner's Son heads Parker's first volume of South Sea folk, with later volumes promising the High Court of Budgery-Gar, an epic in yellow, Dibbs, a masquerade, and derelict tales. Parker recalls, in a foreword to Donovan Pasha from 1902, that twelve years had passed since he began giving tales of lands well known to him.

The first tales came from Australia and southern Pacific islands, where he lived and roamed in the middle and late eighties. Those far south sketches appeared with prodigality, though not at first in book form, while he also wrote Canadian tales far from their scenes.
6243-the-right-of-way-volume-01:
A jury foreman's treble cry of not guilty lifts a smothering weight from a crowded courtroom, as hundreds of eyes race between judge, prisoner, and the prisoner's counsel. The verdict shocks everyone, and a woman laughs outright in a far gallery corner before the clerk calls for silence. Charley Steele, the counsel at the centre of it all, has won by a discovery that left him dull and blank one moment and seeing things like crystal the next.

This first volume follows the trial, what came of it, and five years after, as Charley makes a discovery and meets a woman in heliotrope. Chapters on the wind and the shorn lamb, a false peace, and the cost of an ornament set his new life in motion. Parker opens a story of law, guilt, and second chances, where a courtroom triumph proves only the start of the reckoning.
6653-voyages-of-samuel-de-champlain-volu:
Charles Pomeroy Otis gives, in this first volume, a faithful English rendering of Samuel de Champlain's voyages, with notes by a learned editor. The notes, long and many, are set as endnotes to each chapter, and old spelling is kept, save for tall s turned to plain s and a few French marks made plain. Algonquian words get a careful note of their own.

An opening essay on Champlain's life admits how much of his youth, home, and habits we know only in faint rays, and refuses to fill gaps with fancy. What stands firm is his public career, given in records that last. Volume one thus offers Champlain the explorer, in a scholarly, readable dress.
6759-the-adventures-of-ferdinand-count-f:
Tobias Smollett's Ferdinand Count Fathom, part one, opens with sage observations that usher in an important history. Chapters trace the hero's infancy, his start in military life, his mother's prowess and death, and his own early sagacity. A brief schooling leads to schemes of importance and a partnership with a female associate.

Their first attempt, with a digression some readers may deem impertinent, and a change of battery lead to a remarkable adventure. An introduction by G. H. Maynadier frames the tale. Volume one of Count Fathom is a rogue's progress, full of Smollett's bite and wit.
6770-the-thirty-years-war-volume-01:
Schiller's History of the Thirty Years' War, volume one, opens with a preface to the sixth edition of his collected works in English. The preface praises Schiller as a historian no less than as a dramatist, formed to excel in all departments of letters, with a lucid style and sound, fair judgment. Detached poems and plays, translated over years, join the set.

Volume one then begins the great German war itself, from its Bohemian roots, with Schiller's clear narrative as guide. His history remains a popular, readable account of a tangled age. The Thirty Years' War, volume one, is the opening of Schiller's classic war history.
6776-history-of-the-revolt-of-the-nether:
Volume one of Schiller's History of the Revolt of the Netherlands opens with the same collected-works preface that frames his Thirty Years' War. Schiller, the preface says, was formed to excel in all letters. His histories show a lucid style and sound, fair judgment. Those gifts will always recommend them as popular accounts of their periods. Many small corrections join this edition.

The revolt itself begins in the Netherlands under Spanish rule, with grievances, faith, and pride driving a people toward resistance. Schiller tells that opening with narrative force. Volume one is the start of his classic account of Dutch freedom's birth.
6812-abraham-lincoln-a-history-volume-01:
John Nicolay and John Hay, Lincoln's secretaries, open their great history with a dedication to Robert Todd Lincoln, in token of lifelong friendship. Their preface notes that a generation born since Lincoln died has reached manhood, yet millions still live who shared his toils and mourned his tragic death. Contemporaries, they say, judged him incomparably the greatest man of his time.

Volume one traces Lincoln from youth through law, politics, and the rise that led to the White House. Nicolay and Hay write with insider knowledge and high seriousness. Abraham Lincoln: A History, volume one, is the classic, monumental life, still a foundation for Lincoln study.
6848-the-prince-of-india-or-why-constant:
Lew Wallace opens volume one of The Prince of India with a verse that calls past shapes and shadows to rise from forgotten graves and walk the streets again. Book one, on earth and sea giving up secrets, runs from a nameless bay and a midnight landing to a hidden treasure. Book two follows the Prince of India himself.

A messenger from Cipango, a pilgrim at El Katif, yellow air, El Zaribah, a caravan, and a prince at the Kaaba lead to arrival in Constantinople. Wallace writes a vast, romantic history. Volume one is the sweeping start of a tale that ends with a city's fall.
7003-the-antiquary-volume-01:
Walter Scott's Antiquary opens its first volume with an editor's introduction and twenty one chapters of antiquarian comedy. Illustrations show the Antiquary with Lovel in his sanctum, Sir Arthur and Miss Wardour, their rescue, and Eddie Ochiltree visiting Miss Wardour. Mrs Heukbane and Mrs Shortcake add domestic color, while St Ruth Abbey and its ruins set the antiquarian scene.

The volume opens on Anselmo, shrewd and prudent yet wayward as a child, pleased again by toys such as a book of fables graced with wood prints. Only this first volume's matter is described here, as Scott sets his collector, his laird, and his beggar on the road toward mystery. The tale blends humor, history, and the love of old things.
7023-rob-roy-volume-01:
The first volume of Scott's Rob Roy opens with a Wordsworth verse from Rob Roy's Grave, on taking who have the power and keeping who can. An advertisement to the first edition recalls that the editor, two years earlier with the Antiquary, had promised to intrude no more in his present capacity. Like Junius the phantom, he jests, an anonymous writer cannot be bound to a charge of inconsistency.

A better apology follows from honest Benedict, who swore to die a bachelor and did not think he should live to be married. Only this first volume's matter is described here, as Scott sets his young hero, his father, and the world of trade and outlawry in motion. The novel's famous Highland tale begins in this volume's pages.
7586-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Edward Bulwer Lytton opens The Caxtons with a frank preface. The plot is extremely slight, the incidents few, and, except for those involving the fate of Vivian, no more than ordinary life supplies. The novel is an experiment apart from his previous works, the first in which humor has been employed as a main force. Its narrator is Pisistratus Caxton, telling his family's story.

Pisistratus, as he himself feels, becomes the type of a growing class in modern civilization: one too many in the midst of the crowd, a young man seeking a place. Part one sets the Caxton household, its books, its humors, and its hopes, before the wider story unfolds. The volume is the doorway into Lytton's most domestic and affectionate novel.
7606-zicci-a-tale-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's Zicci opens with a shadow falling across a summer evening in Naples, in the last century. The gardens there are a gay, favored resort, full of music and easy company. Four or five gentlemen sit under a tree with sherbet, talking between tunes. Among them, a young Englishman who had enlivened the whole party falls silent and withdrawn. The change in his mood is the tale's first mystery.

A countryman taps him on the back and asks what ails him, and that question opens Glyndon's story. The beautiful Neapolitan world around him, all music and gardens, now carries a threat. The mysterious stranger Zicci, whose power will test the young man, stands behind the scene. The first book sets that luxury against a gathering darkness, and lets the reader feel both at once.
7609-eugene-aram-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton dedicates Eugene Aram to Sir Walter Scott, and the opening address explains why. The author has long wanted to lay a tribute at Scott's shrine, yet each earlier book seemed unworthy of the great name. Time kept running on, so he seizes this chance rather than wait for a better one.

This first part sets the tale apart from Pelham and Paul Clifford, the two books named in the address. Aram is a scholar of quiet habits, and the story turns on a hidden past that threatens his new life. The volume opens the portrait of a learned man whose learning cannot keep his secret safe.
7615-pelham-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Pelham opens with the rules of good society, and its hero's family shows them at work. Vulgar people, the narrator notes, grasp none of what good society demands, and the credit they extend is as brief as their lineage. From this polished nursery, the novel will send its hero to Paris, to politics, and to a murder inquiry. Rank and fashion shape every habit he will later test.

The family itself fits the code. Henry Pelham is an only child. His mother, Lady Frances, loves diamonds and old china. His father, the younger son of one of England's oldest earls, is a moderate Whig who gives sumptuous dinners. Good society, short credit, and long pedigrees: the part sets Pelham's world in a few strokes, then lets the novel complicate it.
7624-devereux-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Devereux introduces a hero whose story will run from youth through exile and return. What remains is a young author's book, frank and artless in enthusiasm, and the part lets those qualities stand. Youthful faults stay visible, and the author does not hide them. The hero's long road, not a polished plot, is the book's promise.

The part opens with an advertisement to a new edition, in which the author is candid about his early work. The work was composed in early youth, and he leaves its faults of construction standing, since removing them fully would mean rewriting the whole work. He has, however, lightened the narrative of irrelevant episodes and eased some boyish extravagances of diction. Revision here is pruning, not rebuilding, and the book keeps its first energy.
7631-the-disowned-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Disowned opens with a young man cut off from his name and fortune, and his disowning sets the novel's long quest in motion. Clarence steps into the story as a stranger with a grievance, and the novel follows what he does with that loss. His quest, not any single scene, is the part's business. The reader meets a hero defined first by what has been taken from him.

The landscape around his entrance is quiet and English: a soft, warm May evening, twilight gathering over large, still masses of wood beside a green lane. Fern and dwarf furze cover the waste land, and rushes cluster at intervals along the road. Into that calm steps the stranger, troubled by boundaries encroaching, day by day, upon what he has learned to look up to. A green lane, a grievance, and a lost name open the tale.
7640-ernest-maltravers-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Ernest Maltravers is built, by its 1840 preface, as the philosophical story of a moral education, or apprenticeship. Lytton admits his debt to Goethe's Wilhelm Meister, while setting his apprentice amid the events and manners of his own times. Pelham was the first of only three such novels he prized. The design matters more here than any single scene: a young mind formed by the world it moves through.

The dedication frames that design for a particular audience. Lytton dedicates the book to the German people, praised as thinkers and critics, a foreign yet familiar readership, deep in judgment. An English author offers them his work, trusting their criticism. The part thus pairs a German model, a German audience, and an English apprentice, and lets that triangle set the novel's ambition.
7650-kenelm-chillingly-volume-01:
Sir Peter Chillingly of Exmundham, a baronet of old family and fair lands, opens Edward Bulwer Lytton's Kenelm Chillingly. He married young at his parents' wish, gaining a wife with a pretty fortune, good ties, and skill at the piano. The match rounded off his estate and pleased the county.

His son Kenelm grows up under these settled hopes, yet the first book already hints at a restless mind. Debates about real life against high ideals frame his youth, as kin and friends argue how a young heir should be formed. The novel sets up a witty study of an odd, thoughtful hero.
7659-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-01:
Published under the pen name Pisistratus Caxton, Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? opens at a Surrey summer fair, with booths, gingerbread, and sideshows promising a giant, a pig-faced lady, and a two-headed calf. Above them a stage offers a grand melodrama for rural playgoers.

Music, drums, and penny whistles fill the green as the tale's players are introduced with sly wit about trades and manners. A young girl, bound to the stage, longs for the blue river and a free holiday at dawn. The opening sets a comic, wide-ranging novel of English life in motion.
7672-harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-:
A long letter to a friend opens Lytton's Harold, explaining why the author chose the Norman Conquest for a romance. He calls it England's Trojan War, a time before full chivalry and Crusade song, when readers knew little of its kings, customs, and faces.

The first book lays out the Saxon world on the eve of invasion, with courts, priests, and earls jostling for power. Lytton admits the risk of seeming bookish, yet trusts story to carry the research. It is a historical novel built on chronicles, aimed at readers new to the age.
7685-lucretia-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Lucretia, subtitled The Children of Night, was planned as a dark twin to the sunny Caxtons. Both novels test how home training, early scenes, and example shape later character, but Lucretia works through fear and distress where its twin works through humor.

The author notes in his 1853 preface that readers mistook the moral aim, judging a book by pleasure or pain rather than purpose. This first part sets out the St. John household, a proud old man, and a girl whose early lessons will bend her whole life. It is a tragic study of upbringing gone wrong.
7692-a-strange-story-volume-01:
Lytton's A Strange Story opens with a preface on Maine de Biran. The French thinker moved from blind faith in matter to belief in free will and self-knowledge. At last he reached a third life of the soul. That path frames a tale of wonders no plain theory of sense can explain.

The first volume then turns to Dr Fenwick's circle. Mr Vigors speaks in a sepulchral voice of Mrs Ashleigh and strange doings around Dr Lloyd. Mesmerism, gossip, and earnest science mix as the narrator weighs what the mind can do. It is a Victorian romance of mystery and mind.
7715-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons opens with a letter to a friend who urged a fiction drawn from English records. Lytton argues that a good novel does not twist facts but fills them with color, motive, and daily habit, using fair guesswork where history must stay silent.

The first book sets the Wars of the Roses in motion, with nobles and gentry driven less by badges than by deeper aims: land, pride, and freedom from oppressors. Through chronicle detail and invented talk, it seeks a living picture of a single age, not a mere list of battles.
7728-paul-clifford-volume-01:
Lytton's Paul Clifford opens with an 1840 preface that sets it apart from his other novels. It is, he says, the only one where a robber leads the tale. He chose it to expose two faults: prison discipline that corrupts boys, and a bloody code that hangs men for the state's own blunders.

The first volume follows Paul to sixteen, a handsome lad under a dame's care. He is invited to a ball at Bill's house as his start in London life. Between prison-yard lessons and the crowd round Newgate's drop, the novel asks whether punishment reforms anyone, or merely breeds the crime it claims to cure.
7737-the-parisians-volume-01:
A note by the author's son opens Lytton's The Parisians, placing it with Kenelm Chillingly and The Coming Race as a late group with one moral aim. Early satire attacked false respect, later humor defended real social bonds, but these three warn against popular theories that warp character and national life.

The first book sets the scene in Paris, where old nobles like Rochebriant face a new order, and Isaura Cicogna writes letters full of art and feeling. Through salons and streets, the novel tests loyalty, rank, and sympathy in a France on the edge of change.
7821-the-attache-or-sam-slick-in-england:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton's The Attache, or Sam Slick in England, volume one, opens with the same July 1843 letter as its sequel, sending a Yankee attache ahead to Edmund Hopkinson at Edgeworth. His politics please, his humor may try patience, but his quaint talk promises amusement.

Contents of the first volume promise uncorking a bottle, a juicy day in the country, and tying a nightcap, among other comic chapters. Through Sam Slick's shrewd, slangy eye, Haliburton satirizes English customs, American bumptiousness, and the gap between old world polish and new world plain speech.
7901-american-historical-and-literary-cu: Opening part one of Smith and Watson's American Historical and Literary Curiosities in text form gives almost nothing to read. The file holds just the editor's note and the title page. The note warns that the series is a picture book of illustrations and page images, so the plates must be viewed in the HTML edition.
8779-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Dante Alighieri's Inferno opens in the Reverend H. F. Cary's translation, in this first illustrated part covering cantos one and two. Dante finds himself in a gloomy wood midway through life, astray from the direct path, in a forest so savage and rough that remembering it renews his dismay. At the foot of a mountain closing a valley, his journey begins, with Virgil soon to guide him.

These opening cantos set the whole Comedy in motion: the dark wood, the beasts blocking the way, Beatrice's call, and Virgil's promise to lead Dante through Hell and Purgatory. Cary's early nineteenth-century verse, once the standard English Dante, gives the poem a stately, slightly archaic music. New readers can start here and feel why the Inferno's first lines have haunted literature for seven centuries.
9050-a-select-collection-of-old-english-:
Carew Hazlitt prepared this fourth edition of Dodsley's Select Collection of Old English Plays. He arranged the plays in time order for the first time. He added notes from all past editors plus his own. Dodsley's set, first out in 1744, had become scarce and dear, and Hazlitt sought to revive a favorite of lovers of early drama.

This first volume opens the series with a preface on the collection's history through three earlier editions. Inside, readers find plays from the dawn of English drama, with notes that gloss old words and customs. For students of Shakespeare's age, the set is a treasure house of the stage that came before him.
9763-alice-or-the-mysteries-book-01:
Book one of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, opens in a Devonshire cottage in early April. Two ladies sit by open windows, before lawns gay with evergreens and first spring flowers. The sea, blue and calm, bounds the view through the trees. The cottage's owner, a woman past thirty yet looking younger, chose this remote spot for its quiet.

The book's first chapter asks who the fair one is who takes Blanch's place, the lady of matchless grace. Lytton's polished romance begins in seclusion, then widens to mystery. A reader gets the opening book of a Victorian tale of beauty, secrets, and hidden pasts.
9947-queen-victoria-story-of-her-life-an:
This life of Queen Victoria covers her reign from 1819 to 1901, opening with tributes from Tennyson and Norman Macleod to her courage, patience, and goodness. The narrative begins with the outlook for royalty at her birth and her first meeting with Prince Albert.

Chapters follow her accession, marriage, and family life, then the great public events: rebellion in Canada, the Opium War, the Crimea, the Indian Mutiny, jubilees, and the nation's progress. The book also notes Victoria as artist and author. It is a warm, popular royal biography from just after her death.
a-modern-chronicle-volume-01:
Winston Churchill's A Modern Chronicle, volume one, introduces Honora Leffingwell in a chapter asking what's in heredity. Honora was born at Nice, where her father Randolph served as United States consul, and raised in St. Louis. His death leaves her to relations and a conservative old city on the Mississippi. Perdita Recalled and Concerning Providence follow her childhood.

This first of eight volumes carries chapters one to six of Book One, ending as Honora has a glimpse of the world. The whole set's contents are printed here, mapping her rise through society to come. Churchill, the American novelist — not the British statesman — wrote best-selling studies of American manners. Honora's ambition, marriages, and divorces will test Gilded Age St. Louis and New York. The chronicle is a woman's career told as national biography. Heredity, the opening asks, and the eight volumes answer.
a-select-bibliography-of-chemistry-1492-:
A Select Bibliography of Chemistry, 1492-1897, published in 1901, continues Henry Carrington Bolton's great listing of chemical literature. This portion is Section 8 of the second series, devoted to academic dissertations. It extends Bolton's coverage five years beyond his first bibliography, which had closed in 1892, and gathers the university theses of chemistry into one place.

Academic dissertations are among the hardest chemical writings to trace, since they were printed in small numbers by universities across Europe and America. Bolton's section gives them a single ordered list, by the same bibliographer who mapped the science's books. For historians, it opens a view of how chemistry was taught and examined in the universities of the nineteenth century.
a-select-collection-of-old-english-plays: Robert Dodsley revives his select collection of old English plays in this first volume of a fourth edition, chronologically arranged for the first time, revised, and enlarged. The preface notes that after half a century since the last edition, the work had become scarce and dear, though a favourite with lovers of early drama since 1744. Notes of all commentators, with new notes by W. Carew Hazlitt, accompany plays rescued for a new generation.
a-strange-story-volume-01: Edward Bulwer Lytton opens his strange story in this first volume with a preface on French intellectual philosophy. Victor Cousin, he notes, ranks Maine de Biran the most original thinker of his school, a man who began in blind faith in Condillac and materialism. As perplexities opened before him, Biran added a second, human life of free will and self-consciousness to the animal life of impressions and appetites ruled by necessity.
a-thorny-path-volume-01:
A Thorny Path begins in Volume 1 of the Alexandria novel by Georg Ebers, set when the Roman emperor Caracalla holds Egypt. Ebers opens inside the studio of Heron, a gem cutter whose work needs exact light. His daughter Melissa hauls a heavy green screen up and down over the broad window, hour after hour, so the sun will not spoil the stones on his table.

Chapter I stays with that quiet labor: caged birds, low whistling, and gold embroidery set aside when a visitor steps into the outer room. Melissa's calm service hides a household under strain, with a surly father, grown sons, and Christian friends at the edge of a pagan city. Readers meet the family at work before imperial danger reaches their door and turns duty into risk.
a-tramp-abroad-volume-01:
A Tramp Abroad, Part 1, by Mark Twain, opens his comic travel book about walking through Europe, first published in 1880. Twain, whose real name was Samuel L Clemens, starts at Heidelberg, where a grand hotel, an all knowing porter, and German student life supply his first material. The illustrations come from the 1880 first edition, Titian's Moses and the author's own portrait among them.

Chapter III gives the book's most retold piece, Jim Baker's blue jay yarn, a California tale about a bird, a knothole, and the language jays speak. Then the student chapters take over: the five corps, their laws, their dueling ground, and a sickening spectacle of sword fights treated as sport. Twain plays the innocent American abroad, measuring German order and German beer against his own loose habits, and finding both wanting in the funniest possible way.
a-word-only-a-word-volume-01:
A Word, Only a Word opens in Volume 1 of the novel by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers starts in the Black Forest just after May, where a boy named Ulrich laughs under the pines and claps his hands at a wood pigeon. The valley is narrow, the air sultry, and storm clouds gather while every creature seems to hold its breath around him.

Chapter I sets Ulrich's scorn for book learning in his own cry: a word, only a word. He braces his bare knee against a bundle of sticks and mocks the idea of sitting over books all day for one stupid term. Ruth, the girl beside him, answers that not all words are alike. That small argument names the book's theme. A single word, spoken or withheld, will steer love, honor, and survival for everyone here.
abraham-lincoln-a-history-volume-01:
John G. Nicolay and John Hay, Lincoln's own secretaries, dedicate their great history to Robert Todd Lincoln in token of lifelong friendship. Their preface, written a generation after Lincoln's death, says the judgment of contemporaries has already hardened into tradition: he was incomparably the greatest man of his time. This first volume covers the making of the man.

The contents run from lineage and Kentucky boyhood through Indiana pioneer life, New Salem, the Black Hawk War, surveying, the legislature, early law practice, marriage, and the Shields duel, toward Congress. Nicolay and Hay worked from papers no one else held, and their ten-volume life remained the standard Lincoln for decades. Volume one gives the frontier roots in full.
alice-or-the-mysteries-book-01: Edward Bulwer Lytton opens his novel Alice, or the Mysteries in a secluded Devonshire cottage, where two ladies sit by open windows above a spring garden and the sea. The quiet, remote scene sets up a tale of hidden identities, love, and social mystery that will widen far beyond this cottage. Book one plants the central figures and secrets on which the long romance turns.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith assembles the opening part of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, a series made up almost entirely of illustrations and page images. This text file carries only a few passages that could be scanned well, and its editor's note points readers to the fuller HTML version. The plates preserve documents and relics of American history and letters in facsimile form.
an-egyptian-princess-volume-01:
Georg Ebers's An Egyptian Princess, volume one, in Eleanor Grove's translation, opens with the Nile overflowing its bed. At Sais, in the house of Rhodopis, the Greek courtesan whose salon gathers Egypt's court, a supper ends in a fateful embassy. Cambyses, king of Persia, demands Nitetis, daughter of Pharaoh Amasis, as his bride. Ebers's preface to the second German edition promises a corrected text.

Nitetis's brother Psamtik burns with jealousy of the Persians; her brother by adoption, Bartja, loves Rhodopis's granddaughter Sappho. The volume sets Egypt's glittering decline against Persia's rising power. Ebers, an Egyptologist, built his romance on Herodotus and the monuments. Grove's translation carried his historical romances across the English-speaking world. Volume one is all threshold: a princess displayed like a treaty, a court smiling over its fear, and the Nile rising over a kingdom with a generation to live.
apotelesmata-philosophica-mercvrii-trivm:
Apotelesmata Philosophica Mercurii Triumphantis, printed in 1601 by Martinus Copus, is the key to the author's earlier work Mercurius Triumphans. That book first appeared at Magdeburg in 1599 and was issued in an enlarged edition the next year. The present work's five sections correspond to the five books of the 1599 edition, unlocking them in order.

Its Latin title promises the true and supreme medicine of the most ancient philosophers, the heart of the alchemical quest. The dedication, addressed to the Emperor Rudolph the Second, is signed with the initials of Martinus Copus, doctor of medicine. A woodcut coat of arms of the Copi de Calvis family ornaments the book, a piece of the learned alchemy of Rudolfine Europe.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-01:
