Richard F. Burton published the first volume of his Thousand Nights and a Night in 1885. His literal, unexpurgated translation of the Arabic Alf Layla wa Layla became the most famous English Arabian Nights. Shahrazad, wedded to a king who kills his brides, saves her life by telling tales that never quite end at dawn.

Volume one sets that frame and opens the early cycles of merchants, jinn, and porters. Burton kept the verse, the slang, and the frankness that earlier versions cut. His notes draw on years in the East and a scholar's appetite for custom. The full set runs to ten volumes, with six supplemental ones after. This first volume is where the great frame begins.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
Burton's Supplemental Nights began in 1886, adding tales from Arabic manuscripts outside the main cycle. Volume one of the supplement is famed for holding Aladdin and Ali Baba in Burton's full rendering. Those two tales, known to every child in short forms, come here with their complete Arabic frames and details.

Aladdin's lamp and the forty thieves' cave gain depth, violence, and humor in the uncut text. Burton drew these stories from the Wortley Montague manuscript and other sources he names. The supplement was no afterthought: it rounds the Nights toward completeness. Readers who know only the famous pair will find them stranger and richer here. Six volumes carry the supplement to its end.
arachne-volume-01:
Arachne begins in Volume 1 of the novel by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers sets the story in Tennis, a small weaving town in the Nile Delta, during the flood season of 274 BC. Greek rulers hold Egypt, and Greek artists compete for royal favor, wealth, and fame in this opening volume.

Chapter I paints the drowned landscape in slow detail: islands, palms, papyrus reeds, and waterfowl under a hard bright sky. The town sits ringed by floodwater, quiet in the heat. At its heart stands Hermon, a young sculptor whose hunger for fame will shape the tale. Ledscha, a local girl bound to old loyalties and old gods, crosses his path. Art, love, and revenge grow from this still, shining first scene.
arxiv-2412-03201:
Eduardo Brito, Fernando Castillo, Pille Pullonen-Raudvere, and Sebastian Werner argue that software users need proof, not promises, that online services behave fairly. Services now decide access to money, information, and more, yet even open code is hard to check because systems change fast and deployments are complex. Laws and best practice pledges fill the gap, but flaws and data leaks slip through. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the authors propose TrustOps, a practice of gathering checkable evidence at every stage of building and running software.

The approach combines tools and trust technologies that already exist rather than inventing new ones. A small set of adaptable core principles anchors the proposal, so different teams can fit it to their setting. The paper closes with a roadmap for research and development, aimed at a trust model based on continuous evidence.
arxiv-2412-11501:
Naoki Sato and Hideaki Iiduka wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It tests graduated optimization for deep neural networks, a trick that smooths a bumpy loss with noise and then eases the noise away to find a broad low point.

The team grades the explicit form, with a best noise plan from past work, on classic test curves and on real network losses, and notes where it stalls. They then stretch the implicit form, which rides on the noise that stochastic gradient descent makes on its own, to the momentum variant. A convergence study and image tests on ResNet builds show the stretch works.
arxiv-2412-11701:
Ben Dutton and Nikos Katzourakis study a class of math tasks where the goal is to make the peak value of a cost as small as it can be. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

The cost rests on how a map curves, through its second slopes, plus on lower terms for its place and first slope. The tasks are of second order, on a bounded region with fixed edge values. The authors prove that best maps exist under plain terms. In the one-dim case, they prove a stronger form, where the best map is best on each sub-part too. They then draw out a hard third-order equation that any such best map must meet.
arxiv-2412-11801:
Ann-Kristin Malz, Gregory Ashton, and Nicolo Colombo attach honest confidence levels to machine learning classifications of detector glitches, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Gravitational-wave observatories record many brief noise bursts that mimic real signals, and sorting them is a job increasingly handed to algorithms.

A label alone is not enough; scientists need to know how much to trust it. Many machine learning methods give no uncertainty at all. The authors apply conformal prediction, a framework that wraps a point predictor and returns sets of labels with guaranteed coverage. They tune it for the glitch classification task of the Gravity Spy project, which crowdsources and automates the sorting of these artefacts. The paper explores how the method behaves in this setting and what its guarantees mean in practice. Reliable uncertainty, they argue, is what makes algorithmic labels safe to use in measurement.
arxiv-2412-15401:
Canyi Chen and colleagues built a mediation analysis for quantiles in a 2024 statistics paper. Mediation asks whether an exposure reaches an outcome through an intermediate variable, and scientists often care about effects at specific quantiles, say the worst-off tenth, rather than the average. Theory for quantile mediation lagged behind practice, leaving users without guarantees, so the authors define natural direct and indirect effects at each quantile inside the counterfactual framework, both with closed forms.

Testing for no mediation is tricky because that null hypothesis is composite, mixing several ways mediation can vanish. Their adaptive bootstrap controls false positives properly, backed by theory and numerics. Worked examples show the method answering subgroup questions means-based mediation cannot phrase.
arxiv-2501-04401:
Thibaud Ardoin and five co-authors test if the faint radio marks of ultra-wideband tools can be used to track the tools themselves. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Ultra-wideband gives place sense down to a few centimeters, and phone makers now ship it widely. Each tool's hardware leaves a slight mark on its signal. The team built a real data set with off-the-shelf tools, with shifts in place kept in check. A deep learning path pulls the mark out of the raw signal. In calm settings, the marks named the right tool in more than ninety-nine of a hundred tries. In new places, the rate fell, but stayed high.
arxiv-2501-05901:
Ziheng Wu and colleagues at ByteDance present the second generation of their Valley vision-language model, tuned especially for shopping and short video. Multimodal models that read images and text together have raced ahead on captioning and video understanding. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team frames their design as scalable, meant to hold up across many domains while pushing practical applications in e-commerce. The reported numbers headline the release. On e-commerce benchmarks the model beat similar-sized open-source rivals by a wide margin. On a broad public leaderboard it placed second among models under ten billion parameters.

Code and model weights are open-sourced through the project's repository, inviting outside testing of the claims. The paper positions the model as an industry workhorse rather than a laboratory curiosity, with design choices aimed at deployment breadth.
arxiv-2501-08301:
Nick Tusay and fourteen co-authors watch a rocky planet crumble, reading its interior from the dust it sheds. Their paper from twenty twenty-five observes K2-22b, an ultra-short-period world whose dusty eruptions swing its transit depth wildly. The escaping material likely rose from deep layers to the molten surface before sublimating. JWST's mid-infrared instrument caught four predicted transit windows as a slitless spectrograph.

One transit registers strongly, two weakly. The spectra disfavor plain iron core material and fit magnesium silicate minerals, the stuff of mantles. A surprise absorption near five microns hints at gas, possibly nitric oxide or carbon dioxide. Firm claims await better signal, the authors stress. Still, a dying planet is confessing its recipe.
arxiv-2501-10501:
V. A. Fawcett and co-authors studied the radio glow of dusty quasars in 2025. Recent work had found a striking link: the more dust obscures a quasar, the stronger its radio release tends to be, but the cause was unknown. The team built radio readings at four or five rates for a sample of quasars at moderate redshift, joining findings from Indian and British telescope arrays with archival data.

Dusty quasars were far more likely than clean ones to show steep radio spectra, where brightness falls quickly with rate, while clean quasars more often showed peaked spectra. Most of the peaked, dust-free sources matched compact jetted radio galaxies in size and brightness. For the dusty group, the authors discuss shocks driven by outflows. These shocks plow into the surrounding dust and gas. They are the likely engine of the extra radio release, tying the original correlation to quasar winds.
arxiv-2501-13401:
Hiwa Ahmed, Yidian Chen, and Mei Huang use a gravity-like model of strong forces to study how three bound states act in hot, spinning matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The states are mesons, pairs of quarks. One is light, one is mid-weight, and one holds a heavy charm quark. The team reads their spectral marks in still and in spinning heat. The light and mid states show broad peaks at low heat, then melt as heat grows. Spin delays the melt. The heavy state stands firm against heat. They also track how the spin of each state lines up in the plane of a crash.
arxiv-2501-15301:
Xiangxiang Xu and Lizhong Zheng wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It shows that many gauges of information can be computed from learned traits of the data, not from the raw data at all.

Under mild terms on the traits, a class of gauges splits in this way. The list runs from mutual information and f-information to two forms of common information and the information bottleneck. The work draws fresh links between these gauges and the web of dependence in the data. It also gives theory cover for the hands-on designs that gauge information through representation learning.
arxiv-2502-02701:
Atsushi Noda and Takashi Isozaki wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a hands-on way to pick which variables to adjust for when gauging a cause, when more than one valid set exists and data are scarce.

Adjusting for a set that meets the back-door rule strips out confounding, but the right set is often not unique. With thin data, a poor pick can drag accuracy down. The authors give tests for picking from a list of candidate variables, plus an algorithm to guard the gauge. They start with full causal graphs, then extend to partial graphs, with a theorem on when a causal effect can be computed there. Tests on known and made-up data show the method works.
arxiv-2502-08401:
Selçuk Kayacan, a mathematician in Istanbul, studies racks, an algebraic structure built on a single operation with special rules. Racks show up in the study of knots and in abstract algebra. Kayacan asks how racks can be described by generators and relations, in the same spirit as group presentations. That framing lets hard questions about racks borrow tools from group theory.

The paper first rebuilds the needed group theory from scratch. It defines free groups through words and relations, then shows how any group can be presented that way. The same machinery is then turned toward racks. On that base, Kayacan proposes a cryptographic protocol defined on racks. The work links pure algebra to a possible use in secure communication.
arxiv-2502-13501:
Luigi Ferreira studied hot Yang-Mills theory in a 2025 physics paper, using two ways of fixing the gauge. Yang-Mills theory describes the strong-force carriers called gluons, and fixing a gauge means picking one representative field from many equal copies. At the quantum level, leftover copies, named Gribov copies, must be removed for honest results.

Ferreira carries the zero-heat removal of tiny copies over to heated theory, adding thermal masses drawn from simpler calculations. The combined action shows three regimes for gluons as heat rises: fully confined at low heat, partly confined in between, and fully freed at high heat. The picture matches the expected melting of confinement.
arxiv-2502-13701:
Sylvia Kerkhove, Natasha Alechina, and Mehdi Dastani bring the study of cause and effect into games where many agents choose with a plan. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Cause is core to daily life, to human thought, and to smart systems. Yet it had scant study where agents act with strategy. The team gives a step way to turn a causal model into a game frame. In that frame, each move is a set act on an agent's terms in the causal model. A known cause frame then reads the effect of each value. The pair of frames lets one ask how an agent's plan drives the rest. They prove how the two frames tie.
arxiv-2502-14801:
Cheng Li and colleagues built a system in 2025 to create and explain traffic accident videos. Crashes are rare, messy, and hard to predict, so self-driving systems train on too few real examples. Their framework generates crash videos that match detailed written accounts, including what caused the crash and how it might have been prevented.

Pairing generated videos with careful descriptions produced a new training set for accident understanding. Systems trained with that set scored best on both automated measures and human ratings. Better crash data could teach driving software to read danger earlier. The work also gives researchers a safer way to study events too risky to stage.
arxiv-2502-16701:
Irene Solaiman and colleagues argued in 2025 that releasing a generative AI system is only the first question; access is the rest of the story. A release decision says which components are available, but whether anyone can actually use them depends on practical conditions the release headline hides. The authors break access into three axes, each with its own variables for every component of a system.

Resourcing covers the infrastructure a user needs, such as the computing power to serve model weights. Technical usability covers whether the component can be operated at all by its intended audience, and utility covers whether using it delivers real value. Comparing four high-performing language models, two open-weight and two closed, they find the same access variables decide the real openness of all four. The framework then examines scale: wider access multiplies both benefits and the difficulty of intervening when something goes wrong.
arxiv-2502-21001:
Woo Kyoung Han, Byeonghun Lee, Hyunmin Cho, Sunghoon Im, and Kyong Hwan Jin wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It stores images and sound in a neural net with no loss at all, by having the net predict bit planes one by one.

Implicit neural representations trade a signal for a small net's weights. The team first bounds how big such a net must be, and finds the bound soars with bit depth. Splitting the target into bit planes cuts that bound in effect. With the same net size, training then settles faster. Two-dimensional images and audio are rebuilt exactly, even at sixteen-bit depth, a first. A side find, bit bias, shows the net favors the top bit. The trick spreads to depth growth, true lossless squeeze, and hard quantization.
arxiv-2503-02501:
Michael Björklund, Rickard Cullman, and Alexander Fish define a new spectrum for large sets of lattice points, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. They prove it must contain a full scaled copy of the whole lattice's spectrum. For a set of integer points, its Ehrhart spectrum collects the Ehrhart polynomials of all simplices whose corners lie in the set.

Ehrhart polynomials count lattice points in dilated polytopes, so the spectrum packages a lot of geometric information. The authors require only that the set has positive upper Banach density, meaning it is reasonably thick along some sequence of regions. Even then, some rescaled copy of the integer lattice has its entire spectrum inside the set's spectrum. The result generalizes an earlier theorem about volume spectra by two of the authors. It is a rigidity statement: thickness alone forces rich internal structure.
arxiv-2503-08601:
Dušan Malić, Christian Fruhwirth-Reisinger, Samuel Schulter, and Horst Possegger release LiSu, a dataset and method for estimating surface orientation from LiDAR scans, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Surface normals, the directions a surface faces at each point, are basic input for reading three-dimensional scene geometry.

LiDAR point clouds are sparse and noisy, and no large labeled dataset existed for this task. The authors generate one synthetically with a traffic simulation engine, which supplies exact ground truth normals and removes manual labeling. Their estimation method exploits how driving data unfolds in space and time. Two penalties enforce that neighboring points agree on orientation and that estimates change smoothly between consecutive frames. The result is a benchmark and a stronger estimator for self-driving perception. Synthetic supervision sidesteps the labeling bottleneck that held the area back.
arxiv-2503-09201:
Krzysztof Urbanowski questions a claim made for a newer uncertainty relation in quantum physics, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The relation concerns the sum of variances of two observables that cannot be measured sharply at the same time.

Some papers present this sum rule as stronger than the classic Heisenberg-Robertson relation. Urbanowski tests the claim on a clean case: a system sitting in an eigenstate of one of the two observables. In that case, he shows, the sum rule gives exactly the same results as the classic relation. Worse, it places no bound at all on the variance of the other observable. The paper warns against reading more power into the newer relation than it holds. It is a short, pointed piece of criticism aimed at a specific weak point.
arxiv-2503-16001:
Niels Benedikter and colleagues derived an effective equation for many fermions in a magnetic field in a 2025 paper. A large cloud of interacting fermions follows the many-body Schrödinger equation, which is far too complex to solve directly. In a joint limit where particle number grows and quantum effects soften, the cloud should obey the nonlinear Hartree-Fock equation instead, and proving that rigorously is the task.

The proof hinges on trace-norm bounds for commutators of position and momentum with the evolving one-particle density. The authors first prove the bounds for non-interacting starts in a magnetic field, extending a 2020 result, then carry them along the Hartree-Fock flow to all times. Magnetic fields complicate each step beyond the field-free case.
arxiv-2503-22201:
Jaewoo Jeong, Seohee Lee, and colleagues forecast where pedestrians will walk next in a 2025 computer vision study. Self-driving cars and mobile robots need those forecasts to move safely among people. Cameras supply extra signals beyond position, such as body pose and scene text, and text turns out to help fuse those signals into one understanding.

Running a vision-language model live to extract that text is too heavy for small systems. Their method distills the multi-modal knowledge into a lighter model during training. The deployed forecaster then benefits from pose and language insight without paying the live extraction cost.
arxiv-2503-23601:
Thomas O'Brien and Ysobel Sims put GPT-4 in charge of a humanoid robot's behavior and check that the arrangement behaves itself, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Language models can already split a goal into sub-tasks. Earlier work judged those plans for correctness, but practical deployment raises other worries.

Their method feeds the robot's real-time state back to the model inside a reactive behavior framework. Safety, smooth transitions between tasks, and goals with different time horizons all get explicit handling. Experiments ran in simulation and on a real humanoid. For feasible requests, the system produced executable output every time, with clean hand-offs between sub-tasks. User goals were achieved most of the time across short and long horizons. The study is a proof of concept that a language model can run a robot's strategy loop responsibly, not just draft plans on paper.
arxiv-2504-02001:
Abdel Nasser Tawfik, Azzah Alshehri, and Antonio Pasqua test whether a quantum-revised version of Einstein's metric softens the singularities of general relativity. Near such points, spacetime stops behaving like a smooth manifold. The authors follow how bundles of timelike paths expand inside an uneven, spherically symmetric cosmos.

They run the calculation twice, once with the conventional metric and once with their quantum-mechanically revisited one. The quantum version uses a mean-field treatment of its operators. Unlike the classical result, the revised metric appears to control the singularities rather than letting expansion blow up. How strongly the effect works seems to depend on the degree of quantization chosen.
arxiv-2504-03201:
Jonathan Arnaud, Xian-Zhu Tang, and Christopher McDevitt built a fast stand-in model in 2025 for runaway electrons in fusion plasmas. In a tokamak disruption, some electrons accelerate to near light speed and multiply in an avalanche that can damage the machine. Simulating that growth from first principles is far too slow for whole-machine studies, especially when impurities are only partly ionized.

Their physics-informed neural network learns the adjoint of the governing kinetic equation, with power balance and atomic data built into training. A new closure for the fast electron population sharpens accuracy over an older source model. Checked against Monte Carlo runs, the surrogate predicts avalanche growth well across wide conditions, at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2504-06001:
Fiori and a large team of co-authors track the flickering light, in a 2025 preprint, of a black hole system across a long outburst. The system, MAXI J1820+070, flared from 2018 to 2020 and then brightened again. The team combined optical and X-ray records over timescales from months down to fractions of a second. They hunted for rhythms in the light that reveal how matter falls toward the black hole.

Optical light showed a slow rhythm that settled slightly longer than the orbital period. The same rhythm appeared briefly in X-rays. At other times, faster quasi-periodic wobbles showed up in both bands, with the optical wobble at half the X-ray rate. If such wobbles come from a wobbling inner disc, the optical data point to slow spin for the black hole. Later rhythms may come from the outer disc lit by the inner disc's glow.
arxiv-2504-07501:
Xiangge Liu and colleagues proved new graph theory results in 2025 about tough networks. A graph is called tough if cutting out a few points never shatters it into many more pieces than the cut itself. Toughness matters for networks that must stay connected under damage, and the least degree of a point gives a simple local clue.

Their tests use a global measure built from distances between all pairs of points, summed in a special matrix. When that measure stays small enough, the graph must be tough, with the bound tied to size and least degree. Versions cover plain toughness and stronger forms too. Spectral clues can certify strength that is hard to check directly.
arxiv-2504-08801:
Andrew Kiruluta, Priscilla Burity, and Samantha Williams propose replacing attention in transformer models in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Self-attention handles long-range dependencies well but its cost grows quadratically with sequence length, which strains long inputs and small machines. Their Learnable Multi-Scale Wavelet Transformer swaps dot-product attention for a learnable multi-scale Haar wavelet module. Wavelets naturally capture both fine local detail and broad global context at multiple resolutions.

Unlike fixed wavelet transforms, the module's scale-specific coefficients are learned end-to-end, letting the model adapt its decomposition to the task. The authors give the full mathematical formulation and an architectural diagram. On a standard machine translation benchmark they compare against a self-attention baseline using translation quality and accuracy metrics. They also highlight the design's linear scaling and the interpretability gained from visualizing the learned wavelet coefficients.
arxiv-2504-14901:
Eunbi Jang, Junghee Cho, Chanik Kang, and Haejun Chung design a very thin electromagnetic absorber in a 2025 physics study. Absorbers that work at wide incoming angles matter for stealth, wireless systems, and quantum hardware. Classic designs need at least a quarter wavelength of thickness, too bulky for compact devices.

Metamaterials can be thinner but usually absorb poorly when waves arrive at a slant. The authors use an adjoint optimization method to search for structures far thinner than a wavelength. Their designs keep strong absorption across angles, borrowing the slant tolerance of older screens. Efficient computation let them explore many shapes systematically rather than by hand tuning.
arxiv-2504-19201:
Giuseppe Mazzuoccolo and Vahan Mkrtchyan studied a growth operation on cubic graphs in 2025. Graph theorists usually shrink cubic graphs by contracting triangles; these authors run the film backward, expanding chosen points into triangles, and ask how few expansions buy a desired trait. Their first target trait is that the enlarged graph can be covered by four perfect matchings, partitions of the points into disjoint edges.

The minimum number of expansions needed defines a setting tied to the shortest cycle cover problem. If a famous five-cycle double cover guess holds, they show the setting never exceeds two fifths of the points. And they guess a far tighter bound of one tenth, best possible for the Petersen graph, which itself follows from other major guesses. A second setting counts expansions needed merely to admit one perfect matching, and a Gallai-type identity links it exactly to a complementary amount.
arxiv-2505-01601:
Samuel Rhys Cox, Helena Bøjer Djernæs, and Niels van Berkel ask how tools that aid art and design work get judged. Their paper from twenty twenty-five looks at creativity support tools, a class of software now boosted by generative AI. The authors reviewed how past studies measured success when people used such tools.

The review covers a large set of tool tests held in the ACM Digital Library. It lists the scores and checks that studies used most often. The authors find that most tests weigh speed and output quality above all else. They argue that tests should also weigh how users feel, reflect, and grow. They also call for sound checks built for AI-based tools. The paper urges a wider view of what good support means.
arxiv-2505-01901:
Peyman Kiasari asked whether coding paradigms deserve their name in a 2025 paper. Robert Floyd introduced the term in his 1978 Turing Award lecture, borrowing it explicitly from Thomas Kuhn's philosophy of science. A paradigm is the shared setup of a scientific community, overturned only by revolution. Kiasari matches Kuhn's first concept with how work uses the word. Paradigms like object-oriented or working coding coexist and mix rather than overthrow each other.

The verdict is that Floyd's borrowing fundamentally altered the concept's meaning, so current usage departs by a lot from Kuhn's setup. That divergence, the paper argues, calls for a critical reassessment of the term in work discourse. Loose philosophy can smuggle in false implications about how coding styles change.
arxiv-2505-02201:
Simranjot Sapra, Jeng-Kuei Chang, and Rajendra Dhaka trace how a nickel-doped sodium cathode stores charge, using live X-ray views of the cell at work. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies a fluorophosphate cathode family for sodium-ion batteries, made by a pH-assisted sol-gel route. A light nickel dose proves optimal. That sample pairs high capacity at slow rates with strong output at fast ones.

Endurance is the headline: most capacity survives two thousand fast cycles with near-perfect efficiency. Operando diffraction watches the crystal breathe reversibly as sodium comes and goes. Synchrotron microscopy tracks shape changes in step. Impedance analysis splits the losses by relaxation time. Structure and shape both hold up after long cycling, which explains the stamina.
arxiv-2505-03701:
Arturo Cevallos Soto and Zhaohuan Zhu study how young planets move inside the disks that form them, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Planets usually drift inward through their protoplanetary disk. Where they stop shapes the architecture of the final planetary system.

The pair inserted planets into three-dimensional simulations of turbulent, magnetized disks. Turbulence delivered random kicks, which they quantified with a modified Gaussian process. Periodic tugs from slow-moving disk structures also appeared. With the simulated disk's very low surface density, most drift mechanisms slowed dramatically. Earth-mass planets would take longer than the age of the universe to migrate, effectively stalling. Only giant planets could push inward through the turbulent inner disk.
arxiv-2505-07201:
Shubhankar Paul and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on growing ultra clean crystals of ruthenium dioxide. The compound is a candidate for a new kind of magnetism, called altermagnetism. Clean crystals are a must to test such claims. The team grows them by vapor transport, where the solid turns to gas and back in a hot tube.

A neck in the tube and tight control of heat let them steer the crystal shape. Three forms come out: thick plates, blocky columns, and thin needles. Tests show very low left over resistance and a high purity ratio. No sign of magnetic order shows down to low heat. The recipe gives labs a clean source for tests of this much watched material.
arxiv-2505-08901:
Manuel Hauke reviews a century of Diophantine approximation in twenty twenty-five. Metric Diophantine approximation asks how well typical real numbers can be approximated by rationals. Khintchine's theorem is its foundation, now a hundred years old. The Duffin-Schaeffer conjecture stood beside it as a famous open problem for decades.

That conjecture was spectacularly proven in twenty twenty, by Koukoulopoulos and Maynard. Half a decade on, Hauke surveys the field's history and recent breakthroughs. Generalizations of Khintchine's theorem are discussed in turn. Simplified key ideas from the Duffin-Schaeffer proof are presented in accessible form. Those ideas have since found use in other areas of number theory. Readers get a guided tour from a classic theorem to a modern triumph.
arxiv-2505-10601:
Chuang Chen and Wenyi Ge proposed SRMamba in twenty twenty-five to raise the resolution of LiDAR point clouds cheaply. Range-view methods project the three-dimensional cloud into an image and upscale there. But sparsity and irregular structure make the recovery hard, especially from new viewpoints. Holes appear in the projected image, and flattening loses vertical geometry.

Their pipeline patches holes with a Hough voting and compensation step. It then processes the image with a visual state space model — the Mamba architecture — scanning in multiple directions. That preserves long-range and vertical structure. An asymmetric U-Net adapts to sensors with different beam counts. On the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes benchmarks, SRMamba beat competing methods on both visual quality and numerical scores.
arxiv-2505-12701:
Shuyang Dong, Shangtong Zhang, and Lu Feng explain reinforcement learning agents by showing what they could have done instead. Counterfactual explanations answer what-if questions, a natural way to build trust in healthcare and robotics. Continuous action spaces, where actions are dials rather than buttons, have resisted such explanations. The team's method searches for alternative action sequences that improve the outcome while straying least from the original.

A distance metric tailored to continuous actions measures that straying. Constraints, such as states where a fixed policy must rule, are respected during the search. Tests in diabetes control and a lunar lander task show the explanations are effective and cheap to compute. They also generalize across settings. The work gives continuous control agents an interpretable voice: here is the smallest change that would have gone better.
arxiv-2505-17101:
Santiago Acevedo and co-authors wrote this machine learning study, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how neural networks store meaning. Models that read the same text or see linked images tend to build like inner maps, and the team set out to measure that likeness.

Their tool, called Information Imbalance, ranks how well one model's inner map can predict another's. Tests on translations read by a large model showed meaning spread across many words, not held in a few. Meaning was easiest to read in the model's middle layers, across six language pairs. English maps predicted other languages better than the reverse. In vision models, the best layers differed by model type. The authors say meaning converges across languages and model kinds, but the flow of that meaning is not even.
arxiv-2505-20201:
Mohit Chandra, Siddharth Sriraman, Harneet Singh Khanuja, Yiqiao Jin, and Munmun De Choudhury test AI as a mental health talk partner in this two thousand twenty-five paper. People more and more turn to language models for help amid care and long waits. Skill at talks, though, is little tested: most checks score naming an illness or winning a vote. They skip how well a model fits a patient's goals, values, and traits. The team built MedAgent, a frame making lifelike sensemaking talks.

From it they built a data set of twenty-two hundred patient-model talks, and MultiSenseEval, a human grading frame for dialogue. Top models did poorly at patient-first talk and scored on average only thirty-one percent on diagnosis skills. Scores shifted with patient persona and fell as talks grew longer. The work gives data and scores for a skill the field must learn to gauge.
arxiv-2505-23401:
Marta Bílková, Wesley Fussner, and Roman Kuznets built a new proof system in 2025 for logics of knowledge shared among several agents. Multi-agent modal logic, with S5-style knowledge operators for each agent, is a standard language for reasoning about who knows what. Proving things in it cleanly, and extracting consequences automatically, calls for a calculus designed around its structure.

Their formalism merges two known devices: hypersequents, which suit the S5 modalities, and nested sequents, which handle the alternating T-like steps between agents. They prove the calculus sound and complete, free of the cut rule, and guaranteed to terminate, which yields decidability and the finite model property for multi-agent S5. As a payoff they establish the Lyndon interpolation property, counting the agents themselves as part of the shared language, and discuss what blocks extending the results to distributed knowledge.
arxiv-2506-05401:
Yuan Xun, Siyuan Liang, Xiaojun Jia, Xinwei Liu, and Xiaochun Cao defend visual language models in two thousand twenty-five. Backdoor attacks hide in poisoned fine tuning data. Defenders cannot touch frozen encoders or core model weights here. Trigger shapes and target replies stay unknown to them as well.

Their Robust Instruction Tuning touches only adapters and text embeddings. Input diversity jitter breaks the fixed cues triggers rely on. A second rule sparsifies adapter weights with sharp, odd activations. Seven attacks on two datasets fell to near zero success. Training cost rose by less than fifteen percent overall.
arxiv-2506-06801:
Suman Majumder and Saikat Chakraborty watch a polymer chain crumple and find colloid-like rules in the mess. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A stretched polymer quenched below its collapse point shrinks into a globule. Small clusters of monomers, nicknamed pearls, form first. The pearls merge like droplets until one globule remains. Droplet merging echoes cluster aggregation in colloidal systems.

Molecular dynamics simulations test whether the same scaling laws hold. The team tracks cluster size distributions and average growth over time. Bending stiffness of the chain is varied across runs. Power-law scaling appears regardless of stiffness. The collapse thus joins a broad family of aggregation processes. Universal dynamics link polymers to colloids and beyond.
arxiv-2506-07201:
Duško Jojić and Ognjen Papaz look at Sperner marks of big graphs that come from edge wise splits of a shape with flat sides. Each swap of order sets a split, whose side faces form the big graph's edges. Past work by Mirzakhani and Vondrák showed the keen mark gives most one hue edges for the case of no swap.

The team works through the line graph of these big graphs with a help graph. That graph codes which back to back counts stay close in line in the swap. They set those graphs out with cuts of a plain shape with k sides. Sets with no links in the graphs then set new Sperner marks. Those marks beat the keen one for swaps not the same when spun. Some of these marks are also best.
arxiv-2506-08601:
Toki Ikeda, Takashi Shimonishi, Natsuko Izumi, Hiroyuki Kaneko, Satoko Takahashi, Kei Tanaka, Kenji Furuya, and Chikako Yasui wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reports the first clear sighting of outflows and jets from young stars in the outer part of our galaxy, seen with the ALMA telescope array.

The team watched five star-forming zones far from the galactic center. In one, they found a slow wide outflow and a fast narrow jet, with knot-like shots that point to bursts of ejection spaced far apart in time. The traits match those of near systems, so early star growth looks alike in metal-poor zones. One gas ratio does differ, hinting at distinct dust or shock chemistry there. Four more outflow sources are also reported.
arxiv-2506-10201:
Adalyn Gibson, Adam Kowalski, and Adina Feinstein wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It hunts for signs of fast protons in flares on AU Mic, a young red dwarf star, using far-ultraviolet light caught by the Hubble Space Telescope.

Fast protons in a flare should leave a mark called the Orrall-Zirker effect, a red-side boost in hydrogen lines. In six flares from stored Hubble data, that mark did not show. But one strong flare showed a blue-side boost in carbon lines, which the team links to either an erupting filament or gas boiling off the surface. One-dimensional flare models could not match that boost. The line-by-line study still tightens what is known about how such stars flare.
arxiv-2506-10301:
Hossein Rahmani and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on bias in fake test sets for search systems. Test sets need queries and grades of how well each result fits. Both are dear to make by hand. Language models can fake them at scale, and past work hints the fakes can grade systems. The team asks how far bias in the fakes warps the grades.

They show bias in scores from fake sets by direct tests. A mixed effects model backs the claim. For raw scores of one system, the warp can be large. For head to head ranks of systems, the warp shrinks a lot. Code and data are open.
arxiv-2506-10801:
Benjamin Hoover, Zhaoyang Shi, Krishnakumar Balasubramanian, Dmitry Krotov, and Parikshit Ram propose a new energy rule for dense associative memory networks. These networks store patterns as valleys in an energy landscape and retrieve them by rolling downhill. The standard rule uses a smooth exponential form. The new rule borrows a kernel known for best density estimates.

Their rule, called log-sum-ReLU, is built on the Epanechnikov kernel. It still retrieves stored patterns exactly, with the same vast capacity. It also grows many extra valleys that the standard rule never forms. Tests on images show these extra memories score as plausible as the stored ones. Some look novel, even creative, to the authors. The work hints at one design serving both giant storage and idea generation.
arxiv-2506-12301:
Yue Wan, Xiaowei Jia, and Xiang Lorraine Li study confirmation bias in chain of thought reasoning in two thousand twenty-five. Chain of thought prompts help language models reason step by step. Gains vary a lot by task type, though. The team views that uneven record through a bias known from human thought.

They split the chain into making reasons and using them for an answer. Model beliefs, read from direct answer odds, skew both stages. Strong beliefs bend the reasons made and how they are used. Task risk and belief strength jointly explain when the chain helps. The study urges prompts that curb this bias.
arxiv-2506-15001:
Ignacio Sastre and Aiala Rosa wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a curious trick: teaching a language model a secret token that stores a whole passage. When the model is fed that token, it prints the stored text back word for word.

Only the token's inner code is trained, on one fixed passage; the model's own weights stay untouched. The pair tested the trick on English and Spanish texts up to about two hundred forty words long. Models from small to eight billion parameters were tried. The largest model rebuilt every passage exactly. The authors say such memory tokens could serve in search, compression, and tightly controlled text generation. The work shows a recall power in these models that standard use never calls on.
arxiv-2506-15101:
Manuel Aguilera, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, formalizes the Gauss-Landau theorem, a prime-factorization method for greatest common divisors and least common multiples. Teachers use the technique constantly, yet it had never been explicitly named or formalized in the literature.

The paper gives a unified treatment for finite sets of nonzero integers rather than just pairs. Computing both quantities from prime factorizations becomes a stated theorem with a modern structure. Aguilera's aim is adoption: a named, formal version should be easier to teach, cite, and build on. The note is short and elementary, aimed at mathematical instruction as much as research.
arxiv-2506-22401:
Tong Yang, Bo Dai, Lin Xiao, and Yuejie Chi design exploration strategies for online reinforcement learning in a 2025 study. An agent learning by trial must explore enough to find good behavior without wasting trials, and modern agents use deep networks that resist classic analysis. Practical schemes with firm performance guarantees remain scarce.

Viewing the problem through a primal-dual lens, the authors build value-incentivized actor-critic methods. Bonus values encourage visiting uncertain states while the dual side keeps the bonuses honest. Their analysis targets sample efficiency, the number of interactions needed to reach good performance. Guaranteed exploration matters most where trials are costly, such as robotics and clinical settings.
arxiv-2506-22701:
Shi Jie Yu studied lower bounds in twenty twenty-five for estimating the trace of a matrix function — a sum that appears in physics, statistics, and machine learning. Practical estimators combine Hutchinson's randomized method with block Krylov subspaces, which build polynomial approximations to the function's action. The cost question is how many steps such methods must take.

Yu derives upper bounds on needed Krylov steps for functions like the inverse square root, by way of scalar polynomial approximation. He also proves query lower bounds for traces of inverse powers of Wishart matrices. The results tie estimation cost directly to polynomial approximation limits and information requirements, clarifying what no algorithm in this family can beat.
arxiv-2506-23201:
Haoran Li and four co-authors argue that weather and prices should reshape a power forecast model itself, not just feed it more inputs. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Guessing home power use well matters more as solar and wind join the grid. Most models treat outside facts as plain extra inputs, which wastes their value.

Their design uses a helper network that retunes parts of the main model as conditions change. A team-of-experts setup switches on only the parts needed for each case. That choice trims waste and cuts the harm from noisy extra inputs. The model, called M2oE2, beat top past methods across several load data sets. It did so with little extra cost. The team has shared both the data and the code in public.
arxiv-2506-23601:
Weijie Shi, Yue Cui, and eight colleagues make language models produce answers that differ in meaning, not just in wording, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Many tasks want several genuinely distinct responses: picking the best of many tries, group-based training, and synthesizing varied training data all depend on real diversity.

Temperature sampling shuffles word choice, and diverse beam search penalizes repeated phrases, yet the outputs often say the same thing. The team's method, SemDiD, works directly in embedding space, where meaning lives. Three mechanisms cooperate: guidance that pushes new answers in fresh directions, repulsion that keeps answer groups apart, and a debiased scoring of positions. Adaptive gains and constraint optimization balance quality against spread. The goal is a set of answers that are each good and truly different. Semantic variety, the authors argue, is the bottleneck for several modern training recipes.
arxiv-2506-24101:
Rainey Lyons, Vanja Dukic, and David Bortz offered a data-driven way in 2025 to learn how structured populations change. Populations split by age or size need rates for birth, death, and growth, and picking the right rates from noisy counts is slow, hard work. Their method searches a library of plausible rate formulas and keeps only the few that fit.

An added step learns what happens at the edge of the range, such as newborns entering, straight from the data. A tuning check then polishes that edge rule. Tests on known age and size models show where the method shines and where similar formulas blur together. Biologists get a faster path from counts to models.
arxiv-2507-00401:
Xin Xu, Eibe Frank, and Geoffrey Holmes recast a hard learning task: sorting things into classes from just a few shown cases. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, works when the base model cannot be retrained.

In real use, the part that pulls features from data is often a fixed black box. The team turns the few-case task into a run of checks that ask if cases match. On that base they build a small add-on head that fits any base and costs little to run. Trained on a few cases from a new field, the head scored near the best known ways, at far lower cost. Tests span a broad set of image tasks across fields.
arxiv-2507-04901:
Charith Hirimuthugodage, Laalitha Liyanage, and K. Gunawardana twisted iron nanowires in simulation to see what carbon does to them in a 2025 paper. Nanowires of iron and carbon-doped iron, aligned along one crystal direction, were subjected to torsion in molecular dynamics simulations using a potential fitted to iron-carbon interactions in the body-centered cubic structure. The sweep covered carbon content from pure iron up to ten percent, temperatures from near zero to nine hundred kelvin, and three wire thicknesses.

More carbon weakened grain boundaries, lowering the peak shear stress the wire withstands before its critical twist. Heat pushed deformation from elastic toward plastic as atomic vibration grew, and thicker wires showed their own size effects. The atomic-scale picture guides designs where iron nanostructures must survive twisting loads.
arxiv-2507-05301:
Kai-Cheng Yang analyzes news citing patterns in AI search systems in two thousand twenty-five. AI search now gates how users reach news and facts. Its citation habits are still poorly mapped. Data come from a head to head arena for AI search tools.

Thousands of chats and responses span three big providers. Hundreds of thousands of citations sit inside those replies. A small share point to news sources, piled on few outlets. A clear liberal lean shows, while low credibility sources are rare. User delight did not track the lean or quality of news cited.
arxiv-2507-08901:
Zebang Feng and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on making sharp road maps for self driving cars. Maps built with laser scans are costly and slow to make. Maps from a single car lack accuracy, above all in bad weather. Their system, called EGC-VMAP, pools data from many cars on the road.

The system fuses map parts seen by many cars at many times in one learning run. A new network design knows which trip each part came from. A layered match step keeps training fast, and a mixed loss guides the fit. Tests on a large multi city data set beat single car methods. The team reports a steep cut in hand labeling cost, which aids city wide use.
arxiv-2507-11901:
Juscimara Avelino, George Cavalcanti, and Rafael Cruz recommend pipelines in twenty twenty-five. Imbalanced data is common, and regression suffers from it too, not just classification. Rare target values are hard to learn. Balancing algorithms in preprocessing are a standard remedy, but choices abound.

The best resampling method and model pair depends on the data set and metric. Testing every combination is costly. Their framework, Meta-IR, trains meta-classifiers to recommend a full pipeline per task. It works zero-shot, with no trials on the new task. Meta-features describe each task and are mapped to the best pipeline class. Readers get a recommender that turns pipeline search into a single prediction.
arxiv-2507-13801:
Haoang Lu and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on filling in a full three dimensional scene from one camera image. Self driving cars need the layout and the labels of what fills each block of space. Much of a street scene hides behind other things or sits out of view. Past one camera methods leave those parts weak.

Their frame, CF-SSC, fakes a future frame to widen the view. Poses and depths tie past, now, and future frames in true space terms. A space aware build fuses the three with care for their links in time. Tests on two road data sets hit state of the art scores. Gains show most in how well blocked parts are guessed.
arxiv-2507-17901:
Iyen and five co-authors studied in twenty twenty-five how well quantum information survives near a black hole. They used quantum Fisher information, a measure of how much a state reveals about a parameter, as their gauge. Their system is three linked quantum bits carried by Dirac particles around a Schwarzschild black hole, passing through noisy channels.

Noise and the hole's Hawking heat both wear the signal down. Under strong squeezing, one form of the measure became fully shielded from the Hawking heat, though channel heat still hurt it. Squeezing also slowed decay sharply compared with the unsqueezed case. A second form spiked briefly at one channel temperature. Across channel types, channel heat proved the main source of damage, ahead of the black hole's own effects.
arxiv-2507-18701:
Hannah Ambrose and Anthony Whitworth use computer runs to map the orbits of star groups born in small clusters. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The stars are treated as the shards of one dead cloud core, with the gas long gone and no link between each star's first place and speed. Two terms drive the tale: how many stars the cluster holds, and how much of its motion is in shared spin. More stars shrink the tight orbits, but leave wide ones much the same. The spin share rules how the planes of the orbits tilt to each other, and how fast stars are thrown out.
arxiv-2508-00401:
Riddhi Pitliya, Ozan Çatal, Toon Van de Maele, Corrado Pezzato, and Tim Verbelen give man-made agents a theory of mind through active inference, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Theory of mind means recognizing that others hold their own beliefs and goals.

Earlier active inference methods to cooperation needed shared task-certain models or explicit communication. Here each agent keeps split representations of its own and others' beliefs, then plans with an extended tree-search algorithm that reasons recursively about joint policies. In collision avoidance and foraging model runs, theory-of-mind agents cooperated better, crashing less and duplicating less effort. They inferred beliefs purely from observed conduct.
arxiv-2508-04701:
Bobbi Yogatama, Yifei Yang, and colleagues argue that analytical databases should be rebuilt around GPUs, and present Sirius, a prototype GPU-native SQL engine. They contend that recent hardware advances, including larger GPU memory, faster interconnects, and declining cost, have removed the barriers that limited GPU data analytics. Software has matured too, with composable data systems and solid libraries.

Sirius treats the GPU as the primary engine and uses libraries such as libcudf for high-performance relational operators. It offers drop-in acceleration for existing databases through the standard Substrait query representation, replacing the CPU engine without changing the user-facing interface. Integrated with the DuckDB system, Sirius delivered several-fold better cost efficiency on standard analytical benchmarks. Integrated with the distributed Apache Doris engine, it delivered speedups larger still. The argument: CPU-first database architecture is a legacy choice, and the tooling now exists to invert it.
arxiv-2508-04801:
Trong-Thuan Nguyen and colleagues launched a 2025 grand challenge on automated analysis of ear, nose, and throat endoscopy images. Reading these scope images is hard: devices and operators vary, findings can be tiny and local, and small distinctions like left versus right or vocal fold state matter for care. Clinicians also need to retrieve similar past cases by image or by a short written description, a service few public benchmarks support.

Their ENTRep challenge pairs expert-labeled images, marked by body region and normal or abnormal status, with narratives in Vietnamese and English. Three tasks cover fine-grained labeling plus image and text retrieval, scored on hidden test data. Top team results are reported as a baseline.
arxiv-2508-05101:
Junjie Qi, Ming Lu, Jie Liu, and two colleagues show that leaking quantum coherence can create a one-way superconducting device, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The device conducts better in one direction than the other. This one-way behavior is the superconducting diode effect, usually studied in tidy, closed systems.

Their device is a SQUID, a loop with two Josephson junctions, threaded by an external magnetic flux. They couple one junction to a gapless reservoir of electrons, which drains phase coherence and makes the system non-Hermitian. Out of that openness emerges an effective distribution that drives the diode effect. The critical current then differs by direction, as a diode's should. Under alternating current bias, the famous Shapiro steps turn asymmetric too. The work suggests loss and decoherence, usually enemies, can be design ingredients for superconducting electronics.
arxiv-2508-12201:
H. O. Fatoyinbo and colleagues modeled bird flu spread between wild birds and dairy cattle in 2025. The H5N1 virus has lately turned up in cattle, raising fears at the meeting point of wildlife, farms, and the shared environment. Their math model tracks sick and well cattle, wild birds, and virus lingering in the environment, all at once.

Analysis finds when the disease dies out versus settles in, summed up in a threshold number for spread. Computer runs show extinction, persistence, and how each rate shifts the outcome. Cattle recovery, cattle-to-cattle spread, virus decay outdoors, and pickup from the environment mattered most. The ranking helps farms pick which controls to fund first.
arxiv-2508-12801:
Bowen Dong and colleagues propose Maximum Score Routing, a new way to route tokens to experts inside mixture-of-experts language models. Such models send each input token to a few experts. That scales capacity while keeping speed. Old routing sets a cap on experts for hardware-friendly work. But full experts drop tokens, and little-used experts waste work on padding.

To drop the cap instead breaks load balance and speed. MaxScore models routing as a minimum-cost maximum-flow problem. It also adds a SoftTopk operator. The team reports that it fixes core limits of past rerouting and transport forms. At the same compute cost, it gave lower training losses and higher test scores than both capped and uncapped bases. Details and code are public for all.
arxiv-2508-13001:
Divya Patel, Maryam Dehghanian, and Gary Ferland compare X-ray emission line patterns between two active galaxies to test a core idea about how such galaxies work. The unification model says the two Seyfert types differ only by viewing angle and blocking material, so their line ratios should match when both are obscured. One galaxy in the pair is a type one that was temporarily veiled by its own outflowing wind; the other is a classic type two. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they also run a standard plasma code to predict the veiled galaxy spectrum.

The code underpredicted the observed line ratios, which the authors blame on choices in the assumed incoming light shape. More telling, the two galaxies observed ratios differ from each other. The note concludes that extra unknown factors are at play beyond the simple unification picture.
arxiv-2508-16201:
Yicheng Ji and six colleagues speed up video language models with a speculative decoding framework called SpecVLM. Video models use dense token representations that make both prefilling and decoding expensive. Recent token reduction methods cut cost but lose information and accuracy.

The team found that a draft model's guesses are barely affected by heavy video token pruning. SpecVLM therefore prunes up to ninety percent of video tokens during speculation, in two stages guided by the verifier model's attention and spatial uniformity. The result is lossless acceleration: up to 2.68 times faster decoding on one large model and 2.11 times on another. Tests span four video understanding benchmarks.
arxiv-2508-16501:
Roman Zwicky derives a new model free double soft dilaton theorem, counting the space time dependence of the dilation commutator. The work also weighs gravity form factors as a probe of infrared conformality. It came out in twenty twenty-five.

The method restores positive mass for the pseudo Goldstone modes and pins a scaling bound on any single operator that gives the dilaton mass. In a second part, Zwicky asks how far QCD like gauge theories, in the chiral limit, fit this class. The quark pair operator meets the bound. Some results hold in a supersymmetric gauge theory, with an argued reach below its conformal window.
arxiv-2509-00001:
K. Mahesh Krishna, working alone, extends a core idea from sparse signal theory to measure spaces in a short 2025 note. Donoho and Elad set out the spark of a frame in 2003, a count tied to the smallest set of frame parts that depend on each other. From spark they derived an uncertainty principle and a sharp test for when a sparse answer to a hard problem is the sole one.

Krishna shows that spark makes sense for linear maps whose domain is a measure space, a set with a size rule. From that broad form he derives a new uncertainty principle. He also gives a condition that ensures sparse solutions exist for linear systems on such spaces. The note widens a classic tool to far broader settings.
arxiv-2509-00301:
Ninh Van Thu, working alone, gives an explicit account in 2025 of how key complex functions behave near the edge of a weakly pseudoconvex domain. Such a domain is a region in complex space whose edge meets a mild curve condition, held only in a loose sense. The study follows set sequences of points that tend toward a special edge point, called h-extendible.

Three linked objects are tracked along those sequences. The first is the Bergman kernel, a core function that encodes the domain's complex shape. The second is the Bergman metric, a way to measure distance built from the kernel. The third is the set of curvatures tied to that metric. Explicit boundary formulas for all three aid work on how complex domains behave at their edges.
arxiv-2509-00701:
Kun Qiu, with three co-authors, Ying Wang, Baoqian Li, and Wenjun Zhu, presents an unsupervised framework for cleaning encrypted traffic data. Classifying network flows into categories helps enterprise and carrier networks, but encryption defeats deep packet inspection, and machine learning methods need clean training data without useless flows.

Existing cleaning relies on manual inspection of every packet, which is costly and slow. Qiu and his co-authors automate the removal of irrelevant protocols, background activity, control messages, and long-lived sessions from encrypted mobile traffic, without labeled examples. On real-world datasets, their cleaning costs only about two to two and a half percent in classification accuracy compared with manual cleaning, making it an efficient preprocessing step.
arxiv-2509-00801:
Hyungbo Shim, with two co-authors, proposes parameter adaptation for multi-agent systems. The agents differ in their internal dynamics. Such systems are called heterogeneous. Unlike identical agents, they cannot reach perfect synchronization. Strong coupling can still induce approximate consensus among them. That shared behavior is governed by blended dynamics.

The team adds an adaptation law to align the agents' parameters. The law needs no direct exchange of parameters. It reuses the same coupling signal used for state synchronization. The process is thus plausible as a biological or social model. Under a persistent excitation condition, they prove convergence. The agents' dynamics converge to each other over time. The system becomes homogeneous in the limit, with exact consensus of states.
arxiv-2509-01001:
Zhi Zhao, with three co-authors, proposes a generalized promotion time cure model for cancer data. Single-cell tools reveal interplay between cancer cells and their surroundings. The data span survival, cell composition, and single-cell omics. No prior model joined all three scales at once. Their model aims to find cell-type-specific genes for prognosis.

The class is Bayesian in form, as the title states. It joins multiscale data to find cell-type-linked factors. It also aims to improve survival prediction for patients. Simulations cover both low- and high-dimensional settings. They show the models can identify such factors. Survival prediction improves as well in those tests. The framework links cell-level measures to patient outcomes in one model.
arxiv-2509-01301:
Tests of how well language models handle culture often shrink it to trivia questions with short answers. Juhyun Oh, with five co-authors, argues that this trivia-centered habit fails as models grow stronger and spread wider. Culture is not a static list of facts; it shapes even tasks that look neutral.

The authors call for intentionally cultural evaluation, a systematic check of the cultural assumptions built into every part of testing. They map what kinds of cultural questions arise, how they arise, and under what circumstances. They also stress researcher positionality, the way a test maker's own background shapes the test. Oh and the team close with directions for more inclusive, culturally aware language research beyond current benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-01401:
Recognizing emotion in spoken Arabic is hard because data and research for the language are scarce, and large models are costly to run. Ali Abouzeid, Bilal Elbouardi, Mohamed Maged, and Shady Shehata introduce ArabEmoNet, a lightweight model for that task. It reads Mel spectrograms, pictures of sound over time and pitch, with two-dimensional convolutions that keep fine emotional cues.

An attention-equipped bidirectional LSTM then reads those features in both directions to catch how emotion unfolds. With only about one million parameters, the model is many times smaller than large speech systems such as HuBERT base and Whisper, yet the authors report superior results. That small size suits phones and other limited devices. ArabEmoNet aims to bring strong speech emotion tools to a low-resource language in real-world settings.
arxiv-2509-01501: Jingjun Han, Jihao Liu, and Ziquan Zhuang prove the effective termination of minimal model programs of general type in dimension at most five. The minimal model program is a stepwise method in algebraic geometry for simplifying shapes. For dimension at most four, they also give explicit bounds, in terms of topological invariants and divisor volumes, on how many steps the program can take.
arxiv-2509-01601:
Sudden catastrophic shifts, from collapsing structures to failing ecosystems, often arrive without warning in quiet, low-noise systems. Tapas Bar, with four co-authors, studies early warning signals for such tipping points in athermal systems, systems without thermal jitter. Their models are a zero-temperature random field Ising model and thermally deposited cobalt films, both prone to avalanche failures.

As the system nears its tipping point, avalanche activity shows clear critical signs: slowing down, growing variance, and a lengthening spatial correlation range. Those hallmarks can serve as warnings of impending collapse. Crucially, raising disorder in the system made it less vulnerable to catastrophic failure, and in highly disordered regimes the warnings emerged well before the transition. Disorder, usually seen as a flaw, here buys both safety and time to act.
arxiv-2509-01701:
Kazi Hassan Shakib, Muhammad Asfand Hafeez, and Arslan Munir design AmphiKey, a key exchange protocol for smart power grids. Key exchange is how two devices agree on a secret code for safe messages. AmphiKey mixes newer quantum safe methods with classic ones so safety holds if either holds. It runs in two modes: one proves who sent a message, the other lets a sender plausibly deny it.

The signed mode pairs short lived keys with long term keys built to resist side channel leaks, where attackers learn from device behavior. The deniable mode guards privacy while still checking identity during setup. Tests span a strong server and a small low power board. Handshakes finish in well under a few thousandths of a second in most roles.
arxiv-2509-01901:
Saieed Akbari, Jonny Aloni, Arash Beikmohammadi, and Alexander Clow tighten bounds on splitting graphs into cycles and single edges. A long standing conjecture claims any graph splits into a number of such pieces that grows only with its point count. The covering version was proven decades ago with a near matching bound. Best known split bounds still carry a small extra factor.

For graphs where each point has at most four links, the team proves the clean bound conjectured. Claw free graphs, which lack a point tied to three separate others, split into few two-regular pieces and edges. They also improve the covering bound for any graph that holds a cycle. Only trees still need the older covering count.
arxiv-2509-02101:
Matic Fucka, Vitjan Zavrtanik, and Danijel Skocaj present SALAD, a semantics aware detector for logical anomalies in images. Surface detectors catch dents and scratches well but miss logical flaws like missing or misplaced parts. Top logical methods lean on pooled pretrained features or handcrafted descriptors that discard spatial and semantic detail. SALAD adds a composition branch that models how object parts are arranged.

A new extraction procedure builds composition maps without hand labels or category specific data. Modeling the distribution of those maps teaches the system semantic relationships among parts. On the standard logical anomaly benchmark, SALAD sets a strong new image level score. The gain shows composition modeling beats feature pooling for logical checks. Code is released for reuse.
arxiv-2509-02401:
Josefa Lia Stoisser and eight co-authors wrote a 2025 biomedical AI paper on agents that summarise complex multi-table data, such as combined omics datasets in cancer research. Language model agents often sound fluent while overstating what the data supports.

Their agent tracks two doubt signals. Retrieval uncertainty measures spread across repeated table choices, while summary uncertainty blends self-consistency with perplexity, a fluency-based score. Summary doubt feeds reinforcement learning training, and both signals filter outputs at run time and help build cleaner synthetic data. On multi-omics benchmarks, the count of claims that were both correct and useful roughly tripled per summary. Downstream survival prediction also improved sharply. The work treats uncertainty as a control signal for abstaining and reporting confidence.
arxiv-2509-02601:
Piotr Giedziun and nine co-authors present a 2025 computational pathology paper on telling normal mitotic figures from atypical ones in tissue images, the second track of the MIDOG 2025 challenge. Shape cues are subtle, and models must work across hospitals and scanners.

Their entry leans on H-optimus-0, a pathology foundation model chosen after cross-domain benchmarks and local tests. Cheap low-rank fine-tuning adapts it, while MixUp augmentation blends training images. Soft labels encode how strongly human experts agreed on each case. Hard negative mining, focal loss, metric learning, and domain adaptation all support robustness. The authors report reasonable preliminary performance, and they frame the work as evidence of both promise and difficulty for foundation models in this task.
arxiv-2509-02701:
Mathieu Gross, Md Riajul Haque, and Yann Mambrini wrote a 2025 cosmology paper. It computes the gravitational wave background expected from primordial black holes. The inflaton, the field that drove early cosmic expansion, adds its own waves. Signals from several sources overlap across frequencies.

For the first time, the authors combine three sources. They add waves from black hole decay. They add waves from the black holes' own density fluctuations. And they add inflaton waves from before and after inflation ends. The reheating era uses a power-law inflaton potential. A possible memory burden effect is folded in. That effect slows black hole evaporation as information builds up. It reshapes the spectrum. The full picture helps future searches read early-universe history.
arxiv-2509-02801:
Christopher Ewasiuk and Stefano Profumo wrote a 2025 particle physics paper asking how a huge hidden sector of light particles would betray itself through gravity alone. General relativity, read as an effective theory, predicts small quantum corrections to Newton's law from loops of matter fields.

With very many light species, those corrections can grow to levels that precision laboratory and astrophysical tests can see. The authors translate the predictions into the standard language of Yukawa-type deviations from the inverse-square law. Current fifth-force limits then bound how many hidden species can exist and how heavy they may be. Massless hidden states still allow enormous multiplicities, while finite masses face tighter limits. The framework complements cosmological probes, since lab tests constrain the spectrum regardless of cosmic history.
arxiv-2509-03001:
Elena Brylyakova and 4 co-authors searched old low-frequency radio data in 2025 for signals from five quiet binary systems. Each pair holds a visible low-mass star and an unseen companion whose mass fits a neutron star. Finding radio pulses would confirm what those hidden partners really are.

The archive came from a large phased array telescope near Pushchino in Russia. No steady or repeating emission showed up from any of the five systems. One single short burst did appear near one target, bright and brief. Its delay pattern, though, pointed to a distance that does not match that system. The authors weigh other explanations for the burst, leaving its source open.
arxiv-2509-03101:
Chris Blake and Ryan J. Turner examined in 2025 how galaxy motions add error to measurements of the universe's expansion rate. Standard sirens are cosmic events with known loudness, such as colliding neutron stars, whose distance can be read off directly. Pairing that distance with a host galaxy's redshift gives the Hubble constant, the current expansion rate.

Host galaxies also drift with their own peculiar velocities, which distort their redshifts. Reconstructing those motions from nearby matter leaves errors that are linked across galaxies by large flows. The authors show how to carry that full linked error into expansion estimates. In simulations of near-future sirens, ignoring the linkage could understate the error by about a factor of two. Nearby sources with precise distances suffer most.
arxiv-2509-03201:
Abdul Rahoof and 3 co-authors built CapsBeam in 2025, a capsule network beamformer for ultrasound imaging that runs on a programmable chip. Beamforming combines signals from many sensor elements into one image. Newer learning-based versions give cleaner pictures but are too heavy for small edge devices.

CapsBeam works on raw radio-frequency data from non-steered plane wave imaging, where the ultrasound pulse is sent out flat rather than aimed. In living tissue tests it reduced artifacts against the standard delay-and-sum method. In lab and simulated data it raised contrast and sharpened detail along both image directions. The team pruned the model with their multi-layer look-ahead method, cutting most parameters without hurting quality. A custom accelerator then delivered strong throughput on a commercial chip.
arxiv-2509-03601:
In a 2025 theoretical physics paper, Mara Lozano and two co-authors examine topological excitons in flat electronic bands, and on which light they can absorb. An exciton is a bound pair of an electron and a missing electron, called a hole. Topological excitons carry a swirling pattern, or vorticity, in momentum space, set by the band structure's topology.

Selection rules state which kinds of light can create or destroy such excitons. The authors derive them for three model systems, including Hamiltonians whose pseudo-spin textures wrap like skyrmions, plus flattened BHZ and Haldane models. With skyrmion-like textures, every exciton is bright, and the handedness of light it couples to is fixed by the swirl direction. In the BHZ case, bright excitons take circularly polarised light regardless of interaction range. The Haldane case couples to elliptically polarised light, with a phase diagram mapping how polarisation depends on model parameters.
arxiv-2509-04301:
Praveen Muralikrishnan and four co-authors explain how sugars keep proteins folded, using simplified computer models in a 2025 research paper. Vaccines and protein drugs need stabilizers, called excipients, and sugars are common choices. Four sugars enter the study: two glucose forms, fructose, trehalose, and sucrose counted among them. A coarse polymer stands in for the protein while free-energy bookkeeping separates the forces at play.

At low sugar levels, sugar-polymer contacts help folding, while solvent effects push the other way. At higher levels, entropy penalties, the cost of lost disorder, take control. Mixing two sugars added a stabilizing entropy effect favoring the folded state. Formulation designers gain a clearer recipe logic.
arxiv-2509-04401:
Andreas Raab, writing alone, develops classical Monte Carlo methods that mimic a flagship quantum computing task in a 2025 research paper. Random circuit sampling asks quantum machines to draw bit strings from the wild output patterns of random quantum circuits. Such sampling is often cited as evidence of quantum advantage. Raab derives exact probability formulas whose large-system limit matches the expected Porter-Thomas distribution, then builds importance sampling algorithms around them.

Systems from seventy qubits up to more than a million were simulated on an ordinary personal computer at minimal cost, without noise. On that basis, Raab argues the sampling task can be conveniently performed classically. The claim challenges how quantum advantage demonstrations should be judged.
arxiv-2509-04501:
Rohit Patel, writing alone, offers a from-scratch guide to the reinforcement learning methods used to train language models in a 2025 exposition paper. Instruction tuning pipelines stack algorithms with confusing names: supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling, REINFORCE, TRPO, PPO, GRPO, and DPO. Explanations often assume background knowledge or gloss over details. Patel develops each method step by step in simplified notation aimed squarely at language models, cutting detours into the wider reinforcement learning literature.

A literature review then surveys newer techniques beyond the core seven. The closing section presents GRAPE, a proposed generalization of relative advantage policy evolution, as fresh research directions. Students and engineers gain one self-contained map of the post-training toolbox.
arxiv-2509-05801:
Can a forecasting model be steered to imagine a crash it never saw in the current data? Debdeep Sanyal and four co-authors take up that question in a 2025 paper on time series foundation models. These large models predict routine patterns well, but rare, high-stakes events are exactly what users most need to test.

Their method, activation transplantation, edits the model's hidden states mid-prediction, imposing the statistical shape of one event, such as a past crash, onto a calm stretch of data. Forecasts respond in kind: crash features push predictions down, while calm features restore stability. The team also finds that models grade severity, with stronger shocks tied to larger internal vectors. Results held on two different model designs, supporting direct what-if stress tests.
arxiv-2509-05901:
An open-source solver for the one-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation is presented in a 2025 paper led by Sandy H. S. Herho with four co-authors. That equation governs waves in fiber optics, ultracold atomic gases, and ocean swells. The authors prize clear, teachable code over raw speed, aiming at students and researchers learning nonlinear wave behavior.

The solver pairs a Fourier spectral treatment of space with an adaptive eighth-order time stepper, conserving mass to machine precision on smooth solutions. Four standard tests check it: a lone soliton, two solitons colliding elastically, a breather, and instability growing from noise. Entropy measures and phase-space pictures then gauge how complex each solution becomes. Full code, documentation, and example setups are released for reproducible experiments.
arxiv-2509-06201:
A robot hand that keeps adjusting as it closes is the controller Grasp-MPC, presented in a 2025 paper led by Jun Yamada with five co-authors.
