Open-loop grasping fails in clutter when predictions err or objects shift; earlier closed-loop systems handled only simple scenes. Grasp-MPC plans continuously with model predictive control, guided by a learned value function over visual input.

That value function trains on two million synthetic grasp trajectories, successes and failures alike. Combined with collision-avoidance and smoothness costs, it steers six-degree-of-freedom grasps of novel objects in clutter. On the FetchBench suite and in real-world trials, success rises by up to about a third over open-loop, diffusion, transformer, and offline reinforcement baselines, including under noisy conditions.
arxiv-2509-06401:
Commonsense in a language model is strongest in English and thins in smaller languages, measure Ivan Martínez-Murillo and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. Their benchmark, MULTICOM, extends an existing dataset to English, Spanish, Dutch, and Valencian. The task: generate a commonsensical sentence containing a given triplet of words.

A range of open models, from LLaMA and Qwen to regional entries like Salamandra, are scored by automatic metrics, model judges, and human annotators. English wins consistently, less-resourced languages lag significantly, and adding context gives mixed help that tends to favor the underrepresented languages. The dataset is released publicly, and the authors frame the gap as a standing limitation of multilingual generation.
arxiv-2509-06501:
Training web agents that can hunt through many pages for one answer is the subject of a 2025 artificial intelligence paper led by Junteng Liu, with fourteen co-authors. Language models increasingly act as agents that browse the web, but hard, long searches expose weak spots. Good training examples for such searches are scarce.

The authors build data by letting a model explore and then evolving questions from long to short forms, creating query-answer pairs that demand many steps. Training on this data, first with supervised learning and then reinforcement learning, yields an eight-billion-parameter agent. It handles very long contexts and up to a hundred tool calls in one task. On several search benchmarks it beats much larger rivals, and it also generalizes well to a broad knowledge test.
arxiv-2509-06701:
Hidden sub-agents inside large neural networks are given a mathematical theory by Su Hyeong Lee and two co-authors in a 2025 paper on artificial intelligence foundations. The authors model an agent as a distribution over outcomes, scored by a log-score utility that rewards accurate beliefs. Combining agents means pooling their distributions.

Weighted logarithmic pooling, they prove, can strictly improve every member's welfare, something linear pooling cannot do, and binary outcome spaces rule it out too; three or more outcomes are needed. The framework supports recursive structure through cloning invariance, continuity, and openness. As an application to language models, they formalize a persona effect: prompting a benevolent character can summon an antagonistic counterpart. A strategy that first elicits then suppresses the counterpart cuts misalignment more than reinforcing the good persona alone. The theory aims to explain how sub-agents merge into coherent larger agents.
arxiv-2509-07101:
In a 2025 paper, Nathaniel Craig and 2 co-authors build a geometric picture of theories that mix scalar particles, like the Higgs, with fermions, like electrons and quarks. Geometry here means treating the set of possible field values as a curved space. They treat that space as a vector bundle supermanifold, a layered space that holds both kinds of fields at once.

On that space they set up Fermi normal coordinates, a tidy local frame that makes scattering results easier to read. The frame also shows where the field space fails to be smooth. Applied to the Higgs sector of the Standard Model, the work traces what happens when a key symmetry breaks. The results give a cleaner way to read Higgs behavior and possible new physics in real data.
arxiv-2509-07401:
When boson stars collide, the merger can stir up swirling vortices, much like eddies in water. Yuanyuan Zeng, Bokai Zhang, and Jiajun Chen simulate those mergers in a 2025 research paper. Boson stars are hypothetical clumps of dark matter particles. The team solves the Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson equations, which govern such quantum fluids, and varies the self-interaction strength between particles.

Vortices form in every merger they ran. Their size depends strongly on the interaction strength. With repulsive interactions, stronger coupling makes the vortex region expand. With attractive interactions, stronger coupling makes it shrink. The team confirms the pattern through velocity correlations, energy spectra, and vorticity maps. The result connects a basic particle property to a visible feature of dark matter collisions, which future observations might one day test.
arxiv-2509-07601:
Tanmay Patil and 1 co-author work out the Carrollian limits of general relativity in a 2025 paper. The Carrollian limit sends the speed of light to zero. That is the reverse of the familiar slow-motion limit. It gives the geometry for null surfaces, such as black hole horizons and null infinity. Electromagnetism is known to split into electric and magnetic slow-motion limits. The authors ask whether gravity splits in the same way.

They use a 1+3 covariant split of linearized gravity on an expanding universe background. They track how wave perturbations change under Carrollian boosts. The full linearized Einstein equations are not Carrollian-invariant. The theory instead divides into two consistent frameworks. The electric limit has frozen dynamics, ruled by tidal forces. The magnetic limit stays dynamical, governed by the magnetic part of the Weyl tensor. The split mirrors the electromagnetic case in a neat way.
arxiv-2509-07801:
Decheng Duan and 3 co-authors release SciNLP in 2025, a benchmark for extracting entities and relations from full scientific papers in natural language processing research. Structured extraction captures a field's core concepts and emerging trends, but most datasets annotate only abstracts or single sections, because full-text annotation is costly and domains are complex. SciNLP instead covers complete papers end to end.

The dataset holds 60 manually annotated full-text NLP publications, with 6,429 entities and 1,649 relations, described as the first full-text resource of its kind for the domain. The authors benchmark leading supervised models on it and compare performance across papers of different lengths. Cross-comparisons with existing datasets show SciNLP improves performance on certain measures. Full-text benchmarks push extraction systems toward the messy reality of real literature.
arxiv-2509-08001:
When one banker quits, nearby colleagues often follow, and that clustering may be predictable. Abdulla AlKetbi and 3 co-authors study turnover contagion in Hong Kong finance in a 2025 research paper. They built temporal networks from the Securities and Futures Commission public register. The data cover well over one hundred thousand professionals and nearly five thousand firms across seventeen years.

Their graph-based method spreads features across the network to capture peer influence and firm stability. A clear contagion effect appeared: professionals grew much more likely to leave once many peers had recently departed. Adding network signals to machine learning models improved turnover prediction substantially over baselines. The authors suggest uses in regulatory monitoring, talent management, and systemic risk assessment. Workforce moves, it seems, ripple like information through a market.
arxiv-2509-08501:
Thomas Banks and Anish Suresh check an approximation to a hard set of equations on a tiny lattice in a 2025 paper. The equations are the Schwinger-Dyson equations for an electron fluid. They govern how the fluid's parts correlate. In full, they form an endless chain. A large-N limit cuts the chain down to equations for one- and two-point values.

That cut needs a test. Monte Carlo runs on two-by-two and three-by-three lattices supply the test values. The derived equations match those values at large N, to the stated precision. Small, exact checks like these are how bold approximation schemes earn trust. Only then do they graduate to real systems that no one can solve head-on.
arxiv-2509-08701:
Yuanze Li and 8 co-authors report a direct test of charge buildup in a quantum anomalous Hall system in a 2025 paper. In such a system, Hall conductance takes a fixed exact value from surface states. Past tests checked conductance, not the charge on the surface itself.

A capacitor based method senses charge that grows in step with shifts in the magnetic field. Tests on Corbino and disk devices track loss through conductance and frequency. At very low loss, the full exact charge is seen at last. A model fit gives the charge density the theory predicts. The method may aid the search for a related topological effect.
arxiv-2509-08901:
Hannah Wakeling and 2 co-authors present ORLCA, a concept for an open source life cycle assessment repository, in a 2025 paper. Life cycle assessment counts the full environmental impact of a product or service. Such accounting is a first step toward reducing those impacts.

Research experiments and infrastructure increasingly need this accounting across planning, running, and end of life. ORLCA is designed to support that work in an open repository. It aims to follow FAIR principles: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. The paper is a concept proposal, not a finished system. It lays out a base for shared, open assessment in research.
arxiv-2509-09001:
Jingwen Liu and 4 co-authors present a fast attention method called ANNA in a 2025 paper. Attention is the core step in transformers, the models behind much of AI. Standard attention cost grows as the square of input length, which caps model size.

ANNA uses near neighbor search to cut that cost below square growth. Proofs show ANNA models keep the power to mimic parallel algorithms, a key trait of standard attention. They solve match and multi hop tasks at near best depth. Fixed depth ANNA models can also mimic fixed depth low rank models. That gives one frame for judging many fast attention variants.
arxiv-2509-09401: Yi Huang and 1 co-author prove a result in 2025 about volumes assigned to moduli spaces of open strings. For every crowned hyperbolic surface, they show the Mirzakhani volume introduced by Chekhov can be written as a sum involving polylogarithms. The terms are Gaussian rational multiples, evaluated at plus or minus one and at plus or minus the square root of minus one.
arxiv-2509-09501:
Coloring a manga page automatically requires knowing which inked region on one page is the same coat, face, or room on the next. Yingxuan Li and 3 co-authors define that matching task in a 2025 research paper. Manga line art holds only sparse black strokes, none of the shading and color cues natural images offer. No annotations exist to learn from directly.

Their transformer framework trains on region correspondences generated automatically at large scale. It learns to drop noisy matches and reinforce structural links that agree. At use time, each drawing is segmented, then regions are matched through edge-aware clustering. Hand-annotated benchmarks confirm strong patch accuracy and region matching well above chance. The task also feeds in-between frame generation for animation. Teaching machines the identity of a line region is a quiet prerequisite for automating the labor-intensive corners of manga and anime production.
arxiv-2509-09601:
Stéphane Delorme and 3 co-authors describe a classroom pipeline in 2025 that teaches big data skills by asking whether Wednesday arXiv papers earn more citations. Handling huge real data sets is now routine in physics and astronomy, yet undergraduates rarely get to practise the full craft. Their farm-to-table workflow gathers, cleans, and plots records for some eight hundred thousand entries shared by arXiv and the INSPIRE-HEP database.

Everything runs with open Python tools common in scientific computing courses, and a public version built by two undergraduate students works on ordinary laptops. The authors also sketch harder uses for advanced classes, including live monitoring of data-taking and steps toward commercial work. The weekday question gives students a playful hook into serious method.
arxiv-2509-09801:
Brennen Hill's 2025 paper stacks two cheap tuning methods for language models and finds the combination stronger than either alone. Adapting a big model to a specialised reasoning task is usually limited by computing budget. Parameter-efficient methods work in two different places: some adjust the model's weights, others nudge its internal activations. Hill's HEFT strategy applies them in a coarse-to-fine order, broad first, surgical second.

A low-rank weight update lays the foundation, then representation tuning refines the activations on top. Fine-tuned for just three passes over the BoolQ reading task, a Llama-2 model edged past versions trained twenty passes with either method alone. The synergy suggests adaptation budgets can shrink sharply when the two spaces are tuned together rather than in isolation.
arxiv-2509-09901:
N. L. Samuelson and 7 co-authors report measurements from a graphene quantum Hall interferometer in this 2025 physics paper. In such a device, interference patterns carry information about particles trapped inside the loop and how they couple to the edge current. Earlier work assumed those particles enter and leave quickly, so the system stayed near balance during each measurement.

Working at two filling factors, the team watched the interference phase jump as single quasiparticles entered the bulk. Some jumps come from particles joining a shared puddle that couples to the whole edge, others from particles caught at a defect near one part of the edge. At times the settling time stretched to several minutes, far slower than the standard picture assumes.
arxiv-2509-10101:
T. J. Hicken and 15 co-authors pin down the hidden defects inside a candidate quantum material in this 2025 paper. The compound Pr2Zr2O7 is a possible quantum spin ice, a state prized for quantum technology. Disorder inside the crystal is thought to boost its quantum behavior, but nobody knew exactly which defect does the work.

Using neutron and X-ray scattering, backed by density functional theory, the team found the main defect. Praseodymium ions sit on zirconium sites. Oxygen vacancies balance the charge, and a nearby oxygen is pushed out of place. That structure explains the single-ion magnetism seen in tests and the extra features in crystal field spectra. It also broadens the magnetic scattering pattern in a way once blamed on quantum effects alone.
arxiv-2509-10601:
Claims of twin supermassive black holes hiding in galactic centers take a hit from Kareem El-Badry, David W. Hogg, and Hans-Walter Rix in this 2025 astronomy paper. A recent catalog named one hundred eighty-one candidate binaries in Gaia data, based on apparently steady, wave-like brightness changes over roughly a thousand days, the expected signature of two orbiting giants.

The authors extend the light curves with the Zwicky Transient Facility and the Catalina survey. In every one of the one hundred sixteen cases with added data, the supposed period failed to predict what came next; the brightness wandered stochastically instead. Red noise, the natural restless flicker of these galaxies, had manufactured the fake signals. Truly sinusoidal variation, they conclude, appears in at most a few per million active galaxies, which raises hard questions for binary models.
arxiv-2509-10801:
Ken Nagai links odd zeta values to trigonometric kernels in this solo-authored 2025 short note. The values of the zeta function at odd integers have resisted closed forms for centuries. Representations therefore matter. Nagai develops selector kernels. These trigonometric devices pick out the wanted terms. He pairs them with dual hyperbolic counterparts.

A Fourier-Poisson duality stands in the foreground. The work uses finite-part integrals, in the style Hadamard and Galapon gave them. Two classical workhorses emerge as dual faces of one construction. They are the Euler-Maclaurin and Poisson summation formulas. The kernel approach extends earlier integral representations of odd zeta values, of Cvijović-Klinowski type. As a note, its contribution is a unifying lens. Several scattered formulas for these stubborn constants become dialects of one language.
arxiv-2509-11201:
Yihang She and three co-authors tackle a data bottleneck in forest science in this 2025 computer vision paper. Splitting laser scans of forests into individual trees is essential for tracking carbon and ecosystem health, but real annotated scans are too few to train reliable systems.

The team built a pipeline that fakes the data instead, combining game-engine graphics with a physics-based simulation of laser scanning to produce a large, diverse, labeled three-dimensional forest dataset. A state-of-the-art segmentation model pre-trained on the synthetic forest and then fine-tuned on a single small real plot matched models trained on the full real dataset. The authors identify physics, diversity, and scale as the ingredients that make synthetic pre-training work.
arxiv-2509-11301:
Matthias Wüest and four co-authors present UnLoc in this 2025 computer vision paper. It finds where a camera is inside a building. Only a floorplan is used. Floorplans are easy to get. They stay valid for years. Furniture changes do not matter.

Earlier floorplan methods treated depth predictions as certain. They often needed a custom depth network per building. UnLoc models each depth estimate as a probability distribution. The uncertainty flows into the position estimate. General pre-trained depth models replace per-site training. Large synthetic and real datasets were used for evaluation. UnLoc beat prior methods. The biggest gains came on the LaMAR benchmark. Recall rose several-fold on long and short sequences there.
arxiv-2509-11501:
Kartik Ganesh estimates what Hurricane Harvey did to construction labor markets in Texas, in a 2025 economics paper. Harvey struck in 2017, and rebuilding likely raised demand for construction workers in hit counties for years after.

Using quarterly job and wage data from 2016 to 2019, Ganesh compares dozens of federally named disaster counties with unhit southern control counties. His difference-in-differences event study tracks outcomes quarter by quarter. Mean wages in treated counties rose notably within two quarters and stayed high for two years. Job gains came more slowly, turning significant only after six quarters, in line with slow-starting rebuild work. The findings imply disasters create lasting labor demand shocks, with lessons for recovery planning.
arxiv-2509-11701:
Bo-hyun Kwon, Sungmo Kang, and Jung Hoon Lee answer a standing question about three-manifolds. This 2025 topology paper treats Heegaard splittings. A splitting cuts a three-manifold into two handlebodies along a surface. The rectangle condition of Casson and Gordon tests for strong irreducibility. The test is sufficient, but whether it catches every case was unknown.

The authors construct a counterexample. Their genus two splitting is strongly irreducible. It fails the rectangle condition. The example comes from a double branched cover. The base is a three-bridge decomposition of a knot in the three-sphere. That decomposition has the same pairing of traits. The rectangle condition does not detect strong irreducibility. A weaker version that might is the next goal.
arxiv-2509-11901:
Some language features can use a captured continuation at most once. They are called one-shot control operators. Kentaro Kobayashi and one co-author rank their power with care in 2025. Exceptions, effect handlers, and coroutines all package effects neatly. Yet the one-shot family had mostly escaped formal comparison.

The yardstick is Felleisen's macro-expressiveness. The authors confirm a piece of folklore. One-shot effect handlers can be macro-expressed by asymmetric coroutines. One-shot delimited control can be too. The reverse fails in both cases. On the way, they show why an older informal proof of that claim breaks down. They repair it into a valid macro-translation. Language designers get a firm map of what these tools can and cannot mimic.
arxiv-2509-12501:
Yao He and 3 co-authors present a framework for creating artist-style three-dimensional meshes from raw observations in a 2025 paper. Artist-created meshes are valued in commercial graphics because they work well with animation and texturing tools and render efficiently. Sensors such as LiDAR or phone depth cameras, however, produce noisy or incomplete point clouds.

Existing methods often assume clean, complete inputs or use complex multi-stage pipelines. The new method refines the input point cloud and directly produces a high-quality mesh in one end-to-end process. Its core idea reformulates three-dimensional refinement as a two-dimensional inpainting task, filling gaps in an image-like form, which lets powerful generative models be used. Preliminary ShapeNet results show promise for clean, complete meshes.
arxiv-2509-13001:
Lukas Wegmeth, Tobias Vente and two co-authors measure in 2025 the carbon cost of shop hint research. Hint systems shape much online choice. Their field has paid scant heed to energy and carbon so far.

They rebuilt pipelines from two RecSys years and metered real energy use. Deep learning works gave off about forty-two times the carbon of older classic works. One deep paper gave off near three metric tons in carbon terms. That tops a long flight for one person. Guides for leaner work close the study. The plea is to weigh gains against planet cost.
arxiv-2509-13101:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports in 2025 a clear bump near a set mass in paired charmonium spectra at the LHC. Proton hits at high energy and large data volume form the base. Two decay paths to muons, with or without pions, are studied.

Both paths show excess at the same place with joint strength near nine standard steps. No clear signal sits at a higher checked mass, and a cap on its share is set. A joint fit with the twin-pair channel gives a width ratio near one. The bump adds a firm exotic candidate for study.
arxiv-2509-13201:
Thanh Son Phung and Douglas Thain pool spare GPUs in 2025 for throughput-first language model jobs. Demand outstrips cluster supply, and static holds force queues or costly buys. Not all jobs need low delay, so spare capacity can serve them if context moves well.

Shared context reuse is the core fix. Policies let work hop across spare nodes without loss. A test job cut its run time by near all versus static holds. The gain shows spare pools can rival owned clusters for batch jobs. Context care, not raw cards, is the bottleneck named.
arxiv-2509-13401:
Temple He, Prahar Mitra, and Kathryn M. Zurek construct a density matrix for the vacuum in flat-space gravity in a 2025 paper. Their setting is a large spherically symmetric causal diamond, a region of spacetime defined by light signals, in four-dimensional asymptotically flat gravity. The density matrix encodes the quantum state as seen within that region.

The construction uses the soft effective action, which characterizes low-energy gravitational degrees of freedom arising in the long-distance limit. It consists of a soft graviton mode and a Goldstone mode from spontaneously broken supertranslation symmetry. Integrating out the soft graviton yields an effective action for the Goldstone mode alone, from which the density matrix and modular Hamiltonian are extracted. As a corollary, they explicitly compute the mean and variance of that Hamiltonian.
arxiv-2509-13601:
Lorenzo Martinelli and eight co-authors test whether stellar rotation explains odd star cluster diagrams in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Clusters of intermediate age show stretched main-sequence turn-offs and red clumps, features once blamed on mixed ages and now linked to stars spinning at different rates, which mixes their interiors.

The team built synthetic stellar populations from two model grids that differ only in how strongly rotation mixes chemicals, then fit the color-magnitude diagrams of the clusters NGC 419 and NGC 1817. Weak mixing fit both clusters best and matched seismic masses for red clump stars. Strong mixing made later stars too bright, so rotational mixing in intermediate-mass stars must stay modest, and spinning disc effects may explain remaining mismatches.
arxiv-2509-13901:
Saptarshi Ghosh and three co-authors benchmark GitOps tools for intent-based networking in a 2025 paper. GitOps manages infrastructure by declaring the desired state in version control and letting software reconcile reality with it, continuously. Whether the popular operators stay fast and light when network intents pile up had not been measured carefully.

The team ran controlled single-intent and multi-intent experiments on Argo CD, Flux CD, and ConfigSync, recording latency and resource use for each. Clear trade-offs emerged between determinism, efficiency, and responsiveness. They then wired the tools into a realistic orchestration pipeline driven by Nephio, an intent-based orchestrator, and measured end-to-end deployment overhead. Their results give practitioners concrete guidance for choosing and tuning tools in autonomous network systems.
arxiv-2509-14301:
Xin-Li Sheng, Francesco Becattini and Daniele Roselli improve a formula in 2025 for spin in particles emitted by a hot relativistic fluid. The fluid is at local thermal balance as it breaks apart, a stage called decoupling. Simulations of nuclear collisions use the earlier formula widely.

A new expansion method works for decoupling surfaces of any shape. It recovers the known term tied to thermal vorticity, which is local rotation in the fluid. It also upgrades the spin shear term so it captures surface geometry properly. Extra terms appear whose physical meaning still needs assessment. One gain is principled: the method naturally drops gradients along the surface normal, justifying an isothermal rule that was previously imposed by hand.
arxiv-2509-14401:
Ahad Yaqoob and Syed M. Abdullah test in 2025 whether a memory based neural network can forecast share prices on the Pakistan Stock Exchange. Deep learning for emerging market stocks is still little studied. Such markets mix steady blue chips with jumpy, thinly traded names.

Their long short term memory network predicts closing prices for ten major stocks across sectors. Inputs are past price and volume data plus many engineered technical indicators. Training covers several years of records. Forecasts were strong for stable, liquid sectors such as power, cement and fertiliser. Volatile or shock sensitive stocks, such as those tied to world oil prices, proved far harder. The split shows model skill depends on market character, not just model size.
arxiv-2509-14601:
Mushtari Sadia, Amrita Roy Chowdhury and Ang Chen argue in 2025 for computing directly on unstructured data: text, images, audio and video that fill most of the world information. Traditional data systems compute well only on structured tables. Unstructured riches stay hard to query and transform.

Their proposed paradigm runs in three stages. Latent structure is first extracted from raw media. Structured processing tools then transform that structure. Results are finally projected back into unstructured form for people and AI to consume. The two way pipeline aims to keep human friendly richness while gaining analytic power. Position papers matter when they name an architecture: this one gives system builders a concrete loop to implement and test.
arxiv-2509-14701:
V. V. Flambaum, writing alone in 2025, shows how very weak parity effects can grow large during phase transitions, in dense matter and in the early universe. Weak forces split left and right handed chiral systems by tiny energy gaps. On their own, those gaps are too small to use.

In a phase transition, a seed of the new phase grows past a critical size, then fills the whole system. The boost scales with the critical count of atoms in that seed, Flambaum argues. Gauging the share of left against right chiral forms made could thus reveal that critical count. Tests proposed form set spin chiral forms in crossed electric and magnetic fields during a transition. A tiny split becomes a count a lab can read.
arxiv-2509-14901:
An Yan, Leilei Cao, and four co-authors present their second-place technical report for the LSVOS 2025 video object segmentation track, written in 2025. Video object segmentation means outlining a chosen object in every frame of a video. The task is hard when targets are small, look alike, get hidden, or move fast.

Their solution builds on the SAM2 framework and adds a pseudo-labeling strategy. A trained checkpoint generates labels for unlabeled test videos, and those labels join the training data for another round. At inference, two models run in parallel: one favors stability over time, the other robustness at the concept level. A cascaded decision step merges their outputs frame by frame. The combined system scored strongly on the MOSE test benchmark.
arxiv-2509-15001:
Théo Charlot and five co-authors introduce BabyHuBERT, a speech model trained on recordings of children's everyday environments, in a 2025 paper. Daylong child-centered recordings are vital for studying early language development. Models trained on clean adult speech perform badly on them, because children's voices, homes, and languages differ so much from studio data.

BabyHuBERT learns from thirteen thousand hours of multilingual recordings spanning more than forty languages. The target task is voice type classification: labeling who speaks when, among the key child, other children, and male and female adults. Scores across six corpora beat both a model trained on English daylong recordings and a standard clean-speech model. Gains were largest for underrepresented language communities such as Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands. Code and models are shared openly.
arxiv-2509-15201:
Aabhas Gulati, Ion Nechita, and Sang-Jun Park build fresh ladders for testing quantum maps in a 2025 paper. Positive maps are core tools for spotting entanglement. Copositive matrices anchor one classic family of such tests. The authors define a convex cone of pairwise copositive matrices and study it in a systematic way.

That cone is dual to a cone of pairwise fully positive matrices. It also fully marks which covariant maps are positive. A lifting step moves plain copositive matrices into the new cone, which links the two theories. A twin cone handles maps that split into parts. As a use case, a family of maps set by a graph and a real dial gets exact cut points for being positive or splittable, stated through graph values.
arxiv-2509-15401:
Jun Ma, Vadim Marmer, and Zhengfei Yu study how a treatment affects each person, not just the average. In their model, the treatment and a tool that nudges it are both yes or no choices. Effects can differ from person to person in ways that simple models miss. Past work looked at the shape of these effects through density curves, which can be rough.

The trio build methods that use the full spread curve of effects instead. That curve can answer how many people gain, where the middle lies, and how wide the spread is. They prove their estimates settle into a known pattern and build resampling tests on that base. Sets of bands from their method let users judge the whole spread at once.
arxiv-2509-15701:
Ke Wang leads a team that grades pronunciation with large models that take sound and text. Such grading aids language learning apps. It must score at the level of sounds, words, and full sentences, across several traits. Whether big multimodal models can do this fine work was unclear.

They tune such a model on a public data set plus a private one. Tuning beats no tuning by far and rivals public and commercial systems on single level tasks. Word and sentence level scores are strong. Sound level grading stays hard. Two score types split in an odd way, and the team argue the rank based one better shows true order. Future work targets finer modeling.
arxiv-2509-15901:
Frederic Kirstein leads a team that makes meeting summaries more factual and more personal. Language model summaries often invent facts, drop key points, or add fluff. Their pipeline, FRAME, treats the summary as built from graded facts. It pulls salient facts, scores them, groups them by theme, and grows an outline into a full summary.

A second part, SCOPE, personalizes the result. The model answers nine questions out loud before picking content, building a trace of its reasoning. A new grading frame checks whether a summary fits its target reader, with no reference text needed. It flags errors with high accuracy against human marks. On two test sets, the pipeline cuts invention and omission sharply.
arxiv-2509-16001:
How a nucleus stretches in an electric field tells physicists about the forces inside it. Francesco Marino, Miriam El Batchy, and Sonia Bacca compute this trait for oxygen-22, a form of oxygen rich in neutrons. They use a coupled-cluster method joined with a transform tool, and they test two sets of nuclear forces.

One force set counts pairs of particles, while the other also counts groups of three. The team compares their results with measured data from past experiments. They find good agreement in the low energy range. That match supports the use of these force models for other neutron-rich nuclei.
arxiv-2509-16101:
Grouping data that comes in several views, such as text plus images, is harder when the data stays split across many owners. Kristina P. Sinaga builds math tools for this task in shared learning setups where raw data never leaves its home. Her tools swap plain distance measures for heat-based ones and split large data arrays into compact parts.

Four new methods come out of this work, each tuned for privacy, low message cost, or personal fit. Proofs cover how the methods settle, how much they leak, and how much work they take. The aim is sound grouping that respects the split and private nature of modern data.
arxiv-2509-16301:
Sorting cancers into subtypes from several kinds of molecular data at once is hard, since the data types differ and tangle in complex ways. Tiantian Yang and Zhiqian Chen build a graph network that learns directed, weighted links for each data type from the data itself, guided by tree methods. A tensor fusion step then blends single, paired, and triple interactions at low cost.

On three real cancer data sets, the model beat leading rivals across many measures. It also scores which data types and features matter most, which gives biologists usable clues. Clear direction and weight in the graphs aid that reading.
arxiv-2509-16401:
Solar storms can spray energetic particles across a wide span of the inner solar system, and which places get hit depends on fine details. Matthew A. Young and Bala Poduval run a particle transport model with a simple shock in a smooth solar wind, then vary one setting at a time across seven runs. Each run's particle flow over time and energy is compared with a baseline.

All runs show broad spread around the Sun, yet some settings leave far-side watchers with little or no flux. Traits tied to diffusion and shock shape drive the gaps. The mapping helps read real storm patterns and the wind behind them.
arxiv-2509-16601:
Mikołaj J. Gawkowski, Mingjia Li, Benjamin X. Shi, and Venkat Kapil test a shortcut for atom-level models in a 2025 chemistry paper. Learned potentials can predict how atoms push and pull. Training them on small clusters is cheap and can use very exact methods. The open question is whether such training holds for bulk matter.

The team check cluster-trained models against warm, moving ensembles. Some models pass, while others fail in quiet ways. Training without force data proves risky. The authors urge care in checking models before real use. Their guidance could save labs from trusting a model that only looked good on clusters.
arxiv-2509-16701:
Shunyu Liu, Guangdong Bai, Mark Utting, and Guowei Yang improve auto bug fixing in a 2025 software paper. Large language models can now patch code on their own. Yet they often lack facts about the project at hand. The team fetch relevant code from the same project and feed it to the model before it writes a patch.

Their system is called RelRepair. On one benchmark of small Java bugs, fix rates rose by a clear margin. Nearly half of the bugs were fixed in that test. The gains show that project context matters as much as model size. Better patches could cut the time coders spend on dull fixes.
arxiv-2509-16901:
Mandip Goswami, working alone, sets a shared baseline for electric vehicle sound in a 2025 paper. How a car sounds shapes how good it feels. Electric cars lack engine noise, so tones like inverter whine stand out. Goswami links standard psychoacoustic measures with light learning baselines in an open package.

Measures cover loudness, tonality, roughness, and related traits. Scripts rebuild every figure and table in set environments. Code and small audio samples are released under open terms. Teachers and engineers can reuse the package to compare designs fairly. A shared yardstick could raise sound quality across the young EV field.
arxiv-2509-17001:
Irfan Ullah, working alone, studies how far holomorphic functions extend from special orbits in a 2025 math paper. The orbits, named for Matsuki, sit inside complex Grassmannians where two group actions meet. Each orbit carries a natural CR structure. Its envelope of holomorphy is the largest region to which all such functions extend.

Ullah gives a geometric proof built on a fiber bundle view of the orbits. Compact fibers in that view constrain how far extension can go. A worked example inside a concrete Grassmannian shows the method. The results link complex geometry with representation theory, two fields that often meet on such orbits.
arxiv-2509-17601:
Tom Dunstan leads a large team of co-authors on a 2025 arXiv paper about machine learning weather forecasts. Their model, FastNet, is a graph neural network that predicts weather worldwide at a fraction of the cost of classic physics-based systems. The catch is physical consistency: learned forecasts can blur fine detail or draw patterns no real atmosphere would make.

The team redesigns the training loss in three ways. A spectral loss punishes errors in pattern scale, which fights blurring. Gradient terms in the loss suppress artifacts that break smooth flow. A new wind encoding splits speed from direction to catch extreme winds better. Alone, the first two changes slightly hurt the standard error score. Trained together, they gave forecasts that score well and look far more physical, a trade the authors argue forecasters should want.
arxiv-2509-17701:
Mariam Mahran and Katharina Simbeck test language models on math problems in three languages. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds an automated pipeline that generates, solves, and grades school math. The problems follow the German K-10 curriculum, and the team produced hundreds of exercises in English, German, and Arabic versions.

Three commercial models wrote step-by-step solutions in each language. A separate panel of model judges, held out from the solvers, graded the work with a comparative framework. A steady gap appeared: English solutions scored highest, and Arabic often ranked lowest. The same model, the same problems, and the same math still yielded unequal teaching quality by language. The authors frame the result as persistent linguistic bias. They argue that equitable multilingual systems for education need direct measurement of this kind, not assumptions.
arxiv-2509-18001:
Haocheng Luo and 3 co-authors explain why small batches help a training trick that seeks flat minima. Their 2025 paper works on sharpness-aware training, where each step probes how sharp the loss peak is. A known quirk is that smaller probe batches steadily improve the result, a fact that lacked a firm cause.

Noise in the step process holds the key, the team shows. Their maths frame shows that noise acts like an added flatness push, which grows as the batch shrinks. A new weighted variant copies that gain while staying fit for parallel work. Tests back both the theory and the new method.
arxiv-2509-18101:
Guanzhong Pan and 3 co-authors weigh when a firm should run its own language model, not rent one. Their 2025 paper sets out a cost-benefit frame for that choice. Cloud tools from big firms are easy to start and scale, but raise privacy, lock-in, and long-run cost points.

The frame counts gear needs, run costs, and speed scores for top open models. Those sums are set against cloud fees for like use. The result is a break-even line based on how much a firm uses the model and how much speed it needs. Firms can use the frame to plan their AI path.
arxiv-2509-18201:
Xicheng Zhang presents a sampling-based method to find the best point of a function with no slope data. His 2025 paper deals with zeroth-order optimization, used when a task gives values only, not gradients. Mild smoothness terms on the task set the frame for the proof work.

He proves firm rates for how fast the method closes on the best point. Wide tests back the claims on famous bench tasks, smooth and rough alike. The method held up past a hundred dims, a scale where many such tools fade. It also coped with jumps and breaks in the task shape, which suits black-box tasks.
arxiv-2509-18301:
Mirko Weber and 6 co-authors pick RNA shapes that fit live measures of light transfer. Their 2025 paper deals with a hard task: a large RNA can fold in many ways, and its energy map is rough. Models from three known tools gave a pool of shapes for one ribosomal RNA contact.

Each shape was checked for sound base pairing and a set error cap. For kept shapes, the team worked out where two dye tags can sit, and what light transfer each shape would show. Those forecasts were weighed against lab measures from single molecules. Matches show lab values can arise from the pool.
arxiv-2509-18401:
Poetry and stories in Persian carry deep cultural roots that AI models rarely face in tests. Armin Tourajmehr, Mohammad Reza Modarres, and Yadollah Yaghoobzadeh measure how creative language models are in Persian. Their 2025 paper builds a data set of user-written Persian literary texts across twenty topics. Models were asked to write fresh literary pieces rich in local expression.

Outputs were scored on four traits from a classic creativity test: originality, fluency, flexibility, and elaboration. To cut costs, a language model acted as judge, and its scores matched human judges well. The team also checked how well models used simile, metaphor, hyperbole, and antithesis, four core devices of Persian writing. Results show clear strengths and clear limits. The authors say models need more work to handle non-English literary traditions with care.
arxiv-2509-18501:
Surgery guided by scans faces a gap: the scan is taken before the operation, but organs shift and bend during it. Maximilian Fehrentz and five co-authors present BridgeSplat to close that gap. Their 2025 paper couples live 3D reconstruction with the patient's prior CT scan. The live model uses 3D Gaussians, soft blobs that render a scene, tied to the CT mesh.

Each Gaussian is set relative to a triangle of the mesh, so the two stay aligned. Joint tuning adjusts both the Gaussians and the mesh bend, guided by the surgery video. The bend can then flow back to update the CT itself. Tests ran on pig surgeries and on a simulated human liver. The CT bent in sensible ways from a single camera view. The authors share code and data in public.
arxiv-2509-19301:
Robots trained by copying human demonstrations inherit the demonstrator's limits, while pure reinforcement learning on real robots is slow and risky. Lars Ankile and five co-authors merge the two: keep the copied policy as a black-box base, and learn small per-step corrections on top with off-policy reinforcement learning. The residual learner needs only sparse binary rewards, success or failure, which are easy to supply. It is also sample-efficient, a must when every real-world trial costs time.

The method improves manipulation policies on high-degree-of-freedom systems in simulation and in reality. Most notably, the team reports the first successful real-world reinforcement learning training on a humanoid robot equipped with dexterous hands. Results across vision-based tasks reach state-of-the-art levels. The authors present the recipe as a practical pathway for bringing reinforcement learning out of the lab.
arxiv-2509-19501:
Linked groups of atoms could one day form a sensing web that feels gravity with extreme care. Charles Fromonteil and seven co-authors design such a web from entangled atom groups that act as optical clocks. Mass and energy are linked, so a clock held in two places at once gains a phase shift from gravity itself. The design needs only shared control of each group as a whole, not atom-by-atom control.

Starting from simple entangled seed states sent through light channels, the groups build up large shared states. Those states can span wider gaps than single-atom methods allow. Local readouts at each node then reveal the gravity signal. The plan points to tests of gravity and space-time with hardware that scales. It also fits the slow growth of quantum networks for sensing and communication.
arxiv-2509-19701:
Scientific simulations refine their grids where the action is, a method called adaptive mesh refinement. Akash Poptani and five co-authors measured how that method runs on mixed CPU-GPU machines. They used Parthenon, a block-structured benchmark code. Small blocks and many refinement levels hurt graphics-chip performance, they found.

Profiling blamed extra communication, serial leftovers, and idle chip capacity. Memory access patterns added further drag. The team also charted how the code scales across compute ranks and where memory runs short. They propose fixes to raise chip throughput and trim memory use. The findings target the next United States supercomputers, which mix processors heavily. Simulation codes that ignore those quirks will waste much of the machines' power.
arxiv-2509-19901:
Pure exploration asks which arm, treatment, or hypothesis is best, using as few samples as possible. Xinyu Liu, Chao Qin, and Wei You recast that hunt as a game between an experimenter and a skeptic. The experimenter spends measurements to rule options out; the skeptic proposes the hardest alternative. Letting the skeptic mix strategies turns the game into a saddle-point problem.

Their method, Frank-Wolfe Self-Play, needs no projections, regularization, or tuning knobs. Single-arm updates on both sides match how bandit sampling actually works. A linear bandit case study exposes pathologies such as nonunique optima that break naive designs. Efficient exploration underlies clinical trials and A/B testing. A tuning-free method lowers the barrier to principled experiment design.
arxiv-2509-20001:
Video quality is judged by human panels, and crowdsourcing those panels invites cheaters. Babak Naderi and Ross Cutler tackle unreliable participation in subjective video tests run outside the lab. Recent exploits abuse video metadata, and remote-desktop connections let workers fake their setups. Both distort the scores that streaming and call platforms trust.

The authors build detectors, both objective and subjective, for remote-desktop users. Two mainstream crowdsourcing platforms are compared for susceptibility and for how well mitigations work. Test design itself is part of the defense. Subjective scores steer codec and product decisions worth large sums. Keeping the panel honest across platforms is unglamorous, essential work. The study treats fraud detection as part of measurement science.
arxiv-2509-20201:
Albert Kjoller Jacobsen, Johanna Marie Gegenfurtner, and Georgios Arvanitidis wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on machine learning theory. Adding noise to inputs during training is known to smooth the learned function and help generalization. Most earlier work added plain noise in the full input space. Real data, though, usually lies near a lower-dimensional curved surface, called a manifold.

The authors propose noise that respects that geometry. One strategy projects random noise onto the tangent space of the surface, then follows a geodesic curve back onto it. Another lets the point wander by Brownian motion along the surface. On strongly curved manifolds, the geometric noise improved generalization and made results less sensitive to settings. On simpler manifolds it matched ordinary training. Tests on handwritten digits showed the same pattern when the manifold was learned by a generative model.
arxiv-2509-20501:
Grouping items by looks alone misses the rules that make a group useful. Kishor Datta Gupta and five co-authors build rule-guided clustering in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their framework, DARTVAE, extends a variational autoencoder so domain rules shape the learned representation directly. Rules are not filters applied afterward; they are first-class learning signals.

A language model drafts the rules, which are structured into knowledge graphs. The training loss then combines reconstruction, divergence, consistency, and violation penalties. On aircraft and automotive data, the clusters proved more meaningful in practice: drones were isolated, stealth aircraft unified, and sport utility vehicles separated from sedans. Standard clustering metrics improved as well. The authors warn that generated rules can hallucinate or conflict, and that too many rules invite overfitting.
arxiv-2509-20601:
The radio shell of supernova 1993J, the best-studied explosion of its kind, gets a fresh measurement by Joseph Farah and seven co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Decades of interferometry tracked its expanding ejecta from weeks after the blast. Earlier analyses fit a physical spherical shell model to the data. This re-analysis uses a geometric ring model and closure quantities only, which sidesteps calibration errors.

The first seventeen hundred days were remodeled. Expansion followed the same power law that shell fitting had found, confirming the older result independently. For the first time, the shell's width was measured before day one thousand, as early as day two hundred sixty-four. The width held steady at about a quarter of the radius. Brightness around the ring rotated and then grew more complex, quantifying patterns earlier seen only in images.
arxiv-2509-20701:
Tiny heat signatures are easy to lose in a cluttered infrared image. Jiayi Zuo, Songwei Pei, and Qian Li present DENet, a 2025 network for infrared small target detection. Such detection supports remote sensing jobs like disaster warning and watching ships at sea.

Small targets lack clear texture or shape, so models must keep fine spatial detail while also reading wider context. DENet uses two paths with an edge-focused design and global-local attention. This helps it pull out target edges under low contrast and heavy noise, where fixed gradient tools fall short. The authors aim for fewer missed targets and fewer false alarms than earlier approaches, and they test the design on standard detection benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-20901:
Explaining a language model's answer usually means scoring each word's influence, which is slow and often meaningless. Alan Boyle and three co-authors present CafGa, an interactive tool that fixes both problems, in a 2025 paper for the EMNLP 2025 demo track. CafGa lets users explain at customizable levels of detail.

Instead of single words, users can define larger text segments as the units of explanation. The tool computes feature attributions over those segments and draws deletion and insertion curves to judge explanation quality. Interactive segmentation keeps long documents tractable. Semantic units, such as phrases or sentences, carry meaning that single words cannot. The authors position CafGa as a workbench for researchers who need explanations they can adapt and evaluate.
arxiv-2509-21001:
Tilings and patterns that repeat almost, but not quite, periodically underlie the mathematics of quasicrystals. James Walton, writing solo, develops a general theory of such pattern spaces in a 2025 paper of fifty-two pages. The patterns have finite local complexity, meaning only finitely many local arrangements occur.

Walton extends substitution, the inflation rule that generates aperiodic tilings, from tilings to individual patterns and whole pattern spaces. He then proves recognisability: each pattern's substitution pre-images are unique up to translation, with no minimality assumptions. Fibre sizes follow from groups of translational periods. The theorem answers an open question posed by Cortez and Solomyak. Recognisability is the key step that lets researchers decode a pattern's history from its present form.
arxiv-2509-21101:
Eigenvalues of matrix functions can shift under small changes to the model, and the size of that shift is the condition number. Ritwik Prabin Kalita, Anshul Prajapati, and Punit Sharma study such shifts in a 2025 paper on numerical analysis. Their objects are rational matrix functions with built-in symmetry.

The authors find when a simple eigenvalue has the same condition number under arbitrary perturbations and under perturbations that keep the structure. For symmetric, skew-symmetric, and even or odd functions, they give an exact formula for the structured condition number. For Hermitian, skew-Hermitian, and palindromic families, they give tight bounds. The work matters where structured models are used, such as control and vibration problems, since the wrong perturbation type would misstate the true sensitivity.
arxiv-2509-21401:
Jailbreaking a vision language model through its images is the attack studied in a 2025 paper by Md Jueal Mia and M. Hadi Amini. Such models can reason over images and text together. Image based perturbations are a strong route to harmful outputs. Past attacks often gave unstable results or left visible marks on the image. The authors aim for a cleaner method.

Their attack, JaiLIP, perturbs images under loss guidance. It minimizes a joint objective with two parts. One part keeps the adversarial image close to the clean image. The other part pushes the model toward harmful output. Tests used standard toxicity metrics from two public tools. Results show the method can jailbreak vision language models through image space.
arxiv-2509-21901:
Zebin Zhuang and Wang Yang map the phases of a quantum magnet chain in this 2025 physics paper. The chain follows the spin one-half Kitaev model, with two extra interactions added: an XX coupling and a symmetric off-diagonal coupling called Gamma. Such chains are studied because their phases mix magnetic order with unusual quantum behavior. The authors combine an exact transformation with heavy computer simulation.

Using a Jordan-Wigner transformation and a method called DMRG, they chart six distinct phases. Four phases have energy gaps and show magnetic order pointing along two set directions, in both aligned and opposed patterns. The two gapless phases carry helical Majorana fermions, exotic particles that are their own antiparticles, moving at two different speeds. The borders between phases include two kinds of critical lines. The work shows how symmetry, order, and criticality interact in this chain.
arxiv-2509-22001:
Light can scatter off light, and heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider give a rare place to watch it happen. A. Szczurek and M. Klusek-Gawenda examine that process in this 2025 paper, presented at a workshop on ultra-peripheral collisions. In these collisions the nuclei miss each other but exchange photons. Standard theory predicts slightly fewer photon-pair events than the ATLAS and CMS experiments measure.

The authors study extra channels that could fill the gap. In these channels, one or both nuclei break up while emitting the photons, and the breakup is hard to spot, so the events can be mistaken for the clean process. They include photons coupled to single nucleons, not just to whole nuclei, in both quiet and excited nucleon states. For the ATLAS setup it reaches a sizable share of the standard prediction, which makes it hard to ignore in precision work.
arxiv-2509-22101:
Checking numerical claims, like figures in a news report, takes several steps of reasoning and arithmetic at once. Primakov Chungkham and three co-authors study how to spend extra thinking time well on that task in this 2025 paper, accepted at EMNLP. Language models, even reasoning ones, often misread the nuance of numbers. They also suffer reasoning drift, losing the thread of a claim's parts and backtracking.

The team's approach samples many reasoning paths at test time, then uses a trained verifier model to pick the path most likely to reach the right verdict. That search reduced the drift problem and brought solid gains in verification accuracy. To save computing, an adaptive mechanism applies the heavy search only to claims that look complex. The selective version ran much more efficiently than always searching, while still beating single-shot verification by a clear margin. Code and data are shared.
arxiv-2509-22201: Nathan Brownlowe and David Robertson work in theory of tensor categories. Such categories organize objects and the maps between them. Their 2025 paper introduces a new one: the rigid tensor category of tubular partitions. It is built from partition diagrams drawn on tubes. The authors use this category to give a combinatorial model of another category. That other category collects the representations of the quantum automorphism group of a homogeneous rooted tree, an object from quantum group theory. Its representations are hard to handle in other ways.
arxiv-2509-22501:
C. J. R. Murphy-Barltrop and 3 co-authors model how links between extremes change over time. In climate and finance data, the extremes of several variables often move together, and that tie is rarely fixed. Most models for multivariate extremes assume a steady tie, so they miss this drift. A newer geometric approach reads the tie from the limiting shape of a scaled data cloud.

The team extends that approach to non-stationary data and states the conditions it needs. Their semi-parametric framework estimates the limit shape as it evolves. Simulations showed it captures many forms of dependence and stays robust across model choices. Tests on financial returns showed practical uses for risk work.
arxiv-2509-22601:
Yulei Qin and 15 co-authors train tool-using language agents by letting them copy their own wins. Reinforcement learning sharpens such agents, but balancing exploration and exploitation over long tasks is tricky. Pushing entropy up mechanically can destabilize training as multi-turn data shifts. Their recipe, SPEAR, stores good past episodes in a replay buffer for self-imitation, while a curriculum steers entropy across stages.

Early stages reward frequent tool use to speed exploration. Later stages favor proven tactics as the agent masters the setting. On ALFWorld and WebShop, SPEAR lifted success rates for several base methods by wide margins. Math contest gains were smaller but real, at minor extra cost.
arxiv-2509-22801:
Huajing Zhao and 3 co-authors develop standards for robot grasping pipelines inside the COMPARE ecosystem. That ecosystem aims to make open-source robot manipulation products compatible and benchmarkable. Without shared rules, modules for perception, grasp planning, and motion planning rarely plug together cleanly. The paper reports work in progress on three fronts.

First, the team is building repositories of open-source products to find each component's common traits. Second, they study existing modular pipelines to extract best practices. Third, they build new pipelines that advance prior work while following the proposed standards. The goal is component-level and pipeline-level guidelines for how modules should be specified and integrated.
arxiv-2509-23101:
Fake accounts on blockchains hide behind pseudonyms, which frustrates anti-money-laundering work. M Z Haider, Tayyaba Noreen, and M Salman detect fraud with an ensemble of graph networks. One model of each of three types joins the team: convolution, attention, and isomorphism networks. A tuned soft vote blends their calls. Tests used the real-world Elliptic data set.

The ensemble caught illicit transactions with high recall. False positives stayed below one percent. It beat each single model and other baselines. The design adds quantum-ready hooks for future feature maps. Hybrid quantum-classical graph models could plug in later as hardware matures.
arxiv-2509-23201:
A long-standing claim about holomorphic vector bundles gets a fresh analytic proof. Rei Murakami proves Griffiths' conjecture on compact Riemann surfaces. The claim says a bundle is ample exactly when it carries a Hermitian metric with positive curvature. The proof runs through a system of partial differential equations from Demailly. Two toolkits combine in the argument.

Uhlenbeck-Yau techniques for Hermitian-Einstein metrics supply one half. Pingali's reduction of the problem to an a priori estimate supplies the other. The surface setting keeps the geometry to complex dimension one. Murakami presents the route as a new proof, not a new statement.
arxiv-2509-23401:
Underwater 6G networks must place sensors, hubs, and roaming vehicles where signals fade fast. Mustafa Yavuz Engin, Mehmet Ozdem, and Tuğçe Bilen built a simulation model for that layout problem. Fixed hubs, mobile autonomous underwater vehicles, and many sensor nodes form the network. Water traits like temperature, salinity, and conductivity shape signal loss and delay. Physical models compute those effects.

Placement starts with K-means clustering. A genetic algorithm and then particle swarm optimization refine the clusters in stages. The model covers multi-hop relay, leader choice, queues, and load balance. A live graphic interface compares runs with and without cluster leaders.
arxiv-2509-23501:
The role a prompt assigns to a language model, such as expert or teacher, may change how well it answers. Hamidreza Rouzegar and Masoud Makrehchi test that hunch for in-context learning, where models learn from examples in the prompt itself. They vary role setups in zero-shot and few-shot cases. Four models are covered: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o from OpenAI, plus two sizes of Meta's Llama2.

Tasks span sentiment judgments, text classification, question answering, and math reasoning. Across these data sets, role design shifted results in ways the authors read as promising. They argue that structuring prompts by role deserves more care, since prompt wording is often tuned while roles are left as an afterthought.
arxiv-2509-23901:
A deep network can guess a galaxy's stellar mass from its pictures, but which visual clues actually cause the estimate? Wei Zhang and 6 co-authors interpret such a model with causal analysis and mutual information decomposition. Causal paths separate real influence from mere association among variables. Information decomposition then splits the inputs' contributions into redundant, unique, and synergistic parts.

Data come from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the WISE infrared survey. The results give physical readings of how morphology and other image content beyond total brightness feed the mass estimate. The authors argue the pairing of deep learning with interpretability tools can sharpen data-driven astrophysics.
arxiv-2509-24001:
A robot that cannot tell where its human partner is looking misses half the conversation. Matej Palider and 2 co-authors evaluate gaze estimation methods on the NICO robot platform in a shared workspace. They introduce a new annotated data set collected with that robot. Four leading gaze models were tested against it, and their angular errors came close to those on general benchmarks.

Distance tells a harsher story: the best median error in the shared workspace was about fourteen and a half centimeters. The authors discuss what that gap means in practice and recommend how gaze should be integrated as one modality among several in human-robot systems.
arxiv-2509-24101:
Sentiment tools can treat groups of people unequally, and finding that bias takes test sentences that differ only in who they mention. Zsolt T Kardkovacs and 6 co-authors present BTC-SAM, a framework that uses large language models to write such test cases from a minimal spec. Hand-building rich and varied test sets is slow and needs experts or crowd work.

Their method guides the model to vary identity groups while keeping sentences natural and on-topic. Tests show the generated sentences give more language variety and better coverage than plain prompting. The gains held even for biases the system had not seen before. Cheaper test writing could help teams audit sentiment models across a wider range of harms.
arxiv-2509-24501:
Peer Christian Kunstmann and Patrick Tolksdorf survey what is known, and add new results, about the H-infinity calculus of the Stokes operator. That calculus governs how functions of the operator that drives viscous flow behave. The hard cases are rough domains and unbounded ones, where older proofs run long or fail.

An abstract comparison principle anchors the whole account. The authors sketch how it yields the calculus for no-slip conditions in bounded Lipschitz domains. For unbounded domains, the same route shortens past proofs. A fully new result covers Neumann-type boundary conditions in bounded convex domains. The overview doubles as a map of the field's current edge.
arxiv-2509-25001:
Tooba Imtiaz, Lucy Chai, and colleagues rebuild large three-dimensional scenes from photos with a transformer that looks locally in a 2025 computer vision study. Transformers excel at novel view synthesis, but their attention cost grows quadratically with the number of views, choking on big scenes. The Local View Transformer restricts each part of the reconstruction to nearby views, where the relevant information actually lives.

Local windows restore scalability while keeping the learned reconstruction quality that made transformers attractive. Large scene capture serves mapping, film production, and digital twins of real places, all of which outgrow global attention quickly.
arxiv-2510-00001:
Broestl and colleagues bring the idea of code coverage from software testing to retrieval-augmented generation systems, asking whether a test question set actually covers the knowledge base it is meant to probe. Their practical framework embeds document chunks and test questions into one shared vector space using standard embeddings and clustering. It turns the vague worry about blind spots into numbers a developer can act on in their work.

Three complementary metrics are computed, basic proximity coverage, content-weighted coverage that accounts for how much material each area holds, and multi-topic coverage for questions spanning several clusters. Outlier detection flags irrelevant questions for removal. Demonstrated on two distinct use cases, the method pinpoints specific content areas with inadequate test representation and recommends concrete new questions. It helps teams build more genuinely robust test suites for high-stakes systems in practice.
arxiv-2510-00101:
Francesco D'Eugenio and thirteen colleagues published this 2025 astronomy paper on a bright early galaxy nicknamed Irony. The James Webb Space Telescope took the deepest spectra yet of this object, a so-called Little Red Dot. Such dots host growing black holes from the universe's first billion years. Irony shines from a time when the cosmos was very young.

The spectra show hydrogen lines that are both broad and partly absorbed. The absorption splits in speed, with one part moving toward us and another away. Line strengths imply the black hole may outweigh what its host galaxy's mass would suggest. Odd line ratios point to collisions in dense gas rather than plain dust dimming. Rare iron lines also appear, adding clues about the gas around the black hole. The study shows how messy the gas feeding early black holes can be.
arxiv-2510-00501:
Kaixin Wang and eight colleagues published this 2025 paper on helping code models write in programming languages they barely know. Models ace popular languages but stumble on low-resource ones with little training data. Their framework, CodeChemist, transfers know-how at test time instead of retraining. It first writes and runs code in a strong language to build revealing test cases.

Those tests capture what correct behavior looks like, in executable form. The model then drafts candidate solutions in the weak language at several sampling temperatures. Each candidate faces the test suite, and the best passer wins. Benchmarks on multilingual code suites showed consistent gains over rival test-time methods. The boost grew largest exactly where the language gap was widest. No weights changed during the whole process, the authors stress. The recipe gives rare languages a borrowed competence drawn from their richer cousins.
arxiv-2510-00701:
Lin, Zhang, and Lu make concept bottleneck models multimodal and relational in this 2025 arXiv paper on interpretable deep learning. Concept bottleneck models predict human-readable concepts first, then answer from those concepts, which lets people inspect and correct the reasoning. Classic versions handle one modality and treat concepts as isolated slots, ignoring how concepts relate to each other and to the question. The authors' framework, MoE-SGT, adds structure on both fronts.

They build answer-concept and answer-question graphs, then run a Graph Transformer over them to capture multi-level dependencies between concepts. A Mixture-of-Experts module replaces the plain feed-forward layers, routing each input to specialized sub-experts matched to its complexity. On multiple benchmark datasets the model beat other concept bottleneck networks on accuracy. Crucially, it kept end-to-end interpretability, so the concept layer still explains every prediction in plain terms.
arxiv-2510-00801:
Tsuzuki and Ohki settle a long-open question about Oja's flow in this 2025 arXiv paper on applied mathematics. The Oja flow is a continuous-time algorithm that extracts the leading components of data, much like principal component analysis. Its theory was complete only for symmetric positive-definite matrices, where it behaves as a gradient flow. For general square matrices, only local convergence near the answer was known.

The authors prove global convergence for general matrices, showing the flow settles exponentially fast from almost every starting point. In that setting it finds the invariant subspace tied to the eigenvalues with the largest real parts. They also propose a modification that improves numerical stability in practice. As applications, they build new methods for reducing large linear dynamical systems and for designing low-rank stabilizing controllers.
arxiv-2510-01101:
Mazzucato, Wang, and Wei study what happens as fluid viscosity shrinks toward zero in this 2025 arXiv paper on partial differential equations. Viscous flow follows the Navier-Stokes equations, while ideal flow follows the Euler equations. Near a solid wall the two can differ sharply, because friction creates a thin boundary layer. Their setting is harder still, since fluid may enter and leave through permeable boundaries at a general angle.

The authors prove that Navier-Stokes solutions converge to the Euler solution in the energy norm as viscosity vanishes. Interior convergence holds in both the L2 and Sobolev H1 norms at the same rates known for flow normal to the boundary. Their proof builds boundary layer correctors from Prandtl-type equations and pushes the expansion to higher order. A remark shows the method can reach arbitrarily high precision under stronger compatibility conditions.
arxiv-2510-02101:
Lukeš and Krtouš study point particles threaded on cosmic strings in a three-dimensional universe in this 2025 relativity paper. The BTZ solution describes a black hole in two space dimensions plus time. Continuing it analytically removes the horizon and leaves a conical deficit, read as a massive point particle. A cosmic string can hold such a particle in static equilibrium.

The authors define an additive notion of local mass for these static spacetimes. That bookkeeping lets them analyze particles and strings as one mechanical system. A bound pair, two particles joined by a string of finite length, becomes tractable. Going further, they use a cut-and-glue construction to build two particles oscillating on a string. That dynamical system leaves the static realm entirely. The constructions clarify how mass, deficit angles, and strings trade against each other.
arxiv-2510-02301:
Sullivan and co-authors model the radio jets of two candidate double black hole systems. Their 2025 astrophysics paper studies blazars PKS 2131-021 and PKS J0805-0111. Long radio monitoring showed both sources pulsing on a steady beat. Such clocks hint at two giant black holes in orbit. No single source of the known gravitational wave hum is confirmed yet. The authors propose a shared jet picture. A slow wind carves a helical channel outward. A much faster jet then travels along that channel. Viewing angle effects create most of the observed pulsing.

The model reproduces the main features of both sources. Lower radio tones vary later, as seen in data. That delay follows from emission at larger distances. The team predicts radio polarization and imaging signatures. Future telescopes can test those predictions directly. Confirmed binaries would anchor the gravitational wave background.
arxiv-2510-02401:
Szewczyk, Gallo Fernandez, and Townsend generate long music clips with linear recurrent networks. Their 2025 paper models raw audio one step at a time. Audio waveforms are extremely long sequences. Structure lives at many time scales at once. Older recurrent and attention models struggled with that load. Linear recurrent models, also called state space models, run far more efficiently. The team tests design choices across that family. Context parallelism lets them train on full minute long clips. Those clips reach about one million tokens each.

Their model, HarmonicRNN, set new marks on small datasets. It led on likelihood scores and perceptual quality measures. A Beethoven piano set was one test bed. A mixed YouTube music set was the other. Raw waveform generation stays hard at large scale. Efficient sequence models make the task newly practical.
arxiv-2510-02601:
Rim and co-authors capture 3D hand motion in real world settings with a camera rig. Their 2025 computer vision paper attacks a dataset problem. Hand tracking models train mostly on tidy lab recordings. Wild environments break those models quickly. The team built a backpack rig with eight outward cameras. A worn headset adds two first person views. Together they watch hands from ten angles at once. The wearer can move freely outdoors. A tracking pipeline fuses the views into 3D hand poses. Those poses serve as ground truth for training data.

Their annotated dataset pairs synced images with poses. Quality checks validated the pipeline carefully. The setup shrinks the trade-off between realism and accuracy. Future releases will add object poses and contact labels. Text descriptions of interactions are also planned. Augmented reality needs hands understood outside the lab. This rig shows how to gather that evidence.
arxiv-2510-02801:
Chen and a team of co-authors report a close look at a rare nearby galaxy that mimics a puzzling class of distant objects. The distant objects are called Little Red Dots. The James Webb Space Telescope found them in the early universe. The nearby galaxy, named J2048, sits at a redshift near 0.43, far behind the cluster. The team studied it with the Gemini North telescope.

The data show bright blue light spread across the galaxy. That light comes from a fierce burst of new stars. The burst forms stars at a rate near 400 solar masses each year. Fast gas also streams out of the galaxy. At its center sits a black hole that looks far too heavy for its host. The black hole holds about six tenths of the mass of all the stars. Nearby cases like this one help scientists test ideas about the far-off dots.
arxiv-2510-03101:
Tenison and co-authors pick which layers of a network to retrain on small devices. Phones and wearables must adapt models to their owners. Full retraining is too heavy for their chips and batteries. Retraining a few key layers is the usual escape. Picking those layers often needs labels or a full gradient pass. Their method, AdaBet, needs neither labels nor gradients. It reads the shape of each layer's activity instead.

Betti numbers count holes and loops in that activity cloud. Layers with rich topology hold more learning capacity. Forward passes alone supply all the needed data. Sixteen model and data set pairs tested the idea. AdaBet beat gradient-based pickers on accuracy by a clear margin. Peak memory use fell by two fifths at the same time. Retraining thus fits inside tight device budgets. Privacy gains follow, since data never leaves the device.
arxiv-2510-03201:
Jettkant and Søjmark set up a system of Brownian particles whose own death odds move the walls that kill them. Each wandering particle is absorbed when it hits its boundary. The boundary positions depend on absorption chances before a deadline. Those chances are computed backward from the final time. The coupling forms a singular forward-backward equation system. Its analysis yields a tiered moving boundary problem instead.

Each tier of the problem fixes one absorption pattern. The boundary and its condition come from the tier before. The authors prove classical well-posedness for the whole tower. That solution then solves the original particle system. Uniqueness of the forward-backward system follows from it too. Absorption of one particle shifts every other boundary. A weighted connection matrix encodes those mutual influences. Finance and physics both host such coupled hitting problems.
arxiv-2510-03301:
Sedek presents a 2025 arXiv paper on joining two kinds of machine learning models into one flexible team. Tree based XGBoost handles table data well, while neural networks catch complex patterns. Fixed mixing rules cannot adapt when data changes shape. The framework built here uses meta learning, which means a higher level model learns how to pick and blend the two workers for each new case.

The system weighs how unsure each worker is and which inputs matter most. It can choose XGBoost alone, the network alone, or a blend of both. On the California housing data set, the team cut forecast error by about two percent against XGBoost alone. The gain against the neural network alone reached about ten percent in the same tests. Clearer input rankings also made the blended choices easier to explain. The design suits fields where data mixes tables with tangled patterns.
arxiv-2510-03401:
