Instruction-style overfitting may result from that intertwining. Direct preference tuning beats supervised methods in cold start. Their SPECS approach uses self-distilled preference data. No larger teachers or manual annotation are needed. Preference training learns transferable surface criteria, not content. Reinforcement learning then handles deep thinking. Consistent gains appear across benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-26001:
Xinhua Wang, Caibo Feng, Xiangjun Fu, and Chunxiao Liu improve a Mamba based method for brightening low light images by changing how it scans the picture. Mamba is a sequence model that reads an image in a scanning pattern to capture both fine detail and long range links. Their Hilbert Selective Scan follows a Hilbert curve, a space filling path whose fractal shape covers the plane more thoroughly, which raises the pattern Hausdorff dimension.

Wang and the team report that the richer scan captures fine scale detail and local interactions better, while reducing information mismatches across the image. On public benchmarks, existing Mamba based enhancers gained in both measured quality and visual fidelity, while using less compute and finishing faster. The idea may transfer to other Mamba based tasks.
arxiv-2510-26101:
Taku Mikuriya leads eleven co-authors in a benchmark for language models that write quantum programs. Code generation is usually judged by running Python, but quantum programming also interacts with hardware, even if simulated, and human coders write code that runs on a quantum computer. Their QCoder Benchmark judges models with feedback from a quantum simulator, beyond plain Python execution.

The simulator reports domain measures such as circuit depth, execution time, and error class, which can guide better generation. The benchmark also holds human written submissions from real programming contests for comparison. Even advanced models scored low, with GPT-4o at about nineteen percent accuracy in their experiments, which shows how much room remains in quantum coding.
arxiv-2510-26601:
Anirban Ray, Vera Galinova, and Florian Jug sharpen blurry microscope images with a new learning method. Computational super-resolution tries to recover fine detail that a microscope never recorded, which is only possible with a good prior, a learned sense of what real samples look like. Noise in fluorescence images makes that prior hard to learn.

Ray and his two co-authors present ResMatching, built on guided conditional flow matching, a technique that learns to turn noise into data step by step. On four kinds of biological structures from the BioSR data set, it beat or matched seven rival methods. It gave the best balance between fidelity to the data and realistic looks, and it shone most on noisy images. It can also sample many plausible answers, and its per-pixel uncertainty scores were well calibrated.
arxiv-2510-26701:
Akhila Kandivalasa and Marcos Netto speed up a basic check for power grid control. Observability analysis asks whether a system's state can be inferred from its measures. For dynamic state estimation, which tracks the grid's changing state, the established analysis method does not scale.

Kandivalasa and Netto build a graph from the power system model, using only which variables depend on which, and derive a numerical method that runs in linear time in the graph's size. It is, they note, the first graph approach for dynamic rather than static estimation. They test both decentralised and centralised settings. Against the established method in a centralised case, their approach cut computation time by a factor of about one thousand four hundred forty.
arxiv-2510-26901:
Barry T Chiang, Frank C van den Bosch, and Hsi-Yu Schive set universal rules for when simulated dark matter subhalos can be trusted. Subhalos and satellite galaxies in cosmological simulations suffer overmerging: weak resolution makes tides strip them too fast and destroys them early. Past studies of the problem covered few orbits and assumed round, isotropic subhalos.

Chiang and his two co-authors run the first extensive suite on anisotropic subhalos across resolutions and orbits. They report a universal criterion: a subhalo's tidal radius must always span at least twenty cells, or twenty softening lengths, for its evolution to converge. They also give a universal formula for the scatter from discreteness noise. By their estimate, as many as half of all subhalos in leading simulations may be unresolved in force or mass, and they advocate adaptive refinement tied to the tidal radius.
arxiv-2510-27001:
Elise Wolf tackles a quiet problem in bandit research, where an algorithm repeatedly picks among options to learn which pays best. Comparing such methods fairly is hard because results swing with test conditions. Variance-aware versions, which watch how spread out rewards are, look strong in some settings and weak in others, yet few studies use shared, repeatable setups.

Wolf offers a reproducible framework that tests eight classical and variance-aware methods side by side. Scores cover reward, regret, reward spread, value at risk, and how often the best option is chosen, all through an interactive tool. Variance-aware methods win when uncertainty is high and options differ subtly, while classical methods match or beat them when options separate clearly.
arxiv-2511-00001:
Paul Immanuel's thesis explores incarnations of the Fourier transform in algebraic and arithmetic geometry. A central topic is Banach-Colmez spaces, introduced through the theory of perfectoid spaces. The motivation builds from the l-adic Fourier transform and a related transform for perfect unipotent group schemes, following toward recent research.

The endpoint is the 2021 work of Anschutz and Le Bras on a Fourier transform for Banach-Colmez spaces. Graduate readers get a guided path from classical transforms to the p-adic frontier. Fourier ideas recur across geometry because they exchange local and global information, and this thesis traces that theme into modern perfectoid theory.
arxiv-2511-00301:
Ciaran Bench and nine co-authors compare ways for medical AI to say how unsure it is. Their test bed is photoplethysmography, the light-based pulse signal from wearables, used here to detect atrial fibrillation and to estimate blood pressure. A wrong but confident answer outside a clinic could harm a patient, so honest uncertainty matters as much as accuracy.

The team implements eight uncertainty methods, an unusually broad set, and scores them with a careful evaluation plan. No single method wins everywhere: the best choice depends on the task, the uncertainty measure, and the scale of reliability checked. Checking local calibration, patient by patient, revealed behavior that global scores missed. Evaluation, they argue, should match the model's real clinical use.
arxiv-2511-00401:
Mohammad Shirzadi, Emilio Cruciani, and Ahad Zehmakan survey opinion dynamics, the study of how opinions evolve as people interact. The topic matters for politics and marketing, but it is studied in scattered pieces across computer science, mathematics, social science, and physics, often with no shared language. Their overview reviews the well-known models inside one unified framework and sorts them into classes by their properties.

Key findings are organized in three parts. First come convergence properties: whether a model ends in consensus or polarization, and how long it takes. Next comes viral marketing, with its main algorithmic and complexity results. Last, node traits such as stubbornness, activeness, and neutrality are shown to shape how opinions diffuse. The survey aims to spur cross-disciplinary work on a shared foundation.
arxiv-2511-00501:
Nihan Acar-Denizli and Pedro Delicado model the curves from continuous glucose monitors, devices that track blood sugar over time in daily life and clinical trials. Each person yields repeated curves, and the shape of those curves carries health information. After rescaling each curve to a standard interval, the authors model it with a Beta distribution whose two parameters drift with time.

Their local linear likelihood smoothing handles both time-varying parameters at once, extending earlier local methods that managed only one. The approach needs far fewer observations than previous functional methods and can work with a single individual. Tests on synthetic data and a large clinical trial dataset show competitive fit and speed against spline-based rivals. Theory for estimation and for cross-validation error estimates completes the package.
arxiv-2511-00601:
Hokuto Konno, Jianfeng Lin, Anubhav Mukherjee, and Juan Muñoz-Echániz constrain the topology of Lefschetz fibrations whose fibers are four-dimensional, using Seiberg-Witten theory. Their tool is the family Bauer-Furuta invariant, computed by analyzing the framed bordism class of one-dimensional Seiberg-Witten moduli spaces through the Bismut-Freed local index theorem. The payoff lands in the mapping class groups of four-manifolds.

New obstructions show certain compositions of Dehn twists on special spheres cannot be smoothly deformed to the identity. Two firsts follow. Some closed, simply connected symplectic four-manifolds admit Torelli symplectomorphisms that are smoothly nontrivial, answering a question of Donaldson negatively: squared Dehn-Seidel twists do not generate the symplectic Torelli group. And irreducible four-manifolds, symplectic and not, admit exotic diffeomorphisms built from Seifert-fibered Dehn twists.
arxiv-2511-00701:
M Mustamin and M Demirci use dark matter detectors to bound a trait of neutrinos. Sterile neutrinos, proposed partners that barely interact, could arise when plain neutrinos scatter off electrons through a transition magnetic moment, a so-called dipole portal. Direct detection setups built to catch dark matter also record low-energy recoils, and solar neutrinos leave exactly such signals in them.

Using data from PandaX-4T and XENONnT, the authors model the up-scattering of solar neutrinos into sterile states. They derive robust exclusion limits on transition magnetic moments, both flavor-blind and flavor-dependent, for fixed sterile masses and across the mass-coupling plane. Because these detectors see solar neutrino events, they can probe all neutrino flavors at once, and the limits extend into new ground.
arxiv-2511-00801:
Zhihui Chen and colleagues present Med-Banana, a framework for editing medical images from text instructions. Good edits must add the requested feature while keeping anatomy, image style, and clinical sense intact. Earlier data sets kept only edits that succeeded, and threw the failures away.

Med-Banana instead learns from both. Its resource, Med-Banana-80K, stores success and failure editing paths with candidate images, checks, rejection reasons, and revised prompts. Three parts are trained together: an editor, a verifier, and a refiner, so new edits can be checked and fixed in a loop. Tests with model judges, blinded experts, and other probes show steady gains over open medical image editors.
arxiv-2511-00901:
Vincenzo De Martino and colleagues ask how the people who build machine learning systems handle sustainability on the job. Sustainability here spans environmental, social, and economic concerns, not just carbon emissions, and earlier research offered mostly high level principles with little evidence from practice.

The team interviewed eight seasoned machine learning engineers, then surveyed more than two hundred more of them. They asked how engineers define sustainability, what practices they use to support it, and what blocks adoption. The central finding is a gap: awareness of sustainability is widespread, but planned implementation is rare. The authors call for clearer guidelines, ways to measure progress, and regulatory support to close that gap.
arxiv-2511-01001:
Johansell Villalobos and colleagues test whether a GPU based shallow water solver runs well across very different supercomputers. The solver, SERGHEI-SWE, models water flow for hydrology, where climate change is driving demand for finer, faster simulations. It is built on the Kokkos framework, which promises code that ports between hardware vendors.

They run it on four leading machines with AMD, NVIDIA, and Intel accelerators, scaling to more than a thousand GPUs. Speedup and efficiency stay strong, and a roofline analysis shows memory bandwidth as the main bottleneck. Portability scores with tuned problem sizes reach under seventy percent, and the authors point to finer kernel control, through Kokkos teams and device specific settings, as the route to improvement.
arxiv-2511-01101:
Marek Strong and Andreas Vlachos introduce TSVer, a benchmark for checking factual claims against time series evidence. Fact checking often turns on temporal and numerical data, such as trends in official statistics, but existing data sets lack structured evidence, give thin justifications, or invent synthetic claims.

TSVer holds just over three hundred real world claims gathered from forty one fact checking organizations, matched against a curated database of four hundred time series from varied domains. Each claim is annotated with the relevant time frames, a verdict, and justifications showing how the evidence supports it, with strong agreement between annotators. Even a leading reasoning model scores modestly on verdicts and worse on justifications, showing how hard time series reasoning remains.
arxiv-2511-01501:
Yufeng Jin and six colleagues address a robot's basic uncertainty: from one camera view, where exactly is the object it wants to grab? Occlusions and symmetry often leave several poses that fit the image, yet most neural networks answer with a single confident guess. Their system, SE(3)-PoseFlow, instead estimates a whole distribution of possible six-dimensional poses.

The method uses flow matching on the manifold of rigid-body motions to sample likely poses, so downstream software can reason about doubt instead of ignoring it. It reaches state-of-the-art scores on the Real275, YCB-V, and LM-O benchmarks. The authors also show the samples helping real manipulation tasks, such as choosing a better viewpoint or planning a grasp that accounts for uncertainty.
arxiv-2511-01601:
Soheyla Feyzbakhsh and Aliaksandra Novik work at the meeting point of algebraic geometry and stability theory. Their stage is a smooth projective curve of positive genus, and their objects are coherent systems on it, bundles equipped with extra linear data, gathered into a bounded derived category.

Bridgeland stability conditions are a way of declaring which objects in such a category count as stable, organized into a geometric space called the stability manifold. The authors describe an open region of that manifold for coherent systems on the curve. Their main finding is that the stability manifold is sensitive enough to detect the curve's Brill-Noether theory, the classical study of what special divisors and bundles the curve carries. The result ties a modern homological tool back to concrete curve geometry.
arxiv-2511-01701:
Mirco Mannucci asks what kind of map should guide a tree search through a puzzle. Earlier work fed Monte Carlo tree search with features of the puzzle grid itself. Those features came from the grid's Laplacian spectrum. They gave no benefit. Mannucci's diagnosis is blunt: grid topology is the same for every instance. It cannot tell easy puzzles from hard ones.

His fix is to measure the topology of the solution space instead. The method finds pattern rules on its own. It then builds a compatibility graph. Its nodes are cell-color pairs, linked when the two can coexist. Features such as algebraic connectivity and rigidity vary with how hard a puzzle is. Fed into node choice, they guide the search. Tests that remove one piece at a time show connectivity is the strongest signal.
arxiv-2511-02101:
Arjun Rao, Marc Rußwurm, Konstantin Klemmer, and Esther Rolf measure how much information is packed into learned representations of the Earth. Geographic implicit neural representations turn simple longitude and latitude inputs into rich embeddings trained on satellite, image, or text data. The team asks how many degrees of freedom those embeddings actually use, a quantity called intrinsic dimension, regardless of how large the embedding space is.

For models with embedding sizes between 256 and 512, intrinsic dimensions landed roughly between two and ten, shifting with spatial resolution and the kinds of input data used in training. The measure tracked performance on downstream tasks and exposed spatial artefacts. The authors offer it as a label-free tool for evaluating and comparing Earth representation models.
arxiv-2511-02201:
F. F. Nascimento, V. B. Bezerra, J. M. Toledo, P. H. Morais, and J. C. Rocha derive exact solutions that generalise the Bardeen black hole, a regular black hole model without a central singularity. Their construction layers several physical ingredients onto the basic solution at once: electric charge, a cosmological constant, a surrounding quintessence field, and a cloud of strings threading the spacetime.

The most general member of the family combines all of these sources around the charged Bardeen core. The authors then discuss the Kretschmann scalar, which measures how strong the spacetime curvature is, and trace how it depends on the parameter attached to each source. The paper closes by analysing the geodesics, the paths available to particles and light, through the corresponding effective potential.
arxiv-2511-02301:
Kuan-Cheng Chen, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Chen-Yu Liu, and Kin Leung combine quantum computing with federated learning to watch for faults in industrial sensor networks. Factories generate high-dimensional time series from many machines, and spotting faults matters. The data cannot simply be pooled for privacy, scale, and bandwidth reasons. Classical federated learning keeps data local, yet it can miss the curved decision boundaries that separate normal operation from rare faults.

Their framework runs quantum feature maps on edge nodes, which compute compressed kernel summaries from their local data on quantum circuits. Only those summaries go to a central server, which assembles a global kernel matrix and trains the decision function. On synthetic industrial benchmarks the method generalised better than classical federated baselines at capturing complex time patterns, while notably reducing the communication overhead.
arxiv-2511-02501:
Mohan Liyanage, Eldiyar Zhantileuov, Ali Kadhum Idrees, and Rolf Schuster predict network delay for edge computing without pinging the network. Offloading tasks from a device to a nearby edge server only works in real time if the end-to-end latency is known in advance. The usual way to learn it, active probing, is itself intrusive. Their lightweight scheme instead builds a rational model, a ratio of polynomials, from passive features: frame size, arrival rate, and link utilisation.

Across extensive experiments with five-fold cross-validation, the model reached state-of-the-art prediction accuracy, reporting a mean absolute error of 0.0115 and an R-squared of 0.9847, while keeping inference fast. The authors frame the result as a strong trade-off between precision and efficiency against both traditional regression methods and neural networks, suitable for latency-sensitive edge applications that cannot afford heavyweight predictors.
arxiv-2511-02601:
Dakota Murray, Chaoqun Ni, Weiye Gu, and Trevor Hubbard study a small task with outsized influence on how scientists navigate the literature: naming clusters of papers. Bibliometric software groups documents into topics, and the old way of labelling a cluster, gluing together its most distinctive terms, produces terse, cryptic names. Generative language models can write fluent, human-like labels instead, and databases have adopted them quickly, ahead of any careful study of what makes such a label good.

The authors separate two label types, characteristic labels and descriptive labels, and give descriptive labelling a formal definition with its design decisions spelled out. They propose a structured generation workflow for bibliometric practice and an evaluation framework for judging the outputs. In their tests, model-written descriptive labels performed at or near the level of characteristic labels, and the paper closes with design guidance for using them responsibly.
arxiv-2511-02801:
L. Manchon, M. Deal, J. Marques, and Y. Lebreton describe Cesam2k20, the newest version of a code that simulates how stars evolve. The CESAM line began with P. Morel and co-workers and was refined over three decades. It was picked to compute the first grid of star models for the PLATO space mission, and is now public.

The 2025 paper reviews the code's numerical style, in which structure values are built from piecewise polynomials on a B-spline basis. It walks through the options for each physical process. Fresh strength lies in how the code moves chemical elements and angular momentum inside a star, shown with standard and non-standard solar models. Companion tools handle star oscillations, optimization, and Python access.
arxiv-2511-02901:
Zahar Sayapin, Daniil Rabinovich, Nikita Korolev, and Kirill Lakhmanskiy present a cheaper way to clean up results from noisy quantum computers. Their method, CLP-ZNE, extends zero-noise extrapolation, a trick that estimates the noiseless answer by watching how results degrade with added noise. The twist is to use the fact that gate errors vary across a chip's layout.

By cycling a circuit through different layouts and averaging, the method extrapolates to zero noise with far fewer layouts than older permutation schemes need. For twelve-qubit circuits modeled on IBM's Torino machine, typical errors in expected values fell by a factor of ten, beating standard unitary folding. The tests included both depolarizing noise and relaxation effects drawn from real hardware data.
arxiv-2511-03001:
Minseok Kang and five colleagues built LEGO, a benchmark that grades how faithfully a generated 3D scene follows a text description. A prompt like apples on the table hides many fine constraints: which objects, in what arrangement, in what manner. Older scores check only rough similarity or skip spatial checks entirely. Their 2025 benchmark pairs each description with human-written constraints and a reference scene.

The companion scorer, LEGO-Eval, splits a description into atomic constraints and checks each one with tools that locate objects in the scene and reason about their layout. It caught misalignments far more accurately than older metrics. Current scene generators did poorly: the best reached at most a 10 percent success rate, showing how far text-to-3D still is from following instructions closely.
arxiv-2511-03101: Shoumin Liu, Zhaohuan Peng, and Xumin Wang study faithful representations of Coxeter groups. These groups form a broad family of symmetry groups. The family includes the dihedral groups of regular polygons. Their 2025 paper analyzes those representations for the dihedral case. It then proves a clean identification result: a Coxeter group is fully determined by the proper joint spectrum of its faithful representations. In other words, that shared spectral fingerprint carries enough information to recover the group itself. The result is a rigidity statement in representation theory.
arxiv-2511-03401:
Kunrui Cao and co-authors analyze a wireless system where movable pinching antennas also deliver power to devices. Pinching antennas slide along a waveguide to build strong direct links and cut path loss. Powering devices from the same setup could free sensors from batteries in hard spots.

Exact formulas are derived for outage chance and average rate, covering both lossy real waveguides and ideal lossless ones. Guidance on where to place waveguides and users follows from those formulas. Heavier absorption in the guide hurts performance, as the analysis quantifies. The study weighs whether pinching designs keep their edge once energy harvesting joins communication duties.
arxiv-2511-03501:
Siyao Li examines how oscillons, long-lived lumps of a vibrating field, fall apart when coupled to a second field. Earlier work found decay through parametric resonance with a four-way coupling. Li asks whether a simpler three-way coupling shows the same behavior, testing how general the decay route is.

Growth rates for the second field are computed under the lump's steady pulsing, mapping which bands blow up for which couplings and shapes. Full simulations then watch the pair evolve. Resonance can stall before the lump dies, leaving a smaller lump that fades only slowly through plain radiation. Partial decay by resonance thus looks like a generic fate, not a quirk of one coupling choice.
arxiv-2511-03801:
Silvia P Nunes and three co-authors ask what happens to white dwarfs, the dense final stage of most stars, if dark matter collects inside them. Nunes, Jose D V Arbanil, Juan M Z Pretel, and Sergio B Duarte build a new equation of state that treats hot dense plasma and cold dark matter together.

The plasma part adds thermal and radiative effects, while the dark matter part is modeled as a simple fluid with a coupling set inside the star. A smooth mixing rule joins the two regimes. Adding dark matter raised the model radius by about twelve percent and total mass slightly. White dwarfs, the authors suggest, could serve as indirect probes of dark matter.
arxiv-2511-04001:
J Nathan Kutz is the lead author among fifteen authors arguing that machine learning for science needs a common task framework, a shared set of challenge datasets with agreed objectives. Learning methods now forecast, reconstruct, generalize, and control dynamic systems across engineering, physics, and biology, yet diverse goals and noisy, limited data make fair comparison hard.

Shared benchmarks helped speech, language, and vision advance quickly, and the authors want the same discipline for science and engineering. Their framework gathers datasets spanning practical objectives under limited-data and noisy conditions. Objective metrics would let users compare the many algorithms now appearing in practice and see which methods truly advance each scientific task.
arxiv-2511-04201:
Matteo Mio, writing alone, introduces compact quantitative equational theories, where every result of a theory can be derived by a finite proof. Such theories reason about distances and near equality, a setting used for chance-based and metric semantics, and compactness is the finiteness trait that makes such reasoning workable.

The theory of interpolative barycentric, or convex, quantitative algebras due to Mardare and co-authors is proved compact. That central example then yields other compact theories of convex algebras, each fixing some distance on finitely supported probability distributions. Convex combinations sit beneath mixture and averaging operations across semantics, so a compact axiom set has wide formal use.
arxiv-2511-04401:
Subeen Park and four colleagues address a quiet failure mode in deep learning. Models often lean on spurious cues, links that work in training but break for rare groups. Their method, called SCER, reshapes the learned features to cut that reliance.

The team proves that worst-group error depends on how much the classifier uses spurious traits. Their training rule then directly limits that use inside the embedding space. The goal is steady accuracy even for the group the model serves worst. The work matters for real deployments, where the rare group is often the one most in need of a correct answer.
arxiv-2511-04501:
Antonin Boisneault and three colleagues study spurious resonances in coupled FEM-BEM methods. Such couplings solve sound scattering from an obstacle in a mixed medium. Finite elements handle the varied inner zone, while boundary elements cover the open outer zone.

The team focuses on their newer formulation, called the Generalized Optimized Schwarz Method. Classical couplings can fail at certain wavenumbers even when the physical problem is sound. Those wavenumbers act like fake resonances inside the math alone. Pinpointing and removing them keeps large acoustic simulations trustworthy, which matters for noise control and sonar design alike.
arxiv-2511-04601:
Yicheng Xiao leads eight authors with PixCLIP, a method for fine-grained vision-language understanding. CLIP links images and text well at a broad level, but fine detail alignment lags. Most fixes add visual prompts that steer focus to chosen regions.

PixCLIP instead trains with pixel-level alignment at any chosen granularity. Long, detailed captions help, yet CLIP's text encoder has a strict token limit that blocks them. The authors work around that cap so detailed text can guide local image features. Sharper alignment should help tasks like grounding a phrase to the exact part of a picture.
arxiv-2511-05101:
Yu Mao and Mohamed Saïdi use Hoshi's mono-anabelian reconstruction to rebuild a number field from group data alone. Anabelian geometry asks how much of a field or curve is fixed by its Galois group, a group that tracks field symmetries.

Their result rebuilds both a field and its largest extension unramified outside a set of primes, for a density-one set of primes. The input is just a profinite group tied to that extension. Such pure group rules show how tight the bond is between a field and its symmetries at all.
arxiv-2511-05301:
Arthur Satouf and co-authors present QueStER, a method that turns a user query into a clear keyword search plan for a standard retriever. Generative retrieval stores relevance inside a model and can be brittle off its home domain, and costly to scale.

QueStER trains a light language model to write out the keyword query, which then runs on BM25, a classic search method. That mix keeps the broad skill of generated queries with the cheap, open run of classic search. Tests check how the bridge fares against both parent styles.
arxiv-2511-05401:
Alexandr Kostochka and co-authors settle the Turán number for four disjoint copies of a complete graph. The Turán number is the most edges a graph on a set count of vertices can have while it avoids a given pattern as a subgraph.

Here the banned pattern is four vertex-disjoint cliques, each of size at least three. Using ideas from the Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem plus a discharging count, they give the exact value for all sizes. Exact Turán values are prized since they close a counting task fully, with no gap between bound and build.
arxiv-2511-05601:
Cheng-Rong Xie, Hiroki Tsuchiura, and Manfred Sigrist study a superconducting device that lets current flow more easily one way than the other. Their setup joins two parallel chains of a special superconductor in a ladder shape. No magnetic field or spin-orbit coupling is used, so the one-way effect comes from geometry alone.

A phase gap between the two legs breaks time-reversal symmetry, and the lack of leg-exchange symmetry skews the current-phase relation. Splitting transport into two channels shows why: one channel is shifted by the leg phase while the other is not. Their interference, plus a channel tied to Majorana modes, yields a strong diode response that peaks at middle coupling strength.
arxiv-2511-05801:
Yue Fang and Geert Ridder work out the exact uncertainty of a treatment-effect estimate in trials where whole clusters, not individuals, are randomized. In such finite populations the exact variance of the standard estimator depends on outcomes nobody can observe, so it cannot be pinned down directly. Their study uses a common two-stage design: sample clusters, then sample units inside them.

First they derive the exact design-based variance, counting cluster sampling, unit sampling, and random assignment together. Then they extend earlier work to give a sharp upper bound on that variance, plus an estimator of the bound from observed data alone. In simulations and a real application, intervals from the bound stayed valid and were usually tighter than standard cluster errors.
arxiv-2511-06201:
Rodrigo Gallardo, Oz Fishman, and Alexander Htet Kyaw built a design assistant that suggests small changes to public spaces. The human-in-the-loop system uses generative tools to propose street-level interventions and invite more local participation in planning. It treats everyday patterns of objects in a place as evidence for what belongs there.

Object detection runs on a curated portion of the ADE20K dataset as a stand-in for real streets. Patterns of which objects appear together become embeddings, and a chosen anchor object earns five likely companions. A vision-language model then reasons over the scene and suggests a third object to complete the idea, while people keep control of choices and refinements.
arxiv-2511-06301:
Azzanzi Jiomekong and co-authors release Secu-Table, a dataset for testing how well systems interpret the meaning of security tables. Semantic table interpretation links table cells to knowledge graph entries, and progress depends on good test data. The security field lacked a public dataset of this kind until now.

Secu-Table holds more than fifteen hundred tables and over fifteen thousand entities drawn from public vulnerability and weakness databases. Entries were annotated with Wikidata and a cybersecurity knowledge graph, and all construction code is public. The dataset supports a shared challenge on table-to-graph matching, and the authors report baseline scores from two open language models and one closed model.
arxiv-2511-06501:
Antu Saha, Mehedi Sun, and Oscar Chaparro automate the hunt for solution talk inside software issue discussions. When a bug is debated, the thread mixes proposals, code changes, and evaluations, and finding the solution-bearing parts by hand is slow. Reopened bugs, regressions, and code reviews all depend on locating that content quickly.

Three language model strategies were compared: embeddings, prompting, and fine-tuning, across traditional, pretrained, and large model classifiers in sixty-eight configurations. A dataset from three hundred fifty-six Firefox issues grounded the tests. Embeddings beat word-count features, prompting lagged, and a fine-tuned large model scored best, with ensembles doing better still and transferring to other projects.
arxiv-2511-06701:
Karen Sargsyan designs guardrails that stop automated discovery systems from manufacturing fake findings through repeated testing. When software tests hypotheses endlessly, false discoveries pile up unless the error budget is policed. The architecture enforces that policing structurally, at two levels, rather than trusting the code to behave.

A Haskell-embedded language makes it impossible to run a test without updating the error budget, and a sandbox keeps validation data physically unreachable from generated code. The false discovery framework rests on a machine-checked Lean proof of an online control theorem, with threshold arithmetic verified separately. Simulations held the false rate near one percent where a naive setup reached forty-one.
arxiv-2511-07101:
Andrew Kresch, Sho Tanimoto, and Yuri Tschinkel propose new invariants for equivariant birational geometry, the study of geometric objects up to birational equivalence when a finite group acts on them. Invariants are quantities that stay the same under the allowed transformations, so they can prove that two objects are truly different. The objects here are smooth rationally connected threefolds, a central class in the sorting of three-dimensional varieties.

The proposed invariants combine two current machines. One is equivariant intermediate Jacobians, which extract abelian-variety data from a threefold while respecting the group action. The other is the Burnside formalism, which organizes fixed-point data into a workable package. Joining them yields finer blocks than either tool gives alone. The paper sets out the construction for threefolds with finite group actions, adding new tests for equivariant birational rigidity.
arxiv-2511-07401:
Generous offers can backfire when buyers suspect hidden catches, a reaction called phantom costs. Benjamin Lebrun and colleagues test whether that suspicion changes when the seller is a robot rather than a person. They also vary how autonomous and self-interested the agent seems.

Eight hundred fifty five people joined a car buying simulation with small or large discounts from human or robot agents. The robot seemed less self-interested, which lowered phantom cost worries. Larger discounts raised both suspicion and willingness to buy. The study shows perceived motives, not just price, shape how a bargain feels.
arxiv-2511-07501:
Qi Junyi revisits the Tower of Hanoi, the disk-moving puzzle that still tests ideas in recursion and proof. The classic three-peg version yields to self-similar reasoning, and Stockmeyer proved its solution unique. Four pegs raise harder questions settled partly by the Frame-Stewart strategy and later work.

Corrected tables carry a warning. A balanced split that looks optimal stays best only through eight disks, then drifts twenty percent high at nine disks and nearly four times high at twenty. The note pairs elegant proofs with checked computation. Puzzle lovers and algorithm students see why plausible patterns demand proof.
arxiv-2511-07601:
Louigi Addario-Berry, Emma Hogan, and Lukas Michel extend Schnyder woods from finite maps to infinite ones. A Schnyder wood orients and colors the edges of a triangulation under strict rules, encoding the map structure compactly. Every finite triangulation has a unique maximal such wood.

Infinite triangulations with finite boundary, and the uniform infinite half-planar case, also carry a unique maximal wood. For the full infinite planar case, the maximal wood arises as a limit of large finite random ones. Several structural traits are cataloged. The results support probability work on random infinite maps, a central model in modern geometry.
arxiv-2511-07701:
Xiaolin Sun, Feidi Liu, and Zhengming Ding expose a blind spot in defenses for vision-based learning agents. Small image tweaks can mislead reinforcement learning policies, so defenses hardened against pixel-norm attacks report strong results. Closer inspection shows those attacks barely change what the image means, even with generous budgets.

Diffusion-guided perturbations instead alter the state semantics while staying plausible. Such attacks stress defenses where it hurts: meaning, not pixels. Robustness claims built on weak attacks give false comfort for agents heading into open worlds. The study urges evaluation with attacks that match how perception actually fails.
arxiv-2511-08001:
Avishav Engle and co-authors introduce Game Theoretic Nested Search for robot motion planning among other agents. Robots must predict how nearby drivers or robots will react, often without any direct communication. Nash equilibrium offers a principled target, but optimization methods get stuck locally and payoff tables explode as trajectories multiply.

Nested Search explores the joint action space while an inner search discards trajectories that break the equilibrium condition. The method is scalable and provably correct for general dynamical systems, and users can pick among equilibria with a global goal. In driving and racing tests, it found realistic interaction plans within seconds on ordinary hardware.
arxiv-2511-08201:
Zun-Yan Di and Zhi-Gang Wang calculate the strong decay of the exotic particle X(4140) into a J psi and a phi meson using light cone QCD sum rules. They treat X(4140) as an axial vector tetraquark, a four quark state with a specified arrangement of strange and charm quarks and antiquarks. Whether that picture is right can be tested against the measured decay width.

Extra parameters on the hadron side remove contamination from higher resonances and continuum states, giving stable sum rules. The computed width lands near one hundred forty five megaelectronvolts, with an uncertainty of about twenty one, close to the LHCb measurement. The agreement supports the proposed tetraquark assignment for this particle.
arxiv-2511-08401:
C Evans Hedges proves that training a model perfectly for its source task is generally the wrong move when the real goal is transfer to a new task. Transfer learning reuses a source model, and practitioners naturally tune it for source performance first. Working with L2-SP ridge regression, Hedges shows the source optimal regularization and the transfer optimal regularization differ outside a vanishingly special set of cases.

The transfer optimal penalty depends on task alignment. With imperfect alignment, stronger source regularization helps transfer, while in super aligned regimes weaker regularization wins instead. In isotropic settings, whether transfer helps at all depends only on alignment and source traits, not target sample size or noise. Experiments from synthetic data to image and text benchmarks support the mismatch.
arxiv-2511-08701:
Salah-Eddine Chorfi and three co-authors study inverse problems for a Schrödinger equation whose time derivative is fractional, using the Caputo derivative of order between zero and one. Inverse problems ask what can be recovered about a system from partial observations, and fractional time changes how memory of the past enters the dynamics.

The results are uniqueness theorems: under stated conditions, observations on sets of positive measure are enough to pin down the unknown quantities exactly. The authors refine earlier work by weakening the regularity demanded of the initial data, so rougher starting states are covered. Several variants of the recovery problem are treated within the same framework. The contribution is mathematical, aimed at researchers who need guarantees before trusting a reconstruction method.
arxiv-2511-09001:
Yuka Haruki and three co-authors match schemas and entities across messy enterprise datasets with graph embeddings that pay attention to context. Integration projects drown in manual matching, and earlier automation studies rarely asked how a dataset's own traits, its size, missing values, or overlap with another source, change which method wins.

The technique embeds structural details of tabular data together with column descriptions and external knowledge, so a column is represented by more than its values. Across datasets varying in domain specificity, size, missing rate, and overlap, it consistently beats existing graph-based methods, with the largest edges on numerically heavy or gap-riddled data. Genuine failures remain, notably columns that mean different things while looking semantically alike. Two lessons stand out: context improves matching reliability, and dataset characteristics must drive method choice.
arxiv-2511-09201:
Petros Galanopoulos and Daniel Girela characterize when a Rhaly operator stays bounded or compact on classical spaces of analytic functions. A Rhaly operator is built from a sequence of complex numbers, and the question is which sequences work. The spaces covered include Hardy spaces, Bergman spaces, and Dirichlet spaces on the unit disc.

Their conditions connect the operator to the generating function formed from the same sequence, through membership in mean Lipschitz spaces. For Hardy spaces with exponent at least two, sequences decaying like one over n always give bounded operators. Below two, the authors exhibit a sequence of that size whose operator fails to be bounded. They also settle maps between derivative-Hardy spaces, where boundedness and compactness coincide.
arxiv-2511-09401:
Chenyue Guo, Hongzheng Zhao, and Zi Cai study a driven magnet that is frustration-free at rest. They show frustration can appear in it on its own. Under periodic driving with heating suppressed, a classical spin system develops spin-ice physics. The action centers on magnetic monopoles, point-like excitations that wander through the material.

Unlike their equilibrium counterparts, these monopoles perform non-ergodic random walks with power-law waiting times, tunable through the effective temperature. Heating also varies wildly between initial states, again with long-tailed statistics, before the system eventually reaches infinite temperature. The authors trace both long tails to a drive-induced short-range attraction between monopoles. The results link driven magnets to glassy, history-dependent dynamics.
arxiv-2511-09701:
Dylan Possamaï and Mehdi Talbi develop optimal control theory for stochastic equations with memory. In these systems, today's change depends on the whole past path. Their Volterra integral diffusions allow general regular coefficients, not just convolution-type kernels. Memory breaks the usual Markov tools, so dynamic programming needs a new home.

The authors lift the equations into a Sobolev space, whose Hilbert structure supports a dynamic programming approach. In that setting, viscosity solution theory pins the value function as the unique solution of a parabolic equation on the space. Uses include time-inconsistent principal-agent contract problems, where memory and shifting preferences interact. A new Markovian approximation for Volterra dynamics emerges as a byproduct of the analysis.
arxiv-2511-10001:
Greg Hather and Daniel Aranki introduce mailing address aliasing, a privacy technique for online shopping. Shoppers must hand their home address to every merchant, and each copy can be misused, sold, or leaked. Post office boxes, physical or virtual, cut the risk but cost money, which limits adoption. Under aliasing, the customer gives the merchant an alias address that secretly maps to the real one.

Only the carrier sees the mapping, so merchants never learn where the customer lives. Comparing the options, the authors find aliasing likely reduces unsolicited mail more than box services do, and can offer lower cost with greater user control. The caveat is compatibility: some merchants' ordering systems may not accept alias addresses.
arxiv-2511-10101:
Takehiro Ishikawa, writing alone, models how growing forms can be steered by mixing central control with self-organization, a balance shared by embryos and embodied robots. The setup couples a compact convolutional controller to a differentiable Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion surface, a classic pattern-forming system. The controller watches two chemical fields and gently modulates the feed and kill rates that drive pattern growth.

Three regimes were compared: pure reaction-diffusion, a controller-dominant setup, and the hybrid. Only the hybrid converged fully, in about 165 steps, and it used roughly fifteen times less control effort than the dominant controller. Moderate modulation amplitudes formed a sweet spot with fast, reliable convergence. Ishikawa frames the lesson as seed then cede: nudge briefly, then let the material dynamics finish the pattern.
arxiv-2511-10301:
Dongwan Kim, Viresh Ranjan, Takashi Nagata, Arnab Dhua, and Amit Kumar K C rethink the LLaVA design for vision-language models. In that design, a language model reads visual features it was never built to encode. Their system, LLaViT, lets the language model double as an extended vision transformer. Three changes do the work: separate projection weights for the vision modality, bidirectional attention among visual tokens, and representations that carry both global and local visual detail.

Controlled tests across a range of language models showed LLaViT clearly beating the LLaVA baseline on many benchmarks. It even surpassed models with twice its parameter count in their tests. The authors present the dual-role design as a more effective route to vision-language modeling than bolting a foreign encoder onto a text model.
arxiv-2511-10501:
Georgios Chalkiadakis and four co-authors review three families of machine learning methods and how they might work together for modeling opponents in strategic multiagent settings. The methods are graph neural networks, deep reinforcement learning, and probabilistic topic modeling, tools usually built in separate research fields.

The review weighs how well each approach handles uncertainty, differences among agents, and growth to larger systems. The authors argue graph neural networks look most promising because agents and their relationships naturally form graphs. They also survey game theory solution ideas such as fairness and stability, and note where topic modeling has been used outside document analysis. Open problems include non-stationary environments, balancing stability against adaptation, and keeping solutions computable at scale.
arxiv-2511-10801:
Junellie Perez and five co-authors model how the interiors of the TRAPPIST-1 planets shape the atmospheres astronomers are now trying to observe. These rocky worlds around a cool dwarf star are prime targets, but reading their spectra right takes knowing their geological evolution first.

The team extended an atmosphere-interior exchange model with a carbon cycle, surface temperature estimates, oxygen fugacity as an interior input, oxidation chemistry, and escape physics. The model tracks four gases across mantle, crust, ocean, and atmosphere reservoirs. Validated on Earth, the model was applied to planets d, e, and f. Oxygen fugacity strongly influenced hydrogen and carbon dioxide levels, and the initial water inventory drove hydrogen abundance. The authors stress that interior values are key context for reading atmosphere observations.
arxiv-2511-11001:
Anindya Mukherjee and Pabitra Barik study where a special kind of bundle, called an Ulrich bundle, can be shown to exist. These bundles are tightly linked to the shape of a variety, a space defined by polynomial rules. The note starts from a smooth variety that already carries such a bundle.

From that start, the authors build a related sheaf on the space of unordered groups taken from the variety, even though that space can be singular. As a result, they get such a bundle on the space of point sets on a curve. They also treat the case of a blown-up product of a torus-like variety with itself.
arxiv-2511-11201:
Yongcheng Ding proposes a grating-based design for quantum optics with free electrons, where photons and electrons interact at the quantum level. Such setups could serve quantum information tasks, but a fully quantized treatment with practical gates has been missing. In the proposed design, electron-photon interactions map onto classic cavity models through a Bloch-Floquet analysis.

Within that frame, Ding designs ultrafast single- and two-qubit gates that use flying electrons and need no cavity. Those two gate types suffice for universal quantum computing in setups labs can reach. The author frames the work as a platform for probing free-electron quantum optics and for simulation, sensing, and information work.
arxiv-2511-11601:
Elliott Wen and ten co-authors run the first large empirical check of whether the same machine learning model behaves identically on AI chips from different makers. NVIDIA dominates cloud data centers, but AMD, Intel, Apple, and Huawei hardware is marketed as a compatible, cheaper alternative.

An automated pipeline built over one hundred thousand model variants from four thousand real models and ran them on five enterprise accelerators. Newer non-NVIDIA platforms supported noticeably fewer operators, and output mismatches above five percent appeared, traced to operator implementations, handling of extreme numerical values, and instruction differences. Teams porting models between vendors now have measured evidence of where silent divergence creeps in.
arxiv-2511-11901:
Kostiantyn Drach and Kateryna Tatarko settle a conjecture of K. Bezdek about the shape of lambda-convex bodies, sets formed by intersecting balls of a fixed radius. Among all such bodies with a given inradius, meaning a given largest inscribed ball, which one is widest on average?

The answer is the lambda-convex lens, the intersection of just two balls. Mean width is maximized by that simplest shape, giving the conjecture an affirmative answer in every dimension from two up. Under an added symmetry assumption, the analogous statements for general intrinsic volumes and for circumradius are also resolved. Extremal problems of this kind pin down the geometry of a whole class through one clean example.
arxiv-2511-12001:
Eunkyu Park and six co-authors warn that chain-of-thought explanations can make users more compliant, not more critical. Explanations are sold as transparency tools, yet a fluent rationale invites readers to assume the reasoning is right whenever the answer looks acceptable, a confirmation bias with safety consequences.

Vision-language models answer multimodal moral scenarios while the team perturbs their reasoning chains and varies delivery tone. Users equate trust with agreeing with the outcome, keeping their reliance even when reasoning is flawed, and a confident tone suppresses error detection further. Designing explanation interfaces that preserve skepticism, rather than polish it away, is the practical challenge the results pose.
arxiv-2511-12201:
Feng Chen and eleven co-authors introduce OmniSparse, a sparse attention method for language models that process long videos. Attention over long video is costly, and most sparse methods act only at inference, picking key tokens by fixed patterns. That leaves a gap between training and use, and token choice is often coarse.

OmniSparse works in both training and inference, with budgets that adapt. It keeps active queries that carry broad meaning, drops most lazy local ones, and selects key-value pairs with a shared budget set at head level. It also trims the key-value cache to cut redundancy. Together these steps aim for faster long-video models without losing key detail.
arxiv-2511-12601:
Odysseas Boufalis and four co-authors build an autoencoder framework that aligns neural networks which differ only by symmetries of their parameters, such as reordering hidden units or rescaling them. Equivalent networks sit at different points in parameter space, which blocks simple merging by averaging weights. Earlier work handled permutation symmetry through a costly assignment search.

Their method uses graph metanetworks as invariant encoders. Those networks respect both permutation and scaling symmetries. Similar networks thus land in the same basin. No assignment problem needs to be solved to get that result. Once aligned, networks can be merged by smooth interpolation that avoids high-loss regions. Tests cover implicit neural representations and CNNs, two families where such merging is valuable in practice.
arxiv-2511-12901:
Yuesheng Xu and Hector Munoz-Avila teach a planning chatbot to stop asking for help with the same problems. Their system builds on ChatHTN, a planner that breaks tasks into subtasks using hierarchical task network methods, and calls ChatGPT when no stored method fits. The new work adds online learning: when the language model produces a decomposition, the planner generalizes and stores it as a method. Similar future tasks are solved without another call to the model.

Unlike simple memoization, the learned method applies to other instances of the same task, not just the case that triggered it. Experiments in two domains showed the learner cut the number of ChatGPT calls while solving at least as many problems, and sometimes more. The work appeared at a cognitive systems conference. It points toward hybrid planners that use a language model as a teacher whose lessons are kept, checked, and reused.
arxiv-2511-13001:
Pengcheng Shi and five co-authors present Medal S, a foundation model that segments medical scans from either words or marks, at full resolution. Text-only prompting lacks spatial precision, while rescaling volumes to fit prompts introduces errors. Medal S aligns volumetric prompts with text embeddings channel by channel, keeps the full 3D context, and refines results in voxel space with a lightweight convolutional module guided by both prompt types. It handles up to two hundred forty-three classes across CT, MRI, PET, ultrasound, and microscopy in its training dataset.

Two modes are offered: text-only, where the model's own predictions become prompts for self-refinement, and hybrid, where a clinician's annotations join in. Parallel prompting cut inference time by over ninety percent versus sequential prompting on a twenty-four-class task, and Medal S clearly outperformed the SAT baseline on the validation average.
arxiv-2511-13301:
Lisa Lehner, Christian Komusiewicz, and Luca Pascal Staus analyze how hard it is to delete few vertices so a graph becomes c-closed. A graph earns that label when any two non-neighbors share at most c minus one common neighbors. The question is which graphs can be fixed by removing at most k vertices.

Among their findings is NP-hardness even for bipartite graphs with bounded degree, plus upper and lower bounds on kernel size for the parameter k. They add a new parameter based on bad pairs and give a kernel for it. Special graph classes fare better: unit interval graphs allow a fast exact method in a stated range.
arxiv-2511-13501:
Solmaz Golmohammadi, Mina Zarei, and Jacopo Grilli model how predator and prey cycles fall into step across linked patches of habitat. Each patch follows Rosenzweig-MacArthur dynamics, with animals dispersing between patches and births and deaths adding random noise. Spatial synchrony matters because aligned crashes can threaten whole ecosystems at once.

Gillespie simulations capture the noisy patch dynamics, while analytic tools borrowed from the XY model of magnetism describe the phases of each cycle. Together they reveal how noise and migration drive patches toward or away from shared timing. The results give a theory base for reading large-scale ecological synchrony and judging ecosystem resilience.
arxiv-2511-14301:
Eric Xue, Ruiyi Zhang, and Pengtao Xie build a backdoor attack designed to slip past data-poisoning defenses. Fine-tuned transformer models can be secretly taught to misbehave when a trigger appears, and defenses have grown good at spotting crude triggers. SteganoBackdoor instead starts from natural semantic trigger seeds and rewrites them token by token.

Each replacement reduces overlap with the trigger used at inference time while keeping a strong training-time payload, and the payload is spread across ordinary fluent tokens so no single token betrays it. Across eighteen encoder and decoder models, the attack succeeded at sub-percent poisoning budgets and exposed real limits in current defenses.
arxiv-2511-14801:
Jonas Länzlinger, Katharina Müller, and two co-authors present IHearYou, a system that links the sound of a person's voice to clinical signs of depression. Diagnosis today leans on self-reports and interviews, which can miss how someone actually behaves at home. IHearYou listens passively in household settings and extracts acoustic features from everyday speech.

Those features are tied, through a structured linkage framework, to the indicators listed in the DSM-5 manual for major depressive disorder. The system runs locally to protect privacy and shows live results on an ordinary laptop dashboard. Careful testing rules, with corrections for false discoveries, are built in so other teams can reproduce the findings.
arxiv-2511-15101:
Ashutosh Srivastava, Nikhilesh Maiity, and Abhishek Kumar Singh compute how heat flows through a two-layer sheet of rhenium disulfide, a puckered two-dimensional material. Because the layers cling to each other only weakly, the crystal conducts heat unevenly along its two in-plane directions. The team uses first-principles quantum calculations to compare the two natural stacking orders of the bilayer.

Both stackings show a mild directional imbalance in thermal conductivity, and that imbalance survives heating all the way to very high temperatures. The lower-symmetry stacking scatters sound waves inside the crystal more strongly, which slows heat further. Direction-aware heat flow like this matters for tiny electronics that must shed heat along chosen paths.
arxiv-2511-15201:
Qing Wang, Chong-Wah Ngo, and Ee-Peng Lim tackle a bias in systems that match a food photo to its recipe. A recipe causes the dish, but a photo never shows every step or ingredient equally: cooking, plating, and camera angle all hide detail. Standard training treats the recipe as a flat description of the picture, so models latch onto the most visible matches and miss subtle cues that decide the right pairing.

The authors model that mismatch with causal theory, separating what the image truly shows from what the recipe merely says. Learning then corrects for the misleading pull of dominant alignments. The causal framing should make recipe retrieval fairer to dishes whose photos understate their contents.
arxiv-2511-15601:
Giorgos Michailidis and ten co-authors localize the site of a major gamma ray flare in the blazar TXS 2013+370. Blazars are active galaxies whose jets point near our line of sight. This source flared exceptionally in late 2020 and early 2021. The team combine full polarization radio interferometry at three high frequencies with radio and gamma ray monitoring.

Images reveal a compact knot near the core at the time of the flare. The core shows strong linear polarization and a large rotation in polarization angle at the highest frequency. A high, uniform rotation measure points to an external Faraday screen. Gamma rays lead radio variations in cross correlation. Together the data pin down inner jet structure and magnetic topology during outburst.
arxiv-2511-15801:
Luca Chiantini, Łucja Farnik, and five co-authors ask how many points two distinct curves in four-dimensional projective space can share. Both curves have given degrees, neither pair lies in a flat hyperplane, and the question asks for the largest possible intersection count. The plane case is trivial and the three-dimensional case was solved in the nineteen eighties, with extremal curves lying on a quadric surface.

The authors define a bound from the two degrees and prove it when both curves lie on a surface of minimal degree, here a cubic surface. They conjecture the bound always holds and prove it in many cases, including when at least one curve is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay, a strong algebraic regularity condition.
arxiv-2511-16001:
Insang Yoo and three co-authors design waveguide fed metasurfaces for shaping near fields using a coupled dipole model. These radiating systems load waveguides with subwavelength metamaterial apertures. Distributed elements allow field control with subwavelength precision across the aperture. Near field patterns can thus be tailored for imaging, sensing, or wireless power uses.

The coupled dipole model accounts for mutual links between radiating elements during design. Full wave runs and X band tests verify the approach. Predicted near fields match measured patterns well enough for design purposes. Model based design is far faster than blind full wave tuning. The work gives engineers a practical tool for programming near field landscapes with metasurface hardware.
arxiv-2511-16201:
Niki van Stein, Anna V. Kononova, and Thomas Bäck argue that automated algorithm design needs explanation, not just performance. Large language models can now generate full optimization heuristics. They can also search vast design spaces and adapt through feedback. Yet that progress is opaque. Rarely does anyone learn why a generated algorithm works, which parts matter, or how choices relate to problem structure.

Their vision rests on three pillars. First, language-model-driven discovery makes algorithmic variants. Second, explainable benchmarking attributes performance to parts and settings. Third, problem-class descriptors connect algorithm behavior to landscape structure. Together they form a closed knowledge loop where discovery, explanation, and generalization reinforce each other, shifting the field toward interpretable, class-specific design.
arxiv-2511-16301:
Minseok Seo, Mark Hamilton, and Changick Kim introduce Upsample Anything, a method that raises low-resolution feature maps from vision foundation models to full pixel resolution without any training. Such models shrink their features by a factor of fourteen or sixteen, which blocks direct use in pixel-level tasks, and earlier upsamplers need retraining or heavy optimization.

The method runs a short per-image optimization that learns an anisotropic Gaussian kernel mixing position and value cues, bridging Gaussian splatting and joint bilateral upsampling. The learned kernel works across architectures and data types, sharpening features, depth, and probability maps alike. It runs in well under a second per image and reached top results on segmentation and depth tests, making it a strong, simple baseline.
arxiv-2511-16401:
Yi Yao works on quantizing stability in Kähler geometry, following Donaldson's insight that constant scalar curvature metrics correspond to balanced norms on spaces of sections. The setting here is the unstable case, where a polarized manifold admits no such metric and the question becomes what destabilizes it most strongly.

For large embeddings, a projective embedding of an unstable manifold is Chow-unstable, with a unique maximal destabilizing filtration on its section space. K-stability has its own maximal destabilizer as well, the steepest descent direction of the K-energy. Yao uses non-Archimedean pluripotential theory of Boucksom and Jonsson, plus stated assumptions. He lays out a route to prove the maximal K-destabilizer is quantized by the maximal Chow-destabilizers, linking the two notions of worst instability.
arxiv-2511-16601:
Amandip Sangha shows that the curvature of a Riemannian manifold can be read off from how heat spreads on it for very short times. Fix a point and a two-plane in the tangent space, then compare the heat mass carried along that plane with the Euclidean case, using relative entropy as the measuring stick.

The leading small-time distortion of this directional entropy encodes exactly the local curvature. The planar imbalance determines both scalar and sectional curvature, and collecting the values over all planes assembles a tensor that coincides with the classical Riemann curvature operator. No Jacobi fields or variational formulas are used; curvature appears purely as a tiny information defect of diffusion, opening a fresh analytic bridge between geometry and information theory.
arxiv-2511-17501:
Weiwei Cai and nine co-authors present a framework for editing three-dimensional objects by instruction, working natively in 3D rather than through pictures. Editing 3D content by text command could widen access to 3D creation, but optimization-based methods are prohibitively slow. Methods that edit multiple 2D views and lift the results back often produce inconsistent geometry. This system manipulates the 3D representation directly in a single feed-forward pass.

To train it, the team built a large multimodal dataset of addition, deletion, and modification edits, curated so changes follow the instruction while untouched regions stay faithful to the source. They compared two ways of conditioning the model and found a 3D token concatenation strategy both cheaper in parameters and better in performance. Evaluations show the method beating 2D-lifting approaches on quality, consistency, and instruction fidelity.
arxiv-2511-17701:
Alisa Galishnikova, Hayk Hakobyan, Alexander Philippov, and Benjamin Crinquand introduce the general relativity module of Entity, a free particle in cell code for plasmas around black holes. Near black holes, jets and hot coronae hold magnetized gas with almost no collisions, in very strong gravity.

The new module lets Entity model such gas in curved space while staying open, flexible in coordinates, and fast on modern graphics and central processors. It supports two dimensional symmetric simulations around black holes. The work extends the Entity project from special to general relativity for studies of particle heating and jets.
arxiv-2511-17801:
Cuong Pham, Hoang Anh Dung, Cuong Nguyen, Trung Le, Gustavo Carneiro, and Thanh-Toan Do tackle shrinking large language models by quantization, which stores weights with fewer bits. At very low bit counts, accuracy falls mainly because a few high impact weights are handled poorly.

Earlier methods kept a fixed share of such weights in each layer at full precision. The new framework chooses a share per layer through an optimization that accounts for links between layers. It gives high impact weights a moderate bit width and pushes the rest very low, balancing speed, memory, and accuracy under a fixed budget.
arxiv-2511-18001:
Jiaolong Kong, Xiaofei Xie, Yiheng Xiong, Yuekun Wang, and Jian Wang improve automated program repair with language models. Existing tools rely on coarse outside feedback such as test results, which does not show which part of a proposed patch is wrong, so refinement wastes effort and spreads errors.

Their TokenRepair system first looks inside the model, using token level uncertainty to flag suspicious tokens in a patch, and rewrites only those with guided reasoning. A quality check then filters weak candidates before the next round. On two Java bug benchmarks it fixes more bugs than prior methods, with gains across all models tested.
arxiv-2511-18301:
Harsh Rathva, Pruthwik Mishra, and Shrikant Malviya describe their team's entry to a shared task on detecting hallucinations in multilingual scientific text generated by language models. Most entrants focused on model architecture, while this team took a data centric route, since training data for the task were scarce and unbalanced across nine languages.

They merged and balanced five current data sets into a large, evenly split corpus of correct and hallucinated samples, far larger than the original training set. They then fine tuned a multilingual transformer on it. The system placed competitively in every language and second in a language it had never seen in training.
arxiv-2511-18401:
Jean Gutt, Vinicius G. B. Ramos, and Shira Tanny finish a spectral test for two special kinds of flow. The flows run on the rim of a star shaped region in even dimensional space. A flow is called Besse if all its paths close, and Zoll if they all close with the same period, like laps on a track.

A set of numbers called capacities, drawn from the flow, can detect each kind. The team show a flow is Besse just when a set of these numbers all match. It is Zoll just when the first block of them match. The result ends a program begun by three earlier authors. Such tests link shape, motion, and spectrum in one clean rule.
arxiv-2511-18601:
Wenchao Ma, Dario Kneubuehler, Maurice Chu, Ian Sachs, Haomiao Jiang, and Sharon Xiaolei Huang auto rig facial meshes of any layout. A rig bends a neutral face mesh into the standard pose set coded by the FACS system, so animators can drive expressions. Mesh layouts vary, and some faces come in split parts, which breaks tools built for one fixed layout.

RigAnyFace learns surface shape in a layout blind way, with design tweaks to read FACS controls and handle split parts. Training pairs pro rigged faces, a small costly set, with a 2D watch scheme for the far larger unlabeled stock. That mix scales learning past the hand rigged core. Diverse faces can then be rigged with no hand work.
arxiv-2511-18701:
Mustafa Munir and eight co-authors build ObjectAlign, a checker that finds and fixes object flaws in edited video. Edits can make an object flicker or drift in identity across frames, which spoils the watch. Their frame blends learned perceptual scores with formal symbolic checks.

Thresholds for four consistency scores are learned from data: sense match, perceptual gap, color histogram match, and mask overlap. A verifier then pairs a formal solver check, which pledges no identity drift on masked object codes, with a time fidelity check based on chance. Fails can be flagged and sent for correction. The mix aims for proof grade checks where pure scores give only hunches. Edited and synthetic video both stand to gain.
arxiv-2511-18901:
Boquan Chen and three co-authors constrain how the Milky Way's earliest proto galaxy formed by studying its most metal poor stars. The chemical pattern of old stars records how much cold gas the young Galaxy held, how fast gas flowed in, and how efficiently it formed stars. Those factors trade off against each other.

Using metallicity catalogs built from Gaia spectra, they measure the slope of the metal poor tail of the distribution. Chemical evolution models matching that slope favor a moderate initial gas reservoir, sustained by weak steady inflow, with star formation efficiency much like today's during the first billion years. Simulated Milky Way analogs show similar tails.
arxiv-2511-19001:
Ram Dhari Pandey, Marta Galynska, Katharina Boguslawski, and Pawel Tecmer tune charge transfer in carbazole based organic dyes by doping the bridge. Such dyes split into donor, bridge, and acceptor parts; light moves charge across them in a set direction. Their method, built on localized orbitals of a pair coupled cluster model, tracks that flow by domain and grades it.

A dye series is doped at three bridge spots with nitrogen, oxygen, or sulfur, in one, two, or three places. Forward transfer from donor through bridge to acceptor grows in a progressive way as nitrogen or oxygen doping rises. For single doping, a heteroatom at the terminal bridge spot gives the highest forward flow in their runs. Dye design gains a dial with a readout.
arxiv-2511-19201:
Ann-Sophia Muller, Moonkwang Jeong, Jiyuan Tian, Meng Zhang, and Tian Qiu design an array of permanent magnets that stably traps a tiny biomedical robot in a plane, for minimally invasive surgical uses. Permanent magnets pull harder than coils at a distance, but a classic theorem forbids a stable static trap in three dimensions, and feedback control is harder.

Their two dimensional trap floats in open space at a tunable distance suited to human anatomy scales. A graphics processor accelerated optimization finds the best magnet angles fast, scaling to one hundred magnets in seconds. Simulations and experiments with a two magnet array trap a millirobot and steer it along a complex path.
arxiv-2511-19401:
Gongfan Fang, Xinyin Ma, and Xinchao Wang test a new control channel for video generation: instructions drawn inside the frames themselves. Text prompts describe a scene globally and coarsely, which makes it hard to tell one object to do one thing and another object something else. Their paradigm, In-Video Instruction, embeds guidance in the visual domain instead, as overlaid text, arrows, or drawn trajectories placed right on the subjects they concern, giving explicit, spatially precise commands.

Modern video models already predict future frames that respect the logic and physics of what they see, and the team harnesses that skill to follow the drawn instructions. Experiments span three leading commercial generators. The results suggest a future where directing a generated video feels less like writing a prompt and more like sketching on a storyboard.
arxiv-2511-19601:
Juan Pablo Gatica and Callum R. T. Jones model how spinning compact bodies, such as black holes, absorb radiation while scattering off each other. The approach works with scattering amplitudes, the core quantities of particle physics, and pushes quantum results with finite spin toward the classical large-spin limit. Spin universality and Casimir interpolation make that jump controlled.

Absorptive effects are packaged into a finite set of Wilson coefficients tied to simple three-particle processes the authors call classical spin transitions. Explicit formulas give the leading push from absorbing scalar, electromagnetic, and gravitational radiation, for spin changes up to two units. Surprising universal patterns appear across the results.
arxiv-2511-19701:
Paulin Aubert, Etienne Chevalier, and Vathana Ly Vath solve an insurer's money problem: when to pay dividends and when to inject capital. Claims arrive in clusters, modeled by a self-exciting Hawkes process inside a classic Cramér-Lundberg risk model. Clustering is common in real portfolios and changes the optimal policy.

The authors characterize the best capital injection rule through an explicit threshold and prove the value function is the unique well-behaved solution of the governing inequality. A finite-difference benchmark is matched by a reinforcement learning method using policy gradients and actor-critic training. The learned policies stay stable across starting reserves.
arxiv-2511-19801:
Olivia Liebman, Jonathan B. Curtis, Emily Been, and Prineha Narang study excitons in two stacked layers of MnBi2Te4, a magnetic topological material tied to axion physics. An exciton pairs an electron with a hole, and here excitons in separate layers may condense into a shared quantum state. The layers are gapped by the material's own magnetic order.

Mean-field theory maps when a spin-singlet exciton condensate forms, tuned by an electric displacement field, temperature, and Coulomb pull. Beyond that, many-body methods give the collective mode spectrum and the exciton spectral function. Mode softening tracks the contest between layer detuning and heat, offering signatures experiments can look for.
arxiv-2511-19901:
Subhasis Nalui and Subhra Bhattacharya design wormhole solutions inside a modified theory of gravity called f(R) gravity. They use the Morris-Thorne wormhole metric with uneven matter described by a new linear equation of state. The goal is to solve the field equations for both the wormhole shape and the gravity model at once.

They obtain four wormhole models supported by four power-law versions of f(R) gravity. Some have a solid angle deficit, most cannot be extended without limit, and one is flat far away with zero tidal force. The models are checked for cosmological sense, restated in scalar-tensor form, and probed with photon spheres, whose link to a complexity factor matches the pattern in Einstein's gravity.
arxiv-2511-20201:
Brilli, Mallis, Pitsikalis, and Maragos answer video questions through human-centered scene graphs. Their 2025 paper presents GHR-VQA for video question answering. Pixel-based methods struggle to reason about interactions. Videos center on humans acting on objects over time. Questions usually probe exactly those relations.

Each frame becomes a scene graph of entities and links. Human nodes across frames connect to one global root. That yields a single video-level graph for reasoning. Graph neural networks turn it into rich embeddings. Question features merge inside a hierarchical network. Different abstraction levels handle local and global clues. Tests used the AGQA dataset of action questions. Object-relation reasoning improved by 7.3 percent over the prior best. The gain beat the previous state of the art clearly. Graph steps can be inspected and explained afterward. Perception and reasoning stay cleanly separated modules.
arxiv-2511-20301:
Hu, Doneva, Yazadjiev, and Shao simulate black hole mergers in a modified gravity theory. Their 2025 paper studies ringdown in scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity. After two black holes merge, the remnant rings like a bell. That ringing decomposes into quasi-normal modes. Mode frequencies fingerprint the final black hole.
