Amplitudes and phases depend on the merging pair instead. Computing them needs full nonlinear simulations. The team ran mergers in shift-symmetric scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity. A scalarization-allowing variant was simulated as well. Extracted frequencies matched perturbative theory predictions. Polar and axial mode frequencies split in this theory. Excitation changes stayed surprisingly small overall. The dominant mode shifted by only about two percent. Worst-case modes deviated near ten percent. The largest coupling used neared the theory's validity edge. Frequency deviations grew with coupling squared, as predicted.
arxiv-2511-20601:
Shakeri names a failure of glucose forecasting models: they ignore what drives glucose. His 2025 paper calls the pattern driver-blindness. Insulin, meals, and activity plainly move blood sugar in the body. Deep sequence models get those signals as inputs too. Yet adding them barely improves forecasts over glucose history alone.

A metric called delta-drivers measures that missing gain directly. Across the literature the gain sits near zero in study after study. Three causes interact to produce the blindness. Model designs favor copying the recent past of the target itself. Driver data arrive noisy, mistimed, and confounded in practice. Bodies differ so much that population models wash out individual patterns. Fixes include physiology-based feature encoders for the drivers. Causal regularization and per-person personalization also help partly. The paper urges journals to require the delta-drivers number. Driver-blind models should not pass as state of the art.
arxiv-2511-20701:
Nitya Tiwari, Parv Maheshwari, and Vidisha Agarwal ask in 2025 whether a reasoning method that shines on science questions survives broader topics. The method, Multimodal Chain-of-Thought, first writes out a short rationale, then infers the final answer from it. Image features enter a T5 language model through a gated fusion step. The method had set records on the ScienceQA benchmark, so the team carried it to three different datasets.

They tested A-OKVQA and OKVQA, which demand commonsense and world knowledge about images. They also tested ChartQA, which asks questions about data charts. Ablation studies, removing one part at a time, showed that vision features significantly reduced invented details in the rationales. Even so, reasoning quality swung widely by question type. Commonsense questions proved the hardest to handle well. The authors close with practical guidance for builders of multimodal reasoning systems and the weak points where generalisation still fails.
arxiv-2511-20901:
Andrea Bonito, Alan Demlow, and Joshua M. Siktar study in 2025 how to solve a Poisson equation when its boundary values are unknown. The missing information is replaced by a finite set of point measurements taken inside the domain, a setup arising in inverse heat conduction, fluid dynamics, and wind engineering. An earlier finite element algorithm handled measurements anywhere, including on the boundary. Restricting sensors to the interior lowers the smoothness demanded of the solution, widening the method's reach.

The recovery works through Riesz representers, one per measurement, which the finite element method must approximate. The paper's main result bounds the error of those representers pointwise, sharper than what was known. Feeding it into the recovery analysis improves the algorithm's error bounds in several norms, including uniform control on interior subdomains. The estimates quantify exactly how sensor placement and mesh quality govern reconstruction accuracy when boundary data cannot be had.
arxiv-2511-21101:
Manish Jain and colleagues at Firstsource build in 2025 MortgageLLM, a language model specialised for mortgage finance without losing its manners. Domain pretraining usually erodes instruction-following. Their fix has two parts. An instruction residual, the weight difference that encodes instruction skill, is transferred back into the domain-adapted model. And instead of one compromise model, they train two experts from the LLaMA 3.1 8B base: a conversational question-answerer tuned for dialogue, and a structured-task expert handling classification and summarisation, with a router sending each query to the right expert.

On mortgage benchmarks, the final model beat the base instruct model on every judge score: summarisation rose to 4.58 from 3.99, question answering to 4.09 from 4.0, and classification more than doubled, reaching 2.6 against a baseline of 1.2 on the same scale. BERTScore semantic similarity also improved across all three tasks. The recipe targets other regulated industries facing the same specialisation trade-off.
arxiv-2511-21401:
Antonín Jarolím, Martin Fajčík, and Lucia Makaiová test whether language models can pull courtroom-grade receipts for fact-checkers, in 2025. False claims flourish in comments under news articles, and rebutting them takes pinpoint evidence: the exact span of text that supports or refutes a claim. The team built a new dataset of Czech and Slovak claims with fine-grained evidence spans, each sample annotated twice by paid annotators.

Jarolím and his coauthors find that models often fail to copy evidence verbatim, inventing or trimming text and producing invalid outputs. Size is no guarantee: the small llama3.1 model with 8 billion parameters earned a high share of correct outputs, while the far larger gpt-oss-120b underperformed. Mid-sized qwen3:14b, deepseek-r1:32b, and gpt-oss:20b balanced size and agreement with humans best, measured by token-level F1 matching against the double annotations.
arxiv-2511-21601:
Meilakhs derives the central equation of gas kinetics from quantum mechanics in one clean sweep, in a 2025 foundations paper. Classical mechanics is usually pulled from the Schrödinger equation through wave-packet limits or decoherence arguments. The Boltzmann equation's two halves, free flight and collisions, are typically glued together with plausible but loose reasoning. His method avoids the patchwork.

The derivation passes through the Liouville equation, the law for how densities flow, by a route in line with the quantum theory of transition rates. The collision-free part of the Boltzmann equation then follows from Liouville, while the collision term follows from the rate matrix. Together they deliver the full Boltzmann equation out of the Schrödinger equation in a single piece of formal math. The same machinery reproduces the main formulas of kinetics, suggesting the bridge from quantum dynamics to the classical theory is shorter than textbooks suggest.
arxiv-2511-21901:
Huwyler builds a standardized taxonomy for AI threats, letting security engineers and lawyers share one language. Technical teams use frameworks like MITRE ATLAS, while regulators work from the EU AI Act, NIST guidance, and similar rules. The mismatch leaves firms unable to price AI risk, set reserves, or justify security controls financially. It is built for quantitative risk assessment.

The framework sorts AI-specific risks into nine domains, including misuse, poisoning, privacy, adversarial attacks, bias, unreliable outputs, drift, supply chain, and intellectual property threats. There are 53 operationally defined sub-threats in total across the whole scheme for practitioners. Each domain maps directly onto business loss categories such as legal and reputation damage. Validated against 133 documented AI incidents from 2025, it achieved 100 percent classification coverage, and it aligns with ISO/IEC 42001 and NIST framework functions for audits.
arxiv-2511-22001:
Isztl, Spitznagel, Somfai, and Santos are ophthalmology researchers in Zürich. They ask whether large domain-specific foundation models earn their cost in retinal imaging. They benchmark 12–13 model configurations across four classification tasks spanning OCT scans and color fundus photographs: eight-class OCT, diabetic macular edema, diabetic retinopathy grading, and glaucoma detection.

Pretraining always helped, with accuracy gains running from 5.18 to 18.41 percentage points and larger benefits on harder tasks and fundus photos than on OCT. Compact models of 27–29 million parameters dominated the accuracy-versus-size frontier. SwinV2-tiny reached top-two performance on all four datasets. All models were trained under identical conditions so the comparison isolates initialization and architecture alone. The 303-million-parameter RETFound justified itself only on the diabetic retinopathy grading, reaching 71.15 percent accuracy, while ImageNet pretraining sufficed elsewhere, hitting 99.24 percent on edema and 97.96 percent on OCT classes.
arxiv-2511-22101:
Zhang, a researcher, reports a replication and extension of a study that used deep reinforcement learning to provide liquidity on Uniswap V3. Uniswap V3 is the decentralized cryptocurrency exchange where liquidity providers choose price ranges for their funds. The original system is an adaptive dueling double deep Q-network trained on ETH/USDC and ETH/USDT pool data pulled from the Uniswap Subgraph. It reportedly beat its baselines on gas costs, earned fees, loss-versus-rebalancing, and profit and loss over 2021 to 2023 data.

Zhang rebuilds the pipeline, documenting data collection and choices, then proposes Mamba-DDQN, swapping in a Mamba sequence model alongside the dueling double Q-network and a redesigned reward function. Zhang uses cleaned data and two new baselines for comparison. The extended model shows stronger support and better baseline-test performance, though it has not been run across datasets, and the report reflects on stages.
arxiv-2511-22201:
Guo, Zhu, Yu, and colleagues defend radar against its hardest jamming case. Mainlobe jamming pours interference straight into the receiver's main beam, exactly where targets of interest live, so spatial filtering tricks that work on sidelobe jamming distort the signal or fail. Their DMDD approach splits the problem by nature. The structured jamming is learned from pure jamming recordings by a score-based diffusion model that can sample realistic jamming on demand, while the targets. Sparse in range, are estimated with sparse Bayesian learning.

Expectation-maximization updates the hyperparameters and even the noise variance. Because only the jamming gets a diffusion process while target states come from direct posterior inference, the method stays computationally leaner than fully diffusion-based rivals. In simulations DMDD suppresses false alarms more effectively and detects multiple targets better than existing methods under structured mainlobe jamming, .
arxiv-2511-22301:
Zwonek, a complex analyst in Poland, examines left inverses in the Lempert theorem, a cornerstone result saying that in nicely convex domains in complex space. Two competing notions of distance, built from holomorphic maps into and out of the disc, coincide. Equality is witnessed by complex geodesics, disc maps that realize the distance; a left inverse is a map back from the domain to the disc undoing a geodesic. The paper studies special Lempert left inverses whose fibers are cut out by affine hyperplanes.

The paper asks whether they exist, are unique, and extend through the boundary. The work refines the theory of Lempert domains. The taut domains where the distance equality holds, clarifying what the equality's witnesses can and cannot do at the edge of the domain. The work sits in the invariant-metric tradition descending from Lempert's original breakthrough.
arxiv-2511-22501:
Nogales, Luz-Burgoa, and Martins build a cosmology in modified gravity where matter can be created by gravity itself. Rastall's gravity lets the energy-momentum tensor fail to be conserved, in proportion to how curvature changes, unlike Einstein's theory. The authors propose a Rastall-like version derived from a proper Lagrangian, then study its thermodynamics, treating particle production as an irreversible process in an open system.

Within this framework they construct a bouncing universe: instead of beginning in a Big Bang singularity, the cosmos contracts, reaches a smallest size, and expands again, possibly in cycles. The bounce needs the null energy condition violated near the turning point, and their model accommodates that without breaking consistency. They also show regimes where entropy per particle stays constant, mimicking adiabatic evolution, and check stability via the speed of sound. Observational tests are left for future work.
arxiv-2511-22701:
Spera, Yeomans, and Thampi show that a quiet fluid layer beneath an active one smooths away small-scale chaos. Active nematic fluids, driven by molecular motors, develop active turbulence, chaotic swirling across scales. The authors model such a layer coupled by friction to an ordinary isotropic liquid substrate and simulate what the substrate inherits. The substrate does become turbulent, driven by random forcing from above, but only at larger scales.

Short-scale structures are filtered out: the system acts as a de facto low-pass filter. The authors derive the layers' transfer function analytically and use it to predict the large-wavevector decay of the substrate's energy spectrum. It also predicts how tensorial quantities such as strain rate and stress transmit, including a misalignment between substrate strain and active fields. The analysis matches recent microtubule experiments and matters for traction force microscopy, where cell stresses are inferred from the substrate.
arxiv-2511-22801:
Kato and colleagues explain an optical effect in the mineral Co2SiO4. The mineral is an antiferromagnet, and it hosts a magnetic toroidal monopole. They differ from plain monopoles in how they act when space or time is reversed. A recent test saw an electric field change how the mineral absorbs light by direction. That was the first case of a magnetic toroidal monopole. Its cause at the atomic scale stayed unclear.

The team builds a spin model for the mineral, with cobalt and oxygen linked by shared electrons. The model matches the measured dielectric constant and how it shifts with heat and field direction. It also tracks how the toroidal monopole and its moment change with heat. It predicts a second-order nonlinear response, in line with the mineral's class as an altermagnet. The same approach should extend to sister olivines with like magnetic order.
arxiv-2511-22901:
Ravishankar separates the two halves of an Ahmad pair, an obstruction in the enumeration degrees. A pair of sets forms an Ahmad pair when the first is not reducible to the second, yet everything strictly below the first is reducible to the second. Such pairs block attempts to extend embeddings of partial orders. Earlier work characterised them only partially.

Working in the Sigma-2-0 enumeration degrees, Ravishankar characterises the left halves: precisely the degrees that are low-3 and join irreducible. The right half must be high-2, a separation significantly strengthening previous results. A hierarchy of join irreducibility notions extends this to Ahmad n-pairs, left halves low-3 and n-join irreducible, right halves high-2. For every n some set is the left half of an n-pair but not of an n-plus-one pair. The results also yield new definability consequences, including definitions of the low-3 and high-2 classes.
arxiv-2511-23201:
Azim and colleagues propose a channel model for integrated sensing and communication, the 6G idea of using one radio system both to send data and to sense objects like a radar. Their framework splits the bistatic channel in two, a target channel carrying reflection off the sensed object, described by its radar cross-section and scattering points. The background channel is for all other paths.

The model is built as an extension of the standard 3GPP TR 38.901 model with hybrid clustering that mixes deterministic and stochastic path clusters. It keeps communication performance on par with the standard in bit-error rate and capacity across urban macro, urban micro, and indoor factory scenarios. At the same time it unlocks sensing evaluation the standard cannot do, including target ranging error for localization and detection-probability curves, cross-checked against simulated and measured channels.
arxiv-2511-23401:
Bellah and colleagues advance the strong approximation conjecture for the Markoff equation, the claim that every solution modulo a prime p lifts to an integer solution. Progress comes from studying the graph of mod p solutions under the Vieta group action. Where solutions in the connected component called the cage are known to lift. And the authors use Pisano periods of the Fibonacci sequence to place points into that cage.

For Mersenne primes congruent to plus or minus 2 modulo 5, they show the point (1,1,1), which is fixed under reduction modulo p. Lies in the cage, and that any mod p solution whose matrix has order at least p plus 1 possesses an integer lift. They also bound how often this can happen, proving the density of such primes is below one half while numerical experiments suggest it is roughly 40 percent.
arxiv-2512-00101:
The classic birthday problem asks how many people are needed before two likely share a birthday. Chijul Tripathy introduces a variant in 2025, called the Bottleneck Birthday Problem. The twist limits how many birthdays may fall on any single day.

The problem asks for the largest group one can choose under that limit. No day of the year may collect more than a set number of birthdays, with probability at least one half. It is a playful question with a serious combinatorial core. Such variants sharpen probability intuition and often connect to scheduling and hashing problems in computing. Tripathy presents it as a fun problem, and the bottleneck rule gives it fresh bite.
arxiv-2512-00201:
Algebraic geometry studies shapes defined by polynomial equations, and group actions add symmetry to those shapes. Alexandre Roy studies an algebraic group action on a hybrid compactification in 2025, writing in French. The compactification was defined by J. Poineau using hybrid Berkovich spaces.

Compactifications add boundary points so that a variety's behavior at its edges can be studied cleanly. Roy considers varieties over the complex numbers whose group action is closed. The work blends Berkovich's non-Archimedean geometry with classical complex geometry, a meeting point that has become fruitful for arithmetic questions. Hybrid spaces mix archimedean and non-archimedean geometry, which is what makes them hybrid. Closed actions behave well at the boundary, so the extension is natural to ask for. The work is slow, deep math. It is meant for the small set of folks who build such spaces and need to know how groups act on them.
arxiv-2512-00601:
Reasoning models for medicine must do more than land on the right answer; their reasoning must be faithful and complete. Boyang Gu and co-authors present Clinical-R1 in 2025, training language models with a clinical objective relative policy optimization. Popular post-training methods mainly reward correctness.

Correctness alone is misaligned with multi-dimensional clinical objectives, where a lucky guess with sloppy reasoning is dangerous. The new objective rewards reasoning that is faithful to the evidence and comprehensive in coverage. Work like this pushes medical AI toward explanations a clinician can audit, not just conclusions to accept. Clinical reasoning objectives were defined with the field's real demands in mind. Faithfulness means the stated reasoning matches the evidence the model actually used. For care teams, the gain is trust. A tool that shows its work, step by step, can be checked by the staff who must sign off on the call.
arxiv-2512-01401:
Jung Hon Yip proves a claim about dense matchings in a class of graphs. A matching pairs up points in a graph with edges. The class here has independence number at most two. That means any three points hold at least one edge among them.

For large graphs in that class, Yip finds a matching of set size. He also bounds how many non-adjacent pairs the matching can leave. Dense matchings help in tasks like pairing users or jobs. A firm proof for this class adds a tool for cases where the graph is near-complete.
arxiv-2512-01501:
Hirohito Arai proposes one frame for viewing and running models in N dimensions. Tools for higher dimensions tend to split tasks. Geometry code is strong but lacks a live test space. Scholars must hop between tools to try ideas.

Arai's frame joins simulation and viewing in one place. It covers the four-dimensional case as a test. Users can tweak a model and see the result at once. That loop lowers the bar for work on higher spaces. It serves math, physics, and design teams that think in more than three dimensions.
arxiv-2512-02101:
Neutrino masses are tiny and puzzling, and one proposed explanation hides a fifth dimension where a partner particle lives. Arturo de Giorgi, Dhruv Pasari, and Jessica Turner give a 2025 overview of neutrino masses and mixing in large extra dimension scenarios, organized around that five-dimensional bulk fermion.

In a flat extra dimension curled into a circle with a twist, the bulk fermion appears in four dimensions as a tower of right-handed neutrinos, the Kaluza-Klein tower. The paper works through the phenomenological impact: what experiments would see. Such overviews help phenomenologists judge whether extra dimensions remain a live answer to the neutrino mass puzzle.
arxiv-2512-02201:
Speech recognition for South African languages lags far behind English, mostly for lack of training data. Vukosi Marivate and a large team introduce Swivuriso in 2025, a multilingual speech dataset of about three thousand hours built under the African Next Voices project.

The dataset covers seven South African languages and three topic areas: agriculture, healthcare, and general speech. It is meant both to train and to benchmark automatic speech recognition systems for these languages. Resources of this scale are the groundwork for voice technology that serves speakers whom the current market largely ignores.
arxiv-2512-03001:
Thomas Rivasseau argues that controlling large language models must reach inside their working context. Current operator control relies on preference training, prompting, and filtering of inputs and outputs. Those tools score good results, yet models stay open to abuse, and jailbreak odds grow with context length.

Long conversations give attackers more room to steer a model off course. Rivasseau's invasive context engineering seeks robust security guarantees for long context situations. Stronger in context control matters as agents take longer tasks in law, medicine, and infrastructure, where a hijacked session can do real harm. Long chats are where harm can hide in plain sight, one mild turn at a time. Guards must live in the chat, not at its gate.
arxiv-2512-03201:
A classic number in topology counts how loops link. Oleg Musin and Timur Shamazov offer a way to compute the Hopf invariant in this 2025 work. Heinz Hopf defined his map in 1931 and showed it differs from a constant map.

The authors start from Whitehead's integral formula for the invariant. They turn it into an algorithm for maps built from simple pieces. A working algorithm lets computers handle questions that are hard by hand. It may aid study of shapes in geometry, physics, and data analysis. Computing a classic invariant by algorithm brings hand proofs into the software age.
arxiv-2512-03501:
AI tutors work best when they guide rather than tell. Karthik Sunil and Aalok Thakkar present SocraticAI in this 2025 work. The system brings large language models into undergraduate computer science classes through structured constraints.

Rather than banning AI, SocraticAI enforces well-formed questions and reflective engagement. It also sets daily usage limits and gives Socratic dialogue scaffolds. Guided use could help students learn problem solving instead of copying answers. The design offers a model for schools facing generative AI in class. Scaffolds keep students active, since the tutor asks and prompts rather than solving outright.
arxiv-2512-03601:
Videos mix motion and meaning across time. Haoran Zhou and Gim Hee Lee present Motion4D in this 2025 work. Foundation models for 2D vision improved dynamic scene analysis from single-camera videos.

Those models often lack 3D consistency, a basic need for scene geometry and motion. The gap causes spatial misalignment and temporal flickering in complex scenes. Motion4D learns 3D-consistent motion and semantics for 4D scene understanding. Consistent 4D models help robotics, video editing, and virtual reality. 4D understanding joins space and time, the frame robots and editors both need.
arxiv-2512-03801:
Dark photons are hypothetical particles that could be made inside the Sun and absorbed by detectors on Earth. Theresa M. Backes, Riccardo Catena, and Michael Krämer ask which detector material would do that job best. Their 2025 preprint covers dark photon masses between one and one hundred electronvolts, where sunlight could plausibly produce them.

The authors first derive a material-independent ceiling on how fast absorption can happen, using Kramers-Kronig relations applied separately to the two polarisation modes of the dark photon. Whether a real material can approach that ceiling depends on how its plasma frequency compares with the particle's mass. They then grade commonly used detector materials against these criteria. Metamaterials with tunable plasma frequencies earn a special mention as a promising direction. The result is a general, model-independent framework for designing the next round of solar dark photon experiments.
arxiv-2512-04001:
Most mesons are a quark paired with an antiquark, making a proposed three-body molecule of three vector mesons look thoroughly exotic. Wen-Hao Jia and colleagues study such a bound state in a 2025 particle physics preprint. Their system combines three charged mesons, carries triple charge and spin three, in an arrangement no ordinary meson can match.

The construction starts from a two-meson cluster earlier work found bound, then adds a third meson with spin aligned. The extra pair interaction is repulsive but weak against the cluster's attraction. The calculation finds a state bound by roughly one hundred megaelectronvolts, with width about ten, narrow enough to spot experimentally. The authors suggest hunting it through the invariant mass of a kaon, a D meson, and a vector kaon. A confirmed find would enrich the exotic hadron catalogue.
arxiv-2512-04301:
Apostolos Giannopoulos and Natalia Tziotziou prove a result about the best way to place a smooth hill-shaped function in space. Such functions, called log-concave, show up across probability and geometry. For solid shapes, a classic result by Pisier gives a placement where covering counts stay tame at every scale. Covering counts say how many small copies of a shape are needed to blanket a larger one. Their 2025 arXiv paper seeks the same control for functions.

The pair show that every isotropic log-concave function already sits in a nearly ideal spot. From that spot, all four covering counts between the function, its dual, and the standard bell curve stay below one shared bound. The bound holds at every scale at once. This gives function theory the same firm footing that Pisier's result gave shape theory, and it can feed work on sampling and volume estimates.
arxiv-2512-04601:
Joey Hong, Kang Liu, Zhan Ling, and co-authors present Natural Language Actor-Critic, a way to train language model agents using feedback written in words. Agents that browse, use tools, and chat over long tasks rarely get expert demonstrations to copy. Standard training leans on sparse final rewards, which makes learning noisy and slow. Better actions must also be found in the vast space of possible wording. Their 2025 arXiv paper replaces numeric-only feedback with language.

The actor is the agent that acts. The critic judges each move in natural language, naming what worked and what to change. Learning runs off-policy, so past experience can be reused. Rich verbal critiques give denser guidance than one score at the end of a long task. The authors report steadier training and better sample use. Language-space feedback may help agents improve at jobs where success is hard to score.
arxiv-2512-04801:
John Stenger, C. Stephen Hellberg, and Daniel Gunlycke propose a hybrid quantum algorithm that shares its tuning knobs between the quantum circuit and the classical optimizer that follows. The Variational Quantum Eigensolver guesses a molecule's ground state with a parameterized circuit. Its cascaded cousin refines the guess in stages. Their 2025 arXiv paper welds the two: one set of parameters drives both the circuit and the classical cascaded stage.

The circuit itself is built by diabatic state preparation, a fast, imperfect ramp between states. Measurement results then steer the classical optimization, which polishes the energy. Tests on a system of interacting electrons ran on IBM's Brisbane quantum processor. The energies landed well within chemical accuracy, the tight bar chemists demand. The design suits both today's noisy machines and future error-corrected ones.
arxiv-2512-05101:
Frederik Brooke Barnes and nine co-authors demonstrate quantum key distribution over more than two hundred kilometres of optical fiber using a realistic single-photon source. Quantum key distribution promises secret keys whose safety rests on physics, and decoy-state methods strengthen it against attacks that exploit imperfect light sources. Here the source is a single emitter converted to telecom wavelengths, the band where fiber loss is lowest.

The decoy states are made by varying how the emitter is excited, which changes the photon-number mix it emits. The authors analyze the scheme with established security proofs, including the corrections needed when only finite keys are exchanged. The setup still delivers positive secret key rates at the full distance, tolerating about ten times more loss than the same source could manage without decoys. The work widens the role single-photon sources can play in future quantum networks.
arxiv-2512-05201:
Ali Al Housseini and five co-authors present MuMeNet, a network simulator built for the Musical Metaverse — shared virtual spaces where people attend concerts, compose together, and interact live. Such sessions stress networks in unusual ways: many participants, mixed media, and one-to-many traffic, all inside future mobile networks. Before engineers can provision services for them, they need models and tools that capture that behaviour, and none existed.

The authors first formalize the problem, building service and network graph models around a reference scenario of live audience interaction at a virtual concert. MuMeNet then simulates these sessions as discrete events, following their traffic dynamics in detail. As a showcase, they run an orchestration policy based on linear programming on the reference scenario and analyze performance under realistic workloads. The simulator gives researchers a first testbed for asking how musical metaverse sessions should be served.
arxiv-2512-06401:
Zhenzhen Yang and six co authors automate a dull but vital step in software work: turning written use cases into test cases. A use case spells out, in plain words, how a user steps through a system and what branches each step can take. Tests built by hand from such text are slow to write and easy to leave with gaps or repeats.

Their method first asks a large language model to turn the use case into a control flow graph stored in a structured format. That graph lays out every branch the story allows. Software then walks the graph to list the distinct paths, and test cases are written from those paths one by one. On six use case sets the method gave fuller, less redundant coverage than direct prompting. The payoff is tests that trace back to what users were promised the system would do.
arxiv-2512-06501:
Maxim Gritskov and Saveliy Timchenko classify the simplest possible conformal field theories: quantum systems in one dimension whose space of states is finite. Conformal symmetry, a rigid kind of scale symmetry, shapes such theories strongly. Following a classic definition of quantum field theory, the authors state exactly when a one dimensional quantum system carries that symmetry.

They then give a complete list of the energy operators, the Hamiltonians, that fit the bill at each finite size. A neat pattern emerges: the correlation functions of these theories are polynomial functions of the geometric data behind them. The conformal Ward identities, the symmetry's bookkeeping rules, fix how those functions scale, so the observable correlators turn out to be tidy homogeneous polynomials. The work fully maps a small corner of the theory landscape that larger theories are built against.
arxiv-2512-06701:
Andres Salcedo and five co authors ask what galaxy clusters, the largest bound structures in the universe, say about dark energy and the expansion rate. Clusters are counted and weighed by surveys, and their abundance over time is a sensitive probe of how structure grew. The team combines cluster counts with two other low redshift probes, joint maps of galaxy positions and lensing, and the full shape of galaxy clustering.

In the standard model, all these probes agree with each other and with the geometric data from the early universe, giving tight joint limits. In an extended model where dark energy can evolve, adding the clusters pulls the evidence for evolving dark energy down, and eases the well known tension over the expansion rate. The authors read this as a point for the standard picture, with a hint that the sound horizon may differ from its standard value.
arxiv-2512-06801:
Yi Chen examines the inner spin of the nucleon, the heavy core particle found inside atoms, using a set of weak-force measures. Three related quantities, called axial-vector form factors, describe how that spin is spread through the particle's volume. Chen works out, for the first time, how these measures shape the full three-dimensional picture of charge and spin. The setting is a special frame where the particle is viewed at rest.

One result overturns a common reading of the data. A quantity long treated as the particle's axial size, Chen argues, cannot serve as a true three-dimensional radius at all. A different spin radius, built from the same measures, does have a clear physical meaning. Chen also derives formulas for neutrino scattering off protons, giving future experiments a fresh way to probe how spin sits inside matter.
arxiv-2512-07101:
Emily Adlam brings reference frames to bear on one of quantum theory's strangest puzzles, the extended Wigner's friend scenario. In it, an observer measures a system inside a sealed lab while a second observer treats the whole lab quantum mechanically, and the two accounts seem to clash. Adlam sorts the properties in play using symmetry: some facts about a system only make sense relative to an outside frame, while others stand on their own.

On that distinction she proposes that what each observer saw is always a well-defined fact. What may fail to exist is a well-defined relation between the observers' frames. Without such relations, there is no single joint distribution over everyone's outcomes to compare against quantum predictions, and the contradiction dissolves. The same move blocks a threatened regress, where each relativization would demand another frame behind it.
arxiv-2512-07301:
Boyuan Ning and Yasutaka Shimizu estimate a key dial in a workhorse model of interest rates and asset prices from data sampled very frequently. The CKLS diffusion lets the noise's size scale with the level of the process, and the exponent of that scaling, the elasticity, is the target. Direct estimation stumbles on a technicality: the process may touch zero, where standard likelihood recipes break down.

Their detour changes the problem's clothes. A smooth change of variables and measure turns the CKLS diffusion into a cousin of the CIR process, for which inference tools exist. In the new clothes they estimate the drift using the process's long-run visiting pattern, valid at high frequency. Then translate the drift estimate back into an elasticity estimate through the exact relationship the transformation imposes.
arxiv-2512-07501:
Weilin Luo, Xueyi Liang, Haotian Deng, Yanan Liu, and Hai Wan wrote this 2025 software engineering paper. Writing code that a machine can prove correct is valuable but hard to adopt. Language models give the old dream of automatic formal code a fresh push.

In practice, model-written code often carries syntax and meaning errors. Training data for formal work is scarce, and hidden knowledge stays unspoken. The authors answer with AutoICE, an evolutionary search driven by a language model. Its goal is verifiable C code grown from plain-language requirements. Varied starting points and a cooperative crossover step keep the search diverse. That diversity slows the way a single agent's errors can snowball. A self-reflective mutation step hunts for knowledge the prompt left implicit. In tests, the system verifies a large share of its generated code. It beats the prior best method on both standard and friendlier datasets.
arxiv-2512-07601:
C. Azam, D. Davesne, Y. Lallouet, L. Próchniak, M. Frosini, and A. Pastore wrote this 2025 nuclear physics paper. It studies how atomic nuclei in the gadolinium family change shape as neutrons are added. Their tool is a generalised Bohr Hamiltonian, a classic model of nuclear vibration and rotation.

A Hamiltonian alone needs mass parameters that describe how stiff the nucleus is. Here those numbers come from a microscopic source, the Gogny interaction between nucleons. With that input, the team maps the potential energy surface for each gadolinium isotope. They also track how the first excited state of a set kind evolves along the chain. Energies and electromagnetic transitions of low-lying states come out much alike across the Gogny variants tried. The results also agree well with measured data. The study shows a classic collective model can still speak with a microscopic voice.
arxiv-2512-07801:
Raunak Jain wrote this 2025 position paper on human-AI teamwork in expert decisions. AI agents now advise doctors, analysts, and other specialists in high-stakes settings. Yet teams of human plus agent still fail to reliably beat the best individual.

Jain calls that shortfall the complementarity gap, and blames a design mismatch. Agents are trained as answer engines that deliver verdicts on demand. Experts, though, decide through collaborative sensemaking with their colleagues. They build causal explanations together, surface uncertainties, and adapt their goals. Current training pipelines neither build nor measure that partner-like skill. Jain proposes Collaborative Causal Sensemaking as a research agenda. New training environments should reward collaborative thinking directly. Shared representations should hold a joint mental model for human and agent. Evaluation should center on trust and complementarity, not raw answer accuracy. The aim is AI teammates that reason with people over shared decisions.
arxiv-2512-08001:
Junfeng Xu, Sujoy Majumder, and Lata Mahato, complex analysts, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is uniqueness for entire functions, asking when a function and its higher derivatives sharing values must in fact be the same. They study cases where a function partially shares two values with its derivatives of higher order.

The results improve and generalize earlier theorems by Li and Yi, by Lu and coauthors, and by Sauer and Schweizer. The authors also show that this sharing behavior connects deeply with the analytic structure of a certain nonlinear differential equation. Examples throughout the paper show why each condition they impose is truly needed. For specialists in value distribution theory, the work tightens what can be said about how much sharing forces identity.
arxiv-2512-08101:
Patrick Kline, an economist, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025 about two way fixed effects models. Other researchers often reuse estimates from such models, for example on how firms affect wages, but judging the uncertainty in borrowed estimates is hard. Kline proposes a way to communicate that uncertainty more honestly and usefully.

His method, called branching fixed effects, splits network data into statistically independent branches. Each branch yields its own unbiased estimate of the same parameters, which supports uncertainty checks, moment estimation, and shrinkage. He draws on graph theory results about tree packing to build algorithms that extract branches from large networks efficiently. A widely used dataset from the Veneto region of Italy, long used to study firm wage effects, illustrates the approach. The proposal gives applied economists a practical tool for reporting how much trust a fixed effects estimate deserves.
arxiv-2512-08401:
Elyse Laurent, Ricardo Javier Pena Roman, Sarah Miller, and colleagues, physicists in France, posted an experimental study on arXiv in December 2025. They sharpen a microscopy technique that makes atom thin semiconductors glow under a scanning tunneling microscope, then photographs the light. The tunneling tip excites a tiny spot, but the glow spreads in ways that reveal how excitons, bound electron hole pairs, move and interact with charge. 

That spread normally sits below the diffraction limit, unresolved. The team applies an iterative sharpening algorithm, Richardson Lucy deconvolution, and recovers the emission pattern beyond that limit. They show it on single layers of tungsten diselenide and tungsten disulfide. Two overlooked effects stand out. One is how the emission pattern depends on the tunnel current setting. The other is why bright hot spots appear far from the excitation point. Both findings speak directly to exciton and charge transport in these materials.
arxiv-2512-08601:
Orit Davidovich and coauthors build a unified theory for using reinforcement learning to solve hard combinatorial problems. In practice, neural networks are often trained as fast heuristics for such problems, with good results and quick answers. Yet the theory behind why those methods work, and when they fail, has lagged behind the experiments.

The authors show how to frame combinatorial problems as Markov decision processes that keep the same best solutions. They then give clear conditions under which value based learning methods approach good solutions, with a bound on the gap from optimal. The analysis covers batch size, update steps, accuracy targets, and the choice of state representation. It also helps explain the success and limits of deep Q learning in this setting.
arxiv-2512-08701:
Igor Strakovsky and coauthors study how strongly a J psi meson interacts with a nucleon, using light based production near threshold. Recent data from Jefferson Laboratory, taken on a helium target in Hall D, are of high quality. A measurement near the free nucleon threshold also looks feasible, which opens new uses for this kind of production.

Using a standard vector meson model, the authors estimate the scattering length for a bound proton and compare it with the free proton value from another collaboration. They then project what a recently approved experiment could achieve, using simulated data from a plane wave model. The projected precision is competitive with the free proton result. Comparing bound and free values would help reveal how the nuclear medium changes the interaction.
arxiv-2512-08801:
Chuanzhong Li, Xiaoman Luo, and Bao Shou propose an exact duality map for rigid surface operators in four dimensional gauge theories. Surface operators are two dimensional defects that generalize line operators and probe the non perturbative structure of a theory. Rigid ones have no continuous deformation parameters, and a closed duality map among them has long been expected.

Progress had been limited to special cases, in part because many operators share the same invariants. A deeper problem is a mismatch in the count of rigid operators between dual theories when they are sorted by invariants. The authors give a direct map that moves the longest row between the two partitions defining an operator, with a box added or removed to balance the total. By including non rigid operators, the map resolves the mismatch. It applies to gauge groups of all ranks and clarifies several old puzzles.
arxiv-2512-08901:
Ziyin Song and coauthors build a unified symmetry classification of magnetic orders based on spin space groups. Those groups constrain magnetic patterns in real space and in momentum space in fundamentally other ways. As a result, the link between the two views is far richer than traditionally assumed, and a systematic classification was needed.

Building on the full enumeration of spin space groups, the authors classify all spin arrangements those groups allow. Standard magnetic orders, altermagnetism, and p wave magnetism appear as distinct symmetry classes in one method. The classification also predicts new phases. A highlighted discovery is the coplanar even wave magnet, which is non collinear in real space yet collinear in momentum space. Study of a minimal model and first principles calculations support the idea, and a candidate compound is proposed. The method is extended to layered systems for two dimensional magnets.
arxiv-2512-09101:
Lipeng Zhuang and coauthors present Masked Generative Policy, a framework for robot control learned from demonstration. Actions are represented as discrete tokens. A conditional masked transformer generates those tokens in parallel and then refines only the tokens it is least confident about, which speeds inference while keeping quality.

Two sampling modes are proposed. A short mode suits tasks where the next action depends mainly on the current state, using parallel generation with score based refinement. A long mode predicts full trajectories in one pass and revises low confidence action tokens as new observations arrive. That gives coherent global plans with adaptive execution. Tests span a large set of manipulation tasks on two standard benchmarks. The method raises average success rates over leading diffusion and autoregressive policies while cutting inference time sharply. It also improves success in dynamic settings with missing observations and solves hard non Markovian cases where rivals fail.
arxiv-2512-09201:
Aditya Ganeshan and colleagues present a way to turn a detailed 3D shape into a small set of simple building blocks. Designers want shapes they can edit easily, but faithful copies of real objects usually need huge numbers of parts. Their framework, called ResFit, tackles that trade-off directly.

ResFit works in rounds. Each round fits simple solids to whatever part of the shape is still unexplained, then repeats on the leftover error. The blocks it uses are a new shape type called SuperFrustum, described by only eight numbers yet able to form cylinders, spheres, cones, and tapered or bent versions of them. On standard 3D test sets, the method scored clearly better than earlier work while using nearly half as many pieces, giving shapes that stay accurate and easy to change.
arxiv-2512-09301:
Mikołaj Frączyk introduces a new notion in measured group theory called infinitesimal weak containment. The setting is measure-preserving actions of a countable group, systems where the group moves points around a probability space. The new notion says one action is contained in another if the statistics of the first action on very small sets can be mimicked inside the second.

Frączyk shows that the Bernoulli shift, the most random action, built on all configurations indexed by the group, is infinitesimally contained in the group's own left-regular action. For exact groups, this implies that sparse random-like subsets of the group are approximately hyperfinite, a strong structural simplicity. He uses the result to quantify a theorem of Chifan and Ioana about subrelations of Bernoulli shifts. The proof introduces entropy support maps, which weight the coordinates that matter most for a small set's structure.
arxiv-2512-09401:
Anita Pahi and colleagues review photophoretic trapping, a way to hold and move tiny particles using light. When a particle absorbs light unevenly, the surrounding gas pushes it with a force far stronger than ordinary radiation pressure. That strength allows stable three-dimensional trapping at remarkably low light intensities.

The review explains the physics behind these forces and how they produce stable trapping of absorbing particles. It surveys the experimental setups that achieve robust trapping and the physical parameters that control the force's size and behavior in each setup. The authors also discuss the rich motions trapped particles display, from steady levitation to complex dynamics. Applications range from aerosol science and free-space 3D displays to deploying lightweight payloads in space. The paper aims to unify the theoretical, experimental, and applied sides of a fast-growing field and to point out where future work should go.
arxiv-2512-09601:
Edison H L Au-Yeung works out valuations for elliptic nets on curves with complex multiplication. Such curves carry division polynomials that encode the coordinates of multiples of a point. Their kin, net polynomials, handle integer combinations of points at once and form the nets, arrays obeying the same recurrence as division polynomials.

Complex multiplication is extra structure: the curve's maps to itself include an order from an imaginary quadratic field. Au-Yeung assumes that setting and proves a formula for the common valuation of the two net polynomials tied to multiples of points by elements of that order. It measures how divisible the values are. The formula shows that elliptic divisibility sequences indexed by elements of the order satisfy a recurrence, under conditions on the indices. The result extends the theory of divisibility sequences into that setting.
arxiv-2512-09701:
Binbin Xu presents FineFreq, a dataset counting how often every character occurs in text across more than nineteen hundred languages. Character frequencies are basic infrastructure for linguistics, typography, and language technology, but existing counts are small and cover few languages. FineFreq is derived from the FineWeb and FineWeb2 web corpora, processing tens of trillions of characters from a decade-plus of text.

For each language, the dataset gives per-character counts both in aggregate and broken down by year, allowing fine-grained study of how usage changes over time. It keeps naturally occurring features such as cross-script borrowings, emoji, and acronyms instead of filtering them away, so the counts reflect real writing. Each character entry carries Unicode metadata on category, script, and block, enabling users to filter for their own purposes. The dataset is released in CSV and Parquet formats with associated metadata, on GitHub and Hugging Face.
arxiv-2512-09801:
Tien-Dat Chung leads a team proposing a new method for outlining brain tumors in scans when only a small share of images come with expert labels. Their setting is semi-supervised learning across several MRI sequences at once. Each sequence shows the tissue differently, and older methods often fail to combine what each view uniquely offers, because the views differ in meaning and alignment. The framework gives each modality its own enhancement step, then fuses the views adaptively.

An enhancement module strengthens cues unique to each sequence through channel wise attention. A fusion module learns how to exchange complementary knowledge between sequences. Training mixes a supervised loss on labeled scans with a consistency rule across modalities on unlabeled ones. On the BraTS 2019 data, using only tiny fractions of labeled scans, the method beat strong baselines on overlap and sensitivity scores. Removal tests confirmed both modules contribute to the gain.
arxiv-2512-10001:
Karim Benakli constructs consistent equations of motion for massive particles with high spin in electromagnetic fields. The particles carry spin two and spin three halves, and move through constant background fields. A puzzle drives the work. For pointlike particles, quantum consistency forces a universal gyromagnetic ratio. Real composite particles, like the omega minus baryon, deviate from that value. Naively allowing other values triggers pathologies: faster than light propagation or lost degrees of freedom. Benakli's cure is to treat the system as an effective field theory.

In that view, the theory is expanded systematically in powers of the background field strength. By adding specific operators, the author shows algebraic consistency can be restored order by order, for arbitrary gyromagnetic factor. The pathologies are pushed beyond the theory's range of validity rather than appearing inside it.
arxiv-2512-10101:
Koen Schouten and Mikhail Isachenkov give a model at the frontier of quantum gravity a firm operator algebraic home. The model is the double scaled SYK model, a quantum mechanical system of many fermions whose low energy dynamics mimic a two dimensional black hole. Its hidden symmetry is a quantum group, a deformation of the symmetry of anti de Sitter space. The authors construct, for the first time, the von Neumann algebraic quantum group description of that symmetry, including the normalizer extension that the symmetry secretly requires. 

Dynamics on the quantum anti de Sitter space then reduces exactly to the double scaled SYK dynamics. The reduction works only at the normalizer level.
arxiv-2512-10201:
Huan Li proposes a new way to turn an ordinary semiconductor into an ideal Weyl semimetal, a prized topological state of matter. Weyl semimetals host special band crossings that behave like magnetic monopoles in momentum space. Reaching them usually requires breaking time reversal symmetry or precisely engineering the crystal's symmetry, which limits the materials and knobs available. Li's mechanism needs neither. Chemical doping shrinks the band gap while strengthening spin orbit coupling, until the valence and conduction bands invert. At that closure, the topological transition happens by itself.

First principles calculations demonstrate the idea in a family of copper tin selenide materials. Two pairs of Weyl points appear almost exactly at the Fermi level, the energy that matters for transport. The bulk Fermi surface shrinks to nearly points, while the surface shows only the characteristic Fermi arcs.
arxiv-2512-10601:
Akhil Agnihotri's doctoral thesis looks at how reinforcement learning systems can be taught to act well while also respecting safety limits. The work covers control problems, learning from human preferences, and the alignment of large language models. It brings these topics together under one view of learning with several goals at once.

Early chapters present methods for constrained decision problems, including approaches for long-run average costs and for shorter episodes with clear end points. Later chapters turn to preference learning, where feedback from different raters varies in skill and reliability. The final work scales these ideas to large language models, giving practical tools for safer and better aligned decision making.
arxiv-2512-10701:
Mostafa Anoosha and co-authors improve privacy-preserving diagnosis across devices that each hold part of the picture. In vertical federated learning, partners hold different features for the same patients, as in mobile health, where images might sit on one device and other data on another. Nothing raw is shared, but the usual way of fusing the features is crude, and accuracy suffers.

HybridVFL disentangles features on each client device first, separating the strands of information before anything is combined, then fuses them on the server with a cross-modal transformer that can weigh context. The authors evaluate the system on HAM10000, a multimodal skin lesion dataset, a fitting test for medical classification. HybridVFL significantly outperformed standard federated baselines, which the authors read as proof that smarter fusion, not just privacy machinery, decides whether such systems work.
arxiv-2512-10801:
Juan Augusto Paredes Salazar and co-authors squeeze more pressure out of an S-shaped diffuser, the bent duct used in engines and ventilation where flow tends to separate and waste energy. Blowing small jets of air into the duct can reattach the flow. And experiments had shown a sweet spot: an injection frequency in the low hundreds of hertz at one percent of the free-stream mass flow gave the best pressure recovery.

The team applies a data-driven retrospective cost optimisation technique to tune the injection frequency automatically. High-fidelity simulations of the compressible, unsteady flow, run with Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes models, explore different jet speeds and pulse frequencies. And two-dimensional results agree relatively well with experiment. With the data-driven tuning switched on, simulations improved on the baseline case, raising pressure recovery and shrinking the recirculation region inside the diffuser, while three-dimensional runs continue.
arxiv-2512-11001:
Zoi Kaoudi and Ioana Giurgiu argue that data pipelines built from language model agents need a new kind of query optimisation. Current agentic pipelines are assembled by hand with fixed structures, chosen models, and single engines. Nobody systematically optimises them across mixed data sources and tools, the way databases optimise queries.

Their vision, called NOMA, treats choices of pipeline shape, model, and engine as one joint problem covering speed, cost, and accuracy. A controlled test on a real ten agent pipeline showed huge variation in cost and speed between plans, with the best plans mixing components in ways users would not pick by hand. The authors propose a loop where plan generation, cost estimates, runtime refinement, and semantic caching improve each other across runs.
arxiv-2512-11201: Ryoma Sato and Shinji Ito point out that EXP3, a classic algorithm for choosing among options under uncertainty, can be run in constant time per round. EXP3 belongs to the adversarial bandit family, where rewards may be set by an opponent and the learner must still limit its regret. Earlier implementations were slower than necessary, which matters when rounds are numerous.
arxiv-2512-11601:
Antoine Renard and Michel Rigo use a proof program called Walnut to settle questions about the Wythoff game. Wythoff is a classic two pile taking game tied to the Fibonacci number system. New versions add blocked moves or set end positions.

Walnut checks number patterns on its own, giving short, firm proofs. The pair confirm and extend results from Larsson in 2011 and Komak and others in 2025. They also treat brand new versions with the same tools. For games where end positions obey x plus y at most a set limit, they add classic recursive and pattern based descriptions. The work shows how auto proof tools can crack game puzzles.
arxiv-2512-11801:
Reginald Anderson counts special sets of line bundles on a family of shapes called toric Fano fivefolds. These sets, called exceptional collections, can be used to rebuild the whole shape from a short ordered list. A known method for splitting the shape, due to Hanlon, Hicks, and Lazarev, gives the test used here.

Anderson checks when that method yields a full strong set of line bundles in dimension five. Out of 866 smooth shapes of this kind, 300 pass the test. No count like this existed before. The work builds on a famed result by Beilinson for the simplest shape of all, projective space.
arxiv-2512-12801:
Anurag Dutt and five co-authors present PIE-P, a fine grained energy prediction framework for parallel language model inference, in a 2025 paper. Running large models costs growing amounts of energy, yet measuring that use is hard: hardware power monitors are not always available, and software tools are often wrong. Past tools also cover only single GPU setups, while modern inference spreads across many GPUs.

PIE-P handles tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism. It tackles nondeterministic inter-GPU data exchange and extra overhead. It also handles the difficulty of isolating energy during sync phases, using precise sampling and detailed modeling of that exchange. In evaluations it gave accurate, detailed predictions across parallel setups, beating baselines by a wide margin, the authors report.
arxiv-2512-13401:
Mahum Pervez, Ariq Haqq, Nathan McMahon, and Christian Arenz develop quantum algorithms that prepare ground states, the lowest energy states of a chosen Hamiltonian, using Riemannian gradient descent. Ground state preparation is a core task for quantum simulation of materials and chemistry. Guarantees on the cost were the missing piece.

They bound the number of descent steps by the Hamiltonian's spectral gap, the starting overlap, and the target precision. On an Ising chain, steps grew linearly with the number of spins; with all-to-all coupling, growth was quadratic. Random projections of the gradient make the method efficient, and they ran small versions on IBM quantum devices.
arxiv-2512-13701:
Zheng Xing and Junting Chen build radio maps without location labels, a task they call blind radio mapping. Radio maps show how channel traits vary across space and support smart wireless uses. Standard methods need large amounts of location-labeled data, which is costly to gather indoors.

Their method infers user paths from MIMO-OFDM channel measures alone. They prove channel data stay spatially continuous under a quasi-specular model, giving a distance metric in channel space. A Bayesian frame with spatial regularization then estimates channel features, sorts line-of-sight from blocked paths, and recovers user paths. On ray-tracing data, mean localization error was 0.68 m and beam map error was 3.3%.
arxiv-2512-13801:
Sujatha Ramakrishnan and co-authors present HOLCon, a framework to build halo lightcones from universe simulations. Sound mock catalogs are vital for large sky surveys, and lightcones must track how galaxies form and evolve with redshift. Their tool builds dark matter halo lightcones after a simulation has run.

HOLCon optimizes the lightcone's orientation inside the simulation box to reduce repeated structures when the survey volume exceeds one box. A linear scheme tracks halo traits across snapshots, filling the gaps. Applied to the Uchuu simulation, they built a 50 square degree lightcone out to redshift 10. They checked halo clustering against the source snapshots, then added galaxies with an extended SciPIC method. The mock predicts clustering for H-alpha emitting galaxies.
arxiv-2512-15301:
Yanhao Sun and five coauthors rebuild the theory of a quantum key method so it matches real hardware. Continuous variable quantum key distribution lets two parties share provably secure keys using standard coherent optical gear. As systems go digital, device flaws push the light from a single mode into a continuous spread of modes, breaking the old models.

The authors introduce temporal modes to build an entanglement based scheme that captures those flaws, plus a method to compute secret key rates in the continuous setting. Tuning the pulse shape helps a lot when detector bandwidth is the limit. A digital signal processing method, linear weighted reconstruction, raised the key rate by about 50 percent in a 30 kilometer fiber test, with no new hardware. The framework covers more real conditions and can guide digital system design.
arxiv-2512-15501:
Christoph Aistleitner, Zakhar Kabluchko, and Joscha Prochno show that cumulant growth in lacunary sums depends delicately on arithmetic in a 2025 paper. Lacunary trigonometric sums add cosine terms whose frequencies grow fast, leaving large gaps. Cumulants measure the shape of the sum distribution beyond its mean and variance.

When the frequency ratio limit is a transcendental number, every cumulant matches the independent model, growing linearly. When that limit is algebraic, the match can fail. For one sequence the sixth cumulant grows quadratically, and for others, including powers of two and the Fibonacci sequence, growth stays linear but at a different rate. Many other limit theorems for these sums show no such sensitivity.
arxiv-2512-15701:
Kyle Sargent and co authors present VLIC, an image compression system that uses vision language models as perceptual judges, in a 2025 paper. Compression tuned to plain distortion scores often clashes with what human viewers prefer. Older perceptual losses needed neural networks calibrated on large sets of human judgments.

The authors find, surprisingly, that leading vision language models can repeat human two choice judgments about image pairs with no extra training. VLIC, a diffusion based compressor, is post trained directly on those binary model judgments instead of distilling them into a separate loss network. The system reaches competitive or state of the art human aligned compression on several data sets and user studies.
arxiv-2512-16201:
Sarosij Bose and five co-authors improve automated X-ray reporting in an arXiv paper released in 2025. Vision-language models can draft radiology reports from chest X-rays, but they often hallucinate findings the image does not show. The root cause is weak alignment between what the model sees and what it says.

Their system, VALOR, attacks the problem in two stages. First, clinically informed text training rewards reports that use precise terms and cover the right findings. Second, a frozen expert model scores how well each draft matches the actual image, and those scores steer the model toward visually grounded wording. No preference pairs, retrieval databases, or extra labels are needed. Across several benchmarks, VALOR improved report quality and clinical accuracy over leading medical report generators.
arxiv-2512-16301:
Pengcheng Jiang and a large team of co-authors survey how AI agents keep improving after training in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025. Language model agents now do more than answer prompts: they call tools, remember past work, and reuse skills. Research on these abilities is scattered across post-training, retrieval, memory, and skill systems.

The survey unifies the field under one idea, adaptation, with four paradigms. Two improve the agent itself, through fine-tuning and reinforcement learning guided by tool results or output quality. Two improve the tools: reusable modules any agent can call, and memory or skill systems trained from the agent's own outputs. The authors compare costs, flexibility, and generalization, review evaluation in research, coding, computer use, and drug discovery, and flag open problems like safety and lifelong learning.
arxiv-2512-16601:
Pietro Baratella finds an escape hatch from a stuck universe in an arXiv paper released in 2025. Some scalar fields have a nearly scale-invariant potential with a false resting point at zero. During cosmic evolution the field can get trapped there because bubble nucleation, the usual escape to the true vacuum, is too inefficient, leaving eternal supercooling.

Baratella adds a conserved charge carried by the field, with a matching chemical potential in the hot early plasma. Temperature stabilizes the trap while the chemical potential destabilizes it. When one species decouples from the plasma, the balance can tip toward the chemical potential. The field then condenses, triggering the long-delayed transition to the stable phase. The mechanism offers model builders a new way to end inflation-like supercooling without fine-tuned bubble rates.
arxiv-2512-16701:
Giovanni Adorni argues for Cyber Humanism in Education, a frame for keeping human agency at the center as AI tools spread through schools. Large language models now reshape reading, writing, and coding into joint human-AI work, raising risks of blind trust and deskilled teachers.

Adorni casts AI-rich classrooms as shared systems co-built by people and machines, with teachers and learners as active agents who shape them. Three pillars guide design: reflective skill, algorithmic citizenship, and dialogic design. Case studies from higher education, built on prompt-based learning and a new teacher certificate in the EPICT system, show the frame in action, along with strains over workload, fairness, and control.
arxiv-2512-17301:
Ratbek Dzhumashev and Ainura Tursunalieva propose a new way to untangle cause and effect when outside instruments are hard to find. Economists use an instrumental variable, a factor that nudges a treatment but touches the outcome only through it, to cut through hidden bias. Good instruments are scarce, and weak ones can mislead more than they help.

Their Synthetic Instrumental Variable method builds a valid instrument from the data already on hand. A data-driven check, called the dual tendency condition, certifies the built instrument without any outside variable. The method holds up when noise levels vary and can even reveal the sign of the hidden correlation. Simulations and real cases show cleaner causal estimates for economics, health, and policy work.
arxiv-2512-17401:
Jiajun Sun, Zhanrui Cai, and Wei Zhong tackle a quiet scandal in data work: run a top false-discovery method twice and it may name different findings. Such methods cap the share of false alarms among claimed discoveries, but many flip a random coin inside, so results wobble from run to run. Their remedy, the FDR Stabilizer, wraps around any base method.

The wrapper runs the base method many times and merges the runs into one consensus ranking. Each feature then gets a steadied score, and a final rule picks the winners. The team proves error and power bounds, and shows the picked set settles to a fixed answer as runs pile up. On tests and real data, the steadied version beat the raw methods it wrapped.
arxiv-2512-17701:
Bernardo Flores and three co-authors build a statistical model for data where each item carries an unknown shopping list of features, and the lists are not independent. Feature allocation models guess those hidden lists, say which diseases explain a patient's drugs, but classic versions assume features pop up freely, ignoring that age, place, and time tie them together.

Their model paints the chance of each feature over a random field, split into a part explained by known covariates and a leftover wobble. A sparse neighbor graph keeps the math tractable in high dimensions. A dynamic version lets item effects drift over time like a fading memory. On pharmacy records, the model inferred patients' latent health conditions from drug profiles alone.
arxiv-2512-18001:
Raffaele Tito D'Agnolo, Manuel Ettengruber, and Lian-Tao Wang ask whether the landscape of possible universes could show up at a collider. Some theories hold vast numbers of long lived states, called vacua, and they offer the only firm account of why the cosmic constant is so small. The energy of those states is unknown, and some may sit within reach.

If so, collisions could spray out many particles at once with modest total energy, a pattern searches may have missed. Exotic decays of the Higgs boson are one place such events could hide. The authors also sketch a model tying the small cosmic constant and the Higgs mass to one shared low energy landscape.
arxiv-2512-18101:
Richard A. Shaw leads a large institute team measuring the scientific payoff of MAST, the archive that holds data from more than twenty NASA space missions. They built mission by mission reading lists from nearly 40 journals. The count passes 37,000 peer reviewed papers that used archive data for real science.

Most missions stayed highly productive long after their working lives ended, and citations kept growing for over a decade. For the Hubble telescope, papers by outside teams using old data passed the original teams' papers within ten years and now run more than three times higher. Half of Hubble programs saw a first paper within 1.5 years. Archives, the study shows, are engines, not store rooms.
arxiv-2512-18201:
Jose Guerrero and Mirko Gamba review a laser method for reading hot gases inside engines and power plants. A tunable diode laser shines through the gas, and the dips in its beam reveal temperature, pressure, gas mix, and flow speed. No probe has to touch the harsh stream.

The review builds the math of gas absorption from the ground up, covering line shapes, broadening, and how to pick clean lines to read. It then turns to a wobbled beam variant that shrugs off noise, and a calibration free form of it. Bench advice closes the survey: how to test the laser, strip background glow, and debug the rig.
arxiv-2512-18701:
Felisia Angela Chiarello, Alexander Keimer, and Lukas Pflug study conservation laws of the kind used to model traffic, where a flow's speed depends on conditions averaged over a stretch of road. Such laws are called nonlocal. Standard versions average with the L1 norm; their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, generalizes the averaging to the Lp norm, even for p between zero and one.

They prove weak solutions exist and are unique when the starting density stays away from zero, and they handle the zero case under tighter assumptions. When the averaging kernel shrinks to a spike, the solutions recover the classical local law's entropy solution for every positive p, extending a celebrated result known for p equal to one. They also check monotonicity, study the limit as p approaches zero, and close with numerical experiments.
arxiv-2512-19101:
Ryota Hatami, Nozomu Tominaga, Takashi Yoshida, and Hideyuki Umeda ask what conditions inside an exploding star make the elements scandium, titanium, and vanadium. They simulate element building in a core-collapse supernova, including the effect of neutrinos streaming through the hot layers. Abundance patterns in very old, metal-poor stars serve as the target.

Using the silicon layer of a thirteen-solar-mass star with no initial metals, they scanned temperature, density, and neutrino exposure. Matching the old stars required a set neutrino dose and a temperature band near two to three billion degrees. Density mattered little. They then check whether real explosions reach those conditions.
arxiv-2512-19201:
Sebastian Zimper, Ana Djurdjevac, Carsten Hartmann, and Christof Schütte study crowds steered by a few leaders. Think of opinion dynamics, where a handful of committed voices can pull a large population. Each follower acts with randomness, and the leaders act with randomness too, while choosing how to steer.

Letting the follower count grow without bound gives a limiting system: a McKean-Vlasov equation for the crowd, tied to controlled equations for the leaders. The team proves the best control of the finite crowd converges to the best control of the limit. A stochastic gradient method then computes the limit control, giving a practical handle on huge systems.
arxiv-2512-19301:
P. A. Duverne, W. K. Mouici, A. Coleiro, and J.-G. Ducoin plan the optical chase after the next galactic supernova is caught by its neutrinos. A collapsing star floods space with neutrinos hours before its light show starts. That early warning is precious, if telescopes can find the spot fast enough.

The team modeled where such events occur in the Milky Way, dust dimming included, for three progenitor kinds. Neutrino networks from IceCube to JUNO would triangulate a rough error box. Scheduling software then turns those sky maps into an observing plan, aiming at signatures such as shock breakout. The study weighs how well the whole chain could work.
arxiv-2512-19401:
Anupam Das, Abhishek De, and Stepan Kuznetsov prove that several theories of semirings with fixed points admit no decision procedure at all. A semiring is a set with two operations that act much like plus and times, but with no need for minus. A fixed point adds a way to name the least solution of an equation, much like a loop in a program.

The authors use a method from recursion theory to show that no algorithm can settle all true claims in these systems. The verdict covers Conway and Park mu-semirings and Chomsky algebras, and more systems of the same kind.
arxiv-2512-19501:
Esmée Theewis proves a large deviation principle for stochastic evolution equations that refuse to be coercive. Large deviations price the rare paths of a noisy system as the noise shrinks. Classic proofs lean on coercivity, a strong grip the equation keeps on its solutions, which many real systems lack.

The weak convergence approach lets her drop that grip. Well-posedness plus two checkable a priori estimates take its place, and a modified criticality condition tames strong drift terms. Vanishing drift tweaks are allowed too, covering the Itô-Stratonovich correction. A non-coercive reaction-diffusion system illustrates the reach, and joint work applies it to ocean-style primitive equations.
arxiv-2512-19701:
Yuxuan Yin and five co-authors present LASER, a tool for a cloud scheduling chore. The chore is to guess how much resource a workflow job will use, and how long it will run. Job records are messy mixes. They hold shell commands, tool settings, dependency graphs, and metadata. Old machine learning flattens all that into fixed vectors and loses meaning.

LASER fine-tunes language models on the job records as text instead. The models learn to output several numbers at once. A science-style number format handles values that span huge ranges. A checked decoding step keeps outputs valid and cuts the time to answer. On chip-design workloads and a new public test set, LASER beat human experts. The test set draws on over half a million GitHub Actions runs.
arxiv-2512-20201:
Heekang Song and Wan Choi tackle a bottleneck in distributed computing: moving data between machines during the shuffling phase. Their setting is wireless, with multiple antennas at each end, and they combine embedded index coding with transmit beamforming. Index coding uses data already cached at nodes to shrink transmissions, while beamforming aims the radio signals.

Finding the best joint design is an NP-hard problem, and an exhaustive search quickly becomes too slow. Song and Choi therefore build a multi-agent reinforcement learning system whose agents decide from local observations. Simulations show performance close to the costly optimum at far lower complexity. The approach suits wireless systems whose channel conditions keep changing.
arxiv-2512-20401:
Leonid Fel bounds how well a mixed material can conduct electricity. The setting is a flat composite made of three or four symmetric phases, each with its own conductivity. The effective conductivity of the mixture depends on microstructure, but some bounds hold no matter how the phases are arranged.

Fel's algebraic approach produces an upper and a lower bound for both the three- and four-phase cases. The bounds respect every property physics demands: homogeneity, symmetry under permuting phases, Keller self-duality, positivity, and monotonicity. They also agree with the trivial uniform case and with Dykhne's ansatz. Comparisons against numerics, asymptotics, and exact results show complete agreement, and the new bounds beat the previously known variational ones.
arxiv-2512-20601:
