Those forecasts become variance estimates feeding a convex optimization that sets each prompt allocation under a hard compute cap. Tests on several benchmarks show VIP beats uniform and heuristic allocation, lifting sampling efficiency and performance.
arxiv-2602-01701: Ruyu Li and colleagues unify language model query systems for multi modal data, where meaning hides in semantics beyond queries. Fragmentation comes from interfaces and the specialization generality tradeoff. Specialists excel but struggle across modalities, while all in one systems handle modalities but lag specialists. Their Meta Engine, a query system on query systems, integrates systems. It has five parts: a language query parser, an operator generator, a query router, adapters and an aggregator. In tests it beats baselines, with several times higher F1 and higher on some sets.
arxiv-2602-01801: Dvir Samuel and colleagues speed up video diffusion, whose attention layers bottleneck inference as the KV cache grows. They find three redundancies: duplicate keys across frames, slowly evolving queries, and cross attention over long prompts where few tokens matter per frame. Their FAST-AR combines TempCache compressing the cache by temporal correspondence and AnnCA picking frame tokens by nearest neighbor matching. AnnSA sparsifies self attention to semantically matched keys. Tests show five to tenfold end to end speedups with near identical visual quality, stable throughput and memory over long rollouts.
arxiv-2602-01901: Jiedong Zhuang and colleagues cut multimodal inference costs, where excess visual tokens burden computation and cache. Token pruning damages cache integrity and fails long text generation, so the team studies decode layer attention instead. They find attention in over half of decode layers semantically similar, letting later layers inherit earlier attention. Lazy Attention shares patterns across layers, and Q Cache reuses queries across layers, cutting redundant computation. Q Cache stays lightweight and compatible with Flash Attention, works alone or with pruning. Tests show cache use falling over thirty five percent.
arxiv-2602-02001: Yoonjun Cho and colleagues balance rank budgets for error reconstruction. Quantization Error Reconstruction writes weights as Q plus LR with a rank r correction, but full rank for error reconstruction wastes budget when directions corrupt. Structured Residual Reconstruction keeps the top k subspace, quantizing only the residual, and using spare rank for reconstruction. A criterion selects k balancing exposed and lost error. The resulting Q plus LR form supports QPEFT, stabilizing tuning via gradient steps, cutting perplexity with a five point nine point two bit GLUE gain.
arxiv-2602-02301: Min Cai and others present Modular Gradient Surgery, resolving gradient conflicts when training one general-purpose thought model across diverse domains. Studying sequential and mixed reinforcement plans, the team finds both suffer substantial cross-domain interference at behavioral and gradient levels, limiting overall gains. The new method resolves conflicts at the module level inside the transformer. Applied to Llama and Qwen models, it aids average scores over standard multi-task reinforcement learning across math, general chat, and instruction following, and remains effective under prolonged training.
arxiv-2602-02401:
Xinshun Wang and 7 co-authors unify seeing human motion and generating it inside one model, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The field is split: perception models read video but only output text, while generation models cannot take raw visual input. Motion vocabularies built from skeletons alone also lose the link to images.

Their framework, Superman, starts with a vision-guided motion tokenizer. Because 3D skeletons align geometrically with visual data, the tokenizer learns jointly from both and builds a shared motion vocabulary. A single multimodal model trained on that vocabulary then handles pose estimation from video, motion prediction, and filling gaps between poses. On standard benchmarks such as Human3.6M, the unified system reaches top or competitive scores across all tasks. One model replaces a fragmented pipeline.
arxiv-2602-02801:
Barrett T Smith and 3 co-authors bend microscopic fibers with flowing water to measure how stiff and springy they are, in a 2026 paper. Soft hydrogel fibers and rods serve tissue engineering, flexible electronics, soft robotics, and drug delivery, yet their viscoelastic properties are hard to characterize at that scale. Conventional mechanical testers are built for far larger samples.

Their flow-induced bending rheometer parks a fiber across a glass capillary entrance. Pressure-driven water inflow exerts a quantifiable force while video microscopy records deflection and flow simultaneously. An analytical hydrodynamic model plus beam theory converts deflection into material properties. Steady flow yields the bending modulus; stepwise, cyclic, or oscillatory flow reveals creep, recovery, and time-dependent moduli. Demonstrations span natural and synthetic materials from five to three hundred microns wide and across six orders of magnitude in stiffness. Water loading suits hydrated samples especially well.
arxiv-2602-03101:
Quantum annealing for hard decision problems is reviewed by Rudraksh Sharma and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Combinatorial tuning underlies critical choices in science, engineering, and industry, but its NP-hard nature limits classic methods. Quantum annealing encodes a problem into a real energy landscape and uses quantum tunnelling to explore answers, a specialized form of analogue quantum computing.

The review covers theory, hardware designs, method strategies, and encoding and vector schemes. It connects adiabatic motion and Ising models to modern flux-qubit annealers and emerging platforms, plus hybrid quantum-classic methods. Benchmarking plans and application areas are surveyed. The analysis finds vector overhead, not qubit count alone, is the largest determinant of scalability and results.
arxiv-2602-03301:
Q-learning that stays stable under function approximation is pursued by Hyukjun Yang, with 2 co-authors, through periodic regularization. In tabular settings Q-learning is guaranteed to converge, but that guarantee fails with linear function fitting, where updates can diverge. Such techniques have been introduced to restore stability, and this work regularizes at the level of the projection operator itself in the value iteration behind the method.

The authors construct a regularized projected value iteration and show it becomes a contraction with apt regularization. Extending that projection into the stochastic, sample-based setting yields their method, Periodic Regularized Q-Learning. A rigorous theory-based analysis gives finite-time settling guarantees under linear function fitting. The contribution is mainly theoretical, giving practitioners a provably stable variant.
arxiv-2602-03501:
Model-based reinforcement learning can learn from few trials by differentiating through a simulation of the world. Hai Zhong and 3 co-authors widen the policies that method can use in a 2026 paper. Earlier reparameterization policy gradient work mostly allowed Gaussian policies, which limits their expressive range and ignores modern generative models.

The authors observe that flow policies, which produce actions by integrating a differential equation, fit the framework naturally. Their method, RFO, backpropagates jointly through action generation and system dynamics, avoiding hard likelihood math. Two penalty terms add steadiness and exploration, and a variant chunks actions together. Across locomotion and manipulation tasks, including a soft-body quadruped, RFO nearly doubles the best baseline's reward.
arxiv-2602-03701:
Mohammad Abdulaziz and Thomas Ammer verify minimum-cost flow algorithms inside the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant in a 2026 paper. Minimum-cost flow routes goods through a network at least total cost, and fast algorithms for it usually rest on pen-and-paper proofs. These authors formalize the correctness of executable versions, leaving nothing to trust.

Two of the algorithms use capacity scaling, including Orlin's algorithm, which has the fastest known running time; its worst-case argument is formalized too. Stepwise refinement turns the proofs into code that actually runs, now part of a reusable graph-algorithms library. A verified reduction extends the results to the general problem. The work also produced sharper proofs and theorem statements than existing expositions.
arxiv-2602-03801:
Drones flying shared aerial corridors must pick a base station and a beam, fast, while the radio channel changes around them. Pulok Tarafder and 5 co-authors build a digital-twin training pipeline for that decision in a 2026 paper. Exact optimization is too slow for real time, and learning methods normally need large site-specific datasets that do not exist.

A channel twin, built from ray tracing with geographic context, simulates the site's propagation faithfully and precomputes good beam directions. A multi-head PPO agent then trains on the twin's data to decide station and beam jointly from channel state. In dense drone scenarios it beats a deep Q-network baseline and heuristic schemes by large margins. Inference latency falls by orders of magnitude as well.
arxiv-2602-03901:
Searching for the best trade-offs among many goals is expensive when each test costs real computation. Rong Fu and 6 co-authors present NeuroPareto, a 2026 system that hunts Pareto-optimal designs, meaning designs where no goal improves without hurting another. It targets vast parameter spaces with strict evaluation budgets.

A Bayesian classifier ranks candidates by quality tier and estimates uncertainty. Gaussian process models split that uncertainty into parts that testing can and cannot reduce. A small network, trained on past gains, picks which candidates deserve full evaluation. On standard suites and an energy extraction task, NeuroPareto beat comparable methods.
arxiv-2602-04201:
A handful of sensors must stand in for a whole evolving field. Yanjie Tong and 1 co-author present STRIDE, a framework for reconstructing spatiotemporal fields from sparse point measurements, in a 2026 paper. The setting is parametric partial differential equation dynamics, where fields change across trajectories and parameter values.

A temporal encoder compresses a short window of sensor readings into a latent state. An implicit neural decoder then rebuilds the field at any query location, freeing the method from fixed meshes. A Fourier-based network backbone represents complex spatial patterns more stably than sine-based alternatives. Theory ties the reconstruction to delay observability of the measurements.
arxiv-2602-04501:
J. A. Dixon presents a deliberately simple model in a 2026 paper on exotic invariants, special symmetry quantities in supersymmetric theories. The example uses just two chiral electron supermultiplets, named E and P, which keeps the mathematics manageable.

Adding a mass term creates a constraint on the exotic invariant. Dixon shows that the constraint is easy to solve in this simple case. He also offers a conjecture for the completion terms, extra pieces needed to finish the construction. The value of the example is practical. The larger exotic model, built on the supersymmetric standard model, has a similar constraint. Its completion terms also look similar, so the small model serves as a guide.
arxiv-2602-04801:
Four drones carrying one load on cables must share tension sensibly, or cables slacken and drones drift toward each other. Lamberto Vazquez-Soqui and 3 co-authors add a real-time optimization layer for that task in a 2026 control study.

Their method uses sequential quadratic programming, an iterative optimization technique, on top of a hierarchical controller. It minimizes the sum of squared cable tensions. A penalty on small angles between cables discourages dangerous convergence, without changing the planned trajectory. Simulations with four quadrotors ran the routine in a few milliseconds on standard hardware. Sensitivity analysis showed the safety penalty can be tuned online, trading safety margin against energy use with no measurable tracking loss.
arxiv-2602-05001:
Sherzod R Otajonov and Fatkhulla Kh Abdullaev wrote this 2026 physics paper on Bose-Einstein condensates, matter cooled until atoms act as one wave. Their system holds a two-component condensate in a trap with two cores, so atoms can tunnel back and forth like current in a Josephson junction. Quantum fluctuations beyond the mean field are included through a standard correction.

For a uniform condensate, the authors map regimes of tunneling, self-trapping, and revival, and derive the frequencies of two oscillation modes. The zero-phase mode shows two bifurcations, giving bistability and hysteresis. They then study droplets and vortices: droplet pairs oscillate at predicted frequencies, a nondissipative drag effect appears, and small vortices break into fragments while large ones stay stable. Numerical simulations back the predictions throughout.
arxiv-2602-05101:
Rogue waves in optics and oceans can be modeled by soliton solutions of the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Aikaterini Gkogkou and 2 co-authors study the extreme members of that family in this 2026 mathematics paper. The solutions are built from many solitons that reach the largest amplitude the theory allows, growing without bound as the count rises.

The twist is chance. The solutions' eigenvalues are drawn from sub-exponential distributions, and the authors ask what shape survives once chance washes out the details. Two universality classes emerge, set by the overall layout of the spectrum. In one regime the rescaled solutions settle onto a profile ruled by the Painlevé-III equation; in the other, by Painlevé-V. Either way, the limiting rogue wave does not depend on the set distribution used. The result shows Painlevé-type rogue waves form robustly, not as fragile accidents of special initial data.
arxiv-2602-05201:
At extremely low bitrates, conventional video compression runs out of redundancy to exploit. Maojun Zhang and 4 co-authors take a generative route in this 2026 signal processing paper, accepted at ICASSP 2026. Instead of squeezing pixels, their codec sends a compact description of what the video means, and a diffusion model rebuilds the frames at the other end.

The semantic description is kept lean by splitting motion into two cheap parts. Background movement is summarized by camera trajectory parameters, while the moving foreground is carried by sparse segmentation masks. Conditioned on those semantics, the diffusion model synthesizes frames that preserve the scene's content and layout. The authors report decent reconstruction quality at bitrates where traditional and learned codecs, tied to low-level spatiotemporal redundancy, break down. The work points toward compression built on understanding first and pixels second.
arxiv-2602-05501:
Ending cosmic inflation through a sudden vacuum change has long looked unworkable, since bubbles of the new phase may form too slowly to finish the job. Jintao Zou, Ligong Bian, and Shao-Jiang Wang propose a first-order phase transition at the grand unification scale inside Starobinsky inflation, a well-known model of the early universe. Their trick is a potential barrier that shifts as the inflaton field rolls, holding bubbles back early on.

Near the end of inflation, that barrier lets bubbles form in huge numbers, so the transition can complete. Lattice simulations match earlier analytic estimates. The gravitational-wave spectrum shows a distinctive wobble at high frequencies, a possible fingerprint for future detectors. The paper offers a route around the graceful exit problem that has blocked this class of models.
arxiv-2602-05601:
Blazars are active galaxies whose jets point near Earth, and their sudden flares across many wavelengths carry clues about the tiny regions that emit the light. Paloma Thevenet, Andreas Zech, Catherine Boisson, and Anton Dmytriiev model such flares with a one-zone synchrotron self-Compton framework, where one compact blob of energetic particles both shines and scatters its own light. Their goal is to find flare signatures that tell competing physical processes apart.

The team systematically varies how particles are injected, accelerated by shocks or turbulence, and lost through escape or radiation. Each mix produces a distinct light curve shape over time and energy. Energy-dependent time delays and the shape of a flare's rise stand out as fingerprints of the underlying process. A simplified application to a flare from the blazar Mrk 421 shows how the method would work on real data.
arxiv-2602-05901:
Magnets on a triangular lattice frustrate simple order, because neighbors cannot all satisfy each other at once, and the resulting phases are still debated. Songtai Lv, Yuchen Meng, and Haiyuan Zou point to an overlooked player: parity symmetry, which looks trivial yet shapes what frustration produces. In a weak longitudinal field, phases follow an implicit rule of thumb tied to spontaneous parity breaking.

For the spin S antiferromagnetic XXZ model on that lattice, a controversial parity broken phase appears at intermediate values of S. In bilayer systems, stronger frustration adds phases such as supersolids, classified by their parity features. Improved tensor network contraction techniques let them confirm the picture with large scale calculations. The study offers a systematic viewpoint on how spin, symmetry, and frustration interact. It should interest condensed matter theorists who map phase diagrams of frustrated magnets. The parity lens, they argue, predicts where nontrivial phases emerge.
arxiv-2602-06101:
Hidden marks inside AI-made pictures can prove ownership and curb misuse, but placing them well is tricky. Liangqi Lei and 3 co-authors present ALIEN, a watermarking method for latent diffusion models, which build pictures in a compressed space. Older methods tune the mark by slow trial and error.

ALIEN instead derives the guiding formula directly, on paper. A time-dependent coefficient steers how the watermark signal spreads during picture generation, so the embedding pattern can be controlled. Two versions were tested. One led on picture quality across several measures. The other resisted attacks and edits better than rivals under many test conditions.
arxiv-2602-06301:
Grouping units into clusters is central to mixture models, and one knob, the concentration parameter, steers how many clusters appear. JoonHo Lee offers a principled way to set the prior for that knob in Dirichlet process mixtures. Too often, the choice is left at a default that quietly shapes the answer.

Analysts state how many clusters they expect, and how unsure they are, when the unit count is set by the design. Software then turns those judgments into a prior and shows what it implies about cluster sizes. When count and size wishes conflict, a dual-anchor step picks and reports the trade-off. Trials in a multisite study, a meta-analysis, and a vocabulary test showed real sensitivity.
arxiv-2602-06501:
Vacancy-ordered halide double perovskites conduct heat exceptionally poorly, which suits insulation and thermoelectric devices. Lingzhi Cao and 3 co-authors investigate why, using first-principles calculations across a family of cesium compounds with varying metals and halogens. All the compounds showed ultralow thermal conductivity at room temperature, deviating from the usual inverse temperature law.

Surprisingly, weak chemical bonding, not rattling phonon modes in the structure's voids, did most of the work. Low sound speeds from that weak bonding throttled heat flow in most compounds. The team also mapped how each metal and halogen choice shifts phonon dispersion, anharmonicity, and scattering. The microscopic picture gives designers rules for tuning heat transport in this family.
arxiv-2602-06801:
Sohan Venkatesh and Ashish Mahendran Kurapath challenge a popular way of reading language models from the inside. Activation steering nudges a model's behavior by pushing its inner states along a chosen direction. Those directions are often read as meaningful signs of what the model represents. The paper argues that reading is unfounded, because the directions cannot be pinned down from behavior alone.

With white-box access to a single layer, the authors show that large families of different steering vectors produce the same outward behavior. Tests find that unrelated nudges work nearly as well as the intended directions, across models and traits. That match holds across the practical steering range and varied prompts. The result sets a basic limit on steering-based reading of models, and calls for hard rules about structure beyond mere behavior tests.
arxiv-2602-07001:
Yueyi Yang and three co-authors offer a two-phase system that joins positioning and communication, built on orthogonal time frequency space modulation. It is designed for real low-resolution analog-to-digital converters. In the uplink phase, a positioning signal yields channel parameters, which then yield the user's position. Angle of arrival comes from a spatial smoothing multiple signal classification algorithm, while an iterative interference cancellation scheme handles the rest. Lower bounds of Cramér-Rao type are derived for channel parameters and for user position.

In the downlink phase, those estimates improve beamforming at the base station. Simulations test how converter resolution shapes results. Better uplink positioning yields better downlink bit error rates, while low-resolution converters cause clear performance loss. The work thus quantifies the hardware-cost trade-off for joint positioning and communication.
arxiv-2602-07201:
AKLT states are prized resources for measurement-based quantum computing, but preparing them beyond one dimension is hard.  Wenhan Guo and four co-authors investigate a constant-time scheme that uses fusion measurements to create high-D AKLT states on a given graph.

The states come out with random spin-1 decorations, yet the paper shows those decorated states carry at least as much computational power as clean ones. For Bethe lattices the preparation can be made deterministic.  Random-bond variants are covered too.  The result widens the set of states known to be useful for quantum computing, including states that arise naturally rather than by careful design.
arxiv-2602-07401:
The kagome lattice hosts frustrated magnetism where competing forces create unusual phases.  Yutaka Okabe and one co-author investigate the Ising model on that lattice with antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor and ferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor couplings.

Using level spectroscopy, Monte Carlo simulation, and machine-learning phase classification, they find two Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transitions and a phase diagram of three phases. The phases are a low-temperature ordered phase, an intermediate BKT phase, and a high-temperature disordered phase, varying with the coupling ratio.  Machine learning confirms six-state clock universality.  Statistical experts get a thorough, triple-checked phase diagram for a frustrated model.  Three independent methods converging on the same phase diagram strengthens confidence in the two-transition picture.
arxiv-2602-07601:
DNA storage promises dense, durable archiving, but distributing data across DNA containers raises a new question: how long does recovery take when a container fails?  Adi Levy and three co-authors initiate the study of DNA-based distributed storage, where each read samples a random strand from a container.

Several erasure-correcting codes are analyzed for expected recovery time of a failed container's contents, through generalized versions of the classic coupon collector problem that may interest probabilists on their own.  Storage teams get the first recovery-time analysis for a medium where reading itself is random sampling, a constraint classic distributed storage never faced. Slow reads stall the whole rebuild, so read time is the key cost here.
arxiv-2602-07701:
Sound waves inside a cold gas of bosons behave in ways that are hard to pin down, and this mathematical physics paper works out how quickly they fade. Jan Dereziński and Lorenzo Pettinari study a uniform Bose gas in a large box, kept at low temperature and disturbed only slightly.

Using perturbation theory, they compute the damping of the gas's sound-like excitations, called phonons, at low momentum. Two routes lead to the same picture: one tracks resonances near zero energy, the other studies a two-point correlation function. Readers get a careful, rigorous account of phonon damping in a model system that underlies much of cold-atom theory.
arxiv-2602-08101:
Plague models often miss extreme super-spread events, the dragon kings that deviate from standard spreads and drive outbreaks. Jose de Jesus Bernal-Alvarado and two co-authors bridge tiny random SIR motion with large-scale wave analysis using the Moyal spread.

Treating spread as a random crash process, they derive a Moyal-Poisson mixture for later cases that gets extreme events in SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 data where negative two-part models fail. Spectral split of German pandemic waves then shows large-scale social friction emerging directly from tiny crash shocks. Public-health modelers gain a unified retrospective method that captures both the average wave and its wildest outliers.
arxiv-2602-08201:
Virtual reality feels less real when hands meet objects without real feedback. Kun-Woo Song and two co-authors explore finger tendon buzz, a method that creates an fake feeling of finger motion by buzzing tendons, as a body cue for virtual object contact.

Three sense studies first map short buzzes under five seconds, shaping six example VR scenes and four haptic display plans across the design space of object contacts. Weighing tendon buzz against no buzz and simple buzz, the authors find it improves realism by conveying resistance on the finger and strengthening body ownership. VR designers gain evidence-based guidelines for applying an unusual but promising haptic illusion.
arxiv-2602-08701:
Health wearables in low- and middle-income countries face cost, literacy, and comprehension barriers that limit their use. Mohammad Shaharyar Ahsan and six co-authors present Guardian Angel, a cheap screenless wearable linked to a WhatsApp language-model agent. Their arXiv paper targets plain-language, personalized health guidance from raw, noisy sensor waveforms.

Guardian Angel pairs a cheap wearable with no screen to a WhatsApp agent that reads the signals directly and stays robust to poor signal quality. Where a standard open tool gave valid outputs for only about seventy percent of segments, Guardian Angel reached full coverage under field noise, a measure of availability distinct from accuracy. A ninety-six-hour study with twenty participants showed significant gains in comprehension of vital signs and mindfulness about them. Readers get a practical design for health literacy in resource-limited settings.
arxiv-2602-08801:
Meaning-based communication systems send only task-relevant traits, saving bandwidth for cars and factory devices, but hostile tampering with those traits can cause crashes. Thanh Le and three co-authors present VSCAN, a checking tool that provides math proofs of toughness for deep-learning SemCom systems. Their arXiv paper casts hostile noise making as mixed-integer coding across encoder, decoder, and task networks.

Real attacker limits on power and stats-based stealth become logical rules for state-of-the-art checkers. Across six hundred checking cases, VSCAN matches attack methods at finding flaws while proving toughness for forty-four percent of cases. A speed trade-off emerges: compact 16-D latent spaces prove at fifty percent versus 64-D spaces. Readers get formal proofs where ad-hoc defenses offered none.
arxiv-2602-08901:
Language models sometimes recite training text word for word, a privacy and copyright risk. Xuanqi Zhang and two co-authors show that blanket fixes hurt: most tokens behave normally, while a small minority carries most of the memorization signal. They locate those spots with a token-level likelihood ratio against a reference model less exposed to the tested passages.

From that insight they derive Gated Subspace Steering, a probe-and-steer fix that corrects only activations the probe flags. Its best form has a closed-form solution from a gradient-weighted activation matrix. Across four benchmarks it matches or beats the best memorization cuts while using ten to one hundred times less compute than optimization-based rivals.
arxiv-2602-09001:
Mixture-of-experts models usually route tokens with a Top-k plus Softmax rule that cannot be differentiated cleanly, tangling two choices: which experts to use, and how much each should contribute. Amirhossein Vahidi and six co-authors introduce DirMoE, a fully differentiable router built on a Dirichlet variational autoencoder. A Bernoulli part picks experts, while a Dirichlet part shares weight among the chosen ones.

Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation and implicit reparameterization keep the whole forward pass differentiable. The training objective adds a sparsity penalty that controls the expected number of active experts, plus a schedule that moves routing from exploratory to decisive. DirMoE matches or beats rival routers while improving expert specialization.
arxiv-2602-09101:
Carlos Heredia derives a sped-up, smooth-time version of Adam, the widely used optimizer, by modeling it as a second-order system with memory. The inertial model with far-reaching links connects to an existing first-order Adam flow with far-reaching links through an alpha-refinement limit, and Lyapunov analysis establishes stability and convergence. An Adam-inspired Lagrangian formulation adds a variational viewpoint.

Numerical tests on Rosenbrock-type examples confirm the proposed dynamics track discrete Adam closely. The work gives users a principled smooth lens on why Adam behaves as it does, and a base for designing related sped-up methods with guarantees.
arxiv-2602-09401:
Live-streaming recommendation must model shifting content meaning under strict real-time limits, and standard approaches each lose something. Discrete abstractions blur descriptive detail through clustering, while dense multimodal embeddings sit weakly aligned with ranking goals. Ruochen Yang and sixteen co-authors propose SARM, a 2026 end-to-end ranking design that weaves natural-language semantic anchors straight into ranking optimization.

Each anchor becomes learnable text tokens trained jointly with ranking features, yielding fine-grained author profiles conditioned on multimodal content. A lightweight dual-token gated design captures live-streaming semantics, while an asymmetric deployment plan keeps online training and serving fast. Offline tests and large-scale live experiments beat production baselines consistently. The system is fully deployed, serving hundreds of millions of users each day.
arxiv-2602-09501:
Masked diffusion language models write by filling blanks step by step, facing two linked choices each round: which positions to open, and which tokens to place. Training optimizes token choice directly, but opening order at inference usually follows confidence heuristics or costly reinforcement learning rollouts. Hikaru Asano and three co-authors propose learning the order from ground truth instead.

Their score, Gt-Margin, measures the gap between the correct token's probability and its strongest rival at each position. That margin yields an oracle order that opens easier positions first under each partial masking, and using it markedly improves generation quality on logical reasoning tests. A supervised planner trained by learning-to-rank then imitates the oracle order from masked context alone. Plugged into standard sampling, it lifts reasoning accuracy without touching the token prediction model.
arxiv-2602-09601:
Comet 73P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 3, a short-period comet fragmented repeatedly in recent decades, may feed cometary pickup ions through its dust trail rather than its ion tails alone. Samuel R. Grant and two co-authors test that idea in their 2026 paper, tracing two encounters. In mid-2006, fragments passed sunward of the Sun-Earth Lagrange point while ACE and Wind spacecraft detected pickup ions concurrently.

In August 2011, a fragment passed directly sunward of STEREO-B, with ions shown to originate at fragment 73P-AM. Solar wind velocities extrapolated in three dimensions let the team estimate separations between ion tails and spacecraft. Major-fragment alignment proved poor for ion transport by solar wind, yet the encounter came near enough for immersion in the diffuse ion tail enveloping an extended dust trail. The trail, the authors conclude, significantly sourced cometary ions at that distance.
arxiv-2602-09701:
Sandesh Hegde and three co-authors report strong benchmark wins for fine-grained referring segmentation in their 2026 paper. Their best model beats its instruct baselines by a wide margin on RefCOCOg validation and tops a rival method under identical evaluation. A variant built for GRefCOCO also handles negative prompts, and the smaller model leads on the ReasonSeg test.

Those gains come from training, not from hand-written reasoning examples. Inside the GenSeg-R1 framework, Qwen3-VL models of four and eight billion parameters learn through group relative policy optimization. That training uses no supervised reasoning-chain annotations. At run time, the trained model turns a natural-language query and an image into spatial prompts. Each referred instance gets one bounding box plus two interior keypoints. A frozen promptable segmenter then turns those prompts into high-quality masks, splitting reasoning from segmentation.
arxiv-2602-09801:
Most machine learning ways to science finding frame guesses as end-to-end forecasts, hiding the stepwise structure of science thought. Agnieszka Dobrowolska and eight co-authors propose The Guess Game, a symbol frame for guess polish. Language model agents work on a shared guess state using a fixed grammar of thought moves. Their 2026 paper is sparked by the note that science progress often proceeds through small, local edits grounded in domain context, rather than wide redos.

A minimal game with language model agents is tested on pathway-level machine polish tasks. In damage repair, where guesses contain set errors, the game-based approach often removes more errors and reaches higher care than strong prompting rivals, while keeping valid structure through stepwise edits. In rebuild from partial cues, it performs evenly to the strongest rival, showing move-based polish strong even when ground-truth repair is hard.
arxiv-2602-10201:
Rare top-quark flavor changes that skip charge would betray physics beyond the Standard Model, but they are tightly constrained. A 2026 paper by Subhajit Kala and Soumitra Nandi studies top-quark flavor-changing neutral currents model-independently within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. A general top-flavor parameterization is matched onto the effective theory basis for a global fit.

The fit combines low-energy flavor data, electroweak precision numbers, Higgs measurements, collider limits on top-flavor decays, and electric dipole moment constraints. Allowing complex dipole operators, the authors derive stringent bounds on real and imaginary coupling parts and robust constraints on Wilson coefficients. Predictions for rare branching ratios and CP asymmetries follow, with benchmarks showing how CP-violating observables complement flavor probes.
arxiv-2602-10301:
Surge wave energy converters capture wave energy with a flap hinged at the seabed or a floating platform, and dual-flap arrays raise a spacing question. A 2026 paper by Alaa Ahmed, sole author, investigates how flap spacing affects each flap's performance, estimating absorbed wave energy and yearly energy output at the PacWave South site. Friction-free numerical simulations predict converter response, checked against a one-tenth scale model in a wave tank.

For short flap gaps, flap interaction proves harmful or helpful depending on wave frequency, yet those effects largely balance across varied wave excitations. For longer gaps, interaction always proves helpful. The results guide array spacing for dual-flap converters, balancing per-flap performance against total yearly energy output.
arxiv-2602-10401:
Optical networks change over time, so failure-detection models trained once can drift out of step with the network they monitor. A 2026 paper led by Yousuf Moiz Ali, with six co-authors, presents an online learning approach to concept drift adaptation for optical network failure detection. Rather than relying on a fixed model, the method learns continuously, adjusting as conditions shift so that detection keeps pace with the evolving network. The paper's central claim is performance: the adaptive approach improves on conventional static models by up to seventy percent, while keeping latency low.

That combination matters because a detector that adapts slowly, or one that adapts only at the cost of delay, would be of limited use in live network operations. By pairing a large performance gain with low latency, the work points toward failure detection that stays accurate as networks evolve, without asking operators to trade responsiveness for adaptability.
arxiv-2602-10601:
Katarína Cechlárová and Ildikó Schlotter study a question about party-based elections in a 2026 paper. Each party nominates exactly one candidate, and the election runs over all nominees. A candidate is a necessary president if nomination promises victory no matter what other parties nominate.

The paper maps the machine hardness of deciding this trait across voting rules. For Borda, Maximin, and Copeland rules the problem is solvable in formula time. For general positional scoring rules, including approval-style and veto-style variants, it becomes coNP-complete even when parties have at most two members. Parameterized results refine the picture: hard in the number of parties, tractable in other settings.
arxiv-2602-10701:
Cedric Faas and four co-authors study how decision support reshapes moral responsibility in a 2026 paper. Safety-key AI oversight exists to keep a human genuinely responsible when things go wrong. But support systems that recommend, alert, or restrict interventions can undermine that very purpose, mainly when their recommendations err.

In a simulated oversight test, two hundred seventy-four people monitored an autonomous system. The team tested how a support system that restricted ready interventions affected perceived moral responsibility. The focus falls on cases where support errs: does the human still feel responsible, or does the machine's constraint absorb the blame? The findings matter for making oversight that preserves human accountability rather than quietly transferring it to software.
arxiv-2602-10901:
Adrien Girardot and four co-authors describe the test bench for a new space light meter in a 2026 paper. Pollux, a high-detail light meter put forth by a European group for the Habitable Worlds Observatory, holds four light channels, three in the ultraviolet. Near- and mid-ultraviolet meters use wave plates and prisms of double-bending magnesium fluoride.

No such double-bending material works for the far-ultraviolet channel, so its meter uses mirrors alone in a new assembly. The test bench, running in an airless chamber in a clean room for the airless-ultraviolet range, will check all the meters' results. The paper details the bendable system that lets one bench qualify every other ultraviolet meter for space.
arxiv-2602-11101:
A dye-water mix can sort itself into patterns with no glue at all. A. Bensabat and seven co-authors combine theory, simulation, and tests on Sunset Yellow-water chromonic mixes. Their minimal model needs only a coupling between local density and orientational order.

When that coupling grows strong, defects in the nematic field seed isotropic droplets. Droplets merge under elastic and surface tension, until strong anchoring at interfaces halts coarsening. The result is a stable layered microphase with wavy layers, uneven spacing, glassy defect patterns, and lamellar onions. The authors name orientational-density coupling and elastocapillarity as the guiding mechanisms.
arxiv-2602-11201:
Step-by-step accounts may not show how a model truly reasons. Donald Ye and four co-authors propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay, a metric that corrupts single thinking steps and measures the drop in answer confidence. Standardized scores allow fair match across designs.

Across three model families and syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, they find a steady Thinking Horizon late in the chain, beyond which tokens barely affect the answer. Models can also hold correct internal forms while failing the task outright. The work shows scores alone cannot prove thinking, and offers a tool to measure when chain-of-thought actually matters.
arxiv-2602-11401:
Latent diffusion discards image detail in encoding and needs a separate decoder. Alan Baade and six co-authors propose Latent Forcing, a modification that keeps latent-diffusion speed while operating on raw natural images. Latents and pixels are processed jointly with separately tuned noise schedules.

Latents act as a scratchpad for middle computation before high-rate pixel traits appear. The order of conditioning signals proves key, explaining differences between distillation placements, conditional versus unconditional making, and tokenizer quality versus diffusability. On ImageNet, Latent Forcing sets a new state of the art for diffusion-model pixel making at its compute scale.
arxiv-2602-12101:
After a violent cosmic event, the standard picture says a black hole remnant quickly settles into a linear ringdown that gravitational-wave astronomy reads like a fingerprint. Cheng-Yong Zhang and two co-authors argue that a distinct nonlinear stage can come first and dominate the evolution.

A saddle-node ghost in phase space can trap the remnant, delaying linearity by a span that follows a universal power law. The ghost leaves a quiescence-burst signature: a long silence, then a violent burst, then the delayed ringdown. Rooted in bifurcation topology, the same pattern should extend to neutron and boson stars, offering future observations a clear target beyond the linear paradigm.
arxiv-2602-12201:
Close-in exoplanets lose air to space, and that loss does not take all gases equally. Marilina Valatsou led this work with three co-authors, asking how escape and chemical sorting together shape sub-Neptune atmospheres. Light hydrogen tends to flee first, while heavier oxygen tends to stay behind, changing the mix that remains.

The team built BOREAS, a model that joins a one-dimensional wind picture to a mass-based sorting rule, and ran it across planet sizes, heats, and star fluxes. Oxygen stays put over most settings, escaping mainly under strong flux or on low-gravity worlds. Where hydrogen escapes well with some oxygen dragged along, sub-Neptunes grow markedly water-rich over about 200 million years, a path that may explain water-rich worlds near the radius valley.
arxiv-2602-12301:
Music searchers often say more than a list of genres: they like, dislike, or merely mention a sound, and that intent changes what counts as a good answer. Marion Baranes led this work with two co-authors, building MusicRecoIntent, a hand-labelled corpus of 2,291 Reddit music requests. Descriptors fall in seven categories, each marked as positive, negative, or merely referential.

The team then tests how well large language models extract those descriptors. Models capture explicit descriptors fairly well, but stumble on context-dependent ones, where meaning hinges on phrasing and surrounding talk. The corpus doubles as a benchmark for fine-grained intent modelling, pointing toward music systems that hear not just what a user names, but what they actually want.
arxiv-2602-12801:
Sturmian words are infinite sequences with a famously even distribution of symbols, and rectangles built from them raise a natural balance question. Ingrid Vukusic studies m-by-n matrices formed from Sturmian words of slope alpha, and fully characterises when they are balanced. The characterisation is given in terms of Ostrowski expansions of m and n with respect to alpha.

The result extends earlier work by Anselmo and colleagues, and by Shallit and the author, which handled only quadratic irrational slopes. Unlike those papers, the new argument rests on the distribution of multiples of alpha modulo one. That shift in method is what lets the balance classification reach arbitrary slopes, closing a gap left by the special cases.
arxiv-2602-13001:
Supercongruences are congruences that hold to surprisingly high prime powers, and Whipple's hypergeometric formula is a rich source of them. Chen Wang and He-Xia Ni establish a parametric supercongruence tied to Whipple's hypergeometric formula and to Dwork's dash operation. As a consequence, for any prime p congruent to 3 modulo 4 and any odd r, a specific finite sum matches an expression involving p^r and a harmonic number, modulo p^{r+3}.

That consequence confirms a conjecture of Guo and Zhao. The proof rests on a new parametric Wilf-Zeilberger pair that transforms the sum into a computable congruent form, plus properties of Dwork's dash operation. For number theorists, the paper adds a verified supercongruence and a method that may unlock others in the same family.
arxiv-2602-13601:
Putting the Lennard-Jones potential into Direct Simulation Monte Carlo is hard. Its long range complicates collision rates and makes scattering-angle calculations expensive. This study builds an LJ-DSMC framework around two advances. First, a generalized collision-selection treatment for Bird's DSMC variants uses a Variable Effective Diameter model matched to local viscosity. That matched model gives a collision-rate closure for the Lennard-Jones potential, checked in helium-argon shocks, cold Couette flow, and fast cylinder flows.

Where attractive forces matter, Lennard-Jones effects appear. These include reduced shear stress and larger cryogenic wakes, against agreement with simpler models in hot repulsive regimes. Second, a Deep Operator Network predicts bend angles from detailed scattering data, replacing a costly integral. It cuts the collision step time by 40 percent and wall time by 36 percent, with tiny errors. Ahmad Shoja Sani leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14101:
Thiem Hoang, writing alone, develops a 2026 arXiv model of dust grains with magnetic inclusions. Grain magnetism shapes how dust aligns with ambient fields and emits magnetic dipole radiation. Under the radiative torque view, superparamagnetic inclusions should boost susceptibility and alignment, but past work assumed one inclusion size.

Hoang instead allows a power-law spread of inclusion sizes. The effective zero-frequency susceptibility then equals the uniform-size value at a critical blocking size, scaled down by a factor near 0.1. It rises slightly with dust temperature, unlike the steep fall for single-size grains. For spinning grains, one resonance size dominates the response, and the frequency-dependent susceptibility follows its peak value.
arxiv-2602-14301:
Songyuan Li and five co-authors present a 2026 arXiv framework for federated training of mixture-of-experts models. Large expert models need vast, diverse data, and federated learning taps private data on edge devices. Yet classic federated methods force devices to host full expert models, impractical for resource-limited hardware.

DeepFusion instead fuses heterogeneous on-device language-model knowledge through federated knowledge distillation, yielding a knowledge-rich global expert model. Each device trains its own model matched to its needs and hardware limits. A View-Aligned Attention module integrates multi-stage features from the global model to build predictive representations, making expert training scalable across diverse devices.
arxiv-2602-14601:
Quantum entanglement once looked like a puzzle at the edge of physics. Yu Shi traces its road from Einstein's early doubts to the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. The review covers Bell inequalities and the tests that turned abstract debate into lab results.

Shi stresses the key physical ideas behind each step, not just the dates. Early work by C. S. Wu on photons from electron-positron annihilation gets a full place in the story. Later tests and later growth of the field follow in turn. The result is a clear map of how entanglement moved from doubt to prize-winning science.
arxiv-2602-14901:
Pramit Saha and others fix a pick problem in health agent gear: no lone expert wins each task, from spot checks to site finds to note writing. Each task has a pool of rival experts, and each expert wins on its own slice of cases.

For each ask, the agent must pick the right tool from that mixed pool, with trust, not habit. Their ToolSelect learns that pick by cutting a pool-wide risk over tried experts, with a fair stand-in for task-wise pick risk. Health agents thus gain a learned picker, not a fixed fave.
arxiv-2602-15001:
Davies and colleagues introduce Boundary Point Jailbreaking, a fully black-box automated attack on frontier language model safeguards. Defenders now field classifier systems that have survived thousands of hours of human red teaming. Earlier attacks lean on classifier scores, gradients, or libraries of known jailbreaks. BPJ needs only one bit per query: whether the classifier flags the interaction.

The core trick is judging whether a proposed change improves an attack. BPJ turns a target harmful string into a staged curriculum of intermediate targets, then picks evaluation points that best reveal small shifts in attack strength. The authors claim the first fully automated universal jailbreaks against Constitutional Classifiers and against GPT-5 input safeguards without human seeds. They note BPJ triggers many flags while tuning, so batch-level monitoring may be the better defense.
arxiv-2602-15501:
Steiner and colleagues turn the ESPRESSO spectrograph on the hot Jupiter WASP-31 b, watching two and a half transits to map its air and its orbit. High-resolution spectra of such worlds are often spoiled by planet-occulted line distortion, a star effect that mimics planet signals. The team corrects for Earth air lines and models that distortion before pulling out the planet transmission spectrum.

They confirm and sharpen the planet low sky-projected spin-orbit angle, to about minus 0.09 degrees, but they detect no atmospheric species, not even potassium or CrH seen in past work. In most cases the null results trace to strong distortion or to missing lines in the ESPRESSO range, so old detections are not ruled out. The lesson is blunt: distortion still caps what high-resolution spectra can prove.
arxiv-2602-16201:
Large language models train on web-scale corpora with steep power-law spreads, so most knowledge appears infrequently. Sanket Badhe and coauthors develop an ordered taxonomy and analysis of long-tail knowledge in such models, synthesizing prior work across technical and social views. Scaling has improved average performance, yet misses persist on low-frequency, domain-specific, cultural, and temporal knowledge. Those failures remain poorly characterized.

Their analytical framework spans four axes. First, how long-tail knowledge is defined. Second, how it is lost or distorted during training and inference. Third, which fixes might mitigate them. Fourth, what they imply for fairness, accountability, transparency, and user trust. Existing evaluation practices can obscure tail behavior and complicate oversight for rare but consequential misses. The paper closes by naming open challenges around privacy, sustainability, and governance that constrain long-tail knowledge representation. It offers a unifying conceptual frame for the field.
arxiv-2602-16301:
Marissa Weis and coauthors show how cooperation can emerge among self-interested agents without hardcoded assumptions about co-player learning. Achieving teamwork among such agents remains a basic challenge in multi-agent reward-based learning. Prior work induced mutual cooperation between learning-aware agents that account for and shape co-player learning shifts. Existing approaches typically rely on hard-coded rules, or enforce a strict separation between naive learners and meta-learners.

The authors demonstrate that in-context learning skills of sequence models allow co-player learning awareness without hard-coded rules. Training sequence model agents against a diverse spread of co-players induces in-context best-response plans. Those plans function as learning methods on the fast intra-episode time scale. The cooperative mechanism from prior work emerges on its own: in-context adaptation renders agents vulnerable to extortion, and mutual pressure resolves into team behavior.
arxiv-2602-16501:
A. El Mendili and M. E. Zhitomirsky derive a rigorous quantum-to-classical mapping for interacting spin systems when warm. In the large-spin limit, the partition function takes the form of a classical model for vectors of a related length, with quantum corrections forming a series in inverse powers of spin.

The authors compute the leading temperature-free quantum shift to the magnetic anisotropy constant. The mapping justifies Monte Carlo simulation for realistic magnetic Hamiltonians, including anisotropic and frustrated interactions. As a test, they compute Curie and Néel points for several materials with known microscopic constants, finding good agreement with measured values. They also compare Monte Carlo susceptibility results for manganese fluoride with experiment.
arxiv-2602-16601:
Nail Khelifa, Richard Turner, and Ramji Venkataramanan analyze model collapse in score-based diffusion models trained repeatedly on synthetic data. Such recursive training is known to drift away from the target distribution. The authors study a realistic pipeline where each round mixes synthetic data with fresh samples from the target. They obtain upper and lower bounds on the accumulated divergence between generated and target distributions.

Notably, the lower bound is claimed as the first of its kind even for standard diffusion models. Different drift regimes emerge from score estimation error and the share of fresh data. In one regime, total divergence becomes a discounted sum of per-round score errors. Synthetic and image experiments illustrate the theory, giving practitioners a quantitative guide to how much fresh data retraining needs.
arxiv-2602-16901:
Tanqiu Jiang and co-authors present AgentLAB, the first benchmark for language model agents against long-horizon attacks. Agents now work in long-horizon, complex settings, but that expansion exposes them to attacks exploiting multi-turn user-agent-environment interactions to achieve goals infeasible in single turns. AgentLAB measures susceptibility to adaptive, long-horizon attacks across five novel attack types.

The attack types include intent hijacking, tool chaining, task injection, objective drifting, and memory poisoning, spanning twenty-eight realistic agentic environments and over six hundred security test cases. Tests of representative agents find they remain highly susceptible to long-horizon attacks, and defenses built for single-turn interactions fail to reliably mitigate long-horizon threats. AgentLAB is public, giving security researchers a benchmark for tracking progress on securing agents in practical settings.
arxiv-2602-17201:
Diego Díaz-Domínguez led a two-author paper on squeezing text indexes for large repetitive collections. Compressed suffix arrays index such collections, and the r-index pairs run-length Burrows-Wheeler Transform data with suffix sampling to size the index by the count of equal-symbol runs. But as variation grows, run counts swell with edits, and existing designs trade space against query speed.

The authors introduce variable-length blocking, which adapts index detail to local compressibility. The transform is split into blocks of at most a set run count and arranged as a tree. Compressible zones sit near the root with little extra data. Incompressible zones sit deeper with more data for fast access. A sampling trick that stays correct only along valid backward-search states trims space further. Tests beat the r-index and its subsampled kin on query time at near-equal space.
arxiv-2602-17401:
Mohamed Omar, writing alone, improves the constants in a universal quadratic bound linking two permutation pattern limits. For a permutation matrix, the Stanley-Wilf limit is the exponential growth rate of pattern-avoiding permutation matrices, while the Füredi-Hajnal limit is the limiting density of ones in pattern-avoiding zero-one matrices. Cibulka proved a universal quadratic bound relating the two limits.

This note improves Cibulka's constants through a block contraction argument. Defining an auxiliary function of the Füredi-Hajnal limit leads to a revised inequality with a smaller leading constant in the limit and an improved constant once the Füredi-Hajnal limit grows large. The note thus tightens the known quadratic relationship between Stanley-Wilf and Füredi-Hajnal limits, sharpening a universal bound that had stood since Cibulka's proof.
arxiv-2602-17501:
Bach Tran, writing alone, gives a lower bound for the first non-zero basic eigenvalue for a singular Riemannian foliation. On a closed singular Riemannian manifold with basic mean curvature, the bound rests on a given floor for Ricci curvature and on the diameter of the leaf space. For foliations made of points, the results cover older estimates of first nonzero eigenvalue floors: the Zhong-Yang estimate, the Yang estimate, and the Shi-Yang estimate.

Tran also proves a rigidity result for the case of positive Ricci curvature. That result widens Hang-Wang rigidity, the equality case of the Zhong-Yang estimate. The work thus carries classical eigenvalue estimates into the singular foliation setting, with rigidity marking the extremal case.
arxiv-2602-17701:
Yun Song and team evaluate deep neural net designs for ECG classification, aimed at automated arrhythmia detection. ECG traces remain essential for non-invasive detection of heart abnormalities, and heart disease keeps rising. Data scarcity in minority classes is eased by augmenting the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia set with a generative adversarial net.

Four designs are compared: convolutional nets, convolutional nets with long short-term memory, that pair with a focus step, and one-dimensional residual nets. They capture local shape traits and long-term time links, judged by scores, F1-score and area under the curve with confidence intervals, plus Grad-CAM checks on how readable the models are. The convolutional-LSTM design gives the best stand-alone balance of sensitivity and specificity, while a Top2-weighted ensemble tops overall performance.
arxiv-2602-17901:
Junkai Liu and team propose MeDUET, a pretraining frame for 3D medical image synthesis and analysis. Self-supervised learning and diffusion models have advanced coding learning and making modeling for high-dimensional 3D visual data as separate paradigms. Yet unification stays challenging under multi-source mix, since body content must be preserved for analysis while scan style varies across centers and affects synthesis.

MeDUET casts pretraining as a factor sorting problem. It aims to learn domain-invariant content factors for anatomy and domain-specific style factors for looks. Token demixing with a rival domain rule first establishes content-style split. Mixed Factor Token Distillation plus Swap-invariance Quadruplet Contrast further reduce mixed-region factor leakage and organize factor spaces. With those learned factors, MeDUET transfers to both synthesis and analysis. Synthesis gains closeness, settling and control. Analysis gains strong domain transfer and efficiency across sets and tasks.
arxiv-2602-18101:
Aljona Blöcker and two co-authors study the hot gas giant WASP-18 b, a planet whose dayside air is charged enough for magnetic forces to grip it. Their 2026 paper asks how uneven magnetic drag shapes winds and weather on such a world. Earlier hints from light curves pointed to strong drag, but its effect on the planet's full wind pattern was still unclear.

The team added a new drag formula to a three-dimensional wind model of the planet, with drag that shifts with local charge and adds heat from friction. The model shows drag slowing and bending dayside winds, shifting heat patterns, and forming two warm spots off the equator. Morning and evening edge zones prove most sensitive to the drag model. The work gives a path to read the planet's magnetic strength from its observed heat map.
arxiv-2602-18201:
Joseph Bingham and two co-authors show that hiding sensitive traits from training does not keep them out of unsupervised maps. Their 2026 paper tests SOMtime, a high-capacity self-organizing map method that preserves neighborhood structure. The team asks whether age and income still surface as main axes when those traits are left out of the inputs.

On the World Values Survey, spanning five countries, and a large census income dataset, SOMtime recovered orderings lined up with the hidden traits, reaching correlations up to zero point eight five. Standard rivals stayed far lower, mostly below zero point two three. Clustering the maps alone also produced demographically skewed groups, a fairness risk with no supervised step at all. The paper argues fairness checks must cover unsupervised parts of pipelines, since unawareness fails at the representation level.
arxiv-2602-18301:
Ivan Bondarenko and two co-authors ask what two learned proto-tokens actually encode. Their 2026 paper builds on a striking result: frozen language models can rebuild hundreds of tokens from just two proto-tokens in one forward pass, hinting at life beyond token-by-token generation. The team disentangles what each token carries.

Experiments separate meaning from syntax across the two tokens, test the stability of the e-token, and visualize attention to it during rebuilding. Under standard training the m-token leans more semantic than the e-token. Anchor-based constraints that impose meaning trade off sharply against rebuilding accuracy, while relational distillation transfers batch-level meaning relations into proto-token space without hurting accuracy. The findings support future systems that predict proto-tokens as a middle step.
arxiv-2602-18401:
Josue Casco-Rodriguez and two co-authors improve replay in recurrent networks modeled on the hippocampus. Their 2026 paper revisits noisy recurrent networks trained to path-integrate, where replay has been described as Langevin sampling. Newer replay modifiers have outgrown that description, so the team re-examines replay as sampling in three moves.

First, they prove replay gradients should vary over time and resist estimation, yet readily motivate hidden-state leakage for replay. Second, they confirm hidden-state adaptation, a form of negative feedback, encourages exploration but imposes non-Markov sampling that slows replay. Third, they propose the first model of time-compressed replay in such networks through hidden-state momentum, linked to underdamped Langevin sampling, which with adaptation counters slowness while keeping exploration. Tests cover 2D triangular and T-maze paths and high-dimensional synthetic rat place-cell paths.
arxiv-2602-18701:
What are the basic laws for circuits that can contain other circuits as parts? Matt Wilson, writing alone in 2026, sets out a theory of higher-order circuit diagrams. The laws cover how circuits nest inside each other, how they join in time and space, and how a lower-order bipartite process pair matches a higher-order bipartite state pair.

In category-theoretic language, the laws use enrichment and cotensors in symmetric polycategories, with a Frobenius-like coherence tying them together. The laws capture the key features of higher-order quantum theory, and they yield a ceiling: every higher-order circuit theory fits inside the theory of strong profunctors. The result gives a clean, general frame for reasoning about nested processes.
arxiv-2602-18801:
Neural PDE surrogates that predict one step at a time tend to drift over long rollouts. Amplitudes warp, phases slip, and modes interact in wrong ways. Jiayi Li, with five co-authors, introduces the Spectral Generator Neural Operator, or SGNO, in 2026. It is a structured autoregressive operator built to stay stable over long horizons.

Each step is a spectral update. A real-valued nonpositive diagonal generator gives a gain-controlled backbone. A learned correction path with complex spectral mixing handles the rest of the change. That shape suits dissipative, dispersive, transport-dominated, and nonlinear problems with Fourier structure. Across ten matched benchmark tasks, SGNO cuts long-horizon error sharply against strong baselines. Gains are largest on dispersive and transport-dominated tasks. Spectral checks confirm better energy and phase fidelity.
arxiv-2602-19001:
Personal assistants are expected to reason over multi-modal life history, from recognising people to summing up patterns. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test concept recognition. Xia Hu, with six co-authors, introduces Life-Bench in 2026. It is a fully synthetic, human-verified multi-modal benchmark of over eleven thousand question-answer pairs across ten tasks.

Tasks are organised by evidence scope, from concept identification to event understanding to combined reasoning. Photo-centric user histories match real user accounts distributionally. The linked structure of user data invites graph solutions. The authors propose LifeGraph, a user knowledge graph frame with structured lookup and on-demand access to source visual evidence. Evaluation of four lookup paradigms shows accuracy falls sharply with evidence scope, below four-tenths on combined tasks, and no paradigm dominates across categories. Personalisation over multi-modal history remains an open challenge.
arxiv-2602-19101:
Do language models value moral, grammatical, and economic good separately, as humans do? Seong Hah Cho, with two co-authors, tests that question in 2026. Value tuning requires measuring models' actual learned value views. Humans tell kinds of good apart. Models may not.

Probing behaviour, vectors, and later signals reveals pervasive value mixing. Grammar and economic valuation bend too far toward moral value, relative to human norms. Distinct kinds of good collapse into one another. The conflation is then repaired. Selective ablation of morality-linked activation vectors restores separation. Value representation in models thus proves mixed, but also surgically fixable.
arxiv-2602-19401:
Generative AI has entered daily life, and for people with obsessive compulsive disorder it has entered their symptoms too. Grace Barkhuff examines 100 Reddit posts from a popular OCD forum, tracing how AI shapes new obsessions and compulsions. Obsessions are distressing repetitive thoughts, and compulsions are behaviors meant to ease that distress; both now take AI-based forms.

The author argues that generative AI in its current form harms people with OCD by becoming what she calls reassurance robots. These machines feed the cycle of seeking reassurance. Future designs of generative AI must take OCD into account, she contends, and further work should explore the intersection of OCD and generative AI. Readers get a qualitative map of a new clinical terrain.
arxiv-2602-19601:
Y. Chapovskyi and A. Petravchuk study derivations on polynomial rings and the Lie algebra they form. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, every derivation on the polynomial ring in n variables is a sum of coefficient functions times partial derivatives. Together, such derivations make up the Lie algebra W_n(K), the paper's central object.

For each s from 1 to n-1, the authors prove that a certain subalgebra m_s(K) is maximal in W_n(K). Its ideal I_s is isomorphic to a tensor product Lie algebra, and the quotient m_s(K)/I_s is isomorphic to W_s(K). Since W_n(K) is a free module over the polynomial ring, ranks of subsets are defined, and properties of maximal subalgebras are explored.
arxiv-2602-19701:
Knowing how strongly atomic nuclei inside diamond are polarized matters for quantum sensing, but measuring that polarization directly is difficult. A 2026 arXiv paper by Mateusz Kuniej and Katarzyna Roszak offers a way to infer a lower bound on it from the behaviour of a single nitrogen-vacancy centre spin qubit.

The method runs a simple scheme on the qubit so that information from its surroundings flows into the qubit state, then reads the difference in how coherence evolves after preparation. The result depends mainly on how many spin-bearing nuclei cause decoherence, not strongly on the applied magnetic field. Tests on simulated surroundings with up to fifteen nuclei placed at random show the method gives a fair estimate when the surroundings are polarized.
arxiv-2602-19801:
The core equations for air motion lack an equation of their own for up-down momentum. Up-down velocity must instead be worked out from other quantities through hydrostatic balance. A 2026 arXiv paper by Rupert Klein and three co-authors studies the compressible version, with heat allowed to vary, with diffusion only in the up-down direction, and without gravity.

That gap costs one spatial derivative and sharpens the coupling between terms. Analysis is thus harder than for the classic Navier-Stokes equations for compressible flow. The authors prove local existence and uniqueness for strong solutions. They also prove that small changes in initial data give small changes in solutions. These hold for any regular enough starting data, with starting velocity and pressure taken one derivative smoother than starting density. The result gives the model a firm local well-posedness footing.
arxiv-2602-20001:
Recommender systems choose features from thousands of candidates, and judging which features matter most decides both online quality and computing cost. A 2026 arXiv paper by Xianquan Wang and five co-authors diagnoses three biases that skew that judgment in deep learning systems.

Gate-based and sensitivity-based selection methods can end up leaning on only part of the model layers, samples, or gradients, producing layer bias, baseline bias, and approximation bias. The proposed method, FairFS, regularizes importance estimates across all nonlinear layers, introduces a smooth baseline feature near the classifier boundary, and aggregates approximations to ease the other two biases. Tests show FairFS curbs all three biases and leads rival feature selection methods.
arxiv-2602-20101:
Matching a new solar spectrum against a high-resolution standard should be quick. Tools differ in range and resolution, slowing the job. A 2026 arXiv paper by A. G. M. Pietrow, working alone, presents HelioSpectrotron 5000, an interactive solar spectral atlas built on the Hamburg Fourier transform spectrometer atlas.

The atlas supplies absolute intensity spectra and continuum-normalized spectra at any wavelength range and detail. It adds curated line labels and optional telluric effects. That combination supports fast wavelength calibration and line finding, plus context images. Users can compare high-resolution reference spectra straight against readings from a wide range of ground-based instruments.
arxiv-2602-20201:
Some sums of three Fibonacci numbers can be written as concatenations of three repdigits in a given base, and classifying those sums is a Diophantine problem. A 2026 arXiv paper by Passimzouwé Dagou and three co-authors investigates such sums for bases from two through ten.

The paper proves only finitely many such sums exist for those bases and determines all of them explicitly. The largest solution occurs for base four. Readers gain a complete enumeration for small bases, with the finiteness result showing the phenomenon is exceptional rather than common, and the explicit list settling every case in the range studied.
arxiv-2602-20701:
S. A. Fldzhyan and two co-authors set out a light-based way to compute the QR factorization of a matrix. Their method uses a tunable mesh of light paths, routing power step by step and reading the upper factor straight from the light outputs.

The step count grows only as matrix size times its logarithm, beating the cubic growth of usual digital QR routines. The same setup also handles repeat spectrum work, plus Hessenberg reduction and bidiagonalization as prep steps for QR and SVD work. It compares well with systolic arrays on blocked QR decomposition.
arxiv-2602-20901:
Vision-language models handle everyday visual questions well but stumble when a task needs spatial sense plus multi-step logic. Yuechen Xie and eight co-authors name that gap spatial logical reasoning and build a benchmark for it in this 2026 arXiv paper. SpatiaLQA draws thousands of question-answer pairs from hundreds of real indoor scenes.

Tests on dozens of leading models show even the strongest still struggle with spatial logical reasoning. The authors also propose recursive scene-graph assisted reasoning, which breaks complex scenes into task-relevant graphs step by step using visual foundation models. That method beats prior approaches. Readers get both a yardstick for a real weakness and a promising way forward.
arxiv-2602-21301:
Higher Berry phases describe the topology of spaces of gapped many-body systems, but measuring them is challenging. Chih-Yu Lo and Xueda Wen develop a boundary-scattering probe in this 2026 arXiv paper for one-dimensional gapped free-fermion systems. Coupling a gapless lead to the gapped system lets the higher Berry invariant be read from the higher winding number of the boundary reflection matrix.

The resulting invariant resists perturbations such as disorder, and the approach links higher Berry invariants to transport properties. Readers get a potentially experimentally accessible route to parametrized topological phases, turning an abstract invariant into a scattering measurement. The work bridges topology and transport in a concrete, testable way.
arxiv-2602-21401:
Tassilo Klein and one co-author argue that agentic AI reshapes the boundary of the firm. Classic theory ties that boundary to coordination cost. In older modular systems, integration cost grew with the square of the number of components. In protocol-mediated agentic systems, it falls to linear growth. Verification cost then scales with task throughput.

That shift favors a new equilibrium, the Headless Firm. It is shaped like an hourglass. A personalized generative interface sits on top. A standard protocol waist sits in the middle. A competitive market of micro-specialized execution agents sits below. The model yields two testable predictions. One concerns constant marginal cost of adding providers. The other concerns stable cost per task as ecosystems grow. The model also predicts a domain-conditional Great Unbundling toward small agents and thin orchestrators.
arxiv-2602-21501:
Lars van der Laan alone authors a researcher's guide to empirical risk minimization, a reference for high-probability regret bounds. The presentation is modular. Opening sections build intuition and outline proof approaches before presenting widely applicable guarantees under abstract assumptions, with methods for checking them against particular losses and function classes.

Many rate derivations follow a three-step recipe: a basic inequality, a uniform local concentration bound, and a fixed-point argument. From that recipe comes a regret bound expressed through a local-complexity radius, measured with localized Rademacher averages, provided a gentle Bernstein-style variance-risk link holds. The guide bounds that radius with local maximal inequalities and metric-entropy integrals, recovering familiar rates for VC-subgraph, Sobolev and Hölder, and bounded-variation classes. It also treats nuisance components, regret transfer, sample splitting, and the in-sample regime, where fast oracle rates remain attainable.
arxiv-2602-21601:
Kart Leong Lim and one co-author predict inter- and intra-layer stress in mixed IC chips with a deep grouping boundary-decoder net. High stress hits when 3D mixed IC packages face heat cycling at extreme heat, mainly at joints between unlike materials. The team studies stress images via latent space code using a deep maker model.

Most deep maker models are label-free, resorting to image pairing of input and output for training. Instead, the team relies on a recent decoder net using edge rules plus image pairing for stress modeling. The decoder net maps material settings to latent space shared with its image twin. Because that setup is by size ill-posed, deep grouping is coupled to the decoder net. On a mock dataset of 1825 stress images, the method beats decoder versions and a baseline in train and test error cuts.
arxiv-2602-21901:
Davide Carbone and three co-authors test the TTCF (Transient Time Correlation Function) method for computing nonequilibrium transport coefficients, against the usual time-average route. The usual route reads transport traits from long, settled runs and throws away the early changes. TTCF does the reverse, mining brief early shifts after a fresh outside push and dropping the later run once things settle.

They try it on two cases, the Lorentz gas and a chain of oscillators held by an anharmonic pinning potential. For the Lorentz gas, TTCF gives the same transport numbers as time averages in both linear and nonlinear regimes, at lower cost. It is sharper in the linear-response regime, holds up where ergodicity fails, and exposes phase-space patches with distinct behavior and possible phase transitions. For the oscillator chain, it proves a scalable, low-cost option for the numerical study of nonequilibrium transport.
arxiv-2602-22001:
Robots learn to transfer skills at many levels, from words and plans down to muscle-like motor control. Freek Stulp and five co-authors survey how foundation models and transformer networks have touched each of those levels, asking whether they point toward full-stack transfer. They look across large language models, vision-language models, and vision-language-action models through the lens of robotic transfer learning.

The survey draws out shared ideas that recur across model types, beyond any single system, and weighs the hard problems that remain: gathering useful robot data and building fair transfer benchmarks. The authors expect foundation models to stay a key technology on this road, even if full-stack transfer is not yet in hand. Readers get a map of where transfer works today and where it still stalls.
arxiv-2602-22101:
Data streams for regression arrive continuously, and Hoeffding trees have long been a go-to tool for learning from them on the fly. Pantia-Marina Alchirch and Dimitrios I. Diochnos adapt two batch-learning tricks to streaming: kernel density smoothing for imbalanced regression, and hierarchical shrinkage as post-hoc regularization for trees. The density method is recast through a telescoping form for incremental use.
