On standard online regression benchmarks, the density smoothing clearly improves early-stream performance, while shrinkage adds only limited gains. The combination keeps tree structure untouched while steadying predictions where data are thin. The code is public, giving stream-learning practitioners two tested add-ons with honest, measured trade-offs.
arxiv-2602-22201:
Quantum computing's Clifford hierarchy ranks gates by power, and climbing its levels is a route to more capable quantum circuits. Yichen Xu and Xiao Wang build a simple, systematic path upward by coherently controlling Clifford operations. Their key tool is Pauli periodicity: the smallest power that turns a Clifford gate into a Pauli operator, up to phase.

The authors prove a sharp controlled-jump rule: controlling a gate lands it exactly two levels higher in the hierarchy. They also bound the cost, showing that large jumps demand target-qubit counts growing exponentially with the desired level. Explicit infinite families of Pauli-periodic gates round out the picture, giving builders both a ladder and its price tag.
arxiv-2602-22401:
AI agents that run multi-step research workflows mark a qualitative shift from chatbots that answer isolated questions. Yongjun Zhang introduces vibe researching, the AI-era parallel to vibe coding, and examines it through a scholar-skill plugin covering the full pipeline from idea to submission. Agents can now read files, run code, query databases, search the web, and invoke specialist skills autonomously.

Zhang builds a cognitive task framework sorting research activities by codifiability and tacit-knowledge demand. It locates a delegation boundary that is cognitive, not sequential: it cuts through every pipeline stage rather than between stages. The paper asks whether such agents replace or augment social scientists, and maps where delegation helps and where human tacit knowledge still rules.
arxiv-2602-22501:
Black-hole solutions with several horizons per repeat unit extend earlier computer work on steady, symmetric spacetimes. Omar Ortiz and Javier Peraza build repeat steady symmetric solutions holding multiple horizons in each repeat unit, focusing on two identical evenly spaced counter-spinning horizons. These solutions are described by their period, mass, and spin size.

The authors give strong computer evidence that such setups exist, with no limit on the gap between horizons. That contrasts sharply with the single-horizon case, where spin is impossible when horizons sit too close together. The solutions carry no struts on the axis, while unevenly spaced horizons do grow struts between black holes, and other global traits are also presented.
arxiv-2602-22901:
Jielin Feng and seven co-authors help humans and AI co-write storytelling infographics. Existing authoring tools poorly maintain story consistency or track user story goals through design. Formative interviews plus quantitative analysis of layout patterns pin down what designers need.

The answer is a narrative-centred workflow in three phases: story construction, visual encoding, and spatial composition. InfoAlign, built on that workflow, turns long or messy text into stories, suggests semantically aligned visuals, and drafts layout blueprints. Users can step in and refine at any stage, keeping intent intact and the process transparent. Evaluations show story coherence holds across stages and co-creation genuinely works.
arxiv-2602-23001: Filomena De Filippis proves that solutions to fractional porous-medium-type equations stay locally bounded in the fast-diffusion regime, under optimal tail assumptions. Porous-medium equations model flow through porous matter; the fractional version spreads mass through long-range jumps rather than to neighbours. Fast diffusion means thin regions empty quickly, which can threaten blow-up. Local boundedness rules out infinite spikes on any bounded patch. Optimal tail assumptions are the weakest far-field conditions that secure the result, so no stronger decay at infinity is needed.
arxiv-2602-23101:
Paul Kielty and two co-authors introduce Locally Adaptive Decay Surfaces for high-speed face and landmark detection with event cameras. Event cameras record luminance changes with microsecond resolution, but turning their sparse, asynchronous output into dense tensors for neural networks remains hard. Fixed temporal parameters trade spatial structure in still periods against sharp edges in rapid motion.

Locally Adaptive Decay Surfaces modulate temporal decay at each location by local signal dynamics, using event rate, Laplacian-of-Gaussian response, and high-frequency spectral energy. The adaptive schemes preserve detail in quiet regions while reducing blur in dense activity. At thirty hertz the method beats non-adaptive baselines on detection accuracy and landmark error. At 240 hertz it sustains about two and a half percent normalized mean landmark error with nearly ninety-seven percent mean average precision, setting benchmarks for event-based face analysis with lighter networks.
arxiv-2602-23201:
Max Bennett and two co-authors propose a neural memory system users can steer with plain-language instructions. Modern models work in shifting settings where they must keep adapting to new tasks and new knowledge. Continual fine-tuning and in-context learning are costly and brittle, while neural memory methods promise light updates with little forgetting.

Existing memory models, however, assume one fixed goal and one uniform stream of information. They leave users no control over what the model keeps or drops over time. The new system takes learning instructions in natural language and updates selectively from varied sources. That control matters in settings such as health care and customer service, where fixed-goal memory updates fall short.
arxiv-2602-23301:
Bert Dobbelaere and three co-authors give a method for counting block-like structures on tilings, the polyhedral complexes that generalize Tetris pieces. Such structures appear in contemporary art, play structures, climbing equipment, and modular construction toys. The paper counts n-celled shapes built from flat and solid cells of certain periodic flat and solid tilings.

Counts are given up to translations, rotations, and reflections of the tiling, so congruent placements count once. The authors describe the algorithm through the snub square tiling, provide numerical data tied to existing solid art and objects, and suggest puzzles based on these constructions. The result turns a playful counting question into a systematic enumeration with concrete data and puzzles to explore.
arxiv-2602-23401:
Faruk Alpay and one co-author study grammar-constrained reachability in graphs, where paths must obey a context-free grammar. The paper presents an algorithmic framework for answering such reachability queries and analyzes its theoretical runtime bounds. Reachability under grammar constraints matters wherever graph queries must respect structural rules, from program analysis to data schemas.

To complement the theory, the authors run an extensive empirical evaluation on a benchmark of real-world schemas, comparing algorithmic variants and reporting performance trade-offs. Results highlight how grammar structure and graph characteristics shape reachability computation. The paper closes with guidance for picking efficient approaches in practice, matching method to grammar and graph at hand.
arxiv-2602-23501:
Zhenghao Li and 13 co-authors demonstrate a sample-optimal, hardware-efficient plan for estimating quantum similarity, the overlap between quantum states. Quantum machine learning promises gains by judging state functions that are classically hard, but only if costly profiling of each data item can be bypassed in favor of direct similarity measurement.

Their method uses bosonic quantum interference, with sample needs free of system size and near-optimal in theory up to a constant factor. Implemented on Prakash-1, a fully programmable photonic chip, it prepares and mixes qudit states on-chip to extract overlaps directly. Classification and online learning of quantum data then succeed with high accuracy in realistic noisy tests, making joint overlap measurement a scalable building block for networked quantum learning.
arxiv-2602-23601:
Shadeeb Hossain surveys extended reality (XR) as the next frontier in learning. XR, with virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality, creates deep, hands-on learning worlds that can enhance student interest, hands-on learning, and skill growth.

High rollout costs, tech hurdles, and ethical concerns, above all around student privacy and body-scan data guards, still pose large barriers to uptake. The talk highlights rule needs under GDPR and FERPA plus the need for cyber-safety rules to shield private learner data. In the end, the article weighs new ideas with access and ethics in the growth of XR-based learning.
arxiv-2602-23801:
Xinbu Cheng and four co-authors study spanning structures that use many distinct colors in properly edge-colored graphs. The 2026 paper asks how a Dirac-type rule, which forces each vertex to connect to at least half the graph, guarantees color variety in cycles and matchings.

The authors prove two sharp results. Every such graph contains a Hamilton cycle, a loop through all vertices, with nearly as many distinct colors as the degree bound allows. Likewise, every dense subset of a Latin square contains a permutation with nearly as many distinct symbols as the row and column bound allows. Both bounds are best possible up to a small error term. The work extends a classic result on complete graphs to a much wider class of dense graphs.
arxiv-2602-24101:
Matthew Yoko and Wolfgang Polifke use Bayesian inference to identify flame impulse responses, the key quantity for predicting thermoacoustic stability in combustors. The 2026 paper notes that recovering an impulse response from sparse, noisy data is an ill-posed inverse problem. System identification methods usually handle it, but need hand-tuned regularization. They offer no principled way to include prior physical knowledge.

The Bayesian reformulation represents the impulse response as a physically motivated distributed time-delay model. Parameters are inferred for a given number of pulses, and the pulse count itself is chosen by Bayesian model comparison, which balances fit against complexity to favor the simplest adequate model. Demonstrated on large-eddy simulation data from a turbulent swirl burner, the method selects a three-pulse response consistent with earlier physical interpretation. In short, three pulses capture the flame's reply.
arxiv-2602-24201:
Egor Antipov and five co-authors present a flow-based method for density ratio estimation between intractable distributions, with applications in genomics. The 2026 paper addresses a core problem in probabilistic modeling. Comparing sample likelihoods across conditions is hard. Exact-likelihood models such as normalizing flows are promising.

The method uses flow matching to derive a single dynamical formulation that tracks density ratios along generative trajectories. Tests on simulated benchmarks show competitive performance. In single-cell genomics, likelihood-based comparisons of cellular states support treatment effect estimation and batch correction evaluation, giving biologists a principled tool.
arxiv-2603-00201: Roy and Bhattacharya present AdURA-Net, a geometry-driven uncertainty-aware system for reliable chest disease sorting. Its dilated convolution, multiscale deformable alignment and DenseNet backbone capture anatomical detail of medical images. A Dual Head Loss joins masked binary cross entropy, logit terms and a Dirichlet evidential goal. The design lets the model hold back firm predictions when evidence is thin, rather than forcing a firm answer on unclear labels.
arxiv-2603-00401: McGuinness demonstrates random number certification that trusts nothing about the device producing the data. Past demos needed assumptions about how data were made, or a biased source could pass off fixed data as random. His black box test defeats even an adversary with unlimited compute, since no fixed strategy can earn certification. The method needs only single particle measurements and no seed, yielding numbers provably random from the measurement itself.
arxiv-2603-00601: Sapunov asks whether code agents truly grasp software architecture, beyond excelling at isolated tasks. His Theory of Code Space benchmark has agents explore generated codebases under partial observability, opening files on a budget and periodically writing out their architectural beliefs as structured data. Tests with four baselines and six frontier models reveal an active passive gap that varies by model, and belief maps in context help some models but not others. Smaller models can even hold steadier beliefs than larger siblings.
arxiv-2603-00701: Yan, Stenger, and Gunlycke tackle data flow scheduling for high throughput multi beam satellites, a hard combinatorial problem where classic methods trade quality against real time feasibility. Their hybrid quantum classical framework casts multi beam time frequency slot assignment as a QUBO binary optimisation problem, folding throughput goals and operating limits into a compact form by rescaling parameters. A layer wise training scheme grows circuit depth gradually to dodge barren plateaus and rugged loss landscapes. Tests on quantum hardware against classic and hybrid baselines use realistic simulated satellite traffic.
arxiv-2603-01001: Yano formulates a data-free finite-volume convolutional network for steady compressible Euler flow around a cylinder at eight Mach numbers from 2 to 15. Shared-face fluxes enforce conservation while automatic differentiation supplies gradients, and the paper derives the derivative mismatch of an earlier network. Accuracy against finite-resolution simulations varies widely by case, local sharpness and balance metrics persist, but initialization-robust superiority over the earlier method is not established.
arxiv-2603-01201: De Giacomo and four colleagues study stepwise synthesis for finite-trace time logic, where an agent already running one goal gets another mid-run. The agent must abandon its current plan and build a new one meeting both old and new goals from the current moment. Machine-based methods using aids built during the work handle multiple goals well. While formula growth can blow rules up fast, their minimal machines stay bounded. Naive rework from scratch each time proves too slow.
arxiv-2603-01301: Jeddi and six colleagues disentangle what reinforcement learning adds to medical vision-language models beyond vision and supervised fine-tuning. On MedMNIST they benchmark vision towers, track support via Accuracy@1 versus Pass@K, and test when RL closes the support gap. RL works best with non-trivial support present, sharpening outputs and lifting accuracy and efficiency, while fine-tuning expands support and makes RL effective. Their boundary-aware recipe RL post-trains an OctoMed-initialized model on a small PMC VQA subset and performs strongly across six medical VQA benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-01401: Song and three colleagues model how probing affects teamwork in multi-agent talk, combining signals with a giving game in a two-stage evolving model. Agent-based tests across layouts reveal a single best probing rate lifting system-wide teamwork. Middling probing shakes cheating hold and sparks self-built cooperative teams, enabling their cycling success. The teamwork peak comes from a fine balance between swing period and growth, hinting planned probing beats fixed stiffness.
arxiv-2603-01601:
Large 3D models can build a scene from one image, but they sometimes invent odd holes or bumps. Xiwen Wang, Shichao Zhang, Ruowei Wang, and colleagues name and fight those flaws in this 2026 work. Fake parts hurt most when a model is printed or placed in a virtual scene.

The flaws often start when sparse views with wide gaps guide the rebuild. Their tool, Dehallu3D, forces smooth shifts across many close views while it guards sharp real edges. Two rules do the work: one keeps nearby views in geometric agreement, and one adapts smoothing to spare fine detail. A new score counts outlier risk, so gains can be measured, not just seen. Tests show cleaner meshes that keep true detail while stray parts vanish.
arxiv-2603-01901:
Hannah Selder, Charlotte Beylier, Nico Scherf, and Arthur Fleig test whether brightness tricks fake users in interface simulations. Their 2026 study trains simulated users with reinforcement learning on pointing and tracking tasks. If scores hinge on rendering artifacts, the simulation says little about real design quality.

The team trains hundreds of simulated users while varying luminance of targets, distractors, and background. Settings include no distractors, still distractors, and moving distractors around the task. With still distractors, luminance becomes decisive and both performance and robustness drop sharply. Motion cues soften that effect, which points to dynamics as a buffer against brightness bias. Robustness also tracks the ordering between luminance levels more than their exact values, a subtle rule for fair simulation design.
arxiv-2603-02001:
Johannes Wehrstein, Timo Eckmann, Matthias Jasny, and Carsten Binnig synthesize a database engine fitted to one fixed workload. Their 2026 work argues that general analytical engines pay for their flexibility in overhead. Runtime schema reading, indirection layers, and abstraction walls persist even in highly tuned systems.

A bespoke engine can drop those costs and use data structures shaped to the actual queries. Hand-building one was never worth the effort, but language-model code synthesis changes that math. Naive prompting fails, so their pipeline adds performance feedback, structured refinement, and validation loops. The autonomous system builds an engine from storage to query execution in minutes to hours. Order-of-magnitude speedups over a modern general engine show what workload-specific synthesis can win.
arxiv-2603-02101:
Anna Geisler, Mihyun Kang, Michail Sarantis, and Ronen Wdowinski study random sampling from a physics model in this 2026 paper. The model assigns weights to sets of graph points, with sets that contain many edges weighing less. They focus on split graphs where every node has the same number of links. Such graphs also spread out well, in a sense called expansion.

A standard random walk sampler turns out to mix far too slowly here. Across wide settings, it can take huge time to give a fair sample. The authors give a fast sampler built on cluster methods instead. Their method also estimates the model's total weight to high accuracy. The contrast shows sampler choice can matter more than the model itself.
arxiv-2603-02201:
Kilian Sandholzer, Ian Berkman, Peter Deák, and colleagues review single-photon sources in silicon in this 2026 paper. Single photons can carry quantum data over long distances. Solid chunks of matter that emit them one by one are handy and can be mass-produced. Add a spin, and the source can also store quantum states.

Silicon stands out for its fine chip making and very pure makeup. That purity lets spins hold their state for a long time. The review covers color centers and erbium atoms placed in tiny silicon light guides. It sums up what works now and what blocks coherent sources at scale. Such sources could anchor quantum networks and spread-out quantum computers.
arxiv-2603-02301:
J Kunc, B Morzhuk, V Stará, and colleagues study light-absorbing molecules layered on graphene in this 2026 paper. Clean interfaces are vital for devices that copy quantum behavior, yet factory steps often dirty them. The team presents a building protocol that restores graphene's atomic purity to vacuum-lab levels. Diffraction and microscopy checks confirm the clean surface.

On that surface, a molecular layer shows wide, coherent light effects. Its crystal symmetry splits one key light transition into bright and dark branches. Several light and vibration probes map the split pattern in detail. A fitted model quantifies coupling and energy terms behind the split. The dark branch dominates light emission, they find. The platform could support studies of dark states and molecular quantum memories.
arxiv-2603-02501:
Donggyu Kim, Rose McCarty, and Caleb McFarland answer a labeling question about graph trails in this 2026 mathematics paper. Edges carry labels from a group, and labels can be inverted along the way. An Eulerian trail uses every edge exactly once. The authors ask when every such trail between two fixed points earns the same total label.

Their answer is structural and precise. Each highly connected part of the graph must be labeled over a very specific group. That group is a power of the two-element group, for some exponent. They also show the decision problem reduces in fast time to the group's word problem. That link ties a graph question to a classic algebra computation.
arxiv-2603-02601:
Varun Pratap Bhardwaj argues that AI agents need a new kind of software testing, and his 2026 report AgentAssay supplies one. Agents built on large language models can act differently on each run, even with the same prompt and tools. Normal tests assume fixed outputs and simple pass or fail marks, so they miss real regressions.

AgentAssay replaces fixed verdicts with chance-based outcomes backed by confidence ranges and staged checks. It adds coverage measures for tools and choices, fault-injection tests, and gates for release pipelines. Trials across five models and three agent setups cut testing cost sharply while keeping the same statistical strength. Recorded traces also allow free re-checks of past runs.
arxiv-2603-03201:
Simone Betteti, Giacomo Baggio, and Sandro Zampieri build a mathematical theory of how associative memories move from one stored pattern to the next. Hopfield networks are classic models of memory that settle into stored patterns, and their still-frame retrieval is well understood. Chained retrieval, where one memory hands off to another like steps of reasoning, lacked theory.

Working with a recent input-driven plasticity variant, they analyze a two-timescale design: fast retrieval paired with slow reasoning dynamics. Explicit conditions emerge for self-sustained transitions between memories, including gain thresholds for switching, escape times, and regimes where the chain collapses. The results connect classical memory dynamics to the sequential reasoning that modern machine learning systems increasingly display.
arxiv-2603-03301:
Dvir David Biton and Roy Friedman study semantic caching, a speed trick for large language model services. Classic caches reuse exact repeats; a semantic cache reuses answers for new requests that merely mean something close to an old one, judged by embedding vectors. Their 2026 paper asks which requests such a cache should keep when space runs out.

The authors prove that even with full hindsight, picking the perfect offline policy is computationally intractable, then offer fast heuristics that run in reasonable time. They also design live policies mixing recency, frequency, and semantic closeness. Tests on varied datasets show frequency-based rules are strong, while their new variant improves semantic accuracy further. All of the code is open source.
arxiv-2603-03601:
Aida Abiad, Anuj Dawar, and Octavio B Zapata-Fonseca bring logic to two questions about when graphs count as the same. Controllable graphs and distance-regularized graphs are usually characterized algebraically, through spectra and eigenvalues. Whether two such graphs are isomorphic, or merely share a spectrum, had never been studied through definability in first-order logic. Their 2026 paper is the first to do so, extending and unifying earlier results.

The headline result: cospectral distance-regularized graphs cannot be told apart by counting first-order logic with three variables. The same holds for the broader pseudo-distance-regularized family. Earlier theorems of this kind covered only strongly regular graphs and distance-regular graphs separately. The new work subsumes both, giving logicians and graph theorists one common frame for these equivalence questions.
arxiv-2603-03701:
Tonmoy Dey, Lin Jiang, Zheng Dong, and Guang Wang let city services trade favors instead of competing. Smart city research usually optimizes one service at a time. Their 2026 framework, UrbanHuRo, jointly optimizes two: crowdsourced delivery and urban sensing. Human couriers can gather traffic and air quality data along their routes, while sensing robots can deliver packages at peak hours, each side covering the other's weakness.

Two designs make the joint optimization tractable in real time. A distributed MapReduce module handles order dispatch through a submodular maximization scheme. A deep reinforcement learning algorithm, also built on submodular rewards, plans the sensing routes. On real data from a food delivery platform, the system raised sensing coverage by about thirty percent and courier income by about forty percent on average, while significantly cutting overdue orders.
arxiv-2603-03801:
Reece Robertson and five colleagues prepare thermal quantum states on real trapped-ion hardware and catch the machine heating its own work. Gibbs states, the equilibrium states of statistical mechanics, are prime targets for quantum simulation. Their 2026 experiment runs a variational algorithm for the transverse-field Ising model on IonQ computers, training parameters classically and reading the prepared state back by tomography.

Fidelity falls as the target gets colder and as the system grows, though not monotonically. The telling result is a mismatch of identity: a state prepared for one temperature matches better the Gibbs state of a warmer temperature. Hardware fluctuations act as digital heating, silently raising the prepared state's temperature above intent. The finding sets a practical caution for near-term thermal state preparation.
arxiv-2603-03901: Javier López-Pedrares and others develop mathematical models of tumor response to radiotherapy using the Linear Quadratic model for cell survival. Uncontrolled cancer proliferation and contact with healthy tissue pose a major oncology challenge. Analytical study reveals expected motion under varied treatment scenarios, and numeric tests back the theory and highlight how optimal control reduces tumor burden with minimized collateral damage.
arxiv-2603-04001: Akila de Silva and others report STEM faculty perspectives on making AI in higher education from a focus group study. Generative AI tools now pervade higher education, yet adoption is largely student-driven, forcing instructor replies to embedded classroom technologies. Some faculty embrace the tools for content output and curriculum design, while others proceed cautiously over learning, validity, and integrity.
arxiv-2603-04101: Rafaj and others study kink scattering in Frankensteinian potentials as bubbles of exotic mass and phase. They picture kink-anti-kink scattering in two special potentials of piecewise quadratic and linear pieces, focusing on models lacking skin and core regions. They interpret these models as nearly free massive theories with an inbuilt pair-production process above certain thresholds. Results cover kink characteristics versus thresholds and bouncing-window spreads. The second model shows phase-transition-like conduct where collisions switch from massive-wave disintegration to oscillon production at low thresholds.
arxiv-2603-04201: Harari and Szamuely study the defect in the generalized Grunwald-Wang problem. In the special case, a group of order 2 measures the obstruction. They show both answers are negative in general, even for rational function fields and discrete valuations from points of the affine line. This bears on the arithmetic of function fields over the rationals and p-adic numbers.
arxiv-2603-04301: Weng and colleagues study in hand rolling with a robot hand whose compliant fingers carry tactile fingertips. Each fingertip reports contact location and wrench, giving rich feedback during a grasp. The authors derive motion equations for compliant quasistatic rolling and build a multi finger controller for a desired object twist. Simulations check the contact mechanics before the controller runs on a real experimental robot system.
arxiv-2603-04401: Garcia-Gallego and colleagues bound axion isocurvature with Lyman-alpha forest data. Post-inflationary axion-like particles add isocurvature ripples to the ordinary power spectrum. Sherwood-Relics simulations fit high resolution forest flux spectra. Published noise models give a tentative nonzero detection, after allowing for thermal evolution degeneracy. A conservative noise model weakens this to an upper bound and a mass lower bound, beating large scale structure probes. The forest thus sets a strong limit.
arxiv-2603-04601: Tran and colleagues test AI models on full web app building with Vibe Code Bench. Past benchmarks test lone tasks, not the full zero-to-one path from spec to working app. The bench holds 100 web app specs with 964 browser workflows and 10,131 substeps. An autonomous browser agent judges the specs on live apps. Across 16 frontier models, the best reaches 61.8 percent accuracy on the test split. Self-testing during generation strongly predicts performance, and evaluator choice shifts outcomes widely.
arxiv-2603-04701: Kang and McCosker analyze Terms of Service on social media platforms. Platforms usually obtain consent through Terms of Service at account creation. The study asks whether consent information is clearly communicated within ToS documents. A three-dimensional framework covers Textual Access, Meaning Clarity, and Screen Design. Auto and close reviews assess ToS from 13 major platforms. Findings show high language tangle, non-binding language, and limited notes on data keeping and sharing. Consent sits inside ToS yet constrains clarity and real choice. The study recasts ToS as consent-bearing documents.
arxiv-2603-04801: Awal and Rahman show load leakage persists beyond EM shielding in the bypass. Shielding cuts leaked waves and limits passive side-channel leakage, but ignores active probing. A foe injects radio-wave signals and observes echo replies from the device. State-tied load shifts stay visible outside the shields' primary cutoff band. Tests on FPGA and MCU units under three common shields show passive readings losing telling power. Echoes stay distinct, so active probing can expose run acts even in shielded systems.
arxiv-2603-05401: Edoardo Bocchi and team study Couette-Taylor flow of steady viscous fluid in a cylindrical annulus with one cylinder still, under Dirichlet and vorticity conditions from the weak formulation. The study's outcome is twofold. First, the authors determine all answers with geometric partial invariance, coinciding with spiral Poiseuille or Poiseuille-Couette flows. Second, for small boundary data, such answers prove stable, with no steady finite-energy perturbations persisting. Under vorticity conditions, a large math gap depends on which cylinder is still.
arxiv-2603-06201: Wang and his team set out point supervision for skeleton based action segmentation, labeling only one frame per action segment. They encode joint, bone, and motion data with a pretrained unified model, then build pseudo labels through a prototype similarity method joined with an energy function. Multimodal pseudo label integration makes labels more sound and guides training, next to constrained K-Medoids clustering. New tests on PKU-MMD, MCFS-22, and MCFS-130 show competitive results, at times beating fully supervised methods while cutting annotation effort by a lot.
arxiv-2603-06601: Ale and team bring SWAN, a tool giving each neural unit with an input-dependent binary gate, learning when each unit should be active or inactive for work allocation. Deep networks and large generative models achieve performance yet carry cost blocking resource-tight deployment. Dropout steadies training, while pruning and low-rank splitting turn models post hoc into static forms with flex. Unlike pruning, SWAN learns context-set activation patterns backing efficient dynamic inference and switch to compact dense models, joining sparsity, pruning, and adaptive use in one plan.
arxiv-2603-06701: Ken Nagai builds a unified recursion that links two families of Clausen-type functions. From a polylogarithmic master function he forms two round functions, with real parts and imaginary parts that match the classic Clausen shapes. Swapping the trig seed for a Jacobi theta function gives an elliptic version on the same spine. The round case falls out as a limit, and one generating deformation gathers the recursion.
arxiv-2603-07001: Muslim and Grégoire present a privacy-first, patient-first ID system for health care access. Good care depends on long-term health records and easing patient worries about privacy. Patient identity checks matter, yet reusing IDs exposes people to linking, tying multiple visits as one, and tracing, tying visits to real people. Their setup holds day-to-day trust with privacy safety through a rooted trust anchor, hidden code names, and a limited tracing rule. It is set out in full and tested through design analysis and proof checks.
arxiv-2603-07101: Liu and colleagues probe whether language models can turn game design ideas into playable Unity code that respects both form and meaning. Goal patterns describe common player-objective relationships, and Goal Playable Concepts turn them into working Unity implementations. The team frames the task as constrained executable synthesis: output must satisfy Unity's syntax and architecture rules while keeping the gameplay meaning of the pattern. Their probing measures how well models meet both demands at once.
arxiv-2603-07401: Ananth, Liu and Cai attack caption quality as the bottleneck in training text-to-image and text-to-video models. Vision-language models hallucinate and reason poorly about composition, yielding misaligned image-caption pairs. Their VIVECaption approach works both sides: a list of quality metrics plus a gold-standard dataset built by layered sampling, and alignment through context matching and fine-tuning. A tuned character-detection model in the pipeline lifts overall alignment markedly.
arxiv-2603-07501: Hu, Zhou and Bu bound graph independence numbers from spectra, extending the work to even uniform hypergraphs. They carry the Hoffman bound over to even uniform hypergraphs and offer a simple spectral test for pinning down independence number, Shannon capacity and Lovász number. The Lovász-number Hoffman bound is likewise stretched from regular graphs to general graphs. The paper thus unifies several spectral estimates under one roof.
arxiv-2603-08101: Raillard and colleagues rethink how French offshore wind farms should be sized for a warming sea. Old design rules assumed steady conditions, a premise climate change has undone. They fit non-stationary Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) models to monthly maxima of significant wave height, drawing on CMIP6 climate models and reanalysis data. Along the Atlantic and Channel coasts, seasons pull further apart, with harsher winters and calmer summers. The Mediterranean stays harder to read, and the team ends with a new design level for a structure's full working life.
arxiv-2603-08201: Qiu and colleagues study shape control for microswimmer navigation in turbulence, a challenge for living and built swimmers alike. Most existing work adapts motion or steering, leaving active shape change largely unexplored. The authors task a shape-changing spheroidal swimmer with maximizing distance from its start in two-dimensional random and turbulent flows. With reinforcement learning, the swimmer learns to adapt its aspect ratio from its heading and local flow signals, turning body shape into a navigation tool.
arxiv-2603-08301: Liu and colleagues investigate three eigenfunction constraints of two differential-difference integrable systems in 2+1 dimensions. They revisit the known squared constraint of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili system, which yields a semi-discrete AKNS system. They then introduce a linear constraint for the same system and obtain a combined semi-discrete Burgers system. A further linear constraint for the modified system yields the same system. All results follow from recursive algebraic structures from master rules.
arxiv-2603-08401: Kozak extends Horndeski's theory into the Palatini approach, where the metric tensor and the symmetric connection stand a priori apart. The author introduces an extra transformation and writes down an action formula. It is form-invariant under both the disformal change of the metric and the new change. Such a theory reduces on-shell to a metric subclass of Horndeski's gravity called kinetic gravity braiding. A fixed metric and connection are also added, and values defined this way lead to a metric theory.
arxiv-2603-08501: Ummar Abbas and colleagues build Fanar-Sadiq, a two-language system for Islamic questions grounded in source texts. Plain chat models often invent quotes or cite wrongly, a sharp risk where users expect Qur'an and Hadith backing. The system routes each query to a fit tool, checks exact verses, and runs fixed Sunni calculators for alms and inheritance. It has logged over a million accesses.
arxiv-2603-08601: Aitor Fernández and César Fosco study a massless Dirac field trapped between two thin parallel walls. When the setup mirrors evenly about the middle plane, the Casimir pull attracts, but the odd, mirror-flipped setup pushes apart. They also track wall-bound current links and show that, in two space dimensions plus time, an outside electric field drives a sideways Hall-like current whose shape follows the trap.
arxiv-2603-08701: Le Nagat Neher and colleagues ask whether ultra-fast outflows from active galaxies can be seen in very-high-energy gamma rays. Shocks from these outflows should accelerate particles and glow in gamma rays and neutrinos. Their models find several nearby outflows within reach of next-generation telescopes even when Fermi-LAT sees nothing, favoring hard proton spectra, strong acceleration, and boosted magnetic fields.
arxiv-2603-08901: Pratyay Kumar and colleagues fool deep-learning network attack guards with diffusion-made trick traffic. Natural trick samples look real enough to fool humans and models alike, making them key for testing defense. Their NetDiffuser sorts traffic features into split groups, perturbs them lightly to keep flows valid, and injects meaning-true diffusion tweaks, lifting attack success and cutting guard scores.
arxiv-2603-09201: Egor Lifar and colleagues build a fully data-driven separator that pulls a signal of interest out of unknown non-Gaussian interference. They first learn a discrete tokenizer for the target signal, adapting a SoundStream design with extra transformer layers and finite-scalar quantization. A transformer trained with cross-entropy loss then beats mean-squared error training by a wide margin. On MIT RF Challenge mixtures the method cuts bit-error rates sharply and adapts to new interference with no side information.
arxiv-2603-09601: Elisabeth Sommer James and colleagues build MM-algorithms for traditional and convex NMF under Tweedie and Negative Binomial cost functions. Standard NMF rests on Gaussian or Poisson noise, which can misfit overdispersed data. A Majorize-Minimisation frame gives multiplicative update rules for every model they treat, with new rules for convex NMF under Poisson and Negative Binomial costs. Tests on mutational and word count data show the noise choice strongly shapes fit and feature recovery.
arxiv-2603-09801: Cláudio P. Fonte and coauthors model how yield stress fluids move through messy two dimensional porous rock. Their pore network uses a physics based rule for flow through each narrow throat, with no fitted resistance values. Against direct simulations, the model matches pressure drop and the shift from spread flow to narrow channels. Wall slip lowers the needed pressure and reopens blocked paths.
arxiv-2603-09901: Dominik Hangleiter argues, in this perspective piece, that quantum computational advantage has in fact been achieved. Claims first made in 2019 have grown stronger, even as machines with a hundred logical qubits are being built. He compares today's status to Bell tests in the 1980s: real, with scalability and checking still open. Three milestones for the next era aim to close those gaps, ending with classically checked advantage.
arxiv-2603-10301: Hiroki Naganuma and co-authors ask what shape a near-optimal learning rate schedule takes for a given training workload. Their search separates schedule shape from the base rate, so shapes can be compared fairly across families and tasks. Trials cover linear regression, CIFAR-10 image classification, and small-scale language modelling. Warmup and decay prove robust features of good schedules, while common schedule families fall short of optimal here. Weight decay, they find, can strongly shift which shape works best.
arxiv-2603-10501: Matthias Ludewig shows that quantum cellular automata sit naturally inside coarse homology theory, as its degree-zero part. That framing has a neat payoff. A recent result of Ji and Yang says the space of such automata is an Omega-spectrum, in algebraic topology terms. Ludewig notes this is no special miracle: it follows at once from the formal properties that coarse homology theories carry, once the automata are placed inside that general structure.
arxiv-2603-11101: Yongjian Guo and a large team describe a cloud platform that trains embodied intelligence models. It runs on a thousand graphics processors and builds on the LeRobot framework. They reworked the data pipeline, training stack, and infrastructure together. This cut one model's single-round training time from fifteen hours to twenty-two minutes. Storage, an RDMA network, and an elastic data lake keep data, communication, and computation in step. An end-to-end evaluation loop closes the path from training to simulation to assessment.
arxiv-2603-11201: Haihua Luo and coauthors move continual learning finetuning out of weight space and into representation space, arguing that standard parameter-efficient methods never directly control how representations drift. Their framework, CoRe, acts inside a low-rank linear subspace of a pretrained model's hidden representations, with stated goals. It holds stability for old tasks while keeping plasticity for new ones. Across several continual learning benchmarks, it stays highly parameter-efficient and outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a lot. The authors frame representation finetuning as the clearer path.
arxiv-2603-11401: Jan Frahm and Quentin Labriet pin down a theta correspondence by decomposing a minimal representation on a dual pair. The setting is the conformal group of a simple split Jordan algebra, containing its automorphism group paired with a rank-one group of Möbius type. Cases include the exceptional group of type F4 in its complex, compact, and split real forms. Their direct integral decomposition matches the two sides' representations one-to-one, with the occurring ones characterized through the Plancherel formula of a rank one symmetric space.
arxiv-2603-11501: Chen and co-authors present KEPo, a poisoning attack on graph-based retrieval-augmented generation. GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from outside data, which opens a new attack surface. Older attacks fail here, since the graph rebuilds injected text before the model reads it. For a target query, KEPo plants a toxic event and a forged path from old facts to it, and linked corpora back each other up. Across several data sets, KEPo posts top attack success rates for single and multi-target cases.
arxiv-2603-11601: Baghel and Chopra test whether symbolic scene descriptions help vision-language models play games better. Such models describe scenes well, yet they struggle to turn what they see into precise actions. Four setups face off across Atari games, VizDoom, and AI2-THOR: frames alone, frames with self-drawn or true symbols, and symbols alone. Every model gains when the symbols are accurate. When models extract the symbols themselves, gains hinge on model strength and scene complexity. Noisy symbols can drag decisions down, so perception quality is the bottleneck.
arxiv-2603-11701: Cavus studies why decision trees trained on the same task can disagree, tracing the cause to label noise. Observed labels are one draw from true probabilities, so near-equal trees can grow from the same data. He splits this observational multiplicity into two parts: leaf regret and structural regret. Leaf regret measures prediction wobble inside a fixed leaf from finite-sample noise. Structural regret captures wobble from the tree shape itself changing. Structural regret dominates, at over 15 times the leaf level in some sets.
arxiv-2603-11901: Pan and co-authors propose FlexRec, a reinforcement learning method that adapts LLM recommenders to shifting needs. Most recommenders chase one fixed target and cannot retool on demand. FlexRec ranks a fixed candidate set by generation, guided by user context and a stated need. Sequence-level rewards give coarse credit, and user feedback is sparse and noisy, so plain RL struggles. FlexRec answers with item-level rewards from counterfactual swaps and critic-guided scaling that discounts shaky rewards. It lifts NDCG@5 by up to 59% across scenarios, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-12101: Majozi and Zweni lift Takahashi convexity onto a hull built for spaces with asymmetric norms. Earlier work by Künzi and Yildiz set up convexity ideas for T0-quasi-metric spaces. The hull here carries its own canonical quasi-metric and vector-space operations. On that base the authors define a lifted convexity structure with a mixing rule. They show the result is a convex T0-quasi-metric space. The structure also fits the canonical embedding and W-convexity for minimal function pairs.
arxiv-2603-12501: Singh and Funcke extend a normalizing-flow density-of-states method to lattice gauge theory. Earlier work used the same flow-based route to rebuild the partition function of a scalar lattice theory. Here gauge-equivariant flows reconstruct the density of states of pure U(1) gauge theory in one space and one time dimension. Without a theta term, the rebuilt density matches known analytic results. With a theta term, the method can generate gauge-field configurations at fixed topological charge. The study is presented as preliminary work.
arxiv-2603-12801: Yizhou Liu and co-authors test how massive, asymmetric neutrinos change halo abundance and clustering. Most past work stressed neutrino mass, while asymmetry stayed underexplored. Their N-body runs refit cosmology to CMB data for each case. Mass cuts the count of the heaviest halos, by up to about 30% in the top case today. Asymmetry instead raises counts across a broad mass range. Both effects grow stronger at high redshift, and bias shifts in opposite ways too.
arxiv-2603-12901: Lorenzo Bardone and co-authors explain the order in which diffusion models learn data statistics, from easy to hard. Tests on natural images show a simplicity bias: pair-wise statistics come first. Higher-order correlations are learned only later. A minimal data model with controlled correlations reproduces that pattern. The authors define a scalar invariant that sets sample complexity for each level. Pair-wise traits need linear sample counts, while a fourth cumulant needs at least cubic. Shared latent structure can cut that cost back to linear.
arxiv-2603-13101: Masato Nagatsuka and co-authors update the nucleon axial-vector charge from the PACS10 lattice ensembles at the physical point. The set spans volumes over 10 fm across and three lattice spacings, from coarse to superfine. Work on the new superfine ensemble is still underway in this report. Low-energy relations from the partially conserved axial-vector current are also checked. Three-point functions test if the data match continuum physics within errors. The update tracks progress toward a sharp value of this key charge.
arxiv-2603-13201: Xin Chen and co-authors propose NAIT, a way to pick instruction tuning data for large language models. Too much tuning data can hurt a model, while a small, well-chosen set can help it. NAIT reads neuron activation patterns from data tied to a target skill. It then scores candidate samples by how well their patterns match the target. Training on the chosen tenth of Alpaca-GPT4 beat rival selection methods on many tasks. The team also finds that neuron patterns transfer across skills.
arxiv-2603-13301: Varun Kotte asks when prompt-only LLM query rewriting helps or hurts dense retrieval. Such rewriting is common in production RAG pipelines, yet its effect was poorly known. Kotte tests three BEIR benchmarks, two dense retrievers, and many training setups. Rewriting hurt scores on FiQA, helped on TREC-COVID, and had no clear effect on SciFact. Harm came when rewrites swapped out domain terms that already matched the right texts well. Gains came when rewrites moved queries toward the terms the corpus uses most.
arxiv-2603-13401: Jiashu Han and co-authors introduce MAD, a pretraining strategy for virtual spatial omics from microscopy. Reading molecular states from images would bypass the cost and throughput limits of omics tools. Their method learns cell-centric embeddings by self-distilling two views of the same indexed cell. One view shows cell morphology, the other its microenvironment, and both map into one space. Across tissues and imaging types, MAD set state-of-the-art scores on cell subtyping and transcriptomic prediction. It even beat foundation models trained on much larger datasets.
arxiv-2603-14201: Huang and co-authors study frequency-resolved multi-photon correlations in the ultra-strong coupling regime of cavity QED. A qubit couples so strongly to one cavity mode that counter-rotating terms reshape its states. Frequency-selective detection then reveals strong multi-photon antibunching in the emitted light. Bunching also appears, traced to cascade steps among the dressed states. Breaking parity symmetry opens new paths and boosts output of photon pairs and triplets at mixed frequencies.
arxiv-2603-14301: Barhdadi and co-authors present 4D Synchronized Fields, a representation that joins shape, motion, and language for moving scenes. Older methods split these parts: rebuilds drop motion structure, and language tags are pasted on after motion is learned. Each object's motion is factored into a shared object path plus a small residual. A ridge map tied to that motion predicts how object meanings shift over time. On HyperNeRF, the method posts the best scores among language and motion rivals, and finds target moments well.
arxiv-2603-14601: Groisman and co-authors study k-means clustering when the metric itself must be learned. Both the data measure and the distance start out unknown. Their core result says k-means centers move continuously under the measured Gromov-Hausdorff topology. The Voronoi clusters they define stay stable as well. No uniqueness of the center set is assumed. The frame yields consistency proofs for many metric learning tools at once. Cases cover Isomap, diffusion and Wasserstein distances, plus percolation and length space uses.
arxiv-2603-15101: Villani and co-authors use Gaussian mixture models to find where a simulation model goes wrong. Engineers must trade physical fidelity against practicality, so gaps between simulation and measurement persist even after calibration. Their non-intrusive method maps sensor readings to clusters of physical parameters. The clusters expose systematic discrepancies and model bias, which point to targeted fixes. The setup is Bayesian and uses expectation-maximization. Tests include a toy example and a real study of heat transfer in a concrete bridge.
arxiv-2603-15301: Siedentop studies the Csanyi and Arias energy functional for multi-particle fermion ground states. The functional is built from the reduced one-particle density matrix. He shows it sits between two known bounds: the Muller functional below and the Hartree-Fock functional above. With that sandwich in hand, he derives an asymptotic expansion of its ground state energy. The expansion agrees with the true quantum energy through third order.
arxiv-2603-15801: Smolkovič and Stangl make global new-physics fits fully differentiable. Effective field theory likelihoods now guide hunts for heavy unseen physics. Their framework chains running, matching, predictions, and data limits in one flow. Every step stays differentiable end to end. Gradient-based frequentist and Bayesian inference then scale to big spaces. Two 374-parameter SMEFT studies show the method in action. Basis-independent, multi-scale global fits become practical, they report. The design targets routine use in phenomenology work.
arxiv-2603-16201: Huang and co-authors work on scoring the quality of AI-generated audio. Automatic score models often learn dataset quirks instead of real quality cues. The team uses domain adversarial training to strip out those false cues. They test ways to define the domains, from plain metadata labels to data-driven clusters. No single choice wins for all score types. Their aspect-specific choice beats baselines and holds up on unseen generators.
arxiv-2603-16601: El-Haj introduces Tarab, a vast corpus of Arabic lyrics and poetry. The corpus comprises 2.56 million verses and more than 13.5 million tokens. Songs and poems share the collection in near balance. Varieties span Classical and Modern Standard Arabic plus six regional dialects. Artists come from 28 modern states across fourteen centuries. Each verse carries metadata on variety, origin, and era. Baselines cover variety identification and genre sorting.
arxiv-2603-16701: Chen, Chew, and Kunz map dyonic black holes in Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theory. These holes carry both electric and magnetic charge, plus a scalar field. Scalarized versions split into three branches of existence. Cold and hot branches split off at a minimal charge. Both charges together allow regular extremal holes, unseen in the pure electric case. A third branch shows a sudden plunge in Hawking temperature. Extremal holes take a special scalar value at the horizon. The team demonstrates the plunge for an exponential cubic coupling.
arxiv-2603-16901: Nacar and a large team present an Arabic function calling framework for language models. Models that turn speech into structured tool calls often break down badly in Arabic. Their system builds on a 270M parameter FunctionGemma backbone. Training used dataset auditing, schema repair, tool aware prompts, and full supervised fine tuning. On held out tests, parse failures fell from 87 percent to below 1 percent. Function name accuracy rose more than eightfold, and argument alignment improved across dialects. The authors also test a variant that adds explicit reasoning before each tool call.
arxiv-2603-17301: Sufiyan and co-authors present WINFlowNets, a generative flow network framework that trains its two networks together. Flow networks learn stochastic policies for sequential decisions, but the continuous variant needs a pretrained retrieval network. That pretraining is a burden in shifting robot settings. WINFlowNets warms up the retrieval network first, then co trains both networks with a shared architecture and replay buffer. In simulated robot tasks, it beat the older framework and strong RL baselines on reward and stability. It also adapted well in fault settings.
arxiv-2603-17501: Rasoulzadeh classifies smooth alignable Voss surfaces, grid shells that fold flat into a strip. Such nets ship compact and open on site with a scissor move at the joints. He sorts all non-developable cases that also carry a geodesic-conjugate net. One class rests on helicoidal surfaces and comes with explicit formulas. The other forms families of surfaces of revolution ruled by Painlevé III solutions. One family fills a gap in Eisenhart's older list.
arxiv-2603-17601: Crossley, Falco, and Baker recast wave speed selection in reaction-diffusion systems as optimal control. Travelling waves model spread in biology and physics, from species to fronts. Any test function in their setup yields a lower bound on invasion speed. They test the porous-Fisher equation and multi-species systems with weak coupling. Nonlinear selection can beat the classic linear rule, they show. Simulations confirm the predicted speeds closely.
arxiv-2603-18601: Naser and co-authors propose putting data centers in orbit to support direct handset-to-satellite links for 6G. Low orbit craft would handle radio access and fast inference. Higher layers in medium and geostationary orbit would aggregate data and steer compute. Energy-aware scheduling and AI control tie the layers together. The design turns a passive relay fleet into an active multi-layer system. The authors map the key enabling tools and list open research problems for scale and resilience.
arxiv-2603-18801: Lamata-Otín and co-authors extend the classic SIR epidemic model so infectiousness can evolve. Fixed viral traits underpin standard forecasts of peak infections and policy effects. Evolution changes both the peak and the timing of early growth. The peak then moves in a non-monotone way with the reproduction number. Lifting controls too early can leave a population worse off than no action at all. Formulas give the critical mutation rate and intervention time behind this effect. Shorter infectious periods avoid feeding viral evolution.
arxiv-2603-18901: Canelo and co-authors study a dust band at 6.2 microns in spectra from 175 galaxies. The galaxies are led by starbursts, active nuclei, or a mix of both. They fit the band and sort sources by where its peak falls. One class covers eighty percent of the sample, which may point to nitrogen built into the dust grains. Ice absorption near the band has little effect. A second feature near the band changes fits when it is modeled too.
arxiv-2603-19101: Liu and Papadimitratos defend road condition sorting against poisoning in federated learning. Cars train a shared model without pooling their images. Rogue cars can flip labels, say calling a rough road smooth, to skew the shared model. Their FedTrident checks each local model neuron by neuron to spot such attacks. It rates clients over rounds and drops bad actors based on past behavior. It then unlearns the harm done to the shared model. Tests across many attack setups hold near attack-free scores, they report.
arxiv-2603-19301: Hörmann and co-authors survey data sharing rules at 171 journals in materials science. Nearly all journals now post a data policy, and most ask for a data availability note. But firm demands stay rare, and open deposit of raw data is seldom required. Rules for research software lag far behind those for data. Versioning, identifiers, and run environments get little attention. A shared score shows wide gaps between journals. Neither impact factor nor access type predicts how strict a policy is.
arxiv-2603-19601: Li presents K-GMRF, a training-free method for tracking covariance matrices that change over time. Covariance tracking matters in vision, but estimates often lag during fast change. The method recasts tracking as forced rigid-body motion on Lie groups. Observations act as torques on a latent angular velocity, moved by a symplectic integrator. Theory shows zero steady-state error under constant rotation, unlike first-order methods. On synthetic ellipses, angular error drops thirtyfold versus a Riemannian baseline. Tests on rotation tracking and motion blur also improve.
arxiv-2603-19701: Shibatani and Yamaguchi apply fair division theory to school redistricting with two student groups. Earlier work showed that near-fair plans for many groups can need many added seats. For three or more groups, few added seats cannot always give an almost envy-free plan. The authors define a weaker rule, 1-relaxed envy-freeness. It caps the overload at each school at one seat. They prove such a plan always exists for two groups. They also give a fast method to find it.
arxiv-2603-19901: Anglès Munné and Huber make semidefinite bounds on quantum codes fully rigorous. Such bounds limit how large a code of given length and distance can be. Numeric solvers give strong bounds, but rounding errors block strict proofs of non-existence. The authors build rational infeasibility certificates for a range of codes. They use a clustered low-rank solver plus careful rounding to exact forms. The work improves 18 upper bounds for codes of 6 to 19 qubits.
arxiv-2603-20001: Ling and co-authors give the first soundness frame for program verifiers built by translation. Such verifiers turn a source program into an intermediate language, then prove that version correct. Soundness needs the translated proof to imply the source program is right. Past work assumed both sides share the same state model, which rarely holds. The new frame only assumes a homomorphic link between the two state models. A fresh condition, backward satisfiability, secures the translation step. The frame is formalized for separation logic verifiers.
arxiv-2603-20101: Haklay and co-authors warn that judging automated interpretability agents is full of traps. Their test case is circuit analysis, explaining what model parts do on a task. They built an agent that designs experiments and refines hypotheses on its own. Against human expert accounts on six tasks, the agent looked competitive. Closer checks exposed flaws in that replication-based scoring. Human accounts can be subjective or incomplete, and outcome scores hide the research process. Language models may also echo published findings from memory rather than discover them.
arxiv-2603-20301: Rahman and co-authors propose judging voice privacy by speaker attributes, not signal matching. Voice anonymization aims to hide who spoke, but benchmarks compare waveforms directly. They measure speaker uniqueness from true, inferred, and protected attribute sets. They also test an attack setting with a single utterance per speaker. Inferred attributes still carried risk, despite errors in guessing them. Future voice privacy work, they argue, must weigh attribute-based threats and defenses.
arxiv-2603-20501: Wei and co-authors present CICDWOA, an enhanced whale optimization algorithm for hard search problems. The base whale algorithm can converge too early and lose diversity. Their variant starts with a good nodes set for even initialization. A collective cognitive sharing step boosts group collaboration. A Cauchy-based spiral update strengthens global and local search balance. Gaussian-Cauchy mutation and a nonlinear factor add further diversity. Tests span 23 benchmarks, robot and drone path planning, and design tasks. The method ranked first among rivals on average Friedman score.
arxiv-2603-20801: Xu and co-authors link iterative neural constraint solvers to large neighborhood search. Neural heuristics refine candidate assignments step by step, much like LNS does. They rebuild the ConsFormer method as an explicit LNS loop. The destroy step picks which part of a solution to redo. Prediction guided variants use the model's own scores for this choice. The repair step then refills the gap, by sampling or greedy picks. On Sudoku, graph coloring, and MaxCut, the LNS form won clear gains.
arxiv-2603-21201: Muneeb and Ascher benchmark forty six polygenic risk score tools in one harmonized frame. The tools differ in assumptions, inputs, and complexity, which makes fair comparison hard. Their frame runs all tools on seven binary UK Biobank traits and one continuous trait, with five-fold cross-validation. They track accuracy plus runtime, memory, input needs, and failure modes. Rankings differ significantly across traits, and no tool wins everywhere. Performance depends on trait structure and practical software traits, not just statistics.
arxiv-2603-21301: Sharma and Jain compare three inference-time strategies for improving language model reasoning, with no extra training. Self-consistency samples the model many times and takes the most frequent answer. Dual-model agreement trusts only reasoning that two models share. Self-reflection has the model critique and revise its own work. All use chain-of-thought prompting. Self-consistency with nucleus sampling gives the largest gains, about nine to fifteen points over greedy decoding. Dual-model checks suit higher risk uses. Self-reflection adds only marginal gains for smaller models.
arxiv-2603-21601: Yu and Sun argue that graph foundation models should be built on Riemannian geometry rather than on graph neural networks or language models. Neural networks struggle with memory and interpretability across domains, while text serializations lose graph structure. Geometry, they contend, captures structure directly and still fits semantic learning. Their proposed Riemannian Foundation Model centers on intrinsic graph geometry, with built-in structural inference and generation. They sketch a staged agenda toward general-purpose graph intelligence driven by such models. The piece is a position paper, not an experimental study.
arxiv-2603-21701: Wang and co-authors cut the visual token load of large vision-language models for multi-turn question answering. In multi-turn chats, later questions are unknown in advance and may point anywhere in the image. Prompt-based pruning discards regions those questions need, while heuristic scores prune poorly. Their MetaCompress method learns the compression mapping directly, covering both pruning and merging in one objective. A data-efficient training scheme keeps learning costs low. Across benchmarks and model architectures, MetaCompress kept accuracy high while trimming tokens across dialogue turns.
arxiv-2603-22201: Zhao and co-authors present NMR, a method that retargets human motion onto humanoid robots. Classic retargeting solves an optimization problem for each motion. The authors show the problem is non-convex and trap-prone. The symptoms are joint jumps and self-penetration in the output motion. NMR instead learns the data distribution of good retargeted motion. Physics experts first repair noisy human demos. A CNN-Transformer model then learns from that cleaned data. On a Unitree G1 robot, NMR cuts self-collisions across tasks like dance and martial arts.
arxiv-2603-22301: Mabrok reads the hidden states of language models as points on a curved semantic surface. Models compute in continuous vector spaces but must output discrete tokens. That mismatch warps meaning in ways that are poorly mapped. Mabrok equips the surface with the Fisher information metric. Tokens then act as Voronoi regions that tile the surface. He defines an expressibility gap for the distortion this tiling causes. Two theorems bound the gap for any fixed vocabulary. Tests on six transformer models confirm the predicted scaling.
arxiv-2603-22401: Belis and co-authors build probability models over permutations on a quantum computer. Permutation data shows up in tasks like tracking many objects and ranking items. A strong way to model such data uses non-Abelian harmonic analysis. Low Fourier frequencies mark simple links, and high ones mark complex links. A Markov chain can then mix diffusion steps with Bayesian updates. Their quantum algorithm packs the exact model into a quantum state's amplitudes. It leans on the fast quantum Fourier transform over the symmetric group.
arxiv-2603-22501: Gómez and co-authors prove that chirality cannot act as a primary ferroic order in certain crystal classes. Some had suggested that handedness itself could order, like magnetism or polarization. The team uses group theory and a full subgroup survey to test that idea. They show no achiral parent can reach an enantiomorphic pair through a zone-center instability. Since a ferroic order must transform at the zone center, such transitions cannot be primary ferroic ones. Any critical fluctuations should appear at finite wavevector instead.
arxiv-2603-22601: Van Dam, Monzillo, and Penjić study graphs tied to one special spectral object. They look at a connected regular graph and an algebra built from one of its spectral idempotents. When that algebra has dimension two, they seek a plain structural account of the graph. They give such an account in terms of equitable partitions. The authors present many examples and sort the distance-regular graphs with this trait. They also sort graphs that yield a three-class association scheme. A final part covers graphs with two such eigenvalues.
arxiv-2603-22801: Zhang and co-authors prove that transformers trained by gradient descent can learn a class of teacher models. The teachers include convolution layers, graph convolution layers, and classic statistical models. A one-layer transformer with simple position-only attention is the student. The authors prove it can recover all teacher parameter blocks and reach optimal population loss. The trained student also generalizes to out-of-distribution data under mild conditions. A shared bilinear structure across tasks makes the unified proof work.
arxiv-2603-23201: Martinez, Benvenuto, and De Vito test whether star rotation skews mass estimates for type II supernova progenitors. Such masses are often read off pre-explosion images with non-rotating star models. The team instead runs rotating models whose spin rates match observed stars. They check each supernova on its own and the full mass spread as a group. Rotating models shift masses slightly downward, but by less than the usual error bars. They set an upper mass limit near 20.4 solar masses for these progenitors.
arxiv-2603-23501: Khan and seven co-authors build MedObvious, a benchmark for the sanity checks that start medical image reading. Clinicians first confirm the scan is valid: right modality, right anatomy, sane orientation. Most tests skip that step and trust the input. MedObvious packs 1,880 tasks where models must spot a broken panel in image sets. Five tiers climb from mix-ups to triage-style traps. Across 17 vision models, checking proves shaky. Models invent flaws on clean sets and wobble as sets grow. Scores swing with the answer format.
arxiv-2603-23601: Patterson, Wang, and Mann link global entanglement to what a moving watcher sees. Quantum reference frames recast physics from one watcher's stance. They find terms where global entanglement splits into frame-bound links plus coherence. They name that split entanglement transference. For speeding frames, the split reframes an old puzzle: speeding up seems to drain entanglement. In the frame view, the lost links can be offset by growing coherence. The trade hints that frames help track how quantum stores shift.
arxiv-2603-23701: Wei and six co-authors retest early-exit decoding in today's large language models. Early exit stops a model's work mid-stack once its guess looks sure, saving time and cost. New training recipes trim layer slack, which may shrink those chances. The team craft a score for a model's inborn exit fitness and a bench to test it. Exit gains fade across newer model breeds. Dense models beat sparse expert mixes and state space models. Big base models past twenty billion weights show the most promise.
arxiv-2603-24301: Gudmundsson and Löhndorf introduce a new method for building minimal surfaces in four-dimensional spaces. Their method constructs minimal submanifolds of codimension two in even-dimensional spheres and hyperbolic spaces. It rests on the theory of complex-valued harmonic morphisms. With it, they give the first explicit examples of such maps defined on the sphere S4. They also give the first such examples on the hyperbolic space H4. The work adds concrete constructions where few explicit cases were known.
arxiv-2603-24801: Sakib and co-authors dissect segmentation failures for abdominal aortic aneurysms. Models often fail by focusing on irrelevant structures or missing thin targets. Their framework computes an attribution focus map from the final encoder block. That map guides the model twice: predicted mass is aligned with it, and it feeds a refinement path plus a confidence prior. Tested on curated clinical cases, the method improves substantially over a base SAM setup. The gains suggest encoder focus is a practical lever for segmentation.
arxiv-2603-24901: Li and co-authors study the ground state of thin films of the ferroelectric material CuInP2S6. Experiments suggest a state with net polarisation, while density functional theory predicts an antiferroelectric ground state. The team combines first-principles calculations with the deep potential method. For films thicker than a bilayer, the lowest-energy state mixes both orders: antiferroelectric inside, ferroelectric at the two surfaces. A ferrielectric state lies very close in energy. Phonon free energy calculations flip the preference for the monolayer, where the ferroelectric ordering wins.
arxiv-2603-25001: In and co-authors rethink how to blame a failure in a team of AI agents. Older tests assume one root cause, but real failures often allow several fair readings. The team defines multi-perspective failure attribution, which keeps that ambiguity in view. They built MP-Bench, a benchmark made for this setting, plus a scoring rule to match. Their tests show that claims of weak language model skill came mostly from narrow test design. Wider views give a truer read on debugging skill.
arxiv-2603-25401: Le and Simonetto follow a physics-style flow that solves rough convex problems fast. Their system is a high-grade view of Nesterov's acceleration, adapted to objectives with kinks. A time-varying Moreau smoothing softens the kinks, and a rescaled gradient with Hessian damping steers the path. They prove the flow is well posed and build an energy that drains at the right rate. Paths settle weakly onto minimizers under mild conditions. A twin system covers monotone operators, and numeric tests show the knobs at work.
arxiv-2603-25601: San reviews the WKB method for semiclassical operators and its fix at caustics. The method gives approximate solutions to the Schrödinger equation. It seems to fail where caustics form. Maslov showed how a wider version gets past that failure. San uses modern microlocal analysis and sheaf theory to give a unified account. The framework proves the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization rules for general operators in one degree of freedom. The paper also surveys applications and extensions of the method.
arxiv-2603-25801: Ahn and co-authors demonstrate a chip device that calms laser intensity noise without any feedback loop. Laser noise limits quantum sensing, metrology, and computing. Feedback loops are slow, and optical resonators are narrow and need locking. Their device uses second-harmonic generation in nanophotonic lithium niobate waveguides. It runs at a pump-depletion point where input swings barely move the output. The authors report noise cuts of 25 to 60 decibels from DC past 10 gigahertz. A noisy fiber amplifier output was steadied to the shot-noise limit.
arxiv-2603-26501: Harbater, Hartmann, and McNinch discuss when Levi factors exist for algebraic groups over one-variable function fields. A Levi factor complements the unipotent radical of a group. The question is whether local data can guarantee a global factor of this kind. The authors give examples of disconnected groups where the local-global principle fails. They then prove a strong local-global principle when a Levi descent condition holds. The work sorts which extra structure makes the passage from local to global safe.
arxiv-2603-26601: Thy, Diekmann, and Thiele study compound drops that slide down a slope on a solid surface. Each drop joins two immiscible, partly wetting liquids that do not evaporate. A two-layer flow model with full curvature drives the study. The team maps how drop shapes shift as force, volume ratio, and viscosity ratio change. They track speeds and the dynamic contact angles at the drop's edges. Outside the steady range, drops show a repeating cycle of fusion, overtaking, and splitting.
arxiv-2603-26701: Hashimoto and co-authors simulate opinion dynamics with language model agents grounded in an economic world. Past agent studies let opinions shift through talk alone, ignoring lived outcomes like past pay or losses. In their setup, agents act, earn or lose, and let those results shape their views. Single opinions follow structured paths, and hard times make views rigid. Across the population, shared opinions move with the economy, while inequality sharpens polarisation and price swings widen the spread of views.
arxiv-2603-26801: Cenacchi proposes a single way to make neural networks use fewer features across graphs, text, and tables. The method, called L0GM, adds hard gates to learned features. Each gate can switch a feature off during training. A schedule slowly tightens these gates. This creates a clear trade-off curve between accuracy and sparsity. Tests on three public benchmarks show competitive accuracy with fewer active features. The method also lowers calibration error in the reported tests.
arxiv-2603-26901: Malandii and Uryasev introduce biased mean regression inside the Risk Quadrangle framework. The biased mean adds a chosen excess amount to the expected value of an outcome. That target fits questions like which factors push portfolio losses past a set level. Minimizing their superexpectation error turns out to equal quantile regression under one setup. It also matches least squares when the excess is zero. In portfolio choice, the matching risk measure equals CVaR optimization. The computation reduces to linear programming.
arxiv-2603-27001: Quamer and co-authors present PHONOS, a streaming module that neutralizes accent in anonymized speech. Speaker anonymization changes timbre but often leaves accent cues that betray a speaker's background. PHONOS converts non-native sound segments toward a chosen target accent in real time. Training pairs come from golden utterances built with alignment and voice conversion. A causal translator then maps accent tokens with at most 40 milliseconds of look-ahead. Tests cut non-native accent confidence by 81 percent. End-to-end latency stayed under 241 milliseconds on one GPU.
arxiv-2603-27301: He and co-authors present Decoupling then Perceive, a framework for low-light image super-resolution. Doing enhancement and upscaling in sequence amplifies artifacts and crushes texture. Their method first splits the image into luminance and texture frequency bands. A structural decoupling mechanism performs that split adaptively per image. Two learning paths then rebuild each band with targeted models. A recomposition module merges the paths while keeping structure consistent. Benchmarks improved PSNR by 1.6 percent and SSIM by 9.6 percent. Perceptual error dropped by nearly half against the prior best.
arxiv-2603-27801: Das and co-authors document a myth-inspired sculpture built across continents. Navagunjara Reborn rose at Burning Man 2025. Digital sculpting began the shared workflow. Artisans in Odisha fabricated parts by hand. US teams tuned the modular structure. Photogrammetry and digital twins fed back design fixes. Final assembly happened in one shot in the Nevada desert. Lessons cover craft, myth, and engineering links.
