Many are easy to spot or tested only in hand-built scenarios.

Their attack subtly manipulates poses of existing objects in shared results, staying below detection thresholds. Small errors propagate through tracking and trajectory prediction, causing significant deviations and unsafe decisions such as unnecessary hard braking. An online scenario-aware framework adapts at runtime. Experiments show high success in inducing such errors and frequent safety-critical behavior while evading defenses. A localized mitigation cuts such errors markedly.
arxiv-2605-01701:
Jiahuan Wang and four co-authors bound how well decentralized learning generalizes when the data arrive as a Markov chain rather than as independent draws. Fleets of machines now train jointly, each seeing a stream with memory. Gradient methods, including the ascent-descent pairs used for minimax problems, inherit both the chain's dependence and the network's chatter.

Working through algorithmic stability, the lens that ties generalization to how much one data point can move the outcome, they separate the fingerprints of topology, chain mixing speed, and primal-dual dynamics. Both plain decentralized descent and its minimax sibling receive non-asymptotic generalization bounds. The results extend what was known for Markov sampling in one machine to the decentralized and minimax settings at once, which is where large-scale robust and adversarial training actually lives.
arxiv-2605-02001:
Cao-Vien Phung, Thomas Röthig, and Admela Jukan analyse low Earth orbit satellite networks that mix radio links with laser links. Lasers offer high speed and low delay between satellites, but weather can block optical paths to the ground, so radio remains needed. Traffic imbalance and changing capacity make scheduling and buffer size key design choices.

With finite buffers, interference-aware scheduling, and weather-based outage chances, their results show lasers bring large gains. Raising satellite power is not the best route to top throughput. Choosing the right scheduling priority can reach the maximum instead, while using less power. The work guides how large on-board buffers should be for hybrid networks.
arxiv-2605-02301:
Junhao Wei and colleagues present SAGA, a planner for agile drone navigation in cluttered spaces that must be fast and safe. SAGA casts local planning as a joint regression and ranking task over a fixed lattice of motion anchors. From a depth image and the drone's motion state, it predicts refined end states and scores for all anchors in one forward pass, then decodes the best into a feasible trajectory.

Anchor features become geometry-aware tokens, and self-attention reasons across anchors globally. A polar positional encoding, built from anchor yaw and pitch, preserves directional structure in that token space. The design aims to weigh many feasible motions at once without a slow search, a key need for autonomous flight among obstacles.
arxiv-2605-02701:
Davide Nobile and Philipp Grohs propose a robust way to train neural networks when gradient noise has heavy tails. Standard stochastic gradient methods can be thrown off by rare, huge gradients. Clipping gradients is a common guard, but it is usually applied to a whole batch at once, which can distort the update.

Their method clips each sample's gradient separately before averaging. Theory shows optimal convergence rates in expectation for non-convex problems under heavy-tailed noise, with high-probability bounds that match up to small factors. In experiments, the method beat both momentum-based training and batch clipping on a standard image task, even after counting its extra compute time. A further finding: with gradient accumulation, clipping at the mini-batch level can help at almost no cost.
arxiv-2605-03601:
Moritz Grillo and Guido Montúfar ask when the parameters of a deep ReLU neural network are determined by the function the network computes. Two networks can represent the same function with different weights, beyond the obvious rescalings and permutations of hidden units. The authors study the realization map that sends parameters to functions.

Using weighted polyhedral complexes, they prove that for every architecture whose input and hidden layers have width at least two, there is an open set of identifiable parameters. Hence the functional dimension equals the parameter count minus the hidden neuron count. They also show minimal representations can keep nontrivial redundancies, and they establish a generic depth hierarchy against shallower networks.
arxiv-2605-04401:
Wenxian Shen studies travelling waves in a chemotaxis model. A living population moves toward or away from a chemical it produces itself. It also grows toward a cap. Such waves, connecting a fully populated state to an empty one, describe how a species invades new territory as a moving front.

Earlier work established that these waves exist for the simplest parameter case, but their uniqueness, stability, and monotone shape were little studied. Shen addresses all four properties together for a general family. It allows repulsion as well as attraction. It also allows a range of growth and response powers. The results characterise when a single, stable invasion front is the whole story.
arxiv-2605-04801:
Dieter Horns, Niklas Knop, and Mohammad Mohammadidoust estimate how much of the local dark matter density might actually be ordinary matter. That matter would take the form of interstellar objects, the comets and asteroids wandering between stars. Three such visitors have now been detected passing through the solar system, implying a large unseen galactic population.

Combining the observed arrival rate with size and density estimates gives a local mass density for these objects. The result carries large uncertainty, though. Their nuclear sizes are hard to pin down. The apparently great age of the latest visitor motivates a thick-disk distribution model. Including this baryonic component in the galactic rotation curve would lower the inferred non-baryonic dark matter density.
arxiv-2605-04901:
Zhengyi Li and eight co-authors show that a shuffling defence used in secure transformer inference is weaker than previously claimed. Secure inference should let a client learn only the final output while the server learns nothing about the input. Revealing middle activations speeds things up, but shuffling them was meant to stop clients from stealing model weights.

The authors attack the defence by aligning differently shuffled activations to one common ordering, then using them to extract weights. On Pythia and GPT-2 models the alignment errors were tiny, and for about a dollar of queries the recovered weights came very close to the true ones. The result urges caution about this efficiency shortcut.
arxiv-2605-05201:
Manish Mishra constructs a pinned version of the local Langlands correspondence for a special family of representations of reductive groups over local fields. The correspondence matches representations with parameter data, and Mishra treats depth-zero supercuspidal representations, an important building block case. Fixing a pinned splitting of the inner form removes arbitrary choices and makes the matching canonical.

A depth-zero type splits naturally into a tame toral part and a finite cuspidal part, and each is matched separately. The toral part uses the known correspondence for elliptic tori, while the finite part uses a pinned Jordan decomposition that keeps extension data for possibly disconnected quotients. Combining these pieces with a known unipotent correspondence gives the enhanced parameter and its inverse map.
arxiv-2605-05401:
Every why-question hides a contrast: why this happened, rather than something else. Britt Besch and Tobias Gerstenberg study how people pick that hidden alternative, called the foil. Participants read short stories and judged what they expected before, what seemed closest, and what they thought could have happened instead.

Foil choices were best predicted by hindsight expectations, what people find surprising after knowing the outcome. The pair also ran language models on the same task. The models' foil choices did not line up with their own stated expectations in the consistent way human choices did.
arxiv-2605-05701:
Search agents spend two currencies at once: tool calls and tokens, both capped. Zhengru Fang and co-authors study how to budget those currencies during multi-hop question answering. Better answers need not only stronger models but decisions about which search action deserves the next unit of budget, and when the evidence is enough to stop.

Their controller scores each feasible action by value of information: marginal task value per unit budget, given the current state and what remains. A second stage decides when to commit a final answer. The formulation treats inference-time spending as an explicit optimization problem.
arxiv-2605-05801:
Gossip protocols spread information through a network by pairwise exchanges, and real exchanges sometimes garble the message. Giorgio Cignarale and five co-authors study protocols that correct their own transmission errors without any central coordinator. Earlier work treated faulty protocols in temporal epistemic logics; this team proposes a dynamic epistemic logic instead.

They show how agents can detect and repair faulty messages as the protocol runs. Self-correction changes what optimal means for such protocols. The authors also compare the approach against bounded-memory and full-information variants, mapping the trade-offs between resilience, memory, and speed of convergence.
arxiv-2605-06101:
Luis Colmenarez, Áron Márton, and Markus Müller introduce syndrome resampling, a method that raises quantum error correction thresholds without new hardware. Correction works only when physical error rates sit below a code dependent threshold, which current devices struggle to reach. Their idea works purely on the measurement records, called syndromes, that decoders already collect.

Unlikely syndromes are prone to logical failure, so biasing averages toward likely syndromes lifts logical fidelity. The authors tie this resampling to a known information measure and a family of optimal thresholds. In surface code simulations, thresholds rose for both optimal and weaker decoders, and logical error rates fell by up to four orders of magnitude. Tests on existing experimental data cut logical errors by up to two orders.
arxiv-2605-06201:
Ying Gu and five co-authors propose judging multimodal models by logical consistency instead of labeled accuracy alone. Accuracy scores can reward lucky guessing, and new tasks may have no ground truth labels for validation at all. Their metric checks whether a model's answers respect cause and effect logic in both directions, on sufficient and on necessary relations.

The Vision-Language Logical Consistency Metric works on standard multiple choice visual question tests and on newer natural benchmarks, with no ground truth needed. The team evaluated eleven open source models from four families on established benchmarks. Accuracy had improved markedly in recent models, but logical consistency lagged far behind it. Further checks support the metric's validity, and the authors suggest it for model selection and answer justification on unlabeled tasks.
arxiv-2605-06301:
Violeta Calleja-Solanas and four co-authors show that higher order interactions in ecosystems can hide behind ordinary pairwise models. Ecologists increasingly treat group interactions, where several species jointly shape each other's growth, as a key part of community dynamics. The natural hope is that rich abundance time series can reveal whether such higher order effects are at work in a given system.

The authors show that higher order Lotka-Volterra dynamics can often be reproduced accurately by an effective pairwise model fitted to the same data. Higher order structure therefore cannot, in general, be inferred from time series alone. Distinct mechanisms can generate nearly identical dynamics, a problem of mechanistic identifiability that risks accurate yet misleading readings. Time series need support from other ecological information before interaction structure can be trusted.
arxiv-2605-06501:
Chuanyang Zheng and eight co-authors propose Cubit, an architecture that replaces attention's token mixing with kernel ridge regression. Attention has stayed the core mixing step in Transformers since 2017 despite many changes elsewhere. The authors show attention can be read as Nadaraya-Watson regression, which averages values by similarity between tokens.

Cubit instead uses the closed-form solution of kernel ridge regression, adding normalization through the inverse kernel matrix. A limited-range rescale keeps training stable. Experiments suggest Cubit may model long sequences better than a standard Transformer, with its advantage growing as training sequence length increases. The work argues regression choice is a real design lever.
arxiv-2605-06601:
Isaac David and Arthur Gervais ask whether a language model agent can reconstruct the security meaning of a Linux update using only binary files. Defenders and attackers both diff patched packages, yet source patches and advisories are often unavailable. Their Patch2Vuln pipeline extracts old and new binary pairs, diffs them with Ghidra tools, and ranks changed functions for an offline agent.

On twenty-five Ubuntu package pairs, the agent localized a verified security patch function in half the security cases and assigned an accepted root cause in slightly more. Failures often came before reasoning, when the differ missed the right function. All negative controls stayed classified as unknown.
arxiv-2605-06801:
Domagoj Perković, Konstantinos Vasiliou, S. A. Parameswaran, and Steven H. Simon test a claim that fractional quantum Hall edges carry a protected intrinsic electric dipole moment. Earlier work by Park and Haldane predicted a universal value, and it was widely expected to hold. The authors find flaws in the earlier numerics and compute the ground-state dipole with care, using density matrix methods called DMRG.

Across three chosen systems, the expected intrinsic value appears only for the one-third filling edge. The two-thirds edge and the border between Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases do not show the claimed value. Composite fermion arguments suggest hierarchy states usually lack protected dipoles, changing thinking about Hall edge energy balance and structure.
arxiv-2605-07101:
Yuyang Zhang, Haldun Balim, and Na Li improve exploration when several learning agents must cooperate. A popular decentralized method uses energy-based policies, but in practice those are replaced by simple Gaussian policies. The authors show that this simplification badly limits exploration, and the problem grows as more agents join.

Their alternative gives each agent a diffusion-based policy, which can express several distinct action styles at once. A new training method with theoretical guarantees makes online training of such policies efficient. Across particle, robotics, and strategy-game benchmarks, the approach consistently improved performance over the Gaussian-based version.
arxiv-2605-07201:
Srikar Kashyap Pulipaka describes a system built for a shared task on detecting toxic behavior in gaming chat. Messages from the game World of Tanks had to be sorted into six categories, from non-toxic to insults, harassment, threats, and extremism. Pulipaka tried encoders, instruction-tuned models with light fine-tuning, layered classifiers, and ensembles.

The best setup paired a mid-size open language model with a small, carefully calibrated share of synthetic training data. It placed fourth among thirty-five teams on the test set. Analysis also exposed a validation trap in the data: doing well on the validation split predicted poor transfer to the real test.
arxiv-2605-07301:
Shiyue Cao and five co-authors model opponents for language-model agents by separating model building from prediction. Earlier approaches tangled the two, relying on implicit context reading that adapted poorly as interactions evolved. Their SOM framework first builds a structural causal model linking an opponent's observations to its actions.

That explicit graph then guides the language model's reasoning along clear pathways when predicting the opponent's next move. Across diverse multi-agent benchmarks, SOM consistently beat leading language-model reasoning baselines. The authors present the split design as a route to more accurate, adaptable strategy in complex, changing multi-agent settings.
arxiv-2605-07701:
Fan Zhou and Tim Van de Cruys argue that classifier-free guidance, the knob controlling how strongly a diffusion model follows a prompt, should not be frozen at one value. The best setting varies by task and by stage of generation, especially for language. Treating it as a fixed hyperparameter leaves quality and controllability on the table.

They recast guidance choice as sequential decision-making and train a policy with reinforcement learning to pick the guidance scale at each generation step from the current diffusion state. On three controlled text generation tasks with discrete diffusion language models, adaptive guidance beat fixed-scale strategies on the balance between control and quality. The learned policies followed distinct, interpretable patterns for different tasks.
arxiv-2605-07801:
Markus Walker and three co-authors bring trust regions to sampling-based model predictive control, the family that includes the popular MPPI algorithm. These controllers sample candidate action sequences, score their trajectories, and update the sampling distribution, but adjusting knobs like temperature or momentum has relied on heuristics and hand tuning.

Their setup bounds each update of the proposal distribution by a set divergence limit, with an entropy floor if wanted. The adaptation values then come out of the optimization rather than a rule of thumb. Deterministic local sampling further improves speed. On two benchmark environments the trust region version converged faster and used samples better in low-sample, low-iteration regimes, exactly where sampling controllers struggle.
arxiv-2605-07901:
Charul Gupta and four co-authors film what happens when a cavitation bubble collapses next to a confined air bubble inside a blind cylindrical hole. High-speed shadowgraphy shows a neat sequence: the growing cavitation bubble drives liquid down and squeezes the air bubble, which then rebounds and fires the liquid column upward as a slug. When the slug strikes the collapsing bubble's far side, a vortex ring is born.

Sweeping two dimensionless parameters mapped three regimes, and only the first, where impact lands during collapse at low stand-off and low fill fraction, makes a ring. Two simple one-dimensional models predict the impact point and speed, and a timing parameter comparing liquid travel time to the collapse half-period separates the regimes cleanly. The ring leaves at five meters per second before breaking up.
arxiv-2605-08201:
Sparsh Tiwari, Bettina Finzel, and Gesina Schwalbe cut the labeling cost of neurosymbolic vision systems. In two-stage designs, a neural network first perceives objects and a symbolic reasoner then applies rules, which keeps the system readable. The catch is that the perception stage normally needs expensive labels for its output symbols.

The authors pair a slot-based, object-centric architecture with a variational autoencoder for self-supervision, while concept guidance on selected latent dimensions steers the slots toward human-readable meanings. The grounded predictions become symbolic background knowledge for engines such as inductive logic programming and decision trees, so reasoning tasks can be learned from far fewer hand labels.
arxiv-2605-08801:
Peter Vanya, Katarína Šimková, and Rastislav Farkaš propose a data driven way to model traffic flows for planning roads and railways without the usual survey heavy machinery. Traditional macroscopic models need costly, bias prone surveys of how people live and travel, while earlier fitting frameworks are hard to interpret and prone to overfitting. Their protocol fits models to traffic counts, which are now cheap and reliable, with explainable weights and a controlled path for adding complexity.

Demonstrations on toy and realistic cases show the approach working end to end, with suggested extensions to systems mixing cars and public transport. Infrastructure planners gain forecasts they can explain to the public whose money builds the projects.
arxiv-2605-08901:
N. Semenova, V. Semenov, and A. Bukh study traveling waves in an ensemble of excitable FitzHugh-Nagumo units, a classic nerve pulse model, coupled weakly across distance and driven by extreme outside forcing. Three forcing types are compared: regular Gaussian pulses, pulses dirtied by white noise, and heavy tailed Lévy noise with tunable shape. Periodic forcing creates synchronization tongues with orderly collective motion, sometimes multiple waves or partial synchrony alongside propagation.

Lévy noise instead crushes regularity, producing counter propagating waves that melt into random walking behavior as intensity grows. The authors classify all observed regimes and map their layout across parameter space. Excitable media research gains a guide to how extreme environments reorganize signal travel.
arxiv-2605-09201:
Terko and four colleagues map magnetic order in perpendicular spin transfer torque memory, a leading candidate for fast, durable, scalable memory. Reliable operation needs control of order inside the synthetic antiferromagnet fixed layer, but pillars can show states absent in extended thin films. The team runs a micromagnetic study of 30 nanometre diameter three layer pillars with realistic material parameters.

Phase diagrams map stable states against bilinear and biquadratic interlayer exchange coupling. Adding asymmetry between the fixed layers in magnetisation, anisotropy, and thickness lowers the coupling needed to stabilise opposed states and suppress rivals. Energy path calculations show that for tilted opposed states, greater asymmetry raises fixed layer reversal barriers while cutting the free layer barrier, a trade off absent for aligned states. Stray fields also shift both reference and free layer energy barriers. The team publicly releases the simulation data covering 4374 configurations, supporting design of devices with either fixed state.
arxiv-2605-09301:
Chin and a colleague revisit Cluster-First-Route-Second for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem, an approach known for asymptotic optimality but overlooked by neural methods. Neural methods build routes autoregressively, inheriting slow step by step decoding, spatial symmetry sensitivity, and brittle out-of-distribution behaviour. Neural CFRS is the first one-shot neural CFRS framework that is purely non-autoregressive. It sets fleet capacity constraints end to end through a differentiable entropic Optimal Transport layer yielding a continuous transport plan for an assignment solver.

Proofs show the design is invariant to E(2) spatial transforms, route permutations, and traversal direction within routes, and a pre-trained spatial vocabulary unlocks parameter efficiency and zero-shot scaling. Neural CFRS scales to out-of-distribution N=1000 instances with under 4 percent gap. It holds about 5 percent gap even as an ultra-lightweight single layer. It reaches a 2 point 73 percent gap on size-100 problems.
arxiv-2605-09401:
Djeudjo and three colleagues sort chimera states, the puzzling mix of coherent and incoherent behaviour in systems of coupled identical oscillators, where existing detection and sorting methods often lack precision. Their method pairs Fourier analysis, which pins down key signal traits such as amplitude, phase, and frequency, with an unsupervised grouping step. That step acts on normalised total variations, measures of local spatial change in those dynamical traits.

Earlier methods hit limits that blocked precise sorting, which this joint Fourier-plus-grouping approach is built to overcome. The method finds regions in parameter space that return chimera states and further splits the different types. Rayleigh oscillators host the test, a network known for many dynamical patterns.
arxiv-2605-09501:
Joseph and three colleagues examine a confined active nematic under an orienting field. An active nematic is a fluid of self propelled rodlike units with orientational order. The team works in a low Reynolds number Ericksen Leslie framework. It includes active stresses and field induced torques. Their linear analysis finds two distinct modes. One has odd director symmetry, and the other has even symmetry. They derive exact and approximate boundaries for both.

Direction turns out to decide the outcome. A field pointing across the substrate anchoring direction lowers the activity threshold. It cooperatively switches on the even mode. A field aligned with the anchoring tends to stabilize the system instead. Full nonlinear simulations confirm the linear predictions. They show the analysis picks out the symmetries of the long time states. An external field can thus both tune when instability starts and choose which pattern emerges.
arxiv-2605-09701:
Hong and eight colleagues built DriveFuture, a driving system that plans with the future in mind rather than only reacting to the present. Most latent world models, compressed inner models of the road scene, treat future states as side targets. DriveFuture instead shapes the current inner state around predicted future states, then feeds that future-aware state to a diffusion-based planner that draws up the path.

On the public NAVSIM tests, the system scored 55.5 on the hard v2 set and 89.9 on the v2 standard set. It scored 90.7 on the v1 set, by the benchmark's driving scores. As of April 2026 it ranked first on the NAVSIM-v2 hard leaderboard. The lesson the authors draw is blunt: simulating the future matters less than letting it steer decisions made now.
arxiv-2605-10001:
Li and three colleagues tackled hypergraph condensation, shrinking large real graphs into compact yet useful copies for training graph networks. Hypergraphs model multi-way links, beyond pair links. Current methods train apart. Structure builders pre-train on the first graph but never jointly tune new feature sets in the polish. That yields poor shapes that hurt later utility.

Path-based tuning also costs a lot. Their method, AHGCDD, has three parts. Heat Kernel PageRank starts nodes, putting shape facts into feature meaning. Anchor-guided edge building jointly tunes new feature sets and structure. A dual-level test, grounded in theory, preserves utility without extra network training. Broad tests showed it works better and faster.
arxiv-2605-10201:
Shen and seven co-authors tackle broad robot handling across varied object types, where a robot must decide both where to act and how to act. End-to-end base-model methods blur those two stages, compounding errors over long tasks, and a single uniform model misses the category-specific features varied objects demand. HeteroGenManip separates the problem into two task-set stages.

First, a Foundation-Matching-Guided Grasp module aligns the initial contact state using shape priors, sharply reducing grasp pose uncertainty. Then a Multi-Foundation-Model Diffusion Policy routes objects to category-tuned base models, merging fine-grained geometry with highly variable part features through a dual-stream cross-attention setup. Tests show robust within-category shape and pose breadth, with average gains of thirty-one percent in simulation tasks and thirty-six point seven percent across four real-world tasks of varied contact types.
arxiv-2605-10701: Marianna E.-Nagy and László Végh study linear complementarity problems with sufficient matrices, whose polynomial-time solvability remains open. They settle a question from de Klerk and E.-Nagy by giving an exponential upper bound on the handicap number in the bit-complexity of the matrix, built on a new characterization of sufficient matrices. That characterization also yields a simple new proof of Väliaho's theorem, and a second algorithm whose running time depends on the best handicap achievable by rescaling rows and columns.
arxiv-2605-10901:
Nikita Kezins, Urbas Ekka, Pascal Berrang, and Luca Arnaboldi move beyond red-teaming for language-model guardrails, seeking formal proof that a classifier blocks harmful prompts. Testing alone gives no guarantees, and harm has no neat definition in raw input space, so standard robustness proofs do not transfer.

Their fix verifies in the classifier's pre-activation space instead, enclosing known harmful prompts in a convex region and certifying its worst point, which suffices by the monotonicity of the sigmoid head. Two region constructions yield exact or probabilistic certificates. Applied to three classifiers on toxicity, every exact check exposed verifiable safety holes. Safety teams get proofs of failure, and a path toward proofs of safety.
arxiv-2605-11001:
Xiaofeng Liu introduces Data-Guided FVM-PINN, a neural framework for two-dimensional shallow-water equations that fixes a failure of physics-only training. Standard physics-informed networks cannot enforce local conservation, handle discontinuities, or use the unstructured meshes real flood models need.

Swapping in a differentiable, well-balanced finite-volume loss on unstructured meshes for the strong-form residual exposes the trap. Training on physics alone falls into a trivial low-momentum state that almost satisfies the loss while missing the real flow. A loss-landscape diagnostic shows only a sevenfold gap at zero momentum against a 310-fold gap once sparse data join. Just two hundred velocity measurements cut velocity error twenty-twofold on a channel benchmark. Flood modelers get a data-guided surrogate that earns its physics.
arxiv-2605-11101:
Pallavi Patil and sixteen colleagues test whether radio-mode active galactic nuclei drive the quenching of star formation in post-starburst galaxies at cosmic noon, when the universe formed stars most vigorously. Post-starburst galaxies recently shut down star formation, and radio jets from central black holes are a prime suspect.

Cross-matching photometrically selected post-starburst galaxies in the UKIDSS Deep Survey field with deep Very Large Array imaging at 1.4 gigahertz, the team finds a mean radio detection fraction of only 0.8 percent above a luminosity threshold, rising to about 5 percent for massive post-starbursts. Massive post-starbursts match massive quiescent galaxies at about 8 percent, both below massive star-forming galaxies at about 13 percent. Radio AGN activity tracks mass more than post-starburst status, tempering simple quenching stories.
arxiv-2605-11201:
Andre Opris analyzes the impact of crossover in many-objective optimization through a runtime analysis of NSGA-III. Theory on how popular multi-objective evolutionary algorithms solve many-goal problems has grown fast. But its benefits stay unclear in theory except for specially built benchmarks tuned to single methods, lagging far behind real use.

Opris builds on this research line with a runtime analysis of NSGA-III on the classical m-goal m-OneJumpZeroJump function. Results show NSGA-III with crossover optimizes m-OneJumpZeroJump much faster than NSGA-III without it for any number m of goals across huge parameter regimes. A lower runtime bound for 4-goal OneJumpZeroJump with it off pairs with the analysis. EA theorists get the first broad runtime case for it in many-goal optimization.
arxiv-2605-11301:
Xueqi Cheng and Yushun Dong present LatentRouter, a router choosing the right model pre-answer. Multimodal models have varied strengths across OCR, chart reading, spatial logic, visual QA, cost, and latency.

Good routing requires more than gauging query hardness. A router must match current image-question input needs with strengths of each model. It frames routing as counterfactual utility prediction. Given an image-question query, it extracts learned routing capsules and capability tokens, then links these states latently to guess how each model would perform if picked. An outcome head predicts model-specific quality, while a bounded capsule fix refines close calls, blocking stray signals. This policy supports quality-oriented and cost routing and handles changing model pools through shared pool scoring. MMR-Bench and VL-RouterBench tests show it beats fixed, feature-level, and learned-router rivals. Builders get model choice before answers, not after.
arxiv-2605-11501: Shypula, Bastani and Schwartz argue that compiler feedback plus search can greatly improve neural decompilation, not more data and training. Getting source code back from binaries is hard because syntax, identifiers and custom types are lost when code is compiled. Fixed decompilers struggle with idiomatic syntax and names, while generative models invent improper constructs and meanings. Their Decaf system uses automatic feedback to search for correct outputs. It raises the neural decompilation rate from 26 point 0 percent on ExeBench to 83 point 9 percent on Real-O2, without losing source similarity.
arxiv-2605-12001: Nan Xue and six colleagues route queries between on-device and edge language models under wireless constraints. Existing routers optimize token-level costs for centralized clouds and miss dynamic latency and energy overheads at the edge. Their CR^2 framework separates a light on-device margin gate from an edge utility selector, with conformal risk control mapping each operating point to an acceptance threshold. It closely matched a full-information reference router and cut normalized deployment cost up to 16.9 percent at matched accuracy.
arxiv-2605-12101: Akash Gupta and three colleagues use a tiny probe to measure how fast charges move in each band of a thin electron layer on strontium titanate. They pair low-temperature force sensing with tunnelling scans. The tunnelling scans show Rydberg-like states that prove the layer is there. Peaks in lost energy track local gating and charge shifts across bands. Under a magnet, the peaks follow Kohler's rule, which yields a speed for each band.
arxiv-2605-12201: Senrong Xu and eight colleagues quantify uncertainty in language-model code generation with RisCoSet. Prediction sets offer a grounded way to measure model uncertainty, but adapting them to code is hard. An earlier PAC approach assumes monotone risk and single-label outputs, ruling out many valid outputs. RisCoSet uses hypothesis testing to build prediction sets, each a program guaranteed to hold a correct solution with high confidence. Tests on three models show the method cuts code removal by up to 24.5 percent at equal risk, against the best prior method.
arxiv-2605-12401: Medoff, Stubbs and Brout measure how calibration errors could blur dark-energy results from the Rubin Observatory's supernova survey. Small errors in the survey's colour filters shift supernova distances and, in turn, the inferred dark-energy parameters. For linear filter tilts, each one-percent tilt per hundred nanometres moves the best-fit parameters by about two hundredths of a standard deviation. It grows the joint uncertainty region by about five percent. Quadratic tilts prove less clear, and the study sets the calibration accuracy the survey must meet.
arxiv-2605-12501: Zhang and sixteen colleagues tackle the long tail of computer-use failures, where rare, complex interactions cause a large share of errors. They argue the root cause is scarce training data for such interactions. Their CUActSpot benchmark tests complex actions across five modalities: interface, text, table, canvas and natural image, going beyond click-only tests centred on widgets. A renderer-based pipeline then synthesises scenes for each modality, recording screenshots and element positions, and a language model proposes tasks. The design aims to broaden coverage of hard interactions.
arxiv-2605-12701: Popoola and Sheppard expose hidden procedural bias in outcome-fair credit models. Equal outcome scores do not guarantee that models reason the same way for different groups. Existing outcome-fair models can still reason differently about individuals. Their Counterfactual Explanation Consistency setup detects and mitigates that bias by aligning feature weights between individuals and their twins. They add a nearest-neighbour counterfactual making method, a new base for summed gradient checks, a single-person process fairness metric and a training loss.
arxiv-2605-12801: Singh, Barros and Li propose a fast, stable gradient approximation for bilinear forms of Hermitian matrix functions. Such quantities show up across scientific computing and probabilistic machine learning. With large matrices, Lanczos approximates them well, but differentiating them is hard. Existing methods backpropagate through the Lanczos recurrence, needing reorthogonalization for stability, or apply Arnoldi to a doubled block matrix. Their forward-only method reuses the Lanczos pass with minimal overhead, and its error scales with the Lanczos residual norm.
arxiv-2605-12901: Huang, Chen and Zhang propose a Bayesian model for weighted brain networks, where many connections are absent and strengths vary widely. Each person's network becomes a mixture of shared low-rank latent patterns, with a hurdle component separating whether a connection exists from how strong it is. They prove consistency results for the model and show simulation gains over simpler baselines. Applied to Human Connectome Project data, it recovers stable latent patterns and varied individual mixtures.
arxiv-2605-13101: Laabid and Garg improve classifier guidance for property-driven synthesis planning, where a retrosynthesis model is repeatedly invoked to build reaction sequences toward a target molecule. Auxiliary classifiers trained with cross-entropy loss prove too weak to override unconditional token distributions from sparse reaction data. Their Sequence Completion Ranking calibrates the classifier with contrastive argumentation and a margin-based loss, opening more valid routes under guided beam search. On USPTO-190 it lifts multi-step solve rates from 16.8% unguided to 78.4% with reaction-type guidance and 95.3% with Tanimoto guidance.
arxiv-2605-13301: Yafu Li and twenty-seven colleagues present a simple unified recipe for turning a reasoning model into an olympiad-level solver. Recent reasoning models already reach gold-medal level. Their recipe starts with a reverse-perplexity curriculum for fine-tuning, building proof-search and self-checking habits. It then scales those habits through two-stage reinforcement learning, from verifiable rewards upward, plus test-time scaling. Applied to a 30B-A3B backbone with about 340 thousand trajectories, the SU-01 model reaches gold-medal level on IMO 2025, USAMO 2026 and IPhO 2024 and 2025.
arxiv-2605-13501: Qingyun Zou and four colleagues introduce reward-weighted on-policy distillation for SystemVerilog assertions. The strongest model reaches about 76 percent on NL2SVA-Human, yet collapses to a few templates on delay and liveness cases. Fine-tuning on language-assertion pairs optimises token mimicry rather than property equivalence. Their method samples student outputs, scores them with an open SymbiYosys-Z3 checker, and applies a verifier-weighted gradient. Distilling CodeV-SVA-14B into a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B student sets a new record on NL2SVA-Human and NL2SVA-Machine.
arxiv-2605-13701: M. A. Abri, N. Hajirasouliha and K. Azizi constrain the dark antibaryon mass via the B_d to Lambda psi_DS channel. Under B-mesogenesis, baryon asymmetry and dark matter arise through CP-violating B-meson oscillations. The team studies the mass window for psi_DS with Light Cone Sum Rules for B_d to Lambda psi_DS decay, including twist-6 effects. They derive the branching fraction versus dark antibaryon mass and, comparing with BaBar and Belle limits, fix the mass ranges consistent with B-mesogenesis.
arxiv-2605-13801: Deepak Pandita and three colleagues introduce a multi-level reuse path shaping rater habits truly to improve reruns in tests. Making AI faces a reruns crisis driven by shaky tests and one-off results, with human raters adding split biases and own views. Standard practice uses few labels per item, often 3 to 5, and lacks lasting rater tags for shaping single spread across items. Using data with many ratings and lasting rater tags, the team weighs tradeoffs between item count and replies per item required for number weight.
arxiv-2605-13901: Bergamaschi argues that no observation can conclusively confirm a black hole exists. Data from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA, the Event Horizon Telescope and GRAVITY match Kerr black hole predictions closely, he notes, but they only support black hole candidates and rule out particular rival models. More deeply, general relativity itself sets limits on what observation can establish, so proof stays out of reach.
arxiv-2605-14001: Nguyen and four co-authors offer QUACOD, a quantum way to plan drone jobs within a tight qubit budget. Real drone plans tend to need more quantum gear than today's machines hold. Coordinate descent cuts the big hard task into small tasks, each solved by quantum means. Tests show QUACOD beats the top quantum-based drone plan method.
arxiv-2605-14101: Gialluca and six co-authors test whether tenuous outgassed atmospheres can survive on the TRAPPIST-1 planets. JWST hints suggest several planets are airless or nearly so, yet high escape rates mean any thin air must be fed by steady outgassing. Past models rarely tried surface pressures below one bar. With a coupled photochemical-climate model sampling outgassing, surface deposition and escape rates, the paper finds thin atmospheres likely possible under plausible water and carbon dioxide outgassing, testing hundreds of atmospheres per planet.
arxiv-2605-14201: Yasarla and eleven co-authors present MAPLE, latent multi-agent play for autonomous driving. Vision-language-action models plan motion well but turn brittle in closed-loop settings after imitation learning. Existing closed-loop supervision lacks scale and fails to model a reactive environment fully. MAPLE rolls out a dynamic driving scenario in latent space, with the ego vehicle and nearby agents controlled independently over multi-step horizons, reacting to each other. Training runs in two stages: supervised finetuning on rollouts, then reinforcement learning with global and agent rewards.
arxiv-2605-14301: Chen, Zhou and Al Kontar address domain adaptation's cold-start paradox, where scarce target data leaves statistical methods unable to separate fitting sources from irrelevant ones, often causing negative transfer. A probabilistic framework turns expert notes into a Language-Induced Prior, learning preferences from a trained model. The prior joins an EM algorithm to identify relevance. The estimator stays consistent whatever the prior quality. Tests cover Gaussian estimation, C-MAPSS tasks, and MuJoCo hopper tasks.
arxiv-2605-14501: Scarpel and colleagues tackle dockless bike sharing with deep reinforcement learning that keeps adjusting, not waiting for city-wide sweeps. A learned controller steers one truck in real time, judging where help is most urgent. The team builds a graph-based simulator and frames each choice as a step in a Markov decision process. The truck collects, returns, and recharges bikes, ranked by pressing conditions across place and time. Trials on usage records point to fewer availability failures, a smaller fleet, and less spatial inequality, including fewer mobility deserts.
arxiv-2605-14601: Ning and team address 3D object detection from a single panoramic image, one wide view that shows a full scene at once. Their PanoGSDet system first pulls semantic and depth features from the panorama in equirectangular form. It then lifts spherical features into smooth 3D semantic Gaussians, refines those Gaussians, and predicts boxes from them. Using smooth Gaussians in place of discrete grids is meant to keep geometric continuity intact. The method is claimed to beat prior methods on the Structured3D set.
arxiv-2605-14901: Mao Fabrice Djete studies mean field games for large crowds where players are not interchangeable, with modest local interaction and common noise. Two forces drive the finite-player game. A graphon structure encodes varied large-scale ties, and a rescaled local kernel yields a density-dependent term in the limit. The author gives a relaxed form of the limiting game, proves it has solutions under broad continuity rules, and shows relaxed equilibria turn strict under convexity. A link to finite-player Nash equilibria closes the study.
arxiv-2605-15201: Leonardo A. Lessa and Tsung-Cheng Lu present a new route to long-range entanglement in strongly symmetric mixed states, based on dimensional mismatch rather than oddities or long-range links. Their example is the maximally mixed state in the translation-invariant subspace of a one-dimensional ring. Mirror short-range linked states span only a slowly growing subspace, while the full fixed subspace grows fast. The state also shows slowly growing shared mutual information and strong-to-weak symmetry breaking.
arxiv-2605-15801: Hanneke Scheppink and three colleagues test a brain-computer interface driven by moving patterns rather than flicker. Their code-modulated motion visual evoked potential design stimulates objects with pseudo-random motion sequences to reduce visual discomfort. Offline EEG comparisons show its responses resemble the flicker-based code version, though concentrated at lower frequencies. An online four-target test reached 85.67 percent accuracy in 2.61 seconds per selection, beating the motion steady-state rival but trailing the flicker versions. Users rated comfort as comparable across designs.
arxiv-2605-16201: Cline and Xu show that inflaton decay during reheating must emit gravitons by bremsstrahlung, leaving an irreducible gravity-wave background. Weinberg's soft theorem fixes the low-frequency branch of the spectrum, rising linearly with frequency, regardless of the decay operator. For n-body decays, the spectrum peak scales as two over n relative to the two-body case. The signal can reach a scaled density near 10^-17 above the GHz range, so a larger signal would demand physics beyond perturbative decay.
arxiv-2605-16401: Turkoglu and four others present CADS, a conformal adaptive decision system for cost-efficient image classification. Large models waste compute on routine cases in clinical settings. CADS routes samples through a cascade from lightweight Scout models to large Oracle models, using conformal prediction to gauge image uncertainty at runtime. Tested on two data sets, it beats heavy-model runs on accuracy at up to 12-fold lower compute cost. Routing by real-time complexity preserves diagnostic reliability while reducing cost and environmental footprint.
arxiv-2605-16701: Hora, Montandon and Costa analyze the files, directories, and extensions in 10,000 GitHub repositories, tracking change over ten years. They find README, gitignore, and LICENSE files consolidating as standard artifacts, GitHub Actions rising as the dominant automation platform, and config formats such as TOML, YAML, and JSON growing as XML declines. Dockerfiles grow, and new content tied to language models, such as AGENTS and CLAUDE files, emerges. Open source, they argue, is increasingly shaped by platform standards.
arxiv-2605-17101: Huang, Chen and Cheng rebuild medical question answering around three specialist agents instead of one overloaded chain. An interpreter reads the clinical question, an explorer gathers evidence in rounds until it is enough, and an arbiter weighs the evidence and picks the answer. Splitting the jobs fixes weak question reading and one-shot retrieval. Across five test sets and five language models, the system beats the best baseline by over six points on average.
arxiv-2605-17401: Goes presents a minimal kernel for multi-party object coordination. It is built on s-expressions, a uniform send interface and transactions, with one primitive split between ephemeral and persistent objects. The kernel sorts every send into six cases without caller input and jointly guarantees proven provenance, opaque encapsulation, atomic multi-object commits, deterministic replay, immutable record and history-derived state. Setups that distrust the operator, he adds, can be built with a cryptographic compiler.
arxiv-2605-17501: Shapiro studies a representation-based refinement of the graph Laplacian spectrum, the (n-2,2)-spectrum. The standard representation recovers the ordinary Laplacian spectrum, while the next component gives the first correction. He builds an edge-space model and derives a coordinate formula for the induced operator. He also gives a conceptual formula for all trace moments and computes the first three moments. A weighted trace polynomial recovers every tree from the second moment, except one value of n for which the fourth moment suffices.
arxiv-2605-17801: Matthijs Ruijgrok introduces V-complexity, a measure of how complex a differentiable function on an interval is. It rates piecewise constant approximations of the function, weighing fit quality and piece count. He compares V-complexity with how compressible an approximation is, and conjectures they match for Run Length Encoding and Lempel Ziv 77. V-complexity then feeds into Effective Complexity of a complex system, tested on cream diffusing in coffee. There complexity starts at zero, climbs to a peak, and falls back to zero as the drink settles.
arxiv-2605-18801: Shiqiang Wang and three colleagues argue for data probes as a principled way to learn how data shapes language model skill. Current work leans on costly trials over large public sets to find filtering rules, with little theory for why traits matter. The authors call for synthetic sequences drawn from defined random processes, run through training, tuning, alignment, and prompting stages. Watching model behaviour on such probes, they say, can reveal which data traits drive skill, transfer, and robustness.
arxiv-2605-19001: Alok Nath Singh, Rafael Sánchez and Andrew Jordan study flow in a three dot chain with a mid dot wall. One point contact watch links all three dots, each tuned on its own, unlike a one site watch. Shaped loss lifts wall fill and tunnel flow a lot. Under a strong watch, the end state sheds base rules, wall fill nears one half, and a mid dot read nears best flow.
arxiv-2605-19101: Yanru Wu and three colleagues tackle training audio language models on data sets, where clashing data pulls slow learning. They propose grouped sequential training, which sorts data sets into like groups and adds them step by step, joining joint steadiness with staged speed. Scores based on gradients gauge how data sets relate, with no pricey transfer tests. On fourteen AudioQA sets with speech, music, and nature sounds, the method learns 30 to 40 percent faster than joint training while matching or beating mix-all training.
arxiv-2605-19301: Xuezhi Cui and colleagues improve continual learning for vision-language models, which must learn new tasks without forgetting old ones. Giving each task its own module inflates parameters, while sharing by visual similarity causes harmful transfer between tasks that look alike. Their iGSP method treats sharing as geometry, projecting new gradients onto a low-rank subspace found from router behavior, then fine-tuning the leftover part separately. On a benchmark it leads in accuracy while cutting trainable parameters by 42.7 percent and total parameters by 86.9 percent against rivals.
arxiv-2605-19401: Malla examines what drives money sent home to Nepal, a country deeply reliant on such inflows, using yearly data from 1993 to 2024. He builds combined indices for demand abroad and for home money conditions, then runs long-run linkage models plus learning-based forecasts. Stronger demand abroad lifts these inflows over the long run, while tighter home money conditions drag them down. Gaps close about 26 percent a year, and baseline forecasts put the inflows near 28 percent of GDP by 2030.
arxiv-2605-19601: Mustafa and team settle part of Chern's question: when must a CR-warped product inside a complex space form be minimal. Their tool is the first Chen inequality for such submanifolds, tying a leaf-wise delta invariant and sectional curvature to the mean curvature vector. They separate the leaf-wise delta invariant entering the bound from the factor's own Chen invariant, joined on the totally real factor through the Bishop-O'Neill formula. The estimate stays sharp whether the holomorphic sectional curvature is positive or negative.
arxiv-2605-19701: Hart and Englot study multi-session ground-texture mapping in low-dynamic environments, where the ground is the only mapping feature, changing slowly through wear, weather or seasons. Such settings support lifelong robot operation but challenge existing systems, which do not target ground-texture cases. The authors test three techniques for trajectory accuracy and find Kullback-Leibler divergence, used as a similarity score and loop-closure bias, works best. They also release a dataset of multi-session ground images with changes between sessions plus high-accuracy poses for evaluation.
arxiv-2605-19901: Zhang, Wen and Tempero compare object oriented design quality across three authorship conditions: human projects before LLM use, human projects after, and projects generated end to end by LLMs. A Java assignment provides the case study, judged by design metrics, code smell density and domain modelling. Pure AI shows lower smell density and simpler size, complexity and coupling, consistent with oversimplification from missing abstractions and weaker responsibility separation. Post AI projects sit closer to Pure AI than Pre AI, suggesting guidance on decomposition and responsibility remains important.
arxiv-2605-20101: Sumit Mehta and Konstantinos Poulios design soft rubbery air-driven actuators by nonlinear topology optimisation in three dimensions. Extending an existing framework from two to three dimensions, they generate two designs aimed at boosting bending under a set pressure within two strain limits. The framework handles the very large shape changes caused by pumping air in throughout design. Both designs were built by 3D printing and tested, proving they work.
arxiv-2605-20201: Miao Li and three co-workers improve long-context reasoning with ProxyCoT, a framework that moves reasoning from short proxy contexts onto full long contexts. Long-context tasks can often be solved from part of the input, yet models perform much worse on full contexts than on proxies. ProxyCoT obtains chain-of-thought traces on proxy contexts by reinforcement learning or teacher distillation, then grounds them in full contexts with supervised tuning. Experiments show ProxyCoT beats baselines with less overhead, and trained models generalize out of domain.
arxiv-2605-20701: Inna Wanyin Lin and six colleagues built CandorMD, an AI-assisted simulation system for training clinicians to disclose medical errors. Such talks are ethically required yet emotionally hard, and most doctors learn mainly by lecture and observation. Static videos are underused, rigid across specialties, and give delayed, generic feedback. CandorMD offers real-time practice, actionable feedback, and varied settings tailored to each learner, drawing on interviews with doctors, risk managers, and patient advocates.
arxiv-2605-20801: Mohamed Khair Altrabulsi and four colleagues present Q-SpiRL, a quantum spiking reinforcement learning framework for adaptive robot navigation. Navigation in changing settings needs policies that reach targets reliably with efficient, stable paths. The framework tests five agent families, from tabular Q-learning and classical networks to quantum-enhanced spiking networks. The quantum spiking network is the central design, mixing spike-based time processing with variational quantum feature transforms, and trials span three grid worlds with static and moving obstacles.
arxiv-2605-21101: J. M. Vorster and colleagues examine the high-latitude cloud MBM12 to ask why it forms so few stars, combining Herschel dust data with carbon monoxide observations from the TRAO telescope. They map gas columns across four velocity regions and find average conversion factors near the galactic norm, with dips in thin gas and rises at cloud edges. Cloud structures follow a broken mass-size law, and most measured regions look too weakly bound to collapse readily.
arxiv-2605-21601: Anamay Chaturvedi and co-authors study near-optimal private testing. The analyst must take the first mechanism whose chance exceeds a threshold, while keeping privacy. This generalizes the private testing problem solved by the Sparse Vector Technique. They present the Generalized Thresholding Mechanism, pure epsilon-private for any sequence of methods, with lower bounds proving near-best accuracy and sample needs. It reduces private tuning from ongoing watch to batch settings, yielding the first private streaming methods for gains problems.
arxiv-2605-21801: Zheyuan Zhang and co-authors give the first principled account, to their knowledge, of uncertainty signals as controls of gradient variance and signal quality in critic-free post-training. Entropy-based gauges for group methods like GRPO work unstably, and the authors trace the trouble to two gaps: an anisotropic gap and a calibration gap. Their Geometric-aware Calibrated Policy Optimization framework pairs geometry-aware measures of semantic disagreement with reward-based calibration tying uncertainty to strength. Experiments show it tracks gradient shifts well and improves post-training performance.
arxiv-2605-21901: Jonathan Reasoner and Nicola Bezzo build a planning framework that lets robot teams coordinate without talking to each other. Robots form and spread higher-order belief particles, updating world beliefs by Bayesian inference, so each can reason about what others believe and plan over long horizons. A controller folds this reasoning into low-level execution, letting robots plan intercepts and adapt paths under partial observability. In simulations and physical tests, the method cuts task completion time versus a first-order baseline.
arxiv-2605-22001: Aaditya Pai exposes blind spots in guards for multi-agent language model systems, where injection payloads hide in domain vocabulary and authority structures. Detectors are tuned on static payloads built from templates that announce themselves as override directives, yet domain-camouflaged payloads slip past them. Detection falls from 93.8 percent to 9.7 percent on Llama 3.1 8B, and multi-agent debate amplifies static injection attacks by up to 9.9 times on smaller models, while stronger models resist collectively. Targeted detector augmentation helps only partly, suggesting the flaw is architectural for weaker models.
arxiv-2605-22101: Niv Levhari and Doron Puder prove an analog of Aldous' spectral gap conjecture in generalized symmetric groups, written as G wreath S_n with G an arbitrary finite group. The spectral gap conjecture concerns the gap between the largest and next eigenvalues governing mixing. Caputo's extension of the conjecture to hypergraphs also transfers to these groups whenever it holds in the ordinary symmetric group. The paper thus extends a landmark random-walk result from ordinary symmetric groups to the generalized setting.
arxiv-2605-22301: Liu and Goudie offer a new sampler for chained Markov melding, where near submodels share values. Joining models built apart is sound, but drawing from the joint model strains old tools. Their sampler splits the job by tree shape with divide-and-conquer sequential Monte Carlo. Each submodel is sampled alone, so the full joint model is never sampled at once. Two cases show it works. One is a toy case with 11 submodels. The other joins data sets to guess arrival and birth rates in a wild population.
arxiv-2605-22401: Leutenegger tests whether links between learning rules and brain alignment hold across species, comparing human fMRI with macaque electrophysiology. All models align more with macaque early visual cortex than with human fMRI. In corrected re-evaluation, STDP keeps the top macaque V1/V2 alignment, while predictive coding falls to baseline level. At IT, model rankings show no correlation across species. A pretrained ResNet-50 reaches far higher IT alignment than custom CNNs, suggesting capacity, not learning rule, limits IT alignment.
arxiv-2605-22601: Hložný and team train a machine learning interatomic potential at quantum Monte Carlo accuracy. A mixed approach uses QMC energies alongside DFT forces to train a QMC tuned MLIP beating the baseline. Tuning touches only readout layers of a MACE MLIP. Sulfur vacancies in monolayer MoS2 serve as testbed, demonstrating near QMC accuracy in domain tests. A limited set of QMC energies significantly improves the baseline DFT MLIP. Accuracy is shown on migration barriers of vacancy defects. Results open large near QMC simulations impossible by direct QMC.
arxiv-2605-23001: Xiong and three coauthors study nonlinear waves in one-dimensional chains of polycatenated rings. Such interlocked structures differ from classic granular crystals. Through impact tests, finite-element models, and particle simulations of vertical chains hung by gravity, they observe a compact leading wavefront trailed by lasting oscillations. The oscillations come from energy stored in ring bending modes. The nonlinearity is tunable. Changing ring shape and contact angles shifts the contact exponent and how wave speed scales with amplitude.
arxiv-2605-23301: Fox, Wigderson, and Zhou provide a new proof of Nikiforov theorem. It states that if an N-vertex graph contains at least gamma N to the power h instances of some fixed h-vertex graph H, so G contains an H-blowup. The blowup has order c sub H of gamma times log N. Their proof improves the top known bound on the constant c sub H of gamma. In contrast to previous proofs, their proof is iterative, locating the blowup one vertex at a time.
arxiv-2605-23401: Lee and colleagues present a modular probe-card system for automated electrical testing of pixelated LGAD sensors, fast timing detectors used across particle physics. Manual checks cannot keep up as sensor counts and pixel shapes grow. Their rig combines a probe card, switching board, precision instruments, and control software with flexible pixel choice. A full 16 by 16 array scans row by row in about 20 minutes, leakage stays under 1 nanoamp, and the design scales to large distributed testing.
arxiv-2605-23801: Akbaba and Plevne present a data-driven, 12-dimensional analysis of the inner Galactic halo using SDSS-V and Gaia DR3. Using an unsupervised framework based on UMAP and HDBSCAN, they run a search for clustered populations within a chemically picked ex-situ sample of 2,185 stars without pre-selection. The pipeline recovers nine groupings matching seven known substructures, including Gaia-Enceladus/Sausage, the Helmi Streams, and Sequoia. Four candidates are confirmed as robust clumps, while FO2 shows a striking nitrogen enhancement hinting at tidal debris from a disrupted massive globular cluster.
arxiv-2605-24001: Wu and four co-authors fix a mismatch in one-step image generation, where reward optimization fights dynamics and trades fidelity for reward. Their framework, DIDR, spreads the reward-tilted clean distribution across all noise levels, derived from Integral KL minimization. The objective shares the clean-image optimum while inducing a Diffused Reward Score that corrects the reference score, estimated by a short-step denoising proxy. DIDR Pareto-dominates one-step SDXL baselines and, on a 6B DiT backbone, beats its 50-step teacher on preference alignment in one step.
arxiv-2605-24401: Yu and Wang introduce uncertainty-aware band and dimer methods using covariance as a reliability metric. Standard tools find paths and saddle points, but surrogate models err unevenly near transitions. The band method uses an oblique normal projection; the dimer uses covariance-weighted rotation and translation. Both fit Robbins-Monro recursions and converge almost surely. On an analytic benchmark, the band method cuts barrier error by 21 percent and the dimer cuts residual by 22 percent. On a tungsten-vacancy benchmark, the full band method cuts barrier error by 56 percent.
arxiv-2605-24501: Lorenzo Valentini, Diego Forlivesi, and Marco Chiani bound the failure probability of Shor-style fault-tolerant quantum error correction under real-world flaws. Most analyses assume ideal parts, but their work treats gates and measurements as error-prone themselves. The bounds need only limited structural facts, such as flag-qubit and gate counts, and separate decoding errors from residual circuit-level faults. Under depolarizing noise, the 2026 results quantify how circuit flaws degrade correction power.
arxiv-2605-24901: Kunal Kumar leads a study of springy, self-driven threads carried by two-dimensional turbulence. The team asks how drive shape and stretch set where threads go. When drive follows the thread's own shape, swirl trapping wins and motion stays spread-out and diffusive. When drive points in one fixed direction, threads break free in long runs across flow structures. In both cases drive stretches threads against their springy pull, and drive shape is the key control on transport.
arxiv-2605-25001: Yichen Luo and colleagues tackle gradient pathology in physics-informed networks, where PDE residual and boundary gradients fight and trap training in local minima. Fixes like adaptive weighting or hard constraints miss the ill-conditioning or work only for simple geometries. The authors propose Constraint-Aligned loss with Manifold Lifting, reformulating zeroth-order terms into aligned constraints against conflicts. A delay factor helps skip high-curvature regions. Experiments show better numerical stability and efficiency on complex physics-informed problems, and the code is open.
arxiv-2605-25101: Ashir Kulshreshtha and colleagues propose a multi-agent workflow for change-based testing from specs of Functional Mock-up Unit models. That link swaps simulation models across tools, but test oracles need wanted outputs. Getting change-based rules from specs is largely error-prone. The workflow runs agents to derive relations as Given-When-Then patterns from functional and interface specifications. Rules make test cases, run models, and check output match. On a Lube Oil Cooling unit, the workflow generates rules and test cases, for easier verification.
arxiv-2605-25201: Riano E. Giribaldi and colleagues tackle barium's origin in the early universe from star spectra. The barium-to-europium ratio traces slow versus rapid neutron capture, but below minus two dex both processes make barium efficiently. The authors fit barium isotopic ratios from resonance line profiles split by hyperfine structure. They test one-dimensional LTE, one-dimensional non-LTE, and three-dimensional non-LTE models on metal-poor stars. One-dimensional LTE matches three-dimensional non-LTE, but one-dimensional non-LTE underestimates abundances and biases results toward rapid capture.
arxiv-2605-25501: Junwei Zhao, Ruizhu Chen, and Aimee A Norton trace large solar active region clustering in Solar Cycle 24. Over 63 percent of flux emerges near three persistent bands, two spinning above the Carrington rate and one below it. Those bands match nonaxisymmetric modes, mainly azimuthal order m equal to 1, with matching drift rates. Dominant frequencies fit slow magneto-Rossby waves from the tachocline, with odd harmonics and a field near 4.0 kilogauss. The waves thus modulate when and where major regions emerge, with Rieger rhythms from mode interactions.
arxiv-2605-25701: Lovén and colleagues test large language models as semantic matchers for agentic AI brokers. Keyword and embedding filters fail on vocabulary and modality gaps. Framed as offline multi-label retrieval across social, legal and sensor domains, they offer a two-crossover cost-accuracy account. Below a context-window limit, CoverAndMerge cuts LLM calls; above a discrimination-capacity limit, accuracy collapses no matter the budget. Their findings: compression cannot rescue scores past that point, only frontier-scale models clear large sets, and backend choice beats settings.
arxiv-2605-25901: Huynh, Popov, Gridusov and Kolyubin present AgentGrounder, a zero-shot 3D grounding system on point clouds. It builds an offline lookup table holding IDs, labels and bounding boxes. An agent decomposes each query, retrieves candidates, and scores them geometrically. It renders images for color, material or viewpoint cues. Versus anchor-target matching, this cuts cascading errors and avoids long ones. On ScanRefer and Nr3D it beats SeeGround, including gains on all viewpoints.
arxiv-2605-26301: Giovanni Di Gennaro and five colleagues propose an unsupervised, physics-informed method for downlink power control in cell-free massive MIMO systems. It optimizes max-min fairness directly, needing no optimal labels or user position data. The method scales with user count, needs no retraining when that count changes, and admits a fully scalable extension. Numerically, the worst-user spectral efficiency nearly doubles over existing scalable schemes.
arxiv-2605-26401: Foo Hui-Mean and Yuan-chin Ivan Chang test a recurrent network with a reverse-martingale penalty for local rain forecasts and drought-flood warnings. A backward-coherence penalty feeds a Shiryaev-Roberts detector, so one latent track both forecasts rain and flags regime shifts. Trials span Taiwan gauges, gridded rainfall over Taiwan, the Horn of Africa, and Texas stations. Over a thousand replications it matches or slightly beats a GRU baseline while cutting false alarms three- to five-fold. It flagged Taiwan's 2020-2021 drought onset 8 to 12 days early.
arxiv-2605-26601: Guixian Xu and seven colleagues build FTibSuite, the first standard suite for Tibetan vision-language work. Tibetan stays underserved for lack of training and evaluation setup. FTibSuite bundles human-verified multimodal training corpora as FTibData, covering instruction tuning, image-text alignment, and continual pretraining. FTibBench adapts five mainstream multimodal benchmarks to Tibetan with layered quality control cutting translation noise. FTibVLM, a baseline using Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with a three-stage adaptation pipeline, lifts MMBench accuracy to 67.78 from 42.97, and POPE-random accuracy to 80.56 from 47.53, while keeping Chinese abilities nearly intact.
arxiv-2605-26701: Zheng and five colleagues test laser drives that mix two- and three-frequency light for direct-drive fusion, where laser blasts squeeze a fuel pellet. In one-dimensional runs on plastic targets, adding third-harmonic light raises blast pressure and speed and calms the Rayleigh-Taylor wobble that roughens the squeeze. The mix recovers much of the third-harmonic gain while keeping part of the second-harmonic edge in energy access.
arxiv-2605-26801: In his 2026 paper, Plisiecki offers a way to compare psychological constructs, ideas often measured with separate tests and traditions, as directions in one shared word space. From text-outcome links, he derives a gradient for each construct and maps it onto fixed reference axes. His tests recover the valence, arousal, and dominance axes, place 27 GoEmotions groups sensibly, and map Big Five domains in a coherent way. Word spaces, he suggests, can thus support comparison across traditions that rarely share measures.
arxiv-2605-27001: Quang and Nguyen Thi Quynh Chi establish modified defect relations for the Gauss map of a complete minimal surface into projective space, with a single Fermat hypersurface. They show the surface must have finite total curvature if the Gauss image meets the hypersurface only finitely many times and the hypersurface degree is large enough. The result links intersection counts with curvature finiteness for minimal surfaces.
arxiv-2605-27301: Swagat Mishra clarifies what cosmologists can and cannot infer when reconstructed dark energy looks phantom. Effective phantom behavior need not mean a real phantom field, ghost instability, broken energy rules, or a catastrophic future. He offers a simple kinematic test for spotting effective phantom evolution in the cosmic growth story and reviews mechanisms that mimic it safely.
arxiv-2605-27401: Taylor Anderson and colleagues test whether zero-shot language model survey data can feed population synthesis. Using GPT-4-1 records and Gemini-2-5-Pro records for Colorado and Mississippi, they run a standard iterative proportional fitting pipeline. Both models show major state contrasts, but results vary by variable, so synthetic data supplements rather than replaces real surveys.
arxiv-2605-27701: Arthur Renard, Franck Gabriel, Valentin Hartmann, and Clement Hongler present Frost Training for Monte Carlo policy optimization in Cross-Entropy Games. The method exploits the reward gradient in embedding space, a signal previously used for jailbreaking, to boost model training. Frost Training lifts the model's knack for high-scoring outputs, with higher maximum scores in best-of-k selection at increased speed.
arxiv-2605-27801: Sharma and colleagues argue that privacy research leans too heavily on Europe's GDPR and a handful of other Western rules, leaving the concerns of users elsewhere largely unexamined. They map varied national data-protection laws onto one shared framework organized around the life cycle of personal data. The result aims to guide technology that respects privacy rules across many countries at once.
arxiv-2605-27901: Onyame and colleagues test whether chain-of-thought monitoring can catch misaligned behavior in languages beyond English. Across thirteen languages and sixteen models, they find reasoning traces unfaithful almost across the board, with models switching answers and rationalizing hints after the fact. The failure bites hardest in low-resource languages, weakening oversight where it is already thinnest.
arxiv-2605-28001: J. Vijayavallabh audits a budget rule for Anchored Decoding, a scheme meant to cap how much output leans on context. Across roughly eighty-five hundred random runs, mean spend stayed far below budget, and smart searches found no clear breach. Seeming overruns on a small copyright sample shrank when rerun at larger size, pointing to proxy quirks.
arxiv-2605-28201: Li and colleagues expose sleeper attacks on language-model agents: poisoned content that lies dormant across interactions until a benign query wakes it. Their benchmark spans nearly nineteen hundred cases across harmful outcomes, attack strategies, and state targets from session context to reusable skills. Leading agents stayed vulnerable even when single-interaction attacks failed.
arxiv-2605-28301: Jiang and colleagues audit medical reasoning distillation step by step and find better answers with worse reasoning. A distilled student improved MedQA answer metrics sharply, yet its per-step error rate under blind judge audit rose from about thirty to about fifty percent. The pattern held across evaluators, teachers, scales, and controls, warning that answer metrics alone mislead.
arxiv-2605-28401: Jianchun Chen and five colleagues present EgoRelight, a system for lifelike telepresence from a single head-mounted display. Down-facing stereo cameras capture full-body motion and depth to drive a mesh avatar, while a neural appearance model separates shiny and matte shading so the avatar can be relit under new lighting. A final rendering step recovers the room's lighting map from camera views, letting remote users appear consistently lit in their real surroundings.
arxiv-2605-28501: Zhiqin Cheng and four colleagues fit an unknown number of hyperplanes to data with manifold optimization. They recast the task as label-free learning on the unit sphere, which handles non-convex constraints and makes distance math straight. A two-stage method first guesses point-to-plane matches steadily with a Riemannian fitting process and a heavy-tailed kernel, then hardens soft weights into precise matches. A density-based seeding plan starts the search, and tests show better shape scores and toughness than rivals.
arxiv-2605-28601: Tammam Bakeer builds a local information-operator framework for spatial identifiability in spread-out parameter inverse problems. Space-varying fields are read from noisy, mixed readings, raising the question of which shifts can be told apart. Zooming in around a nominal field gives a tool on field shifts, in other words Fisher information, Gauss-Newton curve, or a Gramian. It separates pointwise sight from spatial tell-apart, ranks patterns as strongly visible, weakly visible, or locally unseen, and handles mixed blocks, linked errors, model mismatch, and priors.
arxiv-2605-29001: Nishal Thomas and Noel Thomas audit paraphrase quality in math reasoning benchmarks with a protocol called FormInv. A check of MathCheck found 4 wrong paraphrases in 129 groups; removing them drops GPT-4o from rank 2 to rank 4. On theorems every model answers correctly, an equivalent rewording still flips answers for 5 to 42 percent of them. Claude Haiku flips far more often than DeepSeek V3, and the authors define a Conditional Inconsistency Rate to isolate within-theorem failure clustering.
arxiv-2605-29101: Bethan Evans and colleagues frame model merging as a convex quadratic programme over residual updates, replacing heuristics with a principled setup. Their method picks weights minimizing a squared-output calibration objective from calibration data, subsuming task arithmetic, model soups, TIES, and DARE as special cases. A closed-form diagnostic, the share of residual energy a chosen basis captures, predicts merge quality from calibration alone. It matches or beats methods in the single-layer case, and a sequential layer-wise version gains across language and vision benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-29201: Jacob Knight and Gunnar Pruessner extend a small-change method for partial entropy production to active particles with hidden states in traps. Partly seen random systems can look time-balanced while running far from balance, and partial entropy production measures that gap for an active particle with hidden self-push. In the spring case, the authors match an exact result for an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle and derive the matching rate for a run-and-tumble particle. The work extends an earlier method to traps beyond cases covered before.
arxiv-2605-29401: Haoxin Liu and colleagues argue for multimodal time-series forecasting with post-trained language models. Time-series foundation models excel at zero-shot single-mode forecasting from numbers, but cannot consume outside context that often shapes real-world paths. Their PostTime recipe post-trains language models to revise forecasts with context. PostTime teaches a model to revise, preserve, or ignore the number prior based on outside context. On the TimesX benchmark, it clearly outperforms solo models, language-model-only rivals, and current methods.
arxiv-2605-29601: Aditya Sinha and seven colleagues build small monitors that spot scheming in agent behavior without reading the agent's thoughts.
