Existing monitors need chain-of-thought access, internal signals, or costly frontier models. Their method draws reasons from a frontier teacher, then a judge filters them, and the best are distilled into open-weight monitors. Trained on five datasets and tested on six new benchmarks, a Qwen3.5-27B monitor beats low-cost frontier monitors at lower cost. Stronger frontier monitors score higher but cost roughly sixteen to thirty-four times more.
arxiv-2605-29701: Yuepeng Guan, Mamiya Kawaguchi, Shinya Matsuzaki, and Akio Tomiya study heat behaviour in the symmetry-improved Cornwall-Jackiw-Tomboulis formalism for low-energy QCD. Here, Ward-Takahashi identities return through auxiliary sources fixed by the equilibrium state. That repair sharpens symmetry in the truncated two-particle-irreducible theory yet muddies pressure's meaning. The team sets out pressure recipes, including vacuum-subtracted, source-matched, and pulled-back forms, tested in a three-flavour sigma model. Structure stays stable across recipes, with gaps near the crossover and first-order zone.
arxiv-2605-30101: Isaac M Hair and Amit Sahai establish list recovery for random low-rate linear codes over large prime fields. For fixed dimension, error share and accuracy target, a random code is list recoverable for all list sizes up to an exponentially growing bound. The proof blends a graph certificate, a nonvanishing determinant test and the Schwartz-Zippel lemma. A matching lower bound shows codes of dimension at least two cannot do better for large feasible lists. The result is thus nearly optimal.
arxiv-2605-30201: Mohamed Sana and four co-authors propose Hysteretic Policy Optimization, a small change to GRPO-style learning for sparse verifiable rewards. Early updates hold more negative responses than positive ones, and length normalization ties update size to output length. HPO down-weights negative updates and swaps length normalization for mean-length normalization. Adaptive HPO sets the hysteretic weight from batch advantage-sign statistics, removing fixed-weight tuning. On TeleLogs and Countdown, Adaptive HPO beats GRPO on reward per update, most in early sparse regimes, by balancing advantages.
arxiv-2605-30301: Siheon Park and five co-authors improve sample bounds for sample Lindbladian work with the Wave Matrix Lindbladization. For a jump operator, they derive a bound cutting size dependence from squared to linear. Extra cost disappears when the operator norm squared shrinks as size grows. This likely holds for random Lindblad cases, yielding typical cost linear in time squared over error. In the worst case, the method needs samples linear in size, shown by a rank-one Lindblad operator example. Results reveal a split between typical and hostile sample costs.
arxiv-2605-30501: Zhihao Wu and four co-authors reveal a basic weakness in marking AI-made text: when users access multiple models, marks easily fail. In theory, mixing output spreads regains the unmarked spread. They present WASH, a method solving word-list mismatch and token-split gaps. Tests across six marking schemes and three LLMs show mixing across 3 models cuts spot z-scores from 5 to 300 to below 2, below the spot threshold of 4. It reduces true hit rate at 5 percent false positive rate to below 50 percent.
arxiv-2605-30601: Kozyra and Reinert present TASER, a training-time plan that steadies deep networks against distribution shift using data shape. TASER couples model derivatives to density scores by penalizing the Langevin Stein operator, with a weighted Sobolev reading and bounds under stronger and stronger assumptions. A lighter first-order variant, TASERLight, needs neither direct tangent-space math nor an inner search. Tests on spectroscopy, body motion, ECG, and image benchmarks show gains under shift and added benefits beside plain regularization.
arxiv-2605-30701: Zheng and colleagues devise a sensitive broadband mid-infrared upconversion spectrometer for fast spectroscopy. Older devices suffer from narrow-bandgap detectors and dim broadband sources. Their device pairs a supercontinuum source spanning 1.5 to 4.2 microns, built on a silicon nitride waveguide, with high-efficiency low-noise upconversion from coincidence pulsed pumping. Silicon detectors then enable single-photon spectral work at a fifth of a photon per nanometer per pulse. Spectral acquisition beyond 200 kilohertz runs about ten times faster than FTIR rates, for infrared transient work.
arxiv-2605-30901: Tan and colleagues make counterfactual explanations more reliable on tabular data, where low-density regions make classifiers unstable. Their DensityFlow builds them by following continuous dynamics guided by a density score, steering away from uncertain, low-density areas toward the data manifold. The density score is learned by noise contrastive estimation with a multi-way discriminator. For black-box models, a local proxy step aligns a light surrogate with the target along the path, cutting query costs. Tests show better results across models at lower query cost than ensemble baselines.
arxiv-2605-31401: Masala and colleagues build a vision-language model for Romania. Vision-text models shine on English tests but fade on low-resource languages. The team renders English training and test corpora in Romanian, using machine translation for textual notes. Training and testing models isolates the roles of vision bases, wide and Romania-tuned language bases, and OCR-style image-text data. A new HoraVQA test set from daily scenes in Romania completes the pipeline. Romania-tuned models beat same-sized and larger-category rivals.
arxiv-2605-31501: Dsouza and colleagues study Kohn-Luttinger superconductivity of Weyl Fermi arcs in PtBi2. This is a noncentrosymmetric Weyl semimetal where tests point to unusual superconductivity on topological surface states. Focusing on the arcs, they work out the pairing interaction from electron repulsion. Over much of the phase diagram, the leading instability has i-wave symmetry, with a node at each arc's centre. The i-wave state proves robust when model settings change.
arxiv-2605-31601: Warman, Gai, and Schafer-Nameki present twin phases for a symmetry: inequivalent phases whose order parameters belong to the same shared charge under it. Stable, direct shifts between such twin phases never break symmetry on their own, even after partly gauging it. For illustration, they use an anomalous finite group symmetry in two spacetime dimensions, which yields an intrinsically beyond-Landau transition and a deconfined quantum critical point.
arxiv-2606-00001:
Lican Huang proposes treating East Asian calligraphy as performance with a written score, much like music, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Image-based representations freeze a character as a static picture and lose the timing, pressure, and movement that define the craft. The Calligraphy Writing Score Representation instead encodes each brush stroke as an ordered, executable action. Characters sit within a structured grid, and strokes carry details such as type, execution order, and brush pressure.

The framework, Shu Dao, draws on Japanese Shodo and tea ceremony practice, where ritual matters. It organizes the score at three levels: strokes, character structure, and whole-composition layout, including rhythmic dynamics. The contributions are the notation system itself, the score-mediated view of calligraphy as scored performance, and a computational foundation for studying and generating such works. The author offers it as support for human-AI co-creation in computational art and digital humanities research.
arxiv-2606-00101:
Huidong Feng and co-authors build a benchmark of AI-generated videos good enough to fool existing detectors, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Detection datasets rely on open-source generators far weaker than commercial systems, and the few pro samples often carry watermarks that give them away. Their dataset, CoCoVideo-26K, covers thirteen mainstream pro systems and pairs fake videos with matched real ones. That pairing lets analysts isolate what differs between real footage and high-fidelity synthesis.

Their detector, CoCoDetect, pairs a spatio-temporal video network with contrastive learning, which teaches representations by comparing matched and mismatched pairs. A confidence gate sends uncertain cases to a multimodal language model that reasons about physical plausibility and scene fit. Experiments on the dataset and benchmarks reached state-of-the-art results in their comparisons. The authors release code and data, aiming to reset what forged video hunting must handle at pro grade.
arxiv-2606-00301:
Ye and co-authors split false-speech spotting by the kind of flaw at work. Big chat models err in more than one way. One doubt score for all flaws can miss that mix. Their tool, FLaG, treats spotting as a blend of proof from groups.

Each case is soft-sorted into more than one hidden group. Each group holds its own trust marks from traits and word cues. A log-sum blend then joins group marks in a set, sound way. The tool sits as a light head on a frozen model. It adds scant cost and needs no change to the base model. Math ties the blend to best proof use under mixed flaws. Tests span many sets and base models with top marks.
arxiv-2606-00501:
Dey and Kasbekar frame a joint plan for rent of quantum bits and spread of a circuit. An agent may hold no quantum rig of their own. They can rent bits from linked rigs on a quantum net. Four linked picks then shape the whole task at hand.

Picks span bits per rig, bit homes per time slot, gate sites, and hop times. Their full math form is set as a whole-count line plan. The task is proved NP-complete in full. Some slim cases yield to fast exact tools, they show. A greedy hunt with local polish takes the big cases on. It lands near the best known marks at far less time cost. In two slim cases, it hits the best mark in full.
arxiv-2606-00601:
Wu and Zolnikov turn step-bound chains in code into group scans a chip can run in ranks. State-space tools like Mamba rest on such chains for fast line work. Those chains force a strict one-by-one order, though. That order caps how much a chip can do at once.

Their frame, ScanWeaver, recasts such chains in a scan form that groups well. It then lowers that form end to end to GPU code. MLIR steps carry the chain from high form to Blelloch scan runs. The test case is the pick-scan at Mamba's heart. Real GPU runs are built and timed from the made code. Marks are set next to PyTorch and CUDA runs. A fused Mamba core gives the work its systems frame.
arxiv-2606-01401:
Shupletsova and Stegailov study the flat interface between two forms of ice. Low-density amorphous ice turns into a high-density form under pressure. The mechanism of this shift has stayed unclear for years. States between the two forms sit at the heart of the puzzle. Their work gives the first full account of the flat interface. Its thickness at equilibrium links to medium-density amorphous ice.

The layer keeps the same thickness under compression. Its position shifts into the low-density region and back. On release, the shift lags, like a memory effect. A neural network sorts the ice forms with high precision. It uses local atomic position data to tell them apart. MDA-like states sit at the interface, not as a bulk phase.
arxiv-2606-01501:
Franz and Mulet revisit a classic problem: the longest increasing subsequence. They study it at a set temperature, as in statistical mechanics. Two energy scales stand out in their results. A Schottky-like crossover marks the first scale. A condensation transition marks the second, at lower temperature. Below it, the count of longest configurations grows slower than exponential. Exact algorithms solve the ground state in polynomial time, they note.

Yet local Monte Carlo moves get trapped after fast quenches. The stuck states show glassy signs at low temperature. Two-step relaxation, stuck overlaps, and aging all appear. Slow logarithmic annealing tracks the true balance down to the ground state. Sparse counts, not energy barriers, make local search fail here.
arxiv-2606-01601:
Xiang, Li, and Dai explain detection transformers from inside the model. Object detection is hard to explain, since many instances appear at once. Post-hoc tools probe a trained detector with gradients or perturbations. Both routes cost extra passes or repeated runs. EIVE instead emits an instance-level saliency map after the forward pass. Decoder cross-attention becomes the attribution pathway in their design. Each object query's attention maps to its predicted instance.

A fusion module pools attention signals across decoder layers. The maps come out stable and compact from that pooling. No gradient pass or input perturbation is needed at all. The method fits single-scale and multi-scale DETR-like detectors. A joint training scheme adds spatial limits on attention. Detection scores and clarity of the maps both improve.
arxiv-2606-01901:
Hakimov and co-authors turn image rebuilding into a dialogue game. A vision-language model guides an image generator over turns. It issues corrective instructions as rounds progress. Shared common ground becomes visible in the rendered image. That makes the buildup of shared context measurable.

Tests cross two describer models with two generators. Seven image categories span the benchmark set. The describer is the dominant factor in quality. The generator decides if refinement helps or hurts. Math and geometry images prove hardest to rebuild. Token budget strongly shapes how rounds converge. Short budgets give sparse first images with room to grow. Strong describers use richer spatial and numeric correction terms.
arxiv-2606-02001:
Shi and co-authors build training data for agents from grounded real interaction. Agent skill hinges on using diverse real-world tools. Quality interaction data drives that capability directly. Human annotation is too costly to scale for it. Current methods let chat models synthesize everything. Unconstrained generation drifts into biased random sampling instead.

Internal model priors then dominate the synthetic data. Real domain diversity and difficulty are missed. Long-horizon tasks of high fidelity are rare too. Their GAIS framework grounds synthesis in two phases. Protocol-anchored environments derive from real Model Context Protocol sources. Tasks are built to match those environments closely. The result is more diverse, harder agent training material.
arxiv-2606-02101:
Raab proposes a way to make synthetic data that is safe by design. Synthetic data stand in for real records in sharing. Two advantages set this method apart from rivals. The first is transparency about what is preserved. Users know which relationships hold approximately in the data.

The second advantage is a disclosure safety guarantee. The synthetic data derive only from pre-checked information. Margins where relationships are kept are defined first. Each margin then passes statistical disclosure control. Top-coding, bottom-coding, and category merging are applied. Small counts may be modified by the custodian's standards. Further tweaks ensure the margins stay consistent overall. The method suits custodians who must prove safety.
arxiv-2606-02201:
Goncharov and co-authors give a gate based route to squeezed Schrödinger cat states of light. Such states are a key resource for tests of quantum theory. They also serve modern quantum technologies. The scheme uses a measurement assisted gate built on a controlled-Z operation. An ancilla starts in a small amplitude cat state.

The target oscillator starts in a squeezed vacuum or coherent state. The two interact through a quantum nondemolition entangling step. A projective homodyne measurement then completes the gate. The output states have high fidelity, the authors report. Their size and squeezing can be controlled by design. A tunable trade-off links fidelity and success probability. An iterative protocol then amplifies cat states step by step.
arxiv-2606-02301:
Mahajan and co-authors measure how chronic pain patients move, using one smartphone video. Chronic pain lowers quality of life by limiting function. Measuring that impact in daily settings is hard to do well. Optical motion capture gives high precision for movement quality. It is costly and restricted to labs, though.

Their Quantitative Movement Testing pipeline uses computer vision. It extracts 3D movement markers from standard monocular phone video. Deep learning based 3D pose estimation powers the pipeline. The team validate it against optical motion capture. Thirteen healthy controls took part in that validation. A leave-one-subject-out calibration corrects bias in the output. Two clinical cohorts then used the tool in practice.
arxiv-2606-02401:
Xu and Zhuang, with Guenancia, study what survives when a singular space is pushed to a limit shape. The space has a Kawamata log terminal singularity. Such a point comes with a built-in limit. The limit is set by the normalized volume minimizer at the point. The team asks which forms on the space stay sound in that limit.

They prove that non-degenerate reflexive differential forms do survive. One case matters most for the field. If the point is symplectic, the limit point is symplectic too. A rigidity result for such limits joins the proof. Together, the two results confirm Kaledin's conjecture. The formal completion of any symplectic singularity is conical. Two more uses follow from the proof. Bases of nilpotent orbit closures are K-semistable Fano varieties. Volume minimizers for hypertoric cases come from the standard dilation.
arxiv-2606-02601:
Ascarate and co-authors warn that a common anomaly detection test can mislead. Class-split evaluation holds out one class as the anomaly. It proxies for unconditional out-of-distribution detection. When the held-out class overlaps the normal mixture in representation space, the protocol breaks. Anomaly scores can fall to chance level. They can even invert.

The preferred score direction may depend on the unknown anomaly class. The team introduces a training-free diagnostic called neighborhood class leakage. It predicts score-direction instability before it strikes. Tests span Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Imagenette. Both pixel space and VAE latent space are covered. Class-split benchmarks, the authors argue, are geometry-dependent stress tests. They should not be read as unconditional proof of detection skill. Benchmark users get a cheap check to run first.
arxiv-2606-02801:
Roth asks what separates a true organism from a mere colony of cells. In an organism, each cell's function is defined by the whole. In a microbe colony, each cell keeps its own life. The whole is just a sum of stand-alone parts. Roth maps that split onto coherence in physics. A coherent system is described by a single state vector. Classical coherence, unlike the quantum kind, is sustained by metabolic work.

A Lagrangian-style model makes the idea concrete. Genetic sequences act as coordinates, and mutation rates as velocities. The equations yield a collective coordinate for the coherence of the whole. The model predicts broad spread in infection outcomes across matched samples for coherent organisms. Colonies should give steady responses instead. A test uses Dictyostelium discoideum, which lives as single amoebae or as multicellular slugs. Infecting both states with the same virus can confirm or kill the hypothesis.
arxiv-2606-02901:
Pharr and co-authors tackle a coordinate problem. Fourier spectra of resonant quantities depend on which magnetic coordinates a researcher picks. Earlier work showed that one area weighting keeps the resonant coefficients fixed on rational surfaces. The external spectrum, which links to perturbation coils and error fields, was left open.

The team pairs a square-root-area weighted vacuum field with a full-area-weighted resonant field. The resulting coupling matrix has singular values that do not change under coordinate changes. Its right singular vectors also rebuild into one consistent real-space pattern. Calculations with the GPEC code confirm the math. Badly weighted matrices could give dominant modes whose overlap differed by a factor of two to three between coordinate systems. The gap grew for strongly shaped, low aspect ratio plasmas. The authors say the fix applies to any tool that computes such spectra on flux surfaces.
arxiv-2606-03201:
Yang and co-authors teach a reinforcement learning agent from expert videos shot in a unlike domain. The agent sees no reward signal. Its own look may differ from the expert's in color, shape, or the sim-to-real gap. Their method, XIPER, turns cross-domain video prediction into a reward source.

XIPER trains a model that maps the agent's views into the expert domain and predicts what comes next. The likelihood of that prediction serves as the reward. Tests span eight tasks in a color suite and three in a body suite of a control benchmark. XIPER beat baselines in both, despite gaps in agent color and shape. The team also tests on a sim-to-real set. Given only simulated expert video, the method gave sane reward signals for real robot views. The work targets learning from video when no reward can be written by hand.
arxiv-2606-03301:
Pennec and co-authors build a benchmark for reasoning over whole TV series. Past video benchmarks stress local sense: frames or clips that sit side by side. SagaQA asks for high-level grasp of long stories told across full shows. Its questions need hops that link facts from wholly unlike episodes. Models must track events and acts across a long multimodal arc.

The team also studies how agent planners cope with such hops. Planners are sorted into three classes: parallel, sequential, and hybrid. Each is graded on how coherent and complete its plans are. Hybrid planners won in the tests. They made higher-quality plans and showed stronger skill at complex story sense. The authors offer SagaQA as a test of narrative grasp at full length. It targets a skill that clip-based tests cannot see: holding a whole show in mind while a question crosses it.
arxiv-2606-03401:
Li and co-authors tackle a weak spot in how scientific images are judged. Such images act as key evidence in research reports. AI-made content can now plant subtle but serious errors in them. Standard quality scores track looks, not scientific truth. Language models also lack the domain skill to verify such images.

Their framework, SIU2A, scores images on utility and upgradability. Utility covers finding errors and judging if a fix is feasible. Upgradability grades how well a fix restores the image. Errors are sorted into four types: detail distortion, missing parts, false content, and entity confusion. A benchmark with expert labels supports tests of both stages. Trials show current multimodal systems do poorly at finding scientific errors. They also struggle to repair images without harming correct parts. The gap between seeing and scientific use is made plain.
arxiv-2606-03701:
Roy finds when a smooth functional can be extended without losing smoothness or norm. The setting is spaces with polyhedral norms. A smooth functional lives on a subspace first. The question is when it extends to the whole space while preserving its norm. The answer turns out to be purely geometric.

Extension is possible exactly when one special point behaves the right way. That point is the unique absolute norm-attaining point of the functional. It must be an extreme point of the unit ball of the subspace. It must also be an extreme point of the ambient unit ball. A counterexample shows the result fails for non-polyhedral norms, even under strong extra assumptions. Related questions about extreme functionals and their restrictions are treated too. Functional analysts get a crisp test for smooth Hahn-Banach extension.
arxiv-2606-03801:
Sabatini proves that Cayley graphs of quasirandom groups expand well and stay small in diameter. A finite group is quasirandom when its nontrivial representations all have high degree. Expansion in such a group was tied to its simple quotients by recent work. That link drives the results here. The Bourgain-Gamburd expansion machine is simplified as a first payoff.

The product theorem drops out of the machine's assumptions. Crown theory then shows a sharp sampling result. Just over one over epsilon random elements yield an expander Cayley graph with high probability. Diameter results generalize work of Breuillard, Green, and Tao, and of Pyber and Szabó. Any connected Cayley graph of a quasirandom group has polylogarithmic diameter. Group theorists get cleaner expansion criteria and tight size bounds in one package.
arxiv-2606-04701:
Yao and colleagues benchmark AI agents on screens that refuse to sit still, in a 2026 arXiv evaluation paper. Today's GUI agents assume a static screen frozen between actions. The authors formalize this as the living-screen-native agent task and introduce LivingScreen, the first benchmark for it on short-video platforms, with a faithful browser-based environment and a three-tier task suite.

Its metrics jointly score accuracy and information efficiency, rewarding agents that gather enough but not too much. Evaluating extensive frontier models, they find none reaches the human cost-accuracy performance. The dominant failure mode is observation control: models over-observe, watching too long, or under-observe, acting before seeing enough. The authors identify observation control as a missing capability axis for future GUI agents, one invisible to static benchmarks where looking longer is free and the world politely waits.
arxiv-2606-04801:
Le Breton, Szustakowski, and Piraud present the fastest implementation of cubical persistent homology for images, in a 2026 arXiv paper on topological data analysis. Persistent homology tracks how shapes appear and merge as an image is thresholded at varying levels. Their software, Flash Cubical, computes persistence on a V-filtration, built around three ideas.

First, properties of cubical complexes allow the highest-dimensional persistence to be computed through union-find and duality. Second, pruning certain edges makes that union-find fast in practice. Third, a lookup table exploits the regularity of cubical grids to precompute local information. The authors report this is the most efficient implementation of its kind in both time and memory.
arxiv-2606-04901:
Kohli, Bhattacharjee, Shailendra, and Sikdar fingerprint the behavior of links to catch attacks inside mega-constellations, in a 2026 arXiv security paper. Constellations like Starlink and Kuiper route traffic over optical links. Link integrity becomes a commercial and national security concern. Existing real-time security works only at the physical layer, leaving network-layer and attacks invisible. Their CLIF framework fuses onboard physical measurements with network-layer data in fingerprints.

They simulate the first shells of Starlink with 1,584 satellites, Kuiper with 1,156, and a joint peering scenario with 2,740. Their detector achieves recall of 99.5 percent on Starlink, 99.4 percent on Kuiper, and 94.8 percent on the joint constellation, with false positive rates below 0.7 percent. Cross-layer fusion, they conclude, is necessary for comprehensive constellation security and cheap enough for satellites' strict energy budgets.
arxiv-2606-05101:
Sepehr Dehdashtian and co-authors introduce FoeGlass in this 2026 arXiv paper, an automated red-teaming method for audio deepfake detectors. Detectors that flag synthetic speech guard against misuse of text-to-speech models, but testing them needs datasets that expose their blind spots. Manual collection is slow, and blind spots are hard to find on purpose.

FoeGlass is the first black-box automated approach. It uses a language model's in-context learning to explore a speech generator's input space, producing samples that fool a target detector with only black-box access. A diversity-based context design curbs the mode collapse that plagues automated red teaming. Across open-source detectors and generators, FoeGlass data raised false negative rates by up to 94 percent over baselines. Its attacks transferred across detectors, and fine-tuning on its samples improved robustness by up to 41 percent.
arxiv-2606-05301:
A 2026 arXiv paper co-authored by Greg L. Bryan proposes line-intensity mapping as a probe of active galactic nuclei, the accreting black holes at galaxy centers. Intensity mapping measures the glow of a spectral line across a volume instead of cataloging sources one by one. The authors target the neon-five line, whose ionization potential makes it an uncontaminated tracer of black hole activity, visible in heavily obscured nuclei.

By cross-correlating intensity maps with redshift surveys, emission becomes detectable below survey thresholds. Fisher forecasts for two instruments, one CDIM-like and one PRIMA-like, promise constraints on the product of AGN intensity and bias across redshifts two to three. About ten percent of the signal comes from sources below the detection threshold. That sub-threshold population is detectable at signal-to-noise between nine and four, offering a route to the black hole-halo connection at low luminosities.
arxiv-2606-05401:
Reiko Liu, Wen-Jie Ma, Hu Zheng, and Yu-fan Zheng construct Carrollian conformal bases for particles of any mass in this 2026 arXiv paper, using an agentic AI workflow. Carrollian holography aims to rewrite flat-space scattering as correlators of a boundary theory, but its dictionary was known only for massless particles, leaving massive ones without a local description.

The central method is the Poincaré-Carrollian intertwiner, which reproduces the known celestial and Carrollian bases for massless particles and then constructs the missing bases for massive and tachyonic ones. The tachyonic basis keeps real momentum support while the massive one requires the complex shift in the scattering amplitudes. The work used LACIA, an agentic workflow built to keep physical reasoning apart from technical work. It reduces the risk of hallucinated derivations and deceptive self-checks, with human checks confirming the results.
arxiv-2606-05501:
Emre Girgin and Cagri Kilic learn contact detection for legged robots without force sensors, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Leg odometry rests on the assumption that a foot in its stance phase has zero velocity relative to the world. That lets the leg's kinematics correct the body estimate. Everything hinges on knowing precisely when each foot touches the ground. Force sensors at the foot tip usually do that job, but many robots lack them, and they miss events like slipping.

The proposed framework is self-supervised and uses only the standard joint encoders. A denoising autoencoder, trained to reconstruct clean signals from corrupted ones, learns representations of the legs' estimated motion with no human labels. The latent space is modeled probabilistically as two overlapping distributions for stance and swing. Experiments confirmed the learned detector outperformed supervised methods needing extra sensors and labeling. The authors release their code publicly.
arxiv-2606-05601:
Yarndley, Lantoine, and Armellin plan propellant-free orbits skimming the Moon in a 2026 arXiv paper. Orbits below fifty kilometers give close views of the surface. The Moon's lumpy gravity field warps such orbits fast, raising drop risk and fuel costs. A solar sail, pushed by sunlight, offers thrust that never runs out. The team builds a two-stage planner around a pattern in how these orbits drift.

The first stage uses mixed-integer optimization to pick orbit and sail setups suited to station keeping. A second, lighter stage polishes the choice into precise flight paths. A test case modeled on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter kept a realistic sail craft in the low band for at least a year. It burned no propellant at all. The plan still worked with course fixes only once a month. It also proved steady under perturbed inputs, hinting longer stays may be feasible.
arxiv-2606-05801:
Jinbo Yang and colleagues solve black holes exactly in a gravity theory that breaks Lorentz symmetry in a 2026 arXiv paper. Bumblebee gravity adds a vector field with a preferred direction in spacetime. Earlier studies of its black holes leaned on numeric work. The team constructs analytic solutions for still, round spacetimes where the field has only a time component. They map the parameter region where the solutions flatten out at large distance, as real black holes should.

Formulas for two special thermodynamic quantities fall out of the solutions. With them, the first law and Smarr relation check out exactly. The exact results confirm the older numeric findings and expose cases the numerics missed. One regime allows an unbounded charge-to-mass ratio. Overcharged solutions in another regime open into traversable wormholes. The Hawking temperature also bends non-monotonically, and the heat capacity shows two blow-up points.
arxiv-2606-06101:
Hrebeniuk, Klen, Karuseichyk, Treps, and Semenov find the quantum speed limit for measuring air turbulence in a 2026 arXiv paper. Turbulence blurs starlight and degrades free-space optical links. Its strength is captured by the Fried parameter, a coherence radius. Direct imaging infers it from spot size but hits a diffraction wall when the receiver aperture is smaller than that radius.

Borrowing spatial-mode sorting from superresolution imaging changes the game. In the weak-field regime the authors pin down the ultimate precision limit for estimating the coherence radius. Mode sorting beats conventional direct imaging by a wide margin in exactly the small-aperture regime. The result is a hard measurement bound, not just a better instrument: no measurement strategy can surpass it. Telescope sites, adaptive optics, and quantum communication links all budget around such estimates. Knowing the floor tells engineers when to stop optimizing hardware and start accepting physics.
arxiv-2606-06701:
Some infinite products, when expanded as power series, have long runs of coefficients that are exactly zero. Daniels, Huber, McLaughlin, and Ye pin down new families of those vanishing runs in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their objects are products of quintuple products, classical building blocks from the theory of q-series, where each factor steps by powers of a base variable.

For primes that leave remainder one when divided by four, the authors write out explicit arithmetic progressions, evenly spaced index patterns, along which the coefficients must vanish. When the prime splits as a sum of two squares, they give a formula for the exact shift that locates the zero run. The proofs use involutive transformations, symmetry flips on integer lattices that pair terms up so they cancel. The work extends a line of results reaching back to Richmond and Szekeres.
arxiv-2606-07201:
Auclair and colleagues examine how mechanical stress limits the design of tokamak fusion power plants in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tokamak confines hot plasma in a doughnut shape using powerful magnets. The toroidal field coils and central solenoid, the magnets producing the main fields, must be thick enough to withstand enormous magnetic forces. Their sizing models feed a system code that estimates plant dimensions and cost.

The authors built two analytical models, a simple teaching version and a refined one using thick-cylinder stress theory and realistic conductor structure. Comparing them shows where simplified assumptions misjudge the needed coil thickness on the cramped inner side. Their analysis suggests compact machines with major radius under four meters appear feasible when several innovations are combined. Those include high-temperature superconductors and structural tricks that redirect forces, though the authors flag the added risk of stacking new approaches.
arxiv-2606-07401:
Joshi and co-authors benchmark document parsers on the messy regulated documents businesses process, in this 2026 arXiv paper introducing RealDocBench. Mortgage files, financial reports, logistics forms, and clinical records drive high-stakes workflows, yet benchmarks mostly use clean academic layouts and report one similarity score. What downstream agents need is the value for a field on an ugly page. The benchmark's question track holds over 1,300 field-level questions across 581 documents in four domains, each with reference answers.

A second layout track provides 1,500 human-verified page images with bounding boxes under a 9-class taxonomy. Eighteen systems, spanning commercial parsers, vision-language models, and open-source OCR tools, were evaluated under one protocol with cost and latency reported beside accuracy. The results exposed a wide performance spread hidden by single-number benchmarks. Medical documents proved hardest, and trade-offs appeared between accuracy, per-page cost, and response speed across systems.
arxiv-2606-07601:
Ha, Yoon, and Lee unify families of neural differential equation solvers by splitting dynamics into what fades and what persists, in this 2026 arXiv paper on LFNO. Neural operators learn mappings between functions to solve equations. Fourier-based operators excel at steady periodic behavior, while Laplace-based operators handle transients, the decaying response. Their Laplace-Fourier Neural Operator runs two branches, one for each component, and recombines them, covering systems with both regimes.

9 benchmarks tested the design: 3 ordinary systems including the chaotic Lorenz system, and 6 partial systems from heat flow to Navier-Stokes fluid motion. LFNO outperformed existing ones on the ordinary systems, where transients dominate, and beat the Laplace-only operator on partial equations, staying competitive with the Fourier specialist. The split improved stability and made predictions easier to read, since engineers can inspect the transient and steady parts. The split is the key to one solver for many regimes.
arxiv-2606-07701:
Zhang offers a pointed correction to a widely cited verification result in this short 2026 arXiv paper. The subject is diagnosability, whether faults in a discrete event system can be detected from the events an observer can actually see. A 2011 paper claimed a polynomial-time test for decentralised diagnosability of labelled finite-state automata that needed no extra assumptions.

Zhang shows three separate problems. First, he gives a counterexample system that can deadlock or loop invisibly, on which the published algorithm gives the wrong answer. Second, the suggested fix of adding invisible self-loops at dead states can itself change whether a system is diagnosable, so it is not safe. Third, verifying the related property of co-diagnosability is PSPACE-hard, a complexity class above polynomial time, so a fast general algorithm is unlikely to exist. The note is brief but it removes a result other researchers had relied on.
arxiv-2606-07801:
Lv and co-authors argue that multimodal reasoning should be graded by its weakest link, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A reasoning path must stay sound across many constraints at once, from visual grounding, tying claims to what is in the image, to logical consistency. Process reward models score such paths, but averaging rewards lets a strong dimension hide a failing one, such as a visual hallucination covered by fluent logic.

Their framework, MMS-PRM, builds a detailed reward space for the risks and refuses to average failures away. A Chebyshev-based tree search steers exploration toward whichever dimension is worst, and a curriculum form of preference training teaches balanced skills gradually. In experiments the approach avoided the dimension-collapse failure and improved the reliability of multimodal reasoning. It reached competitive results across challenging tasks, supporting the case that robust reasoning means optimising the worst dimension, not the average.
arxiv-2606-08101:
Laurent Bartholdi founds a theory of group actions that computers can reason about, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An automatic action is a group or semigroup acting on a space encoded as an omega-regular language, the kind automata on infinite words can recognise. Each element's action is itself recognised by such an automaton. Many examples once studied apart fit this single framework.

The paper focuses on bounded actions, where the encoding automata have no two connected nontrivial cycles. For bounded actions of inverse semigroups, Bartholdi proves the orbit relation, which pairs of points lie in the same orbit, is also omega-regular. From this, minimality, transitivity, aperiodicity, and element order are all decidable. Indeed every first-order statement about the action and its orbits is decidable. An application reaches complex dynamics: for post-critically finite polynomials, the encoding of Fatou components can be computed.
arxiv-2606-08201:
Sosnov proves results about the structure of matrix Lie rings in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Lie ring is a set with addition and a bracket operation that captures how elements fail to commute. The question is uniqueness of addition: if a map between such rings preserves brackets and is a bijection, must it also preserve addition automatically? Sosnov studies the rings of all square matrices and of trace-zero matrices over an arbitrary field, where trace zero means the diagonal entries sum to nothing.

He shows that any bracket-preserving bijection out of the full matrix ring is automatically additive on the trace-zero part, for matrices of size at least two by two. He also proves the first result of its kind for injections, maps that need not cover the whole target: any bracket-preserving injection of the two-by-two trace-zero ring is additive.
arxiv-2606-08401:
Jiangdong Ai and Shi improve a forty-year-old bound in graph theory in this short 2026 arXiv paper. A Hamilton cycle in a directed graph visits every vertex exactly once and returns to its start. A classical theorem of Chvátal and Erdős gives a condition guaranteeing such a cycle in undirected graphs, based on connectivity and independence number. Jackson extended the question to digraphs and bounded the connectivity needed to force a Hamilton cycle by a factorial-sized expression.

Jackson asked for better bounds and wondered whether a linear one might hold. Later researchers noted even a polynomial bound would be interesting. Ai and Shi deliver that polynomial bound: the required connectivity grows at most like twice the cube of the parameter, plus a constant, replacing the old factorial growth. The improvement is dramatic, shrinking an astronomically large sufficient condition into a practical range.
arxiv-2606-08601:
Peiliang Gong and a large team make language models interrogate a time series before forecasting it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language models show promise for forecasting, but existing methods rely on passive modality alignment, mapping numbers into the model's representation space, which often misses fine-grained, non-stationary temporal patterns. Their method, InA-Probe, shifts the paradigm from passive alignment to an active, instruction-driven probing mechanism that questions the data.

A multi-level instruction injection mechanism enriches the model with both global task objectives and fine-grained, patch-level semantic priors, hints about what each segment of the series may mean. An adaptive query generation module then produces sample-specific probes, dynamically modulated by the temporal context. The probes are refined through a dual-stage attention process. The result is a forecaster that adapts its questions to each series rather than applying one fixed encoding.
arxiv-2606-09001:
Liu, Fan, and Wang bring supercomputer-grade equation solving into the JAX machine-learning ecosystem, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sparse linear systems from discrete partial differential equations sit at the heart of computing. JAX, Google's differentiable programming framework, lacked a solver combining GPU acceleration, AMG, and distributed multi-GPU execution. Algebraic multigrid, or AMG, solves huge systems by working across grid resolutions. JAX-AMG wraps Nvidia's AmgX solver suite as a JAX primitive to fill it.

Through one interface, users get AMG and Krylov methods with tunable preconditioners, helpers that speed convergence. The library supports JIT compilation, batched solves, and MPI-based distribution. Derivatives flow through solves by adjoint methods, enabling optimization and inverse problems. Caching reuses solver setup across solves, spreading the overhead. Published in SoftwareX under an Apache license, JAX-AMG targets simulation in physics and scientific machine learning.
arxiv-2606-09201:
Hui, Sacramento, and Yu map a classic model's phases once electrons interact and hops reach further, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a chain with alternating bonds, is the textbook topological insulator with protected edge states. Adding electron-electron interactions and extended-range hoppings, jumps beyond nearest neighbors, enriches it beyond non-interacting predictions. They chart the ground-state phase diagram and its order parameters.

The diagram holds several topological phases, 2 novel superconducting-like phases, mimicking paired-electron behavior without true superconductivity, and 5 charge-density-wave phases, where charge settles into periodic patterns. Those phases and two charge-density-wave phases trace to imbalanced coupling plus extended hoppings. The order parameters check out in large-system runs against entanglement entropy and fidelity. Surprisingly, coupling allows non-unidirectional hoppings in those phases, unlike the non-interacting case.
arxiv-2606-09601:
Berker Demirel and his co-authors build a trust score for AI-made samples when the asked-for mix is brand new in this 2026 arXiv paper. Conditional generators make samples to order, like cells with a set mix of traits. That skill is prized for rare or untested cases. But grading such samples hits a loop: the usual scores need real samples from the target, which by premise do not exist.

Their post-hoc score needs only the training data. One part checks global realism, whether a sample fits the shape of real data. The other checks faithfulness, whether it sits closer to the asked traits than to near rivals. In tests on cell images, picked samples kept true cell forms better and lifted downstream scores. The same score can run mid-generation, so a system can abstain before it wastes effort on a bad sample.
arxiv-2606-09701:
Blake Bullwinkel and his co-authors train language models to attack and defend each other in turns in this 2026 arXiv paper. Safety tuning often leans on fixed attack lists. Fresh attackers then slip past, since they adapt. Automated red teaming answers with an attacker that learns. Co-training goes further: defender and attacker grow together, each forcing the other to improve.

Past co-training used PPO or DPO, while GRPO, a leaner reinforcement method, proved shaky here. Their AdvGRPO makes GRPO work with dense multi-channel rewards and split advantage scaling. Training climbs a ladder: single-turn attacks, then closed-loop multi-turn ones, then full co-training in turns. The learned attacks proved strong and moved well to fresh targets. Co-trained defenders beat set baselines on safety tests. The loop, in effect, arms both sides at once.
arxiv-2606-09801:
Oliver Janzer, Sean Longbrake, and Liana Yepremyan settle growth rates for a two-pattern graph count in this 2026 arXiv paper. The generalized Turán number asks: in a graph on n points that bans one pattern, how many copies of a second pattern can fit? Both patterns here are complete bipartite graphs, split sets with all cross links. That case stayed wide open for decades.

For split sizes two or three on the banned side, with the counted side larger, the team proves the count grows like n to the s, for large enough far side. One subcase answers a question posed by Spiro. A second Spiro guess falls too: for each graph with at least one edge, there are endless real growth powers that some banned partner can force. The proofs close a long gap for bipartite pairs.
arxiv-2606-10201:
Zheng and his team turn area coverage by robot teams into a contest between cooperators and adversaries, in a 2026 arXiv paper on control theory. Standard coverage control allocates agents according to a risk density field, spreading them to monitor what matters. Their version lets a second group of adversarial agents generate the spatial risk field itself, creating a two-player zero-sum game. The area coverage metric becomes the game reward, linking the two groups' dynamics and inducing coupled gradient-descent-ascent controllers for each side.

Analysis of a low-dimensional case reveals a Hopf bifurcation, a transition to oscillation, dictated by the ratio of the groups' control gains. When ordinary agents dominate, it converges to a fixed layout. At Nash equilibrium, ordinary agents settle into a generalized centroidal Voronoi tessellation, the classic optimal coverage pattern, while adversarial agents settle at their own equilibrium centroids.
arxiv-2606-10401:
Zhang and colleagues give multimodal language models an external spatial memory so they can reason about places across long visual experiences, in a 2026 arXiv paper on artificial intelligence. Spatial intelligence requires coherent representations over time, and grid-based cognitive maps built from multi-frame input help, but limited context windows still choke understanding. Existing fixes need architectural changes, memory modules, or fine-tuning, limiting use with off-the-shelf pretrained models. Their framework, CoCoSI, is a plug-and-play multi-agent system that collaboratively constructs cognitive maps as structured spatial memory.

Local and global agents coordinate the construction, with atomic commits keeping the shared map consistent and cross-agent verification checking entries between agents. The design borrows from human spatial cognition, where maps are built incrementally and checked. It applies that pattern to model agents rather than changing any single model's weights.
arxiv-2606-10501:
Minsoo Jo and co-authors study a deployment risk for robot control models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models turn camera input and instructions into robot motions, assuming the body executes commands faithfully. Real joints degrade through wear, damage, safety limits, or friction, so realised motion drifts from commanded motion. The team shows these joint-level faults hurt task success unevenly across joints. Even faults that leave a task physically feasible, like extra friction, cut success rates sharply through growing closed-loop mismatch.

Their remedy is J-PARC, a lightweight calibrator added on top of a frozen policy. It infers the current fault regime from recent joint motion and adjusts the policy's actions through a shared residual correction, conditioned on that regime. Simulation and real-hardware experiments show J-PARC improves robustness under faults while leaving fault-free performance intact, a practical step toward reliable deployment.
arxiv-2606-10601:
Kalyan and co-authors automate mesh generation for engineering simulation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Before a structure can be simulated, its shape must be divided into a mesh of small elements, and quad meshes are prized but tedious to build by hand. Their framework, Dmsh, is a fully automated reinforcement learning pipeline with three agents: one simplifies topology, one regularises geometry, and one generates the mesh. Meshing is cast as a Markov decision process, solved with a Soft Actor-Critic method adapted to mixed discrete and continuous actions.

A curriculum trains the agents from simple domains toward complex ones. Recursive decomposition lets subregions be meshed in parallel, joining into one conforming all-quad mesh with no post-processing. Across wide benchmarks, Dmsh reportedly beats existing methods in automation, robustness, and mesh quality.
arxiv-2606-11101:
Di Pinto and Viganò examine supersymmetry in a charged black hole solution in a 2026 arXiv paper on supergravity, the framework joining gravity with supersymmetry, a symmetry pairing particles with partners. Their setting is the static Reissner-Nordström black hole, a charged non-rotating hole, in a Bertotti-Robinson universe, a background shaped like two-dimensional anti-de Sitter space times a sphere. The work uses four-dimensional supergravity.

After reviewing it, they work out the constraints guaranteeing supersymmetry and compute the Killing spinors explicitly. Killing spinors are the fields whose existence certifies that a background preserves it. They show the solution saturates the BPS bound, a sharp inequality linking mass and charge for such states. That saturation lets them compute the black hole's mass cleanly and analyze its heat behavior. Finally they generalize the extremal solution, the limiting case, to include a cosmological constant.
arxiv-2606-11201:
Gan, Li, and Luo improve inference-time alignment of language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. This approach steers a model's answers during generation using guidance from an aligned model, avoiding retraining. Existing methods accept or reject that guidance in binary fashion, never asking whether it is reliable. The authors show guidance quality varies drastically across models. Bad guidance triggers confusion, more interventions, and worse answers.

BlendIn, their framework, replaces the binary switch with blending. It forms hybrid output distributions mixing both models, weighting each contribution by assessed reliability. Good guidance keeps its influence; unreliable suggestions are downweighted rather than blindly accepted. BlendIn also yields diagnostic signals and mitigation strategies for misaligned guidance. Across challenging model pairs it improved performance by up to fifty percent over existing methods. The intervention paradox they document, where more intervention signals worse performance, motivates the softer design.
arxiv-2606-11301:
Saurabh studies a family of knots and their Alexander polynomials in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Alexander polynomial is a standard invariant in knot theory. His family is the 4-strand Turk's head knots Th(4, 2n+1), closures of a repeated braid. The goal is their coefficient structure, governed by Fox's Trapezoidal Conjecture, still open for this family.

Using the reduced Burau representation, Saurabh derives a recurrence of order at most eight and a rational generating function. A resultant elimination then gives an exact factorization of the scaled polynomial via Chebyshev functions. This yields a convolution formula for a coefficient sequence and an expression as a finite hypergeometric series. The saddle-point method shows negative curvature in the asymptotic main term. He closes with obstructions to global discrete error bounds this way.
arxiv-2606-12201:
Mutke and co-authors check whether Europe's planned energy transition needs more rare materials than Europe can fairly claim, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Energy system models chart how to cut emissions, but most ignore the metals their wind turbines, solar panels, and batteries require. The team reviews fifty-nine highly decarbonized European studies. They then compute the material demands of five key technologies across nineteen materials, comparing them with Europe's population-based share of world reserves.

For seven materials, modeled demand passes that fair share of current reserves. Gallium, indium, iridium, and tellurium overshoot clearly; silver, selenium, and vanadium exceed it less sharply. Demand from non-energy uses tightens the squeeze further. New technology can ease or worsen the gaps, depending on design choices. Efficiency and recycling help only partly, the authors conclude. They call for sufficiency measures, using less energy overall, alongside supply expansion to close the material gap.
arxiv-2606-12301:
Liu and co-authors speed up a physics-based decoder for quantum computers by splitting its hardest problem in two, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Ising approach turns decoding into finding the lowest-energy state of a magnet-like model. Under realistic noise, error types correlate, creating terms linking up to ten spins at once. Such high-order terms slow solvers, break convergence, and inflate the hardware needed to run them.

Their iterative decoder, ILOD, alternates between the two error types. Each pass uses Bayesian priors from the other type's current guess to reweight its own couplings, halving the maximum interaction order. Spin counts for hardware embedding drop 2.5-fold. On the toric code the error threshold reaches 4.73 percent, nearly the joint method's 4.83 percent, while runtime shrinks geometrically with code size. On the color code, ILOD keeps converging at large distances where the joint method fails outright.
arxiv-2606-12401:
González Picos and co-authors read the carbon fingerprints of a giant planet to reconstruct its birth, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Isotope ratios, the relative amounts of an element's variants, record where a planet gathered its material. For the super-Jupiter Beta Pictoris b, the team measures carbon-12 to carbon-13 in its atmosphere. Eleven nights of high-resolution spectroscopy with CRIRES+ at the Very Large Telescope resolve both carbon monoxide variants.

The ratio comes out at fifty-eight, with an uncertainty band of fifteen to eighteen. That matches today's interstellar medium and sits below the Sun's value. It resembles ratios in other young super-Jupiters. The retrieval gives a temperature near 1,629 kelvin, near-solar metal content, and a solar-like carbon-to-oxygen ratio of 0.52. Hints of thick clouds appear. The planet orbits inside its disc's carbon monoxide snow line, benchmarking formation models for close-in gas giants.
arxiv-2606-12901:
Trenggana and Zen show how propagating modes of the quantised gravitational field can entangle 2 particles held in a harmonic trap, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setup belongs to the quantum-gravity-induced-entanglement programme. Because entanglement cannot be created by local operations and classical communication, a classical gravitational field could never entangle the particles. So observed entanglement would certify gravity's quantum nature.

They find that the gravitational field's effect on the entanglement is encoded in the field's commutation relations. Within this model the entanglement arises through the quantum action of the field rather than its classical background. Entanglement does not form at once: there is a time delay before it is set, proportional to the distance between the particles, showing the propagation of interactions at finite speed. Choosing squeezed states as the particles' quantum states lifts the effect, although the entanglement remains very small.
arxiv-2606-13101:
Haba studies an SU(5) grand unified theory supplemented by a 45 Higgs field and a DFSZ axion sector, in this 2026 arXiv paper. He derives predictions for proton decay channels and the axion mass. The Georgi-Jarlskog flavour structure is imposed at the unification scale to fix the charged-fermion mass relations that the minimal model gets wrong.

A 1-loop gauge coupling unification analysis, including threshold masses of the light multiplets from the 45-dimensional Higgs, identifies the region of the unification-scale parameter space. Through the relation between the unification and Peccei-Quinn scales, that region yields correlated predictions for the QCD axion mass. Because the Georgi-Jarlskog assumption reduces the flavour ambiguity of the dimension-6 baryon-violating operators, the model gives constraints and predictions for antineutrino proton decay modes. It also gives them for charged-lepton modes, such as a proton decaying to a positron and a neutral pion.
arxiv-2606-13201:
Dubey and colleagues propose a minimal model of bounded trade-off screening for multi-attribute choice, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Classical decision models assume compensatory utility aggregation, where gains on 1 attribute offset losses on another without limit. Human behaviour often violates that assumption: people reject options doing poorly on a critical attribute despite strengths elsewhere. Current non-compensatory accounts rely on thresholds, lexicographic rules, or sequential filtering.

The proposed framework weighs the balance between gains and losses across attributes rather than adding up utility. A screening process applies a max-min comparison rule, asking whether the largest gain offsets the largest loss, governed by a trade-off tolerance parameter that controls allowed imbalance. Through simulation, the authors show the mechanism yields preference patterns that differ from standard utility-based models and captures context-dependent trade-off choices.
arxiv-2606-13301:
Li studies how Ricci flows settle near their singular times in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ricci flow deforms shape geometry so that curvature spreads out, a process central to geometry and topology. In 3 dimensions the flow can develop singularities, places where the geometry breaks down. A singular Ricci flow continues past those events by surgery and completion. Li considers the completion equipped with a spacetime distance, and equips time-slices with a metric defined through heat kernel measures, which record how heat would diffuse.

He proves that each time-slice of the completion is a metric limit of the part of the flow, in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense of metric spaces converging. For any time and any connected component of the slice, the closure of the regular region converges to it as the time approaches from below. Convergence holds at the first singular time, the hardest case.
arxiv-2606-13401:
Brylle, Andersen, and Madsen argue that dynamic electricity tariffs are the scalable way to flex demand in this 2026 arXiv paper. Denmark's grids face strain from electrification and renewable generation: too little reserve capacity, overloaded components wearing out, unstable voltage, and investment needs. Demand-side flexibility means shifting when customers use power. Explicit mechanisms, where an operator controls devices, give certainty but cannot scale across millions of customers. The authors champion implicit flexibility, where changing prices nudge households and businesses to move consumption.

They draw on consumption data showing strong price-responsive behaviour, and on Denmark's market and tariff models, which vary network charges over the day. Their analysis estimates savings of tens of millions of Danish kroner per constrained substation from deferring or avoiding grid reinforcement. Because the scheme can be revenue-neutral for the grid operator, they present dynamic tariffs as the pathway to system-wide flexibility.
arxiv-2606-13501:
Qiang and colleagues present GF-DiT in this 2026 arXiv paper, a runtime for serving diffusion transformer models. These models dominate image and video generation, and demand for serving them is growing. Systems assign each request a fixed parallel setup, a set number of processors, for its lifetime. But requests differ, stages within a request differ, and system conditions change, so a static setup wastes hardware and degrades service quality. The authors argue parallelism should be a first-class schedulable resource, adjusted while requests run.

GF-DiT is a runtime that adapts the parallel settings of running requests to workload demands and service objectives. Its asynchronous design decomposes each request into schedulable tasks, enabling processors to move as conditions shift. Policies can be programmed to trade latency against throughput for service tiers. The design targets cloud operators who must keep accelerators busy without breaking quality promises.
arxiv-2606-13701:
Gu and colleagues test a contactless way to estimate blood pressure from two sensors at once in this 2026 arXiv paper. Continuous non-contact monitoring promises cardiovascular care without cuffs. Single-modality approaches, imaging photoplethysmography, which reads blood volume changes from facial video, are limited by artefacts, skin-tone sensitivity, and the lack of information about the heart's motion. The authors combine facial imaging with millimetre-wave radar facing the back, capturing paired cues: optical volume fluctuations and cardiac micro-motions.

Bridging the two streams takes a deep learning architecture combining multi-scale dilated convolutions for feature extraction with bidirectional recurrent layers for time modelling. The study asks whether fusion beats either modality for blood pressure. Radar contributes motion information that video cannot see, such as chest-wall vibration, while video contributes pulse-wave detail. If the synergy holds, camera-plus-radar sensing could move blood pressure tracking into homes.
arxiv-2606-14101:
Đurić, Yu, and Sengupta melt a new kind of magnetic order with frustration and find an exotic phase in the wreckage. Altermagnets combine traits of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, including chiral splitting of magnon modes, the spin-wave excitations. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies a spin-half square-lattice model with first and second neighbor couplings plus an exchange modulation. The method is notable: symmetry-enhanced neural network wavefunctions optimized by variational Monte Carlo.

At low frustration the model confirms an altermagnetic ground state with the expected chiral magnon splitting. At high frustration with large modulation, the order melts into a disordered phase. That phase hosts two coexisting orders: a bond-nematic order, born from condensation of magnon pairs, and a symmetry-protected topological valence bond solid. Its spectrum shows chiral splitting of triplon-like levels, echoing the altermagnetic regime. Possible deconfined quantum critical points between phases are flagged for future work.
arxiv-2606-14301:
Quiriny and colleagues argue simulation software should tolerate degenerate tetrahedra mesh generators cannot remove. Three-dimensional Delaunay triangulations, unlike 2D ones, guarantee no minimum angle, so slivers, nearly flat tetrahedra, appear even from regular point sets. Over ninety percent can be removed by local fixes, but eliminating every sliver can take longer than meshing itself. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a robust framework on the Tempered Finite Element Method (TFEM).

Their stiffness-matrix analysis shows the difficulty: flat tetrahedra generate high-energy modes acting as increasingly strong constraints as the Jacobian shrinks toward zero. For isolated degenerate elements these stay local and do not prevent convergence, which holds when the Jacobian is bounded below by machine precision. The framework extends earlier, mostly two-dimensional TFEM demonstrations to demanding settings including incompressible fluid flow. Their position: a mesh of millions of elements should not be rejected over a few dozen slivers.
arxiv-2606-15101:
Lim and coauthors optimize a quantum resource called Wigner negativity using energy-based shortcuts in a 2026 study. Wigner negativity marks non-Gaussian light states that quantum technologies rely on. It can be created when a coherent pulse scatters off a two-level atom in a one-dimensional reservoir. Directly scoring negativity is too costly, since it needs the full Wigner function per output mode.

The authors introduce energetic cost functions that flag which output modes likely host large negativities. Plain incoherent energy works when few output modes matter, but fails as mode counts grow. A refined quantity, the non-Gaussian energy, tracks negativity far better in that regime. Both measures correlate strongly with true negativity across short intense pulses and driven finite-energy ones. The most energy-efficient generation uses under one input photon on average. The approach turns a hard optimization into an energy accounting exercise.
arxiv-2606-15201:
Zinihi and coauthors combine two learning ideas to model epidemics in a 2026 methods paper. Physics-informed neural networks fit epidemic equations, but they can train unstably and forecast poorly long-term. Koopman theory instead lifts nonlinear dynamics into a space where they act linearly. The authors merge both into K-PINN, a network that learns that lifted space while obeying the epidemic equations. They apply it to an SEIRSD model with susceptible, exposed, infected, recovered, and deceased groups.

Training data came from a structure-preserving simulation scheme for monkeypox cases. Real COVID-19 data from Germany, Morocco, and Sweden tested the method. K-PINN estimated epidemic parameters better than physics-informed networks. It beat Koopman methods based on extended dynamic mode decomposition. Its trajectory reconstructions and long-term forecasts were more stable. The authors argue the hybrid suits epidemic systems too. Better parameter inference from sparse data is the payoff.
arxiv-2606-15301:
Malhou and coauthors teach a neural policy to beat the classic LLL lattice reduction algorithm in a 2026 cryptography-adjacent paper. Lattice reduction rewrites a basis of skewed vectors into shorter, more orthogonal ones. LLL is the standard tool, but its handcrafted swap rule leaves quality on the table as dimension grows. The authors cast reduction as a single-player game over LLL's primitive moves. A network learns sequencing through AlphaZero-style self-play with tree search.

Their policy, Delta-Star, trained only on eight-dimensional lattices. Yet it needs fewer primitive operations than LLL to finish a reduction. It also generalizes without retraining to unseen moduli and dimensions up to thirty-two. The resulting bases approach the quality of the stronger BKZ algorithm. Extracting an algorithm from the learned weights is a stated next goal. The result hints other handcrafted heuristics in computational mathematics may yield to self-play.
arxiv-2606-15601:
Tsim and Gutoreva propose SCAN in 2026, a decision framework that helps learners decide which parts of a task to hand to generative AI. It rests on Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, the gap between what a learner can do alone and with help, together with metacognition, thinking about one's own thinking. SCAN sorts any task into four sub-zones that set the right level of AI involvement.

The zones are Substitute, where AI does the task; Complement, where it extends the learner; Aid, where it supports; and Non-negotiable, where the learner must act alone to keep learning. Workers and students can scan their own AI use with it before starting a task. They connect it to cognitive load theory, cognitive offloading, and AI sycophancy, and to deskilling risks at work. The aim is hybrid intelligence: people and AI each doing what keeps human skill growing over a lifetime.
arxiv-2606-15801:
Al-Bayaty introduces MAPS in 2026, a sphere-based picture for visualising qudit states, quantum systems with more than two levels. Qubits map elegantly onto the Bloch sphere, but that picture cannot extend to qutrits or higher systems without severe topological complications. It also fails to show the phases of even qubit states along its axes.

The multi-axial projective sphere threads the familiar sphere with several intersecting axes, up to one fewer than the number of levels. Each axis carries one basis state with its relative phases, so the whole state becomes readable geometrically. New phase gates swivel and shift states along these axes. Since each axis can stand for one feature, the picture doubles as a visualisation for high-dimensional data in machine learning and chemistry. One sphere that scales with dimension replaces the abstract constructions qudit visualisation usually requires.
arxiv-2606-16301:
Cho and co-authors introduce GENIE in 2026, an optimizer that helps models generalize to domains they never trained on. Domain generalization fails when models latch onto domain-specific cues, the spurious correlations of their training data. Gradient methods tend to follow one dominant direction, which can reinforce exactly those cues. GENIE instead scores every parameter by its One-Step Generalization Ratio, a measure of how much each parameter's update reduces loss.

A preconditioning factor then equalizes those ratios during training, so no small subset of parameters dominates the optimization. The theory shows GENIE balances convergence contribution and gradient alignment while keeping the convergence rate of plain stochastic gradient descent. Across five domain generalization benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art optimizers, per the report, and stays robust under strong domain shifts and limited data. It also plugs into existing generalization methods and improves them.
arxiv-2606-16701:
Gu presents recent LHCb results in a 2026 proceeding on open heavy flavor production. Heavy quarks are born early in collisions because of their large mass, then travel through the whole evolution of the quark-gluon medium. Watching the particles they finally form reveals how the medium transports them and how they shed their color charge to become neutral hadrons.

Results span proton-proton, proton-lead and lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. LHCb's forward detector probes parton distributions at very low momentum fractions, a region other detectors reach poorly. Its fixed-target program, using gas injected into the beam pipe, covers an energy range between older fixed-target work and top collider energies. Proton-lead data help separate cold nuclear matter effects, such as changed parton densities and energy loss inside nuclei. Those baselines matter before lead-lead results can be read as signs of a hot medium.
arxiv-2606-16801:
Chen and colleagues present MixGuard in a 2026 paper on privacy-preserving split learning for large language models. Split learning lets a weak device keep its raw data while a server runs the heavy layers of a model. The intermediate values sent to the server can still leak the data to reconstruction attacks.

MixGuard defends by mixing, in the spirit of mixup training. It scrambles data at three levels: token-level obfuscation, representation-level obfuscation, and adaptive gradient perturbation during backpropagation. A small calibration model, fitted on public data, first sharpens an estimate of the target representation so the mixing hides content without destroying the learning signal. Across four classification and four generation tasks, spanning model families and tuning styles, MixGuard keeps accuracy close to non-split training. It also beats existing defenses against state-of-the-art reconstruction attacks, including attacks that adapt to the defense.
arxiv-2606-17201:
Mar and Boska present a 2026 arXiv paper on the ends and tangles of infinite graphs. Ends describe the ways a graph extends out to infinity. They compactify a locally finite graph, and tangles extend that idea to any infinite graph. Both constructions rest on vertex connectivity, but edge versions were less complete.

Switching to edges gives edge-ends and a larger edge-direction space. The authors define edge-tangles in a natural way and prove they yield exactly the edge-directions. They also build certain Boolean algebras in a purely combinatorial way. Stone duality then recovers the tangle and edge-direction spaces from those algebras. Functorial versions of the constructions are pursued as groundwork for future work in the field.
arxiv-2606-18101:
Huang and colleagues fix a trust problem in teaching vision models to point at the right button, in a 2026 paper. GUI grounding asks a model to find tiny interface elements in dense screenshots and name exact coordinates. On-policy self-distillation is attractive here because the teacher signals are dense. But the teacher grades the student's partial answers. Once a prefix coordinate drifts off target, its guidance can turn unreliable.

Their quality-aware method gates those signals softly. A check asks whether the teacher's current coordinate token could still be completed into the true bounding box under the student's prefix, and down-weights signals that fail. Teacher probabilities are also scaled to tune supervision strength. Across six grounding benchmarks the method beat the base model and strong post-training rivals, making spatial verifiability a practical design rule.
arxiv-2606-18201:
Ji and colleagues settle how hard it is to compute a quantity that links quantum circuits to counting problems, in a 2026 complexity paper. Any quantum circuit's amplitudes can be written through a low-degree polynomial over the binary field, scaled by a parameter called the circuit width. That width fixes how precisely a quantum computer can estimate the polynomial's gap, so it measures the qubit resources the counting approach needs. Montanaro had asked whether the width is efficiently computable.

The answer is no. Deciding whether a degree-three polynomial has width at most k is NP-complete, and even approximating the width within a constant factor is NP-hard, ruling out efficient approximation schemes. The paper's five results are not all negative, though: under a natural parameterization, efficient algorithms do exist. The work draws a sharp line around what the polynomial method can say about quantum advantage.
arxiv-2606-18401:
Terças and Mantsevich explain how excitons, bound electron-hole pairs that carry energy through a semiconductor, can appear to diffuse backwards in two-dimensional materials, in a 2026 condensed matter paper. Experiments have found this puzzling negative diffusivity, and earlier accounts leaned on nonlinear effects or thermodynamic oddities.

Their minimal hydrodynamic model treats excitons, electrons, and holes as three coupled fluids exchanging momentum. In the collisional regime, that coupling reshuffles transport coefficients between the fluids but keeps exciton diffusion positive. Once plasma inertia and collective charge waves enter, the slow exciton mode mixes with fast acoustic plasma modes. The blend turns dynamically unstable, which shows up as negative diffusion. A clear fingerprint follows: an exciton cloud should briefly contract before growing again as the plasma relaxes. The authors present shared plasma dynamics as a control knob for exciton transport in semiconductors.
arxiv-2606-18801:
Jang and the team correct the language bias of multilingual search engines at indexing time, without any training, in a 2026 information retrieval paper. Multilingual dense retrievers should rank documents by meaning. But they strongly prefer documents written in the query's language. So top results fill with one language's documents, even when matches exist in others. That hurts search and multilingual retrieval-augmented generation.

Their method Shift uses parallel translation pairs to estimate, for each language, a language vector. It captures that language's offset in embedding space with respect to a source language. Shift then subtracts the vector from document embeddings while indexing, matching the meanings across languages. Because the fix happens on the index side, queries and models stay as they are. Testing across four multilingual retrieval benchmarks and models showed Shift eased language bias and improved retrieval performance, making it a cheap add-on for multilingual indexes.
arxiv-2606-19101:
Sarti argues in 2026 that structure, not nonlinearity, should drive learning models for dynamical systems.
