Defoe traces English blood through Romans, Saxons, Danes, and Normans in a mongrel national pedigree of fun. He mocks pride of pure descent as folly in a nation built by wave on wave of settlers. The verse is rough, quick, and quotable, and it sold in huge numbers across England in 1701. Later critics hail it as the first great poem of English multiculturalism in the language itself. It made Defoe's name before the novels that now eclipse his verse entirely.
dekker-satiro-mastix-1601:
Thomas Dekker's Satiro-Mastix, played in 1601, is his blow in the War of the Theatres. The London playwrights were mocking each other on stage, and Ben Jonson had hit Dekker in Poetaster. Dekker answers by putting a Jonson figure, Horace, on stage to be scourged.

The satire rides on a wedding plot drawn from the same events Jonson used, turned inside out. Captain Tucca, a swaggering braggart, carries much of the fun. Scholars prize the play for its picture of the stage world at war with itself. It also shows Dekker's gift for London speech and low-life comedy at full stretch.
descartes-method-meditations-veitch-1901:
John Veitch, a Scottish professor, translated the core works of René Descartes in the volume of 1901 given here. The book holds the Discourse on Method, the six Meditations, and selections from the Principles of Philosophy. Veitch's rendering differs from the better known Haldane and Ross version, and scholars use it as an independent check.

Descartes begins by doubting everything that can be doubted, and finds one stone that will not move: I think, therefore I am. From that point he rebuilds knowledge of God, soul, and world step by step. The Meditations remain the most assigned work in modern philosophy. Veitch's plain Victorian English keeps their drama of doubt and recovery clear.
devereux-volume-01:
Book one of Lytton's Devereux fills this first volume, with the author's 1852 advertisement at its head. Lytton there calls the novel a work of early youth, kept in plot but pruned in style. The character of Algernon Mordaunt, formed by his studies in morals, is named as its core.

Within the tale, the Devereux brothers live as dependants on an uncle's favour. Aubrey argues that the eldest, as heir and favourite, need not strive as the younger ones must. The wish to earn an independence stirs the talk. Love, court manners, and family pride fill the opening book. This file holds book one only, and the story runs on past its close.
dnb-ferdinand-james-de-rothschild-1901:
Thomas Seccombe wrote this life of Ferdinand James de Rothschild for the 1901 add-on to the Dictionary of National Biography. The DNB add-on took up lives the main work had missed or that had closed since. Seccombe was a sound hand at such lives, with a clear, dry style.

Ferdinand was a baron of the Austrian arm of the house who made his home in England. He sat in the Commons, built Waddesdon Manor, and filled it with art and fine things. The life is the standard short record of the collector in the great reference work.
doe-osti-3015051-state-tribal-collaborat:
State and tribal collaboration on energy is introduced in a September 17, 2025 slide deck by Smith, Cory, and Pakes, presented to a NASEO working group. The deck opens with the laboratory's partnership record: support for more than 3,000 communities, tribes, jurisdictions, utilities, and businesses on energy transition planning and technical assistance.

Legal groundwork follows, because tribal sovereignty shapes every joint project. Slides trace the doctrine through Cherokee Nation v. Georgia in 1831, which named tribes domestic dependent nations, and Worcester v. Georgia in 1832, which held that state law has no force in Indian lands. Later material distinguishes federally designated tribal land from land used for cultural activities, framing why collaboration must start from tribal self-governance rather than state process.
encyclopaedia-biblica-vol2-1901:
Volume Two of the Encyclopaedia Biblica appeared in 1901, covering E to K. Cheyne and Black held to their critical plan: test every tradition against the evidence. The contributor list reads like a roll of the era's boldest Bible scholars.

Entries here handle Egypt, the Exodus, the Gospels, Israel's history, and the geography of the holy land. Long signed articles argue their cases with full notes and sources. The editors print rival views where the experts split. Together with the other volumes, this made the most advanced Bible reference of its time, still consulted for its learning.
english-act-of-settlement-1701:
Parliament passed the Act of Settlement in 1701 to decide who would inherit the English throne. The law looked past Catholic heirs and settled the crown on Sophia of Hanover and her Protestant descendants. It also set conditions that future monarchs would have to accept.

Beyond the succession, the act protects judges by letting them serve during good behavior, not royal pleasure. It limits pardons in impeachment cases and bars monarchs from leaving the realm without consent. Together, these clauses strengthened Parliament against the crown. The act still shapes the British monarchy and its rules of succession today.
ernest-maltravers-volume-01:
Volume One of Ernest Maltravers holds Edward Bulwer Lytton's dedication to the German people and his preface to the edition of 1840, then Book the First of the novel. Lytton ranks the book above Pelham and Godolphin, the most mature and comprehensive of his works. Young Ernest begins his course of love and ambition.

The middle of the volume finds Alice in a conservatory, blushing and trembling as Maltravers kisses her hand. She asks if she must now leave him; he answers, Never, and her face grows radiant. Alice knows no remorse, the narrator notes, though she feels agitated. The volume sets the pair's unequal love at the center of Ernest's education. Readers meeting the novel in parts start here.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-01: Volume one of Michel de Montaigne's Essays, in Charles Cotton's translation as edited by William Carew Hazlitt in 1877, is given over to front matter in this hosted file. A preface argues that Montaigne shaped minds from Bacon to Shakespeare. A life of the essayist follows, covering his tower retirement, his mayoralty of Bordeaux, and his death in 1592. His letters come next. Montaigne's own address to the reader closes the file, promising an honest self-portrait for family and friends. The essay chapters begin in the following volume.
eugene-aram-volume-01:
Volume 01 of Eugene Aram holds the dedication to Sir Walter Scott and the first book of Edward Bulwer Lytton's tale. The story then settles into Grassdale, a quiet country place of fields, a brook, and long June evenings. There the reader meets the Lester household and Walter Lester, who fishes the brook and chafes at his uncle's displeasure.

Into this calm comes Eugene Aram, the Student, a scholar living apart with his books. Book I sets the pieces in place: the village, the family, the young men, and the learned stranger whose reserve hides more than shyness. Readers starting the novel here get its groundwork: place, people, and the first shadow over Aram's name, before love and suspicion take hold in later volumes.
europmc-pmc10100201: Liu and Wang review how extracellular vesicles, tiny parcels released by cells, carry messages between cells and how that traffic is regulated. The review covers how vesicles form, what cargo they load, and how target cells take them in. It shows why these parcels matter for health, disease, and new treatments.
europmc-pmc10291001:
Hu and colleagues review spinal cord injury in a 2023 paper, covering its molecular mechanisms and treatment options. A spinal cord injury can paralyze and disable for life, and full repair remains out of reach. The damage unfolds in stages, from the first crush or cut to weeks of swelling, cell death, and scarring that block regrowth.

The review explains each stage at the molecular level. It then surveys interventions in testing, from drugs and cells to implants and stimulation. The paper shows why repair is so hard and where progress is real.
europmc-pmc10719501:
Larsson, Butterworth, and Burgess explained Mendelian randomization in 2023, a method to test cause in heart research. Gene studies of the past decade found many variants tied to heart traits. The method uses those variants as a natural trial. Genes are dealt at birth much like lots in a trial, which cuts bias.

If a variant that raises a risk factor also raises disease, the factor likely plays a causal role. Larsson sets out the rules that must hold for that logic to stand. Uses span tests of new heart drugs before costly trials start. Old drugs can also be checked for fresh uses this way. The review gives the steps and the traps of the design.
europmc-pmc10758001:
Li and co-authors reviewed in 2024 how tiny carriers can deliver drug pairs for human disease. Pairing drugs can hit a disease on two paths at once. Gains include lower doses, less harm, and slower drug resistance. Pair care is now sought for cancer, heart disease, and brain decline, among others.

Nanoparticles, minute spheres of fat or plastic, can carry both drugs to one spot. Li shows they can stretch release, guard the drugs, and aim them at sick tissue. Forms in use or in tests span liposomes, polymer spheres, and nanocrystals. The review maps disease targets and the pairs matched to them. Hard parts remain: factory scale and proof in patients.
europmc-pmc10855901:
Chandrasekaran and Weiskirchen explain how excess weight drives type 2 diabetes in this 2024 overview. Type 2 diabetes is a long-term illness where blood sugar runs too high. Obesity, meaning a harmful build-up of body fat, is its strongest risk factor at all ages. Both illnesses are spreading worldwide.

Trials show that modest, lasting weight loss can improve blood sugar and insulin action, the authors note. Insulin is the hormone that moves sugar from blood into cells. Some patients then need fewer diabetes drugs. Diet, exercise, and daily habit changes form the core plan and can even help prevent the disease. The review lays out how fat and sugar control are linked inside the body. It closes with recent care plans for people who carry both conditions.
europmc-pmc10901501:
Buttenschoen, Morris, and Deane test whether AI docking tools produce shapes that could exist in the real world in this 2024 paper. Docking means predicting how a drug molecule sits in a protein pocket. New AI tools claim top accuracy and speed. The authors suspected many outputs break basic rules of chemistry and shape.

Their test suite, PoseBusters, checks bond lengths, flat rings, clashes, and other physical rules. They ran five AI tools and two classic tools through it. Judged by pose closeness alone, the AI tools looked strong. Once the physical checks were added, much of that lead vanished, the authors report. They argue that only tools passing both tests should be called state of the art.
europmc-pmc11071201:
Li and a large team uncover a self-feeding loop that drives pancreatic cancer in this 2024 study. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a lethal cancer with fast, aggressive growth. Cancer cells often burn sugar by glycolysis, a process that makes lactate. Lactate can tag histones, the spools DNA wraps around, in a mark called lactylation.

Tumour samples showed high levels of this mark, and high levels tracked with shorter survival, the team found. Blocking glycolysis or silencing a key enzyme cut the mark and slowed tumour growth in cells and mice. Screening found the mark switches on two growth genes, TTK and BUB1B. One of those genes binds the sugar enzyme itself, closing a positive feedback loop. The authors present the loop as a driver of the cancer's onset and a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc1480401:
Kodner and Spreeuwenberg took stock of a rising buzzword in 2002: integrated care. Health services for chronic illness often come in pieces, split across many providers. Integrated care promises to join those pieces. The authors saw a young field with fuzzy terms.

They argue the idea needs clear meaning before theory or practice can grow. Their paper maps what the term could cover and what follows from each reading. At its heart, they press for a patient-centered drive. Kodner hopes the paper sparks debate on what integrated care should be. The stakes are high for people whose care spans years and many hands.
europmc-pmc1538601:
One protein sits at the heart of Alzheimer's disease. Zheng and Koo reviewed its wider life in 2006. The amyloid precursor protein, APP, is cut to make the beta-amyloid pieces that form brain plaques. Faults in its gene cause some early, inherited forms of the disease.

Yet APP does more than yield plaques. Lab studies assign it roles in cell growth, sticking, and signaling. Fly and mouse mutants, with the gene added or removed, show it matters for normal brain work. Zheng urges the field to study the whole protein, not just its toxic fragment.
europmc-pmc1618401:
Copying RNA to boost tiny samples can bend the very ratios labs want to measure. Diboun and co-authors quantified that risk in 2006 for a common amplification protocol. Boosting is unavoidable when tissue is scarce.

Distortion struck when a signal shift in one sample fell outside the scanner's range. The bend usually shrank ratios, weakening their statistical proof. Strong changes survived well: 87 percent of top genes kept their significance. Moderate changes kept it only 69 percent of the time. Diboun found the limma analysis method coped better with amplification than a rival approach.
europmc-pmc1664601:
Deaths worldwide are shifting to older ages and chronic diseases. Mathers and Loncar projected that shift in 2006, updating global forecasts from 2002 to 2030. Older projections had badly underestimated HIV/AIDS.

Their models run three scenarios, baseline, optimistic, and pessimistic, tied to economic and social trends. In all three, deaths move from infections, childbirth, and nutrition causes toward noncommunicable diseases. The risk of death for children under five falls by nearly half in the baseline case. Mathers aims the projections at health policy and priority setting worldwide.  Their findings update the widely quoted 1996 forecasts, which rested on 1990 data.
europmc-pmc1847501:
Evans and colleagues mapped the immune defenses of the honey bee in 2006 from its newly read genome. Bees are social insects that fight germs both as a colony and as individuals. The team focused on individual defenses in Apis mellifera and compared them with the fruit fly and the malaria mosquito.

They built bee models for four signaling pathways tied to immunity and found plausible matches for nearly all expected members. Yet across 17 gene families linked to insect immunity, bees carry only about one third as many genes as the fly or mosquito. The authors suggest bees can afford a leaner kit because colony behaviors block many infections. Or bees may face a narrow set of pathogens that evolved closely with them, such as the foulbrood bacterium.
europmc-pmc1939701:
Pfenninger and Schwenk asked in 2007 whether cryptic species, distinct species that look identical in effect, cluster in particular animal groups or regions. Reports of such hidden species had grown sharply over two decades. Some researchers proposed their spread was uneven, which would skew global diversity counts.

The team analyzed a literature database of cryptic animal species reports by taxon and by biogeographic region. Regression models corrected for how many species each group holds and how intensely it has been studied. After those corrections, cryptic species spread almost evenly across major animal groups and regions. That evenness suggests stasis in outward form, long-term look-alike evolution, is a constant of animal life. Hidden diversity thus inflates true species counts in a predictable way everywhere, with direct effects for biodiversity estimates and conservation planning.
europmc-pmc2125401:
William DeB. MacNider studied uranium poisoning and its antidote in 1916. The metal's toxicity, he argues, runs through acids: uranium leads the body to form organic acids such as diacetic acid and acetone. Age matters: young animals suffer less from both the metal and from anesthetics. Sodium carbonate lessens the poisoning.

Not, he insists, by blunting the metal itself. The carbonate delays the acids forming and lowers the amounts appearing in urine. The kidney tells the story under chloroform. The protection is credited to blunting those organic acids, plus the hydrochloric acid chloroform itself frees during anesthesia. Carbonate treatment, in effect, puts an old animal in a young one's position. Readers get an antidote explained as acid handling, not metal binding.
europmc-pmc2125801:
G. N. Stewart and J. M. Rogoff cut the spinal cords of cats at set levels to learn which cord region controls the steady release of epinephrin from the adrenal glands. Their 1917 Journal of Experimental Medicine paper used sensitive test tissues, including the denervated eye and strips of rabbit gut and uterus, to detect the hormone's flow.

Cutting the cord in the neck, as low as the last neck segment, left epinephrin release unchanged in rate and character, running through the same nerve paths as in an intact animal. Cutting in the mid-back, by contrast, stopped detectable release. The controlling cord region seemed to end near the third chest segment. Under urethane, neck-level cuts also produced no change the tests could catch, which narrows where the release signal leaves the cord.
europmc-pmc2128201:
Wade H. Brown, Louise Pearce, and William D. Witherbee described the bone and tendon lesions of rabbit syphilis under the microscope. Their paper belongs to the sixth part of their series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1921. The rabbits had been inoculated with two old strains of Treponema pallidum, and the team studied the lesions' gross forms and fine structure.

Localized infection of bones and tendons occurred frequently and produced varied lesions, with the face bones and the feet and legs as the usual sites. Most lesions began in the periosteum, the bone's outer membrane, though some arose inside the bone, in the marrow, or at growth lines. Periosteal lesions took two gross forms: a bounded, hard, nodular mass, or a spreading process. Under the microscope they showed the layered structure of syphilitic granulomata. Invasion of the bone, with absorption and tissue death, was constant.
europmc-pmc2128501:
Gerald S. Shibley, of Columbia's medical school and Presbyterian Hospital in New York, opened an agglutination series with streptococci that clump by themselves. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. Self-clumping strains wreck the specific clumping tests used to type germs, so he studied the spontaneous process itself.

The self-clumping, he argues, comes from a cohesive force between the bacteria, stronger than usual in salt solutions of the strength used for tests. Many granular self-clumping strains can be made smooth-growing by culture at room temperature, and then lose their clumping habit. Anything that lowers the cohesive force, or raises the repelling force above it, makes a stable suspension instead. Shibley closes with practical methods for handling stubborn self-clumping strains so their specific reactions can still be read. The physics of sticking, treated plainly, rescues a diagnostic test.
europmc-pmc2128601:
Ernest G. Stillman and Arnold Branch finally produced true lobar pneumonia in mice by the inhalation route, after many failures by others. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924, from the Rockefeller Institute hospital. The recipe had two parts: mice partly immunized by earlier inhalations, then alcoholized and exposed to a spray of virulent pneumococci.

Plain non-immune mice, alcoholized and sprayed, die of blood poisoning but rarely show any lung localization. The partly immunized mice, treated the same way, often developed a genuine lobar pneumonia instead. Immunity to one type gave no safety against another: mice protected against one type often developed lobar pneumonia from inhaling a different type. A little immunity, paradoxically, is what lets the lung disease form at all. It holds off the flood of blood poisoning that otherwise kills first.
europmc-pmc2131501:
Frederick Hammett and Vilma Wallace wrote part seven of their biology of metals series in 1928, testing lead on the chick embryo. Lead is a known poison, but its action on a growing embryo had fine points to fix. They exposed developing chicks to the lead ion and measured growth of the whole body and of its parts.

Overall growth was retarded by the lead. Growth of the somites, the blocks that form the spine and muscles, lagged even more than body length and width did. The head and the eye-forming regions were especially sensitive, and their shaping was strongly held back. The authors read the pattern as proof that lead picks out the areas of fastest growth by cell division.
europmc-pmc2140901:
Cecil Murray, at Bryn Mawr College, applied the principle of minimum work to artery branching in a 1926 paper. Blood flow through an artery costs work against friction, and keeping blood itself costs upkeep. For a short arterial section at steady flow, Murray writes the total cost as an equation in the vessel's radius and the flow. Earlier work had found the radius at which that cost is least.

This paper extends the principle to the angle at which an artery divides. At a branching, the parent and daughter vessels must split flow and change direction. The minimum work condition fixes how the angles should be set for the given flows and radii. The result gives a physiological rule for the geometry of the arterial tree, to be checked against real vessels.
europmc-pmc2169301:
Kubica and co-workers found in 2008 that Staphylococcus aureus bacteria can hide silently inside human macrophages. This bacterium is usually classed as an outside-cell pathogen, though it can invade other cells and die quickly there. In macrophages grown from human monocytes, its behaviour differed sharply. After being engulfed, the bacteria sat inside vacuoles for three to four days before escaping and bursting the host cell.

Until that escape, infected macrophages showed no signs of death and kept working. Pre-treating them with interferon-gamma let them kill the bacteria at human therapeutic doses. Survival depended on bacterial regulators called sigma factor B and agr. Mutants lacking alpha-toxin or other factors were killed efficiently. Alpha-toxin was the key survival molecule. Mobile macrophages may thus carry the infection around the body.
europmc-pmc2222601:
Deary and co-workers described the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936 in 2007, a study of cognitive ageing across a lifetime. All Scottish children born in 1936 took a general intelligence test in 1947, as part of a survey of 70,805 children. Survivors living near Edinburgh form this cohort of 1,091 people. They retook the same mental ability test at age 70, alongside medical exams, fitness tests and detailed thinking assessments.

The protocol also gathered personality, quality-of-life and food questionnaires, plus blood samples for DNA and biomarkers. Cognitive testing covered reasoning, memory, processing speed and executive function. The cohort's rare strength is a true measure of lifetime cognitive change, from age eleven to seventy and beyond. Rich accompanying data let researchers hunt for what drives differences in that change.
europmc-pmc2245901:
Zhang presented the I-TASSER server in 2008, an automated system predicting three-dimensional protein structure from amino acid sequence. The method had ranked best in the server section of the recent CASP experiment, a blind community test of prediction methods. The online server at the University of Kansas had already answered thousands of modelling requests from over 35 countries. Each query returns up to five full-length models.

A confidence measure called C-score estimates each model's accuracy from template consensus and clustering density. In large benchmark tests, C-score correlated strongly with the true structural similarity score, at 0.91 on that scale. Using a C-score cutoff gave false positive and false negative rates below 0.1 in these tests. The score reliably separates correct from incorrect overall folds. Average prediction error was just 0.08 on that similarity scale. The server is free for academic use.
europmc-pmc2361201:
Hamilton and colleagues compared survival across three aggressive womb cancers in 2006. The types were uterine papillary serous carcinoma, clear cell carcinoma, and grade 3 endometrioid carcinoma. All three are high-risk forms of cancer of the womb lining, and earlier small studies disagreed on which was worst.

Using a national US registry for 1988 to 2001, they tracked 4,180 women. Five-year disease-specific survival was 55% for the serous type, 68% for clear cell, and 77% for the grade 3 endometrioid type. The gap held for both early and advanced disease. The serous and clear cell types made up only 10% and 3% of womb cancers but caused 39% and 8% of deaths. The authors urged that these poorer outlooks shape patient advice and future trial design.
europmc-pmc2362801:
Forsyth and colleagues measured three tissue-chewing enzymes in brain tumors in 1999. The enzymes, called MMPs, cut through the protein mesh around cells. Two of them, gelatinase-A and gelatinase-B, were suspected of helping gliomas invade brain and grow new blood vessels. Gliomas are tumors of the brain's support cells.

The team measured enzyme levels in 46 tumor samples and seven healthy brain samples. Gelatinase-A ran higher in tumors than in normal tissue, even in low-grade tumors, and stayed high in the most malignant kind. Gelatinase-B rose more steeply with tumor grade and sat strongly in blood vessels at growing edges. A third enzyme, MT1-MMP, appeared in neurons, tumor cells, and vessels. The authors assigned gelatinase-B mainly to vessel remodelling, and the other two to both invasion and vessel growth.
europmc-pmc2481301:
Milano and co-authors split scleroderma into molecular subsets using skin gene activity in 2008. Scleroderma hardens and scars the skin and can damage internal organs, but patients vary wildly. The team read gene activity in 61 skin biopsies from patients with the diffuse form, the limited form, a localised form called morphea, and healthy controls.

Forearm and back skin from the same patient gave nearly identical profiles, a property they used to define each patient's intrinsic pattern. Diffuse and limited patients separated cleanly from each other and from controls. Inside the diffuse group sat three distinct subsets, and inside the limited group two. Each subset's signature pointed to a different program: cell growth, immune infiltration, or scarring. A 177-gene signature tracked how severe the skin disease was in diffuse patients. Subsets also mapped onto lung, gut, and finger complications.
europmc-pmc2577301:
Huse and colleagues validated in 2008 a shortcut for censusing microbial communities by sequencing only short variable stretches of a universal gene. Surveys of the small subunit ribosomal RNA gene identify microbes, but reading the full gene is slow and costly. Their method reads just the hypervariable tags, the stretches that differ most between species, using high-throughput pyrosequencing.

They compared tag results with full-length sequences from human gut and deep-sea vent communities. The tags gave equivalent identifications and relative abundances. This held even for tags differing from their nearest reference by up to 15 percent. The method samples communities hundreds of times deeper per dollar, exposing the rare biosphere of scarce species. It also skips the cloning step that biases older surveys. The authors offer it for projects like the Human Microbiome Project.
europmc-pmc2631701:
Donlan surveyed biofilms on medical devices in 2001, the slimy microbial communities that make device infections so hard to cure. Bacteria and yeasts stick irreversibly to surfaces such as catheters, heart valves, pacemakers, prosthetic joints, and contact lenses, then secrete polymers that encase them in a protective matrix. In that state they resist antimicrobial treatment far beyond ordinary cells.

Biofilms may start as a single species but grow multispecies with time, drawing organisms from patients' skin, staff hands, or tap water. Donlan calls for reliable sampling and measurement techniques so biofilms on devices can be compared between studies. Open questions include how much biofilms drive drug resistance and how firmly contamination of a device links to patient infection. Answering them is presented as the path to controlling device-associated infections.
europmc-pmc2662801:
Weinert and co-authors traced in 2009 the family history of Rickettsia, bacteria that live inside the cells of insects and other creatures. Some cause grave human diseases such as typhus, spread by ticks and lice. Many more live only in insects, and those were barely known. The team found 20 new strains in arthropods and built a family tree from several genes.

The tree shows Rickettsia are mainly insect partners, not mammal parasites. They do not evolve in lockstep with their hosts; instead they jump hosts often, usually to a related insect. About 150 million years ago the genus split in two, and a burst of new forms followed near 50 million years ago. Some lines gained tricks such as passing through mammals or killing male hosts. One strain proved a mix of two distant lines, a rare case of gene swapping.
europmc-pmc2695001:
Bucan and a large team scanned in 2009 the genomes of 912 families with autism, hunting rare structural variants that delete or duplicate whole gene pieces. Autism's genetics is famously tangled, and earlier work had shown such copy changes matter in a slice of cases, but too coarsely to name single genes. The team used dense typing and compared against 1,488 healthy controls.

Prioritizing changes that hit gene exons, they found over 150 spots where rare variants struck several unrelated patients but no controls. Twenty-seven held up in an independent check of 859 more cases and 1,051 controls. Known sites confirmed the method, including deletions of NRXN1 and duplications around UBE3A. New candidates emerged too: BZRAP1, a synapse protein adjuster, was hit in twelve unrelated cases and zero controls. Most variants were seen just once, a sign of how many roads lead to autism.
europmc-pmc2724101:
Gandhi and co-authors traced in 2009 how faults in PINK1, a mitochondrial kinase, make neurons prone to die from calcium stress in Parkinson's disease. PINK1 faults cause an inherited, recessive form of the disease, but what the protein normally does was unknown. Mitochondria are the cell power units, and they also handle calcium, a signal that can kill in excess.

In PINK1-deficient neurons, calcium left mitochondria too slowly through its sodium-calcium exchanger, so calcium built up inside. Overload raised reactive oxygen species, harmful oxygen forms, which blocked glucose entry and weakened respiration. That lowered the threshold for a lethal pore to open, so normal calcium pulses could trigger cell death. Feeding complex substrates partly restored respiration.
europmc-pmc2725801:
Elbasha, Dasbach, and Insinga modeled in 2007 whether a four-type HPV vaccine could cost-effectively cut cervical cancer, precancerous lesions, and genital warts in the United States. HPV, human papillomavirus, causes cervical and several other cancers and warts in both sexes. Simple cohort models cannot capture herd immunity, the indirect protection when spread falls, so policy needs a dynamic population model.

Their dynamic model tracked infection and disease across the population under several vaccination strategies added to current screening. Routine vaccination of young girls proved cost-effective in the model, and broader strategies could be judged on the same terms. The abstract frames the four-type vaccine as able to reduce cancer, precancer, and wart incidence at acceptable cost.
europmc-pmc2726301:
Seghier reviewed in 2008 the laterality index, a number used in functional MRI to state which brain half dominates a task such as language. Brain scans measure activity in each hemisphere, and the index compares left and right contributions. Small method choices can shift that number a lot, which affects both research and clinical use.

The review works through each choice: how activity is quantified, where volumes of interest sit, which statistical threshold is used, and how baseline tasks are picked. It also covers thresholding the index itself and whether values repeat well on rescan. Seghier urges that these factors be reported and kept in mind whenever index values are compared between people or studies.
europmc-pmc2727001:
Hotez and Kamath reviewed in 2009 the prevalence and burden of neglected tropical diseases among the poorest five hundred million people in sub-Saharan Africa. These diseases are chronic, disabling conditions tied to extreme poverty. Worm infections cause about eighty-five percent of the burden, they estimate.

Hookworm affects almost half of the poorest people, including tens of millions of school children and pregnant women, where it drives anemia. Schistosomiasis follows with about one hundred ninety-two million cases, then lymphatic filariasis and river blindness with tens of millions each. Together the burden may reach half that of malaria in the region. Data on many non-worm diseases are missing, so the true total is likely higher.
europmc-pmc2777001:
Hruz and co-authors described in 2008 Genevestigator V3, a web-based reference database for exploring gene expression across many biological contexts. Earlier versions let biologists query expression data, but scaling limits, single-organism storage, and missing heavy analyses held them back. The new version pairs a client-server design with large-scale manual curation and quality control of microarray data for several organisms, plus curated pathway data for mouse and Arabidopsis.

On top of better querying, V3 adds tools to study genes across many contexts at once. Users can hunt for biomarker genes, cluster genes into expression modules, and model responses inside metabolic and regulatory networks. As a reference expression database with approachable tools, it serves discovery research and the checking of new hypotheses. The system is built for meta-analysis, drawing conclusions across hundreds of experiments at once.
europmc-pmc2855701:
Rapin, Lund, Bernaschi, and Castiglione merged immune simulation with sequence-based prediction in 2010, upgrading their agent-based simulator C-ImmSim. Earlier simulators caricatured molecular binding, the step that decides whether the immune system notices an invader. The upgraded version represents germs and immune receptors by their actual amino acid sequences. It uses prediction software to forecast which fragments will bind and trigger a response, including a new scoring method built on protein binding energies.

Test runs reproduced classic vaccine studies and the growth of immune memory. Simulated people with two different tissue-type gene sets handled flu better than those with matched sets. Under chronic exposure, the highest-affinity defender clones outgrew all rivals, matching basic immune science.
europmc-pmc2883601:
Yesylevskyy, Schäfer, Sengupta, and Marrink built in 2010 a water model that adds electric responsiveness to fast, simplified computer simulations of biomolecules. Coarse-grained simulations lump atoms into beads to reach larger scales, but their usual water beads cannot polarize, so they screen electric forces wrongly. Their model packs four water molecules into three linked beads that can reorient like real water.

The new water reproduced bulk water's electric screening while keeping the density and oil-water behavior of the standard MARTINI model it extends. Two hard test cases showcased the gain: ions crossing a membrane and charged molecules in mixed environments behaved more realistically. Better water physics at coarse scale opens longer, larger simulations of membranes and proteins that finer models cannot reach.
europmc-pmc2929501:
Podhorecka, Skladanowski, and Bozko reviewed the role of the histone variant H2AX in the DNA damage response in a 2010 article. Breaks across both DNA strands are among the most harmful lesions a cell can suffer.

When such breaks form, H2AX near the damage gains a phosphate mark, creating a signal known as gamma-H2AX. The mark helps gather repair proteins at broken sites and pauses the cell cycle through checkpoint controls. Measuring the mark can reveal the harmful effects of toxic agents, track how well cancer treatment works, and hint at how sensitive a tumour may be.
europmc-pmc3003701:
Eldh and colleagues showed in 2010 that tiny vesicles shed by stressed mast cells can protect other cells from oxidative stress. Exosomes carry RNA and protein between cells, and their cargo was suspected to change with the sender's state.

Vesicles from peroxide-stressed mouse mast cells carried a different messenger RNA mix than vesicles from calm cells, and both differed from the parent cells. Receiving cells given stress vesicles lost less viability when later stressed themselves. Ultraviolet light exposure reshaped what the stressed cells loaded. The findings cast exosomal RNA as a courier of protective instructions.
europmc-pmc3087801:
Elshire and colleagues introduced in 2011 a streamlined way to genotype many individuals at once by sequencing only the DNA next to chosen cutting sites. Falling sequencing costs made reading DNA cheap, but reading whole genomes for every sample in a breeding population was still wasteful. Their method, genotyping by sequencing, uses enzymes that cut DNA at fixed spots and avoids the repetitive stretches that clog analysis.

Applied to maize and barley breeding populations, it mapped hundreds of thousands and tens of thousands of sequence tags respectively. For barley, which lacked a finished genome, the shared tags themselves served as the reference map. The approach is quick, highly repeatable, and needs no prior markers for a new species. Breeders can use it for genomic selection on fresh material, and conservation biologists can survey wild populations with no genome in hand.
europmc-pmc3097201:
Chang and colleagues calculated in 2011 how many years of life serious mental illness takes away, using a large London mental health case register covering more than thirty thousand patients. They built life tables for schizophrenia, related psychotic disorders, bipolar disorder, substance use disorders, and depression, and compared them with national figures for the same years.

Every diagnosis carried a large loss. Men lost roughly eight to fifteen years of life expectancy depending on diagnosis, and women lost roughly ten to seventeen years. The heaviest losses fell on men with schizophrenia and women with schizoaffective disorder. The authors note these gaps exceed the measured life impact of smoking, diabetes, or obesity. They call urgently for work on why these patients die early and how services can prevent it, since general healthcare gains are not reaching this group.
europmc-pmc3101201:
Zimmerman, Kiss, and Hossain opened in 2011 a journal series on migration and health by proposing that policy should follow the whole journey, not just the destination. Migrants' health is shaped long before arrival and long after, yet governments handle each phase in separate silos with clashing goals. Their framework splits migration into five phases: before departure, travel, destination, interception by authorities, and return.

Each phase carries its own health risks and its own chances to intervene, from pre travel screening and safe passage to workplace protection abroad and care on return. The authors argue mobility and health protection are fully compatible when agencies coordinate across borders and sectors. The article sets up five companion pieces, one per phase. Its aim is practical: give policy makers a shared map so migrant health stops falling between jurisdictions.
europmc-pmc3146901:
Michael Reddy and colleagues watched malaria mosquitoes bite outdoors on an island in Equatorial Guinea in a 2011 paper in Malaria Journal. Indoor spraying and bed nets had been the island's main defences, but those tools only work against mosquitoes that come inside. Volunteers collected landing mosquitoes indoors and outdoors across villages, seasons, and two years.

Outdoor biting proved surprisingly heavy all night, including early evening and morning hours when people are outside unprotected. The region's main malaria vector now sought hosts outdoors at least as much as indoors, a sharp change from its indoor-only habit recorded before control began. Roughly two fifths of bites came at hours people spend outside. The authors propose years of indoor insecticide pressure pushed the mosquitoes outdoors, and call for added outdoor measures.
europmc-pmc3215701:
M. Aleksi Kallio and colleagues introduced Chipster, analysis software for high-throughput biology data, in this 2011 paper in BMC Genomics. Microarrays and next-generation sequencing were producing data faster than most biologists could handle, and new analysis methods usually demanded programming skill. Chipster was built to put those methods within reach of non-programmers.

The software offers a graphical interface over a large collection of analysis tools for gene expression, microRNA, and genome copy-number data. Interactive charts let users click on data points and build new gene lists from their selections. Analysis steps can be saved as reusable workflows and shared with collaborators. The paper walks through the microarray tools using three case studies, and notes the platform also handles proteomics and sequencing data.
europmc-pmc3316601:
Sawyer, Krause, Guschanski, Savolainen, and Pääbo examined how DNA decays in remains that are centuries to tens of thousands of years old, reporting in 2012. DNA recovered from bones and museum specimens always arrives broken and chemically altered. The team compared mitochondrial DNA from tissues aged between eighteen and sixty thousand years, asking which kinds of damage build up steadily with time.

Fragment length, it turned out, does not shrink in a dependable way as remains age. Breaks in the DNA backbone did favor certain letters in patterns that suggest more than one decay route. One kind of chemical change, where one DNA letter masquerades as another near fragment ends, did climb reliably with age. The authors propose that pattern as a practical test for telling genuinely ancient DNA from modern contamination.
europmc-pmc3348501:
Kirilina and colleagues uncovered the bodily origin of a false signal that haunts a popular brain scanning method, in a 2012 study. The method, near infrared spectroscopy, shines light through the scalp to watch brain activity, but blood changes in the skin itself can mimic brain signals and create false alarms. During a sustained attention task, the team recorded the light signals alongside MRI scans, blood pressure, heart rate, and skin blood flow.

The fake signal sat exactly where veins drain the scalp, and it tracked the body's stress response rather than brain work. Mental effort triggered a sympathetic squeeze on scalp arteries, followed by a drop in blood held in the veins. A statistical fix that models the skin signal cleanly separated it from real brain activity. The authors warn that nearly any thinking task will stir the same bodily response, so cleanup is essential.
europmc-pmc3360701:
Sokolove and collaborators traced how the autoimmune attack in rheumatoid arthritis builds before joints ever become painful. Using stored blood from 81 people who later fell ill, some samples reaching back twelve years before diagnosis, they tracked antibodies to citrullinated proteins with a multiplex array.

The antibody response widened over time, a spread across more and more targets. Early antibodies aimed at citrullinated histones, fibrinogen, and biglycan, and as their range grew, inflammatory signals in the blood rose in step. A joint profile of antibodies and cytokines flagged whose symptoms would start within two years. The authors see this quiet phase as a chance to step in sooner.
europmc-pmc3395601:
Kamiya and a large team reported in 2012 that a single letter change in one gene decides sex in the tiger pufferfish, or fugu. The gene, Amhr2, helps build reproductive organs. By mapping the sex region and testing relatives, the team pinned down the one change that tracked perfectly with being male or female.

Females carry two copies of one version, while males carry one of each. The swap alters a single building block inside the gene's working region. The same link holds in two cousin species, and a matching defect in medaka fish also produces females. Oddly, the fugu sex chromosomes show none of the usual wear, marking them as very young proto-chromosomes.
europmc-pmc3483701:
Barrera reviewed how oxidative stress and damaged fats shape cancer growth and treatment, in ISRN Oncology in 2012. Cancer cells carry an altered chemical balance, with more reactive oxygen molecules than healthy cells. Those molecules attack the fatty walls of cells, leaving breakdown products that act as signals. One product, shortened to HNE, drew the author's focus.

At high levels, such stress can kill cancer cells, and many cancer drugs and radiation work partly by pushing it higher. Yet some tumor cells adapt to steady stress and become drug resistant. Barrera weighs both faces of the process: stress helps tumors arise, then becomes a weapon against them. Learning how resistant cells adapt could sharpen future treatments, she argues.
europmc-pmc3511201:
Healthy urine was long taught as sterile, and Derrick E. Fouts leads a fifteen-author team dismantling that dogma in 2012. They combine 16S gene sequencing with metaproteomics, the reading of proteins present, in urine from 26 healthy controls and 27 people with spinal cord injury and neuropathic bladder.

Clean-catch healthy urine is not sterile; it carries a real microbiome that differs between men and women. The no-symptom bacteriuria state in neuropathic bladder has its own distinct community, differing from both health and infection. Sorting harmless colonization from true urinary infection matters: overtreating breeds drug resistance, undertreating risks serious illness. Microbiome signatures may one day guide that call.
europmc-pmc3521101:
Many tumors wear folate receptors on their surface, and Grant L. Zwicke, G. Ali Mansoori, and Constance J. Jeffery review using that badge to aim cancer nanomedicines in this mini-review. The folate receptor grabs the vitamin folate, and cancer cells of many types display far more copies than healthy tissue.

Attaching folate to nanoparticles steers imaging agents and drugs straight to those cells. Targeted delivery promises higher efficacy with less collateral damage to the immune system and fast-growing healthy tissues, the usual price of chemotherapy. Some conjugates show up to tenfold higher efficacy than untargeted drug in the studies surveyed. Early detection plus precision delivery, the authors argue, is the direction of travel.
europmc-pmc3524801:
DNA where it should not be triggers immune alarms, and Brian J. Ferguson and five colleagues identify an unexpected sensor in 2012: DNA-PK, a protein known for DNA repair. Working with cells and mice, they show DNA-PK binds stray cytoplasmic DNA and starts an antiviral program.

The response runs through the regulators IRF-3, TBK1, and STING, switching on interferon, cytokine, and chemokine genes. Cells and mice lacking the DNA-PK catalytic subunit answer DNA and DNA viruses weakly, while RNA viruses still register normally. Since DNA-PK loss also causes severe immune deficiency through its repair role, the new sensing job complicates the picture, with implications for vaccines and autoimmunity.
europmc-pmc3708701:
Sturrock and colleagues assess active case detection for malaria in regions nearing elimination, where the remaining infections hide in people with no symptoms. Finding and treating these silent carriers is attractive, but the authors note the evidence that it cuts transmission is still sparse.

Current field tests miss very low density infections, imported parasites keep arriving, and reaching high coverage is operationally hard. The right form of detection, they argue, depends on the local transmission pattern and on who carries the risk, and every campaign should build in standardized monitoring. In some settings, targeted mass drug treatment may serve better than screening and should be evaluated head to head.
europmc-pmc3730701:
Karl Friston wrote a theory paper in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface in 2013 titled Life as we know it. He asks whether living organization must be rare and special, or whether it follows from basic physics. His tool is the Markov blanket, a statistical boundary that separates a system's inner states from the world outside.

Friston argues that any random, changing system with short-range links will develop such a blanket. Once it exists, the inner states act as if they were doing Bayesian inference, the math of updating beliefs from evidence. They seem to model their world and act to keep themselves intact, which gives rise to balance-keeping and a simple form of self-making. Computer simulations of a primordial soup support the claim that life-like order can be nearly inevitable.
europmc-pmc3743401:
Siqi Liu and co-authors reported a study in eLife in 2013 on how the protein MAVS switches on antiviral defenses. When RNA viruses infect a cell, sensors pass the alarm to MAVS, a protein on mitochondria that clumps into large polymers. Those polymers switch on two kinases that in turn activate the factors NF-kB and IRF3, driving production of interferons.

The team found that MAVS polymers recruit several TRAF proteins, TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6, through separate binding spots. Breaking those spots, or removing the TRAF proteins, shut down IRF3 activation. The TRAFs also drove tagging reactions that pulled another protein, NEMO, into the MAVS complex, which was needed to switch on both kinases. The work maps a core step of antiviral signaling.
europmc-pmc3744901:
Wing-Hin Lee, Ching-Yee Loo, Mary Bebawy, Frederick Luk, Rebecca Mason, and Ramin Rohanizadeh wrote a review in Current Neuropharmacology in 2013 on curcumin. Curcumin is the yellow polyphenol in turmeric, a spice and traditional medicine used in India, China, and Southeast Asia for over two thousand years. Modern work links it to diseases that share an inflammatory base.

The review covers curcumin's history, chemistry, stability, and its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and anti-cancer actions. It then focuses on brain diseases: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and brain tumors. Curcumin's benefits there seem to run through several paths at once, including control of the inflammation switch NF-kB and of enzymes and signal proteins tied to it. The authors also weigh its limits as a treatment.
europmc-pmc3756401:
Toshinori Ozaki and Akira Nakagawara wrote a review in Cancers in 2011 on p53, a protein that guards against cancer. p53 is a transcription factor that can trigger cell death, and over half of human cancers carry mutations that disable it. Mutant p53 can also block the normal protein and gain cancer-promoting powers of its own.

When DNA is damaged, p53 builds up in the cell nucleus and switches on target genes. Those genes pause the cell cycle so damage can be repaired, or push the cell into apoptosis so the damage cannot spread. The review explains how p53 is controlled, including its breakdown by the protein MDM2 under normal conditions. It also covers treatment strategies that aim at p53, including for cancers that resist chemotherapy.
europmc-pmc3759801:
Mohammed Nuruzzaman, Akhter Sharoni, and Shoshi Kikuchi wrote a review in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2013 on NAC transcription factors in plant stress responses. NAC proteins form one of the largest families of gene regulators found only in plants. They help reprogram gene activity when a plant faces attack by germs or harsh conditions such as drought and salt.

The review maps the family tree of NAC genes in rice and Arabidopsis, then focuses on a stress-responsive group called SNAC. Raising the activity of some of these factors can improve a plant's tolerance, which makes them targets for crop engineering. The picture is tangled: one NAC gene often answers several stresses, the proteins can act as brakes or accelerators, and they regulate each other in webs.
europmc-pmc3787301:
Sara Di Rienzi and a large group of co-authors reported a discovery study in eLife in 2013 on a new candidate phylum of bacteria. Cyanobacteria changed Earth's history by filling the air with oxygen, but their relatives were unknown, leaving their evolution a puzzle. The team rebuilt whole genomes from human fecal samples and from a subsurface aquifer.

The genomes belong to a new candidate phylum, sister to Cyanobacteria, which they name Melainabacteria. Its members do not photosynthesize: the analysis suggests they are anaerobic, motile, and live by fermentation. The subsurface member can fix nitrogen with an enzyme unlike the cyanobacterial one, hinting nitrogen fixation evolved twice. The authors propose the two lineages split around the gain of oxygen-making photosynthesis, with Melainabacteria staying in oxygen-free niches, including the mammal gut.
europmc-pmc3907301:
Iain C. Macaulay and Thierry Voet review the young field of single-cell genomics in PLoS Genetics in 2014. New methods can now copy and read the tiny amounts of DNA and RNA inside one cell. That opens a view of how cells differ from each other, a view lost when thousands of cells are ground up and read together as one sample.

The review covers the main technical and biological advances so far in genome, epigenome, and gene-activity studies of single cells. It also sets out the hard problems that remain, from copying errors to sparse data, and looks at what these methods could reveal about normal development and disease as they improve.
europmc-pmc3919201:
Jonathan Flint and Kenneth S. Kendler review what genetics has learned about major depression in Neuron in 2014. Depression is the most common psychiatric disorder, and in the United States it causes more disability than any other biomedical disease. Finding its biological roots has proven hard, and the authors take stock of how far genetic methods have actually gotten.

Large genome-wide searches and family linkage studies together limit how common and how strong the risk variants can be. Against those limits, the authors rejudge the long list of candidate-gene claims, many of which look weaker than first reported. They also discuss whether depression mixes several distinct conditions, and whether narrower subtypes would give genetic studies a cleaner target.
europmc-pmc3922601:
Li Shang, Karin Nienhaus, and Gerd Ulrich Nienhaus review how the size of engineered nanoparticles shapes their dealings with living cells, in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology in 2014. Man-made nanoparticles now appear in catalysts, sensors, solar cells, vaccines, drugs, and medical imaging. Knowledge of their biological effects, and of possible health risks, has not kept pace with that spread.

The review first covers how particle size is measured, then the evidence on how size affects entry into cells, by both active uptake and passive routes, and where particles end up inside. Cell damage from particles of different sizes is also weighed. For designers of medical nanoparticles, and for safety assessors, size emerges as a basic dial that must be set deliberately.
europmc-pmc3938901:
Juan Pablo Domecq and a large team review what is known about involving patients in designing health research, in BMC Health Services Research in 2014. The ethical case for engagement is strong, and it is widely assumed to make research more relevant to patients' real concerns. What was missing is evidence on how best to do it. The team searched eleven databases plus grey literature and expert advice, and included 142 studies.

Engagement proved feasible in most settings, done most often at the start, in setting agendas and drafting protocols, and less during the running and reporting of studies. Reported benefits included better enrollment, help winning funding, and choosing outcomes patients care about. The common costs were time, money, and a worry that engagement was only token. No comparative studies singled out a best method.
europmc-pmc3965101:
Ross Overbeek and colleagues describe the SEED and its RAST annotation service in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. The SEED, started in 2004, exists to annotate microbial genomes consistently and accurately as their numbers explode. It combines a genome database, a website, programming access, and server tools, and scientists use it to predict gene functions and to spot new pathways.

Its core is a set of subsystems, collections of related protein families, and the FIGfam family library derived from them. When a genome is submitted to RAST, its genes are called and matched against those families to assign functions. Public genomes then join the SEED and feed the family library in turn. The authors argue this cycle has scaled with the genome flood without losing consistency.
europmc-pmc3967101:
Brian J. Raney and colleagues describe track data hubs in Bioinformatics in 2014, a way to display your own genome annotations inside the UCSC Genome Browser without running a copy of it. A hub is a collection of annotation files hosted anywhere on the internet, in compact formats such as bigWig and bigBed. The browser reads the hub's small configuration files and pulls the data on demand, drawing it with the full browser interface beside the public tracks.

Hubs can be organized and configured like built-in data, and they spare labs the overhead of maintaining a private browser mirror. The supporting software is free for non-commercial use. The short paper is the formal reference for a feature that became a standard way to share genome-wide results with collaborators and reviewers.
europmc-pmc4032901:
Elke Eggenhofer, Franka Luk, Marc H. Dahlke, and Martin J. Hoogduijn review the life and fate of mesenchymal stem cells, in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. These cells live in most tissues, help repair damage, and calm inflammation. They grow easily in the lab, which makes them a hot prospect for therapy.

Early hopes cast them as spare parts that would travel to injury and replace failed cells. Trials tell another tale: most given cells lodge in fine blood vessels and die within days. Growing them in dishes also changes their travel and homing traits. Yet patients and animals still gain. The benefit seems to flow from signals the cells shed in their short stay, which nudge local repair and immune cells. The review sums up what is known about their movement, survival, and this signal-based route to effect.
europmc-pmc4072001:
Maximilian Muenchhoff and Philip J. R. Goulder reviewed sex differences in infectious diseases of childhood. Their review appeared in The Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2014. Boys and girls differ in how often infections strike and how severe they become, with differences visible from fetal life onward.

Overall, illness and death from infection run higher in males. Sex hormones shaping the balance of immune signals is one proposed reason. In the few diseases that hit females harder, damage from the immune response itself may be to blame. The authors note unexplained exceptions and stress that few studies have directly measured immune responses by sex in children. Bias patterns also shift with age as hormone levels change.
europmc-pmc4116801:
Thandavarayan Ramamurthy, Amit Ghosh, Gururaja P. Pazhani, and Sumio Shinoda reviewed bacteria that stay alive under stress yet refuse to grow on standard culture media. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Public Health in 2014. This viable but non-culturable state has been reported in several human pathogens.

Such bacteria keep their viability and disease-causing power while evading the culture tests used in food and water checks. Molecular studies confirm the state is real and reversible under the right conditions. A key advance was finding a resuscitation-promoting factor, a bacterial signal that wakes them, in both major bacterial groups. The authors stress the state's weight for outbreak tracing, food safety, and infection control, and the need to learn its triggers.
europmc-pmc4179701:
Jiangfeng He, Ziqin Li, and four co-authors promoted genotyping-by-sequencing for plant breeding in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2014. Breeders improve crops faster when gene markers flag the plants worth keeping, a method called marker-assisted selection. Big crop genomes like maize and wheat made marker hunting costly.

Genotyping-by-sequencing cuts the genome with enzymes, tags each sample with a barcode, and reads many samples in one sequencing run. One pass both finds new single-letter markers and scores them in each plant. The authors describe the lab steps and the computer pipelines the data need. They report the method already serves association studies, diversity surveys, and linkage mapping at low cost per sample, which puts genome-wide selection within reach of ordinary breeding programs.
europmc-pmc4208401:
Benjamin D. Auerbach, Paulo V. Rodrigues, and Richard J. Salvi reviewed a volume-control theory of tinnitus in Frontiers in Neurology in 2014. Damage to the inner ear cuts the signal reaching the brain, yet the central hearing system often ends up more active, not less. That overactivity may underlie both tinnitus, phantom ringing, and hyperacusis, painful sensitivity to sound.

The review gathers evidence that the brain turns up its central gain to make up for lost input, like raising the volume on a weak station. Several mechanisms may drive the rise, acting at different levels and timescales, from lost inhibition to homeostatic plasticity. Sorting out which mechanism acts where is, the authors argue, the step needed before targeted treatments for either disorder can be built.
europmc-pmc4228501:
Krishna R. Kalari, Hugues Sicotte, and ten co-authors described the Mayo Clinic's RNA sequencing pipeline in BMC Bioinformatics in 2014. RNA sequencing reads the messages active in a sample, but turning raw reads into usable answers takes many steps, each with its own tool. Labs that wire the steps together ad hoc get uneven results.

The pipeline, MAP-RSeq, runs six modules in a fixed order: aligning reads, checking their quality, counting gene and exon activity, spotting expressed single-letter variants, hunting fused transcripts, and writing a summary report. It was tuned on simulated and real data and already serves clinical and research projects at the clinic. The software runs on a single machine or a computing cluster and adapts to other genomes.
europmc-pmc4332301:
Veselin Petrov, Jacques Hille, Bernd Mueller-Roeber, and Tsanko S. Gechev review programmed cell death in plants under environmental stress. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. Plants cannot run from drought, salt, or heat, and when stress runs too high they sacrifice damaged tissue on purpose to save the whole organism.

The death program is active and gene controlled, and reactive oxygen species carry much of the trigger signal. Those same molecules double as stress messengers elsewhere in the plant, so dose and place decide the outcome. The review explains the program's steps and its links to farming, since crops that time this sacrifice well may yield better under harsh conditions.
europmc-pmc4372801:
Madhusoodanan Mottamal, Shilong Zheng, Tien Huang, and Guangdi Wang reviewed a class of cancer drugs in Molecules in 2015. Histone deacetylases are enzymes that strip acetyl tags from histones, the spools DNA wraps around, and in doing so they can silence tumor suppressor genes. Drugs that block these enzymes can restart cell controls and push cancer cells to mature or die. Three such drugs had won approval for certain lymphomas.

The review groups the blockers in trials into four major structural classes. It then surveys computer modeling tools used to reshape those starting drugs into stronger candidates. Modeling-guided design has already yielded varied new structures with different properties. The authors aim to guide chemists toward blockers with greater benefit, for blood cancers and solid tumors alike.
europmc-pmc4374501:
Alison O'Mara-Eves and co-authors pooled trials on involving communities in health programs for disadvantaged groups, in BMC Public Health in 2015. Poorer groups suffer worse health in many rich countries, and engaging their communities is often proposed to close the gap. The team gathered controlled trials from wealthy countries published since 1990, found through systematic reviews and databases, and combined results on behavior, health, confidence, and social support.

Programs that engaged communities did improve several outcomes on average, the pooled results showed, though effects varied. The review also tested whether the style of engagement changed the payoff, comparing approaches where residents merely receive services with ones where they help design or deliver them. Community outcomes were summed up in narrative form. The work gives planners evidence on when engagement helps, rather than treating it as a slogan.
europmc-pmc4433701:
Stefan Hienz, Sweta Paliwal, and Saso Ivanovski reviewed how bone is lost in periodontitis in the Journal of Immunology Research in 2015. Periodontitis is gum disease in which the bone holding the teeth is slowly eaten away, and stopping that loss is a central goal of treatment. The damage is done not by bacteria alone but by the body's own immune response to them.

Cells called osteoclasts carry out bone removal. They form from blood cell ancestors under control of key signals, and inflammatory signals boost their activity in diseased gums. Plaque bacteria under the gum line start the process, and immune cells, including T cells, B cells, and neutrophils, push the balance toward loss. The review maps these steps in detail, showing where future treatments might interrupt the chain before bone is gone.
europmc-pmc4444601:
Silvia Portugal and a large team of co-authors studied atypical memory B cells in people exposed to malaria, reporting in eLife in 2015. Protective antibodies against the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum take years of repeated infections to build. Long exposure also grows a large set of unusual memory B cells, like those seen in lasting viral infections, whose job was unclear.

Gene profiles and mutation patterns showed these atypical cells share a developmental past with normal memory B cells. Yet their surfaces carry many brakes, and signaling through their antibody receptor is blunted. As a result they divide poorly, release fewer signals, and make less antibody when triggered. The authors suggest that, under chronic malaria, normal memory cells turn into this muted state, which may slow the gain of real immunity and complicate vaccine design.
europmc-pmc4536801:
Alice Conigliaro leads a twelve-author team on how liver cancer stem-like cells coach blood vessel cells, in Molecular Cancer in 2015. A subset of liver cancer cells marked CD90 behaves like stem cells, aggressive and prone to spread. The team asked how these cells talk to endothelial cells, which line vessels and feed tumors.

Exosomes from CD90-positive cells, but not from ordinary liver tumor cells, pushed endothelial cells toward forming vessels and sticking to each other. The cargo behind it was H19, a long noncoding RNA enriched in the stem-like cells and shipped out in their exosomes. Adding or removing H19 reproduced or blocked the effect, marking the RNA as a working part of the tumor's vessel-building signal.
europmc-pmc4557301:
Margaret Alexander leads a ten-author team showing that immune cells mail each other gene silencers, in Nature Communications in 2015. MicroRNAs tune gene activity inside the cell that makes them. The team asked whether they also work between cells, riding in exosomes, the tiny sacs cells shed.

Dendritic cells released two inflammation-linked microRNAs, miR-155 and miR-146a, inside exosomes that sister cells then took up. Once inside, the delivered RNAs muted their target genes and reset how the receiver answered endotoxin, a bacterial alarm molecule: miR-155 sharpened the response, miR-146a dulled it. The same transfer happened in living mice, where exosomal miR-146a curbed and miR-155 fueled endotoxin inflammation, a new channel of immune coordination.
europmc-pmc4611001:
Working with colleagues, Tanya F. Vergeldt published a 2015 systematic review of risk factors for pelvic organ prolapse and its return after surgery. Prolapse, where pelvic organs drop from their normal place, is common and has many possible causes. The review searched PubMed and Embase up to August 2014. Only studies from western developed countries with anatomical definitions and adjusted analyses qualified.

Fifteen studies passed the filters. Among thirty candidate factors for first prolapse, four stood out across studies: childbirth count, vaginal delivery, age, and body mass index. For prolapse returning after repair, only the stage of prolapse before surgery was confirmed across studies. The short list gives clinicians a firmer base for counselling women about risk and likely surgical outcomes.
europmc-pmc4653301:
Susanne Hartmann, Anne J. Ridley, and Susanne Lutz published a 2015 review of ROCK1 and ROCK2 kinases in cardiovascular disease. These enzymes sit downstream of Rho proteins and control the cell's actin skeleton, movement, growth, and death. The two forms were long assumed to do the same job. The review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology.

Knockout mouse studies split their roles: ROCK1 drives heart scarring, while ROCK2 drives heart wall thickening. Raised ROCK activity appears across hypertension, angina, heart failure, and stroke, making it a possible disease marker. Drugs that block ROCK lowered the excess activity in patients and measurably improved their condition. The authors stress that the isoform differences matter for designing safer targeted drugs.
europmc-pmc4661801:
In 2015, Sha Li and colleagues published a review on oxidative stress and of plant-based shields in liver disease. Too many reactive oxygen and nitrogen species harm liver tissue. Drink, drugs, pollutants, and radiation can all drive the process, which feeds diseases such as fatty liver and drink-based liver harm.

Animal work shows that shields against this stress can guard the liver, though trials in people are less clear. Plants used as food or in herbal cures often hold strong shields that also calm swelling. The authors searched the PubMed base in depth, with a keen eye on Chinese herbal cures and natural goods. They sum up what drives liver stress and weigh how far shield-based cures can go.
europmc-pmc4691901:
Zhengming Chen, Richard Peto, Maigeng Zhou, and a very large study group tracked smoking deaths in China in The Lancet in 2015. Chinese men smoke more than a third of the world's cigarettes, after use rose first in cities, then in villages. Chinese women, by contrast, smoke far less than their grandmothers did. Two huge nationwide studies, started fifteen years apart, let the team compare the toll across generations.

About two thirds of men smoked. The extra death risk carried by male smokers roughly doubled between the two studies, and smoking's share of deaths at ages forty to seventy-nine climbed. Men who started before age twenty faced twice the death rate of never-smokers. Those who quit by choice largely escaped the risk after a decade. Among women, smoking uptake had fallen tenfold across generations, so their epidemic is fading rather than growing.
europmc-pmc4705701:
Allison Agus, Jérémy Denizot, Jonathan Thévenot, and nine colleagues tested how a Western diet reshapes gut microbes in mice, in Scientific Reports in 2016. Crohn's disease rose through the last century as fat and sugar intake climbed in Western countries. The team fed mice a high-fat, high-sugar diet and watched the gut. The diet built a mildly inflamed gut environment and shifted the microbe mix toward harmful types.

Harmful E. coli relatives overgrew while protective bacteria fell, and helpful short-chain fatty acids dropped. A receptor for those acids, GPR43, also faded, in mice and in Crohn's patients alike. A drug that activates that receptor protected mice from colitis. Moving stool from diet-fed mice into germ-free mice made them easier to infect. The study ties diet, microbes, and one receptor into a single chain of Crohn's risk.
europmc-pmc4708101:
James Dunbar and Charlotte M. Deane built ANARCI, a tool for numbering antibody sequences, described in Bioinformatics in 2016. Antibodies and T-cell receptors bind targets through variable regions whose positions must be labeled consistently before sequences can be compared or engineered. Five numbering schemes compete, each with its own labels and its own fans in different fields. No free public tool could apply them all. ANARCI closes that gap.

Given an amino-acid sequence, the tool classifies the variable domain and stamps it with any of the five schemes: Kabat, Chothia, Enhanced Chothia, IMGT, or AHo. It runs as a download under an open license, with a web interface at the same address. Consistent numbering underpins antibody modeling and drug engineering, where one mislabeled position can mislead a design. By speaking every scheme's language, ANARCI lets separate research communities compare notes without translation errors.
europmc-pmc4732001:
Christoph Ruttkies, Emma L. Schymanski, Sebastian Wolf, Juliane Hollender, and Steffen Neumann relaunched MetFrag in the Journal of Cheminformatics in 2016. MetFrag helps identify unknown small molecules from mass spectrometry data by searching compound databases and predicting how each candidate would fragment. The update refines its algorithms and scoring, and adds outside knowledge the first version ignored. Candidate lists can now pull reference, source, and patent details from public chemistry services.

New filters cut duplicate candidates that differ only in spatial arrangement, and suspect lists of expected compounds can steer the search. Retention time, how long a molecule lingers in the separation column, can now inform rankings too. On test spectra, adding reference and timing data lifted correct top rankings dramatically, especially paired with a second tool. The message is practical: a spectrum alone rarely names a molecule, but context often can.
europmc-pmc4737801:
Scott, Zheng, De Baetselier, and 15 colleagues test a basic assumption about tissue macrophages: that self-renewing resident cells come only from embryonic precursors, never from blood monocytes. They empty the liver's Kupffer cell niche with a toxin-based mouse model and watch what refills it.

Circulating monocytes move in, settle, and slowly take on the gene profile of the Kupffer cells they replaced, becoming long-lived and self-renewing. The same handover happens naturally just after birth, when the growing liver opens new macrophage niches. Given an available niche, then, monocytes can found a resident macrophage population every bit as durable as the embryonic one.
europmc-pmc4776701:
Brian M. Bot leads a twelve-author team in Scientific Data in 2016 presenting data from mPower, a Parkinson's disease study run entirely through an iPhone app. Clinic visits catch this movement disorder only in snapshots a few times a year, yet symptoms swing day to day with dose timing and rest. The study set out to catch that swing with phone sensors and short tasks.

People with and without Parkinson's joined from their phones, answered surveys, and recorded frequent sensor tasks such as tapping, walking, and voice samples. The open release shares that data so outside analysts can test new measures of symptom change. The app code is also open for reuse in other diseases. The authors hope the set seeds a shared science of phone-based health data.
europmc-pmc4861601:
Max A. Horlbeck and co-authors showed in 2016 that nucleosomes, the spools DNA wraps around, block the gene-editing protein Cas9. Cas9 is borrowed from bacteria and now edits, images, and regulates genes in many species. Why some guide RNAs work well and others fail was only partly clear. The team mined large screens in human cells with cutting and non-cutting Cas9 forms.

Strong guides sat almost only where nucleosomes were scarce. In test tubes, a nucleosome on the target directly stopped Cas9 binding and cutting, while machinery that slides spools aside restored access. Target choice for editing must thus weigh DNA wrapping, not just the letter sequence, a rule the study spells out.
europmc-pmc4900601:
Matthew J. Eckelman and Jodi Sherman measured the United States health care sector's pollution footprint in 2016 and its toll on public health. Care delivery ties deeply into industry, energy, and transport. Using an economic life-cycle model fed by national health spending from 2003 to 2013, the pair traced direct and indirect emissions to air, water, and soil.

In 2013 the sector accounted for about 12 percent of acid rain impact and 10 percent of greenhouse gases and smog formation. It also held 9 percent of standard air pollutants, plus small shares of ozone loss and toxic releases. Hospitals and drug supply chains weigh heaviest. Care that heals patients thus sickens the wider public a little, a cost green care can trim.
europmc-pmc4915101:
Mohammad A. Jafri and co-authors reviewed telomeres and telomerase in cancer in 2016, plus therapies that target them. Telomeres cap chromosome ends and guard genome stability, but they shorten with each division until cells stall. Most cancers restart telomerase, the enzyme that rebuilds caps, and so survive endlessly.

Genome scans have mapped genes that set cap length and found hot-spot mutations in the telomerase gene's switch that switch it on. A backup lengthening path, tied to ATRX and DAXX faults, serves other tumors. Tests and drugs based on cap length and enzyme activity are in active build. The review weighs which tumors each approach fits, a guide for a target shared by most cancers.
europmc-pmc4964801:
Maria Kyrgiou leads a team weighing how treatment for early cervical disease affects later pregnancies. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in The BMJ in 2016. Local treatment removes or destroys abnormal cervical tissue before cancer develops. It can save lives, but it cuts tissue that holds a pregnancy. The team searched major databases to April 2016 for studies of obstetric outcomes in treated and untreated women, and graded them by cone depth and comparison group.

Women with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia already face higher preterm birth risk than the general population. Treatment raised that risk further, with cutting methods riskier than ablative ones.
