Risk climbed with the depth and volume of tissue taken. For small excisions the added risk over the disease itself looked small, if present at all. The authors urge doctors to weigh fertility plans in treatment choice and to take no more tissue than the disease requires.
europmc-pmc4993001:
Bo Li and a wide team of co-authors analyze tumor immunity across more than ten thousand cancer samples. Their study appeared in Genome Biology in 2016. How tumors and the immune system interact decides prognosis and drug resistance, yet immune cell counts inside tumors were hard to estimate at scale. The team inferred infiltrating immune cells from RNA sequencing data in a cancer atlas covering twenty-three cancer types. Their estimates tied to clinical features, viral status, and genetic changes more strongly than rival methods.

One antigen, MAGEA3, looked like a vaccine target in melanoma but not in lung cancer. Another, SPAG5, emerged as a candidate across several cancers. Melanomas high in the checkpoint CTLA4 split into two groups by T cell content, which may predict drug response. Chemokine networks also shaped infiltration. The authors offer the atlas of tumor-immune patterns as a resource for immunotherapy design.
europmc-pmc5063301:
Aline Koch and a large co-author group spray RNA to fight a crop fungus, in PLoS Pathogens in 2016. Fusarium graminearum blights barley and other cereals. Plants can be engineered to make double-stranded RNA that silences fungal genes, but engineered crops are slow to approve. The team instead sprayed a long double-stranded RNA onto barley leaves, aimed at three fungal genes the fungus needs to make ergosterol, a vital membrane part.

The spray curbed the fungus not only where it landed but in unsprayed parts of the leaf. Tracing the path gave a surprise. The RNA traveled through the plant's vessels, and it was the fungus's own cutting enzyme, DICER-LIKE 1, that chopped it into the small silencing pieces after the fungus took it up. So the pathogen helps arm its own attacker. The authors discuss spray-based, non-transgenic crop protection with high specificity.
europmc-pmc5076301:
José De-Sola Gutiérrez, Fernando Rodríguez de Fonseca, and Gabriel Rubio review cell phone addiction in Frontiers in Psychiatry in 2016. Whether heavy phone use counts as an addiction is contested, and the review weighs the concept, prevalence, methods, psychology, and linked psychiatric problems in the published studies. Research focus has shifted from the device as a whole to the apps and content it carries.

Researchers agree the problem exists but define and measure it so differently that prevalence figures spread widely. The user profile differs from Internet addiction, abuse peaks among young people, mainly females, and social class shows no clear effect. Problem use travels with traits such as impulsivity and low self-esteem, and with disturbed sleep, anxiety, stress, tobacco, and alcohol. The authors blame loose terminology for much of the confusion and call for shared criteria before the field's numbers can be compared.
europmc-pmc5088501:
Andrew C. Singer, Helen Shaw, Vicki Rhodes, and Alwyn Hart review antibiotic resistance in the environment for the people who regulate it, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Resistance is usually framed as a hospital problem, but resistant bacteria and the chemicals that breed them, antibiotics, metals, and biocides, also flow through water, soil, and waste. These are pathways environmental regulators already police. Action plans against resistance say little about any of this.

Writing from England's Environment Agency as their example, the authors map the drivers and routes of environmental resistance and match them against regulators' normal powers and duties. Their verdict is twofold: current action plans leave relevant pathways untouched, and they do so partly because the underlying science is too thin to write policy on. The review runs thought experiments on how mitigation could work and calls for the knowledge gaps to be closed.
europmc-pmc5142301:
Federica Giordani, Liam J. Morrison, Tim G. Rowan, Harry P. de Koning, and Michael P. Barrett reviewed animal trypanosome diseases and their drug treatment in Parasitology in 2016. These parasites, spread by blood-sucking insects, cause wasting diseases in livestock that have blocked farm development in Africa for centuries and are spreading in South America and Asia.

Drugs remain the main means of control, yet research into new ones stalled for decades, and the few available compounds are losing ground as parasites grow resistant. The review covers the main parasite species, the diseases they cause, and every current treatment and prevention option, with special weight on resistance. With fresh investment arriving, the authors urge deeper study of parasite biology to find new drug targets and understand how resistance works.
europmc-pmc515301:
Amy M. Brunner, Igor A. Yakovlev, and Steven H. Strauss validated reference genes for plant studies in BMC Plant Biology in 2004. Measuring gene activity with real-time PCR is precise only if the yardstick gene used for comparison holds steady, yet few studies check that steadiness or compare candidates.

Working with ten housekeeping genes in poplar trees, they borrowed a stability method from plant breeding, using variance analysis and regression to score each gene across tissues, growth stages, and environments. The candidates differed widely in how stable they were. The authors conclude that testing reference genes for each set of conditions is essential, since a wobbly yardstick can hide real changes or invent false ones in gene activity.
europmc-pmc5286201:
Daniel C. Jeffares and nine colleagues studied large structural variations in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe in Nature Communications in 2017. Structural variations, duplications, deletions, inversions, and swapped segments, are harder to read than small mutations, yet they may drive much of the variety between individuals. The team built a curated catalogue of these variants across a worldwide strain collection.

Copy number variants, stretches present in extra or missing copies, turned over fast, appearing and vanishing even between close relatives. They shifted gene activity in proportion to copy number, inside and beyond the changed region. They also fed measurably into traits such as amino acid levels, growth under stress, and sugar use in winemaking. Rearrangements of the other kinds tied strongly to reproductive isolation, the failure of strains to breed. The authors argue these fleeting changes are a major, undercounted engine of evolution and trait variation.
europmc-pmc5303301:
Rosalind E. Keith, Jesse C. Crosson, Ann S. O'Malley, DeAnn Cromp, and Erin Fries Taylor showed how to turn an implementation framework into fast, usable findings, in Implementation Science in 2017. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) organizes studies, but often too slowly to help the managers actually rolling out a program. The authors wanted evaluation that improves delivery while it is still under way.

They demonstrate with the Comprehensive Primary Care initiative, a multi-payer effort to transform primary care led by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Their team studied 21 practices using field notes and interviews with leaders, clinicians, and staff, coding the material with initiative-specific codes plus CFIR constructs, then comparing across cases. The method surfaced the barrier and facilitator patterns fast enough to adjust the intervention in its second year of four. The authors commend the approach for transformation efforts needing rigorous answers quickly.
europmc-pmc5332601:
Robert A. Fleming addressed the outlook for pneumonia in older patients in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1922. The paper was read to a medical audience in February of that year. Fleming starts from a grim rule: risk from croupous pneumonia climbs with each decade past forty, until death is near certain in old age. Heart lesions and long diseases make it worse.

In a strong adult, the chief threat is spread of the disease to more of the lung. In the older patient, Fleming saw two added dangers. The sound lung grows waterlogged, and a spreading inflammation of the lung lining follows. He gives cases that show the heart swelling as the disease grew, with missed beats and fluid at the lung base. His close gives a bold change of treatment plan meant to guard against those two late turns.
europmc-pmc535701:
Shahrad Taheri, Ling Lin, Diane Austin, Terry Young, and Emmanuel Mignot linked short sleep to hunger hormones in PLoS Medicine in 2004. Large surveys had tied short nightly sleep to higher body weight, but the path was unclear. Two gut hormones pull appetite in rival ways: leptin curbs it, ghrelin stokes it. The team checked if sleep length moves those hormones in a long-run sleep study group.

More than a thousand adults from the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort had a night in the sleep lab, kept diaries, and gave morning blood after fasting. Weight tracked sleep in a U shape, with short sleepers heaviest. In those who slept under eight hours, less sleep meant more weight in step. Short sleep also came with low leptin and high ghrelin, a mix that should drive eating. The gaps held when body weight itself was counted out.
europmc-pmc5370101:
Hélène-Marie Lanoiselée led a team that screened French families for early Alzheimer's genes, in PLoS Medicine in 2017. Three genes can hand down the disease in a dominant way when flawed: APP and the two presenilins. They were found in the nineteen nineties, but sorting which variants truly cause harm stays hard. Large case sets help sort them, and France has tracked such families since 1993.

This update adds five years of screening at twenty-eight hospitals. The national set of mutation families now stands at one hundred and seventy. Fifty-three of the families were new in this round. The team also screened lone cases with onset before the early fifties. About one in eight of those carried a flaw too, and where parent DNA could be checked, each flaw had arisen fresh in the patient. The set sharpens variant calls for clinics.
europmc-pmc5388101:
Yuelong Shu and John McCauley trace the rise of GISAID in a 2017 article in Eurosurveillance. GISAID is a global system for sharing flu virus data fast. It began after bird flu spread in 2006, when key virus data sat in a closed archive that few could reach. That block slowed the world response and raised charges of unfair access.

The new system opened in 2008 with a deal: those who share data get credit, and users agree to work with the teams that sent samples in. The authors say this trust-based model won wide backing from health bodies and labs. It now serves as the main route for rapid sharing of flu gene data during outbreaks.
europmc-pmc5393901:
Lasse Folkersen leads a large author group in a 2017 PLoS Genetics study that maps gene spots tied to blood proteins linked to heart disease. New lab tools can now measure hundreds of blood proteins in thousands of people at once. The team paired such measures for 83 proteins with gene scans in people who carried several heart risk factors, then checked the finds in separate groups.

They found 79 gene spots tied to protein levels, and most held up in the check groups. For many spots they could sketch a likely path from gene to protein. They also tested whether the spots affect heart artery disease itself. The work gives later studies a base for judging which blood proteins truly drive disease and might serve as drug targets.
europmc-pmc5446901:
Yue and co-authors compare genome change in tame baker's yeast against its wild cousin. Their research article appeared in Nature Genetics. Big structural changes shape evolution and disease. Short-read sequencing misses many of them. Long reads can span the tricky zones. The team built end-to-end genomes for twelve yeast strains. Seven came from domesticated Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Five came from wild Saccharomyces paradoxus.

The two species change in opposite styles. In chromosome cores, the wild yeast gains balanced swaps faster. Those include inversions and translocations. The tame yeast gains unbalanced changes faster. Those include fresh insertions, deletions, and duplications. Near chromosome ends, both species reshuffle heavily. The tame yeast reshuffles even faster there. The authors link the contrast to human handling. Brewing and baking may have bent genome evolution. The assemblies give a sharp base for yeast population genetics.
europmc-pmc5462901:
Bonnet and co-authors argue that the harmless microbes inside ticks matter as much as the harmful ones. Their review appeared in a journal on infection and cell biology. Ticks rank among the top disease carriers in the world. Most research focuses on the germs that cause disease. Ticks also host many microbes that do no harm. Before 1990, those residents were mostly ignored. Any microbe found in a tick was presumed a threat.

Gene sequencing changed that view. Ticks carry a rich inner community. Their effects run from harmful to helpful. They aid feeding, growth, and breeding. They help ticks cope with stress and tune their immune systems. They may even shape how disease germs pass to new hosts. Some famous disease genera, such as Rickettsia, have mostly harmless kin in ticks. Sorting out these ties could yield new ways to control ticks.
europmc-pmc5486101:
Chude and Amaravadi present a review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences on blocking autophagy in cancer. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system for worn parts and proteins. Advanced tumors lean on that recycling to survive stress. Blocking it could make other therapies bite harder. Lab evidence for the idea keeps growing.

Hydroxychloroquine is the only approved drug that blocks autophagy so far. Trials use it alone and alongside standard treatments. Early results show added tumor shrinkage in lab models. The drug is weak, though, so stronger blockers are in development. The review sorts candidates by the recycling step they target.
europmc-pmc5512801:
Ormond and Freeman present a review in Materials on dye sensitizers for photodynamic therapy. This cancer treatment pairs a light-absorbing dye with light and oxygen. The excited dye spawns reactive oxygen that kills nearby tumor cells. Photofrin, the first approved sensitizer, remains highly effective. A handful of related dyes have since won approval.

Most approved agents are porphyrin-like compounds, they note. Some are given as precursor drugs the body converts itself. Dyes outside that family remain experimental so far. Anthraquinone, cyanine, and curcumin-based candidates are in trials. The review explains how the therapy works and grades each class.
europmc-pmc5558801:
Bickerdike and co-authors present a systematic review in BMJ Open. Their subject is social prescribing in British primary care. Doctors refer patients to a link worker, who connects them with community support. The aim is better health and well-being without more medicine.

Such programs are spreading fast in the National Health Service. The team searched nine databases and found 15 evaluations. Most were small and weak in design. All carried a high risk of bias. Few used control groups or standard measures. Still, most claimed positive results. The authors say the evidence cannot yet judge success or value for money. Future studies must compare groups and report costs. Readers get a sober check on a popular idea.
europmc-pmc5602001:
Schoonenboom and Johnson explain how to build a mixed methods research design. Such studies combine at least one qualitative and one quantitative part. Done well, the mix gives breadth and depth. Done carelessly, it gives a muddle.

Seven major design choices come first. They cover purpose, the study's theoretical drive, and timing. Timing asks whether parts run at once or in sequence. The point where results merge needs a clear choice too. So do fixed versus flexible plans and overall complexity. Ten further choices sit below those. Two case studies show full designs being built step by step. Validity stays in view throughout. Readers get a checklist-style guide for planning sound mixed studies.
europmc-pmc5618501:
Vizoso and co-authors review the mesenchymal stem cell secretome in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Stem cell therapy was once credited to cells settling in and turning into new tissue. Implanted cells, it turns out, rarely last long. Their benefits likely flow from what they release.

That output, the secretome, can be bottled as conditioned media or exosomes. A cell-free product is easier to make, store, and ship. It could sit ready to use off the shelf. Safety and quality rules still need to be built. One promising source is the human uterine cervix. Its stem cells come from a routine Pap smear, with little pain. They grow fast and in bulk. Readers get the logic of therapy without cells.
europmc-pmc5640601:
Carhart-Harris and co-authors report a brain imaging study in Scientific Reports. It tests psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression. Patients got the drug with psychological support. Brain scans were taken before and after treatment. The scans measured blood flow and resting-state connectivity. Good data came from 16 of 19 patients.

Symptoms fell in all 19 patients at one week. At five weeks, 47 percent met response criteria. Blood flow dropped in the temporal cortex after treatment. That drop included the amygdala, and it tracked symptom relief. Connectivity rose within the default-mode network. Some connectivity shifts predicted response at five weeks. The authors propose a reset mechanism for the benefit.
europmc-pmc5660601:
Ponomarova and co-authors report a microbial community study in Cell Systems. It shows how yeast feeds lactic acid bacteria. The yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, used in food and drink. In nitrogen-rich settings, yeast adjusts its metabolism. It secretes a pool of compounds, especially amino acids. That overflow lets two bacterial species survive. They are Lactobacillus plantarum and Lactococcus lactis.

Nitrogen supply and gene control pathways jointly tune this niche creation. In grape juice, the overflow aided L. plantarum growth. In a lactose medium, mutual benefit emerged with L. lactis. The work shows how one species' metabolic choices help others. Such cross-feeding can build stable mixed communities.
europmc-pmc5742601:
Picard and co-authors report the 2017 IUIS committee listing of inborn errors of immunity. The catalog counts 354 such errors as of February 2017. Work began under the World Health Organization in 1970. The union took over the task twenty years later.

The report sorts the errors into tables by shared disease workings. New sequencing tools have sped the growth of the list. Groups changed most include antibody faults and immune dysregulation. The authors present the listing as a key reference for the field. A companion paper gives a version sorted by patient signs.
europmc-pmc5742801:
Bonser and Erle review airway mucus in asthma, with a focus on two mucin proteins. Asthma airways make too much mucus, and it clears poorly. Plugs can block airflow and drive much of the illness. The gel forming mucins MUC5AC and MUC5B form the core of that mucus.

Gene activity for both mucins shifts in asthma, the authors note. Fresh work shows how each one shapes the bad mucus gel. Changes in stored and secreted mucin add to the faulty gel. Sorting their roles may point to treatments that clear plugs without harming defense.
europmc-pmc5748601:
Kuzmich and co-authors review drugs that tune the TLR4 signaling pathway. TLR4 starts innate immune responses when it senses bacterial endotoxin. Overactivation drives chronic inflammation and sepsis, a life threatening state. No specific drug for sepsis exists yet.

The review covers small molecules in early or clinical testing. Some block the TLR4-MyD88 path, others the TLR4-TRIF path. Results in animal sepsis models are set out and weighed with care. The authors stress how often rodent gains fail to carry into humans. Natural and synthetic leads both get a full hearing.
europmc-pmc5850801:
Ogilvie, Bouckaert, and Drummond introduce StarBEAST2, a faster engine for species tree inference. Their paper appeared in Molecular Biology and Evolution. Bayesian coalescent methods read species history from many genes at once. The gold-standard tool slowed to a crawl on modern data.

StarBEAST2 integrates population sizes analytically instead of sampling them. New search operators speed the chain's mixing. Real data sets ran more than ten times faster. Simulated ones averaged roughly thirty times faster. A relaxed clock model now tracks each species' own substitution rate. Concatenation, the speedy shortcut, distorts exactly those rates.
europmc-pmc5855601:
Sciacchitano and co-authors review galectin-3, a protein tied to many diseases. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Galectin-3 helps control cell growth, cell contact, and inflammation. Because it touches so many basic tasks, it shows up in many illnesses. The review works through those illnesses in alphabetical order. They range from cancer and fibrosis to chronic inflammation and scarring.

The authors gather studies on what galectin-3 does in each condition. They weigh its value as a diagnostic and outlook marker. They also discuss it as a possible drug target. Interest in this protein has grown fast over recent decades. Readers get one wide survey of a molecule with many roles.
europmc-pmc5871901:
Chen and co-authors review why breast cancer spreads to certain organs. Their article appeared in NPJ Precision Oncology. Spread accounts for about 90 percent of breast cancer deaths. Yet cancer cells do not land in organs at random. Tumour subtype and host organ features steer the pattern. Signals pass between cancer cells and host tissue before arrival. That talk prepares a niche that welcomes arriving cells.

The review covers gene and epigenetic changes in tumour cells. It also covers stem-like traits, exosomes, and small RNAs. Circulating tumour cells and immune responses get attention too. Local tissue structure shapes whether colonies take hold. The authors aim at better prediction and new therapies.
europmc-pmc5908901:
Sproston and Ashworth review the role of C-reactive protein at inflamed sites. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. This blood protein can rise a thousand-fold during infection. It is made mainly in the liver. It comes in two forms with opposite traits. The native form can split into five single units.

The two forms act in opposing ways, the authors report. The native form aids cell eating and orderly cell death. The single-unit form draws immune cells to inflamed tissue. It also delays cell death and lifts some signals. Early studies often failed to say which form was used. Readers learn why that detail changes past results.
europmc-pmc5995401:
Taciak and co-authors test the stability of the RAW 264.7 cell line across serial passages. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. This mouse macrophage-like line has served labs for over forty years. Its stability across passages was often debated but never proven. The team tracked cells from passage 5 to passage 50. They checked macrophage genes, surface markers, and cell functions. Phagocytosis and nitric oxide output were among the tests.

Traits stayed stable from passage 10 to passage 30, they report. Beyond that point the line should not be used. Late-passage drift could undermine data reliability. The paper gives labs a clear usage window.
europmc-pmc6030101:
Legon and co-authors test focused ultrasound on the human motor cortex. Their research article appeared in Scientific Reports. The method sends acoustic energy into the brain. It aims to change neuron activity without surgery. Effects on movement areas were still unknown.

The team paired ultrasound with magnetic stimulation. That pairing let them probe motor neuron responses. Ultrasound lowered the size of evoked muscle responses. It also weakened one form of cortical facilitation. A separate inhibition measure stayed unchanged. Volunteers reacted faster on a simple response task. The authors read this as net neuronal inhibition. Readers get the first report of such effects in humans. The work points toward new brain treatment tools.
europmc-pmc6052101:
Greene and co-authors test whether tasks beat rest for reading traits from brain scans. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Functional connectivity maps how brain regions work together. Models built from resting scans predict traits only weakly. The team drew on two large, independent data sets.

Scans taken during cognitive tasks predicted fluid intelligence far better. The best model explained over 20 percent of score variance. Rest-based models explained under 6 percent. Which task worked best varied by sex. The authors compare tasks to a cardiac stress test for the heart. Readers get a strong case for task-based scans in brain-behavior research.
europmc-pmc6146601:
Shen and co-authors wrote a review in Journal of Hematology and Oncology on anlotinib, a new cancer drug taken by mouth. Anlotinib blocks several tyrosine kinases, enzymes that help tumors grow and build blood vessels. Its targets include receptors for VEGF, FGF, and PDGF, plus c-kit.

The review sums up the drug's clinical development. In a phase III trial, it beat placebo on survival in advanced lung cancer that had progressed after two prior treatments. China's drug agency approved it as a third-line option for that cancer. A further trial showed longer time without growth in soft tissue sarcoma. Readers get one account of where this multi-target drug stands.
europmc-pmc6162501:
Zhang and co-authors wrote a review in Cancers on the p53 pathway in glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor. p53 is a tumor suppressor that orders damaged cells to die and guards genome stability. Its pathway is faulty in 84 percent of glioblastoma patients and 94 percent of cell lines.

The review explains how broken p53 signaling helps tumor cells invade, grow, and dodge death. It also supports cancer stem cells, the cells that regrow tumors. Small RNAs that tune the pathway are covered as well. Attempts to exploit p53 for therapy have so far disappointed. The authors call for better models of mutant p53 to close the knowledge gaps.
europmc-pmc6261201:
Nkhata and co-authors review how fermentation and germination raise the food value of grains and legumes. Their review appeared in Food Science and Nutrition. Grains and beans hold rich nutrients, but many stay locked away. Plant compounds such as phytates bind minerals and block protein digestion. Those locks keep nutrients from reaching the body. Both old processing methods can open them.

Soaking seeds until they sprout wakes up enzymes inside them. Fermentation wakes the same enzyme set through microbe action. Enzymes such as phytase break down the blocking compounds. They also split large starches and proteins into simpler forms. The body can then absorb more iron, zinc, and protein. Both methods are cheap and long used in home kitchens. The review explains the enzyme steps behind their benefit.
europmc-pmc6323901:
Noronha and co-authors introduce the Virtual Metabolic Human database. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The database links five resources on metabolism. They cover human metabolism, gut microbes, disease, and nutrition. A set of metabolic maps ties them together. The system holds 5,180 distinct metabolites. It also holds 17,730 reactions and 3,695 human genes.

Microbe coverage spans 818 gut species. Food items number 8,790 in the nutrition arm. Users can design diets with a built-in tool. Seven maps let users visualize metabolic data. A friendly website and code interface give access. Links reach 57 other web resources. The database supports hypothesis building across biomedicine.
europmc-pmc6351101:
Yao and co-authors show mitochondrial fusion fuels dividing cells' energy rise. Their study appeared in eLife. Dividing cells burn more glucose and release more lactate. That pattern is called the Warburg effect. Yet these mouse fibroblasts also raised real respiration. Oxygen-based energy output nearly doubled in growth. Coupling efficiency rose about 30 percent too.

Joined, fused mitochondria supported both increases. Blocking a fusion protein, Mfn2, slowed cell division. Adding extra Mfn2 sped division up instead. Without fusion, energy output fell while ATP held steady. Cells switched from releasing to consuming aspartate. A cancer gene, Ras, pushed mitochondria to multiply. That raised energy output even higher. Fusion thus backs growth in normal and cancer cells.
europmc-pmc6355901:
Hart and co-authors show how surface chemistry tunes MXene conductivity. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. MXenes are flat, two-dimensional materials that conduct well. They already lead in shielding and sensing uses. They also store energy in devices. Theory predicted surface groups control their electrons.

The team tested that idea inside an electron microscope. Heating in vacuum stripped surface groups away. Conductivity rose as the groups left. Spectroscopic tools tracked the surface during the process. Adding material between the layers also changed behavior. Transport flipped between metallic and semiconductor-like modes. The work gives a direct handle on MXene tuning. Better control could lift device performance further.
europmc-pmc6360801:
Zhang and co-authors report a research article in Molecular Cancer on a circular RNA in stomach cancer. The RNA, called circNRIP1, is found at higher levels in gastric cancer tissue. Circular RNAs can act as sponges that soak up smaller RNAs.

Tests show circNRIP1 soaks up miR-149-5p, a small RNA that normally holds back growth. Freeing the AKT1 and mTOR signals then lets cancer cells grow and move. Blocking circNRIP1 slowed tumor traits in cell tests. The authors present this RNA chain as a driver of gastric cancer spread. It may also serve as a target for future drugs.
europmc-pmc6375701:
Zhang and co-authors present a research article in eLife on tau filaments made in the test tube. Tau clumps drive several brain diseases, and each disease shows its own filament shape. Labs often grow tau filaments with heparin, but whether those match disease forms was unclear.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team solved structures for filaments from two tau forms. The four-repeat form made several filament types with a kinked hairpin fold. The three-repeat form made one uniform type with a paired core. Both differed from the Alzheimer and Pick disease structures. The authors question how well heparin-grown filaments model real disease.
europmc-pmc6409601:
Bohnsack and co-authors review RNA methyltransferases in Genes. These enzymes add a methyl mark, called m5C, to RNA letters. The mark appears on many RNA kinds, from transfer RNAs to messenger RNAs.

Two enzyme families do this work in eukaryotes, the NSUN family and DNMT2. Recent work has named which RNAs each enzyme marks. Shape studies show how each one picks its exact target letter. The marks help control protein making and cell growth. Faults in these enzymes link to disease, which the review also traces. Each mark sits at a known site.
europmc-pmc6441201:
Huang and co-authors identify a circular RNA from the AKT3 gene that helps gastric cancer withstand cisplatin, a mainstay chemotherapy for the disease. circAKT3 ran higher in resistant tumors and cell lines than in sensitive ones, and patients on cisplatin whose tumors carried more of it showed more aggressive disease and shorter disease-free survival.

The circle works as a sponge for miR-198, freeing the growth signal PIK3R1 to rise. With that signal up, cancer cells repaired cisplatin's DNA damage faster and resisted programmed death, in culture and in animals. Silencing circAKT3 reversed the protection. The findings nominate the circle as a drug target for patients whose tumors stop answering cisplatin.
europmc-pmc6447501:
VanderWeele lays out practical principles for choosing which confounders to control in observational studies when a full causal diagram is not available. Wrong choices can leave bias in place or create new bias, so selection rules matter for any causal claim. The proposal assumes researchers know, for each covariate, whether it causes the exposure, the outcome, or both.

Control every covariate that causes the exposure, the outcome, or both; drop anything known to be a pure instrument; and add proxies for unmeasured common causes of both. Warnings follow about proxy variables that may open collider paths instead. Statistical selection methods are then judged against these causal principles.
europmc-pmc6459001:
The GBD 2016 Neurology Collaborators deliver the Global Burden of Disease estimates for brain and nerve diseases across 195 countries from 1990 to 2016. Fifteen groups are covered, from stroke and migraine to dementia and meningitis. Bayesian models combined how common each disease is, new cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost, by age and sex.

In 2016 these diseases were the world's leading cause of health loss, at 276 million DALYs, and the second cause of death, at 9.0 million. Stroke alone took 42.2 percent of the DALYs; migraine, dementia, and meningitis followed. Total deaths rose 39 percent as the world grew and aged, even while rates for a fixed age mix fell by about a quarter. Only tetanus, meningitis, and encephalitis shrank outright.
europmc-pmc6496801:
Zeng and co-authors review pyroptosis, the inflammatory form of programmed cell death, as a driver of cardiovascular disease. Unlike quiet apoptosis, pyroptosis bursts cells open: caspase enzymes activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, which matures interleukin-1β and interleukin-18 and lyses the cell, spilling inflammatory contents into tissue. First spotted in infected macrophages in 1992, the pathway now implicates itself in atherosclerosis and heart attack.

In diabetic heart muscle, high glucose and oxidative stress recruit the inflammasome through the TXNIP protein, killing cardiomyocytes and degrading pump function. The review assembles mechanisms across heart cell types and surveys therapies aimed at throttling pyroptosis, some already in clinical trials, while weighing how much cell death a tissue can afford to lose.
europmc-pmc6499401:
Poggio and co-authors report a research article in Cell on how tumors use PD-L1 to evade immune attack. PD-L1 on tumor cells binds PD-1 on T cells and shuts those cells down. Antibody drugs that block PD-L1 help some patients, but many tumors resist them. The team studied whether tumors also release PD-L1 on exosomes, tiny vesicles shed by cells.

They report that many tumor cells secrete most of their PD-L1 on exosomes, not on their surface. Removing exosomal PD-L1 slowed tumor growth, even in models resistant to antibody drugs. It also let T cells activate in draining lymph nodes. Exposure to cells lacking this form suppressed wild-type tumors at distant sites months later. Blocking both forms worked better than either alone, pointing to a new treatment target.
europmc-pmc6520701:
Gai and co-authors review lipid buildup in chronic kidney disease. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Obesity and high blood lipids are top risk factors for this disease. That hints that fat stored in kidney tissue harms its function. Free fatty acids look most harmful of all.

Fat builds up when uptake rises and burning falls. Uptake routes include the CD36 receptor and fatty acid transport proteins. Excess fatty acids damage podocytes and tubule cells. They do so through reactive oxygen species and lipid peroxidation. Mitochondrial harm and inflammation follow. Not all fats are bad, though. EPA and DHA may slow disease progress. Diet change and lipid drugs may help patients.
europmc-pmc6524401:
Velazquez-Salinas and co-authors give their view on interleukin 6 in viral infections. Their opinion note appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. It follows their work on vesicular stomatitis virus in swine. There, strong IL-6 rise tracked with a more virulent strain.

IL-6 is a cytokine made by many cell types. It signals mainly through the JAK/STAT3 pathway. Some studies show IL-6 is vital for a sound immune response. Knockout mouse work backs that view for flu and vaccinia. Other studies link high IL-6 with worse viral disease. The authors weigh both sides. They suggest IL-6 can help the host or aid virus survival.
europmc-pmc6585101:
Kruger and co-authors round up the latest trends in cancer immunotherapy as of 2019, writing in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research. Two engines drive the field: checkpoint inhibitors that release T-cell brakes, and CAR T cells engineered to hunt cancer. The review distills the newest clinical and translational findings from major meetings and journals.

For checkpoint blockade, the frontier is combinations — with chemotherapy, radiation and each other — plus use around surgery, new tumor types, response prediction and safer toxicity handling. For CAR T cells, larger cohorts confirmed the early results in leukemia and lymphoma, while strategies multiply to carry the approach into other blood cancers and solid tumors. A geographic note closes the survey: CAR T trials now cluster in the US and China.
europmc-pmc6586801:
Lee, Ko, Ju and Eltzschig review hypoxia signaling and its drug targets, writing in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. When oxygen runs low, cells stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor, or HIF. In plentiful oxygen, enzymes tag HIF for destruction within minutes. In hypoxia the tags stop, HIF survives, and it switches on a couple of hundred genes — from erythropoietin, which orders more red cells, to vessel growth and sugar-burning programs.

The review follows HIF through four organs: heart, lung, liver and kidney. Its role flips with timing, protecting tissue in acute injury yet feeding harm in chronic disease. The closing sections survey efforts to drug the pathway, stabilizing HIF where repair is wanted and blocking it where it is not.
europmc-pmc6610901:
Guzon-Illescas and co-authors study death rates after osteoporotic hip fracture. Their cohort study appears in the Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research. Hip fractures in older people carry heavy costs in health and function. Only a minority regain their prior independence. Death rates after such fractures stay debated.

The team used discharge records from a hospital near Madrid. They tracked 3,992 patients treated from 1999 to 2015. Most patients were women, with an average age near 84. One third had died within twelve months. The one-year death rate rose about 2% per year. Men died at higher rates than women. Age, dementia, heart failure, and care-home residence all raised risk.
europmc-pmc6626501:
Bouillon and co-authors review the actions of vitamin D in bone and beyond. Their review appears in Endocrine Reviews. Vitamin D prevents rickets and soft bones. It works mainly by aiding calcium uptake in the gut. Deficiency speeds bone loss and fracture risk in the elderly. Supplements with calcium cut that risk in deficient groups. The vitamin's receptor sits in tissues throughout the body. That spread hints at many further roles.

Animal and genetic studies support wide extraskeletal effects. These span immunity, muscle, skin, and reproduction. Observational work links low status to many diseases. Trial results, though, remain mixed overall. Mendelian randomization best supports a link with multiple sclerosis. The authors call for sharper trials to settle causality.
europmc-pmc6729001:
Peng and co-authors traced a chain by which a gene regulator spreads colorectal cancer. The regulator, METTL3, adds chemical marks to RNA. It is turned up in many cancers, including this one. The team measured it in large patient samples and tested its role in cells and animals.

High METTL3 matched abnormal RNA marking and more tumor spread. Raising it made cancer cells migrate and invade more, in dishes and in mice. METTL3 marks a precursor of a small RNA called miR-1246 and helps it mature. That RNA then silences SPRED2, a brake on the MAPK pathway. Cutting this chain may slow the cancer's spread.
europmc-pmc6733901:
Xia and co-authors examine pyroptosis, a fiery form of programmed cell death, in cancer. Pyroptosis is run by the gasdermin protein family. It comes with inflammation and immune responses. Its effect on cancer cuts both ways, depending on the tissue and genes involved.

Driven pyroptosis can stop tumors from forming and growing. Yet as an inflammatory death, it can also build a setting where tumors thrive. Many tumor cells silence a key gasdermin gene, making pyroptosis hard to trigger. Some chemotherapy drugs can raise that gene's activity again. Choosing drugs by gasdermin levels may sharpen treatment, the authors suggest.
europmc-pmc6750801:
Fettweis and co-authors link the vaginal microbiome to preterm birth. More than 10% of births worldwide come early. In the United States, women of African ancestry bear a far higher risk. The team followed pregnant women, most of them of African ancestry, with repeated sampling. Their project shared data from about 12,000 samples.

The study compared 45 preterm births with 90 term controls. Women who delivered early had lower levels of a protective bacterium, Lactobacillus crispatus. They had higher levels of several other microbes, including BVAB1 and Sneathia amnii. Those microbes tracked with inflammation signals in vaginal fluid. The first full genomes of two of the microbes are reported here.
europmc-pmc6778101:
Spohn and co-authors tested how easily germs learn to resist antimicrobial peptides. Such peptides are promising new antibiotics, but fears of resistance dog them. The team grew E. coli in the lab against 14 diverse peptides and 12 standard drugs. They then measured how much protection the germs gained, and whether it crossed from one drug to the next.

Against some peptides, such as tachyplesin II and cecropin P1, the germs stayed nearly defenseless. Gene changes and gene gains gave them only weak shields. Germs already proof against standard drugs gained no extra safety from these peptides. DNA from soil germs conferred none at all. Plain physical and chemical traits foretold which peptides would hold up. Such peptides could make durable new drugs.
europmc-pmc6818701:
Meites and co-authors report updated vaccine advice in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. The paper comes from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which guides vaccine use in the United States. HPV vaccine prevents infections that can lead to several cancers. Routine shots at age 11 or 12 years were already advised. Catch-up rules for adults were the open question.

The committee extended catch-up vaccination to all persons through age 26 years. For adults aged 27 through 45 years, it advised shared clinical decision-making with a doctor instead of a blanket rule. The report reviews falling infection rates since vaccination began. It also weighs cost studies behind the change.
europmc-pmc6828701:
Liang and co-authors report a study in Cell Death and Disease on a long non-coding RNA in bowel cancer. Such RNAs do not build proteins but steer cell behaviour. One, named RPPH1, was found at high levels in colorectal cancer tissue. High levels tracked with later stage disease and poorer survival. Spread to distant sites is the main danger in this cancer.

The team showed RPPH1 drives spread in cell and animal tests. It binds a structural protein, TUBB3, pushing cancer cells into a mobile state. Cancer cells also package RPPH1 into exosomes, tiny parcels that reprogram nearby macrophages into a tumour-helping form. Blocking this RNA, the authors suggest, could slow metastasis.
europmc-pmc6863901:
Steen and co-authors dispute a claim about how much of microbial life science can reach, in The ISME Journal. A recent paper had argued that high proportions of bacteria in most environments have been grown in culture. If true, the famous dark matter of microbiology would shrink. The authors reanalysed part of that paper's data and found fault.

They identify technical errors, above all a similarity calculation that ignored gaps in gene sequences. The original also leaned on 16S gene surveys biased toward cultured kinds. Deeper still, they argue, similarity of one gene cannot prove an organism can be cultured. Their verdict: most bacterial and archaeal taxa remain uncultured.
europmc-pmc6908601:
Malik and co-authors propose a trait-based scheme for soil microbes, in The ISME Journal. Soil microbes decide the fate of most carbon entering the ground, whether it returns to the air or stays stored. That balance shapes the climate. Predicting how it shifts as the world warms requires knowing how microbes live, not just which kinds are present.

The authors borrow life-history thinking from plant and animal ecology. Microbes can be sorted by strategy: fast growth when food is rich, tough survival when it is scarce, or investment in enzymes that mine complex carbon. Enzyme gene families that cut plant cell walls illustrate the mining strategy. The scheme is meant to plug into soil carbon models.
europmc-pmc6928101:
Maier and co-authors set out principles for stroke neurorehabilitation. Their synthesis appeared in Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience. It draws on motor learning and brain plasticity research. The goal is real recovery, not just compensation. Lasting gains cut impairment and lift quality of life.

The authors unify findings from neuroscience and clinical practice. They identify fifteen principles of motor learning. They include massed and spaced practice, plus dosage. Task-specific and goal-oriented practice also feature. So do rising difficulty and variable practice. Feedback, rhythmic cueing, and motor imagery round out the set. Each principle is tied to trials that used it well. Evidence spans healthy subjects and stroke patients.
europmc-pmc6973101:
Owen and co-authors present MetaInsight, a free web tool that lets non-programmers run network meta-analyses. Their article appeared in Research Synthesis Methods. Network meta-analysis compares many treatments at once, even ones never tested head to head. Health decision makers rely on it, but existing software demands heavy statistical coding skill.

MetaInsight wraps established R packages in a point-and-click web page. Users need only a standard browser. Results appear as visual plots that can be questioned in real time. Sensitivity checks can test how sturdy a published analysis is, live, in front of decision makers. An example shows the tool at work. The authors hope it widens who can run and challenge such analyses, and inspires similar tools for other specialist methods.
europmc-pmc7010701:
Khalil and co-authors measure a blood marker of nerve damage across normal aging. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Neurofilament light protein leaks from injured nerve fibres into fluid and blood. New ultra-sensitive tests can read it in serum, allowing repeat checks without a spinal tap.

The team tested 335 people from a population cohort, with brain scans and cognitive exams, and retested 103 after about six years. Levels rose with age and spread wider past 60, hinting that quiet nerve injury speeds up late in life. Higher levels tracked with shrinking brain volumes, both at one time point and over the follow-up. Hidden illnesses likely drive part of the rise. The authors argue serum levels can flag subclinical brain change in apparently healthy older people. That makes the marker a candidate tool for watching brain health and testing protective treatments.
europmc-pmc7020001:
Desforges and co-authors review respiratory viruses and the brain in the journal Viruses. These viruses usually cause mild illness in the airways. In newborns, older people, and those with weak immunity, they can cause far worse disease. The authors focus on a less known risk: spread into the central nervous system.

The review gathers evidence that several respiratory viruses can invade nerves and brain tissue. Human coronaviruses get special attention. Once in the nervous system, a virus may harm cells directly. It may also trigger immune responses that damage tissue. The authors link such infections to encephalitis and to longer-term nerve disorders. They argue that these pathogens are under-rated as a cause of brain disease.
europmc-pmc7020601:
Coetzee presents an updated identification key in Malaria Journal, as sole author. The key covers adult female Anopheles mosquitoes of the Afrotropical region. Some of these species are among the world's most efficient carriers of malaria parasites. Correct identification is a basic tool for malaria work.

The key builds on the pictorial key that Gillies and Coetzee published in 1987. Species described in the 32 years since then are now included. New drawings and new paired choices were added where needed. Subspecies are left out. Anopheles stephensi appears for the first time as found on the African continent. A full list of known species, with their naming and classification, supports the key itself.
europmc-pmc7034601:
Krumbhaar surveys the early history of anatomy in the United States in the Annals of Medical History, writing as sole author. In a young country, he notes, the growth of a science can be traced from its beginnings. The first settlers relied on educated leaders, midwives, and ships' surgeons, yet the need to learn the body from actual dissection was recognised early.

The hard part was getting bodies to dissect, a problem everywhere but worst in a healthy, thinly settled land. Krumbhaar follows the first anatomy teachers and lectures, including William Shippen Jr., whose course at the College of Philadelphia began in November 1765 with about sixty lectures on the fresh subject. The essay records how anatomical teaching took root in America despite scarce material and public suspicion.
europmc-pmc7045401:
Yang and co-authors investigate how oesophageal cancer recruits helper cells in Molecular Cancer. Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma carries a poor prognosis, and earlier work tied the chemokine CCL2 and tumour-associated macrophages to its development. How those macrophages arrive, switch into a tumour-friendly mode, and shield the cancer was not clear.

Using human tissue arrays and a cancer genome database, the team found rising CCL2 alongside macrophage build-up, both predicting poor survival. In rat and mouse models, blocking the CCL2-CCR2 axis sharply cut tumour incidence by stopping macrophage recruitment. The macrophages in turn support immune evasion through PD-1 signalling. Experiments with knockout mice and cultured cells pinned down the chain. The work names the CCL2-CCR2 route as a treatment target for a cancer that badly needs new options.
europmc-pmc7082301:
Tangye and co-authors deliver the 2019 update of the IUIS list of inborn errors of immunity, in the Journal of Clinical Immunology. An expert panel of the International Union of Immunological Societies compiled the report. These inherited faults leave people open to infection, autoimmunity, allergy, and cancer.

The update documents 430 inborn errors of immunity. It adds 64 gene defects found in the two years since the prior update, or confirmed since then. Faster gene sequencing keeps expanding the list and sharpening treatment choices for single genes. Doctors get a handbook for diagnosing these disorders, and researchers get a map of the immune pathways behind them.
europmc-pmc7116101:
Casewell and co-authors review why snake venom differs so much between and within species, and what that means for bite victims, in Trends in Pharmacological Sciences. Snakebite strikes about 1.8 million people a year worldwide. Venom mixtures vary, and that variation can make standard antivenom fail.

New laboratory technologies now let researchers catalogue venom ingredients in full and trace how gene duplication and natural selection reshaped toxin families over time. Different toxin mixes produce different illnesses in victims, from bleeding to paralysis. The review closes with treatment designs meant to work across venom variants, aimed at the world's most lethal neglected tropical disease.
europmc-pmc7118901:
Shen and co-authors show that a chemical mark on RNA speeds up sugar burning in colorectal cancer and drives its growth, in Molecular Cancer. The mark, called m6A, is the most common chemical edit on messenger RNA. The team linked the mark-writing enzyme METTL3 to glucose uptake scans in patients.

METTL3 directly stabilised two genes the cancer needs for glycolysis, HK2 and the glucose transporter GLUT1. Reader proteins called IGF2BP2 and IGF2BP3 carried out the stabilisation. Blocking the pathway slowed tumor formation in cell and animal models. The authors name METTL3 and its pathway as treatment targets. The study ties an RNA editing system to the altered energy habits of tumors.
europmc-pmc7172701:
Loeffelholz and Tang review lab testing for emerging human coronavirus infections. Their article appeared in Emerging Microbes and Infections. Three major outbreaks this century showed the need for fast, exact tests. Older standard methods are giving way to newer assays. The review focuses on the COVID-19 outbreak that began in Wuhan. Good sampling is a key theme.

The authors explain why a nasopharyngeal swab is the usual sample. Viral pneumonia rarely yields thick sputum for testing. A swab can still miss some infections, they note. Deeper samples or repeat tests may be needed. The review covers real-time PCR and serology methods. It also looks at point-of-care molecular devices now in development. Such tools could let local clinics test patients quickly and safely.
europmc-pmc7182001:
Lefevere and co-authors review how plants make salicylic acid, a key defense hormone. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science. Salicylic acid switches on plant responses against attacking pathogens. Plants build it through two routes, named the ICS and PAL pathways. Both routes start from the same raw material, chorismate.

Which route matters most depends on the plant species. Studies of Arabidopsis made the ICS route look dominant overall. Other plants lean mainly on the PAL route instead. Pathogens can interfere with both production and signaling. The authors compare evidence across species to avoid overgeneralizing. Understanding these routes helps explain how plant immunity works. It may also guide efforts to breed hardier crops.
europmc-pmc7226101:
Groot and Lee review how cells sort microRNAs into extracellular vesicles for export. Their article appeared in Cells. Vesicles are tiny membrane packages that carry proteins, lipids, and RNA between cells. Cells do not load them at random. Specific RNA-binding proteins, such as hnRNPA2B1 and Argonaute-2, help choose which microRNAs go in.

Membrane proteins involved in building vesicles also shape the cargo. Stress changes the sorting: oxygen-starved or overloaded lung cells altered their vesicle microRNAs. Disease states from lung illness to diabetes show disturbed vesicle content. Those changes may drive disease, not just mark it. The review connects sorting machinery to specific conditions. It also weighs vesicle microRNAs as possible diagnostic signals.
europmc-pmc7250901:
Han and co-authors review gene faults in IDH enzymes in glioma, a brain tumor. Their review appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. IDH enzymes help cells make energy and keep chemical balance. Faults in their genes occur in most lower-grade gliomas. They also occur in some blood, bile duct and cartilage cancers.

Mutant IDH gains a new job. It makes a substance called D-2-hydroxyglutarate, which builds up in tumor cells. That buildup reshapes cell metabolism and gene control. It also affects how tumors resist treatment. Patients with the fault often live longer than those without it. New targeted drugs are being developed against the mutant enzymes.
europmc-pmc7325801:
Assem and co-authors map a brain system for hard thinking in Cerebral Cortex. The system is called the multiple-demand network, a set of areas that switch on across many different tasks. Earlier scans had located it only roughly, so the team used detailed brain maps from 449 people in the Human Connectome Project.

Combining three task contrasts, they find a core of 10 areas in each half of the brain, strongly active and strongly linked to each other. A wider ring of 17 more areas surrounds that core. Parts of the caudate and cerebellum also join in. The areas lean slightly toward some tasks but mostly switch on together. Readers get a sharper map of the brain core behind complex thought.
europmc-pmc7426501:
Rossi and co-authors survey the mental health of people in Italy during the first COVID-19 lockdown. The web survey ran from March 27 to April 6, 2020. It drew 18,147 responses, and 79.6% came from women.

The team measured post-traumatic stress symptoms, depression, anxiety, insomnia, stress, and adjustment problems. Post-traumatic stress symptoms were most common, at 37%. Being a woman and being younger raised risk for every outcome. Quarantine, stopped work, and recent COVID-linked stress all raised risk too. Losing a loved one to COVID-19 linked with stress symptoms, depression, and insomnia. The authors call for close watch of public mental health as such crises unfold.
europmc-pmc7461801:
Wang and co-authors review T helper cell profiles in pregnancy and in repeated pregnancy loss. A mother's immune system must tolerate a fetus that is half foreign. T helper subsets help run that balance.

Naive helper cells split into subsets such as Th1, Th2, Th9, Th17, Th22, and follicular helpers. Th1 responses aid implantation at first, then Th2 responses take over to shield the fetus. Regulatory and Th9 cells calm local inflammation that could harm the pregnancy. Th17 cells guard against microbes, yet excess Th17 activity can draw in harmful cells. When this balance breaks, losses and preeclampsia can follow. The review maps each subset's role and ways to tune responses in care.
europmc-pmc7488201:
Swann and co-authors describe children and young people admitted to United Kingdom hospitals with covid-19. The prospective study ran in 260 hospitals across England, Wales, and Scotland. Enrollment used a shared international protocol for severe infections.

The cohort held 651 patients under 19 years, admitted to 138 hospitals between January 17 and July 3, 2020. About 42% had at least one other health condition on record. A mucocutaneous-enteric symptom cluster matched the syndrome now called MIS-C. About 18% of children went to critical care in the cohort during their hospital stay. Six patients died, all with profound prior illness. About 11% met the MIS-C case definition used in the study. Those children were older and more often of non-white ethnicity.
europmc-pmc7499501:
A Western Cape Department of Health team, working with the National Institute for Communicable Diseases, studies risk factors for COVID-19 death in South Africa. Effects of HIV and tuberculosis on outcomes were unknown there. The team linked records for adults in public care.

The cohort held 3,460,932 patients, of whom 22,308 were diagnosed with COVID-19 and 625 died in the window studied. Male sex, rising age, diabetes, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease all raised death risk. Living with HIV also raised the risk of death. Current and past tuberculosis did the same in their models. The pattern of age, sex, and other illness matched other settings. The authors warn that leftover confounding may inflate the HIV and tuberculosis figures. Still, the twin epidemics clearly intersect here.
europmc-pmc7568301:
Knott and co-authors characterize a two-enzyme system that breaks down PET plastic. Nature breaks tough polymers with enzyme teams over time. A similar pair was found for this synthetic plastic.

One enzyme turns PET into soluble intermediates. The second, called MHETase, makes the PET monomers. The team studied how MHETase works in detail. They also tested how the pair acts together. Synergy between the enzymes sped the breakdown process. Work on the pair may guide enzyme cocktail design. Such cocktails could support plastics upcycling in future. The study links natural deconstruction logic to a man-made material problem.
europmc-pmc7569401:
Bell, Clarke, Mounier-Jack, Walker and Paterson study parent views on a future COVID-19 vaccine in England. Uptake by families would shape how well a vaccine works. The study used mixed methods with parents and guardians.

Most parents said they would likely accept vaccination. That held for themselves and for their children. Ethnicity and household income predicted refusal in the data. Self-protection was the main reason for acceptance. Safety fears about a rushed vaccine led concerns. Efficacy doubts also featured in parent responses. The findings can guide how a rollout is framed. Clear safety evidence may matter most for hesitant families.
europmc-pmc7583501:
Gold and co-authors track race, ethnicity and age trends in COVID-19 deaths in the United States. Their report covers May to August of that year. National vital statistics data supplied the death records.

A total of 114,411 COVID-19 deaths were reported then. Of those, 78.2% were aged 65 or older. Men made up 53.3% of those who died. White decedents made up 51.3% of the total. Hispanic decedents were 24.2% and Black decedents 18.7%. Deaths fell from 37,940 in May to 17,718 in June. They rose again in July before easing in August. The South share of deaths grew sharply over the period.
europmc-pmc7587101:
Addetia and co-authors link neutralizing antibodies to protection from SARS-CoV-2 in a vessel outbreak. A fishing vessel saw a high attack rate at sea. Tests before departure and after return were available.

Data covered 120 of 122 persons on board. Follow-up ran a median of 32 days in the study. The team checked prior antibody levels against later infection. Neutralizing antibodies tracked with protection from the virus. Human proof of this link had been lacking before. Animal models alone had shown such protection. The results may help vaccine design for COVID-19. Knowing immune correlates can speed how vaccines are judged. Durability of protection was not settled by this work.
europmc-pmc7599101:
Li and co-authors study YTHDF2 in prostate cancer and its effect on tumor suppressors. YTHDF2 reads a common chemical mark on RNA. It usually drives marked RNA messages toward decay.

Higher YTHDF2 and METTL3 levels marked worse survival. That pattern appeared in prostate cancer patient data. Knocking down either gene slowed tumor growth and spread. Tests ran in cells, grafts and metastasis models. Two tumor suppressors were direct shared targets. They were LHPP and NKX3-1 in this work. YTHDF2 bound their marked sites and sped decay. Their loss raised AKT signaling in cancer cells. Restoring them copied the effect of gene knockdown.
europmc-pmc7617101:
Wang and co-authors track body-mass index and obesity in urban and rural China from 2004 to 2018. Mean BMI had risen steadily since the early 1980s. Recent national and subgroup trends lacked a sound check.

Six national surveys covered 645,223 adults aged 18-69. Height and weight were measured in each survey. Mean BMI rose from 22.7 in 2004 to 24.4 in 2018. Obesity rose from 3.1% to 8.1% over the span. The pace of rise slowed after 2010 overall. Urban groups slowed most in the later years. Rural women kept a steady rise through 2018. About 85 million adults in China were obese by then. Trends split by sex, place and social status in the data.
europmc-pmc7659001:
Yesbolatova and co-authors present a sharper tool for switching off proteins in cells. The tool builds on the auxin-inducible degron method, which marks a chosen protein for rapid removal. The old method leaked and needed high doses of the trigger chemical.

The new system, called AID2, pairs a changed plant protein with a new ligand. It shows no clear leak and needs a 670-times lower dose. It also removes target proteins even faster than the old method. The team proved it in yeast, in human and other mammal cells, and in mice.
europmc-pmc7677301:
Orgilés and co-authors survey how COVID-19 quarantine affected children in Italy and Spain. Parents of 1,143 children aged 3 to 18 years filled in a survey. They reported on mood, behavior, and daily habits during home confinement, compared with life before it.

Most parents, 85.7%, saw changes in their child's mood or behavior. Trouble focusing led at 76.6%, then boredom at 52%. Children used screens more, moved less, and slept more. Spanish parents reported more symptoms than Italian parents. When home life grew tense, parents reported more problems in their children. Other common signs were irritability at 39% and restlessness at 38.8% among the children surveyed.
europmc-pmc7678301:
Zhao and co-authors trace how a tumor signal helps colorectal cancer spread to the liver. The signal is a small RNA, miR-934, packed into vesicles shed by cancer cells. Such vesicles can prep distant tissue for tumor arrival. The team tested this loop in cells and living models.

Cancer vesicles carried miR-934 into macrophages, a type of immune cell. It pushed them into a state that aids tumors, by lowering PTEN and firing a growth pathway. Those macrophages then released a factor that fed back to raise miR-934 in cancer cells. High miR-934 tracked with poor outlook for patients.
europmc-pmc7808901:
Morris and co-authors measure how the pandemic changed colorectal cancer care in England. Many feared that COVID-19 would harm cancer services. Hard numbers on that harm were scarce. The team used population data for the whole country.

The authors tracked how cancers were found during the pandemic. They also tracked how patients were managed and treated. Referral and diagnosis flows came under strain as services shut or slowed. Comparing pandemic months with prior norms shows the scale. The results give planners a firm count of missed or delayed care. They also highlight where recovery efforts should aim first.
europmc-pmc7833401:
Di Lorenzo and co-authors review polyphenols and human health, with a focus on bioavailability. Polyphenols are plant chemicals with possible health gains. They split into flavonoid and non-flavonoid groups. Trials link eating them to lower chronic disease risk. The weak point is how little the body absorbs.

Food mixing, liver processing, and gut microbes all cut uptake. Breakdown products made in the body may do much of the work. Those metabolites show antioxidant and calming effects. The authors review animal and human studies on uptake. They compare the main food sources of polyphenols. Factors that sway each class are weighed. The message is that dose on the plate is not dose in the blood.
europmc-pmc7836001:
Buschmann and co-authors review nanomaterial systems that deliver mRNA vaccines. mRNA vaccines won their first big success against SARS-CoV-2. Lipid nanoparticles made much of that success possible. They carry the mRNA into cells after a shot in the arm. They also act as mild immune boosters.

The authors first survey delivery systems in broad terms. They then focus on the lipid particles used in COVID-19 vaccine trials. Each part of the particle gets a close look. The last section sorts out what sets performance. Size, charge, and lipid mix all matter. The review serves teams designing the next mRNA products.
europmc-pmc7961001:
Nagy and co-authors report a survival analysis of cancer hallmark genes across many tumour types. Hallmark genes drive the core traits of cancer, from fast growth to spread. The team asked which of them forecast how long patients live. They drew gene activity and survival data from a large cancer atlas. The data covered 26 different tumour types.

Two hallmarks stood out: genome instability and invasion. Their genes reached significance in most cancer types. Thyroid cancer and glioblastoma broke the pattern, with few such genes. Kidney clear cell cancer and low-grade glioma held the most predictive genes. The paper lists the eight genes with the strongest effects, each tied to a hallmark. Some raised risk sharply, while others marked better survival. The results give doctors candidate markers by cancer type.
europmc-pmc8019501:
Ding and co-authors test whether a simple blood index predicts atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. The triglyceride-glucose, or TyG, index stands in for insulin resistance. Insulin resistance helps drive artery disease, but it is awkward to measure directly. The team pooled cohort studies of people free of such disease at the start. They searched PubMed and Embase for the relevant work.

Eight cohort studies with 5,731,294 participants met the bar. People in the highest TyG group faced a hazard ratio of 1.61 for new disease. The risk held when the index was treated as a continuous measure. Coronary artery disease showed a hazard ratio of 1.95 in the pooled analysis. Stroke showed a hazard ratio of 1.26 across the same cohorts.
europmc-pmc8165101:
Zhong and co-authors survey small molecules in targeted cancer therapy. Targeted drugs now lead cancer care, with better effect and safety than older chemotherapy. The first tyrosine kinase inhibitor, imatinib, won approval in 2001.

By December 2020, 89 such drugs had won approval in the United States or China. The review traces how these drugs are built and how they act. Low response rates and drug resistance still limit them. The authors weigh fixes now in study and likely next steps. Readers get a full map of a fast-moving drug class.
europmc-pmc8185001:
Ashton and co-authors validate plasma neurofilament light as a sign of nerve damage. The protein can be measured in blood as well as spinal fluid. The team tested its worth across many brain disorders.

Two cohorts took part, with 805 people in London and 1,464 in the Swedish BioFINDER study. Plasma levels rose in 13 neurodegenerative disorders and in Down syndrome groups. The test helped tell atypical parkinsonian disorders from look-alikes. It also flagged dementia in Down syndrome and in psychiatric settings. Cut-off values drawn from the data sharpened its use.
europmc-pmc8208001:
Betran and co-authors chart caesarean section rates worldwide and project them to 2030. Rates keep rising in rich and poor countries alike. The team gathered national data from 1990 to 2018.

Sources included health system reports and household surveys. They computed weighted regional averages from the latest data. Trend analysis ran at national, regional, and global levels. Models then projected rates and case counts for 2030. The results show where surgical birth is climbing fastest. Health planners can use them to weigh access against overuse. Subregional detail sits inside the global picture they built.
europmc-pmc8329701:
Du and co-authors assess pyroptosis across metabolism and the tumour immune setting. Pyroptosis is an inflammatory cell death. Cells trigger it when they sense danger signals or infection inside.

Gasdermin proteins execute the death by cutting open the cell. Whether the fire helps or harms depends on context. Timing and response size decide much of that. The review covers how pyroptosis is controlled step by step. It then weighs its roles in metabolic disease. Its place in tumour immunity gets equal depth. One death path, many outcomes. Metabolic disease forms one large test bed for its roles.
europmc-pmc8336501:
Liu and co-authors survey cytokines from clinical meaning to measurement. Cytokines run immune and inflammatory responses through tangled networks. Their levels also serve as markers for many diseases.

Measuring them can guide diagnosis and treatment. The review splits cytokines by pro- and anti-inflammatory effect. It covers what skews a measurement in body fluids. Native levels, sample handling, and freeze-thaw effects all matter. Soluble receptors can mask readings too. New quantification methods close the survey. Careful measurement turns a noisy signal into clinical value. Both lab biology and bedside medicine use these numbers.
europmc-pmc8397301:
Twohig and co-authors compare hospital risk between the Delta and Alpha variants of SARS-CoV-2. Delta was first found in England in March 2021 and spread fast. Many feared it caused worse illness than Alpha, the variant it replaced.

The cohort study covered all COVID-19 patients in England from March 29 to May 23, 2021, whose virus was genome-sequenced. Patient records were linked to data on vaccines, emergency care, hospital stays, and deaths. The team then compared admission and emergency care risk between the two variants. The design lets health planners judge Delta's true added burden. Vaccination status was part of the linked record set.
europmc-pmc8437801:
Kabinger and co-authors work out how molnupiravir forces errors into SARS-CoV-2 RNA. This oral antiviral drug was in late-stage trials for COVID-19 care. It raises the rate of viral RNA mutations and curbs virus growth in animals and humans.

Lab tests showed the viral copying enzyme uses the drug's active form in place of normal building blocks. When the enzyme later reads that RNA as a template, the drug residue can pair with either of two bases. That slip yields mutated RNA. Structural views of the enzyme at work confirm the loose pairing. The two-step trick may explain the drug's broad reach across viruses.
europmc-pmc8597301:
Zhao and co-authors test fecal microbiota transfer in mice with a Parkinson-like illness. Gut problems often come with Parkinson disease. Changes in gut microbes may send signals to the brain. The team used rotenone to cause the illness in mice, then gave a transfer of gut microbes.

Rotenone changed the gut mix and harmed gut function and movement. Two microbe groups grew more common in the sick mice. The transfer restored the gut mix and eased gut and movement problems. It also lowered gut inflammation and repair harm to the gut wall. The authors link the benefit to a gut signal path that involves a known immune sensor.
europmc-pmc8668901:
Han and co-authors discuss the ionizable lipids that make RNA delivery work in lipid nanoparticles. RNA drugs can target almost any gene, but RNA breaks down fast. It also cannot cross cell walls on its own due to size and charge. Fat-based particles solve both problems and have reached the clinic.

Among the particle's four parts, the ionizable lipid does the key work. It carries a charge in acid, so it can pack the RNA in. At body pH it turns neutral, which limits harm. The lipid also helps the RNA escape into the cell's main space. The authors sort the main lipid types and look ahead to new designs.
europmc-pmc8712501:
Wang and co-authors review macrophage polarization and its role in liver disease. Macrophages are front-line immune cells that can shift into distinct states. In diseased tissue, local signals push them toward M1 or M2 forms. Each form plays a different part in harm or repair.

The review first covers where liver macrophages come from. It then maps the signal pathways that set their state. Routes include TLR4 and NF-kB, JAK and STAT, and several others. Each major liver disease gets its own account. Acute injury, hepatitis, fatty liver, fibrosis, and liver cancer are all covered. The authors aim to clarify a complex two-way link.
europmc-pmc8746501:
Rahman and co-authors review phenolic compounds and their roles in human disease. These plant compounds can calm inflammation and block enzymes tied to illness. Some work alongside standard anti-inflammatory drugs. Others act on gene switches that control antioxidant defenses in cells.

Phenolics have been used against high blood pressure and metabolic problems. Blocking one enzyme helps treat type 2 diabetes. Blocking another is used in Alzheimer disease care. The compounds also show value for skin disease and arthritis. The review sums up current knowledge across these uses. It closes with prospects for new drugs built on these compounds.
europmc-pmc8776501:
COvid-19 Multi-omics Blood ATlas (COMBAT) Consortium presents a blood atlas of COVID-19 that defines hallmarks of disease severity. Severe disease is hard to treat because patients vary and immune markers were poorly mapped. The team combined many data types from blood across severity levels. Influenza and sepsis patients, plus healthy volunteers, served as comparisons.

Severity hallmarks spanned immune cell subsets and their signals. Features of the immune repertoire, metabolism, and clotting also stood out. Lasting activation of one pathway marked COVID-19 apart from the other illnesses. Blood protein patterns split patients into clusters that predicted outcome. The atlas aims to guide drug work and trial design.
europmc-pmc8786601:
Röltgen and co-authors study immune imprinting and variant recognition after SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination. They compared antibodies from mRNA shots, other vaccine types, and infection. Human lymph nodes were analyzed after infection or mRNA vaccination. The team asked how first exposure shapes later antibody breadth.

Antibody breadth against variants was lower after infection than after any vaccine. It improved over several months, though. Infection with a variant raised variant-specific antibodies. Prior mRNA vaccination instead pulled responses back toward the first strain. Infection disrupted the lymph node centers where antibodies mature. mRNA shots kept those centers active for weeks in some cases.
europmc-pmc9086501:
Quail and co-authors give a consensus statement on neutrophils in cancer, drawn from a meeting of field experts. Neutrophils are white blood cells that fight infection as a first line of defense. In cancer, they can either help a tumor grow or help destroy it. Their states and jobs vary far more than once thought.

The statement maps what shapes these varied states inside and near tumors. It names key disputes in the field and why study results often clash. The authors suggest ways to name, measure, and test neutrophil states more alike across labs. Readers get shared terms and a research agenda. The goal is firm ground for future work on these cells in cancer.
europmc-pmc9151701:
Wicks and Semenza review hypoxia-inducible factors in cancer growth and in therapy. These factors are master switches that match oxygen supply and demand in the body. Cancer cells hijack that system to fuel their own progress. The factors switch on thousands of genes in response to low oxygen.

Those genes drive new blood vessels, cell movement, and shifts in fuel use. They also help tumors invade, spread, and evade the immune system. The review sets out how the factors are turned on in cancer cells. It then weighs the current state of small-molecule drugs that block them. Future prospects for such drugs get frank treatment. Clinicians and researchers get a guide to a core cancer pathway.
europmc-pmc9247101:
Zhao and co-authors review fibrosis, its mechanisms, and drugs now in clinical trials. Fibrosis means excess matrix deposits after a faulty repair response. It can strike the liver, kidney, heart, and lung. Diseases like liver cirrhosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis carry a heavy global burden.
