A key driver is the lasting activation of myofibroblasts, the cells that lay down matrix. Signals like transforming growth factor keep them switched on. The review first covers causes and spread for several organs. It then maps the abnormal cells and their interactions. Aberrant pathways that control matrix cross-linking, metabolism, and inflammation are detailed. Drugs aimed at those targets are assessed trial by trial.
europmc-pmc9252801:
Thumuluri and co-authors present DeepLoc 2.0, a tool that predicts where proteins sit inside cells. Knowing a protein's location aids functional annotation and drug target search. Some proteins live in several compartments at once. The new version predicts multiple locations, not just one.

DeepLoc 2.0 uses a pre-trained protein language model and needs only the sequence as input. That makes it faster than profile-based rivals. It reached state-of-the-art scores on strict new data sets. Two features aid interpretation: an attention map along the sequence and prediction of nine sorting signal types. The attention map aligns well with true signal positions. A free webserver serves the tool.
europmc-pmc9467401:
Schmauck-Medina and co-authors summarize a Copenhagen meeting on new hallmarks of ageing. Nine hallmarks were set out in 2013 by López-Otín and colleagues. They range from genomic instability to stem cell exhaustion. The list has guided ageing research for a decade.

The meeting took stock of what the nine still explain. It also weighed new candidates from recent work. Proposed additions include compromised autophagy and microbiome disturbance. Altered mechanical properties and splicing dysregulation were also raised. Inflammation featured as a further theme. Sessions covered telomeres, senescence, and DNA repair. Heart, brain vessel, and muscle ageing got their own talks. The authors argue that old and new hallmarks joined give a fuller picture. That picture can steer trials aimed at healthy old age.
europmc-pmc9477501:
Hulse and co-authors present the first complete connectome of the Drosophila central complex. This deep brain region runs directed movement and sleep. Its recurrent circuits support navigation that bends with context and past experience. Such circuits are hard to study in larger brains.

The map was built with electron microscopy at synaptic resolution. It covers every neuron and circuit in the region. The team found new neuron types and new sensory and motor paths. Network motifs in the map fit known jobs of the region. One motif extracts the fly's head direction. Attractor dynamics can then hold that heading steady. Other paths may let context and inner state pick behavior patterns. The authors offer the map as a blueprint for circuit studies.
europmc-pmc9735601:
Batty, Bennett, and Yu review the role of oxidative stress in atherosclerosis. The disease is a slow vessel wall inflammation. It underlies most heart and vessel disease worldwide. Excess reactive oxygen species drive much of its harm.

Those species also serve as signals that keep vessels healthy. The harm starts when their output outruns the cleanup systems. Inflammation, wall lining failure, and lipid shifts follow. The review names the main enzyme sources of the species. Vessel antioxidants and their failure in disease get equal space. Human plaques show changed source and shield levels. Lab and animal work explains how each part acts. Antioxidant drugs draw strong interest as a fix. Trials so far show no clear shield effect from them. The authors weigh fresh routes to rebalance vessel stress.
europmc-pmc9748301:
Santos and co-authors price the health care cost of doing nothing about physical inactivity. Too little movement is a changeable risk for major diseases. The team aimed to count what inaction will cost health systems. Their figures are meant to guide policy spending choices.

They used a population fraction method across 194 countries. The window ran from 2020 to 2030 in their model. Diseases covered heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and several cancers. Dementia and depression joined the list of outcomes. If inactivity rates stay flat, costs would be huge. Direct care costs would reach about INT$520 billion total. Low and middle income lands would see 74% of new cases. High income lands would bear 63% of the costs. Dementia care alone would take a large cost share. The authors call the burden fully avoidable through action.
europmc-pmc9951101:
Chen and co-authors estimate the global economic cost of 29 cancers across 204 countries and territories. Their modeling study spans the years 2020 to 2050. The team asked how large the total cost will be and how it will spread. Costs were counted in international dollars at constant 2017 prices.

The authors put the global cost of cancers over that span at $25.2 trillion. Burden fell unevenly across countries, regions, and income groups. Health burden and money burden did not match in their spread. High-income countries faced a greater burden per person in disability terms. The authors argue that global action is needed to curb the projected rise. The study gives planners a long-range cost map for cancer control.
evelyn-diary-1901:
John Evelyn kept a diary across most of his long life, from 1620 to 1706. Evelyn was a gentleman, a gardener, and a founding member of the Royal Society. The 1901 edition prints his record in full.

He describes the Civil War years, the court of Charles II, the Plague, and the Great Fire of London. Gardens, books, and new science fill the quieter pages. Evelyn was Pepys's friend and great fellow diarist, though calmer in tone. Read together, the two diaries give the fullest picture we have of Stuart England. His notes on trees and planting reflect his other famous book, Sylva.
freeman-portion-of-labor-1901:
Harper issued The Portion of Labor in 1901, naming Mary Wilkins as author of Jerome and A New England Nun. She dedicated the book to Henry Mills Alden. Chapter one finds young Ellen, seven and a half, watching Norway spruces by her father's house.

Ellen is sure the trees mean to walk north toward their cold home land. That child's fancy opens a tale that soon leaves the village for the factory town. A strike, a love story, and the slow grind of mill life cross in its pages. The novel counts among the first American books to treat labor as a grave and central subject.
frus-1861-d101:
Writing on 18 October 1861, William H. Seward kept up his brisk exchange with Lord Lyons. The letter is document 101 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Day after day in October, the two men traded notes across a short distance in Washington. The pace shows how much of the war's fate was argued in that one city. Seward's note keeps the exchange moving on his terms as far as he could. The exchange kept a rhythm that let both men save face while holding firm. Both men prized the rhythm, since it let each claim be met on its merits.
frus-1861-d201:
Cassius Clay wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 August 1861. The dispatch is document 201 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Clay wrote in August with the news of Bull Run on its way to Russia. The czar's court did not waver in its warmth for the Union. His report gave Washington a firm point of light at a dark hour in the war. Russia's warmth held through the war and bloomed, in time, into a famous friendship. Famous friendship in time grew from these plain, dated seeds of 1861.
frus-1861-d301:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from Mr. Thayer, dated 29 June 1861. Congress received it as Document 301 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d101:
By the date of 14 July 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 101 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d201:
On 8 January 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed another note to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, printed as Document 201 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three days of steady notes mark the reopening of normal business.

January 1862 also brought a change of war secretary in Washington and fresh Union plans for the spring. Britain watched for signs of where the war was heading. In that setting, frequent short notes between Seward and Lyons kept small disputes from growing while larger questions waited on events. Washington was a small town in 1862, and the envoys met socially as often as officially.
frus-1862-d301:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 8 August 1862 in a letter printed as Document 301 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

That week a new battle was opening in Virginia at Cedar Mountain, the first move of the campaign that ended at Bull Run. Dayton could not know it as he wrote; his concern was the French court. His reports are read today for exactly that split view: Paris gossip and policy, written in full ignorance of the week's fighting. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d401:
Dated 22 April 1862, this order from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Horace J. Perry, secretary of the American legation in Madrid. It is Document 401 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the printed record of the year's diplomacy.

Spring 1862 brought the fall of New Orleans and fresh strain over Spain's part in the Mexican expedition. Seward's letters to Madrid balanced protest with courtesy, since Spain held Cuba and could open or close ports to Confederate ships. The dispatch belongs to that careful exchange, where each instruction tried to keep a proud old empire neutral while the Union fought for its life.
frus-1862-d501:
James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 May 1862. It stands as Document 501 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Pike wrote as the Union's armies pressed in Virginia and the West, and Dutch opinion followed the campaigns in the papers. His reports weighed the ministry's formal correctness against the merchants' wish for an end to the fighting. He also kept Washington posted on the Dutch colonial questions that touched the war at sea. A mid-May report like this one is a typical brick in the Hague file: modest in itself, part of a wall of steady information.
frus-1862-d601:
Spain's minister of state addressed this instruction on 22 March 1862 to the commander of the Spanish expeditionary force in Mexico. It is Document 601 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, in the appended Spanish correspondence.

By March 1862 the allied front in Mexico was cracking, and Madrid's orders to its general reflect the strain. Spain soon concluded that France meant more than debt collection and pulled its troops out, a decision shaped in letters like this one. Printed in translation in an American volume, the document shows the State Department at work. It was assembling the fullest record it could of a crisis on the Union's border. The record even included papers written by governments it could not control.
frus-1862-d701: On 15 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. Yrisarri for the last time in this file. The letter is document 701 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, closing a short exchange that ran from late August. The evidence names both men and the date, but it does not state Yrisarri's post, his land, or the letters' subject.
frus-1863p1-d101:
On 2 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams for the fifth time that day, by the volume's count. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 101 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The dozen letters of 2 March read like a table of contents for the London brief. Each took up one thread — a claim, a ship, a talk, a tone to hold. This one holds its own thread in the set. Such batch writing was desk craft of a high order, and it kept a far-off envoy fully armed for his next round of talks.
frus-1863p1-d201:
An instruction dated 18 May 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 201 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d301:
The State Department's mail for London dated 28 September 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 301 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In the fall of 1863 two ironclad rams built for the Confederacy waited in a British yard. Washington's orders to Adams that season pressed hard for the ships to be held. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d401:
A formal note dated 23 February 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 401 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Trade bound the countries tightly, from Southern cotton to British mills. Both sides had much to lose from a break, and the notes reflect that caution. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d501: Document 501 in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs is a letter dated 2 May 1863, from Major Turner to Mr. Hunter at the State Department. It was printed with the year's diplomatic papers, laid before Congress with the President's annual message. The record gives the two men's names and the date, and little more, so its exact business cannot be told from the heading alone.
frus-1863p1-d601:
Document 601, dated 4 August 1863, records a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late summer of 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1875v01:
Volume I of the 1875 papers opens with a Hawaiian convention. The reciprocity treaty with the island kingdom leads the book. Grant's message then looks back over a century. He counts thirteen states grown to thirty-eight. Population has passed forty million, he reports. The country files run from Argentina to Hawaii. China takes the longest section.

Its reports describe a China arming its coasts. Four more gunboats are ordered from England, one consul writes. Troops move into Formosa against its native peoples. Arsenals drill men by foreign methods. Austria, Brazil, and Central America fill their usual places. Britain and Germany stay brief this year. The volume's weight sits in the Pacific. Trade and arms point the same way.
frus-1901:
One event echoes through the 1901 volume country by country. President McKinley has been assassinated. Argentina files condolences and notes Roosevelt's accession. Austria-Hungary and Belgium send their own messages. Bolivia and Brazil repeat the pattern. Each section pairs local business with mourning. Passports, expulsions, and arrests fill the local files.

Brazil reports riots over street-railway fares in Rio. A sacked Baptist church at Nictheroy draws an indemnity. Greece supplies a quieter mid-volume scene. Its queen funded a Bible translation into modern Greek. The books went free to hospitals and charities. The gift met no public favor, the report admits. Grief for a president thus shares the year. So does a queen's unpopular kindness.
frus-1914-20v01:
The Lansing Papers open with America's neutrality years. Volume I sorts the Secretary's files by problem. Peace proposals and Far East neutralization lead. Recruiting of Americans and methods of warfare follow. The Belgium legation acts for Edith Cavell in one file. Munitions sales and loans to belligerents fill large blocks. Britain's interference with American commerce fills a larger one.

Submarine warfare then consumes the volume's second half. Relations with Germany run to hundreds of documents. They end in severed ties and war. A mid-volume note weighs the Gulflight's torpedoing. Three crew lives lost would demand vigorous protest, it argues. Deferential complaint would satisfy no one. The volume is a decision record. Neutrality collapses under its own files.
frus-1917Supp01v01:
Supplement 1 of 1917 opens with peace terms exchanged and refused. The Allies answer Wilson's December suggestion on January 10. Their terms reach Washington in full. Wilson then addresses the Senate on January 22. He lays out bases for a durable peace. Germany sends its terms in secret. Wilson offers Austria-Hungary assurances against dismemberment. Vienna refuses a separate peace all the same.

Mexico proposes ending the war in February. Greece wins American intercession in its crisis. Part II turns to submarine warfare and neutral rights. The mid-volume wires work the hemisphere. Panama is pressed to act with America. Cuba and Brazil, Washington notes, dislike one conference plan. The supplement catches a neutral becoming a belligerent. Peace feelers and war measures share its pages.
frus-1917Supp02v01:
Volume I of Supplement 2 covers America's entry into the war. War with Germany is announced on April 6, 1917. British and French special missions arrive to plan cooperation. Austria-Hungary severs relations two days after the declaration. Turkey follows on April 20. Russia's Provisional Government states its war aims in May. The American Federation of Labor messages Russia's soviets. A permanent French High Commissioner, Tardieu, takes post.

The Expeditionary Force's staff sails in these papers. Belgian, Rumanian, and Japanese missions follow the first two. A mid-volume paper laments the Balkan front's neglect. No one guarded the gates there, it argues. That blunder gave the war new life. The volume is mobilization in documents. Missions, fleets, and armies align within weeks.
frus-1918Russiav01:
Russia Volume I follows the revolution's political year. Chapter one opens with the March Revolution. The Emperor abdicates, and America recognizes the Provisional Government. Prince Lvov leads, with the soviets beside him. Milyukov and Guchkov resign after protests over war aims. Wilson's May message reaches a straining ally. The Root mission travels to Russia in chapter three. Bakhmeteff brings Russia's case to Washington.

Kerensky's premiership fills chapter four. The July crisis breaks the offensive. Kornilov's episode and the Democratic Conference follow. A mid-volume wire watches the east. Trotsky sends a French officer; railroad men wait at Harbin. Stevens tracks the Siberian lines for Washington. The volume ends before October's storm. It is a government dissolving in real time.
frus-1918Supp01v01:
War aims open Volume I of the 1918 war supplement. Lloyd George speaks on January 5. Wilson answers with the Fourteen Points on January 8. Hertling and Czernin reply for the Central Powers. The Supreme War Council holds its third session. Allied premiers denounce the enemy peace program. America objects to collective pronouncements all the same. Professor Herron carries unofficial peace talk in Switzerland. He meets a Bulgarian emissary, then Lammasch of Austria.

Emperor Charles writes Wilson on February 17. Wilson's February speech answers both enemy ministers. A labor conference memorandum states Allied workers' aims. The mid-volume text quotes Wilson's September speech. Plain people demand plain statements of war aims, he said. The volume is diplomacy by public speech. Each capital argues before the world.
frus-1919Parisv01:
Volume I of the Paris Peace Conference papers covers preparation. Hostilities end; the Inquiry begins its work. That expert body plans America's peace in secret. Wilson's trip to Europe fills a long file. The Commission to Negotiate Peace takes shape. Nations and peoples petition for representation. Finland, the Hejaz, Liberia, and Poland all appear. Russia's place stays unsettled in its file.

The Allies confer in London in December 1918. League of Nations proposals close the main list. Labor questions and aerial rules join the agenda. A mid-volume paper recalls wartime ship inspections. Eastbound ships were held on general suspicion, it says. Inspection during loading was the proposed cure. The volume is the conference before the conference. Hopes arrive in Paris with paperwork.
frus-1919v01:
Wilson's message of December 2, 1919 opens the year's first volume. America then walks away from the conference table. It refuses seats on the treaty's new commissions. The delegation sails home on December 9. Ambassador Wallace stays on as an observer. The first Labor Conference meets without that machinery. A second Pan American financial conference is prepared. Gold clearance fund conventions appear in the list.

Old treaties die under the Seamen's Act. Norway, Spain, and Sweden settle their terms in files. A mid-volume paper promotes a Chinese-American bank. Chinese and American groups reach a deal in principle. Hsu sails to America to close it. The volume mixes retreat and routine. Empires of paper shrink; banks still charter.
frus-1920v01:
The 1920 opener carries Wilson's December message to Congress. America keeps an observer's seat near the Supreme Council. Wilson calls the League's Council and Assembly to meet. A world court statute takes shape in drafts. An American joins the Aland Islands commission. Teschen splits Poland and Czechoslovakia in a long file. The Allies settle that border by agreement in July. Spitzbergen wins a treaty of its own. Brussels hosts a financial conference that autumn.

A mid-volume argument defends Canada's fishery boats. Their shore privileges, it says, are brief and earned. A lasting treaty would not be abused, it argues. The volume looks outward despite the Senate's mood. Courts, islands, and conferences fill its year. Isolation was never quite the word.
frus-1921v01:
Harding's two 1921 messages open the year's first volume. Washington prepares its great naval conference in long files. The League writes about mandates; Washington answers. Central America tries federation again in its papers. Costa Rica and Panama dispute their border first. America urges the Loubet and White awards. Panama objects to both settlements. Tacna-Arica returns in a shorter run.

A mid-volume brief defends a wireless claim. The China Electric Company, it argues, never bought wireless rights. Its deal, read plainly, excludes such supplies. A rival Chinese wireless firm proves the point, it says. The volume is a new reign's inbox. Disarmament leads, but cables and borders crowd in. The Harding era starts with old maps.
frus-1922v01:
The Washington Conference fills the front of the 1922 opener. Four powers sign a Pacific treaty first. Naval limits follow in their own long file. Submarines and poison gas win a joint pledge. Nine powers sign the China treaties last. Harding reports the results to the Senate in February. Ratifications roll in through the year. America declines the Genoa Conference in a firm file. War debt talks open with Europe's treasuries.

Three presidents meet on a warship in Fonseca Bay. Nicaragua, Honduras, and Salvador sign peace aboard Tacoma. A Central American conference follows in December. The mid-volume pages argue Tacna-Arica. Chile, the text says, long refused broad arbitration. It now accepts judging the plebiscite question itself. The volume is conference diplomacy's triumph year.
frus-1923v01:
Coolidge's December message opens the 1923 volume. He asks the Senate to join the World Court's protocol. Gun elevation on kept battleships stirs talks with two powers. America refuses the old arms trade pact. Its delegates join talks on warfare's rules instead. Opium traffic work proceeds with the League's committee. A new trade rule is adopted in these files. Unconditional most-favored-nation treatment becomes policy. Liquor smuggling then fills the longest run. Treaties would let officers search ships near shore. Ottawa talks with Canada pursue the same end.

A mid-volume warning goes to Bolivia. Pay the bond contract, or credit collapses, it says. Final bonds must reach holders before May. The volume mixes courts, cargoes, and rum-runners.
frus-1924v01:
The 1924 opener begins with Coolidge's message. Russia's bid to join the Spitzbergen pact is weighed. Britain protests bigger gun angles on American battleships. Arms traffic drafting proceeds with the League. Refugee papers from the League win acceptance. Russians and Armenians may travel on them. Drug traffic control fills a solid file. America refuses a joint board for relief loans. War debt talks continue in their own run.

Austria and Hungary join a claims pact in November. Liquor treaties then crowd the contents' end. A mid-volume letter answers Canada on the St. Lawrence. A joint board may grow, Ottawa is told. Its first charge covers the waterway scheme's two big questions. The volume pairs dry laws with deep channels. Prohibition shapes half its diplomacy.
frus-1925v01:
Scrapping warships opens the 1925 volume. Three navies sink tonnage under the Washington pact. Calls for a new disarmament conference follow. America keeps clear of Europe's security pacts. Geneva's protocol and Locarno both pass it by. Its delegates do join the Geneva arms traffic talks. Warfare's new rules fail to win adoption. War debt settlements then fill the volume's heart. Belgium, France, Italy, and others sign funding deals. Greece, Latvia, Rumania, and Yugoslavia follow.

Russia's Spitzbergen bid is refused this time. A mid-volume dispatch reports Tacna-Arica's pause. An appeal, Collier writes, may bring a truce. Figueroa's government gains time to choose its course. The volume is debts and disarmament. Europe pays slowly and arms carefully.
frus-1926v01:
The World Court proposal opens the 1926 volume. America would join with reservations stated in full. Disarmament's preparatory work takes the next long run. The Reparation Commission loses its American observer. Alien property held since the war awaits disposal. A sanitary convention signs in June. Ships' oil pollution gets a Washington meeting. The League's slavery work wins sympathy. Narcotics control gets a circular statement. Panama's Bolívar Congress must stay free of politics.

Tacna-Arica then swallows the volume's second half. The plebiscite ends; good offices begin again. Peru rejects the settlement Washington proposes. A mid-volume Peruvian note states the price plainly. Friendship waits until Chile returns both provinces. The volume ends where the dispute began.
frus-1927v01:
The Geneva naval conference opens the 1927 volume. Three powers meet from June to August. Their talks fill the book's first long run. Disarmament's groundwork continues in Geneva sessions. A draft pact on private arms making is prepared. The Washington treaties' status is reported in one paper. America's team joins Geneva's economic conference in May. Trade bans draw an October conference of their own. Tax experts meet in London on double levies.

A radio pact signs in November to close the list. A mid-volume note cites that trade conference's records. The League's own volumes hold its full acts. The yearbook feel is strong in this volume. Conference follows conference without pause. Diplomacy had become a circuit.
frus-1928v01:
The pact renouncing war fills most of the 1928 opener. Coolidge's December message stands at its head. The Paris treaty signs on August 27 that year. Its negotiation takes the first long run of papers. Nations then notify their adherence in a second run. Disarmament's preparatory fifth session follows. A Franco-British naval compromise wins rejection. A House resolution against submarines wins approval. Trade bans fall under a Geneva convention. A second conference on them meets in July.

Copyright's Rome revision and the slavery pact appear too. A mid-volume case frees seized German securities. The Supreme Court's Disconto ruling guides the Custodian's hand. Enemy property still haunted the peace's tenth year. The volume joins high ideals to old loot.
frus-1929v01:
Hoover's December message opens the 1929 volume. Joining the World Court's statute leads the general files. The war renunciation pact needs strengthening, some suggest. Disarmament's sixth preparatory session follows. London's five-power naval talks take shape in long papers. Geneva signs new rules for the wounded in July. Prisoners of war gain a matching convention. Sea safety confers in London that spring. Drug traffic data is swapped by agreement. Forged currency draws a Geneva conference too.

Status talks fill the volume's tail. Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, and others weigh dual nationality. Service in two armies is the core problem. A mid-volume note prefers a formal treaty. Quick deals on single articles, it warns, fall short. The volume is law being built clause by clause.
frus-1930v01:
The London Naval Conference fills the 1930 opener's front. It sits from January to April that year. Hoover's December message precedes the papers. France and Italy's shipbuilding gap takes the next run. Disarmament's groundwork resumes in the autumn. The Hague codifies parts of world law in spring. Dual nationality's army duties win a protocol there. The League's charter draws a cautious American view. The Basel settlements bank gets a policy too. Tariff truce talks draw unofficial observers.

Foreigners protest America's new tariff law. Seamen's deportation bills draw more protests. Load lines are set at a London meeting. A mid-volume British letter tests a report's worth. Could it ground world discussion, London asks Washington. Such feelers fill the conference year's gaps. The volume is procedure with fleets attached.
frus-1931-41v01:
This special volume gathers a decade of Japan papers. Manchuria's seizure opens the record in 1931. America's answer refuses to bless the taking. Shanghai burns in the 1932 fighting file. Japan then pushes deeper into China by stages. It tears up the Washington naval pact. It walks out of the London talks in anger. Gun limits and fleet news swaps are refused. Civilians die under bombs in yearly files. The gunboat Panay sinks in December 1937. That file runs long with protests and amends.

China's customs and salt funds need guarding throughout. A mid-volume Tokyo statement eyes Spain's war. Franco, it notes, now holds most of the country. The Anti-Comintern camp, it vows, will widen its reach. The volume is a road to war, filed yearly.
frus-1931v01:
Hoover's debt moratorium fills the 1931 opener. His two December messages frame the fight. A one-year pause on war debts is proposed in June. France's acceptance takes the hardest bargaining. Experts meet in London through the summer. Each debtor nation answers in its own file. Congress approves the pause at year's end. Credit flight from Germany must also stop. Basel's Young Plan committee meets in December. France and Italy's fleets take the next long run. A one-day armaments truce begins in November.

Stimson tours Europe in the general files. Press briefings fill slips between the cables. A September conference transcript sits mid-volume. The Secretary fields questions on the crisis. The volume is finance as foreign policy. Debts, not armies, threaten the peace here.
frus-1932v01:
Disarmament at Geneva fills the 1932 opener. Hoover sends two December messages with the papers. The conference opens in February after long waiting. America's nine points come on February 9. A second plan follows on April 11. Stimson travels to Geneva for private talks. Hoover's own plan lands on June 22. An adjournment formula closes the first phase in July. The Bureau works on into December. Germany demands equal arms in its own file. Sea questions run alongside throughout.

Stimson's August speech reviews the peace pact's three years. Debtors then plead for easier war debt terms. The moratorium is legalized country by country. A mid-volume British paper warns of paradox. A disarmament meeting that spurs rearming would shame all. The volume is hope administered in sessions.
frus-1933v01:
Geneva's disarmament endgame opens the 1933 general volume. The bureau works from January into March. American planning fills the spring recess. Deadlocks crowd the general commission into June. Direct talks break down by October. Germany walks out that month in anger. Four powers confer in December without it. Arms export bans need Congress's grant in one file. British and Japanese eyes watch America's shipyards. A four-power pact signs at Rome in July. Nazi pressure on Austria's Dollfuss follows. The Polish Corridor adds its own tension.

London's money conference closes the contents. Roosevelt sounds out foreign leaders in Washington first. A mid-volume note arranges a premier's quiet visit. No formal urging must leak, the envoy stresses. The volume is two conferences failing slowly.
frus-1934v01:
The 1934 opener joins Geneva's endgame to London's naval prelude. Talks run side by side from January to May. The bureau and general commission meet into June. America then sponsors an arms trade treaty alone. Naval talks with Britain fill the summer. Japan joins them in the autumn session. Tokyo then denounces the Washington naval pact. Foreigners protest the Senate's munitions inquiry. The old arms traffic pact wins consent with a caveat. The Persian Gulf reservation needs many powers' assent.

A mid-volume count sizes that chore. Thirty-seven powers signed; others must each agree. Letters must explain the caveat capital by capital. An eastern pact for Europe is weighed meanwhile. The volume is limitation by correspondence. Every weapon needs a paper trail.
frus-1935v01:
Geneva's arms trade talks open the 1935 general volume. A special committee sits from February to April. America's draft text gets its first reading. Its Geneva delegation office then closes. London's naval conference fills the next run. Berlin and London cut their own naval deal in June. That pact draws a short, wary file. Envoys analyze Europe's drift toward war. Selling war goods on credit wins no official help. The Nye Committee's work fills two files. Foreign governments protest its reach in one.

The Senate kills World Court membership in January. Debts from the first war sit unpaid in a status file. Liquor smuggling talks close the contents. A mid-volume talk plans Atlantic air routes. Bermuda and Newfoundland are weighed as stepping stones. The volume is peace machinery winding down.
frus-1936v01:
The 1936 general volume opens at Geneva's last act. Disarmament's conference flickers in a short file. London's naval talks then run from January to March. A new naval treaty signs on March 25. Other powers are wooed to join its terms. Britain's bid to revive a Washington clause fails. Kept tonnage is counted under the old pact. Submarine rules win a formal restatement in November. Neutrality law draws the Department's careful views. Envoys report Europe's slide in a long run. Berlin and Tokyo sign their anti-Comintern pact. That November accord closes the political files.

Liquor treaties fill the tail by country. A mid-volume ruling backs seizing smuggler ships. Revenue law, it argues, reaches their unlawful trade. The volume mixes fleets with rum-runners again.
frus-1937v01:
Spain's civil war fills the heart of the 1937 general volume. Geneva's disarmament bureau meets once in May. Envoys report Europe's dangers in a long run. Then Spain takes three thick sections. Its war's world politics fill the first. Guarding Americans and others fills the second. Planes and war goods must not reach Spain. That ban's policing fills the third. Italy joins the anti-Comintern pact in its file. Big naval guns stay capped only if Japan agrees. Tokyo refuses, and the limit fails.

Van Zeeland tours America on trade's obstacles. Hull states his peace principles on July 16. Foreign capitals comment in a thick tail. A mid-volume case strands a man in Seville. Fernandez holds Spanish papers, not American proof. His release cannot be claimed as a right. The volume is neutrality's hard year.
frus-1938v01:
Europe's road to Munich fills the 1938 general volume. Envoys report the drift in a front file. London floats joint action for peace in talks. Rome and London sign their April accord. Roosevelt's comment follows in the record. Spain's war then takes four sections. Guarding lives and banning planes fill two. Refugees win a relief file of their own. Austria's annexation follows in a thick run. The Czech crisis then builds by stages. May's scare, summer pressure, and September's brink pass in order. Berchtesgaden and Godesberg head the fourth part. Munich's surrender closes the sequence on September 30.

Evian's refugee meeting ends the contents. A mid-volume French report blames Berlin and Rome. Franco's softer reply was hardened at their insistence. Spain and Czechoslovakia, Paris warns, are one problem.
frus-1939v01:
The road to war in Europe fills the 1939 opener. Guesses at Axis designs open the record. Germany swallows Czechoslovakia on March 15. America refuses to call the republic extinct. Tension mounts through April's middle weeks. Roosevelt begs Hitler and Mussolini for pledges on April 14. Pressure on Poland builds all summer. London, Paris, and Moscow fail to unite. Berlin and Moscow then sign their pact on August 23. Roosevelt's last appeals fill August's closing days. Invasion comes on September 1 in the next part. Russia enters Poland on September 17.

The two aggressors sign a friendship pact on September 28. Peace feelers after Poland fall flat. A mid-volume report lists bombed Polish towns. Officers swear to strikes beyond military targets. Their escape route ran south to the Russian frontier. The volume is a countdown kept in cables.
frus-1940v01:
Peace feelers open the 1940 general volume. Sumner Welles tours Europe's capitals that winter. Neutrals are sounded on the postwar world. Myron Taylor goes to the Vatican as Roosevelt's man. Envoys to Turkey's faith leaders are proposed too. Then Germany strikes Norway and Denmark in April. The Low Countries fall in the next section. France collapses in the third. Italy attacks Greece at the tail. Russia's eastern moves take four sections. Finland's Winter War ends at Moscow in March. The Baltic states are swallowed by force. Bessarabia is seized from Rumania in turn.

Berlin and Moscow cooperate through it all. A mid-volume wire from Belgrade reports Balkan whispers. Bulgaria's envoy retails Yugoslav thinking that January. The volume is a continent partitioned. Its sections tick off the victims.
frus-1941v01:
Russia anchors the 1941 general volume. Finland's road to war beside Germany opens it. Washington pleads with Helsinki to stay out. That file runs longest at the front. Berlin and Moscow cooperate until June 22. Their pact's collapse is dated in the contents. London and Paris had courted Moscow in vain earlier. Poland's exiled government bargains with Russia next. Balkan moves by both dictatorships follow. Greece's fight with the Axis is noted. Roosevelt and Churchill meet at sea in August. Their Atlantic session takes a short file.

Neutrality law is loosened by November's repeal. Repatriation and refugee files close the list. A mid-volume statute text frees some aliens from the draft. Men who drop citizen plans escape service thereby. The volume is realignment year. Old neutrals choose sides by winter.
frus-1942v01:
The United Nations are born in the 1942 opener. Their declaration signs on January 1 in Washington. A world court's future wins no joint study. German atrocities draw allied condemnation in files. A war crimes board is proposed in turn. Looted property transfers are denounced by plan. A relief administration is designed in long talks. Postwar money and trade are sketched beside it. Citizens trapped in enemy lands need exchange. Deals with Berlin, Rome, and Tokyo follow. Refugee aid runs through the same machinery.

Neutral states protest the draft's reach. Wheat men meet in Washington into 1942. Their pact is initialed that April. A mid-volume letter backs a tin pact's renewal. Full output will be needed, it argues. An escape clause guards the signers meanwhile. The volume builds the postwar world early.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d101: On November 8, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill, four days before sailing for the Mediterranean. The letter is Document 101 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The president's party was packing maps, staff lists, and arguments for two conferences at once. The record gives the date and the two names and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the last Washington days of the story.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d201:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius sent President Roosevelt a memorandum on 9 November 1943 about trusteeship for disputed islands in the Central Pacific. It carries two hasty enclosures and a chart, and Stettinius warns that the State Department's full studies of trusteeship were still unfinished.

The enclosure favors placing the contested islands under an international trusteeship shared by the United States, Britain, Australia, New Zealand, and China. Day-to-day rule would be split by friendly agreement, while defense would rest with the United States alone or jointly with Britain. The paper also urges Roosevelt to hear the Joint Chiefs of Staff before raising the plan with Churchill, since nearby American islands might be drawn in.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d301:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 308/7 at Cairo on 24 November 1943, on the boundaries of the Southeast Asia Command. It records Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek's objection to the boundaries set at the Quebec conference, and his counter-proposal, worked out with Mountbatten and Somervell.

Chiang backs one command under Mountbatten for the Burma campaign, but holds that Thailand and Indochina must stay in the China theater. Moving them, he argues, would wound Chinese morale, feed Japanese propaganda about British empire-building, and chill relations among the three allies. His plan has Chinese troops attack from the north and Mountbatten's from the south when the time comes, with political questions handled by a joint committee. Mountbatten accepts the boundaries but objects to the committee; the American chiefs and Roosevelt approve Chiang's proposal as it stands.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d401:
President Roosevelt wrote to the Shah of Iran from Tehran on 1 December 1943, a letter of thanks for his welcome in the Shah's country. The Shah had met him, offered his palace, an airport greeting, and a guard of honor, and sent a magnificent carpet.

Roosevelt says the circumstances of his visit made it impossible to accept those offers, much as he would have liked to. He leaves Iran with regret. He regrets not seeing more of the country and its people. The carpet, he promises, will remind him and the American people of Iranian hospitality. Iran, he writes, holds a warm spot in American hearts. It is warmer now that the two nations are brothers in arms. He hopes their wartime partnership will continue unchecked in the labors of peace. Below his signature he added, in his own hand, a hope that the Shah would visit Washington.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d501:
Harry Hopkins sent a message to President Roosevelt himself on December 6, 1943, the last day of the Second Cairo Conference. Hopkins traveled as the President's special assistant and closest adviser, yet still put matters to him in writing. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

A Hopkins note to Roosevelt is the inner circle talking on paper. Hopkins saw everything at Cairo, from the leaders' tempers to the staff's disputes, and his written word carried a weight no other aide could match. Readers interested in how Roosevelt actually made decisions will find these short staff messages among the most revealing records of the trip.
frus-1943v01:
General topics open the 1943 Diplomatic Papers in Volume I of Foreign Relations of the United States. Wartime conferences among heads of government lead the volume. Other sections cover prisoner exchanges, aid for Americans in enemy lands, and help for refugees, notably the Bermuda Conference on refugees.

Papers also record the Moscow foreign ministers' meeting and early plans for postwar relief. Much space goes to UNRRA, war crimes warnings, and talks on money and trade after the war. The mix of cables and conference records shows Allied leaders building new world bodies while the war still raged.
frus-1944-quebec-d101:
On August 30, 1944, Hull wrote to Lord Halifax in Washington. Halifax served as Britain's ambassador to the United States. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. Such letters kept allied channels warm between summits.

Ambassadors in Washington handled much of the alliance's daily business. A letter from Hull to Halifax joined the two foreign services directly. The Quebec Conference opened less than two weeks later. For readers, the message shows preparation running through diplomatic channels too. Not every question waited for Roosevelt and Churchill to meet. The conference opened at Quebec City on September 12.
frus-1944-quebec-d201:
An editors' note sets out the Roosevelt-Churchill agreement of September 15, 1944, on occupation zones in Germany, learned from Leahy through Morgenthau's diary. The southwestern zone went to American forces and the northwestern to British. Boundary changes moved Hessen-Nassau and Oberhessen to the American zone, and the Saarland, Palatinate, and Rheinhessen to the British.

American forces were guaranteed access through the western and northwestern seaports, with rights of passage through the British zone. The Joint Chiefs added American control of Bremen the next morning, and the Combined Chiefs' decision was approved on September 16. No evidence shows the two leaders discussed dividing Berlin's sectors, which the London protocol of September 12 had also left open.
frus-1944-quebec-d301: A joint public statement was drafted for Roosevelt and Churchill on 19 September 1944, though a draft is not a released text. The wording survives as document 301 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the Quebec Conference. Comparing proposed language with what leaders finally said in public is one reason historians value drafts preserved in records like this one.
frus-1944v01:
Volume I of the 1944 Diplomatic Papers gathers general questions that crossed many borders. The European Advisory Commission leads, with its work on surrender terms and zones for Germany and Austria. Peace feelers and the reach of unconditional surrender follow.

A second thread builds a new world body, from first talks to the Dumbarton Oaks meetings. Other sections aid refugees, warn on Nazi crimes, and probe war crimes charges. The papers show planners drafting the peace while the war ran on. Cables and draft plans sit side by side. Draft texts let readers watch each plan take shape.
frus-1945-50-intel-d101:
Irwin, the interim activities director of the Strategic Services Unit, wrote to Assistant Secretary McCloy on 28 January 1946. The SSU had just passed to new interim leadership as Magruder's time ended. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A change of chief, marked by a new name on the same channel to the same patron, shows an institution outliving its founder. Irwin wrote days after the president created the Central Intelligence Group, when the SSU's remnant faced absorption into the new body. Readers can watch the handover in the paper itself: the unit's needs unchanged, the hand presenting them new. The thread continues because the work, and the danger, continued.
frus-1945-50-intel-d201:
On 2 December 1946, the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) sent a memorandum to the President’s Special Counsel (Clifford). It is document 201 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d301:
On 1 October 1948, Acting Secretary of State Lovett sent a letter to Secretary of Defense Forrestal. It is document 301 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

Between offices that did not answer to each other, a letter was the polite but firm way to press a point. The tone is formal, but the stakes were real: turf, money, and the shape of the new agencies. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d401:
Secretary of Defense Louis Johnson wrote to Secretary of State Dean Acheson on 7 October 1949. The letter is document 401 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Johnson and Acheson were the two cabinet officers whose departments used intelligence most. The armed services ran large intelligence shops of their own, and the Pentagon guarded them with care. A direct letter between the two secretaries shows how disputes and deals at the top shaped the young intelligence system below them. Both men left office within two years, but the habits their letters set outlived them.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d101:
Leo Pasvolsky pressed the same cause twice in one week. In this short note of 23 January 1945, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, he returns to the Emergency High Commission for Liberated Europe. He writes to the Secretary of State from his post working on the general world body.

Pasvolsky says agreement on the commission at the coming meeting is a need, not a wish. From his side of the work, it is the strongest answer the allies can give to fast-growing opposition at home. Critics charge that the Dumbarton Oaks plan would merely bless a system of one-sided grabbing by the great powers. A joint commission for the freed countries would prove them wrong.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d201:
The de Gaulle visit was over, and Stalin reported it to Roosevelt on 3 December 1944. His secret and personal message is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The talks, he says, allowed a friendly exchange on Franco-Soviet relations.

De Gaulle raised the two questions Stalin had forecast: the Rhine frontier and a Franco-Soviet pact. On the frontier, Stalin answered that it cannot be settled without the knowledge and consent of the main allies, whose armies are fighting on French soil. He stressed how complex the matter is. On the pact, he called for close study of its legal nature. One open point is who could ratify such a pact in France as things stand. He ends by asking the President's reply and comments.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d301:
Eden and Stettinius sat down at Malta to tie up the loose ends on Germany, and these are their agreed minutes. Printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, the record opens with Eden asking the Secretary of State what points he wished to raise. Zones of occupation come first.

Agreement exists between London and Washington on the zones, Stettinius says, but small points remain, above all the ports of Bremen and Bremerhaven. They should be settled at once. The Russians may soon be in Berlin, and might form views of their own if the negotiated protocol stays unapproved. Eden agrees the points can be cleared with the military authorities forthwith. The two also take up a zone for the French, which the President favors and which might be cut from the southern British zone.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d401:
Open items blocking the call of the United Nations conference are listed in this delegation paper of February 8, 1945. France's status came first. At Malta, the British and Americans had agreed France should be a fifth sponsoring power. Its name would join China's on the invitations.

How to consult France and China came next. The United States would do it for Britain and Russia; Grew stood ready in Washington to start at a flash from Yalta. The form of invitation followed: America could issue it for all five sponsors, and a draft was in hand. Trusteeships close the list. The paper measures how close San Francisco was.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d501:
Formal where the communiqué is warm, the Protocol of Proceedings records what the Crimea Conference actually decided. The conference of the three heads of government, it states, took place from February 4 to 11 and came to set conclusions. The first section covers the world organisation.

A United Nations conference would be summoned for Wednesday, April 25, 1945, in the United States of America. Invitations would go to the United Nations as they stood on February 8, and to Associated Nations declaring war by March 1. Ukraine and White Russia's candidacy follows. Later sections carry Poland, reparations, and the rest. Lawyers and historians cite this text, not the speeches.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d101:
General Deane reported fresh pressure on Moscow in an extract of a telegram to General Bradley dated June 26, 1945. The extract is document 101 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The omitted part of the cable sums up Vyshinsky's stiff reply of the day before, which had put off the American requests until Zhukov returned.

Deane says the importance of General Stoner's signal crews going to Berlin had been stressed when the request to enlarge Parks's group was made. On receiving Bradley's latest cable the night before, he took the matter to General Antonov again, while Harriman took it to Vyshinsky. He plans to see Antonov or his staff that day and press further. The fragment shows the daily grind of extracting approvals from the Soviet machine.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d201:
Ambassador Harriman described Molotov's first questions about the agenda in a telegram dated July 8, 1945. The message is document 201 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Harriman had handed Molotov the list of topics the President might wish to raise, sent from Washington on July 5.

Molotov asked whether reparations would be discussed. Harriman pointed out that Pauley was coming to Berlin and felt sure the President would discuss the subject if the Soviets wished to raise it. Molotov then asked whether the whole administration of Germany would be covered, and Harriman said he assumed the Germany topic covered it. Molotov would bring the list to Stalin's attention and report any comments or added topics. The exchange gave Washington its first feel for Soviet priorities.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d301:
Washington explained a deliberate silence to Ambassador Harriman on June 29, 1945. Molotov's note of March 17 had refused American requests for consultation on Rumania's political situation. The Department had left it unanswered on purpose, while the main effort went to the Polish question.

Now, the Secretary of State ad interim wrote, a detailed reply would serve no useful purpose. The subject would come up at the coming conference of heads of government, alongside the other former satellite states. The cable shows how Washington saved its Balkan complaints for the summit table at Potsdam. The Balkan questions, in short, would wait for the heads of government.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d401:
The left bank of the Rhine is treated in a briefing book paper of June 30, 1945, as a problem of military security above all. The fair needs of France, Belgium, and the Netherlands should be recognized, it says. But the problem should ultimately be solved by long-range controls over Germany, not by transfers of Rhenish territory.

While allied military government lasts in Germany, the paper adds, western Europe need not fear German aggression. So there is no need now to decide what military posts the Rhine area may require later. Its basic data describe a region of 10,598 square miles and about 6,550,000 people, including the Saar and the Palatinate.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d501:
Recognition of Poland is announced in a White House press release of July 5, 1945, carrying a statement by the President. It is with great satisfaction, Truman announces, that effective today, as of 7 p.m. Eastern War Time, the United States has established diplomatic relations with the newly formed Polish Provisional Government of National Unity, now established at Warsaw. The step fulfills the Yalta decisions on Poland.

The new government, he reports, has informed him in writing that it recognizes in their entirety the Crimea Conference decisions on the Polish question. It has thereby confirmed its intention to carry out the provisions on holding elections. Arthur Bliss Lane, chosen as ambassador to Poland, will proceed to Warsaw as soon as possible.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d601:
The United States Chiefs of Staff answered a British proposal in a top secret memo of July 10, 1945. It is document 601 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The issue was wording in the joint paper on basic objectives for the war.

The U.S. chiefs agree to write British Commonwealth in place of British Isles for one security clause. They add that the clause should no longer link security to war-making capacity. With Germany beaten, they argue, there is no case for widening pledges made for a two-front war. The commitment should be clearly tied to the war against Japan alone. The memo shows both staffs trimming grand wartime language as the conflict shrank to one foe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d701:
A correction to the record of the Molotov-Sarper talks reached Ambassador Wilson in Ankara on July 7, 1945. His top secret wire is document 701 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The source was the Turkish foreign ministry's secretary general, Acikalin.

Acikalin said Ankara had cabled Sarper not to discuss any Soviet proposals made on behalf of the Balkan states. Sarper's reply exposed a garble in his earlier cable. No mention of the Balkan states had in fact been made on June 18. What Molotov had said was narrower and vaguer. If an alliance treaty with Turkey were in question, Ankara would have to examine certain considerations Moscow wished to formulate. No one in Ankara yet knew what those considerations might be. The correction removes a point Wilson himself had built on days before.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1001:
The Acting Secretary of State sent this telegram to the Secretary of State at Potsdam on July 31, 1945. It quotes a message Washington had sent to Stockholm five days earlier. That message answers reports that the Soviet government will ask Sweden to hand over interned German airplanes as war booty.

The Stockholm envoy is told to resist that claim, ideally with British and French support. America cannot accept the war booty theory for such property, the text says. All German assets now sit under the joint jurisdiction of the four occupying powers. None may be removed or disposed of without the consent of the Allied Control Commission.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1101:
Staff of the United States team at Potsdam drafted this working paper on 24 July 1945. Working papers were not public statements. They were the private groundwork that helped American negotiators agree on a stand before they faced the British and Soviet teams across the table.

A paper of this kind set out facts, options, and a line to take on one of the questions before the summit. Germany's future was the chief subject at Potsdam, and the first full week was spent mapping out stands. The text lets readers watch Washington sort out its own case in private. It is the homework behind the handshakes, kept in the official record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1201:
Hayter, secretary general of the British team, wrote to Cannon, a first secretary at the embassy in Portugal, on 17 July 1945. The note went out on the summit's opening day. It joined the Potsdam staff to a quiet post in a neutral land.

Portugal had stayed out of the war, but its Atlantic islands held air bases the Allies prized. Lisbon was also a crossroads of spies, trade, and quiet deals. A line from the summit's staff to the Lisbon post shows how far Potsdam's reach ran. Small posts felt the great talks too, and this note is the touch.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1301:
The Acting Secretary of State set down this memorandum on 24 July 1945. It dates from the middle of the summit, the day the Polish deputy premier sent his three papers and the talks pressed on Poland. Grew's note is the home office thinking on paper at that hour.

Memoranda from the acting chief fixed stands for the desks in Washington. They also formed the record of what the home half of the department knew and when it knew it. This one belongs to that Washington layer of the Potsdam story. It shows the department's stand-in chief at his daily work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1401:
François Lacoste, the French chargé in Washington, wrote to the acting secretary of state on 6 August 1945. A chargé speaks for his country when the ambassador is away. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Lacoste's letter came five days after the Caffery and Bidault exchange in Paris, and it works the same tie from the other capital. While ambassadors talked in Paris, the French mission in Washington kept its own channel warm. The date also fell on the day of the Hiroshima bombing, though the letter belongs to the ordinary flow of allied business. Together, the papers show a two-ended alliance being tended at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-101: An editorial note placed after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume speaks in the editors' voice rather than a delegate's. Notes of this kind in the Foreign Relations series supply context the wartime papers assume. They can explain a missing text or point to a parallel record. The note serves readers moving through the heavy staff traffic of the conference's second week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d801:
Schoenfeld wrote from Hungary on July 18, 1945, in document 801. The representative in Budapest kept up a steady flow of reports as Potsdam began. This letter went to the Acting Secretary of State. It joined the growing Hungary file in the second Potsdam volume.

Daily reporting from a small post builds a record no summary can match. Schoenfeld tracked a country remaking itself under foreign eyes. Readers see the armistice regime from within, week by week. The document shows the value of presence: Washington knew Hungary through this man's desk. His letters let the summit's Balkan choices be judged against ground truth.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d901:
American staff prepared this undated working paper, titled simply Gold, for talks at Potsdam around July 18, 1945. A note on the copy says it served discussion with the President. The subject is the gold captured from Germany, worth about 250 million dollars in American hands.

Most of that gold, the paper says, can be traced to banks in freed nations, and pledges may bind America to return it. Calling the gold war booty might break those pledges and weaken the gold standard. The paper suggests treating the claim as a bargaining chip instead. It could trade against other nations' views on restitution and booty, and against French claims.
frus-1945Berlinv01:
Volume I for the Conference of Berlin, better known as Potsdam, gathers the papers that set up the 1945 meeting. Early letters arrange a three-power session, followed by the Hopkins mission to Moscow and the Davies mission to London. Briefing books then take over most of the volume.

Those briefs cover Germany's treatment, reparations, zones, and its fleet. Poland, Austria, Italy, and Greece each get full sections, as do war crimes and population transfers. Staff wrote these papers to arm President Truman for the talks. They show what Washington wanted before bargaining began.
frus-1945v01:
The United Nations is the whole subject of Volume I of the 1945 Diplomatic Papers. Its core is the San Francisco Conference, told in dated chapters from January through the signing in June. Delegation talks, draft texts, and votes trace the Charter as it took form.

Later papers cover the Preparatory Commission and the choice of the United States as the permanent seat. UNESCO's founding and labor conference work follow. A guide links the Dumbarton Oaks drafts to the final Charter articles. For students of the UN's birth, this is the working record.
frus-1946v01:
General matters and the United Nations open the 1946 series in Volume I. It tracks how Washington set up its work with the new world body. Voting rules in the Security Council, new members, and budget shares take long sections.

Trusteeship for the Pacific islands and atomic energy control mark the hard cases. Aid policy, threat studies, and base rights close the volume. Court jurisdiction and the UN seat also appear. The papers show a great power learning to work through a body it helped design, while guarding its own freedom to act.
frus-1947v01:
General questions and the United Nations fill Volume I for 1947. Headquarters accords, the seat question, and fights over new members lead the record. A sharper tone enters, with the debate on the Soviet-backed warmongering resolution.

Atomic control and arms limits take the longest run. Aid policy, threat studies, base rights, and stockpiles of key materials follow. Pacific trusteeship for the former Japanese islands also appears. The papers show the new body settling into its home while the wartime alliance frayed inside it, vote by vote. Delegation cables show the daily work behind each vote.
frus-1949v01:
National security affairs and foreign economic policy share Volume I for 1949. Arms control at the United Nations leads, with atomic control still deadlocked. Threat studies, military posture, aid abroad, and base rights form the security core.

Atomic energy's foreign side takes its own long block. Trade papers cover the GATT talks at Annecy and new investment treaties. The Point Four aid idea appears near the end, in its first papers. Antarctic policy closes the volume. Planners wrote these files as a long rivalry took shape and aid became a core tool.
frus-1951v01:
National security affairs and foreign economic policy open the 1951 set in Volume I. Objectives, threat studies, and military posture lead the record. The shift to a mutual security aid program follows in its own block.

Arms control and bids to strengthen the UN against attack take the next runs. Trade talks at Torquay fill the long GATT sections, with fights over tariff cuts and empire preferences. Export controls on the East also appear. The papers show a state funding allies abroad while it bargained over trade rules at home and overseas.
frus-1955-57v01:
Vietnam opens the 1955–1957 set as Volume I. The Diem government's first months lead, with the sect crisis in Saigon and a hard choice to back him. French and American training duties are argued through the spring of 1955.

The vote question follows, as all-Vietnam elections due under Geneva were weighed and let slip. A referendum pitted Diem against Bao Dai that fall. Long-range plans close the volume, on home security, land reform, and aid. Diem's Washington visit also appears. The papers trace a deepening pledge to one half of a divided land.
frus-1958-60v01:
Vietnam opens the 1958–1960 set as Volume I. The Diem government's hold on the South fills the record. Aid, army training, and internal security run through the files, with worry over the regime's narrow base.

Insurgent attacks grow in the later papers. Saigon's files weigh land reform, press curbs, and the Can Lao party's reach. The volume reads as a slow slide. Each report of calm sits beside a warning, and the warnings grow longer as the three years pass toward a war still unnamed. Reports from the field grew blunter with each season.
frus-1961-63v01:
Vietnam, 1961 fills Volume I of the 1961–1963 set. General Lansdale's January visit leads. A counterinsurgency plan follows, pressed on Saigon through the spring in these files.

A presidential task force and Vice President Johnson's Asia trip take the middle blocks. Money missions weigh what aid can buy. Rising Viet Cong attacks drive the Taylor mission in October. Its report's adoption closes the year. The record shows a war built by steps. Each paper adds men, money, or a new pledge, none yet called war. Honolulu talks in December close the year's record.
frus-1969-76ve01:
Volume E-1 of the 1969-1976 series gathers documents on global issues from 1969 to 1972. Its first chapter covers terrorism, hijacking, and attacks on civil aviation. Cases include the Israeli attack on Beirut airport and the hijacking of TWA Flight 840. The Munich Olympic attack closes that chapter. A short chapter covers the hijacking accord with Cuba. Later chapters treat drug trafficking, space cooperation, environment policy, and oceans policy.

The drug chapter is one of the longest in the volume. It follows U.S. efforts to curb supply at the source abroad. The oceans chapter weighs claims to wider seas. The volume shows new issues forcing their way onto the agenda.
frus-1977-80v01:
Volume I of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1977-1980, treats the foundations of foreign policy. Its documents are dated 1974 through 1980 and run in one sequence of 163. They print speeches, memos, and studies that set out first principles. Human rights, arms restraint, and aid all get early statements. The Carter team's effort to state a new course after Vietnam fills much of the volume.

The papers include work from before Carter took office, as the series frames the shift. Notes cite Congress and the Nation and the Public Papers for key texts. The volume serves as the stated creed against which the later, country volumes can be read.
frus-1981-88v01:
Volume I of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1981-1988, treats the foundations of foreign policy. A short opening run prints texts from 1975 through 1980. Chapters then proceed year by year, from 1981 to 1988. An appendix closes the volume. The papers print the speeches and doctrines of the Reagan years. They set out the case against Soviet power, for military buildup, and for backing anti-Communist movements. Trade and partnership with allied economies also get their statements.

One address urges the big economies to open markets and invest in each other. The volume serves as the stated creed of the Reagan era. Later country volumes can be read against it.
gao-gaoreports-b-296401:
Sigmatech protested Army task orders for engineering support in GAO decision B-296401, dated August 10, 2005. The orders went to Sverdrup Technology. They sat under a blanket purchase deal. The firm had done like work under its own deal. It said the Army had bundled its work into the big deal.

GAO sustained the protest. The claim was on time. The firm learned the facts when the orders came, and filed in 10 days. On the merits, the Army did no bundling study. It also missed key steps in the rules. Bundling small firm work needs a clear study. That study was absent, so the orders fell.
gao-gaoreports-b-296501:
Computers Universal protested the terms of a Veterans Affairs call for tech services in GAO decision B-296501, dated August 18, 2005. The site was the Naval Medical Center in San Diego. The work was day-to-day tech help, software work, and code work. The firm said staff skill terms were too strict.

GAO denied the protest. The record showed the skill terms fit the need. The center needed high level skill for its many clinics and systems. Strict terms are allowed when they track a real need. The firm had held the work before. That fact did not make the new terms unfair. The call could stand as drawn.
gao-gaoreports-b-298401:
Armor Group International Training, Inc. protested a planned sole-source award by the Department of State. The award to BSR, Incorporated covered anti-terrorism driver training. The work ties to the Diplomatic Security Training Center in Dunn Loring, Virginia. GAO issued B-298401 on August 31, 2006.

Armor Group attacked a geographic limit in the agency's needs. It said the limit skewed the buy toward one source. GAO found the limit tied to real training needs. State staff and students had to reach the site on a set drill. A limit that an agency truly needs can stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-309301:
An unpaid ambassador post is upheld in this GAO opinion, B-309301, dated June 8, 2007. Sam Fox got a recess post as Ambassador to Belgium. A law at 5 U.S.C. section 5503 bears on pay for such posts. Three senators asked how that law and the bar on free work apply here. The State Department said Fox would draw no pay.

GAO agreed with that stand. The law bars pay for Fox in this post. Unpaid service here does not break the bar on free work. That bar guards against forced debts and later claims for pay. A legal bar on pay wipes out that risk. GAO also warned that a stricter read would raise deep constitutional doubts.
gao-gaoreports-b-310801:
NHIC Corporation lost its protest. That ruling is B-310801, dated February 12, 2008. The Medicare agency sought a firm to run claims work. The award went to Palmetto GBA, LLC. The deal joins Part A and Part B claims in one zone. NHIC fought the cost test that backed the pick. It said bid costs were not matched to the work plans.

GAO denied the protest. The agency ran a deep test of each big cost part. It used topic pros to judge if costs fit each bid's plan. The test found the costs real for the work at hand. Deep tests by pros earn trust at GAO.
gao-gaoreports-b-400101:
Jim Swistowicz saw his protest thrown out under GAO decision B-400101, dated July 7, 2008. He spoke for a labor union at Sierra Army Depot in California. The Army ran an A-76 race for base aid work at the depot. He said a law bars the budget shop from calls for such races. The race at stake had roots in a past race from 2000. Its new start came in the fall of 2007.

GAO dismissed the protest. A race begun before January 28, 2008 sits past his stake. The law that grants staff a voice sets that date as a gate. Old races run their course free of the new voice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-101:
Mad Cow Disease, GAO-05-101 of February 25, 2005, reviews how the Food and Drug Administration polices the feed ban that guards U.S. cattle. The ban, set in 1997, bars some animal protein from feed for cattle and other cud-chewing stock. The aim is to stop the spread of bovine spongiform encephalopathy. FDA and 38 states check feed firms to enforce the rule.

GAO first flagged weak spots in the ban's policing in 2002. It now checks what FDA has fixed since then. Gains in day-to-day control are real, the report finds. Gaps in checks and follow-up still blunt the ban's force.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-201:
Interagency Contracting, GAO-05-201 of April 29, 2005, shows how a shortcut in federal buying went wrong in wartime. One agency may order goods or work off a deal another agency holds. The Pentagon used that path to buy interrogation and support work in Iraq through the Interior Department. Interior placed 11 task orders worth over $66 million.

GAO finds cracks in how those orders were run. It names the causes that fed the cracks, from vague needs to weak checks. It then grades the fixes both departments have since made. The case warns that speed in buying still needs firm hands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-301:
Defense Acquisitions, GAO-05-301 of March 31, 2005, is a thick yearly score book on the Pentagon's top arms builds. U.S. arms lead the world when done. Yet for 30 years, GAO has found the same flaws: cost growth, late steps, and weak feats. Cash strain adds a fresh push to hold each build to its sums.

GAO grades a set of major builds one by one. It tests if facts in hand match the facts a sound build would hold at that stage. Gaps flag risk and the acts to cure it. Strong builds earn a nod as models. The book will come out each year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-701:
Screening welfare clients for domestic violence is surveyed in GAO-05-701, a report of August 16, 2005. Forty-eight states have adopted the Family Violence Option or a like policy. Most ask clients directly about abuse; five merely post notice of waivers. Screening tools vary in depth, and caseworkers often lack skill for the topic. Some states hire specialists. The health department shares information but has issued no best-practice guide.

Most states waive work rules, the 5-year cash limit, and child support duties for victims, though 27 demand use of support services. Few clients get waivers. Fifteen states fund marriage programs with welfare money; 28 fund fatherhood programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-801:
