Visa security staffing abroad is assessed in GAO-05-801, issued July 29, 2005. A 2002 law put Homeland Security officers in Saudi Arabia to review every visa request. It also let the program grow to other posts. These officers advise and train consular staff. GAO checked the officers' work in Saudi Arabia. It also weighed plans to expand the program.

GAO found the officers review all requests before final rulings there. Officials said their law enforcement skill strengthens security. But no solid data shows the program's impact. The review-all duty leaves little time for training help. The department has no strategic plan for the program. Chiefs at five new posts held off approval until their questions on goals and staffing were answered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-401:
Federal workers can buy long-term care cover from a federal program. In GAO-06-401 (March 31, 2006), GAO tests how that program stacks up. The Federal Long Term Care Insurance Program began in 2002. Law required the federal offer and this study of its standing in the market. The study period runs three years.

GAO compared benefits, premiums, enrollment rates, and enrollee traits. It set the federal product beside private individual and group products. It also checked early claims against first expectations. GAO found the federal program compared favorably with other products. It said study of the claims trend could guide future choices. Readers get price and design detail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-501:
The Energy Department buys over $20 billion a year, yet small firms get a thin share of prime work. In GAO-06-501 (April 7, 2006), GAO reviews small business contracting at the department. Federal policy gives small businesses the fullest practical chance at prime contracts. Those are direct contracts between the government and a firm. GAO studied the department's key efforts to widen such chances.

GAO also named management challenges the department faces in raising its performance. It adds data on how other agencies run small business programs. Improved program management could help the department reach its small business goal, GAO said. Readers get efforts, obstacles, and comparisons.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1001:
Very light jets, and their effect on busy skies, are forecast in GAO report GAO-07-1001, dated August 24, 2007. These small jets cost less than other business jets and pack new tech. Forecasters see thousands joining U.S. skies over the next two decades. The first were cleared to fly in 2006.

GAO weighed current forecasts and what could shift jet sales. It asked how more light jets could affect sky capacity and safety. It checked agency plans to fit them in. It traced effects on agency costs and trust fund income. GAO made no recommendations. The report maps a new fleet before it lands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1101:
Pension and health benefits in bankruptcy are shaped by many forces, GAO reports in GAO-07-1101, dated September 6, 2007. Debate has grown over firms that use chapter 11 cases to cut or end worker benefits, to stay in the fight with rivals. Congress passed new laws in 2005 and 2006 that touch that choice.

GAO asked if those laws changed how benefits fare in chapter 11. It asked what is known of how far firms have cut worker or retiree benefits. It read filings of 115 public firms that filed from October 17, 2004 to October 17, 2006. Experts aided the work. Agencies agreed with the findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-201:
Farmers hurt by import competition gained their own trade aid program in 2002. GAO assessed its early record in GAO-07-201, issued December 18, 2006. The program offers training, technical help, and cash up to $10,000 a year. The law allows up to $90 million a year through fiscal year 2007. Producer groups must first win certification from the Agriculture Department. Prices must have fallen at least 20 percent, with imports a key cause.

Few producers had taken part so far, GAO found. Of 101 petitions filed, the department fully reviewed 64. It certified 30 and denied 34. Certified crops ranged from Concord grapes and wild blueberries to shrimp and catfish. Petitions fell in fiscal year 2006 from the year before. Officials blamed the strict eligibility tests. Spending stayed well below the sums Congress allowed. The report was meant to guide the program's 2007 renewal debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-301:
Fire, police, and medical radios still cannot always talk across agency lines. GAO measured the push to fix that in GAO-07-301, a report dated April 2, 2007. The homeland security department gave $2.15 billion in grants from fiscal years 2003 through 2005. The money targeted shared communications. GAO reviewed projects in selected states. It also tracked work on common radio standards. Technical help programs were part of the review.

Grants improved many local projects, GAO found. But broad planning lagged behind the spending. Not all states had plans to guide their buys. No national plan tied state efforts together. Full-scale drills were cut back, which weakened progress checks. A federal help program called SAFECOM made limited headway. Its tools often missed what local officials needed. It also skipped links with federal responders. Common standards advanced slowly. GAO urged tighter ties between grants and state plans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-401:
Title insurance buyers pay set prices for a product they rarely shop for, and GAO-07-401, dated April 13, 2007, probes that market. Earlier GAO work had raised doubts about whether premiums match real costs. It also flagged weak oversight of title agents. State and federal probes added to the concern.

GAO studied market traits across states and the forces that shape prices and rivalry. It reviewed the rules in place and the changes regulators had planned. Work rested on industry data and talks with officials in six states. GAO concluded that normal market pressure seemed weak. Buyers had little say over price yet had to buy the cover to close a deal. Stronger oversight was the remedy GAO pressed for.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-301:
Disaster cost forecasting at the emergency agency is reviewed in GAO report GAO-08-301, issued February 22, 2008. A 2007 law told GAO to study how the agency builds its cost estimates. Sound early figures guide the federal reply to storms and floods. They also shape the aid Congress votes in the aftermath.

GAO traced the steps the agency uses to draft and refine a disaster estimate. It checked the forecasts against real costs for smaller disasters from 2000 through 2006. Federal costs in that set ran under $500 million each. The agency has taken steps to learn from past misses. GAO finds more room to sharpen both learning and resource control.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-401:
Coin supply for the nation's banks is studied in GAO report GAO-08-401, issued March 21, 2008. Federal Reserve Banks order new coins from the U.S. Mint and manage stocks of circulated coins. Since late 2006, high metal prices have pushed the cost of making pennies and nickels above their face value.

The Reserve Banks' ordering process has met bank demand since fiscal year 2000. A forecast tool starts each monthly order, offices adjust it for local factors, and transfers of circulated coins cut new coin orders by about 10 percent in fiscal years 2006 and 2007. But no office works to a defined best stock range, so holdings vary widely and skew high. GAO noted that idle coin stocks held in one place can force needless new production elsewhere.
gauss-disquisitiones-1801:
Carl Friedrich Gauss founds modern number theory in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, in Latin from 1801. Primes, congruences, and quadratic forms fall into one grand order. Gauss wrote the book at twenty-four, gathering two thousand years of scattered results into a new and rigorous science of whole numbers.

His proofs set a standard of rigor that math still honors today. Modular arithmetic, now basic to computing, grows from these pages in time. Few first books have ever remade a field so completely at once. The work made Gauss the prince of mathematicians in his peers' eyes, a title the centuries since have never seen fit to revoke.
godelmann-tractatus-de-magis-1601:
Johann Georg Godelmann was a Lutheran jurist at Rostock whose Tractatus de Magis, Veneficis et Lamiis appeared in 1601. The Latin title names his subjects: magicians, poisoners, and witches. The treatise is legal and theological at once, a framework for witch prosecution.

Godelmann sorts kinds of magic, weighs what proofs a court should demand, and questions confessions won by torture. He accepts witchcraft as real yet urges judges toward care that many of his peers lacked. German courts and writers on witchcraft cited his framework through the great trial years that followed. His Latin kept the argument inside the courts and universities that ran the trials.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FerrieDavidWill: A Civil Air Patrol file, numbered 301, concerns David William Ferrie of New Orleans. Ferrie piloted for the Patrol and led cadets, and he later became a figure in the Kennedy assassination story. The surviving record identifies the file by his name and its Patrol number but gives no contents or dates, so it stands as a labeled service file on Ferrie.
grotius-rights-war-peace-campbell-1901:
A C Campbell published his translation of Hugo Grotius's Rights of War and Peace in 1901. Grotius, a Dutch lawyer and scholar, wrote the work in 1625 while in exile in Paris. Europe was deep in the Thirty Years' War, and Grotius asked what law could bind even enemies.

Grotius grounded the law of nations in natural law, rules reason finds in human nature itself. He treated when war is just, what may be done in war, and how treaties and embassies bind states. Later writers built international law on his frame. Campbell's English made the founding text of international law handy for students of law, history, and diplomacy.
guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-volume-0:
Sir Walter Scott's Guy Mannering, volume one, opens in November on a dreary Dumfriesshire road. A young English gentleman, Guy Mannering, fresh from Oxford, has spent the day drawing monastic ruins. Losing his way, he reaches Ellangowan, the Bertrams' decaying house. There a child, Harry Bertram, is born that night.

Mannering, amusing himself with astrology, casts the infant's horoscope and foretells danger at certain years. The gypsy Meg Merrilies hears the prophecy she will drive to fulfilment. Smugglers, the excise, and lawyer Gilbert Glossin's schemes gather round the estate. Harry is kidnapped and vanishes overseas, and Ellangowan passes toward ruin. The volume's thirty-one chapters end with the pieces set for the heir's return. Scott's second novel mixes gypsy romance, smuggling adventure, and a lawyer's villainy in his richest Scottish vein.
haeckel-riddle-of-universe-1901:
Ernst Haeckel published The Riddle of the Universe in German in 1899; this English edition followed in 1901. The book is his monist manifesto: one substance, one law, no split between matter and spirit. It sold in the hundreds of thousands and made Haeckel a world figure.

He applies evolution to everything: the cosmos, the mind, and morals alike. Soul, free will, and a personal God all dissolve into nature's single order. Churches and dualist philosophers answered with fury, and the book became the prime target of the anti-Darwinian backlash. Read today, it is the fullest statement of scientific materialism as a popular creed.
harnack-christianity-saunders-1901:
Adolf von Harnack's What Is Christianity? appears in Thomas Bailey Saunders's translation of 1901. The book prints Harnack's Berlin lectures of 1900. Harnack, a great church historian, seeks the essence of Christianity in Jesus's own teaching. The gospel, he argues, centers on God as father, the infinite worth of the soul, and the ethic of love.

Creeds, rituals, and dogmas are later shells around that kernel. This kernel-and-husk method defines liberal Protestant theology. The lectures drew crowds and stirred wide debate. Critics from several sides attacked his reduction of the faith. The book remains liberal Protestantism's manifesto in classic form. It is short, clear, and still argued over.
harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-volum:
The first part of Lytton's Harold carries the dedicatory epistle to C. T. D'Eyncourt and opens the tale in the month of May, in the year of our Lord 1052. The scene is the England of Edward the Confessor, when the house of Godwin stood at the height of its power and its peril. The banished Godwin's return hangs over the court. Young Harold, the great earl's son, is introduced among the wars and councils of the time.

Lytton builds his Saxon world slowly: feasts, law courts, churches, and camps, with notes to vouch for the details. The Norman duke across the sea is still a name, not yet a conqueror. Readers of the whole novel will find this a self-contained opening act, rich in scene setting. The later parts of the set carry the story through Harold's oath, his crown, and Hastings.
heartsease-or-the-brother-s-wife-pg2601:
Charlotte M. Yonge opened Heartsease in a great park, where Theodora, a stately girl of nineteen, teaches village children to make a cowslip ball under the elms. Theodora's pride is the family trial: brilliant, imperious, and bored, she looks down on the gentle young sister-in-law who enters the story as the brother's wife of the subtitle. Yonge follows the household as Theodora's contempt wounds the timid Violet and endangers the brother she adores.

Slowly, through illness, loss, and self-knowledge, Theodora learns the heart's ease of the title, the peace found in humility and use. Yonge, the great novelist of the Victorian church family, writes domestic drama with theological bones. Few of her many novels cut deeper into pride and repentance.
herbart-outlines-educational-doctrine-19:
Herbart's Outlines of Educational Doctrine, in Alexis F Lange's translation of 1901, renders the Umriss pädagogischer Vorlesungen of 1841. The German title means an outline of his lectures on education. The book is exactly that: Johann Friedrich Herbart's concise system of teaching doctrine, set down late in his career.

Herbart compresses decades of thought on government, instruction, and discipline into a handbook for the teacher. The end is character; the means are lessons that build a many-sided interest in the pupil. Lange's version served American normal schools in the years when Herbart's method ruled them. Readers who want Herbart's whole pedagogy in brief compass start here.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle opens his History of Friedrich the Second with Book One, Birth and Parentage, 1712. His proem pictures the king about fourscore years back, a lean little old man sauntering on the terraces of Sans Souci in the afternoon, alert and slightly stooping. Strangers called him Frederick the Great; Carlyle proposes to learn how he became so.

The volume gives the Hohenzollern rise in brief. It covers the marriage of Friedrich Wilhelm with Sophie Dorothea of Hanover. A sad scene of high words in the Hanover Schloss follows, where low cooings would have suited better. Courts, cadets, and drilling fill the background. Everything in the twenty volumes that follow grows from this seedbed of family and discipline.
history-of-the-revolt-of-the-netherlands:
Friedrich Schiller's History of the Revolt of the Netherlands opens his account of the Dutch struggle against Spanish rule. Schiller, better known as a dramatist, writes history with the same lucidity and impartiality that his English editors praise, aiming at a popular exposition of a great period.

This first volume lays the ground: the Netherlands under Charles the Fifth and Philip the Second, the growth of religious and political grievance, and the early opposition that would harden into revolt. Schiller judges men and measures with a dramatist's eye for character and a historian's care for evidence. Readers coming to the Dutch Revolt for the first time will find Schiller a vivid, humane guide, even in translation.
hobhouse-mind-evolution-1901:
Mind in Evolution, published in 1901, is L. T. Hobhouse's study of mind, from animal instinct to human reason, told as one long growth. The British sociologist and philosopher set out to trace a single line of growth where others saw a gulf between beast and man.

He examines learning, memory, and reasoning in animals, then follows the rise of concepts, language, and self-aware thought in man. Mind, for Hobhouse, is nature becoming aware of its own ends. The book's patient natural history supported his liberal faith in progress. It stands as a founding work of its field in Britain.
homo-sum-volume-01:
Homo Sum opens in Volume 1 with Georg Ebers turning from pharaohs to the early Christian desert. Ebers explains in his preface that research for a history of the Sinai peninsula led him to old tales of monks and martyrs. Clara Bell translated the novel, whose Latin title means I am a man. Its hero is Paulus, a hermit living among the caves near Mount Sinai.

Ebers says the seed was an old account of an anchorite, a monk who lives alone, who took another man's punishment without clearing his own name. The real culprit confessed only later. That puzzle of silence, guilt, and faith drives the book. Around Paulus gather younger Hermas, tempted by the world, and a small colony of desert Christians at the oasis of Pharan.
in-the-blue-pike-volume-01:
In the Blue Pike opens in Volume 1 of the novel by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary T Safford. Ebers begins with a curse that few listeners can even follow. Cyriax, a rough wandering performer, speaks in mangled tones. The Nuremberg magistrates had his tongue cropped for gross blasphemy, meaning reckless speech against God. That punishment left his talk gasping and strange.

Chapter I gathers his whole travelling company at once. His red haired wife leads him by a chain, like a tame bear. A fading, sickly girl walks with them. So do a lame man on crutches and an older, pockmarked companion. The woman slices bread and onions for the pot. Then Cyriax snatches her shawl to cover his head. The city Honourables, the respected council families, are coming. Fairground folk, harsh city law, and rough comedy set the terms of this tale.
jenner-origin-vaccine-inoculation-1801:
In 1801 Edward Jenner summed up his discovery in The Origin of the Vaccine Inoculation. The short London pamphlet tells how vaccination began. Jenner draws a careful line between casual cowpox, caught from cattle, and the disease raised by inoculation. That line mattered for safe practice.

He traces the vaccine from its dairy country roots to its spread among doctors. The history is concise, written by the man who made it. Doubts about where the protection came from get direct answers. The pamphlet served as his own brief account of the origin. Readers meet the discovery in its founder's words. It closes his run of tracts.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-01:
Reuben Gold Thwaites edited the Jesuit Relations in 73 volumes, issued from 1896 onward. Volume 1, from 1896, covers Acadia in the years 1610 to 1613. French priests had just reached the Atlantic shore of North America.

Their reports tell of the first missions among the Mi'kmaq people. Readers learn how the priests lived, what they ate, and how talks began. Hard winters, scarce food, and new tongues fill the letters home. The set became the base record for early North America. This opening volume shows first contact as the men on the ground saw it.
jewett-tory-lover-1901:
Jewett's Tory Lover, issued at Boston in 1901, is her lone historical novel. Chapter titles move from The Sea-Wolf and The Parting Feast to The Sailing of the Ranger. Later heads promise the coast of France and a run against wind and tide.

The scene is the New England coast during the American Revolution. A young woman finds her heart torn between a patriot officer and a dashing Loyalist, the tory lover of the title. War splits families and towns as each side must choose. Jewett's gift for place and character turns the romance into a thoughtful portrait of a community under strain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-worms-101:
Aaron Worms was chief rabbi of Metz and a Talmudist, born on July 7, 1754, at Geislautern. He was the son of Abraham Aberle and died at Metz on May 2, 1836. At fifteen he was already allowed to lecture on a legal subject in the Metz synagogue. He became rabbi of Kriechingen in 1777.

After seven years Aaron returned to Metz and later led its rabbinical college. In 1832 he was chosen chief rabbi by a unanimous vote, though he had not mastered French. A conservative by training, he still backed measured reform. He favored prayer in the vernacular and spoke for Napoleon at the Great Sanhedrin on Jewish duties.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdima-dimi-bar:
Abdima bar Hamar, also called Dimi, was a Palestinian who moved to Babylonia. He was an older peer of Raba and Joseph, in the fourth century. Few legal rulings bear his name, and few of his homilies survive. On the verse that the commandment is not in heaven nor beyond the sea, he taught a hard duty. Were the Law in heaven, man must climb to fetch it.

His preaching often strains a text or plays on like sounds, the entry shows. At the base of the mount, in Exodus, he reads as God bending the mount over Israel. Accept the Law, or here is your grave. A place name in Joshua he links to the word for sorrow. It marks, he says, the spot where men sigh for the lost rites of Shiloh.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abilene-301: Abilene was a small district of Syria on the eastern slope of Anti-Libanus. It took its name from the town of Abila, on the north slope of Mount Hermon. Abila lay about eighteen miles northwest of Damascus. The district was given as a tetrarchy to Lysanias by the emperor Tiberius, about 26 B.C. Claudius later gave it to Herod Agrippa, about the year 41. The town, called Abila of Lysanias, was thought to be the burial-place of Abel, from the likeness of the names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-leri: Abraham of Lerida was a physician, surgeon, and astrologer. All that is known of him is one dated deed. On September 12, 1468, he couched a cataract in the right eye of King John II of Aragon. Afterward he was equally successful with the left eye. The entry names no home, family, or writings for him, and rests on a note in Kayserling's history of the Jews in Portugal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adiabene-801:
Adiabene was a district in Mesopotamia. It lay between the Upper Zab and the Lower Zab. For some centuries from the first century B.C. it stood half free. Its chief city was Arbela. Talmudic texts give its name in forms close to the Syriac Ḥadyab. Under Persian kings it was at times a vassal state. One king held the title King of Ḥadyab before his throne.

Its kings of the first century gave the place its fame. Izates became a Jew before he took the throne. His mother Helena took the faith at about the same time. Parthian kings rose and fell fast in those years. Izates gave refuge to the fleeing king Artaban. He won the Parthians over to set Artaban back on his throne. In thanks he got kingly honors and the city of Nisibis. Josephus is the chief source for this royal house and its wars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agnosticism-901:
Agnosticism is a term made by Prof. Thomas H. Huxley in 1869. He formed it against the Christian gnostic, the one who claims to know all of God. Paul's altar to the unknown God gave the root. In its first sense, the word marks a held-back judgment. Proof backs no claim that God is, and no claim that he is not.

A second sense grew on the word. It holds God not just unknown now but past all knowing. Human knowledge, on that view, can not reach last things. The entry calls the first stance a sound check on pride. Both church dogma and godless matter lore claimed full knowledge of last things. The close gives the Jewish reply. Man speaks of God by likeness, in weak human words, and yet can hold that he is.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agrippa-ii-or-i:
Agrippa II. was a son of Agrippa I., born in the year 28. He was schooled at Rome, in the court life that had harmed his father. When his father died in a sudden way, Claudius wished to give him the full heir's rights. Court favorites talked the emperor out of that step. Judea went back to Roman officers. The young man stayed at court, where he could aid his fellow Jews at times.

In the year 50 he took the land of Chalcis and the overwatch of the Temple at Jerusalem. That watch gave him the right to name the high priest. Within three years he traded Chalcis for wider lands. Nero later added tracts in Galilee and Perea. His coins bear the faces of emperors and heathen signs. The entry faults his free hand in moving high priests in and out of post.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfonso-de-zamo:
Alfonso de Zamora was a Spanish scholar born in Zamora about 1474. He was baptized in the Catholic faith in 1506. He taught Oriental languages at the University of Salamanca. Cardinal Ximenes hired him for work on a large printed Bible. That project kept him busy for over fifteen years.

His own books deal with Hebrew grammar and word lists. He wrote an introduction to Hebrew grammar in 1526. He also turned parts of the Bible into new versions with notes. In 1526 he sent a Hebrew and Latin letter to the Jews of Rome. The letter urged them to accept the Christian faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aloes-1301:
Aloes in the Bible is a sweet scent for clothes and beds. The word shows up four times in the Old Testament. It shows up once more in the New Testament. The scent was a gum from trees of Malacca and Bengal. It was not the harsh aloe used in cures. It was not the American aloe plant either.

One verse in Numbers seems to name a tree. The entry doubts that an Asian tree fits that verse. The Greek version there reads tents in place of aloes. One scholar holds that the first word was worn down. His fix gives a terebinth tree in the line. That tree fits the lines on both sides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amiltai-probabl:
Amiltai is a name that shows twice in Jewish legend. In Greek myth it is the goat of plenty. Her horn pours out the riches of nature. She nursed the infant Zeus on her milk. In Greek dress one of Job's daughters bears her name. That daughter is Keren-happuch in the Hebrew text. She stands as a type of saintly beauty.

The second use names the mother of Abraham. One sage calls her Amiltai, daughter of Karnebo. The entry traces that name back to Job's daughter. Tales of Job and of Abraham were oft woven as one. A cave tale of milk and honey may have fed the link. The entry keeps the whole chain at the level of legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antipatris-1601:
Antipatris was a city founded about the year 10 B.C. by Herod the Great in the plain of Kefar Saba. Josephus shows that a town named Kefar Saba, old village, stood on the site in the days of Alexander Jannaeus. The modern Kefr-Saba keeps the old name.

Talmudic writers treat Antipatris and Kefar Saba as separate names, but the entry argues they meant the town and its whole plain. The plain's people were mainly Samaritans, the entry notes. Josephus places the city 150 stadia from Joppa and 26 miles south of Caesarea, on the high road to Lydda. In Talmudic writing it marks the most northerly limit of Judea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arnstein-benedi:
Benedikt David Arnstein, an Austrian playwright, was born in Vienna on October 15, 1765, and died there in 1840. He was a grandson of Adam Isaac von Arnstein, the well-known Vienna banker. In 1782 he entered his grandfather's banking house, but he left in 1786 for years of travel. On those journeys he met many leading writers of his day.

Contact with men such as Alinger and Liebel taught him to value the Greek and Roman classics. Retzer, Schreyvogel, Kotzebue, and others also shaped his taste. His plays began early and ran for two decades. The list includes Eine Judische Familienscene in 1782, Die Kleinodien in 1796, the comedy Die Maske in 1796, Das Billet in 1800, and Das Geschenk in 1801.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascoli-graziadi:
Graziadio Isaiah Ascoli, an Italian scholar of languages, was born on July 16, 1829, at Goritz in Austria. His father, a paper maker who had grown rich, died while the boy was an infant. The son turned early to languages and fell in love with comparative philology. At sixteen he startled scholars with a study matching the Friulian dialect of Italy with the Wallachian tongue, a subject no one had treated before.

From that start he built Italian language study. In 1854 he founded the first linguistic journal in Italy, the Studii Orientali e Linguistici. Its two volumes won him the chair of comparative philology at Milan. His lectures there, later printed and translated into English and German, took the Bopp prize from the Berlin Academy. The entry follows a career that remade its field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashre-2001:
Ashre is the first word of two verses, Psalm 84 verse 5 and Psalm 144 verse 15. Those verses are always placed before Psalm 145 when it is recited in the synagogue service. In the northern liturgies the opening verses carry a chant taken straight from the Sabbath reading. That chant serves there as the coda, the closing strain, of each reading in the lesson.

The entry is a music note more than a text note. It prints the chant as an illustration and ties the word Ashre to a fixed sound, not just a fixed place in the prayer book. Happy, or blessed, is what the word means, and the verses it opens bless the dwellers in God's house and the people whose God is the Lord.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-attributes-2101:
Attributes are the fixed qualities of a thing, as set against accidents, its passing states. Aristotle drew that line first. Arab and Jewish thinkers took it up for a hard question: what can be said of God? The entry ties the debate to the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, against which Saadia used it in his "Emunot we-Deot."

Saadia denied positive attributes to God, apart from existence, unity, power, and wisdom. His argument runs as a fork. If God has a body, attributes fit, but the result is crude man-shaped thinking. If God has no body, attributes would split his unity, since differences belong to bodies. The entry follows the question through later Jewish and Arab schools. It asks, in the end, how unity can hold together with the many works the Bible credits to God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azarias-2201:
Azarias was a general in the army of Judas Maccabeus. Judas left him, with Joseph son of Zacharias, in command of the Judean army in 165 B.C. Judas himself was away in Gilead, and Simon was in Galilee. The orders left behind were plain. Azarias was to stay quiet and fight no battle until the leaders came back.

Word of brave deeds by others made him restless. Against orders he marched out to fight at Jamnia. The Syrian general Gorgias beat him back, and two thousand of his men were lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacharach-jair-:
Jair Ḥayyim Bacharach was a German rabbi. He was born at Leipnik in Moravia in 1639. He died at Worms on Jan. 1, 1702. At twelve he came with his father Samson to Worms. He studied seven years under his father-in-law and that man's son. In 1660 he won his rabbinical license at Frankfort. In 1666 he became rabbi of Coblenz.

Coblenz law made its rabbi stand for reelection every three years. In 1669 Bacharach was not reelected. Back in Worms he lived as a private man and lectured on the Talmud. The congregation passed him over for his father's seat, and he felt the slight keenly. Late in life Worms at last chose him as rabbi. Nearly deaf and broken in health, he held the post barely two years. Of his many works, he printed only his responsa. He named that book for his grandmother, Eva Bacharach.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barak-2501:
Barak, the son of Abinoam, is Deborah's chief ally in the war against the Canaanites. Deborah calls him from Kedesh in Naphtali and orders him to take ten thousand men to Mount Tabor. There Sisera attacks him, as she had foreseen, and his forces are scattered and mostly slain. Barak will go only if Deborah goes with him. The honor of the expedition thus goes to her, and he joins her in the song of triumph.

The rabbis make Barak another name for Lapidoth, Deborah's husband, and give him a third name, Michael. They tell how this pious but ignorant man made candles for the sanctuary at Shiloh, so that God made his light shine brightly. His modesty is much praised. As actual leader, he was content to take second place and give Deborah the credit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basan-jacob-ben: Jacob ben Abraham Basan was ḥakam of the Portuguese community of Hamburg. In 1755 he published a prayer for a fast-day held by that congregation. The fast had been called after the great earthquake in Lisbon. The entry gives no birth or death dates and no other works. It records only his office, his city, and that one publication from 1755.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bebri-moses-ben: Moses ben Judah Bebri served as ambassador from Sultan Mohammed the Fourth to King Charles the Eleventh of Sweden. He died on May 29, 1673, at Amsterdam, where he was buried with great honors. His son, Judah Berbi, followed him in the same ambassador post. The son then went back from Amsterdam to Constantinople. The entry is brief and names two books where the tomb and the mission are recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belasco-israel-: Israel Belasco was an English prize fighter born in London in 1800, a brother of the better known Aby Belasco. He first fought on July 23, 1817, and lost after thirty rounds. His second bout, in 1819, went forty-one rounds before he was declared the winner of the stake. In 1821 he beat Saunders in fourteen rounds at the same ground. His last named fight, in 1823, ended in defeat after forty-four rounds for a smaller purse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benas-baron-l-2: Baron L. Benas, an English communal worker, was born in Liverpool in 1844. He stayed a leading figure in the Liverpool Old Hebrew congregation, where he served as a trustee. During the Russian emigration of 1882, he helped found the Liverpool branch of the Russo-Jewish committee. That branch carried much of the work of moving emigrants from Russia through England to the United States. He also led the Liverpool Literary and Philosophical Society and wrote papers for it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ben-ze: Benjamin ben Zeraḥ was a liturgical poet who lived in southeastern Europe in the middle of the eleventh century. Later poets called him the Great and also Ba'al Shem, Master of the Name. That second title came from his frequent use of names of God and angels in his poems. He wrote fifteen poems for the Sabbaths before the feasts and forty penitential poems. Those works appear in the prayer book of the German rite. His style is easy and elegant, and his verse leans toward mysticism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berman-jekuthie:
Jekuthiel Berman, a Russian Hebrew novelist, was born in 1825 and died in Moscow about 1889. For more than thirty years he held a weighty post with the railroad magnate Samuel Poliakov. He spent his free hours on writing, living at Tver and later at Moscow. A stroke in 1887 left him unable to work or write.

His first novel, in 1860, told of the Cantonists, the child recruits of Nicholas the First's time. Three more novels followed in Hebrew journals. He stood as a purist who barred foreign words from modern Hebrew prose.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-dagon-3201: Beth-Dagon was the name of several places in ancient Palestine. The second part of the name is Dagon. Dagon was a Philistine god. Joshua assigns one Beth-Dagon to Judah. Another lay in the territory of Asher. Sennacherib's inscriptions mention a Bit-daganna. That seems to be a third place. The name survives in Palestine today. Still, links to the ancient cities stay doubtful. The entry tests two modern candidates. One sits southeast of Jaffa. The other lies in the district of Acre.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-philip-34:
Philip Bloch was a rabbi and author. He was born in Prussia on May 30, 1841. He studied at Breslau's university and seminary. Frankel, Grätz, and Bernays taught him there. He took his doctorate in 1864. His rabbinical degree came in 1867. In 1871 he became rabbi at Posen. His early work treated religious philosophy and Haggadah.

Later he turned to Polish Jewish history. He wrote on the general privileges of Polish Jewry. He also wrote a history of Kabbalah's development. His memoir of Heinrich Grätz appeared in 1898. It prefaced the American edition's index volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bottle-3601:
Bottle in the Authorized Version renders several Hebrew words for skins that hold liquids. The Revised Version corrects that rendering only in a few places. The entry explains what those skins really were.

A goat, sheep, or ox was skinned without a hole in the body. The leg holes were sewn shut, and the neck hole served as the mouth. Skins were greased or pitched to keep them tight. Such vessels suited wandering nomads best and saw wide use in classical lands. True bottle forms were rare in antiquity. Glass bottles found in Egypt and Phenicia seem to have held perfumes, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bride-3701:
Bride is used in allegory for Israel, the entry begins. Hosea's words, I will betroth thee forever, ground that image. Readers joined it with Ezekiel to read the Song of Solomon as God's espousal of Israel.

Palestinian Jews gave that Song a mystical reading, the entry reports. Only men of mature age might study it on that view. In cabalistic teaching, Malkut, the lowest of the ten Sefirot, is the bride. She seeks union with the creative power above her. The entry warns that this mystery led some followers astray. Shabbethai Zebi and his circle are named as a case of that fall in the seventeenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-budny-simon-380:
Simon Budny was a Calvinist priest of Lithuania in the sixteenth century. He founded the Polish sect called the Budnians, nicknamed Half-Jews. At the Academy of Cracow he met disciples of Socinus and other Unitarians. Prince Nicholas Radziwill invited him in 1562 to serve as pastor at Kleck. There he began a Polish Bible translation, printed in 1572.

Budny later joined the Socinians and worked as a missionary in Lithuania. He associated much with Jewish scholars and knew some Hebrew. One Hebrew writer praised him for valuing the Talmud above all other literatures. His death date is unknown, though Grätz placed it in 1584. The entry adds that Catholics collected and burned his rare works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cahn-arnold-390: Arnold Cahn was a German physician born at Worms on April 11, 1858. He studied medicine at the University of Strasburg and graduated in 1881. He served as assistant physician at the university hospital from 1882 to 1885. He then became a private lecturer, and in 1895 an assistant professor. His specialty was the physiology of digestion. His journal pieces treated stomach motion, digestion during hunger, and stomach acid in phosphorus poisoning. He also wrote on how the healthy stomach handles meat and on peptones as food.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-capestang-4001: Capestang was a village in the department of Hérault, near Béziers, in France. Official papers show many Jews there in the thirteenth century. About 1245 one of them, Simon ben Meir, joined a religious debate before the archbishop of Narbonne. Community leaders of Capestang sat in the room. Many scholars of the next two centuries bore Capestang as a surname, spelled many ways in Hebrew. The community also joined the campaign against Maimonides' philosophy. Fifteen of its scholars signed a letter backing that ban.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cheran-4301: Cheran is a name in the genealogy of Seir the Horite, in Genesis xxxvi. 26. The same list appears in I Chronicles i. 41. Dillmann, in his commentary on the Genesis passage, suggests that the name comes from kar, a lamb. The names in these lists are clan names, the entry explains. A number of the clans carry animal names. Dishon, Ayyah, and Shobal are given as examples of that pattern. No person or deed is attached to Cheran beyond the list place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-claar-emil-4401:
Emil Claar, an Austrian poet, playwright, and actor, was born on Oct. 7, 1842, in Lemberg. He reached Vienna meaning to study medicine, bowed to family wishes and tried trade, then quit that too for the stage. His debut came in 1860 at the Vienna Burgtheater, followed by work in Graz, Linz, and Berlin.

Five years at the city theater of Leipsic included a side role as dramatic collaborator of Laube. He then ran court stages at Weimar and Prague. From 1876 he directed the Berlin Residenztheater. Since July 1, 1879, he had superintended the United City Theaters of Frankfort-on-the-Main. The entry lists two volumes of poems and a run of comedies, a drama, and the tragedy Shelley from 1874.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-congregation-46:
Congregation carries three senses in the Bible, and the entry sorts them with care. First, an assembly called together for a set time and purpose, as in I Kings viii. 65. Second, a single community, as in Numbers xxxv. Third, the whole body of Israel, called the congregation of the Lord or the congregation of Jacob.

Greek terms sharpen the split. Synagoge named the Jewish community and its place of worship alike. Ekklesia, assembly of the Lord, became under Paul the mark of Christian communities, while synagogue stayed Jewish. The entry corrects several Authorized Version renderings along the way, where assemblies or synagogues would read truer than congregations. It ends by pointing to community organization, the minyan, and the synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cottbus-4701: Cottbus is a manufacturing city of Prussia. The entry counts about 500 Jews in a total of 40,000 inhabitants. Jews lived there in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, but were later expelled. They resettled in the nineteenth century. By 1902 the community had a synagogue and a B'nai B'rith lodge. It also ran a society for Jewish history and literature and a burial society formed in 1875. Its first rabbi, Dr. Dienstfertig, died in 1895. Rabbi Leo Kamerase then led the community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cumin-4801: Cumin is the seed of an umbelliferous plant from Mediterranean lands. Its name runs much the same in Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic. Writers name wild, Ethiopic, and garden kinds. Palestine grew a special variety of its own. Jews and Arabs used cumin as a spice. It has a pungent taste, like caraway, and flavors bread. The Talmud also used it as a medicine. It stanched bleeding and eased colic and swellings. Isaiah's verse on threshing cumin closes the entry's survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dar-i-moses-or-:
Dar'i, Moses, is a name the entry gives to three different men. The first was a Karaite of Dar'ah, late in the ninth century. Men called him Medaḳdeḳ, the Grammarian. A few of his notes on Scripture survive, and one stanza of a poem. The second Moses was a Rabbinite named in Maimonides' responsa. He moved from the Maghreb to Egypt and traded his phylacteries for ones matching Geonic rules.

The third Moses stands tallest, as the leading Karaite poet of his line. Scholars still dispute his dates. He finished his Diwan in Egypt, after a cold welcome at Damascus. Two of his sons died young. His third son, Uri, heads a family table running twenty generations. His poems often hide his name in acrostics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davis-maurice-5: Maurice Davis was an English physician and philanthropist born on October 8, 1821, who died in London on September 29, 1898. He was one of the first English Jews trained for medicine. At King's College, London, he won first prizes in medicine and clinical surgery. In 1887 he became a justice of the peace for Middlesex, then for the new county of London. He served medical societies and Jewish charities, including the Jewish Board of Guardians and the Anglo-Jewish Association. He also wrote plays for charity benefits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dimi-also-calle:
Dimi, also called Abdimi and Abudimi, was an amora, or Talmud teacher, of the fourth century. He spent his career carrying teaching between two worlds. He brought Palestinian doctrine and Bible notes to the schools of Babylonia, and Babylonian teaching back to Palestine. A banishment decree by Constantius finally settled him in Babylonia.

The entry calls Dimi a perfect storehouse of varied knowledge, which he gathered eagerly and shared freely. He reported sayings in the names of Jannai, Ḥanina, Joshua ben Levi, and, most often, Johanan. Abaye was his most grateful hearer in Babylonia. Asked what Palestinians most avoid in company, Dimi answered: putting a neighbor to shame, which one teacher counted among three unpardonable sins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-divorce-3301:
Divorce, the ending of a marriage, grew in Jewish law from the patriarchal family. The husband, as head of that family, could dismiss his wife at pleasure. Abraham's sending away of Hagar shows the old right at work. The rabbis kept the right but hedged it with limits.

Deuteronomy barred divorce for life in two cases, false accusation and rape before marriage. The school of Shammai demanded a cause, sexual immorality. The school of Hillel required no reason at all, and its view prevailed. The Mishnah added further limits, and courts could force a husband to grant a bill. Only in the eleventh century was divorce at will formally abolished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ebal-septuagint:
Ebal is a bare mountain, 2,900 feet high, north of Sichem. It stands opposite Mount Gerizim. Tombs lie at its northern base, and old wall ruins crown its heights. The Old Testament mentions it only a few times.

On Ebal, Joshua built an altar of unhewn stones, the entry recalls from Joshua and Deuteronomy. Great whitened slabs there bore the words of the Law. Half of Israel stood on Ebal to call down curses on lawbreakers. The other half, on Gerizim, called down blessings on the obedient. The name Ebal also marks an Edomite tribe and an Arab tribe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-el-elyon-5501: El 'Elyon is a name for God that means God most high. In Genesis, Melchizedek serves as priest of El 'Elyon and blesses Abraham in that name. The entry calls God here the maker or owner of heaven and earth. It lists other uses in Psalms, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Daniel. The name also appears among the Phoenicians. A final section gives a debate among scholars. Some saw the Melchizedek passage as a later addition, while Gunkel held that an old custom in Jerusalem may lie behind it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-of-bour: Eliezer of Bourgogne was a French Talmudist. He lived in the thirteenth century. Scholars think he is Eliezer ben Aaron of Bourgogne. In that view he was one of six rabbis who got a famed letter. Meir Abulafia wrote to them on the rising of the dead. Eliezer wrote a Talmudic work called Sha'ar ha-Penim. That book no longer exists today. A later code of Jewish law cites its title. Nothing more of the man is told here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elmaleh-joseph-: Joseph Elmaleh was honorary chief rabbi of Mogador. He was born at Rabat in 1809. He died in London on Jan. 9, 1886. He moved to Mogador at the age of seventeen. In 1840 the flock there chose him as chief rabbi. In 1881 he added trade to his rabbinic work. He also served as Austrian vice-consul in the town. Austria gave him a high order for his service. His standing let him soften hardships laid on the Jews. A girls' school at Mogador rose through his push.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-ben-jud: Ephraim ben Judah was a liturgical poet of the twelfth century. Zunz placed him in the northern part of France. He may be the Ephraim quoted by Jeroham in Toledot Adam we-Hawwah. The Avignon Mahzor holds a poem for the first day of Passover that bears his name. It begins Wayehi ba-hazi ha-layelah. An old Roman Mahzor holds two more poems by an Ephraim ben Judah. The entry gives no birth or death dates for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-etiquette-5101:
Etiquette covers the rules of polite dealings, and the entry finds those rules already in the Bible. Moses, Abraham, and Abigail are held up as models of courteous speech. The rabbis folded manners into derek erez, the way of the world. One rule from R. Eliezer ties good conduct to words of Torah passing from a person's mouth.

Practical rules fill the entry. A person must be called by name before being spoken to, but a parent or teacher is never named. Guests, meals, and table habits all get guidance. Nothing that causes spitting or a bad smell should be eaten in company. One rabbi, smelling garlic in class, ended the session rather than shame the eater. Banquet customs and toast rules close the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-euclid-heb-also:
Euclid was a Greek geometer of the fourth century B.C., and the entry tracks his works in Hebrew dress. Abraham bar Hiyya, who died in 1136, may be the first Hebrew writer to name him. Most old Hebrew copies of Euclid look like one man's work, Moses ibn Tibbon. His first version of the Elements is dated to the year 1270.

Jacob ben Makir made another version about 1273, with the books of Hypsicles. Arabic commentaries by Al-Farabi and Ibn Haitham also passed into Hebrew. Levi ben Gershon and others wrote fresh notes on single books. Euclid's Data and Optics reached Hebrew through Jacob ben Makir as well. After long neglect, fresh versions appeared in Germany and Poland in the late eighteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fetters-6101: Fetters are chains that bind the feet together or to a heavy object, and the entry sorts the Bible's words for them. The usual term is nehushtayim, a dual form showing they came in pairs, pointing to brass as their metal. Iron fetters are kebel, used in the Psalms for feet bound to something else. A third term, zikkim, comes from a root meaning to bind and can stretch even to ropes. The entry ends by pointing to the article on chains.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fines-and-forfe:
Fines and forfeiture, the entry says, are largely unknown to Jewish law as the sages read it. A fine here means money paid as punishment to a king or state. Loss of a whole estate was a point the rabbis argued. Money sums fixed by the Torah go to the injured party, not to the state. The entry gives four such cases from the Torah.

Three of the four cases turn on harm done to a woman. Sums of thirty, fifty, and a hundred shekels are named. Only ordained judges could impose such fines, the entry notes. In later times, courts in the Diaspora did fine some public wrongs. False weights and measures are given as one such case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-zechari:
Zecharias Frankel was a German theologian born at Prague on September 30, 1801. He died at Breslau on February 13, 1875. He founded the school of historical Judaism and was its most eminent member. That school upholds free research, yet in practice keeps the authority of tradition. Frankel came of Vienna exiles of 1670 and of the rabbinical Spira family. In 1832 he became district rabbi of Leitmeritz.

Frankel served as chief rabbi of Dresden from 1836. Berlin invited him to its chief rabbinate in 1843, but he declined. Prussia would not formally recognize the office. In 1854 he became president of the Breslau seminary, and held that post until his death. His first great work treated the Jewish oath, in 1840. His proof that no Jewish doctrine justified that distrust brought a new rule. Jews and Christians were put on the same basis in court. He also edited two journals of Jewish learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frohberg-regina:
Regina Frohberg, a German writer born at Berlin on October 4, 1783, was the daughter of a very wealthy merchant. At eighteen, in 1801, she married a man named Friedlander. The marriage proved unhappy and soon ended in divorce. She then became a Christian and took the name Frohberg. In 1813 she moved to Vienna, where she lived until her death.

Her books came out over more than thirty years. Early works include a tale of childlike duty and love from 1808 and a volume of stories from 1811. Later titles treat pride and love, past and future, and guilt both own and foreign. She also adapted French dramas for the stage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-glasgow-6701:
Glasgow, Scotland's largest city and a seaport, had 760,329 people in 1901, about 6,500 of them Jews. Its Jewish community dates from about 1830. A first synagogue, at George and John streets, was consecrated in 1858. The congregation moved in 1878 to Garnethill, where its new building cost £14,000.

A second congregation in Commerce street led, in 1883, to a merger as the Glasgow United Synagogue. New buildings followed in South Portland street in 1901 and Oxford street in 1899, and the community kept one shared cemetery. The entry names its charities, among them a board of guardians handling about 400 cases a year and loan societies granting some 200 loans, plus schools and literary societies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gomperz-julius-:
Julius Gomperz, Ritter von, was an Austrian merchant and statesman. He was the brother of Theodor Gomperz. He was born at Brünn in 1824. In 1859 he joined the chamber of commerce, rising to its president in 1872. He entered the Moravian diet in 1861. In 1871 he joined the Lower House, moving to the Upper House the next year. That year he was knighted and decorated with the Order of the Austrian Crown. France made him an officer of the Legion of Honor.

He owned part of a Brünn cloth factory. For many years he presided over Brünn's Jewish congregation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gruby-david-690: David Gruby was a French physician. He was born at Neusatz, Hungary, on Oct. 10, 1810. He died in Paris on Nov. 16, 1898. He studied medicine at Vienna and graduated in 1834. Though Jews rarely won hospital posts then, he became assistant surgeon there. London came next, then Paris in 1839, where he practiced. He led in microscope research, the entry says. His free public lectures on microscopy drew large crowds. His two Latin works of 1839 and 1840 hold his findings. As a doctor he treated the younger Dumas and Heinrich Heine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-had-gadya-one-k:
Ḥad Gadya, "One Kid," is an Aramaic song sung at the close of the Passover Seder. Its opening phrase returns as a refrain at the end of each of its ten verses. A father buys a kid for two zuzim. A cat eats the kid, a dog bites the cat, and the chain runs on through stick, fire, water, ox, and slaughterer.

Long read as a deep allegory, the song is, the entry says, a nursery rime modeled on a German ballad with an older French source. Commentators still mapped its chain onto Israel's oppressors, from Assyria to the Turk, with God ending the angel of death. A large body of writing, in many tongues, grew up around the song, and the entry closes with its tunes and settings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hadadezer-or-ha: Hadadezer, son of Rehob, was king of Aram-zobah. Marching to extend his rule to the Euphrates, he met David and lost badly in chariots, horses, and men. Later, after Joab had thrown back the Ammonites and their Syrian allies, Hadadezer saw a chance for payback. He sent his host across the Euphrates under Shobach to aid Maachah, Rehob, and Ishtob. David took the field in person this time. The rout was total: forty thousand horsemen fell, Shobach among them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halford-george-: George Edward Halford was a private in the mounted infantry of the City of London Imperial Volunteers. Born in 1878, he was schooled at University College School, London. He rose to lance-corporal in the 1st Middlesex before the Transvaal war. He fought round Paardeberg and escorted the Boer general Cronje part of the way to Cape Town. On the great march to Bloemfontein the hardships brought on a fever. He died of it at Karee, near Bloemfontein, on May 15, 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanina-b-hama-7:
Hanina b. Hama was a Palestinian halakist and haggadist who died about 250 and is quoted constantly in both Talmuds and the Midrashim. He studied under Bar Kappara and Hiyya the Great, then joined the academy of Judah I., where he gained such command of the Law that he once told Hiyya he could restore a forgotten law by argument alone.

Judah loved him and kept him close, yet an ill-judged show of Scriptural learning delayed his promotion; on his death-bed Judah still named him first among candidates. Hanina declined to pass his senior Efes, waited, and at last headed the academy at Sepphoris, where he also practised as a physician. He taught that 99 per cent of fatal diseases come from colds. Sepphoris still blamed him when a pestilence raged, and the entry closes with his old age spent watching Johanan lecture to crowds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hasdai-abraham-:
Abraham ben Samuel Hasdai, a Hebrew translator living in Barcelona about 1230, was a keen supporter of Maimonides. During the fight over that thinker's books, he wrote sharp letters to opponents in Toledo and Castile. He defended the grammarian David Kimhi as well. He also joined his brother in a letter blaming foes whose zeal led monks to burn Maimonides' writings.

Hasdai rendered many Arabic works into Hebrew. Some survive only in his versions. They include a book ascribed to Aristotle, an ethics work by Ghazali, and Isaac Israeli's book on the elements. He also translated parts of Maimonides. In Ghazali's work he swapped Koran quotes for Bible and Talmud passages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ben-zebu: Hayyim ben Zebulon Jacob Perlmutter was rabbi of Ostropol in Russia in the eighteenth century. He wrote two unusual books. "Elef Omer" gathers sayings that all begin with the letter aleph, built on a well-known work by Jedaiah Bedersi. "Shirah le-Hayyim" sets out the 613 commandments in verse. Each verse starts with a word from the second song of Moses in Deuteronomy. The first book came out at Grodno in 1795. The second appeared at Warsaw in 1814, with later printings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilprin-phineh:
Phinehas Mendel Heilprin, born at Lublin in November 1801, was a Polish Hebraist. Trained in Talmud, he moved on to Maimonides, Arabic, and Greek thought, then to modern German philosophy. He worked as a cloth maker and wool merchant at Piotrkow. In 1859 he reached the United States and made Washington his home.

His chief work argues against the Judeo-German reformers, above all on marriage and divorce. The entry calls it the fairest Hebrew case of its kind, though sharp in its attacks. Other books treat Maimonides, logic, and the right handling of the Talmud text. He died on Jan. 30, 1863.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hillel-ben-elia: Hillel ben Eliakim was a Greek Talmudist of the eleventh and twelfth centuries and a pupil of Rashi. He wrote a comment on Sifra, quoting Rashi and Isaac b. Melchizedek often. He also wrote a comment on Sifre. Both works were known to the tosafists. Later writers quote them as well, including Elijah Mizraḥi on Rashi and Menahem Azariah Fano in responsa. Mordecai b. Hillel also mentions him. No birth or death dates are given in this entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hoffa-joseph-78:
Joseph Hoffa, born at Cassel on Aug. 18, 1803, was a German scholar of language and antiquity. His father was an army paymaster. He entered the Cassel lyceum in 1816 and Marburg University in 1821. He studied a year at Heidelberg as well.

Poverty forced Hoffa out of university. With a historian's letters he taught at Frankfort for two years, then tutored privately. He took his doctorate in 1823 and gained a lectureship in 1827. His many manuals and textbooks spanned Latin, French, and English letters. Editions of Pliny, Cicero, and Isocrates are listed, plus an English learning aid. He died about 1843.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hungary-in-hebr:
Hungary is a kingdom in central Europe, part of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. When Jews first settled there is not known for sure. A Latin tombstone from Roman Pannonia touches Jewish matters, but firm settlement proof comes later. The first clear document is a letter of about 960.

In that letter Hasdai ibn Shaprut wrote to the Khazar king and named Jews in the country of Hungarin as carriers of his message. Laws soon pressed on Jewish life. The Synod of Szabolcs in 1092 barred Jews from Christian wives and slaves. King Coloman added curbs and set Jews in bishop's towns. The Golden Bull of 1222 drove them from high office. The article follows their long history from there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-huppah-2401:
Huppah is the Hebrew word for a canopy, above all the bridal canopy. The word later came to mean a wedding itself. At first the huppah was the chamber where the bride waited for the groom. The festal procession ended when the couple entered it, and the bride stayed seven days.

The canopy itself was rich purple cloth with gold moon-shaped jewels, or a bower of roses and myrtles. Legend gives Adam ten jewel canopies at his wedding to Eve, with angels dancing outside. In time the huppah became a portable canopy on four poles. The couple stood under it outdoors while the rabbi performed the rite. Reform rabbis later dropped it as an empty form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-latif-isaac:
Isaac ben Abraham ibn Latif was a Spanish physician and cabalist, probably born at Toledo. He died at Jerusalem about 1290, having gone there in poverty. Among the cabalists of his day he stood out as the natural philosopher. He tried to give cabalistic terms a firm base in natural philosophy, though the entry says that bid failed.

His chief work, Gate of Heaven, written about 1244, follows the manner of Maimonides' Guide and opens with a history of Jewish science. Other books treat a bundle of myrrh, the shape of the world, and questions of science sent from Jerusalem. He also commented on Job and on Ecclesiastes. A sharp critique by Isaac ben Sheshet is noted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-incunabula-8101:
Incunabula are works printed in the fifteenth century; those of Jewish interest are Hebrew books and books on Jewish subjects in other types. About 101 Hebrew ones can be traced as certainly printed before 1500, plus eight more of which no copy is known or whose date and place are unsure. Lost items include three Talmud tractates printed by Joshua Soncino in 1488-89.

Hebrew printing's start cannot be fixed exactly. The first dated work is Rashi's Pentateuch commentary, printed by Abraham Garton at Reggio on Feb. 5, 1475. Seventeen places printed Hebrew books, eleven in Italy, three in Spain and three in Portugal. After the 1492 expulsion stopped the Spanish presses, only about a dozen more works appeared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-merwa: Isaac ben Merwan ha-Levi was a French Talmudist of the first third of the twelfth century, the elder son of Merwan of Narbonne. Respected in the community as his father had been, he was elected rabbi of Narbonne. His Talmudic decisions were often quoted and treated as settling a question. He directed the yeshibah there. His pupils included his nephew Moses ben Joseph, Moses ben Jacob ha-Nasi, and Abraham ben Isaac, the ab bet din of Narbonne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israelit-der-83: Der Israelit of Mayence was a German Jewish journal, weekly at first and later semiweekly. M. Lehmann founded it in 1860 and edited it until his death. Oskar Lehmann then took over as editor. Each number carried valued literary supplements, the entry says. Its story pages printed some excellent tales. The journal stood for Orthodox Judaism; indeed, it was founded to guard the interests of Orthodox Judaism. The entry gives no closing date for the paper's run.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-david: Jacob ben David Provencal was a French Talmudist of the fifteenth century. The entry first clears away a confusion: he is not the astronomer Jacob ben David Po'el of Perpignan. This Jacob lived at Marseilles, where he worked in sea trade. He later retired to Naples. From there, in 1490, he wrote to David ben Judah Messer Leon at Mantua in favor of secular studies, and of medicine above all. He also wrote an approval for Jacob Landau's "Sefer Agur" and a commentary on Canticles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseffy-rafael-:
Rafael Joseffy was an American piano virtuoso born in 1852 in Hunfalu, Hungary. His family moved to Miskolcz, where he got his first music lessons. At ten he played in public in Budapest with such promise that his father took him to the conservatory at Leipsic in 1864. In 1866 he went to Berlin to study with Carl Tausig.

After two summers with Liszt at Weimar, Joseffy toured Europe with success and lived in Vienna until 1879. That year he came to America and made a strong New York debut at Chickering Hall. He settled in the United States and took citizenship in 1900. He lived at Tarrytown-on-the-Hudson, wrote a manual for advanced piano players, composed many piano pieces, and headed the piano department of the National Conservatory of Music in New York.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-josel-be: Joseph Josel ben Zeeb Wolf Levi was rabbi in Lesla during the first half of the eighteenth century. He wrote Tif'eret Yosef, a supercommentary on Rashi's commentary on the Pentateuch. It was printed at Prague in 1724 and covers the first three books of the Pentateuch. The entry is only a few lines long. It names no teacher, family, or other work, and it rests on a note by Zunz and on Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ha-levi-a:
Judah ha-Levi, in Arabic Abu al-Hasan al-Lawi, was a Spanish thinker and Hebrew poet born at Toledo in the last quarter of the eleventh century. He died in the East after the year 1140. Sent to Lucena, he studied under Isaac Alfasi and befriended that master's pupils. He chose medicine as his trade but showed poetic gift early.

He knew Arabic and Castilian verse well, yet he sang in the Hebrew of the Bible. Moses ibn Ezra, his older friend, praised him warmly. The long entry traces his life, his friendships, and the gathering of his poems into a diwan by later hands. It also treats his thought, the field of his famed book the Cuzari, where Jewish faith is defended in dialogue form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ibn-kurai: Judah ibn Kuraish was a Hebrew grammarian and word scholar born at Tahort in northern Africa. He flourished in the eighth and ninth centuries. In grammar he moved little past those before him, but his work on comparing languages holds great value. He saw that the Semitic tongues spring from one source and obey the same laws. His Risalah, an Arabic letter to the Jews of Fez, is the earliest known work on that study. In it he urges care for the Targumim as keys to the Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jutrzenka-the-d: Jutrzenka, The Dawn, was a Jewish weekly printed at Warsaw in the Polish tongue. Its first number came out on July 5, 1861, and it ran until October 23, 1863. Chief hands on it were Ludwig Gumplowicz and Alexander Kraushar. Gumplowicz wrote there on Polish law as it bore on the Jews. Kraushar gave poems on Jewish life and pieces on the past of Poland's Jews. Christian writers also took part. The paper died with the failed Polish rising of its day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaplan-wolf-ha-:
Wolf ha-Kohen Kaplan was a Russian teacher and Hebrew poet. He was born at Trishki, in the government of Kovno, in 1826. He died at Riga on June 14, 1888. He had studied under M. A. Ginzburg. His school at Riga became a model for Jewish schools across Russia. He was also the driving force of Riga's Progressive congregation.

In 1864 Kaplan spoke with Count Shuvalov on behalf of Lithuanian Jews at Riga. His plea won them fair treatment from the authorities. He wrote to the Russian publicist Katkov as well. He talked Katkov into defending the Jews in print. The entry praises his Hebrew prose and verse. His long poem "Ereẓ ha-Pela'ot" runs to 124 stanzas. It appeared in a Hebrew annual in 1887.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kobner-heinrich: Heinrich Köbner was a German physician. He was born at Breslau on Dec. 2, 1838. He studied medicine at Berlin and at Breslau. Settling as a physician at Breslau in 1861, he founded a dispensary for dermatology. In 1872 he became professor of dermatology and syphilology. Indifferent health forced him to resign all his positions in 1878. After time in southern Europe he settled in Berlin. There he founded another dispensary in 1884. In 1897 he received the title "Geheimer Medizinalrat."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kraus-friedrich: Friedrich Kraus, an Austrian physician born at Bodenbach in Bohemia on May 31, 1851, took his medical degree in 1882. He worked in Prague institutes for body chemistry and pathology. In 1888 he became privat-docent in internal pathology at Prague. A Vienna clinic post followed in 1890. He was made assistant professor at Vienna in 1893 and professor at Graz a year later. His special study was alkalis and the burning of sugar in the blood. His books treat fatigue, mouth and gullet diseases, and the blood glands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lebrecht-furcht: Fürchtegott Lebrecht, a German educator born at Memmelbach in Bavaria on Nov. 16, 1800, died at Berlin on Sept. 1, 1876. Talmud study at Fürth and Presburg under Moses Sofer came first. At Halle from 1827 he trained under Gesenius and aided him in return. Berlin teaching began at the teachers' seminary in 1840. From 1856 he headed a Berlin study house and raised its teaching to wide notice. His 1862 book treats manuscripts of the Babylonian Talmud. A posthumous work on Bethar came in 1877.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-tribe-of-9:
The tribe of Levi, the entry explains, descends from the patriarch Levi, third son of Jacob and Leah. Levi shared in Simeon's attack on the men of Shechem. For that, it was thought, his offspring were scattered in Israel. At the Exodus the tribe, now large, was chosen for the priesthood and the service of the sanctuary.

A sharp line split the house of Aaron, who held the priesthood, from the rest of the Levites. The Levites got the lesser tasks of the service. At the settlement they received no land of their own. Scattered cities were assigned to them inside the lands of other tribes. The entry lists those cities tribe by tribe, from Hebron to Jazer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-meyer-9901:
Meyer Levy, a German jurist, was born in Wollstein, Posen, on Jan. 17, 1833. He died in Berlin on Oct. 18, 1896, killed by a robber. He practiced first as an assessor in Berlin, then as an advocate at Fraustadt. In 1872 he came back to Berlin and built a large, well-placed practice.

Levy rose to lead the Berlin Bar Association. In 1867 he urged the North German parliament to act on the state and the Jews. His main legal works, written with G. von Wilmowsky, explain the German code of civil procedure. That work reached a sixth edition in 1892. He also printed a handy edition of the same code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lion-10001:
Lion covers the animal's many Hebrew names, its home in Palestine, and its place in Bible stories and sayings. Names include aryeh for the lion in general, plus terms for the lioness, the young lion, and the whelp. The entry places lions near the Jordan, in caves, thickets, woods, and desert.

Readers learn how lions hunt, guard prey, and threaten flocks and people. Shepherds fought them with sling and staff, and hunters caught them with pits and nets. The lion also stands for strength and courage. Judah, Israel, and even God are compared to a lion, and lion figures decorated Solomon's throne and Temple vessels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-london-solomon-: Solomon b. Moses Raphael London was a Russian author and publisher who lived at Novogrudok, Lithuania, in the first half of the eighteenth century. He had studied under Samuel Schotten at Frankfort-on-the-Main. He edited many prayer and moral books over nearly forty years. His editions include a work on circumcision, Sabbath prayers in the rite of Isaac Luria, and a collection of rites and prayers with a small vocabulary for learners. Printings appeared in Amsterdam, Venice, and other cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luzki-simhah-is:
Simhah Isaac ben Moses Luzki, a Karaite writer and bibliographer, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Lutsk at the end of the seventeenth century, he knew rabbinic literature well and also studied Cabala. He worked as a tireless and skilled copyist. He died in March 1766, at Chufut-Kale or at Lutsk, by differing accounts.

The article credits him with saving much Karaite literature. In 1751 he went to Chufut-Kale in Crimea, home to a rich Karaite library. There he taught at the study house and copied manuscripts that might otherwise have been lost. His own books include commentaries, a two-volume code, and a work on the calendar. His bibliography of Karaite writings, though sometimes uncritical, became a key guide for students. The entry honors a copyist whose hand preserved a whole tradition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maimon-solomon-:
Solomon ben Joshua Maimon, a Lithuanian-born philosopher, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Nieszwicz in 1754, he mastered rabbinic literature as a child. His father married him off at twelve, and by fourteen he was a father himself. He worked as a tutor while studying through the night.

The article follows his hunger for wider learning. Maimonides' Guide became his guiding star, and he took the name Maimon in the master's honor. His readings in the Cabala angered the Hasidim around him. Turning to secular science, he taught himself physics from old German books. Harassed at home as a heretic, he set out for Germany at twenty-five. Berlin's Jewish gatekeeper first turned him away as a vagabond. After wandering with a beggar, he found shelter at Posen under Rabbi Hirsch Janow. The entry breaks off mid-journey, with the future thinker still fighting toward Berlin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maretzek-max-10:
Max Maretzek, the Austrian opera impresario, is profiled at length in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Brunn, Moravia, on June 28, 1821, he studied under Seyfried at Vienna. After work with Italian opera in London he reached New York in 1848. He died at Pleasant Plains, New York, in 1897.

The article reads as a chronicle of American first performances. Maretzek managed grand opera from 1849 to 1878 at New York's leading houses. His 1855 season gave America its first Trovatore and Semiramide. Rigoletto, Traviata, and William Tell followed within two years. He introduced Adelina Patti to New York in 1858. In 1863 he conducted the first Faust in America. The entry lists dozens more operas he brought to the New York public. It preserves the man who more than any other built grand opera in the United States.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mauthner-julius:
Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar give Julius Mauthner, an Austrian chemist, a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Vienna on September 26, 1852, and was educated at the University of Vienna, taking his medical degree in 1879. There he stayed. He became a private lecturer in experimental medical chemistry in 1881 and assistant professor on June 3, 1885. He belonged to the Leopold and Caroline Academy of naturalists and chemists.

The entry gives him no books, only papers. It names the journals that carried them. His scientific articles appeared in the proceedings of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna. They also appeared in Liebig's “Annalen der Chemie,” in the reports of the German Chemical Society, and in the “Zeitschrift für Biologie.” Viennese medical papers carried more of them, and two Austrian reference works are cited for readers who want the details of his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melchior-nathan:
Nathan Gerson Melchior was a Danish physician and pioneer eye specialist. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906; he was a brother of the merchant Moritz Melchior. He was born in Copenhagen on August 2, 1811. He graduated from its university in 1835. He spent two years studying ophthalmology at Berlin, Leipzig, Dresden, and Prague before making diseases of the eye his specialty at home.

The entry follows a career of firsts and honors: he was army surgeon in the war with Germany of 1848 to 1850. The title of professor came in 1853, and a post as privat-docent in ophthalmology at Copenhagen came two years later. He also won a seat on the board of the newly founded Ophthalmological Institute. In 1856 the king sent him abroad to study how other countries fought the contagious Egyptian eye disease then ravaging Europe. He died in Copenhagen on January 30, 1872.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merom-10701:
Merom is the "waters of Merom" where Joshua fought the northern kings. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price locate it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article identifies the site with Lake Huleh, some fifteen miles north of the Sea of Galilee. Pear-shaped, with the stem pointing south, it runs three miles across and nearly four long. Its surface is seven feet above the Mediterranean, and its depth ten to sixteen feet. The plain by its southwestern shore is judged the probable battle field of Joshua 11.

Jabin of Hazor commanded a host compared to the sand of the seashore, with horses and chariots very many. Joshua came on them suddenly, likely by a night march and a dawn attack as at Gibeon. He routed them. He hamstrung the horses and burned the chariots. After Merom, says the entry, the land could be divided among the tribes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mocatta-10901:
Mocatta, an Anglo-Jewish family among the earliest resettlers of Jews in England, is traced by Joseph Jacobs, Isidore Harris, and Goodman Lipkin in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry's longest life is David Mocatta, a London architect born in 1806. His father Moses translated the anti-missionary classic Faith Strengthened; the son studied architecture in Italy under masters including Sir John Soane.

David Mocatta became the railway age's house architect, employed often by the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway, and inherited fortunes from his father and his brother Benjamin. When Soane left his collection to the nation, Mocatta was made a trustee. He also helped found the West London Reform Synagogue and directed the building of its Margaret Street home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ju:
Mordecai ben Judah Löb of Lemberg was a commentator of the later seventeenth century and rabbi of Dobri in Bohemia, given four lines by Wilhelm Bacher and S. J. Levinson in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His name rides on a single work: Ma'amar Mordekai, a commentary on the Pentateuch.

The book reached print only after his death, at Dyhernfurth in 1719, edited by his son Judah Löb, who served as shammash — beadle and factotum — of the Breslau community. The entry's sources are the standard bibliographies, Steinschneider, Fürst, Azulai, and Benjacob, which is to say the man survives as an entry in other men's catalogues and in his son's piety.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-jacob:
Moses ben Jacob of Russia was a scholar whose life was broken again and again by Tatar invasions. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Schadow in Lithuania in 1449, he lived for years at Kiev. There he wrote sharp marginal notes against the Karaite writer Abraham ben Elijah.
