When the Tatars sacked Kiev they looted his house and carried off the notes, which later surfaced at Kaffa. Moses himself was captured at Lida in 1506 and ransomed at Solchat by Rabbanite and Karaite Jews together. He stayed on in the Crimea and wrote a commentary on Ibn Ezra in 1515. His story shows how fragile scholarship was on that frontier.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-york-11501:
New York held more Jews than any city on earth. Cyrus Adler, Max J. Kohler, Cyrus L. Sulzberger, and D. M. Hermalin wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there about 1654, under Dutch rule. Most were Sephardic exiles from Brazil and the Indies. Ashkenazim from Holland and England joined them soon.

Twenty-three fugitives landed from the Saint Catarina in 1654. Governor Stuyvesant ordered the Jews to leave his colony. The Dutch West India Company overruled him from home. Their letter called his ban unreasonable and unfair. It cited Jewish losses in Brazil and their invested capital. German immigration swelled the city after 1800. Russian persecution drove a far greater wave from 1881. By 1904 the city's Jews numbered about 672,776.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oholibamah-a-v-: Oholibamah was one of the three wives of Esau. Emil G. Hirsch and Bernhard Pick wrote her short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was the daughter of Anah, of the line of Seir. Seir was a Horite, a folk of the hills. In an earlier tale she is called Judith. There she is the daughter of Beeri the Hittite. Her name comes in lists of chiefs in Genesis and in Chronicles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-omer-lag-be-117:
Lag be-Omer is the thirty-third day of the Omer count. The board and Julius H. Greenstone wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Lag is a pair of Hebrew letters worth thirty-three. The day falls on the eighteenth day of Iyyar. It is kept as a half feast day each spring.

No one knows for sure why the day is kept. The tale most told ties it to Rabbi Akiba. A plague struck his pupils in the Omer days. That plague ceased, men say, on this one day. So the day is called the Scholars' Feast by some. Boys spent it in games and in mirth. A second tale says the manna first fell that day. Men of the Cabala hold the day in high regard too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parah-heifer-11:
Parah, or Heifer, is a tract in the Mishnah and Tosefta. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in the order Tohorot, on laws of the clean. The law of the red heifer stands in the book of Numbers. A red cow with no flaw was to be burnt whole.

No yoke had ever lain on that cow in her life. Her ash was mixed with spring water in a set way. That mix was used to cleanse a man made unclean. The rite of the burn and the mix was strict in form. It was a chief point of clash of two schools. The Pharisees set new rites to mark their stand apart. The tract holds twelve chapters and ninety-six parts in all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philippe-felix-:
Félix Philippe was a French Jewish officer of the National Guard. He was born in 1825 and died at Paris in 1848. Isidore Singer and A. Rhine wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He taught artillery to the guard. His life was short and wholly military.

In June 1848 revolution shook the streets of Paris. Philippe was given the defense of the Hôtel-de-Ville. He held the post as a young lieutenant. On June 24 he was fatally wounded in the fighting. He died a month later, at twenty-three. The Jews of France raised a monument to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-placzek-baruch-:
Baruch Jacob Placzek was Moravia's chief rabbi at Brünn. Isidore Singer and S. Funk wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Weisskirchen in 1835. He was son and successor to Abraham Placzek.

At twenty-three Placzek founded a high school at Hamburg. Brünn called him two years later. He raised the bar for Moravian rabbis. Only trained, learned men now win pulpits there. He founded a seminary annex and cantors' school. As Benno Planek he published poems and a novel. He also wrote keen studies of animal life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbinowitz-sau:
Saul Phinehas Rabbinowitz was a Russian publicist and historian in Hebrew. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Taurogen in the Kovno government in 1845. At five he was taken to Wilna to live. His father was rabbi of an old suburb there.

Saul learned Hebrew and Talmud from his father first. His mother's father, rabbi of Taurogen, taught him as well. At fourteen he entered the yeshivah of Jacob Barit. That strict school shaped his mind for his life's work. The entry traces his rise as a voice of Hebrew letters. He wrote for the new Hebrew press of Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rawnitzki-joshu:
Joshua Hayyim Rawnitzki was a Russian author born on August 14, 1845. Herman Rosenthal and Isidor Warsaw wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Odessa. His first writing appeared in the journal Ha-Kol.

The article says he soon wrote often for Hebrew journals. In 1887 he helped publish a German Jewish paper. From 1892 to 1896 he edited Ha-Pardes at Odessa. His books include pearls drawn from the Talmud. He also wrote a novel of Jewish life. An essay treated the new Hebrew of his day. He published Hebrew poems for children as well. The entry shows a writer working in several forms and languages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reuben-tribe-of:
The tribe of Reuben descended from Jacob's firstborn son Reuben. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Reuben's four sons founded its four clans. They were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.

The article gives the tribe's numbers at the Exodus. It counted forty six thousand five hundred fighting men. A plague after Baalpeor worship cut that number down. In camp the tribe marched on the south side. Its camp gave the whole southern host its name. Some Reubenites joined Korah's rebellion against Moses. Rich in cattle, the tribe asked for land east of Jordan. Moses granted it after they promised to help conquer the west. The entry then maps their territory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roe-12801:
The roe is a deer like animal named in English Bible versions. Isidore Singer and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The same Hebrew word is also rendered roebuck or gazel. It appears among animals permitted as food.

The article says roe was furnished for Solomon's table. Scripture praises its swiftness, gentleness, and grace often. A feminine form of the word became a personal name. Zibiah and Tabitha both come from that form. The Talmud uses two Hebrew terms for all deer kinds. That makes each case hard to pin down, they say. Some passages do seem to mean the roe itself. Its horns usually carry only one branch. The entry joins Bible reading with Palestine game lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rostof-12901:
Rostof is a Russian fortified trading and manufacturing town on the river Don. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews settled there about 1827 and grew with the city's grain trade.

A large synagogue and study house rose at Rostof in 1842. Under Alexander II, Jews even sat on the city council there. By 1866 the community numbered 2,342, and it later neared 14,000. Prosperity broke in May 1883, when an anti-Jewish riot struck the town. Three Jews were hurt and much property destroyed, yet the rioters were acquitted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saint-gilles-13:
Saint-Gilles is a French town in the Gard, south-southeast of Nîmes. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In the twelfth century it was an important commercial center of the south.

When Benjamin of Tudela passed through, its Jewish community numbered 100 members. They lived under the protection of Raymond V, Count of Toulouse. In 1216 the Jewish communities of southern France sent delegates to Saint-Gilles. Led by R. Levi, they met to plan against the Lateran Council's resolutions. Those church decrees of 1215 threatened Jewish life across Christian Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ibn-hayy: Schulim Ochser wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel ibn Ḥayyim, a medieval poet who wrote prayers for the liturgy. When and where he was born is unknown. He composed eighty-two liturgical poems in all. The last four listed by Zunz were written for the Simḥat Torah festival. Twice he signed his name in acrostic as Samuel ha-Ḳaṭan ha-Kohen. The entry rests on Zunz's study of the synagogue poetry of the Middle Ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sardis-13201:
Emil G. Hirsch and Louis H. Gray wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sardis. The ancient city stood in Asia Minor, on the river Pactolus. It was the capital of Lydia, some sixty miles from Smyrna. After 133 B.C. it headed a Roman court district. No one knows when its Jewish community began.

By the late first century B.C. that community held real influence. A decree of 50 to 49 B.C., kept by Josephus, proves it. The Jews had their own assembly and their own place for settling disputes. Sardis then passed a decree confirming their freedom of worship. Special steps let them import ritually clean food. Under Augustus the proconsul renewed their privileges. He also let them send money to Jerusalem. The town's site is now the ruined village of Sart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schonhak-joseph:
Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Joseph Schönhak. He was a Russian author. Schönhak was born at Tiktin in 1812. He died at Suwalki on December 10, 1870. He led a retired life given to writing and study. His works join natural science to Bible study.

His Toledot ha-Areẓ, printed at Warsaw in 1841, is a natural history in three parts. It sorts its subjects by kind. Each gets a full account of color, form, and habitat. Creatures named in the Bible get book, chapter, and verse. The same care covers creatures named in the Talmud. His Ha-Mashbir, from 1858, is a rabbinical dictionary. It rests on Nathan ben Jehiel's 'Aruk. His Sefer ha-Milluim appeared at Warsaw in 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seleucid-13401:
Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Seleucidæ. They were a powerful Syrian dynasty. Their rule touched Jewish history for two centuries, from 312 to 112 B.C. Seleucus the First, called Nicator, founded the line. He had been one of Alexander the Great's generals. His victory at Gaza in 312 won him Babylon.

Seleucus counted his reign from 312, opening the Seleucidan era. Legal papers were dated by that era for centuries. The Jews called it the era of contracts. The Books of the Maccabees use that dating. Oriental Jews kept it into the late Middle Ages. The Seleucids pushed Greek culture across the East. They founded cities and gave Jews full civil rights in them. Antioch, the capital, held those rights until Josephus's day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shanghai-13501:
Shanghai, the Chinese port city, gained its first Jewish settler around 1850. Joseph Jacobs and N. E. B. Ezra wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the city. Elias David Sassoon opened a branch of his father's Bombay house there. Clerks from India followed, hired by the Sassoon firm.

The community grew to mix Asiatic, German, and Russian Jews. Jews played a large part in building China's foreign trade. Some sat on the city's French and English councils at once. Early trade in opium and Bombay cotton yarn lay mostly in Jewish hands. Worship began in a hired hall in the 1870s. By 1905 Shanghai had two small synagogues, and the entry maps that growth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shoe-13601:
Shoe examines footwear and its customs among the ancient Hebrews of the Bible. Joseph Jacobs wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the subject. For most people a shoe was a leather sole. Leather bands held that sole around the ankles.

Women likely wore fuller shoes covering the whole foot, even early. A bridegroom owed his bride three pairs each year. One pair served for each of the three chief festivals. Shoes seem a fairly late arrival in Israel, the entry argues. So solemn moments called for taking them off entirely. Moses removed his shoes at the burning bush. Priests served barefoot, and mourners went unshod in grief. At Passover, though, Israel ate with shoes on, ready to depart at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-the-just:
Simeon the Just was a high priest of Jerusalem, but scholars still debate which man he was. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He may be Simeon I, son of Onias I, or Simeon II, son of Onias II. Tales about him fill the Talmud, Josephus, and Second Maccabees.

He was praised for piety and for care for his people. One account credits him with rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. It also says he repaired the Temple and enlarged its cistern. A famous legend tells how he met Alexander the Great. These mixed facts and tales made him a lasting model of the just priest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sloman-henry-13: Henry Sloman was an English actor born at Rochester in 1793. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was a favorite comedian at the Coburg Theatre. He won fame as Watty Wagstaff in Edward the Black Prince. About 1834 he became co-owner of the Rochester Theatre with his brother Charles. He died at Rochester in August 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soferim-scribes:
Soferim, or Scribes, is a Talmudic treatise on the holy books. Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It gives rules for preparing those books by hand. It also gives rules for reading the Law in public. It counts among the so-called smaller treatises of rabbinic literature.

The treatise has twenty-one chapters and 225 paragraphs in all. Early chapters deal with parchment and other writing materials. They cover language, translation, and who may prepare books. Later rules cover spaces between letters, words, and lines. They also cover columns, scroll size, sewing, and mending. The work served as a practical manual for scribes and readers alike.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-zalman-:
Solomon Zalman ben Isaac was a Polish rabbi who died at Warsaw in 1838. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He served as rabbi at Mashelsk and at Praga. He was then called to the rabbinate of Warsaw. He held that post until his death.

He kept a learned correspondence with Akiba Eger. He also wrote to Jacob of Lissa on scientific matters. His Hemdat Shelomoh held responsa on the Shulhan Aruk. It also held novellae on several Talmudical treatises in two volumes. It appeared at Warsaw in 1816 in print. His son later published more of his manuscript novellae.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stein-leopold-1:
Leopold Stein was a German rabbi born in Burgpreppach in 1810. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on November 3 of that year. He studied at Erlangen, Bayreuth, and the University of Würzburg. In 1833 he preached his first sermon at Frankfort.

That sermon pleaded for the introduction of reforms in Judaism. He became rabbi of Burg and Altenkunstadt in 1835. From 1844 to 1862 he was rabbi at Frankfort-on-the-Main. He stood out as a leader of the Reform movement there. He edited Der Israelitische Volkslehrer with S Süsskind for years. He died at Frankfort on December 2, 1882.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-suicide-14101:
Suicide rates vary sharply by people, place, and faith. Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The entry opens with statistics from many European countries. Teutonic peoples show higher rates than Celtic or Mediterranean peoples. In America each nationality keeps its own rate. Environment alone does not explain the pattern.

The article then weighs the role of social setting. Morselli held that religion lowers the suicide rate strongly. Catholics and Jews, he said, are least prone to it. Yet Protestants and Catholics in one country often share rates. Shared conditions can matter more than creed alone. The entry also treats Jewish law and teaching on self-killing. Readers get an early data-driven look at a grim subject. It blends numbers with religious and social analysis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talmud-hermeneu:
Talmud hermeneutics is the science of reading scripture by fixed rules. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The rules pin down both legal and historical meaning. They also derive oral law duties from written law. Halakah counts as an unfolding of the Torah itself.

The rules cover grammar and plain exegesis first. They weigh extra words, prefixes, and suffixes in texts. Dotted letters in words get their own treatment. Letter values can unlock meaning through gematria. A word may be split into two through notarikon. Letters can be swapped or vowels changed by rule. Logic finally deduces one law from another. Hillel's seven rules form the oldest known list. The entry catalogs the tools of rabbinic reading.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temerls-jacob-b:
Jacob ben Eliezer Temerls, also called Jacob Ashkenazi, was a German Talmudist and cabalist. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Temerls was born at Worms late in the sixteenth century. He died at Vienna around 1667.

Young Temerls moved to Poland and ran a Talmud school at Lublin for some years. He then spent most of his life at Kremenetz before settling in Vienna. Contemporaries praised his learning and his great piety. He was said to have fasted for forty years. His printed book gives a cabalist commentary on the Pentateuch. His other writings stayed in manuscript, including responsa and notes on the Talmud and Zohar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-villefranche-or:
Villefranche is a town in the Roussillon district of France. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town was founded in 1095. Jews from Provence were among its early settlers. A Jewish community lived there by the mid twelve hundreds.

In 1274 the community gained leave to lay out a cemetery. In 1328 it could rebuild its ruined synagogue. The town was the birthplace of Levi ben Abraham. The entry warns against mixing it up with two other Villafrancas. One sits in Catalonia and one in Navarre. Both of those towns also had Jewish communities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-way-lewis-14801:
Lewis Way was an English clergyman who worked for Jewish rights. Joseph Jacobs and Eduard Neumann wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Denham on February 11, 1772. He died in London on January 26, 1840. He studied at Merton College, Oxford. A stranger's legacy let him devote his wealth to the church.

In 1808 Way founded a London mission society for Jews. He believed the Jewish nation would rise again. He traveled through Europe at his own cost. He studied Jewish life and pressed for better treatment. In 1817 he won two decrees from Czar Alexander I. They promised baptized Jews protection and farm land. He also pled for Jewish freedom at Aix la Chapelle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiener-leo-1490:
Leo Wiener was an American philologist at Harvard. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Lebovich wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Byelostok, in Russia, on July 27, 1862. He studied at Warsaw and at Berlin's Polytechnic. On emigrating, he worked as a laborer and fruit peddler. Teaching posts in Missouri and Kansas followed.

Harvard called Wiener to teach Slavic languages. He still holds that post in 1905. He writes on language for journals in five countries. Yiddish literature is his special Jewish interest. His history of Yiddish literature appeared in 1899. He translated Rosenfeld's Songs from the Ghetto. He also translated the complete works of Tolstoy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wollemborg-leon:
Leone Wollemborg (born 1859) was an Italian student of wealth and state funds. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Padua, he took his degree there in 1878. He gave his mind to the study of how lands grow rich.

His chief deed was to set up farm loan banks. Those banks served the poor peasants and small farmers of Italy. He sat for Padua in the law house for years. From 1900 to 1903 he held the purse of the state. He served as finance chief in the Zanardelli cabinet. His books treat the cost of goods and farm loans. They also treat joint dairies and grain taxes in his land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-of-magda:
Yizhak of Magdala was a scholar of Palestine in the third century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took part in more than one tale debate of note. One clash was with Levi on a verse in Kings.

That verse treats gold cups in the house of the king. A second clash was with Kahana on Joseph in jail. It asked why Joseph shunned wine from that time on. On the curse of the world he set a calm view. Gnats, flies, and such small things still serve man, he said. The entry rests on the tale study of Bacher in three books. It lists the books where his words may be traced in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-ben-j:
Zechariah ben Jehoiada was a priest who rebuked a king of Judah. Emil G. Hirsch, Bernhard Pick, the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the reign of King Joash. He spoke out against the idol cults of his day.

He warned the folk of the doom of God for their acts. A plot rose against him for that bold speech then. He was stoned in the court of the Temple by royal word. The king had forgot the good his sire had done him. The last words of the priest call on God to see. In tale lore he was the son-in-law of the king as well. He was slain on a Sabbath that was Atonement Day too. His blood was said to boil when the foe razed the shrine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zupnik-aaron-hi:
Aaron Hirsch Zupnik was a Galician writer and editor in Hebrew and Judæo-German. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Drohobycz about 1850, he edited the Drohobyczer Zeitung, a weekly begun in 1883. He also ran Ziyyon, a periodical that moved from Hebrew literature to monthly science.

Zupnik's books cross several forms. One is a historical novel of Jewish life in Spain, adapted from Ludwig Philippson. Another tells the life of Abraham Cohn, a preacher of Lemberg. He translated a work on Jewish teaching and Jewish life into Hebrew and Polish. His own Judæo-German novel follows Jewish life in Galicia from the schoolroom to the workshop.
journal-of-discourses-vol-01:
Volume One of the Journal of Discourses appeared in 1854 in Liverpool and Utah's orbit. George D. Watt reported the sermons in shorthand as they were preached. Brigham Young and the apostles speak here in the Salt Lake Tabernacle.

Doctrine, prophecy, and the building of Zion fill these early discourses. The speakers teach a young church how to live, work, and endure. Their voice is urgent, plain, and sure of divine guidance throughout. No source shows Mormonism's founding generation thinking aloud quite like this. Scholars cite the Journal more than any other Mormon record of its age.
kenelm-chillingly-volume-01:
Volume one of Kenelm Chillingly, Edward Bulwer Lytton's novel, opens Book One at Exmundham. Sir Peter Chillingly, baronet and antiquary, heads the household there. He married Caroline Brotherton young, at his father's and grandfather's wish, though he loved another. Her ample fortune bought two farms and doubled his income without lifting his spirits much.

Caroline played, painted, and spoke French and Italian with real taste and knowledge. Her death left Sir Peter lonely, with books and study for constant companions. Their son Kenelm grows up clever, odd, and hard to satisfy. This first volume sets his upbringing and the quiet, bookish world he must escape. Lytton builds the hero from his parents' mismatched marriage.
king-henry-vi-part-2-pg1501:
This edition of Shakespeare's Henry the Sixth, Part Two prints the cast and full scene plan. King Henry heads the list, with Queen Margaret and the lords of both factions. Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, and his wife Eleanor stand among them. The Cardinal Beaufort and the Duke of Somerset fill out the court.

The contents move from the Parliament House to an abbey at Bury St. Edmunds. Blackheath, Cannon Street, Smithfield, and Southwark mark Jack Cade's rising in London. Kenilworth and St. Albans carry the story toward open war. The plan shows the play's sweep: a murdered duke, a shamed duchess, a mob in the capital, and York's army marching home.
kipling-kim-1901:
Rudyard Kipling published Kim in 1901, a novel set in India under British rule. Kim is an Irish orphan who grows up on the streets of Lahore. He joins a Tibetan lama on a search for a sacred river. At the same time, spies draw him into the Great Game against Russia.

Kim moves between worlds: bazaars, trains, schools, and mountain passes. He loves India in all its noise and color, yet his training pulls him toward secret work. The lama seeks freedom from the wheel of life. Their bond gives the adventure its heart. Many call Kim Kipling's finest novel.
lucretia-volume-01:
Volume 1 of Lucretia opens Edward Bulwer Lytton's dark novel. His 1853 preface explains the plan behind the book. Lucretia was meant to stand beside The Caxtons as its shadow. Both ask how home and childhood fix a person's fate.

In The Caxtons the influence is kind and cheerful. Here it is evil, and the elements are tragic. The children of night of the subtitle are formed by darkness. Lytton defends his design against readers who attacked it. This first volume sets the unhappy schooling in motion. It prepares the crimes and sorrows that follow from it.
mackenzie-voyages-montreal-1801:
Alexander Mackenzie, a Scottish fur trader in Canada, published his Voyages from Montreal in 1801. He had reached the Arctic Ocean by river in 1789 and crossed the Rockies to the Pacific in 1793. His Pacific crossing was the first across North America north of Mexico.

Mackenzie tells of canoe brigades, rapids, and tense meetings with Native nations whose help he needed. The river that bears his name carried him to the northern sea. His Pacific route crossed passes Lewis and Clark later followed in part. The book pushed Britain and America to race for the West he had opened.
maitland-english-law-renaissance-1901:
Frederic Maitland gave the Rede Lecture at Cambridge in 1901 on English Law and the Renaissance. The short work asks how the common law survived when Roman law was sweeping the Continent. Maitland called the Tudor age the law's crisis.

He shows how the Inns of Court, the Year Books, and a stubborn profession kept English law alive. Littleton and Coke become heroes of a quiet resistance. Had England taken Roman law whole, its history would differ deeply. The lecture is brief, brilliant, and quotable, the classic statement of England's legal exceptionalism by its greatest legal historian. It fits in an evening's reading.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume one of Margery opens Georg Ebers's tale of old Nuremberg. Clara Bell's translation avoids speech too modern for its century. The frame tells how Ebers bought the manuscript in Venice. Its seller, a Giustiniani, lamented his family's vanished money.

From those sheets unfolds the life of Margery Schopper of Nuremberg. She writes as 'Gred,' in the voice of a fifteenth-century maiden. Her world is one of council families, forests, and church feasts. Her brother Herdegen stands near the center of her heart. Ebers pours his Egyptologist's learning into German history here. The first volume raises the curtain on her story.
mctaggart-hegelian-cosmology-1901:
Studies in Hegelian Cosmology, published in 1901, continues McTaggart's critical project from method to system. Having tested Hegel's dialectic, he now rebuilds its picture of the whole: the Absolute, the self, and the case for the soul's survival of death.

McTaggart argues that reality is a system of selves bound by love, and that each self is eternal, perceiving the whole from its own point. His famous argument for survival after death is developed here in Hegelian dress. The reasoning is intricate and perfectly clear at once. The book shows idealism's strangest fruit: a godless system of eternal, loving selves.
mead-apollonius-tyana-1901:
G. R. S. Mead turned to Apollonius of Tyana in 1901. Apollonius was a sage of the first years of the Roman Empire. He roamed from Greece to India and was famed for wise words and strange deeds. Some in late Rome set him up as a match for Christ.

Mead draws on the Life by Philostratus, our chief source for the sage. He weighs the tales of cures, flights, and talks with kings. He reads the sage with a theosophist's warm eye. The book gives a clear, short path into a life that still sparks debate.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-01:
Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne wrote memoirs of Napoleon, his private secretary. R. W. Phipps, a colonel of artillery, edited the 1891 set. Volume one holds chapters one to four, through the year 1797.

The editors of 1836 praise Bourrienne's wish to be fair in print. He shows faults as well as merits in a most wondrous man, they say. His graphic power with facts and tales gets their praise too. For fourteen years, they note, Bonaparte's history was the history of Europe. Napoleon stands apart from Alexander, Caesar, and Charlemagne, they argue. No past hero matches him in character, fortune, or reach.
merimee-colomba-carmen-1901:
Prosper Merimee wrote the two novellas paired in the English book of about 1901. Carmen, from 1845, tells of Don Jose and the Romani woman who leads him to ruin in Spain. Colomba, from 1840, is set in Corsica. A young officer returns home, and his sister Colomba presses him to avenge their father's murder.

Colomba is proud, patient, and bound by the code of the vendetta. Her brother must choose between French law and family honor. Together the two tales show Merimee's love of wild places and strong passions. Both are told in clear, ironic prose. They remain his most read works of fiction.
milly-darrell-pg17801:
M. E. Braddon's Milly Darrell reached print first as a magazine serial in Belgravia. The serial ran from November 1870 into January 1871. The text here follows the 1873 Paris volume Milly Darrell and Other Stories. That volume appeared as number seventy-two in Asher's Collection of English Authors.

Braddon, who lived from 1835 to 1915, built her fame on sensation novels. Lady Audley's Secret, from 1862, remained her best-known work. The shorter stories let her compress her usual secrets and passions into brief forms. This foreign-circulation edition shows how widely her fiction traveled beyond Britain.
monsieur-madame-and-be-be-volume-01: Gustave Droz's Monsieur, Madame, et Bébé opens in this first volume of the English edition. The Project Gutenberg header places it tenth in the French Immortals series. Droz's sketches follow a Parisian pair from courtship toward marriage and baby. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the volume itself. It contains only the Gutenberg header, with title, author, and series data. Readers get the volume's identity and place in the set, but none of its sketches.
mr-edward-arnold-s-new-and-popular-books:
Edward Arnold, a London publisher at 37 Bedford Street in the Strand, issued this catalogue of new and popular books in December 1901. Each title comes dressed with review quotations. The sample opens with Mrs. Charles Bagot's Links with the Past. The Morning Post praises its glimpses of a vanishing past and its agreeable personalities.

The World calls Bagot's memoir a trustworthy record of nineteenth-century social life. The Times adds her excellent memory, keen perceptions, and gift of expression. Such catalogues sold books by borrowed authority, stacking newspaper praise page after page. This one survives as a snapshot of Edwardian publishing and the memoir trade.
murray-antarctic-manual-1901:
George Murray put this guide book out in 1901 for the Royal Geographical Society. It was made for Scott's Discovery trip south that same year. Experts in many fields wrote its parts. The book told the men what to study and how to work in the ice.

Chapters cover ice, weather, rocks, sea life, birds, and the south lights. Plain rules tell how to note finds, keep logs, and guard health in deep cold. The guide marks the start of the Heroic Age of Antarctic work. Few books show so well how science planned its push to the pole.
myvyrian-archaiology-wales-1801:
Owen Jones, Edward Williams, and William Owen Pughe brought out this great store of Welsh texts in parts from 1801 to 1807. The text here is from the 1870 reprint. They drew on old Welsh books held in homes and church stores across Wales. The work took years of trips, loans, and close hand work with worn pages.

The set holds poems, tales, and lists of kings and saints from old Wales. It also holds texts by Iolo Morganwg that were not as old as he claimed. True and false side by side, the set fed Welsh lore for a hundred years.
norris-octopus-1901:
Frank Norris published The Octopus in 1901, the first volume of his planned Epic of the Wheat. Norris had covered a famous fight between California wheat ranchers and the Southern Pacific Railroad, which raised freight rates and seized land. The railroad's network of lines and favors reminded everyone of an octopus.

The novel follows ranchers in the San Joaquin Valley as the railroad tightens its grip: false promises, rigged land deals, and armed eviction. A poet, Presley, watches and tries to turn the struggle into art. Wheat itself becomes a vast impersonal force, feeding distant cities regardless of who suffers. The Octopus founded the American protest epic and still frames how novels treat corporate power.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
C. H. Tawney translated Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara in the 1880s, and N. M. Penzer reissued it with introduction and notes in ten volumes from 1924. Volume one opens the Ocean of Story, the great Sanskrit story cycle Somadeva composed in the eleventh century for a Kashmir queen. Its frame promises tales enough to fill an ocean.

Gods, kings, merchants, and rogues pour through the opening books in tales within tales. Somadeva retells older cycles, including the lost great story of Gunadhya, in polished Sanskrit verse. Tawney's English, made in India, keeps the flood ordered and readable. Penzer's notes range across world folklore for parallels. The whole work is one of the largest story collections ever made.
openalex-w1517154901:
Allana LeBlanc, Peter Katzmarzyk, and many co-authors wrote this study. It appeared in PLoS ONE in June 2015. The team studied children aged nine to eleven worldwide. Their project is the International Study of Childhood Obesity. It covers lifestyle and environment across many countries.

Earlier studies used small samples in narrow regions, they note. This study sought factors linked to sedentary time. It also sought factors linked to daily screen time. Sites ran from Canada and Finland to Kenya and China. Comparable measures let the team compare cultures fairly. The work helps target healthy activity programs for children.
openalex-w2015787201:
Marcelo Gehara, Andrew Crawford, Victor Orrico and colleagues studied a widespread South American tree frog. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. The frog is known as Dendropsophus minutus. It lives across a vast continent and many habitats. The team suspected it hides several species under one name.

They gathered DNA data across the frog's whole range. Such wide sampling is costly and hard to organise. Their results uncovered high levels of hidden diversity. Different regions held distinct genetic lineages. The pattern suggests a complex of separate species. Each likely has a smaller range than the named species. The work shows why broad sampling matters for naming species. It also guides later studies of how the group diversified.
openalex-w2100578201:
Roderick Escombe, David Moore, Robert Gilman and colleagues tested air-cleaning methods against tuberculosis spread in hospitals. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2009. TB spreads through air in crowded wards. Drug-resistant strains made control more urgent. Cheap, effective ward measures were badly needed.

The team evaluated two methods in a Lima hospital setting. Ultraviolet lamps treated the upper air of rooms. Negative air ionizers were the second method tested. Both aim to kill or remove airborne bacteria. The study design measured how much infectious air reached test animals. Such ward models descend from classic 1950s experiments. Results inform infection control in high-burden hospitals. Simple air treatment could protect staff and patients.
openalex-w2153509701: Stefanie Engel, Stefano Pagiola, and Sven Wunder wrote this overview in Ecological Economics in 2008. Their subject is payments for environmental services, schemes that pay landholders to protect nature's benefits, such as clean water and stored carbon. The paper reviews design questions in both theory and practice. The hosted sample for this entry preserves no readable abstract or introduction, so no findings are summarized here. Only the title, authors, journal, and year ground this note.
openalex-w2167045801:
Eva Ramírez-Llodra, Angelika Brandt, Roberto Danovaro, and colleagues published this review in Biogeosciences in 2010. They describe what makes the deep sea, Earth's largest ecosystem, deep, diverse, and definitely different. Its geology, chemistry, and biology form habitats unlike anything in shallow water or on land.

Deep-sea study began in the late nineteenth century, and discovery rates for habitats and species remain high. Since 1840, twenty-eight new habitat types have been found, from the shelf break to the deepest trenches. Most have barely been sampled, and their global extent is often unknown. Most deep ecosystems feed on organic matter sinking from sunlit surface waters. The review closes with human threats to these barely known habitats.
openalex-w2757272801:
Nicolas Bertrand, Philippe Grenier, and Morteza Mahmoudi, with colleagues, studied the protein corona on medical nanoparticles in Nature Communications in 2017. When nanoparticles enter blood, proteins coat their surfaces, forming a corona. That coating shapes where particles travel and how long they circulate. Test-tube studies with plasma cannot fully predict behavior inside a living body.

Using a library of polymer nanoparticles, the team tracked corona formation inside animals. They show that the density of a protective polymer layer, PEG, decides early clearance. Below a certain PEG density threshold, particles are cleared from blood rapidly. Above it, they circulate longer. The work explains a mechanism, not just an observation, behind particle fate. It gives drug-delivery designers a concrete surface target to aim for.
openalex-w2785784801:
Collin A. Eagles-Smith, Ellen Kovner Silbergeld, and Niladri Basu lead a team examining mercury risk in Ambio in 2018. Mercury pollution is an urgent global health threat to wildlife and people. Working out who is actually at risk is hard, because mercury moves through food webs in complex ways. Rapid global change keeps shifting those pathways.

The authors examine drivers that raise or lower mercury risk across three domains. First, global change alters how mercury builds up and magnifies through food webs. Second, social and individual factors shape how much mercury people take in. Third, many outside and inside factors modulate mercury's health effects themselves. They argue monitoring must weave all three domains together. Only then can the world judge whether mercury-reduction efforts truly protect health.
openalex-w2805726701:
The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration refined the neutron star merger GW170817 in Physical Review X in 2019. The original detection, in August 2017, located the source well enough for telescopes to find its host galaxy, NGC 4993. This paper reanalyzes the signal with the known position, better models, and recalibrated data. It also extends the analysis to lower frequencies than before.

The tighter analysis shrank the source's sky region to sixteen square degrees. Masses, spins, and tidal squeezing of the two stars all gained sharper limits. The team still found no evidence that either star was spinning noticeably. Tidal measurements probe how stiff neutron star matter is under crushing pressure. Comparing several signal models checked that conclusions were not model artifacts. The paper is the reference statement of what this landmark merger's waves revealed.
openalex-w314366901:
Bronwen Powell, Shakuntala Thilsted, Amy Ickowitz, and colleagues published this paper in Food Security in 2015. It examines how wild and farmed biodiversity across whole landscapes can improve diets in developing countries. Diverse fields, forests, and waters offer far more foods than staple crops alone.

The authors review the evidence tying that variety to healthier, more varied eating. Availability alone does not decide diets: prices, knowledge, and social norms shape what people grow, gather, buy, and serve. They mark where proof is thin and where nutrition programs could join forces with efforts to sustain food systems and nature. The paper argues the two agendas strengthen each other.
openalex-w3153006501:
Andrew Plumptre, Daniele Baisero, R. Travis Belote, and colleagues published this study in Frontiers in Forests and Global Change in 2021. It asks where ecologically intact communities, wildlife assemblages barely touched by people, still survive. Protecting intact ecosystems has been a conservation goal for decades.

Earlier maps of human pressure suggest only a fifth to two fifths of land lies under low human influence. Most measured habitat alone, not whether the full cast of native species persists. The authors set out to locate places where communities remain whole, using species data alongside pressure maps. Those refuges matter doubly: they shelter wildlife now and show what restoration could aim for. Global biodiversity targets increasingly name integrity, not just area.
openalex-w4210971201:
Libor Šmejkal, Anna Birk Hellenes, Rafael González-Hernández, and colleagues present a theory paper on spintronics in Physical Review X in 2022. Spintronic devices read stored information through effects called giant and tunneling magnetoresistance. Until now these effects were thought to need ferromagnetic layers, which hold a net magnetism. The authors had proposed that certain antiferromagnets, with no net magnetism, could do the same job.

Here they work out how both effects could arise in layered stacks of these unusual materials. The models rest on a coupling between electron spin and momentum that alternates across the material. Computer models of real materials predict very large effects, near the hundred-percent scale. If borne out, the scheme could widen the materials open for memory devices.
openalex-w4390345401:
Jonggeol Jeffrey Kim, Dan Vitale, Diego Véliz Otani, and colleagues combined genetic studies of Parkinson's disease across many ancestries, in Nature Genetics in 2023. Parkinson's is a brain disease that slowly damages movement control. Most earlier gene hunts drew mainly on European-ancestry samples, which can miss variants common elsewhere. A meta-analysis pools many studies into one larger search for risk regions in the genome.

The effort joined academic cohorts with data from the company 23andMe and partners worldwide. Diverse samples sharpen the map of risk and can reveal new loci that single-ancestry studies lacked power to see. Findings from such pooled work also transfer better to patients of all backgrounds. The paper is part of a wider push to make genomics serve every population.
openalex-w4411443801:
Toshiaki Iba reviews the history of research on disseminated intravascular coagulation, or DIC. His lecture appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2025. DIC is a dangerous state complicating severe illness. Patients bleed uncontrollably, yet their organs fill with tiny clots.

Iba traces how that paradox was resolved. Excess clotting comes first; it consumes the clotting factors, and bleeding follows. He describes the lab markers that made diagnosis practical: platelet counts, clotting times, fibrinogen, and breakdown products such as D-dimer. Japan set formal diagnostic criteria in 1988. Mixing history with his own research career, the lecture shows how a confusing syndrome became a measurable, treatable condition.
openalex-w7204998101:
Patrícia da Silva Bezerra de Miranda led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on care bundles for preventing infections tied to invasive devices in intensive care units. Bundles group a small set of proven methods that, done together every time, cut infections from central lines, ventilators, and urinary catheters. The review searched four sources for 2020 to 2025 original studies on bundle implementation, adherence, and impact, keeping thirteen.

Structured bundle use greatly reduced central line, ventilator, and catheter infection rates, the authors find, with added impact on hospital mortality and care costs. Multicenter studies showed large drops in healthcare infection risk and large savings. Full adherence to every bundle component proved decisive for lasting results. Systematic rollout and ongoing checks, they conclude, qualify the safety of very ill patients.
openalex-w7213276501:
Guilherme Gallo Costa Gomes leads a team that reads heat maps of the skin as a way to head off sports harm. The tool is a heat-view cam. It reads the skin's warm and cool spots from afar, with no touch. Strain shows as heat: a part worked past its ease glows long before it tears. The team read work from 2020 to 2026; twenty studies made the set.

Most of the work, they find, hugs the legs, and most of that is in the game of kicks and goals. Arms and hands have a few reads, in games of rack and oar. The spine is the blank spot: no read there has yet tried to call a harm ahead of its fall. The next step is proof they can call harm days out, not just show strain once it is there.
openalex-w7213431001:
Vinícius S. Alves leads a mapping of research on girls' futsal in Brazilian schools. Their 2026 state-of-the-art review covers national physical education journals. Sixteen articles published between 2000 and 2022 were found through a systematic search of indexed journals.

Research grew only slowly over that period, the team finds. Production clustered in the South and Southeast, and empirical studies outnumbered theoretical ones. Gender discussion sat at the centre of most work, reflecting strong inequality in school football. Girls' school futsal remains a field still taking shape, the authors conclude, with clear regional and theoretical gaps that call for broader study.
openalex-w7213944501:
Manuel Isaque Bernardes Ferreira Freitas and co-authors review Pilates for posture and muscle and joint pain. Their 2026 integrative review covers studies from 2024 to 2026 on Pilates applied to varied musculoskeletal conditions. Pilates is widely used in physiotherapy to improve posture control and function.

Practice can reduce pain and improve posture and body alignment, the literature shows. Body awareness and muscle strengthening also rise, with gains in quality of life and daily function reported. The authors set out effects across those outcomes rather than on a single condition. Their synthesis supports Pilates as one intervention option within physiotherapy, while its recent and narrow evidence window limits how far the claims can stretch.
openalex-w7214391901:
Michel Haddad and Dener Martins dos Santos examined eco-friendly bricks in a 2026 Brazilian study, weighing them on technical, economic, and environmental grounds. Construction consumes huge amounts of natural resources, so pressed bricks that need no firing attract interest as a cleaner option. The authors compared the material cost of a masonry wall built with eco-bricks against one built with conventional bricks.

Eco-bricks cost notably more to buy at the start. Later building stages cost less, however, bringing the total material cost of the wall down by roughly a fifth. Making eco-bricks also avoids the firing process, lowering environmental impact, and building with them produces less waste. The authors report that the bricks meet the main technical standards for use across many kinds of construction projects.
openalex-w7214908601:
Paula Santos Nascimento and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva wrote a 2026 article on literature as an inclusive teaching tool in special education. Their library study reads national and world work on reading, forming readers, school inclusion, and adapting courses. The question is whether stories and poems can truly include students who are often pushed to the margins of reading culture.

Such texts, the reviewed work shows, develop empathy, widen students' cultural range, and help build classrooms that are more open and caring to diversity. Reading is treated as a social and formative practice, not just sounding out words. When teachers bring literature into their practice, the authors conclude, it becomes a strong resource for inclusion, taking part, and real learning in special education settings.
openalex-w7214937001:
Adriano Nogueira da Cruz led a large team in a 2026 integrative review of the golden hour, the first hour after severe trauma, when fast coordinated care most affects survival. Following standard review methods, the team searched seven databases for studies from 2020 to 2026 and kept twenty-two. Nurses, doctors, pharmacists, radiologists, physiotherapists, nutritionists, and psychologists all have roles inside that hour.

Evidence converged on coordinated teamwork improving both process and outcome measures. Time to control bleeding stood out as a critical driver of death, and a clot-supporting drug given within three hours reduced deaths from bleeding. The review gathers what each profession contributes and when, making it a practical synthesis for trauma teams reorganizing their first response. Speed alone is not the lesson; the lesson is speed with coordination, shared roles, and evidence-based steps done in the right order.
openalex-w7215062801:
Giovanna Azevedo Rodrigues led a 2026 review offering a new way to view developmental dyscalculia, the lasting trouble in learning math. Long treated as a lone deficit standing alone, dyscalculia rarely appears alone when doctors observe patients. The authors combine a literature review with following five patients with severe dyscalculia over time to build a matrix that reads it as one sign of a broader neuropsychiatric disorder.

In those patients, math difficulty came, again and again, with weak visuospatial working memory, finger recognition, lateralization, spatial processing, grasp of relational language, and social reciprocity, partly matching a known childhood syndrome. The math deficit, they argue, is not the central problem but the visible sign of altered shared mechanisms. Understanding dyscalculia, they conclude, needs a whole-system approach joining space, attention, language, and the body's role in thinking, and their matrix is offered as a working hypothesis awaiting tests with patients.
openalex-w7220424301:
Larissa Marcelly Pacheco Zahluth led a ten-author 2026 review on feline sporotrichosis in Brazil, a fungal disease cats transmit to other cats and to people. The review covers its clinical, epidemiological, and zoonotic sides, the limits of conventional treatment, and whether plant products could help as adjuvant therapy, drawing mainly on literature from 2020 to 2026.

The disease is spreading into new Brazilian regions, with a recent rise in the North, tied to social and economic vulnerability, weak surveillance, and underreporting. Itraconazole remains the main treatment, but its long course, adverse effects, trouble giving it, and treatment failures can undo it. Plant extracts and essential oils show antifungal promise against Sporothrix species, though possible antagonistic interactions with standard drugs demand more study. Control, the authors conclude, needs integrated surveillance, treatment access, and safe adjuvant strategies.
openalex-w7220458101:
Junamappe da Silva Cardoso Mendes wrote a 2026 essay on the physical and mental health of health professionals across history. Health work is central to care and to protecting life, yet it carries risks and demands that rebound on the workers. Her essay, grounded in scientific articles, books, and official and normative documents, follows three threads. They are how health work evolved over time, risk factors and their effects, and today's challenges with paths of protection.

Advances in science and technology widened care's possibilities while making work processes more complex. They keep or create risks at work: overload, long shifts, precarious employment, psychosocial factors, and technological change all feed physical and mental wear. Guarding health workers, she concludes, takes more than individual strategies: public policy, enough work organization, permanent education, social and mental support, safe environments, and professional valorization.
openalex-w7220948001:
Eduardo Alexandre Guedes Cidade and José Roque Nunes Marques test a Brazilian environmental law against the knowledge it is meant to protect, in a 2026 article. Law number 13,123 of 2015 governs access to genetic heritage and to the traditional knowledge tied to Amazonian biodiversity, knowledge held collectively by local communities.

Reading the statute beside socio-environmental rights scholarship, the authors ask whether its rules on access, consent, and participation truly guard that heritage. They conclude the law has structural gaps: it smooths the path of economic use while giving prior consent and real community participation less weight. On their account, the framework can repeat old patterns in which outside interests take value from the forest's peoples.
openalex-w7221083601:
Asaph Kalebe Queiroz Ibernon and Denison Melo de Aguiar set legal limits for teaching creationism in Brazilian schools, in a 2026 article. Brazil is formally a secular state, yet religious traditions shape its culture, and bills plus court cases keep pressing the question of what belongs in science classrooms.

Applying constitutional principles to statutes, case law, and doctrine, they conclude that creationism cannot stand beside neo-Darwinian evolution as an alternative scientific theory. Treating it as one, they argue, would damage science education and breach state secularity. Creationism may still appear in religious education classes, where its different epistemological footing is clear. The paper maps where religious freedom ends and scientific standards begin.
paul-clifford-volume-01:
Volume 1 of Paul Clifford presents the opening of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's novel, together with his prefaces of 1840 and 1848. Lytton explains that among all his romances, this one alone makes a robber its hero. He wrote it to expose prisons that teach crime and a law that answers with the rope.

The early chapters are part burlesque, contrasting the slang of thieves with the cant of fashionable society. Young Paul's path into crime begins here. Readers who want Lytton's argument whole will find his case stated most fully in these opening pages and prefaces.
paulus-aegineta-seven-books-adams-vol-01:
Paul of Aegina, a Greek doctor of the seventh century, summed up the whole of ancient medicine in his Seven Books. Francis Adams translated the work into English in 1844 for the Sydenham Society. This first volume opens the set, the last great medical encyclopedia of the ancient world.

Paul gathered Hippocrates, Galen, and the surgeons between them into one ordered handbook. Fevers, wounds, poisons, and the diseases of each part of the body get their chapters. His work became the standard text for a thousand years. Through Paul, Greek medicine passed to the Islamic world and back to Europe. Adams adds notes from the Arabic doctors who used him.
pearson-the-ethic-of-freethought-and-oth: A hosted sample showing only the scanned front matter of The Ethic of Freethought and Other Addresses and Essays, a library gift page and the title page, with no essay text visible. The title page names Karl Pearson, fellow of King's College, Cambridge, and professor of applied mathematics and mechanics at University College, London. The Internet Archive record dates the collection to 1901 and lists Macmillan as its American agents.
pelham-volume-01:
Volume 1 of Pelham introduces Henry Pelham, who narrates his own fashionable life. He describes his parents with amused coolness: a moderate Whig father who gave sumptuous dinners, and Lady Frances, who loved diamonds and old china. When bailiffs seize the house, her diamonds still go visiting, escorted by the chief bailiff disguised as a tutor.

These early chapters set the novel's tone, half confession and half satire of good society. Pelham is a coxcomb with brains, learning the price of credit and show. Lytton's first volume made him the chronicler of the dandy world.
pennsylvania-charter-liberties-1701:
William Penn issued the Charter of Liberties for Pennsylvania in 1701, often called the Charter of Privileges. Penn, the colony's Quaker founder, had governed Pennsylvania for two decades by then. Settlers pressed him for a stronger voice, and the charter answered that demand.

The charter gives real lawmaking power to an elected assembly chosen by the people. It protects freedom of worship for those who believe in one God. It also lets Delaware's counties govern apart, which they soon did. Pennsylvania lived under this frame until the American Revolution, longer than under any earlier Penn plan.
plaw-107-1-2001: Birthday greetings from the nation fill Public Law 107-1, a joint resolution of the 107th Congress approved February 15, 2001, recognizing the 90th birthday of Ronald Reagan. Its recitals praise Reagan's two overwhelming election victories. They cite his pledge to restore the great, confident roar of American progress and optimism. They cite his leadership in extending freedom and democracy around a world divided by the Cold War. And they honor Nancy Reagan's crusade against illegal drugs. Congress extends its best wishes while noting Reagan's courageous battle with Alzheimer's disease.
plaw-107-10-2001:
Taiwan's place in world health work receives American backing in Public Law 107-10, approved May 28, 2001, concerning the participation of Taiwan in the World Health Organization.

Congress found that good health matters to every citizen of the world. Direct, unobstructed participation in international health forums benefits all regions, especially as infectious diseases such as HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria spread across borders. Taiwan's population of 23.5 million is larger than that of three-quarters of the organization's member states. The findings praise Taiwan's health achievements, including high life expectancy, the eradication of cholera, smallpox, plague, and polio, and early hepatitis B vaccination for children. They also note Taiwan's rescue teams and 200,000 dollars of aid after the January 2001 earthquake in El Salvador.
plaw-107-100-2001: Fees in the small business investment company program change under Public Law 107-100, the Small Business Investment Company Amendments Act of 2001, approved December 21, 2001. Amending the Small Business Investment Act of 1958, it raises the cap on subsidy fees from not more than one percent per year to not more than 1.38 percent per year, in two places, and moves a September 30, 2000, date to September 30, 2001. The amendments take effect on October 1, 2001, and a further section addresses conflicts of interest in the program.
plaw-107-101-2001: A single appointment fills Public Law 107-101, a joint resolution approved December 21, 2001. Under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, the vacancy on the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution in the class other than Members of Congress, left when Dr. Homer Neal of Michigan's term expired on December 7, 2001, is filled by the appointment of Patricia Q. Stonesifer of Washington. The appointment is for a term of six years and takes effect on December 8, 2001.
plaw-107-102-2001:
Long leases and a large settlement for an Oregon tribe are the business of Public Law 107-102, approved December 27, 2001. The law concerns the use of the trust land and resources of the Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon.

First, the act amends the 1955 statute on leasing restricted Indian lands. It adds the Warm Springs Reservation to the lands eligible for 99-year leases. It also names lands held in trust for the Tribes in that law. Second, it approves and ratifies the Long-Term Global Settlement and Compensation Agreement dated April 12, 2000. The parties are the Department of the Interior, the Tribes, and the Portland General Electric Company. Included agreements come with it. No provision of federal law is to render that agreement unenforceable or keep the Tribes from pledging or using assets paid under it.
plaw-107-103-2001:
Veterans' benefits grow across the board in the Veterans Education and Benefits Expansion Act of 2001, Public Law 107-103, approved December 27, 2001. The act amends title 38 of the United States Code. It reshapes aid for schooling, pay and pension aid, housing aid, and burial aid for veterans. It also covers job rehab aid and certain powers of the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims.

Title I raises the rates of basic schooling aid under the Montgomery GI Bill and of survivors' and dependents' schooling aid. It restores schooling aid for people being ordered to active duty. It allows sped-up Montgomery GI Bill payments for schooling that leads to work in the high technology industry. Other sections extend who qualifies among Vietnam-era veterans. They raise the yearly cap on Senior ROTC schooling aid. And they expand work-study chances.
plaw-107-104-2001:
Federal long-term care insurance receives two quiet fixes in Public Law 107-104, approved December 27, 2001, which amends chapter 90 of title 5 of the United States Code.

The first change rewrites the definition of an annuitant for the program. It covers any individual who satisfies all requirements for title to an annuity under the federal retirement systems, or another government retirement system. The person must file an application, and must be at least 18 years old. The second change is a preemption rule. No tax, fee, or other monetary payment may be imposed or collected by any state, the District of Columbia, or Puerto Rico on premiums paid for an insurance policy under the chapter. Their subdivisions are covered by the bar as well.
plaw-107-105-2001:
Health care's shift to standard electronic paperwork gained a cushion from the Administrative Simplification Compliance Act, Public Law 107-105, approved December 27, 2001. The act works to ensure that covered entities comply with the standards for electronic health care transactions and code sets adopted under part C of title XI of the Social Security Act.

Under it, a health care provider, a health plan other than a small health plan, or a health care clearinghouse can win extra time. If it submits a compliance plan to the Secretary of Health and Human Services before October 16, 2002, it will not be considered out of compliance before October 16, 2003. The plan must summarize an analysis of the filer's noncompliance and its reasons. It must include a budget, schedule, work plan, and implementation strategy. It must say whether a contractor or vendor will assist. And it must set a testing timeframe beginning not later than April 16, 2003.
plaw-107-106-2001:
Planning for a national museum begins with Public Law 107-106, approved December 28, 2001, which establishes the National Museum of African American History and Culture Plan for Action Presidential Commission. The commission exists to develop a plan of action for the establishment and maintenance of the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, D.C.

The commission consists of not more than 23 members. The President appoints seven voting members, and the Speaker of the House of Representatives and the Senate Majority Leader each appoint six voting members plus two additional nonvoting members. Members are chosen from professional groups. Those groups include professional museum associations, among them the Association of African American Museums. They also include academic institutions committed to the study of African American life, art, history, and culture, including Historically Black Colleges and Universities.
plaw-107-107-2001:
Public Law 107-107, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2002, approved December 28, 2001, authorizes appropriations for fiscal year 2002. The money covers military activities of the Department of Defense, military construction, and defense activities of the Department of Energy. It also prescribes the personnel strengths of the armed forces for that year.

As with the prior year's act, the statute is organized into three divisions: Department of Defense Authorizations, Military Construction Authorizations, and Department of Energy National Security Authorizations and Other Authorizations. Division A begins with procurement authorizations, arranged by service and activity: Army, Navy and Marine Corps, Air Force, and defense-wide activities. An early provision defines the congressional defense committees the act refers to throughout.
plaw-107-108-2001:
The intelligence budget for fiscal year 2002 is authorized by Public Law 107-108, the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2002, signed December 28, 2001. It authorizes funding for intelligence and intelligence-related activities of the United States Government, the Community Management Account, and the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I authorizes the funding under a secret schedule, so the amounts stay secret, and it codifies the Coast Guard as an element of the intelligence community. Title II funds the CIA retirement system. Title III carries general provisions. They include increases in staff pay and benefits allowed by law. They include a restriction on the conduct of intelligence activities. They include a sense of Congress on intelligence community contracting. And they include rules for lodging allowances in an intelligence community assignment benefit program.
plaw-107-11-2001:
Public Law 107-11, approved May 28, 2001, clears the legal path for building the World War II memorial in the District of Columbia, at the dedicated Rainbow Pool site. It orders the memorial constructed expeditiously.

Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the memorial shall be built in line with the special use permit the Secretary of the Interior issued on January 23, 2001. The memorial is the one described in the plans approved by the Commission of Fine Arts on July 20 and November 16, 2000. The National Capital Planning Commission selected it that September and December. The permit allows approved design modifications. Elements of design and construction not yet approved still go through the Commemorative Works Act. The choice of the Rainbow Pool site and the commissions' actions are placed beyond judicial review.
plaw-107-12-2001:
A national medal for public safety officers is created by the Public Safety Officer Medal of Valor Act of 2001, Public Law 107-12, approved May 30, 2001. The act authorizes the Public Safety Officer Medal of Valor as the highest national award for valor by a public safety officer.

After September 1, 2001, the President may award and present the medal, in the name of Congress. The medal goes to a public safety officer cited by the Attorney General. The citation follows the recommendation of the Medal of Valor Review Board. The honor is for extraordinary valor above and beyond the call of duty. The board established by the act has 11 members with knowledge or expertise in public safety. Appointments come in part from the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and from the Speaker and minority leader of the House.
plaw-107-13-2001:
Firefighting and endangered species law meet in Public Law 107-13, approved June 3, 2001. The act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior and the Secretary of Agriculture to spend money appropriated for wildland fire management on interagency work the Endangered Species Act of 1973 requires.

Using funds from the Department of the Interior and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2001, the two secretaries may reimburse two services. They are the United States Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service. The money covers their costs of consulting and conferring under section 7 of the Endangered Species Act in connection with wildland fire management. A sense of Congress says recipients should buy only American-made equipment and products with the money. Agency heads must pass that notice along. And any spending on foreign-made items must be reported to Congress within 180 days.
plaw-107-14-2001:
Survivors of veterans gain wider help from the Veterans' Survivor Benefits Improvements Act of 2001, Public Law 107-14, signed June 5, 2001. The act amends title 38 of the United States Code. It widens health coverage, gives family life insurance, and makes technical amendments.

Its opening section extends CHAMPVA to veterans' survivors who get hospital insurance under the Medicare program. The act then adds family coverage under Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance. It raises the maximum SGLI benefit, with the raise counting for members dying in the line of duty on or after October 1, 2000. Later sections expand outreach efforts to dependents. They make small fixes to the Montgomery GI Bill statute and other laws.
plaw-107-15-2001: Equal tax treatment for the families of fallen officers is the work of the Fallen Hero Survivor Benefit Fairness Act of 2001, Public Law 107-15, approved June 5, 2001. It amends section 1528 of the Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997. The change makes the rule on survivor benefits for public safety officers killed in the line of duty reach further. It also reaches amounts received in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2001, with respect to officers who died on or before December 31, 1996.
plaw-107-16-2001:
A sweeping tax cut arrives in the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, Public Law 107-16, approved June 7, 2001. Congress enacted it to provide for reconciliation under section 104 of the budget resolution for fiscal year 2002, and its amendments run almost entirely to the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

Title I reduces income tax rates for individuals and repeals both the phaseout of personal exemptions and the overall limitation on itemized deductions. Title II delivers tax benefits relating to children. It modifies the child tax credit. It expands the adoption credit and adoption assistance programs. It covers the dependent care credit, and a credit for employer expenses for child care assistance. Title III, opening as the sample ends, takes up marriage penalty relief.
plaw-107-17-2001: Chapter 12 of the bankruptcy code survives four more months under Public Law 107-17, approved June 26, 2001. The act amends the provision of a 1998 law that reenacted the chapter, as already amended by Public Laws 106-5, 106-70, and 107-8. It strikes June 1, 2001, and inserts October 1, 2001. It also rolls two related dates from 2000 into 2001. The amendments take effect on June 1, 2001, weeks before the act itself was signed.
plaw-107-18-2001: Fee money for the manufactured housing program is freed for use by Public Law 107-18, approved July 5, 2001. The act clarifies the authority of the Department of Housing and Urban Development over fees collected under the National Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Act of 1974. Such fees, including ones collected earlier and still unobligated, shall be available to offset the expenses the Secretary incurs under that act. The authority runs during fiscal year 2001 and ends when the first later appropriations act named in the statute takes effect.
plaw-107-19-2001:
The 4-H centennial receives federal seed money from Public Law 107-19, approved July 10, 2001, which authorizes funding for the National 4-H Program Centennial Initiative.

Congress found that the 4-H Program is one of the largest youth development organizations in the country. It operates in each of the 50 states and over 3,000 counties. It is promoted by the Secretary of Agriculture through the Cooperative State Research, Education, and Extension Service and land-grant colleges and universities. And it is supported by the National 4-H Council. Marking the program's centennial in 2002, the Council proposed a public-private partnership on youth development strategies for a global, technology-oriented economy. The Secretary may grant the Council the federal share, fifty percent, of the cost of national, state, and local discussions. The grant also covers a report summarizing them with recommendations and a plan of action.
plaw-107-2-2001: Boston's federal courthouse is named by Public Law 107-2, approved March 13, 2001. The United States courthouse located at 1 Courthouse Way in Boston, Massachusetts, shall be known and designated as the John Joseph Moakley United States Courthouse. Any reference to it in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to that name. The bill passed the House and Senate on consecutive days in February 2001.
plaw-107-20-2001:
Extra money for the closing months of fiscal year 2001 flows from the Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2001, Public Law 107-20, approved July 24, 2001. The act appropriates sums out of the Treasury for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2001, and Title I is headed National Security Matters, arranged in chapters by department.

Chapter 1 directs payment to the Radiation Exposure Compensation Trust Fund, of such sums as may be necessary, for approved claims for fiscal year 2001. Chapter 2 tops up military personnel accounts. It adds 164 million dollars for the Army and 84 million dollars for the Navy. Further amounts go to the Marine Corps and the other services on the same pattern.
plaw-107-21-2001:
Three honors for a late senator make up Public Law 107-21, approved July 26, 2001, an act to honor Paul D. Coverdell.

First, the headquarters offices of the Peace Corps, wherever situated, shall be referred to as the Paul D. Coverdell Peace Corps Headquarters, and past references in federal laws and records are read as pointing to that name. Second, the Peace Corps must call its schools program the Paul D. Coverdell World Wise Schools Program in every public document it produces from enactment onward. Third, the Secretary of Education shall award funds to the University of Georgia to support construction of the Paul D. Coverdell Building at the university's Institute of the Biomedical and Health Sciences, with ten million dollars authorized to be appropriated for fiscal year 2002.
plaw-107-22-2001: Education savings accounts take a senator's name in Public Law 107-22, signed July 26, 2001. The act amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to rename the education individual retirement accounts as the Coverdell education savings accounts. Section 530 is redone phrase by phrase. Each mention of an education individual retirement account becomes a Coverdell education savings account. The section's heading is changed to Coverdell Education Savings Accounts. And the table of contents entry for the section follows suit.
plaw-107-23-2001: A California federal building is designated by Public Law 107-23, approved August 3, 2001. The Federal building located at 6230 Van Nuys Boulevard in Van Nuys, California, shall be known and designated as the James C. Corman Federal Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that building is deemed a reference to the James C. Corman Federal Building. The Senate passed the bill on May 24, 2001, and the House on July 23.
plaw-107-24-2001:
Sanctions authorities are renewed by the ILSA Extension Act of 2001, Public Law 107-24, approved August 3, 2001. The act extends the authorities of the Iran and Libya Sanctions Act of 1996 until 2006.

One section tightens the Libya provisions. In section 5(b)(2) of the 1996 act, the figure of 40 million dollars is struck each place it appears and 20 million dollars is inserted. The change applies to investments made on or after June 13, 2001. The act further requires the President to transmit a report to Congress, not earlier than 24 months and not later than 30 months after enactment. The report describes how far trade actions under the act have been effective in achieving its objectives, and other foreign policy or national security objectives regarding Iran and Libya. It also describes how they have affected humanitarian interests in those and other countries, along with the impact of the actions overall.
plaw-107-25-2001:
In August 2001 Congress passed Public Law 107-25 to answer what it called a continuing economic crisis hurting American farm producers. The short act sends emergency money to farmers through the Commodity Credit Corporation, the government's farm finance agency.

Its main piece is market loss assistance. More than four and a half billion dollars goes to owners and producers under farm production contracts. Each farm's share matches its share of regular contract payments. Smaller sections add extra payments for the 2000 crops of oilseeds, peanuts, and tobacco, each topping up money those growers had already received.
plaw-107-26-2001:
Public Law 107-26, passed in August 2001, kept the Tropical Forest Conservation Act of 1998 running through fiscal year 2004. That earlier law reduces the foreign debt of developing countries as part of protecting tropical forests around the world.

The act authorizes fifty million dollars for fiscal year 2002, seventy-five million for 2003, and one hundred million for 2004 to pay for that debt reduction. It widens which countries can qualify by dropping one word from the eligibility test. It also makes the State Department's representative the chair of the Enterprise for the Americas Board. The money is authorized, not spent; spending bills still had to provide it.
plaw-107-27-2001:
