The Federal Firefighters Retirement Age Fairness Act (Public Law 107-27) fixed an uneven rule, and it passed in August 2001. Federal law set a mandatory age at which law officers had to leave service. Firefighters, whose work is just as hard on the body, were not covered by the same rule.

The act adds one word, firefighter, next to law officer in the age rule. It does so in both federal pension plans, the older Civil Service plan and the newer Federal Employees plan. The result is plain: federal firefighters now face the same forced leaving age as federal law officers.
plaw-107-28-2001: Public Law 107-28 gave land to a city. It ordered the Secretary of the Interior to hand over a former Bureau of Land Management office site. The site held about four and a half acres with some unusable buildings. It went to Carson City, Nevada, for free. The city was to use it for a senior assisted living center. If the land is ever used for something else, it goes back to the United States.
plaw-107-29-2001: Under Public Law 107-29, the United States Postal Service facility at 5927 Southwest 70th Street in Miami, Florida, carries the name Marjory Williams Scrivens Post Office. Congress approved the designation in August 2001. From then on, federal laws, maps, and records refer to that Miami facility by the Scrivens name alone. The naming follows the standard two-section form.
plaw-107-3-2001: Public Law 107-3 solved a problem created by the tied Senate of 2001. The Senate was split evenly between the parties. So the law says the Senate members of the Joint Economic Committee would be five from the majority party and five from the minority. That committee is the joint panel that studies the economy. The even split lasted only while the Senate itself stayed even, and only for the 107th Congress.
plaw-107-30-2001: Public Law 107-30 protects drinking water country in Oregon. It folds more of the Little Sandy River watershed into the Bull Run Watershed Management Unit, a special management area of about ninety-eight thousand acres. Bull Run supplies Portland's water, and the act redraws the unit's governing law so the added watershed gets the same protections as the rest.
plaw-107-31-2001: Public Law 107-31 names a courthouse. It designates the federal building and United States courthouse at 504 West Hamilton Street in Allentown, Pennsylvania, as the Edward N. Cahn Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Approved in August 2001, the law makes that name binding in every federal law, map, and record that mentions the building.
plaw-107-32-2001: Public Law 107-32 designates the Postal Service facility at 1030 South Church Street in Asheboro, North Carolina, as the W. Joe Trogdon Post Office Building. Congress approved the naming in August 2001. The law's second section makes the name binding in any federal law, map, or record that mentions the facility. The whole act runs to two sections.
plaw-107-33-2001: Public Law 107-33 gives the United States courthouse at 40 Centre Street in New York, New York, the name Thurgood Marshall United States Courthouse. Marshall was the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court. The designation was approved in August 2001, and federal references to the courthouse now use his name. The act is two sections long.
plaw-107-34-2001: Public Law 107-34 names the Postal Service facility at 113 South Main Street in Sylvania, Georgia, the G. Elliot Hagan Post Office Building. The designation became law in August 2001. Its second section makes the Hagan name the one used whenever a federal law, map, or record refers to that facility. The act is two sections long.
plaw-107-35-2001: Under Public Law 107-35, the post office at 419 Rutherford Avenue, N.E., in Roanoke, Virginia, is named the M. Caldwell Butler Post Office Building. Butler had represented the Roanoke area in Congress. The designation was approved in August 2001, and the act's references section makes the name official in federal records. The act runs to two sections in all.
plaw-107-36-2001: Public Law 107-36 designates the Postal Service facility at 2719 South Webster Street in Kokomo, Indiana, as the Elwood Haynes 'Bud' Hillis Post Office Building. The naming was approved in August 2001. Under the law's references section, federal laws, maps, and records now use that name for the Kokomo facility. The whole act runs to just two short sections.
plaw-107-37-2001:
Public Law 107-37 was passed one week after September 11, 2001, to speed help to the rescuers hurt that day. Federal law already paid benefits when a public safety officer died or was catastrophically injured in the line of duty, but the claims process had limits and steps.

This act cuts through them for the attacks. When a public agency certifies that its officer was killed or catastrophically injured in the rescue or recovery effort, the benefit is paid on an expedited basis. It was among the first laws Congress passed in response to the attacks.
plaw-107-38-2001:
Public Law 107-38 is the 2001 Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act for Recovery from and Response to Terrorist Attacks on the United States. Congress passed it on September 18, 2001, one week after the attacks, and it is built for speed rather than detail.

Its first account is an Emergency Response Fund for the President, covering emergency expenses to respond to the attacks, assistance to the victims, and dealing with the attacks' other consequences. As a supplemental appropriations act for fiscal year 2001, it put money outside the normal budget cycle so the response could begin at once.
plaw-107-39-2001:
Public Law 107-39 is the joint resolution in which Congress spoke about the September 11, 2001 attacks one week after they happened. It expresses the sense of the Senate and the House of Representatives regarding the attacks, and it carries no new spending or program.

Its opening clauses tell the story as Congress recorded it. Terrorists hijacked four civilian aircraft. Two crashed into the World Trade Center and a third into the Pentagon. Thousands of innocent Americans died, among them passengers, office workers, and rescue workers. Congress called the attacks the deadliest ever launched against the United States, aimed at symbols of American strength to weaken the nation's resolve.
plaw-107-4-2001: Public Law 107-4 fills a seat on the Smithsonian Institution's Board of Regents. It appoints Walter E. Massey of Georgia as a citizen regent, in the class of regents who are not members of Congress, for a term of six years. He filled the vacancy left when Frank A. Shrontz's term expired in May 2000.
plaw-107-40-2001:
Public Law 107-40 is the Authorization for Use of Military Force, passed on September 18, 2001, one week after the September 11 attacks. It is the legal foundation Congress gave the President to respond with the armed forces.

The resolution authorizes force against those responsible for the attacks. Its opening clauses say the attacks made it necessary for the United States to act in self-defense. They say the country had to protect its citizens at home and abroad. They also say the threat of international terrorism went on. Presidents relied on this short text for two decades of military operations.
plaw-107-41-2001:
Public Law 107-41 establishes the Brown v. Board of Education 50th Anniversary Commission. Its job is to encourage and provide for the commemoration of the fiftieth anniversary of the Supreme Court's school desegregation decision, which fell on May 17, 2004.

Congress found a national commission appropriate to plan and coordinate the anniversary. Working with the Department of Education, the commission was to plan public education activities marking the case. That case was Oliver Brown's suit against the Topeka school board. It ended legal segregation in public schools across the United States for good.
plaw-107-42-2001:
The Air Transportation Safety and System Stabilization Act (Public Law 107-42) was the airline rescue law passed eleven days after September 11, 2001. Grounded planes and frightened passengers had thrown the air transportation system into crisis, and Congress acted to preserve its continued viability.

Title I, Airline Stabilization, directs the President to compensate air carriers for losses caused by the attacks. It authorizes federal credit instruments for airlines of up to ten billion dollars in total, along with the subsidy amounts to back them. Later parts of the act address victims' compensation and aviation security.
plaw-107-43-2001:
The United States-Jordan Free Trade Area Implementation Act (Public Law 107-43) puts a trade deal into American law. It implements the agreement the United States and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan signed on October 24, 2000, establishing a free trade area between the two countries.

The act states its purposes plainly. It carries out the agreement. It strengthens economic relations between the United States and Jordan for their mutual benefit. And it establishes free trade between the two nations by removing trade barriers. Jordan was one of the first Arab states to sign such a deal with Washington.
plaw-107-44-2001: Public Law 107-44 is the first stopgap spending law for fiscal year 2002, approved September 28, 2001. Congress had not finished the regular spending bills. So this joint resolution kept the government's departments and agencies funded. It used the prior year's rules and funding levels. Stopgap laws of this kind stop a funding gap while the spending work goes on.
plaw-107-45-2001: Public Law 107-45 makes the 'S' visa permanent. S visas admit a small class of nonimmigrants, informants who help law enforcement, under the Immigration and Nationality Act. The authority had limits written into it; this short act strikes the time limit paragraph and renumbers the rest, so the admission authority no longer expires.
plaw-107-46-2001: Public Law 107-46 adjusts a condition on paying America's United Nations dues debt. Federal law tied payment of the arrears to a cap: no country could be assessed more than twenty-five percent of any U.N. peacekeeping operation's budget. This act raises that cap to twenty-eight point one five percent, loosening the condition so the arrearage payments could go forward.
plaw-107-47-2001: The Defense Production Act Amendments of 2001 (Public Law 107-47) keep a Korean War era tool alive. The Defense Production Act of 1950 lets the government direct industry in emergencies, and it was set to expire on September 30, 2001. This act strikes that date and inserts September 30, 2003, extends the funding authorization the same way, and makes technical corrections.
plaw-107-48-2001: Public Law 107-48 is a one-week extension of government funding for fiscal year 2002. It amends the continuing appropriations resolution, Public Law 107-44, by striking October 16, 2001 as the stopgap's end date and inserting October 23, 2001. Congress passed a string of these short extensions that fall while the regular spending bills were finished. Each one lasted days, not months.
plaw-107-49-2001: Public Law 107-49 names the federal building and United States courthouse at 121 West Spring Street in New Albany, Indiana, for Lee H. Hamilton, the longtime Indiana congressman. The designation, approved in October 2001, makes the Lee H. Hamilton Federal Building and United States Courthouse the building's official name in all federal references.
plaw-107-5-2001: Public Law 107-5 is Congress using its review power to kill a regulation. It is a joint resolution disapproving the Department of Labor's ergonomics rule, the workplace standard on repetitive stress injuries published in late 2000. The resolution states that Congress disapproves the rule and that it shall have no force or effect. It was an early show of the Congressional Review Act in action.
plaw-107-50-2001: The Small Business Technology Transfer Program Reauthorization Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-50) keeps a research funding program running. The program requires big federal research agencies, those with outside research budgets over one billion dollars, to spend a set share with small businesses working with research institutions. The act extends the program and its required spending amounts through fiscal year 2009.
plaw-107-51-2001: Public Law 107-51 memorializes fallen firefighters by lowering the American flag to half-staff in honor of the National Fallen Firefighters Memorial Service in Emmitsburg, Maryland. Its findings say one point two million men and women serve in American fire and emergency services. They answer over sixteen million calls a year. About one hundred of them die in the line of duty each year.
plaw-107-52-2001: Public Law 107-52 is a one-sentence joint resolution with trade consequences. Congress approves the extension of nondiscriminatory treatment to products of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. That treatment is the normal trade status once called most favored nation. The President had transmitted the proposal on June 8, 2001. It was a step in normalizing trade between the former enemies.
plaw-107-53-2001: Public Law 107-53 extends the fiscal year 2002 stopgap funding law a second time. It amends Public Law 107-44 by replacing the end date in section 107(c) with October 31, 2001. The resolution, approved October 22, kept federal agencies funded while Congress and the President finished the regular appropriations bills. The fall of 2001 saw a whole string of these short laws.
plaw-107-54-2001: Public Law 107-54 reappoints Anne d'Harnoncourt of Pennsylvania as a citizen regent of the Smithsonian Institution. Her own earlier term was expiring. This joint resolution fills the vacancy by returning her to the Board of Regents. Her new term runs six years. It took effect December 29, 2001, in accordance with the Revised Statutes.
plaw-107-55-2001: Public Law 107-55 appoints Roger W. Sant of Washington, D.C. as a citizen regent of the Smithsonian Institution for a six-year term. He filled the vacancy on the Board of Regents left by the resignation of Howard H. Baker, Jr., in the class of regents drawn from outside Congress itself.
plaw-107-56-2001:
Public Law 107-56 is the USA PATRIOT Act, passed on October 26, 2001, six weeks after the September 11 attacks. Its full title is the Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act of 2001. Its stated purpose is to deter and punish terrorist acts. It also enhances law enforcement investigatory tools.

Title I, Enhancing Domestic Security Against Terrorism, opens the act, and the table of contents runs on through surveillance, money laundering, border protection, and victims' aid. The act reshaped American security law, and its surveillance powers stayed controversial for the rest of its long life.
plaw-107-57-2001: Public Law 107-57 cleared the way for American aid to Pakistan after September 11, 2001. Law normally barred direct assistance to a country whose elected leader had been deposed by a military coup, which described Pakistan under General Musharraf. This act exempts Pakistan from those bans for fiscal year 2002 and earlier years, and authorizes presidential waivers of other aid restrictions through September 30, 2003.
plaw-107-58-2001: Public Law 107-58 is the third short extension of the fiscal year 2002 continuing appropriations law. Approved October 31, 2001, it amends Public Law 107-44 by moving the stopgap's end date to November 16, 2001. Each of these resolutions bought Congress a few more weeks to finish the year's regular spending bills. Each of these extensions lasted only a few weeks.
plaw-107-59-2001: The Great Falls Historic District Study Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-59) orders a National Park Service study of the Great Falls Historic District in Paterson, New Jersey. The study judges whether the district should be designated a unit of the National Park System. Great Falls, a large waterfall on the Passaic River, powered one of America's first planned industrial cities.
plaw-107-6-2001: Public Law 107-6 names the Postal Service facility at 620 Jacaranda Street in Lanai City, Hawaii, the Goro Hokama Post Office Building. Lanai City is the small plantation town at the center of the island of Lanai. The designation was approved in April 2001, and the usual references section makes the name binding in federal records.
plaw-107-60-2001: The William Howard Taft National Historic Site Boundary Adjustment Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-60) adjusts the boundary of President Taft's historic site in Cincinnati, Ohio. It authorizes an exchange of land connected with the site and redraws the boundary accordingly. The site preserves Taft's birthplace and his boyhood home. The law took effect in November 2001.
plaw-107-61-2001: Public Law 107-61 authorizes the Government of the Czech Republic to build a memorial in Washington, D.C. honoring Tomas G. Masaryk, the founder and first president of Czechoslovakia. The memorial goes on federal land under the Commemorative Works Act, with a few of that act's sections waived. The law is clear about cost: the United States government pays nothing for building or maintaining it.
plaw-107-62-2001:
Public Law 107-62 authorizes the Adams Memorial Foundation to build a commemorative work on federal land in Washington, D.C. honoring former President John Adams and his legacy. It is the first step in a long memorial process; a later law had to approve the site.

The findings say few families have contributed as much to the United States. The family gave the nation its second president and its sixth, John Quincy Adams. It also gave first ladies Abigail Smith Adams and Louisa Catherine Johnson Adams. They note John Adams wrote the Massachusetts constitution, the oldest written constitution still in force.
plaw-107-63-2001:
The Department of the Interior and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2002 (Public Law 107-63) funds the nation's land and resource agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002. Title I covers the Interior Department itself, starting with the Bureau of Land Management.

The Bureau's first account pays for managing lands and resources: protection, use, improvement, surveying, and maintenance of facilities. The act then works through the department's other bureaus and the related agencies. They run from the Park Service and Fish and Wildlife Service to the Forest Service. The Forest Service sits in the Agriculture Department but is funded here.
plaw-107-64-2001: The Military Construction Appropriations Act, 2002 (Public Law 107-64) funds building work for the Department of Defense for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002. It covers military construction, family housing for service members, and base realignment and closure costs. Acts in this series pass every year, paying for barracks, hangars, and homes base by base.
plaw-107-65-2001: Public Law 107-65 is the Eightmile River Wild and Scenic River Study Act of 2001. It designates a segment of Connecticut's Eightmile River for study. The study weighs adding the river to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System. Congress found the river rich in wildlife, ecological, and scenic values, with historic sites tied to America's heritage, and found strong local support for a cooperative study.
plaw-107-66-2001: Public Law 107-66 is the Energy and Water Development Appropriations Act, 2002. It is the yearly spending law for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002. It covers the Army Corps of Engineers' water projects and the Department of Energy. Title I opens with the Corps' civil works, the dams, locks, and flood control projects it builds across the country.
plaw-107-67-2001: Public Law 107-67 is the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 2002. It funds the Treasury Department and the United States Postal Service. It also funds the Executive Office of the President and several independent agencies. The money covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002. It is one of the regular annual appropriations acts that keep the government's housekeeping offices running.
plaw-107-68-2001: Public Law 107-68 is the Legislative Branch appropriations act for fiscal year 2002, the law by which Congress funds itself. Title I is the Congressional Operations Appropriations Act. It opens with the Senate's expense allowances. It then works through the costs of running the House, the Capitol, and Congress's support agencies. The year covered ends September 30, 2002.
plaw-107-69-2001: Public Law 107-69 gives the Bureau of Reclamation police power after September 11, 2001. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to issue regulations for Reclamation projects and lands. The rules maintain law and order and protect people and property. Reclamation runs the dams and reservoirs of the West. Knowingly breaking those rules brings a fine, up to six months in prison, or both.
plaw-107-7-2001: Public Law 107-7 names the Postal Service facility at 2305 Minton Road in West Melbourne, Florida, the Ronald W. Reagan Post Office of West Melbourne, Florida. The designation honoring the former president was approved in April 2001. A references section makes the Reagan name the facility's official one in federal laws, maps, and records.
plaw-107-70-2001: Public Law 107-70 is another short extension of the fiscal year 2002 stopgap funding law. Approved November 17, 2001, it amends Public Law 107-44 to move the continuing appropriations deadline to December 1, 2001. By this point Congress had passed a string of these brief resolutions to keep the government open. It bought about two more weeks. That fall, such laws came one after another.
plaw-107-71-2001:
The Aviation and Transportation Security Act (Public Law 107-71), signed November 19, 2001, is the law that federalized airport security after the September 11 attacks. It creates the Transportation Security Administration inside the Department of Transportation.

The new agency is headed by an Under Secretary of Transportation for Security, appointed by the President with the Senate's consent. The act put the federal government in charge of screening passengers and baggage at airports. It replaced the private screening companies the airlines had hired. And it anchored the airport security system that travelers still pass through today.
plaw-107-72-2001: The Need-Based Educational Aid Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-72) extends an antitrust favor for colleges. Federal law let schools that admit students without regard to wealth cooperate on financial aid methods without breaking antitrust law. That favorable treatment was set to end in 2001; this act strikes the year and inserts 2008. It also orders the Comptroller General to study the exemption's effects.
plaw-107-73-2001:
Public Law 107-73 is a long-titled spending law: the Departments of Veterans Affairs and Housing and Urban Development, and Independent Agencies Appropriations Act, 2002. It covers two cabinet departments and a group of independent agencies. The money runs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002.

Its money flows to veterans' benefits and hospitals on one side, and to housing programs and urban development on the other. The independent agencies sharing the bill include science, space, and environmental offices. Package appropriations acts like this one are how Congress funds very different missions in a single vote.
plaw-107-74-2001: Public Law 107-74 saves paperwork from the shredder. A 1995 law, the Federal Reports Elimination and Sunset Act, was about to wipe out a list of reports Congress must receive. This act lists reports that the sunset does not touch. They include reports under the Department of Energy Organization Act and the Space Act of 1958. They also include reports under the Communications Satellite Act and the National Critical Materials Act.
plaw-107-75-2001: The Internet Tax Nondiscrimination Act (Public Law 107-75) extends the ban on Internet taxes. The Internet Tax Freedom Act had placed a moratorium on new state and local taxes on Internet access and on multiple or discriminatory taxes on electronic commerce. This act strikes the old end of the moratorium and inserts November 1, 2003, keeping the ban in force two more years.
plaw-107-76-2001:
The Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2002 (Public Law 107-76) funds farm and food programs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002.

The bill pays for the Department of Agriculture's work, from farm support and rural development to food assistance. It also funds the Food and Drug Administration, which oversees food safety and medicines, and a set of related agencies. It is one of the regular yearly appropriations acts, passed in November 2001 after the usual series of stopgap extensions that fall. Congress passes a version of it every year.
plaw-107-77-2001:
Public Law 107-77 carries a long name: the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2002. It is the fiscal year 2002 spending law for three cabinet departments. It also funds the federal courts of the United States.

It funds the Commerce Department's trade and census work, the Justice Department's law enforcement, and the State Department's diplomacy, along with the judiciary and related agencies. Passed in November 2001, weeks after the September 11 attacks, it carried the yearly budgets of the very departments then standing at the center of the national response.
plaw-107-78-2001: Public Law 107-78 fights vandalism at federal power sites. It lets the Western, Southwestern, and Southeastern Power Administrations, the agencies that sell power from federal dams, run property protection programs against vandalism, theft, and destruction. The administrators may pay cash rewards to people whose information leads to the arrest and prosecution of those damaging federal property.
plaw-107-79-2001: Public Law 107-79 continues the pattern of late 2001: another joint resolution extending the fiscal year 2002 continuing appropriations law, Public Law 107-44, by changing its end date. Approved December 7, 2001, it kept federal agencies funded deeper into December while the last regular spending bills were completed and signed. The government ran on such stopgaps for months that year.
plaw-107-8-2001: Public Law 107-8 keeps family farm bankruptcy protection alive for eleven more months. Chapter 12 of the bankruptcy code, written for family farmers, was a temporary law that had to be reenacted again and again. This act, approved in May 2001, extends the period for which chapter 12 is reenacted by eleven additional months.
plaw-107-80-2001: Public Law 107-80 designates the federal building and United States courthouse at 550 West Fort Street in Boise, Idaho, as the James A. McClure Federal Building and United States Courthouse. McClure was Idaho's longtime United States senator. The naming was approved in December 2001, and the act makes it binding in federal references.
plaw-107-81-2001:
The Afghan Women and Children Relief Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-81) authorizes educational and health care assistance for the women and children of Afghanistan. Congress passed it in December 2001, as the Taliban fell, with findings about the regime it had just helped remove.

The findings say Taliban restrictions on women's place in society made it nearly impossible for Afghan women to exercise basic human rights, limiting even their freedom of expression. The act directs American help toward the education and health of the women and children those rules had shut out.
plaw-107-82-2001: Public Law 107-82 extends the Drug-Free Communities Support Program for five more years. The program funds local coalitions that fight youth drug use town by town. Congress found the youth population would grow by twenty-one percent over fifteen years, adding six and a half million young people. The act also authorizes a National Community Antidrug Coalition Institute to train and support the coalitions.
plaw-107-83-2001: Public Law 107-83 is the last of the fall 2001 stopgaps: a joint resolution amending Public Law 107-44 to move the fiscal year 2002 continuing appropriations deadline to December 21, 2001. Approved December 15, it carried the government to the edge of the holidays, by which point the regular spending bills were nearly all done. The last regular bills were finished in the weeks that followed.
plaw-107-84-2001:
Public Law 107-84 is the Muscular Dystrophy Community Assistance, Research and Education Amendments of 2001, called the MD-CARE Act for short. It amends the Public Health Service Act to provide for research on the many forms of muscular dystrophy.

The act names the forms in its first lines: Duchenne, Becker, limb girdle, congenital, facioscapulohumeral, myotonic, oculopharyngeal, distal, and Emery-Dreifuss. Its findings call Duchenne the world's most common and catastrophic genetic childhood disease, a rapidly progressive muscle weakness that almost always ends in death. The law ties research to help for the families living with these diseases.
plaw-107-85-2001: Public Law 107-85 designates the Postal Service facility at 4270 John Marr Drive in Annandale, Virginia, as the Stan Parris Post Office Building. Parris had represented Northern Virginia in Congress. The naming was approved in December 2001, and the law's references section makes it binding in federal laws, maps, and records. The act has the standard two sections.
plaw-107-86-2001: In Decatur, Georgia, the post office at 2853 Candler Road became the Earl T. Shinhoster Post Office under Public Law 107-86. Shinhoster was a civil rights leader who had worked for the NAACP. Congress approved the designation in December 2001, and federal records now use his name for the facility. The act runs to two sections, like its sisters.
plaw-107-87-2001:
The Department of Transportation and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2002 (Public Law 107-87) funds the nation's transportation system for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002. Title I covers the Department of Transportation itself, opening with the Office of the Secretary.

That first account alone provides about sixty-eight million dollars for the Secretary's office, with set amounts for the deputy secretary and the general counsel. The act then funds the department's agencies, highways, aviation, transit, and rail among them, plus the related agencies that ride along outside the department itself each year. It was signed on December 18, 2001, well into the fiscal year it funds.
plaw-107-88-2001: Public Law 107-88 redesignates the Postal Service facility at 5472 Crenshaw Boulevard in Los Angeles, California, as the Congressman Julian C. Dixon Post Office. Dixon had represented Los Angeles in the House for more than twenty years. The formal redesignation was approved in December 2001, the year after his death. The act is two sections long, no more.
plaw-107-89-2001:
Public Law 107-89 designates September 11 as Patriot Day in title 36 of the United States Code. The joint resolution, approved in December 2001, three months after the attacks, asks Americans to mark the date each year.

Its clauses recount the day. Four aircraft were hijacked. Two were flown into the World Trade Center and a third into the Pentagon. A fourth came down in southwestern Pennsylvania after passengers tried to retake it. It calls the attacks the deadliest ever against the United States and notes how the country stood united in the aftermath.
plaw-107-9-2001: The Animal Disease Risk Assessment, Prevention, and Control Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-9) creates a federal task force on animal disease. The panel pulls agencies together to stop outbreaks of mad cow disease and foot-and-mouth disease before they start. Congress found that keeping American livestock healthy is a national interest. It also found that fighting an outbreak of either disease could cost billions. Producers, distributors, and consumers would all share that cost.
plaw-107-90-2001:
The Railroad Retirement and Survivors' Improvement Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-90) modernizes how the railroad retirement system is financed and improves benefits for railroad workers and their families. Railroad workers have their own retirement system, separate from Social Security, dating back to the 1930s.

Title I expands widows' and widowers' benefits, restores the retirement age, eases the vesting requirement, and repeals the railroad retirement maximum. It also changes how the system's assets are invested, letting its trustees put the system's money to work more like other big pension funds. It was one of the last laws signed in 2001.
plaw-107-91-2001:
The Detroit River International Wildlife Refuge Establishment Act (Public Law 107-91) creates a wildlife refuge on the Detroit River in Michigan. It was the first international refuge of its kind. Canada shares the river across the water.

Congress found the Detroit River one of North America's great rivers, formed about fourteen thousand years ago as the Wisconsin Glacier retreated. The channel links the upper and lower Great Lakes and links the United States to Canada. The lower river's ecosystem, the act says, is diverse and rich and worth protecting in its own right.
plaw-107-92-2001: Public Law 107-92 names the Postal Service facility at 8588 Richmond Highway in Alexandria, Virginia, the Herb Harris Post Office Building. Harris was a Virginia congressman from the Mount Vernon area the facility serves. Approved in December 2001, the law makes his name the official one for the building in federal records. The act is two sections long.
plaw-107-93-2001: Public Law 107-93 amends the federal charter of Southeastern University of the District of Columbia, a Washington school chartered in 1937 as a YMCA university. The change concerns its board of trustees: it cleans up how trustees are chosen and elected for their terms. Current trustees keep their seats for the terms they already hold.
plaw-107-94-2001: The Veterans' Compensation Rate Amendments of 2001 (Public Law 107-94) give disabled veterans a cost-of-living raise. The law amends title 38. It raises the pay rates for veterans hurt in service. It also raises the rates paid to the survivors of such veterans when they die. Congress passes a version of this raise in most years.
plaw-107-95-2001:
The Homeless Veterans Comprehensive Assistance Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-95) pulls the scattered laws on homeless veterans into one framework. It amends title 38 to revise, improve, and consolidate the benefits and services meant for veterans with no place to live.

Its early sections set a national goal to end homelessness among veterans and state the sense of Congress on their needs and on federal agencies' responsibility. The act then consolidates the existing programs and calls for evaluating how well they work, treating homeless veterans as a problem the government should measure itself against.
plaw-107-96-2001: The District of Columbia Appropriations Act, 2002 (Public Law 107-96) is the spending law for Washington, D.C. for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002. Because Congress oversees the capital's budget, it appropriates even the District's own tax money. Its first federal payment gives seventeen million dollars for resident tuition support, helping D.C. students pay out-of-state college tuition.
plaw-107-97-2001: Public Law 107-97 is the final fiscal year 2002 continuing appropriations extension of 2001. Approved December 21, it amends Public Law 107-44 to move the stopgap deadline to January 10, 2002. With that, the government stayed funded into the new year while the last spending bills of the fall were finished. It closed out a long season of stopgap laws.
plaw-107-98-2001: Public Law 107-98 sets the date Congress comes back. The joint resolution appoints noon on Wednesday, January 23, 2002, as the start of the second regular session of the One Hundred Seventh Congress. It is housekeeping, but a law all the same, of the kind passed at the end of every first session.
plaw-107-99-2001:
The Zimbabwe Democracy and Economic Recovery Act of 2001 (Public Law 107-99) states American policy toward Zimbabwe under Robert Mugabe. It declares that the United States supports the people of Zimbabwe in their struggle for peaceful democratic change, broad-based economic growth, and restoration of the rule of law.

The act works through definitions and conditions aimed at the international financial institutions, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and their sister lenders. American support for money flowing to Zimbabwe's government was tied to democratic reform, making the act the main sanctions framework for that country for years.
plaw-2001: Private Law 107-1, approved on July 17, 2001, is a private law for the relief of Rita Mirembe Revell, also known as Margaret Rita Mirembe. The law treats her as lawfully admitted to the United States for permanent residence as of the date it passed. She must pay the required visa fees within two years. The proper number of immigrant visas for her home country is then reduced to match.
plos-pbio-0020301:
Teresa A. Venezia, Akil A. Merchant, Carlos A. Ramos, and their team profiled blood stem cells in PLOS Biology in 2004. Hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow make all blood cells. Most of the time they rest quietly, a state called quiescence, then wake to divide when blood is needed.

The authors compared gene activity in resting and dividing stem cells. Each state has a clear molecular signature. Those signatures help labs tell true stem cells from their more mature offspring, a long-standing problem. They also hint at what keeps stem cells resting safely for a lifetime. Protecting that rest may matter for both aging and leukemia.
plos-pone-0000001:
Maria Almeida, Alexandre Steiner, Luiz Branco, and co-authors probed odd behavior in very sick animals for PLOS ONE in 2006. In endotoxin shock, the body's extreme response to bacterial toxin, animals seek cold instead of warmth. That cold-seeking may help survival, but the brain circuits behind it were unclear.

The team mapped the neural substrate, the brain areas that drive the behavior during shock. Knowing which regions switch an animal from fever-like warmth seeking to cooling itself matters for understanding how the brain manages body heat in crisis. The work links a survival behavior to specific brain machinery, a step toward explaining temperature control in severe infection.
plos-pone-0000101:
Mette Lundsby Jensen, Sangeeta Dave, Maarten Schim van der Loeff, and a large team studied smallpox vaccine scars in Guinea-Bissau in PLOS ONE in 2006. Vaccinia, the virus in the smallpox vaccine, leaves a lasting scar. Adults in rural areas who bore the scar lived longer than those without it, even though smallpox itself was gone.

That survival edge hints that the vaccine trains the immune system in broader ways than its target disease. Such off-target effects are now a major field of study. A cheap sign, a visible scar, made this long term follow-up possible. The finding adds weight to the idea that live vaccines can shape general health, for better or worse, beyond their named germ.
plos-pone-0000201:
Antonin Lamazière, Fabienne Burlina, Claude Wolf, and colleagues published this biophysics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Certain bioactive peptides, short protein chains with biological effects, can reshape cell membranes without being metabolized. The authors study how these peptides make membranes form tubes and become leaky.

Membrane tubulation and permeability changes sit behind many peptide actions, from killing bacteria to delivering drugs. The authors characterize the physical process in model membranes. Understanding it helps researchers design peptides that enter cells on purpose, and avoid membrane damage where it is not wanted.
plos-pone-0000301:
Ivan Laponogov, Dennis A. Veselkov, Maninder K. Sohi, and colleagues published this structural biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Topoisomerase IV is a bacterial enzyme that untangles DNA, and quinolone antibiotics attack it. The authors solved the crystal structure of its breakage-reunion domain from Streptococcus pneumoniae, at near two-angstrom resolution for the 55-kilodalton piece.

The structure is the first for a quinolone target from a gram-positive bacterium, and it shows a closed dimer shape. Seeing the drug's target in atomic detail explains how quinolones bind and how bacteria mutate to resist them. That guides the design of antibiotics that stay ahead of resistance.
plos-pone-0000401:
Joshua M. Epstein and colleagues modeled whether limiting flights could slow a flu pandemic, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Modern flu spreads worldwide on air routes, and cutting travel is one of the few levers governments can pull early. The team used computer simulation to weigh the value of international air travel restrictions.

Models like this test how much delay restrictions buy and what that delay is worth for preparing vaccines and hospital care. The results inform pandemic planning, where decisions must be made before a real outbreak shows its speed. The study is part of a wider effort to rehearse emergencies in software so that real responses rest on tested reasoning.
plos-pone-0000501:
Duygu Balcan and colleagues analyzed the wiring diagram of yeast gene control, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In yeast, transcription factors switch genes on by binding response elements, short DNA sites near genes. The team showed that the information coded in those response elements accounts for most of the topological properties of the transcriptional regulation network.

Topology means the network's large-scale structure: which factors control many genes, which genes share controllers. If binding-site information alone explains that structure, the network's shape is written in the DNA more directly than expected. The result supports reading regulatory networks from sequence, a goal of systems biology.
plos-pone-0000601:
Karen A. Ocorr, Timothy Crawley, and Greg Gibson measured inherited differences in heart failure in fruit flies, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Genetic variation for cardiac dysfunction in Drosophila means some fly strains' hearts fail under stress while others endure, mirroring human variation in heart disease.

Flies allow large, controlled crosses that human studies cannot, so the genes behind the variation can actually be found. Heart disease genes discovered in flies have repeatedly pointed to human counterparts. The paper establishes the variation itself, the raw material every gene hunt needs first.
plos-pone-0000701:
Arndt Telschow, Matthias Flor, Yutaka Kobayashi and colleagues modeled how a bacterium can push insect populations toward splitting. Their 2007 PLOS ONE subject was Wolbachia, among the most common endosymbionts, bacteria living inside other cells, in the world. In many insects, Wolbachia causes cytoplasmic incompatibility: eggs of uninfected females fail when fertilized by infected males.

That one-way barrier is called unidirectional, and it can separate populations that meet along a mainland-island pattern. The model asks when such a barrier helps drive speciation. A microbe that blocks mating is a surprising engine of species formation, and this study maps the conditions under which it could work.
plos-pone-0000801:
Robert J. Wood, Michael D. Maynard-Smith, Victoria L. Robinson and colleagues measured the speed of a plague bacterium enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA adenine methylation plays an important role in several critical bacterial processes: mismatch repair, timing of DNA replication, and control of gene expression. Dependence of bacterial virulence on the enzyme Dam, DNA adenine methyltransferase, had raised interest in it as a drug target.

Their kinetic analysis used a hemimethylated molecular break light oligonucleotide, a DNA probe that lights up when cut. Kinetics describe how fast an enzyme works and what slows it. Precise rates are what drug designers need to build inhibitors against Yersinia pestis enzymes.
plos-pone-0000901:
Marc Naguib and Andrea Nemitz studied how early hunger marks male zebra finches for life, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Conditions in early growth shape many traits that decide how well an animal does. Most work stops at the youngest stages, but later youth may matter too.

Working with juvenile males, the pair tested how nutritional stress at that stage affects plumage ornaments, the feather displays males show. They also followed how attractive those males were as adults. Poor food in youth, it seems, leaves visible marks that persist. For females choosing mates, such marks may be honest news about a male's past.
plos-pone-0001001:
Li Chen, Prabhat Jha, Bridget Stirling and colleagues reviewed sixty-eight studies of sexual risk for HIV across Africa, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A common assumption says that as HIV epidemics mature, risky behaviors like many partners or paid sex matter less. Under that view, spread becomes general and early risk factors fade.

The team ran a systematic overview of epidemiological studies from early and advanced epidemics in sub-Saharan Africa. Systematic reviews pool many studies to answer what single sites cannot. Whether risk factors hold their force decides where prevention money should go. The review gives planners a firmer basis than assumption.
plos-pone-0001101:
Tanilu Grande, Andrea Bernasconi, Annette Erhart and colleagues trialed a malaria drug pair in the Peruvian Amazon, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Multi drug resistant falciparum malaria is a serious problem in that region. The standing first line treatment there was mefloquine plus artesunate.

Their randomised open label trial compared that standard with dihydroartemisinin plus piperaquine. A head to head trial in the place where resistance bites is the only way to know if a switch is warranted. Malaria drug policy turns on such regional trials, since resistance maps differ valley by valley. The results feed directly into Peruvian treatment guidance.
plos-pone-0001201:
Is beauty in art a matter of taste alone, or does the brain have built-in preferences? Cinzia Di Dio, Emiliano Macaluso, and Giacomo Rizzolatti used brain imaging to address that question in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They showed viewers with no training in art criticism images of Classical and Renaissance sculptures.

The study, sometimes discussed under the phrase the golden beauty, asked whether an objective, biological basis exists for the experience of beauty. Brain responses to the masterpieces were compared to responses to altered versions. The work is an early example of neuroaesthetics, the study of art through the brain.
plos-pone-0001301:
Cytotoxic T lymphocytes kill infected cells, but how fast they kill inside a living body has been hard to measure. Andrew Yates and colleagues revisited those estimates in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Recent experiments had made it possible to estimate in vivo killing rates by tracking target cells in the spleen.

The authors present several refinements to a method that quantifies killing using a dynamical model. Better estimates matter because killing rates feed into models of how infections are controlled and how vaccines work. Their refinements address biases that earlier estimates carried.
plos-pone-0001401:
Benoît Baras and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a flu shot tested in ferrets. A bird flu strain called H5N1 had spread wide and killed many of the people it infected. A shot that guards across strains was a clear need. The team tested a shot boosted with an added agent that lifts immune response.

Ferrets given the shot were then exposed to a lethal dose of H5N1. The authors report that the shot gave cross protection in this test. Ferrets are a close model for human flu. Proof in them is a key step before human trials of a pandemic shot can move ahead.
plos-pone-0001501:
Rick Bright and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a new kind of flu shot. Shots are a cheap, strong guard against seasonal and pandemic flu. Most shots are grown in eggs, which is slow in a crisis. The team built a virus like particle that bears parts of the H5N1 bird flu strain.

That particle drew immune replies that guarded across H5N1 branches. Cross branch guard is the hard test for a bird flu shot. A particle shot can be made fast without live virus or eggs. The work backs this route as a stockpile option for a future outbreak.
plos-pone-0001601:
Tamás Dolinay and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on lung harm from breathing machines. Ventilators save lives, but their stretch can wound the lung itself. A family of signal enzymes had been tied to that wound, yet its exact role was not firm. The team tested mice with and without key members of that family.

Mice that lacked one such enzyme bore the ventilator stretch far better. That names the enzyme as a driver, not a bystander, in the harm. Blocking it could let ventilators run with less self inflicted damage. The work gives intensive care a clear molecular lead.
plos-pone-0001701:
Christoph W. Michalski, Milena Maier, Mert Erkan, and their co-authors tested cannabis-like compounds on scar-forming pancreas cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Pancreatic stellate cells drive the fibrosis, or scarring, of chronic pancreatitis. Cannabinoids had been shown to ease liver fibrosis, but their effects on the pancreas and its stellate cells were unknown.

The team first checked the endocannabinoid system, the body's own cannabis-like signaling, in human chronic pancreatitis tissue. They then tested blocking and boosting it in cultured stellate cells, and report reduced markers of inflammation and fibrosis. The full text gives the tissue results and the cell experiments. The findings mark a possible drug direction for a disease with few treatments.
plos-pone-0001801:
Fiona Robinson, Richard J. Jackson, and Christopher W. J. Smith studied why a human splicing protein is hard to make in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Organisms differ widely in how often they use each synonymous codon, the alternative spellings for the same amino acid. Proteins with spellings rare in the host are made poorly, because the matching transfer RNAs are scarce. Codon content is often adjusted when making foreign proteins.

The team reports that expression of human nPTB, a regulator of RNA splicing, is limited by extreme suboptimal codon content in its own gene. The full text gives the sequence analysis and expression tests. A gene throttling itself through its own spelling is a neat case of regulation built into the code.
plos-pone-0001901:
Eli Zamir, Benjamin Geiger, and Zvi Kam built a sharper imaging method in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cells grip the world at adhesion sites, dense spots where many proteins crowd together. These spots shift fast and mix dozens of parts. Seeing who sits where, and when, calls for imaging at fine detail in both space and time.

Their method uses many colors at once to map the makeup of each adhesion site as it changes. Sorting the sites into true molecular domains shows how the parts sort themselves. Better maps of these grip points help explain how cells move, a key step in wound healing and in cancer spread.
plos-pone-0002001:
Martijn van den Heuvel, Rene Mandl, and Hilleke Hulshoff Pol grouped resting brain areas by shared activity, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Even at rest, far-apart brain regions can rise and fall in sync, forming resting-state networks. Finding those groups in scan data is often done by picking a seed area first, which biases the result.

The trio used normalized cut clustering, a method that splits a network into coherent groups without a seed. Applied to resting scans, it sorts regions into networks on the data's own terms. Unbiased maps of rest networks aid studies of how the brain is wired in health and illness.
plos-pone-0002101:
Benjamin Cowling and co-authors reported early results of a household flu trial in Hong Kong, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Data were sparse on whether non-pharmaceutical steps can reduce the spread of influenza. Face masks and hand hygiene are cheap and need no prescription, yet their real effect in homes was barely tested.

The team ran a cluster randomized trial among Hong Kong household members, testing the feasibility and efficacy of masks and hand hygiene at cutting transmission. Early findings guide whether such simple steps earn a place in flu plans beside vaccines and drugs.
plos-pone-0002201:
Todd Castoe and co-authors found signs of fast adaptation in the core energy proteins of snakes. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Big shifts in basic metabolic proteins are rare, and they are even more rarely tied to major turns in evolution. Snakes, though, rebuilt their bodies radically, losing limbs and evolving extreme feeding habits.

The team ran broad analyses on snake mitochondrial proteins, the machines that release energy in cells. They found several lines of evidence that these proteins underwent adaptive evolution. The finding suggests that even the most basic cell machinery can be reshaped when a lineage takes up a new way of life.
plos-pone-0002301:
Patrick Zeeuwen, Gys de Jongh, Diana Rodijk-Olthuis, and co-authors compared the skin defenses of psoriasis and eczema patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Both psoriasis and atopic dermatitis are chronic inflamed skin diseases. For decades both were blamed mainly on overactive T cells and their inflaming signals, a view that guided treatment.

The authors argue the skin's own host defense differs between the two diseases by genetic program. Epidermal defense proteins, the skin's built-in germ fighters, are set differently in each condition. That contrast helps explain why psoriasis patients rarely get skin infections while eczema patients often do, and it reframes both diseases.
plos-pone-0002401:
Hayashi and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Hisaki Hayashi, Tsutomu Kume, among others. Its subject is foxc Transcription Factors Directly Regulate Dll4 and Hey2 Expression by Interacting with the VEGF-Notch Signaling Pathways in Endothelial Cells. Recent studies have shown that in the developing embryo, arterial and venous identity is established by genetic mechanisms before circulation begins.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002501:
Casas and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names François Casas, Laurence Pessemesse, Stéphanie Grandemange, among others. Its subject is overexpression of the Mitochondrial T3 Receptor p43 Induces a Shift in Skeletal Muscle Fiber Types. In previous studies, we have characterized a new hormonal pathway involving a mitochondrial T3 receptor (p43) acting as a mitochondrial transcription factor.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002601:
Ohta, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Hidenobu Ohta, Shanhai Xu, Takahiro Moriya, among others. Its subject is maternal Feeding Controls Fetal Biological Clock. The daily rhythms of a fetus are widely thought to be shaped by oscillators in the mother's brain.

Those maternal rhythms are coupled to the environmental light-dark cycle. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002701:
In 2008, Angela M. Verdoni and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was defects in actin dynamics lead to an autoinflammatory condition through the upregulation of CXCL5. The catalog record names Angela M. Verdoni first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Destrin (DSTN) is a member of the ADF/cofilin family of proteins and is an important regulator of actin dynamics. A further point appears in the abstract. The primary function of destrin is to depolymerize filamentous actin into its monomeric form and promote filament severing. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002801:
In 2008, Marion Faigle and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was ATP release from vascular endothelia occurs across cx43 hemichannels and is attenuated during hypoxia. Authorship is credited in the record to Marion Faigle and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Extracellular ATP is an important signaling molecule for vascular adaptation to limited oxygen availability (hypoxia). A further point appears in the abstract. Here, we pursued the contribution of vascular endothelia to extracellular ATP release under hypoxic conditions. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002901:
Sol Efroni, Liran Carmel, Carl Schaefer and colleagues offered a new way in 2008 to judge whether a gene is on or off. They treat each gene as being in one of two states, Up or Down, based on measured activity levels. Real biology is messier, but the simple split can be useful if done with care.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors argue that a gene's state comes from stacking several transcriptional behaviors on top of each other. Their technique turns raw numbers into that call. Gene expression analysts gain a tool for sorting active from quiet genes across large datasets.
plos-pone-0003001:
Nicole Harb, Trevor Archer and Noboru Sato examined how self-renewing stem cells hold together in 2008. Embryonic stem cells grow as coherent colonies with tight cell contact. Communication between cells helps set cell identity, but the machinery of those contacts in stem cells was not fully mapped.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors identify the Rho-Rock-myosin signaling axis as the system that determines cell-cell integrity in these colonies. That axis controls tension in the cell's actin skeleton. Labs growing pluripotent stem cells can use the finding to keep colonies healthy and uniform. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003101: Fabrice Paganin, Laurent Schouler, Laurent Cuissard and colleagues reported airway and esophageal stenting in advanced esophageal cancer with pulmonary involvement in a 2008 PLOS ONE clinical article. A stent is a small tube placed to keep a blocked passage open, here in both the food pipe and the airway. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, with an abstract snippet repeating the title. The article concerns patients whose advanced cancer affects both passages, a group facing severe breathing and swallowing problems.
plos-pone-0003201:
Maninder K. Sohi and co-authors report a hard lab case in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper, on the germ that causes most community pneumonia. Streptococcus pneumoniae also causes bronchitis, meningitis and ear and sinus infections. As drug resistance rose, labs turned to new targets in the germ, among them an enzyme called topoisomerase IV.

The team grew crystals of one part of that enzyme, ParC55, and solved its shape, a slow and tricky task. Readers see the grind behind a protein map, not just the end result. Such maps help chemists design new drugs against tough germs.
plos-pone-0003301:
Katerina V. Savelieva and co-authors breed mice that make far less serotonin in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Serotonin is a nerve signal with roles in the brain and the rest of the body. Two enzymes, TPH1 and TPH2, set the pace of its making. The team used gene targeting to knock out both enzymes in mice.

The title reports serotonin fell sharply and behaviour changed in tests that respond to antidepressant drugs. Readers see what broad serotonin loss does to a mammal. The mice help test what those drug-sensitive behaviour tests truly show about mood and nerves.
plos-pone-0003401:
Madeleine J. H. van Oppen and colleagues traced coral travel in this 2008 genetics study. The coral they studied mostly settles its young near home reefs. Such local habits should keep reef groups apart and distinct. The team read DNA from coral groups spread across wide distances.

The DNA carried signs of recent travel over long distances. Some young corals had crossed the gaps between far-apart reefs. That hidden movement links reefs into one larger network. Reef protection works better when planners know how young corals move between sites. Reef rescue plans depend on links like these between far-apart sites.
plos-pone-0003501:
Ntombizodumo B. Mkwanazi and co-authors studied HIV testing in rural South Africa in this 2008 paper. Rapid tests promise same-day results for pregnant women. Faster results should raise testing uptake and improve care. The team followed a cohort of about twelve thousand women.

They compared uptake before and after rapid testing arrived. Same-day speed did not reliably improve uptake or result collection. Counselors offered testing, yet barriers beyond speed remained. Programs may need trust and access work alongside faster kits. Pregnant women are a key group for HIV care, since treatment also guards the baby.
plos-pone-0003601:
Héla Saïdi, Marie-Thérèse Melki, and Marie-Lise Gougeon studied killer cell talks with dendritic cells in this 2008 paper. HIV exploits dendritic cells to spread and to dodge antiviral immunity. The fate of those cells depends heavily on contact with natural killer cells. How that cross-talk works was the open question.

A signal called HMGB1 proved to drive key effects. Through it, NK and dendritic cell contact triggered HIV replication and persistence. Immune teamwork can thus switch the virus back on. The finding warns vaccine designers about this double-edged interaction. Dendritic cells are also the first target of many vaccine designs.
plos-pone-0003701:
Zhen Sun, Zhi Chen, Xiaoli Hou, and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Tests that detect many DNA targets at once save time, cost, and labor. They still need primers, short starter pieces, for each target. The team built primers meant to work universally instead.

Their primers are pentamers made of locked nucleic acid, chains just five units long. These short primers can start DNA copying across genomic DNA in PCR. The design gives labs a tool for amplifying many targets at once without crafting a primer set for each.
plos-pone-0003801:
Kathryn E. Hacker, Caroline Martz Lee, and W. Kimryn Rathmell published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Von Hippel-Lindau disease brings a family of blood-vessel-rich tumors, including kidney cancer. Different VHL mutations cause different mixes of these tumors. Loss of VHL normally breaks the cell's control of its oxygen sensor.

The team tested type 2B mutations of the VHL gene. Those mutations kept the VBC protein complex's form and function intact. Retained function of that kind helps explain why these mutations produce their particular spectrum of tumors rather than the full disease.
plos-pone-0003901:
Elizabeth Whittaker, Andrea Gordon, and Beate Kampmann asked whether a blood marker beats the standard TB test in children in 2008. Current blood tests for tuberculosis measure interferon-gamma release. Those tests cannot tell active disease from latent, silent infection. That gap makes diagnosis in children especially hard.

Their PLOS ONE article weighs a second marker called IP-10 against interferon-gamma. Both markers can be read from a blood sample. A marker that splits active from latent cases would change care for children. The study adds evidence toward a clearer test for a disease that hides well.
plos-pone-0004001:
Fabrice Lopez, Julien Textoris, Aurélie Bergon, and co-authors built a tool for mining gene data in 2008. Public microarray archives keep growing every year. Making that mass of data usable is a growing challenge. The archive they target is the Gene Expression Omnibus.

Their PLOS ONE article presents TranscriptomeBrowser for exploring that archive. They used a clustering method to pull out groups of co-regulated genes. Such groups reveal how genes work together across many experiments. The toolbox helps researchers reuse data that would otherwise sit idle. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004101:
Xueping Zhou, Michael R. Miller, Md Motaleb, and co-authors tested Lyme disease germ products on blood vessels in 2008. Borrelia burgdorferi is the spirochete behind Lyme disease. It causes inflammation across the body and in target tissues. Much of that inflammation is driven by the host's own response.

Their PLOS ONE article perfused single rat mesentery vessels directly. Fluid from virulent germ cultures raised vessel permeability. Leaky vessels help explain swelling and tissue damage in Lyme disease. The setup isolates secreted factors from the germs themselves. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004201:
Daijun Ling and colleagues published this Alzheimer's study in PLOS ONE in 2009. How neurons die across the brain in Alzheimer's disease is still not settled after two decades of work. The amyloid beta 42 peptide is believed to play a causative role in the disease.

The team expressed the human form of this peptide in fruit flies and followed the damage. They report that the resulting neurodegeneration runs through an injury of the autophagic-lysosomal system, the cell's waste-disposal route, and that the injury depends on age. The fly model ties a famous peptide to the failure of cellular housekeeping.
plos-pone-0004301:
Tsuyoshi Watanabe and colleagues published this circadian genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Screening the offspring of wild-caught mice, the team isolated a new circadian variant, an animal whose internal clock behaves abnormally. At first the variant kept weak, fading rhythms, and then lost rhythmicity after transfer from light-dark cycles to constant conditions.

The authors present a genetic and molecular analysis of these wild-derived arrhythmic mice. A clock gene variant caught from wild mice can reveal parts of the timing machinery that laboratory strains have lost. The variant came from Mus musculus castaneus, a wild subspecies.
plos-pone-0004401:
Lab tests guide care only if normal ranges fit the patients tested. Many African countries had no reference ranges of their own. Trials there often used ranges derived from other populations. Etienne Karita, Nzeera Ketter, Matt Price, and co-authors set out to fix that. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper gives blood test ranges for healthy adults. The ranges cover eastern and southern Africa.

The team followed standards from the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute. Their intervals cover hematology and biochemistry tests. Local ranges help trial teams judge side effects fairly. A value normal for local adults should not be flagged as harm. The work fills a long-standing gap for clinics and trials across the region.
plos-pone-0004501:
Two peptides cut from a hormone protein prompt white blood cells to take in calcium, report Dan Zhang, Peiman Shooshtarizadeh, Benoit-Joseph Laventie, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The source protein is chromogranin A, stored in the same glands that release adrenaline-like hormones under stress. Pieces of it act as antimicrobial peptides, part of the body's first-line defense.

The cells studied are neutrophils, the most common white blood cells and key fighters of infection. The peptides made calcium flow into them through a route controlled by calmodulin and an enzyme called calcium-independent phospholipase A2. Calcium entry is a classic wake-up signal for immune cells. The work shows stress hormones and infection defense are chemically linked at the source.
plos-pone-0004601:
Genes for catching sunlight are spread unevenly across the oceans, map Thomas Bibby, Yinan Zhang, and Min Chen in PLOS ONE in 2009. Photosynthetic light-harvesting proteins are the mechanism by which energy enters the marine ecosystem. The dominant photosynthetic bacteria in the open ocean are two cyanobacterial groups, Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus. They are defined by two distinct light-harvesting systems.

The authors study the biogeography of those genes: where each system thrives, and why. Light color and quality change with depth and with distance from shore, favoring different harvesters. A gene-level map of ocean photosynthesis helps predict how marine food webs will shift as oceans warm and stratify. Nearly all sea life runs on the energy these tiny cells capture.
plos-pone-0004701:
Guenter Albrecht-Buehler laid out a new way to read and map long stretches of genome DNA, in PLOS ONE in 2009. His method uses short runs of two DNA letters and the segments next to them. He reports that most of these runs share chains of a repeated four letter motif.

Segments rich in one letter were often found just before these runs. Blocks known as Alu elements also sat nearby, though not as part of the runs. A clear map of such landmarks could help readers move through huge genomes. It treats DNA layout itself as a guide, not just the genes.
plos-pone-0004801:
Elizabeth Gaskell and colleagues described a unique dual activity amino acid hydroxylase in Toxoplasma gondii, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The genome of this protozoan parasite contains two genes encoding tyrosine hydroxylase, an enzyme that produces L-DOPA. The encoded enzymes metabolize phenylalanine as well as tyrosine, with substrate preference for tyrosine in lab tests of their catalytic activity.

Thus the enzymes catabolize phenylalanine by hydroxylation as a second activity. Dual activity is unusual for this enzyme family. The finding matters because Toxoplasma alters host behavior and brain chemistry. Its own dopamine pathway may help to those effects. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004901:
Ariel Cohen and colleagues studied protein dynamics in single human cells combining test and theory, in PLOS ONE in 2009. A current challenge is knowledge dynamics of protein circuits in living human cells. The team addressed whether equations define dynamics and variability of a protein over time. Using accurate time lapse measurements of glowing proteins in single cells tracked for many generations under controlled conditions.

Protein levels fluctuate with surprisingly simple rules. Cell to cell variability follows predictable distributions. Theory and test converge quantitatively. Single cell biology becomes predictive science. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0005001:
Blood platelets have no nucleus. Yet they carry a surprising variety of proteins. Karen Power and colleagues screened them at large scale in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used high-throughput proteomics. The target was alternative splicing. Splicing lets one gene produce several protein versions, called isoforms.

The screen detected novel splice isoforms in human platelets. These tiny cell fragments run a richer protein program than assumed. The catalog is a resource for platelet research. It may also matter for clotting disorders. Platelets are central to both healing and heart attacks. Knowing their full protein set sharpens both fields.
plos-pone-0005101:
The cerebellum coordinates movement and more. Its circuits were hard to trace in living people. Cristina Granziera and colleagues imaged them directly in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used diffusion spectrum imaging. That method follows water movement along nerve fibers. It reveals the wiring of the human cerebellum in vivo.

The structural wiring matched the functional circuits. That match gives the images real meaning. Many diseases, congenital and acquired, alter cerebellar function. A structural map can become a biomarker for them. Doctors could spot circuit damage before symptoms worsen. The work brings cerebellar diagnosis closer to the circuit level. It also validates the imaging method against known anatomy.
plos-pone-0005201:
Hearing depends on tiny bristles, called stereocilia, that project from hair cells in the inner ear. Those bundles move on their own and feed energy into sound sensing, which sharpens hearing. Breneman and colleagues proposed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that the bundles work as flexoelectric motors.

Flexoelectric materials turn bending into electric charge, and charge into force. The study argues this effect powers the bundle motor whose mechanism had been unknown. If right, the idea explains how the ear reaches its striking sensitivity, and it may guide designs for better hearing devices.
plos-pone-0005301:
Coenzyme Q is a fat-soluble antioxidant made inside mitochondria by a set of COQ gene products. It helps cells survive stress, including chemotherapy. Brea-Calvo and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 what switches that production up when cells are under attack.

Survival depended on the NF-kB signal raising transcription of the coenzyme Q building pathway. Cells that could not mount that rise died more easily under treatment. For cancer therapy, the circuit is a shield worth targeting, since blocking it could make chemotherapy hit harder. A shield that helps a cell live through drug stress can help a tumor live too, so this path cuts both ways. Must be read with care in each case.
plos-pone-0005401:
Non-small cell lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in Western countries, largely because it spreads. The biology behind that metastatic capacity is not well understood. Gibbons and colleagues derived gene expression signatures of spreading in a mouse model in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The genetic mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma let the team compare tumors by their ability to metastasize. Expression signatures separated high-spreading tumors from low-spreading ones. Such signatures may forecast patient risk and reveal the pathways a tumor uses to travel. A mouse tumor with a known gene flaw is a clean test bed, since spread can be timed and checked. And a gene mark found there can then be sought in the tumors of men and women.
plos-pone-0005501:
Kyoung-Jae Won and colleagues built a method to find gene control regions in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Finding where control proteins bind on human DNA from the code alone is hard. Binding sites do tend to be kept similar across species, which gives one clue.

The authors combined that clue with other signs to pick out whole control modules, not just single sites. Modules are clusters of sites that work together to switch a gene on in the right tissue. Better maps of these modules help explain how genes are timed and why some changes cause disease.
plos-pone-0005601:
Elizabeth Long, Brandie Millen, and Paul Kubes compared immune triggers from bacteria in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Sensors called Toll-like receptors spot patterns that betray invading microbes. Several bacterial parts trigger one sensor, TLR2, but they plug into it in slightly different ways.

The team compared a cell wall part, lipoteichoic acid, with other TLR2 triggers. The responses it caused were distinct from the rest, not just weaker or stronger. Distinct responses mean the immune system can tell bacterial parts apart in finer detail than a simple alarm model suggests. The study also shows that one sensor can send more than one kind of message, a point drug makers must keep in mind.
plos-pone-0005701:
Anna Sandebring and co-authors studied in 2009 what goes wrong inside cells that lack a working PINK1 gene. Faults in PINK1 cause a form of Parkinson's disease that runs in families. Earlier work showed PINK1 affects both the health and the shape of mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

The team linked the shape changes to a protein called Drp1, which helps split mitochondria. A second protein, calcineurin, controls Drp1 by removing chemical tags from it. When PINK1 is missing, that control shifts and mitochondria suffer. The chain gives drug hunters new points where they might step in.
plos-pone-0005801:
Reginia Yan and co-authors measured finger length ratios across twenty inbred mouse strains in 2009. The ratio of the second to fourth finger differs by sex in many species, lower in males than females. In humans it is thought to reflect hormone exposure before birth.

Mouse strains offer a controlled way to test how much of the ratio is genetic. The team found real differences between strains, showing the trait can be mapped and bred. That opens lab studies of what the ratio truly signals. Human claims about finger ratios often outrun the evidence; mouse genetics can supply firmer ground.
plos-pone-0005901:
Jeffrey Lozier and Nicholas Mills combined habitat models with gene-flow analysis in 2009 to read the recent history of a parasitoid wasp. The wasp attacks aphids across a wide range around the Mediterranean. Its populations may have split apart in separate refuges.

Climate-based niche models pointed to where the wasp could live in the past. Genetic data on gene flow matched a pattern of recent isolation in those separate pockets. Two independent tools agreeing strengthens the story. Such wasps are used in pest control, so their population structure guides releases.
plos-pone-0006001:
Insects change form as they grow, guided by two hormones working in concert. Denisa Liszeková, Maja Polakovičová, Milan Beňo and colleagues focused on one of them, juvenile hormone, in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses a modeling method called 3D QSAR in the fruit fly Drosophila to ask which features of a molecule drive the hormone's action.

A shape-and-activity map of this kind shows which parts of a molecule matter and which can change. Such maps guide the design of compounds that mimic or block the hormone. Since pests also run on juvenile hormone, the work has a practical edge: it can inform insecticides that break a pest's growth while sparing other life.
plos-pone-0006101:
A light receptor is useless if it never reaches the cell's light-catching surface. Ines Kock, Natalia Bulgakova, Elisabeth Knust and colleagues mapped the address label on the fly's rhodopsin in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper targets Drosophila rhodopsin, the receptor at the heart of fly vision and eye development, and tests which of its parts guide its trafficking.

Helix 8, a short segment inside the cell, is required for correct targeting, while the far tail tip is not, the title reports. Human rhodopsin mutations in the same region cause blindness, so the fly map has direct medical echoes. The result sorts the receptor's true address label from dispensable parts.
plos-pone-0006201:
Jumping genes called transposons cut themselves out of one DNA spot and paste into another. Julien Bischerour and Ronald Chalmers studied the bacterial transposon Tn10 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Its cutting enzyme uses one active site for both DNA strands, bending the DNA into a hairpin shape along the way.
