Strip-shaped lesions lined up with the brain's fibre direction far more often than the other types, and their diffusion readings sat between the dot-like and merging groups. Fibre tracking confirmed the alignment. The authors read this as a signature of slow nerve-fibre damage from neurodegeneration, distinct from ordinary vessel wear.
plos-pone-0354601:
Nakajima and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test a whole-body MRI method for staging high-risk prostate cancer. Before treatment, doctors must know whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes or bones. Standard checks use CT scans and bone scans, which involve radiation. The MRI method suppresses background signals so spread lights up, and uses no radiation at all.

Thirty-eight men with newly diagnosed high-risk cancer had all three scans before treatment. For lymph node spread, the MRI matched CT exactly in catching cases and avoiding false alarms. For bone spread, a bone scan caught every case, while the MRI missed one in nine, though it raised no false alarms. For lung spread, chest CT saw all cases and the MRI missed one of three. The authors call the MRI acceptable overall and attractive for sparing radiation, while noting chest CT still earns its place.
plos-pone-0354701:
Syed F Javaid led a team of seven authors on this 2026 survey study of anxiety before surgery at their institute. Patients awaiting operations between late 2023 and early 2024 completed a standard anxiety scale, and the team examined how counseling about surgery and anesthesia, and the surgical technique planned, related to worry.

About two in five patients showed strong preoperative anxiety. Being female, younger, and employment details mattered, as did how counseling was delivered and which technique and anesthesia were planned. Searching the internet, notably, did not move anxiety. Javaid suggests targeting counseling to calm the patients most at risk.
plos-pone-0354801:
Katie Ridsdale and co-authors set out in 2026 a multicentre trial on whether toddlers with a common spiral shin fracture need a cast or boot at all. These stable fractures follow minor falls in children from about nine months to four years, and practice varies because both approaches seem safe. The trial will assign children at random to immobilisation or none.

The main measure is parent rated pain a week later, tested against a small allowed difference. Later checks cover pain, hospital visits, pressure sores, fracture shift, movement recovery, painkillers, costs, and family satisfaction. Families helped design the study, which aims to give clinics firm guidance.
plos-pone-0355101:
Omaymah Abulannaz and colleagues study in 2026 whether prescribed opioid exposure before birth links to how ready children are for school in Manitoba, Canada. Health records matched exposed children with similar unexposed peers, and teachers rated development at kindergarten across five areas. A separate comparison looked within families, between siblings where only one was exposed.

In the matched group, exposed children were more often rated vulnerable in every area, with higher risk when exposure came early, lasted longer, or used higher doses. Within families, the sibling gap vanished. The authors read that contrast as a sign that family circumstances, not the drug alone, may drive much of the link.
plos-pone-0355201:
Phongthana Pasookhush led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of drug-response genes in Thailand. They profiled several thousand Thai adults with a gene chip, covering eleven genes known to change how people handle common medicines, then linked the results to hospital prescription records.

Nearly everyone tested carried at least one gene result that could change prescribing. Stomach acid drugs and cholesterol drugs were the most common exposures, and many users had matching gene findings. Pasookhush argues that testing patients before prescribing, starting with those two drug pairs, would bring the largest early benefit in Thai hospitals.
plos-pone-0355301:
Asma Al Rwaily contributes a pure mathematics paper. It defines and studies a new family of operators on Hilbert spaces. Those abstract spaces are used across quantum theory and analysis. Operators are machines that transform such spaces, and named families help mathematicians sort their behavior. The new family is defined by an equation in which a repeated difference-like map, modified by a polynomial, must cancel out.

Within the paper, Al Rwaily proves basic facts about the family. She checks how it behaves under common operations. She also maps its links to better-known families, such as operators that preserve length in a broad sense. The work is theoretical, with no experiments or data. Its value lies in unifying scattered results and giving later researchers a cleaner framework for operator theory.
plos-pone-0355401:
Songyining Ding and co-authors analysed safety reports for heart assist devices used in children. Children's anatomy and blood clotting differ from adults', so adult device data cannot simply be borrowed. Their 2026 study pulled a decade of reports from the United States device reporting database and compared child and adult patterns.

Child reports numbered only a few hundred, against well over a thousand adult reports, and key fields were often missing. Because of those gaps, true complication rates cannot be calculated from the database. Ding and colleagues expose regulatory blind spots and call for a dedicated children's registry with live, multi-source monitoring to catch device risks earlier.
plos-pone-0355601:
Yasser Mohammad Al-Sharo and co-authors present a federated intrusion detector for networks of medical devices that learns without gathering private data. Hospitals cannot pool patient-linked traffic, yet shared learning catches more attack types. Heavy transformer models detect well but cost too much for small devices. Their 2026 design swaps them for state-space sequence blocks with linear cost.

Traffic features are reshaped into short token sequences for the stacked blocks. Formal privacy noise is added during training, and the merging step resists sabotage by rogue participants. Explanation tools operate at several levels so analysts can audit alerts. Al-Sharo and colleagues aim to square accuracy, privacy guarantees, and robustness in one framework.
plos-pone-0356001:
Maarten Niemantsverdriet and colleagues tested a tissue preserving method that avoids formalin, the toxic chemical standard in pathology labs. Their 2026 study used pressurised carbon dioxide to embed tissues without formalin or xylene. They then checked DNA and RNA quality in samples stored for days, two years, and seven years.

DNA from the new method was in better shape than DNA from formalin-fixed tissue. RNA quality was lower in fresher and two-year samples, but similar in the oldest ones. Even so, RNA from most samples still worked for gene sequencing, the main modern test. The results support a safer embedding route that keeps tissue usable for molecular diagnosis.
plos-pone-0356201:
Wajid Ullah, Fawad Khan, and Laila Al-Essa compare symmetry methods in general relativity in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper. General relativity describes gravity as curved spacetime shaped by matter and energy. Homothetic symmetries are scaling symmetries of a spacetime, and matter collineations are symmetries of its energy-momentum tensor, the object describing matter content.

The study works through static, plane-symmetric spacetimes using three written forms of that tensor. For non-degenerate cases, meaning tensors of full rank, one form gave finite symmetry algebras of several sizes, while the mixed form consistently gave infinite-dimensional ones. Degenerate cases gave infinite results for both forms checked. The three approaches, the authors show, do not agree, so representation choice matters.
plos-pone-0356501:
Xylena Reed and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE asking whether aging leaves a permanent mark on cells that have been reprogrammed back to stem cells. DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA, accumulates age patterns so reliably that scientists use them as aging clocks. The team took blood cells from nearly one hundred healthy adults, reprogrammed them into induced pluripotent stem cells, and compared methylation in both states.

After reprogramming, the age-related signature was largely wiped away: epigenetic clocks read the stem cells as young regardless of donor age. Each cell type also carried its own set of sites where genetic variants influenced methylation, meaning the genetic control map changes with cell state. The reset, they say, supports using donor stem cells to model disease without donor age confounding results, though such cells cannot preserve what aging did to the original tissue.
plos-pone-0356601:
Hongjuan Bai and seven colleagues scan the brains of teenagers with depression, comparing those who injure themselves with those who do not, in this 2026 study. Non-suicidal self-injury is common in this group and poorly understood at the brain level. Just over one hundred thirty adolescents, including healthy controls, lay in a scanner at rest while researchers measured spontaneous activity across brain regions.

Teenagers who self-injured showed stronger activity in a region called the left precuneus, which sits toward the back of the brain and supports self-related thought. That activity, and the region's connection to a nearby visual area, tracked closely with self-injury behavior and with the urge to escape bad feelings. Prediction checks held up well, suggesting these measures could become markers to identify at-risk teenagers and targets for more precise treatment.
plos-pone-0356801:
Alon Tomashin, Ilanit Gordon, and Sebastian Wallot studied how heart signals couple over time, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Hearts do not beat in isolation; patterns in one signal relate to patterns in another, whether within a person or between people. Two analysis tools dominate this work, and the team compared them directly.

Tomashin and his colleagues evaluated multi-dimensional recurrence analysis against cross-correlation, weighing the analytic choices each demands. Their comparison guides researchers toward the right tool for their question, and warns where choices change the answer. Subtle heart coupling is used in studies of stress, bonding, and health, so method care is not a nicety; it decides what findings can be trusted.
plos-pone-0357101:
Zhongqiu Zhang and colleagues tested whether a pharmacist-led cleanup of stroke patients' drug lists could cut waste without slowing recovery. Their 2026 study ran at a Chinese hospital. It covered 416 people with acute ischemic stroke. Care before the change was compared with care after it. The new strategy capped extra brain-related drugs and traditional Chinese medicines. Pharmacists monitored and adjusted each list.

Patients under the strategy received far fewer add-on drugs. They also spent much less on medication and hospital care overall. Their neurological recovery matched the earlier group. Harmful drug events became less common. The results make a practical case that more medicine is not better medicine after stroke. They also show that pharmacists can safely trim crowded prescriptions.
plos-pone-0357301:
Fuchao Xu, Ao Liu, Zhen Liu, and Zinan Fang published a 2026 materials study in PLOS ONE on concrete made from red mud, the caustic waste of aluminum production. The study tests its survival under sulfate attack. Sulfate-rich wetting and drying cycles crack ordinary concrete over time. They added two short fibers, a synthetic polymer fiber and basalt fiber, alone and blended, then cycled the concrete through sulfate baths and examined strength, pores, and microstructure.

Basalt fiber helped more than the polymer fiber on its own, but a specific blend of the two performed best, keeping most of the concrete's sulfate resistance after sixty cycles. Under the microscope, fibers bridged and delayed cracks, gave corrosion products room without bursting the structure, and tightened the pore network. The blend also slowed breakdown of the glue-like gel holding concrete together, pointing to a tougher use for a usually stockpiled waste.
plos-pone-0357501:
Leonie Bourauel and fellow eye surgeons compare a tiny drainage implant for glaucoma across two forms of the disease. The implant lowers eye pressure by giving fluid a new exit, and the team matched patients with the common open-angle form against patients with a flaking form that clogs drainage further. Success was judged at several pressure targets one year after surgery.

Both groups reached far lower pressure than before surgery, but the common form did better on nearly every measure. Its patients needed fewer pressure drops afterward and hit strict targets more often. The flaking form brought more complications and follow-up procedures, though none threatened sight. Bourauel and colleagues support the implant for both forms while warning clinics to watch flaking cases closer.
plos-pone-0357601:
Jinyan Zhang led a team of five authors testing plant extracts against a stubborn fungus, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Malassezia furfur, a yeast linked to dandruff and skin disease, forms biofilms that resist standard treatment. The team tested combined extracts of Angelica dahurica and Ligusticum sinense, two plants used in traditional medicine.

Zhang's group measured how well the extracts inhibit the fungus and its biofilms, and checked their safety. A natural option that works on biofilms could reduce reliance on harsh antifungal chemicals. Biofilm testing matters because microbes in biofilms can survive doses that kill them when free-floating. The study gives product developers and clinicians a careful first look at a traditional pairing.
plos-pone-0357901:
Guanyi Liu, Xuewei Li, and Rui Yang published a 2026 safety study in PLOS ONE on finding the few risk factors that matter most in railway accidents. Modern rail operations are so interconnected that traditional checklists miss how causes chain together. From more than one hundred sixty accident reports, the team extracted risk factors and their causal links, building a directed, weighted network of how one failure triggers the next.

The resulting network had the hub-heavy shape of a scale-free network, where a few nodes matter enormously. Using a combined weighting and ranking method to score node importance. They then simulated attacks that knock out key nodes in different orders. The network stayed robust, and their score identified critical nodes better than standard measures. The practical claim is targeted: fix the highest-scoring risk factors first, and accident chains lose their favorite starting points.
plos-pone-0358701:
Song Jin and three colleagues trace how institutions shape China's energy deals with neighboring countries, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their account runs in two stages: officials form choices about cooperation, and those choices then steer actual energy trade and investment. To test whether choices truly carry the influence of the formal framework, they built a Bayesian model, a statistical approach that handles tangled paths between variables while stating uncertainty honestly.

The estimates supported the chain. Policy choices carried a real share of the influence running from formal frameworks to cooperation outcomes. The indirect effect was clearly positive. The authors also ran example analyses showing how this mediation approach behaves under differing data conditions, a methods contribution in its own right. For policy analysts, the message is that formal rules matter partly by moving the choices of the people who apply them.
plos-pone-0359001: de Oliveira and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the personal cost of devotion to teaching. Based in schools, the study followed teachers over time with number-based methods. It tracked their habits and quality of life. Teaching is often praised as a calling, yet that praise can hide strain. Long-term data can show schools where support would protect both staff and students.
plos-pone-0359101:
Wang Hang and six colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on electric power safety. When extreme weather hits, a power system must keep supply and demand in balance or risk blackouts. The authors present a fast method for judging that risk before and during severe conditions.

Their approach uses deep reinforcement learning, software that learns decisions by trial and feedback, combined with a coupled attention mechanism that weighs which signals matter. Speed is the point: operators need risk answers quickly when storms strain the grid. Grid planners in regions facing harsher weather are the natural readers of this work.
plos-pone-0359301: Afassinou and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on heavy social media use among college students. They built a math model of how too much time on these platforms may drag down study results. A model lets them test how the parts link up before real-world trials. The work speaks to schools weighing phone rules, study support, and guidance on screen habits.
plos-pone-0360301:
Ezgi Şişman and colleagues surveyed clinical nurses in Türkiye in 2026 about sexual prejudice and the factors associated with it. Nurses care for patients of every background, and prejudice from a caregiver can quietly shape the quality and kindness of that care. Their cross-sectional study measured attitudes among working clinical nurses and tested which personal and professional factors tracked with stronger prejudice.

Studies like this give nursing schools and hospitals a factual starting point for training, rather than assumptions. If factors such as education or contact with diverse patients matter, programs can be designed around them. The work adds Turkish evidence to the wider effort to make health care welcoming to lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients.
pmc-10656501:
Xiaochen Wang and three colleagues published a theory study in two thousand twenty-three on imitation and cooperation in networks. Animals and people copy others, but how much self knowledge and outside knowledge they use varies. Past work disagreed on which copying style helps cooperation win.

The authors built one general model that contains the classic copying rules as special cases. Under one-to-one contests, ignoring personal information helped cooperation most. When personal information counted, more outside information helped cooperators. In group contests on loosely clustered networks, the recipe flipped: more personal and less external information worked better. The unifying view explains the clash by the pace and reach of competition each rule creates.
pmc-10669801:
Qi Duan and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-three study testing whether walking patterns can help flag Alzheimer's disease. Gait changes accompany the disease but are rarely used diagnostically. The team broke walking into statistical domains.

Forty-one patients and the same number of healthy peers walked freely and while counting backwards. A sensor system captured detailed gait measures. Factor analysis grouped them into rhythm, pace, and variability domains. Pace linked to the disease in both walking tasks. Variability linked only during the counting task. The domains may serve as an auxiliary diagnostic index alongside standard testing.
pmc-10675001: Andres Carrillo and Maria Vliora introduce a short piece on how fat tissue responds metabolically to eating, published in two thousand twenty-three in a nutrition journal context. Their opening point is simple: the quality and quantity of food we consume strongly shape general health and longevity. Adipose tissue, long treated as passive storage, is the metabolic actor at the center of their topic. The piece frames food intake as a signal that fat tissue answers with hormonal and metabolic adjustments.
pmc-10691101:
Yunheng Han and Erin Molloy present a 2023 theory study on rebuilding the family trees of cancer cells. A tumor's history helps explain how it grows and resists treatment. But single-cell data are sparse and full of errors, and tumor trees are often unresolved. Classic tree-building methods assume clean data, so they can mislead here.

The authors study quartets, small four-cell trees, as building blocks. Under a standard model of tumor growth with unbiased errors and missing values, they prove a key fact. The most likely quartet correctly names the true relationship among four cells. They then prove that a tree chosen to match the most quartets gives a trustworthy estimate of the whole lineage. The result holds even when the true tree is highly unresolved. Their work lays groundwork for quartet-based tools in cancer studies.
pmc-10702401:
Arsalan Salari and colleagues report a severe reaction to misoprostol during a medical abortion. Their case report from twenty twenty-three involves a young woman in early pregnancy. The fetus had a swelling condition found before the procedure. Misoprostol is usually considered a safe, standard drug.

Hours after the final doses, her fingers bent and darkened. Her heart raced and oxygen levels fell sharply. The miscarriage itself completed successfully during the event. Heart imaging afterwards showed normal pumping function. The reaction pattern was unusual for this widely used drug. Clinicians are reminded to watch for rare systemic responses. Case reports keep rare drug harms visible to prescribers.
pmc-10703901:
Zenghui Teng and five co-authors show how a tail shard of a cell-grip protein slows vesicle take-back and so worsens a brain-waste harm. Their study is from two thousand twenty-three.

The waste clumps of the mind ill are held to drive its early harm to cell links. The shard, cut from a grip protein of those links, was known to lift that harm. The team asks how. They watch vesicle out-and-in flow at mouse brain cell links, by a glow tag. Yard drugs lift the shard's count. The find: the shard drags the take-back step, the cell's reclaim of spent sacs. That drag is the path by which the harm grows.
pmc-10704101:
Nurul Amin Rani and a large team of co-authors describe computer based vaccine design work from twenty twenty-three. Their target is varicella zoster virus, which causes chickenpox and later shingles. Current vaccines help, but cover is incomplete and shingles can still return in older or weak patients.

The team used bioinformatics tools to pick six viral coat proteins that matter for infection. They mapped short parts that immune cells can learn to attack. They then built a single multi part vaccine design on paper and in models, with added boosters to make it stronger. The work is a design study, meant to guide later lab tests.
pmc-10710401:
Jeremiah Minich leads a team on saving field samples for genome work. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with preservation methods. Poor storage degrades DNA and blocks good genomes.

Storage fluids, temperatures, and times were compared head to head. Fish and plant species from the field were used. Ethanol guarded fish blood well for weeks at room heat. Plant tissue kept well cold for a few weeks. Genomes built from the oldest samples met project standards. Methylation rates were checked against frozen controls. Remote sampling may no longer need deep freezing.
pmc-10719301:
Xiang-Yuan Ao, Tze San Ong, Roberto Aprile, and Assunta Di Vaio study how new environmental laws shift firms toward green behavior and tax planning in China. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. Communities press firms to act sustainably, and law is one lever.

The team examined the link between firms' green measures and their tax avoidance, an outcome tied to profit choices. Two forces were tested as moderators: how uncertain the environment feels and how far digital tools have spread in the firm. Findings are offered as insight into how green steps connect with business outcomes and finance. The authors stress that green production supports resilient communities and economies, not just compliance with new rules.
pmc-10722301:
Dries Vandeweyer and co-authors map the bacterial groups in the gut of black soldier fly larvae raised on waste streams from industry. Their 2023 study tracks how gut microbes shift along the tract, and how they shift with diet.

The larvae were raised on swill, and on distiller's dried grains with solubles. Both are low-value residual streams. With gene sequencing, the team set substrates, whole larvae, waste left from rearing, and parts of the gut side by side. Both the substrate and the stage of growth shaped the bacterial mix in whole larvae. The work deals with how gut microbes help these insects turn mixed waste into biomass of value. It also deals with why some microbial genera stay put across unlike diets.
pmc-10735901:
Juh Shin and three co-authors test three kinds of regression on nursing home data. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. The goal was to find what links to pressure ulcers among residents. Data came from fifty-one nursing homes over two years. The team weighed thirty-five factors about staffing and how each home is run.

The three methods gave different answers. The Poisson model found that high turnover among nurse aides went with many more ulcers. The linear model found no clear factors at all. The logistic model pointed to residents who depend fully on staff for daily tasks. The authors show how each model reads the data, and why method choice changes the story. Count data, they argue, needs methods built for counts.
pmc-10737201:
Laura Donorfio reflects on how her own aging has changed her work as a professor of gerontology. She describes four unplanned stages in her career: content and logistics, confidence and innovation, generativity and meaning, and a fourth stage she calls being the other. In that stage, she is living the subject matter she teaches.

Donorfio explains that personal aging brought greater empathy, sensitivity, and social awareness to her teaching. She also questions whether her earlier teaching was authentic or quietly ageist. Drawing on existing literature, she argues that gerontologists and geriatricians should use this insight to advance the field and train the next generation.
pmc-10744901:
Zhiwei He, Xin Lan, Lezhou Li, and Yong Cheng use atom-level computer models to watch how atoms drift across a solder joint boundary under heat and electric current. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. As devices pack more power, solder joints face high currents that can push atoms out of place and threaten reliability.

The boundary studied sits between copper and a copper-tin compound. Stronger electric fields lowered the energy needed for atoms to move, so drift sped up. Empty spots left by moved atoms built up, and their growth lagged behind the atom motion, showing the field drives them. Atoms near the boundary broke free of their neighbors more easily under the field. The team proposes a vacancy-driven picture of the drift, useful for designing tougher joints.
pmc-10745501:
Ericka Mochan and four co-authors review how math models explain a synergy. A second pathogen caught alongside influenza can kill, when neither infection alone would. Coinfections with bacteria or other viruses raise the death toll from flu. But the share of each partner is hard to isolate in tests. Timing, order, and dose all blur the picture. Putative mechanisms include cytokine dysregulation, hobbled immune cells, failed mucus clearance, and a damaged airway lining.

Models let researchers measure immune dynamics inside a host. Tests cannot measure those dynamics. The review surveys models of flu paired with bacterial and viral partners. It sets out the insights each model produced. It closes on challenges and open gaps. It frames modeling as the tool for ranking which synergy mechanisms matter most. That ranking can guide which lab tests to run next, and which treatments to try first in coinfected patients.
pmc-10746401:
Sahar Afshar and colleagues test wrist acupressure for nausea after heart attack. Their randomised trial from twenty twenty-three uses the P6 wrist point. Nausea and vomiting trouble many heart attack patients. Some still feel sick despite standard anti-nausea drugs.

Ninety such patients split into three groups. One group wore wristbands pressing the P6 point. A placebo group wore similar bands without the pressing button. The control group received no wristband at all. Nausea severity, comfort, and vomiting episodes were tracked over a day. The acupressure group reported clearly lower symptoms than both other groups. Drug use for nausea was also recorded for comparison.
pmc-10749901:
La Ode Mohammad Firman and three co-workers built a low cost tool to gauge how much heat a phase change stuff can store. Such stuff banks heat as it melts. To size a store tank, staff must know its full heat store. That store is hard to gauge, since traits shift with heat and with phase. Stock calls, based on melt heat on its own, make charge marks wrong. The 2023 work brings a mixed force and heat way in its place.

The kit uses parts that are plain to find and cheap, which peers can tune. It calls full store and plain heat gains as one, from a force sum at each heat step. Checks set its scores next to guide ways. A sound cheap tool counts for small sun and waste heat store work. It counts most where trade heat gauges sit past reach.
pmc-10752001:
Lieguang Chen and a team including Guifang Ouyang test a machine learning method to spot fungal lung infections in blood cancer patients from CT scans. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. These infections are a dangerous side problem of blood cancers and their treatment.

One hundred patients with the infection formed the training set, and eighty more formed the test set. Aspergillus was the most common fungus, followed by Candida and three rarer types. The team pulled measured features from the scans and joined them with clinical facts to train a support vector machine. The model learned the scan patterns of the infection. Such a tool could speed diagnosis where the signs on scans overlap with other lung disease.
pmc-10768501:
Silvia Cocca and colleagues described in 2023 how to recognize and treat two rare but dangerous complications of a standard liver cancer procedure. Trans-arterial chemoembolization, or TACE, starves unresectable liver tumors by blocking their blood supply while delivering chemotherapy. Most side effects are mild and pass on their own. Occasionally, though, patches of liver tissue die or the bile ducts narrow afterward, and late recognition can be costly.

The paper reviews the clinical characteristics of post-TACE hepatic necrosis and biliary stenosis and lays out an endoscopic approach to managing them. Reaching the damaged bile ducts from inside, with an endoscope, can drain and open strictures without new surgery on an already weakened liver. For liver teams, the value is a practical playbook: which warning signs to watch for after embolization, and how to intervene through the least invasive route available.
pmc-10796201:
Soojin Rhee, Sungwook Chun, and Yong Il Ji look for what drives loss of egg reserve after ovary surgery, in a study published in twenty twenty-three. The surgery removes cysts caused by endometriosis, a condition where womb-like tissue grows in the wrong place. The operation can harm the ovary's store of eggs, tracked by a hormone called AMH.

The study covered twenty-two women who had cysts removed from one ovary at a university hospital. Blood was drawn before surgery and three days after. Starting blood counts, white cell counts, and AMH levels all tied to later AMH change. Only starting hemoglobin, the red protein level, tied to the rate of fall. The authors suggest blood health before surgery may shape early reserve loss.
pmc-11535401:
Ming Liu, Haoran Xun, and Liping Wu apply a fuzzy sliding mode control to tame large chaotic shakes in a beam held at both ends, in a multi dimensional model. The beam is non linear and bears an outside load. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

The team derives the beam's motion laws from a classic energy rule, then cuts the system down with a Galerkin step. A neural network model forecasts the chaotic motion, which lets the control act in time. One dimensional and multi dimensional runs are set side by side, and the authors argue the fuller model is needed for true dynamic gauges. The control calms chaos in the full system.
pmc-11537401:
Zhang and three co-authors test plastic film mulch methods for dryland maize, in work from twenty twenty-four. The Loess Plateau in China grows maize with little rain. Film mulch can save soil water and warm soil, but the best layout was unclear.

A field trial in twenty nineteen set up eight mulch methods, plus a bare flat control. Options mixed ridge furrow shapes with black film, liquid film, biodegradable film, and straw in the furrows. The team tracked plant growth, soil water, and soil temperature across the season. Yield and water use efficiency were the final tests. The comparison guides farmers to a layout worth its cost.
pmc-11574301:
Zhicheng Wei and six co-authors use genetics to test whether a cluster of health problems raises lung cancer risk. The cluster, called metabolic syndrome, ties together weight, blood sugar, blood pressure, and blood fats. Plain studies cannot prove cause, so the team used a method that treats gene variants as a natural test. They drew on large public gene databases.

The syndrome raised the odds of lung cancer overall, and most clearly of two types: squamous cell and small cell. It showed no clear link to a third type. Smoking, drink, weight, schooling, and diabetes may carry part of the effect. The paper adds gene-based weight to the case for prevention.
pmc-11598401:
Younes Ledmaoui and five colleagues build an AI system for spotting faults in solar panels, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Photovoltaic fleets need regular inspection to limit energy losses and extend module life. Manual inspection does not scale with deployment.

Their model uses an enhanced convolutional neural network based on VGG16. It classifies physical and electrical changes, such as dust and bird droppings on panels. Oversampling and augmentation balanced the training data. Reported accuracy reached about ninety-one percent, with specificity above ninety-eight percent. A PyQt5 interface wraps the model for everyday users. The authors emphasize explainability, aiming at decisions maintenance teams can understand and trust in the field.
pmc-11602201: Manasi Hegde and Travers Weaver report a man of seventy-three with a central eye fluid ill that showed in odd ways, in twenty twenty-four. The ill was set though two dye scans of the eye read as sound. Such scans are most oft key to the call. The man also sat past the most oft age band for a first find. Fluid sat in the retina, a rare mark for this ill. The pair say this is the first such case they know of in print.
pmc-11604001:
Si Liu leads a team that profiles blood sugar chains in gut cancers. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with serum N-glycans. Three major gut cancers had never been compared this way.

Blood samples from colon, esophagus, and stomach cancer cases were used. A high throughput mass spec assay read the sugar profiles. A random forest model was built to split the cancers. All three showed less mannose tagging on blood proteins. Single sugar tags fell while sialic tags rose. Unsupervised learning showed how the groups separate. Such marks could aid early cancer sorting.
pmc-11604701:
Gao and co-authors show how a two-metal face steers gas-to-fuel picks at charge. Two-metal builds can lift multi-part fuel picks from CO2 at charge. What the face looks like in work, and its role, stayed dim. Their build pairs silver and copper in a crisp two-phase form. A copper-rich face leans to ethylene in the test runs. More silver in the face swaps the top yield to drinks.

At full silver sway, the top yield drops to plain CO gas. A *CO mid part steers how the face re-forms in work. High *CO near the face sends copper bits to the silver side. The new face bends how much it loves the wet part. That love sets the burn pace of the gas path. End picks for rich fuels thus trace to the live face.
pmc-11607901:
Zenghong Wu, Fangnan Xia, and Rong Lin published a global health analysis in twenty twenty-four of cancer burden across two hundred four countries and territories. Using Global Burden of Disease data reaching back to nineteen eighty, they tallied cases, deaths, and disability for thirty-four cancer types. Cancer is the world's second most common cause of death, so the numbers guide prevention spending.

In twenty twenty-one, cancer caused about fourteen point six percent of all deaths and nearly nine percent of lost healthy years. Women showed higher incidence rates, while men died at higher rates. Digestive cancers made up the largest share of deaths. The authors press policymakers to close sex gaps in care and target the biggest killers.
pmc-11612001:
Hendrik Vilstrup and five colleagues review how the liver turns waste nitrogen into urea and what happens when that job fails, in a twenty twenty-four article. Urea making is a high-capacity liver task that keeps the whole body in nitrogen balance. It is also the final exit for ammonia, a waste product that harms the brain when it builds up. Early defenses trap ammonia in amino acids, but only urea making removes it for good.

In liver disease, lost liver mass and poor control shrink urea capacity. The early traps then back up, ammonia spills over, and the brain syndrome called hepatic encephalopathy can follow. The authors argue weak urea making is a required step on that road.
pmc-11612601:
Zhou leads a large team building a digital platform for chronic disease care, in work from twenty twenty-four. China promotes active health management in communities. But separate record systems block sharing among home tests, community clinics, and hospitals.

Their study built a platform to join those data streams and ran it for two years in a single arm design. Residents could self test, and community staff could follow full disease cycles in one place. Mixed methods checked both outcomes and user experience. The aim was better long term control of chronic disease close to home, not just in large hospitals.
pmc-11628901:
Gulfidan Baser and Filiz Hisar meta-analyse interventions helping healthcare students develop positive attitudes toward elderly people. Their 2024 study responds to rising elder care needs as populations age worldwide.

Searches across eight databases retrieved over fourteen thousand studies, of which thirteen entered the meta-analysis. The pooled effect size was statistically significant at about zero point four, a moderate effect favouring intervention groups. Programs during professional education can shift student attitudes positively. However, the authors caution that many existing studies are methodologically weak. Well-designed, high-quality trials are needed before strong evidence claims can be made about which interventions work best.
pmc-11634801:
Hanwei Ke and seven co-authors study a painful bladder state in rats and in human tissue. The state brings bladder pain, a strong urge to pass urine, and frequent trips, yet its cause is still unclear. The team looked at a signal pair called PACAP and its dock PAC1. Both were far higher in bladder tissue from patients and from rats with bladder inflammation.

When the team changed this signal path in rats, bladder inflammation eased and bladder function improved. The paper points to PACAP and PAC1 as possible targets for new care.
pmc-11635101:
Chisembe and co-authors swept drug hold in gut germs from farm hens in Malawi. Drug hold is a world health strain with reach past wards to farms. Farm stock sits at a key cross point, yet facts run thin there. Malawi, a low-stock land, had near no such facts in print. The team took germ bits from hens across the land in 2023. In sum, 115 germ strains came from 116 gut and stool bits.

Drug tests used a set thin-mix way by world lab norms. Full gene reads ran on a bright-read tool for the strains. Near half the strains, 50 of them, held off a key drug. That drug, cefotaxime, lost force on 44 percent of strains. Shield genes of the CTX-M clan showed in the reads.
pmc-11641701:
Reilly and co-authors review injuries suffered by custody officers who guard prisoners. The job exposes staff to hazards during cell checks, recreation oversight, and contraband searches. Yet injury research on this group is thin. The team searched five databases under a registered review plan. From 975 papers, eight studies survived the quality checks. Their average appraisal score was about 69%.

Fatal injury rates in the studies ran from 0.027 upward per the reported units. Sprains, assault injuries, and stress harms recur across the data. The review builds the first broad profile of harm in this workforce. It points prisons toward the risks most worth preventing.
pmc-11643001:
Gulzhanat Aimagambetova and colleagues reviewed heavy bleeding after childbirth in two thousand twenty-four. Such bleeding is the leading cause of mother deaths worldwide. Rates run higher in poorer countries. Health systems there face shortages at every level. Policy, facility, and community barriers all slow care.

Global guidelines exist and save lives where usable. Many clinics cannot follow them fully, though. Local resources and skills vary widely. The authors call for adapted approaches per setting. Training, supplies, and clear local algorithms all matter. Their update gathers current evidence for front-line teams. Faster, fitted care could prevent many deaths.
pmc-11643801:
Guntis Sosins and colleagues characterise aspen wood after heat treatment under pressure. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses a pilot chamber with nitrogen gas. Thermal modification improves wood stability without chemical preservatives. A closed, pressurised process may treat wood more evenly.

Boards were heated for up to three hours at moderate temperatures. Treated wood lost mass and shrank in every direction. Moisture uptake and swelling dropped to less than half of untreated levels. Stiffness rose slightly, while bending strength dipped modestly. Hardness and water capacity of cell walls also shifted. The trade-offs look favourable for building uses. Aspen, a fast-growing wood, gains durability from the process.
pmc-11651501:
Sunyun Qi and colleagues map twenty years of laboratory biosafety research as drawn in a major database, in this review from twenty twenty-four. Using visual analysis software, they charted who publishes, where, and on what, across the Web of Science from the year two thousand to twenty twenty-two. The field guards the public from lab accidents and leaks, so its shape matters.

Two institutions lead, the United States disease control agency and a Chinese academy university, but teamwork between institutions is thin and scattered. A handful of named team leaders anchor the map. Keyword bursts track world events: outbreak and resistance early, Ebola in the middle years, then coronavirus and African swine fever. The authors worry that a field concentrated in few hands lacks diversity, and they urge fairer sharing of funds and collaboration.
pmc-11653801:
Hanbo Feng and colleagues published a 2024 review of reviews on peer-assisted learning. Students in health programs often teach each other. Schools worldwide use this approach heavily. The authors gathered systematic reviews to judge whether it works.

They searched nine databases for eligible reviews. Twenty-four reviews qualified, including nine combined analyses. Quality checks used a standard appraisal checklist. Results were organized with an education evaluation model. Peer teaching appears well established across health training. The summary helps schools see where evidence is strong. It also shows where better studies are still needed.
pmc-11657801:
Yu-Hsin Chang and his team use machine learning with word tools to guess where a sick or hurt case will go from the first check desk. Their 2024 study sets model scores next to the calls made by docs.

Files came from two sites in Taiwan for twenty eighteen and twenty nineteen. One site tested the models from the out side. The models learned from fixed data fields plus free text notes from the first check, worked on by word tools. End points were death or a move to high care, and a move to a ward bed or a new site. Six models were built and set next to a score based on first check grade. Good first checks share beds and gear well and cut stays short, yet hand calls vary and can send a case too high or too low.
pmc-11658701:
Maresova and coauthors study two gene switches that work as a pair in fission yeast. Both switches turn on genes for fat handling in cells. One also steers the cell cycle as cells divide. Their shared targets hinted they work in one path.

Cutting either gene gave a like set of cell faults. Growth slowed and fat balance went off track. Cell division also went awry, with a cut-cell look. The pair proved to act in the same control path. That path guards both fat balance and faithful division. Yeast gives a clean model for those core processes.
pmc-11675701:
Watcharapong Panthong and co-authors join proteomics with machine learning to find a biomarker that can forecast the outlook in sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma. Their 2024 study deals with a rare tumour. Its rate of death in five years is high.

Four types of classifier were trained on protein profiles. The profiles came from tumours, set next to nasal polyps used as controls. Seventeen proteins showed up in all the models. That marked them as biomarkers that may be of use. A check of gene expression across data sets on cancer cut the field to two genes that might fit. One of them, PYCR1, was shown to be in tumour tissues by a standard molecular test. High levels of it were linked to poor survival as a whole. The team puts PYCR1 forth as a biomarker tied to tumours, to forecast the outlook in this rare cancer.
pmc-11676401:
Yuta Kitamura, Shunsuke Ikema, Tomoaki Tatsumi, and Takayuki Baba report a case where a thicker nylon thread inside a glaucoma drain shunt fixed a fluid layer split. The split lay at the back of the eye. The shunt is a small, low cut surgery for glaucoma. The report came out in twenty twenty-four.

A woman in her late seventies had steroid caused glaucoma in both eyes after long steroid care for another ill. Shunt surgery first held eye pressure low, but the back layer split badly in both eyes and the front chamber shallowed. Threads placed inside both shunts raised pressure and the splits healed within a month. Drops then held pressure steady.
pmc-11693601:
Shin Moon and colleagues target an enzyme in immune cells to calm heart attack inflammation. Their study from twenty twenty-four examines PCSK7 in macrophages. Heart attacks trigger fierce inflammation that kills more heart tissue. That response also drives harmful reshaping of the heart later.

Mice lacking PCSK7 carried lower blood cholesterol levels. Their heart injury after infarction was milder in the experiments. Normal PCSK7 pushed macrophages to activate and swallow more lipid. Those actions worsened damage at the oxygen-starved site. Blocking the enzyme therefore looks like a plausible treatment route. The study links a little-known enzyme to both lipids and cardiac immunity.
pmc-11703401: Yuko Harada and Atsuo Mori describe a giant Chiari's network found in a healthy man's heart, in a case report from twenty twenty-four. The forty-year-old had suffered unexplained palpitations for years. Echocardiography showed a bright ribbon-like structure moving vigorously in his right atrium, though a CT scan found nothing. Chiari's network carries risks of clot formation, embolism, and arrhythmia. No clots or atrial fibrillation were found, and monitoring detected none either. He remains under observation without medication while optimal management stays unsettled.
pmc-11705601:

pmc-11713001:

pmc-11728201:
Veleva, Ganeva, and Zhiponova test an electric pretreatment for yeast extracts, in work from twenty twenty-four. Baker yeast is a key raw material for extracts used in food and labs. Breaking its tough cell wall well is the main hurdle.

pmc-11733901:

pmc-11774701:

pmc-11805201:
Anamika Chandra leads a team on COVID-19 vaccine intention in India. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with uptake drivers. Vaccination proved the most promising shield in the pandemic.

pmc-11823001:
Pan and co-authors test whether long-term air pollution raises the risk of major mental disorders. Evidence on that link has stayed limited despite rising concern. pmc-12018401:

pmc-12687301:

pmc-12709001:
Jie-Huei Wang, Zih-Han Wu, Hui-Chen Lu, and Tzung-Ying Guo test ways to pick firm cancer markers, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. pmc-12711601:
Travis McDevitt-Galles and four co-authors test why one Michigan bat colony survives white-nose syndrome while a similar one declines, in a two thousand twenty-five wildlife disease study. The fungal disease has devastated little brown bat populations across North America.

pmc-12715701: Ali Naeim and four colleagues report a brain tumor in an unusual location, in a case report from twenty twenty-five. Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma is a low-grade tumor usually found in the lateral ventricles. It typically accompanies tuberous sclerosis complex. pmc-12716701:

pmc-12727801:
Cramer and seven co-authors review human testing for fungal toxins in food, in work from twenty twenty-five. Mycotoxins from molds pose a health risk in many regions. Testing blood, urine, or milk can measure real exposure better than food records alone.

pmc-12730301:
Sharon Mara Luciano and colleagues tested the cerebellum's role in voice emotion in two thousand twenty-five. People read feelings from pitch, rhythm, and stress in speech. pmc-12730601:
Elisa Pugliese and colleagues test whether a freer style of physical education sharpens young children's minds as well as their movement, in this preliminary study from twenty twenty-five. pmc-12732701:
Michael Daniyan and co-authors probe the heat shock protein 90s of a monkey-born malaria germ for drug-fit shapes. Their code study appeared in twenty twenty-five. pmc-12736101:

pmc-12736701:

pmc-12742201:

pmc-12752901:

pmc-12756201:

pmc-12758101:

pmc-12759301:

pmc-12764201:

pmc-12782601:

pmc-12809901:

pmc-12820501:

pmc-12827101:

pmc-12830901:

pmc-12831401:

pmc-12837001:

pmc-12837101:

pmc-12866401:

pmc-13135501:

pmc-13148301:

pmc-13168401:

pmc-13173101:

pmc-13179401:

pmc-13180101:

pmc-13183601:

pmc-13195201:

pmc-13197301:

pmc-13197401:

pmc-13197801:

pmc-13198501:
