pmc-13289301:
Weronika Grabowska and coauthors report 2026 baseline findings on traditional, complementary, and integrative medicine use in Berlin. Data came from the German National Cohort, known as NAKO, at its inner-city Berlin center for 2017 to 2019. Participants reported use in the prior year of seven non-drug approaches, from meditation to chiropractic care.

Among 1970 people, 1029 said they used at least one such approach in the past year. Meditation led at 26.8 percent, followed by chiropractic care and then yoga in use rates. Frequent users were more often women and reported more chronic pain, joint wear, back pain, and mental health problems than never users. Supplement use was also far more common among users, painting a picture of added care alongside usual medicine.
pmc-13289401:
Hevar Hamah Saed headed a 2026 cohort comparison on home-based drug titration for heart failure with reduced pumping strength. Guideline drugs help most when started fast and raised to target doses, yet routine care often stalls. The TELEFASTER-HF approach used a fixed home plan with remote monitoring to speed that process safely.

The home cohort held 60 patients, compared with 65 patients getting standard care at the same time. Weighting balanced the groups before outcome checks began. Time to best medical therapy was far shorter at home, with a median of 48 days versus 321 days for standard care in the results. Dose levels and target reach were higher at every check, and persistence stayed better through twelve months.
pmc-13289801:
Thibault Genissel, Alexandre Robert, Jane Lecomte, and François Sarrazin define a 2026 concept called evolutionary footprint for conservation science. Human-driven change now alters evolution itself, across fast and slow timescales, through genetics and other inheritance paths. Managers lack a single score for that impact, so the authors propose one that compares change against natural history baselines.

Metrics cover adaptive traits, genetic diversity, large-scale evolutionary processes, and family tree patterns for a species or group. Two cases illustrate scoring: a plant facing pollinator decline, and human effects across mammals as a whole. Mixing timescales, forecasting change, handling non-genetic paths, and building databases remain hard parts. A shared score could bring evolution into routine conservation choices.
pmc-13290601:
Research tying knee osteoarthritis to oxidative stress has boomed, and Yuhang Zhang and colleagues chart the field's shape in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. Pulling the literature from the Web of Science Core Collection, they mapped output, collaborations, and keyword clusters with CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and RStudio.

Publication volume climbed into rapid growth and peaked in 2024. China leads on raw output but sits loosely in the collaboration network, a pattern the authors call high-output and low-integration. Hubs such as Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine anchor the knowledge core. Keywords grouped into three themes: nutrition-based intervention, mechanism work such as cell senescence, and therapy studies such as ozone. The field's arc runs from basic validation through mechanism refinement toward clinical translation, now turning to whole-body interactions.
pmc-13290701:
Yawara Kikuchi and co-authors link tooth loss to heart risk in treated hypertension in a 2026 cohort study. Participants were 5,484 middle-aged and older adults in Japan taking blood pressure medicine, with no past cardiovascular disease. Researchers counted remaining teeth and denture use at entry. They then followed the group for new cardiovascular events over about ten years. Analyses split people by how well their pressure was controlled.

Five hundred sixty-seven participants, about ten percent, developed cardiovascular disease during follow-up. Among those with poorly controlled pressure, fewer teeth and skipped dentures meant higher risk. The highest risk sat in people with almost no teeth who wore no dentures, at roughly double the reference rate. No such pattern stood out when pressure was well controlled. The split between groups passed formal interaction testing. The authors suggest dental care may matter most when pressure control lags.
pmc-13290901:
Genes, a drug, and sex jointly tune fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell anemia, Manoel Ferreira de Magalhães Filho and colleagues report in a study from western Bahia, Brazil, in 2026. Fetal hemoglobin blunts red cell sickling, and both hydroxyurea therapy and variants near two genes are known to raise it; the team measured their combined hand.

DNA from 43 patients was typed for variants in BCL11A and the HBS1L-MYB region. Patients on hydroxyurea carried significantly higher fetal hemoglobin than untreated patients. A factorial analysis found the drug, beta-globin haplotype, and sex interacting to shape levels, and a regression model using the drug, sex, and three variants explained 46.5% of the variation. Several variants also traveled together in linkage blocks. The authors say such markers could guide individualized monitoring of therapy.
pmc-13291001:
Microbes inside digestive tumors get a full review by Huamin Zeng and colleagues in 2026. The cancers covered include stomach, pancreas, colon, liver, and esophagus. These cancers kill many patients each year. Inner microbes may shape how they grow and resist drugs.

The review traces where these microbes come from. It then maps how they affect tumor growth. Herbal medicine ideas to rebalance the tumor habitat get a close look. Drug paths that target microbes are weighed with care. Gaps that block clinic use are named plainly. A microbe-first view may guide future precision care.
pmc-13291401:
Alejandro Guerrero and a large team describe a Colombian family whose genes seem to blunt Alzheimer's, in 2026. Five siblings carry the APOE ε2 variant paired with ε3, a combination tied to lower disease risk. Their ages ran from ninety-four to one hundred five years. The team recorded clinical status, thinking scores, and brain scans for each sibling. Family studies of this kind are rare at such extreme ages.

Cognition across the five ranged from normal to mild dementia. Brain MRI showed less shrinkage than expected for people past ninety-five. A metabolism scan, FDG-PET, showed preserved brain activity patterns as well. The authors read the picture as resilience, where function holds up despite great age. Such families offer clues about the pathways that protect the aging brain. Those clues could seed treatments that mimic the variant's effect. The study adds human evidence to a mostly preclinical research area.
pmc-13291601:
Noisy rhythms in nature carry a hidden energy cost. Daiki Sekizawa, Sosuke Ito, and Masafumi Oizumi break that cost apart in a 2026 study. Heartbeats, brain waves, and chemical pulses all oscillate. Each rhythm burns energy to persist.

A math tool called Koopman decomposition splits motion into modes. Total waste heat splits cleanly across those modes. Each mode’s cost grows with speed squared times strength. Fast modes thus face tight strength limits at fixed cost. One strong mode can drive most waste. Broad spectra can also share the burden. Bifurcation and resonance cases show both patterns. Frequency-level cost maps were invisible before.
pmc-13292001:
Longlong Fang and co-authors merge two diazo reaction paths in one flask with visible light, in a 2026 study. Diazo compounds usually follow one of two roads, shedding nitrogen to form either a carbene or a ketene. Chemists normally force one road and suppress the other. The team instead lit two different diazo starting materials at once. Each followed its own road inside the same mixture.

The carbene and ketene partners then joined in a formal three-plus-two ring closure. Products were densely substituted furanones carrying crowded quaternary carbon centers. No catalyst was needed, and the procedure scaled to gram amounts cleanly. The scope across starting materials proved broad in their tests. Some products showed early antifibrotic activity in screening. The authors frame dual photolysis as a new design principle for diazo chemistry. It turns parallel reactivity into planned convergence for building bioactive scaffolds.
pmc-13292301:
Yaakov Hoffman and co-authors offer a 2026 early study of trauma responses in older adults who survived captivity after the 7 October attack. Almost all captivity research covers young prisoners of war, not elderly civilians. The team assessed 26 Jewish Israeli adults from Gaza-envelope kibbutzim, mean age about 82, half of them released Hamas captives and half displaced survivors.

Apart from stronger prolonged grief among ex-captives, both groups reported similarly low levels of PTSD, complex PTSD, depression, and anxiety. Those treated cruelly on purpose while held fared worse. In the freed group alone, being lonely tracked with grief, and feeling unsafe tracked with PTSD symptoms. The authors read the overall pattern as late-life resilience, consistent with the inoculation hypothesis, while flagging captivity-specific risk factors.
pmc-13293601:
Wenjing Zhou and colleagues run, in a 2026 trial, an unguided online therapy course for major depression in Chinese adults, tracking effects for a full year. Online cognitive behavioral therapy is cheap and scalable, yet lasting benefit in China was unproven.

The eight-week trial in Shenzhen split 317 adults between instant access to a seven-module course plus usual care and a waitlist group. At course end, the instant group had eased depression more, with higher remission and response rates than controls, based on figures the authors report. Dropout was higher in the instant group. Gains were then tracked at three, six, and twelve months.
pmc-13294301:
Jessica L. Hite highlights a smarter way to reconstruct how infections travel from person to person, in a 2026 commentary on contact tracing. Tracing, quarantine, and targeted restrictions remain core outbreak tools, yet they work only when officials understand spread through varied populations. Hite spotlights a recent framework that fuses genetic data with contact records over time inside a Bayesian model, meaning it weighs evidence against prior expectations about the contact network.

Treating the contact network as a prior lets the method capture how individuals differ and untangle cases where genetic evidence alone is too thin. Recording variation at mutation sites rather than whole genomes keeps the evolutionary signal while slashing computing demands, and metadata slot in more easily. Sharper transmission maps could let health officials disrupt spread precisely while imposing fewer social and economic costs on everyone else.
pmc-13294401:
Paolo Niccolò Franco and colleagues count the environmental savings of deep learning CT reconstruction in a 2026 single-center study. Eighteen months of data from four scanners, two with hybrid iterative methods and two with deep learning methods, covered 42,300 body scans. Deep learning protocols also ran lower tube voltage and trimmed contrast dye doses.

Electricity fell from 123,000 kWh in the older group to 66,927 kWh in the deep learning group, with matching carbon drops in the reported totals. Contrast savings reached 434 liters over the period, preserving water as well. Combined carbon from power and dye fell from 49.62 tons to 29.10 tons. Greener scanning need not mean weaker images.
pmc-13294501:
Wenyu Zhang and a large team train machine learners to screen for primary aldosteronism in a 2026 study. The hormone disorder drives much treatable high blood pressure, yet the standard ratio test falters when patients stay on blood pressure drugs. Three datasets totaling 1,380 patients supplied plasma steroids, potassium, and renin to several models, led by a feedforward neural network.

Renin-free models matched accuracy with or without drug washout, while ratio-style models sagged without washout. Three tuned renin-free models reached areas of 0.948–0.954 versus 0.839 for the standard ratio in the reported curves. At high sensitivity cutoffs, false alarms fell by 53–72% in the authors' figures.
pmc-13294901:
Samuele Ruffoli and colleagues create a new family of molecular rings built from malonate units, in a 2026 chemistry study. Macrocycles, large ring molecules, serve as hosts that can recognize and hold guest molecules, but rings of this size tend to grow into unwanted chains instead of closing. By joining malonyl dichloride with substituted benzylic diols under tuned conditions, the team coaxed the reaction to stop at neat two-unit rings.

Crystal structures showed tidy shapes with cavity sizes set by the substituents chosen, plus preferences in how the rings twist. In the solid state the rings stacked into interlocked columns, held by weak hydrogen bonds and, in iodinated versions, halogen bonds. The rings kept their acidic character, while binding of a vanadium-containing ion depended strongly on cavity size and shape. The authors offer the rings as a versatile platform for recognition and materials.
pmc-13295001:
Petru Ifteni and colleagues survey Romanian psychiatrists about long-acting injectable antipsychotics in a 2026 study. Injections given every few weeks can improve adherence and cut relapse in schizophrenia, yet they remain underused. Views were gathered from doctors treating more than 1,000 patients in total.

Eighty psychiatrists rated the four products sold in Romania on benefit, safety, dosing, and monitoring needs. Aripiprazole injections scored best overall, while olanzapine scored lowest on most counts. Better adherence and fewer relapses most encouraged prescribing, named by almost all respondents. Patient distrust and patchy hospital supply were the leading barriers, pointing to fixes beyond the clinic room.
pmc-13295601:
Yiwei Jin and colleagues feed laying hens the leftovers of a traditional herbal drink and watch the eggs improve, in a 2026 study. Xiasangju, a three-herb formula, leaves processing residues still rich in polyphenols and flavonoids. With antibiotics retreating from feed, such plant by-products are candidate additives. The team added the residue to the diets of late-laying hens and tracked production, egg traits, gut inflammation, and gut microbes.

The residue carried active compounds including linarin, rosmarinic acid, and chlorogenic acids. At a modest inclusion level near one and a half percent, hens laid at a better rate with heavier eggs and deeper yolk color. Deeper analysis tied the gains to calmer intestinal inflammation, apparently routed through the COX-2 pathway, alongside shifts in the gut microbial community. The authors present medicine-plant waste as a feed resource hiding in plain sight.
pmc-13295801:
Zachary Green and colleagues track bowel surgery in children as biologic drug use climbed in a 2026 study. A regional British centre followed young inflammatory bowel disease patients from 2007 to 2024. Anti-TNF drugs arrived earlier and reached far more children across three guideline eras.

The cohort held 1,538 children, mostly with Crohn's disease, as yearly patient numbers more than doubled. Treated shares rose from under six percent in the first era to over sixty percent in the latest. Resection rates fell steeply across the same span, driven by Crohn's cases, while ulcerative colitis trends stayed less certain.
pmc-13295901:
Gábor Mátis and colleagues build lab models of infection-driven swelling in pig liver and gut, in a 2026 study. Heavy antibiotic use on pig farms feeds drug resistance, so safer swaps need good test models first. The team exposed pig liver cells and small gut tissue to molecular patterns from bacteria and viruses, the cues that set off inflammation and oxidative stress.

Liver cells reacted strongly, pouring out swelling signals with little cell harm. Gut tissue answered in a milder, more measured way. That split between organs is itself a finding, since a swap drug may act unlike in liver and gut. The authors offer both models as screens for new antibiotic-free options that could cut farm drug use and slow resistance.
pmc-13296001:
Iga Ciesielska-Markowska and colleagues review what is known about the airway microbiome in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, in a 2026 survey. The disease slowly narrows the airways, fed mainly by smoking and dirty air, and its course is hard to foretell. Microbes living in the airways may shape that course, so the team compared the communities of each airway region and of patients versus healthy people.

Each region of the tract holds its own community, with some overlap between sites. Patients' airway mixes parted from healthy ones, and lower diversity tracked with worse lung function and may flag flare risk. The field struggles with tiny sample loads, stray contamination, and uneven methods. The authors look to combined omics and smart analytics to make the microbiome a tool of precise lung care.
pmc-13296301:
Mirko Sergio and a large veterinary team ask, in 2026, whether fat from around dogs' ovaries, taken during routine spaying, beats under-skin fat as a source of repair cells for worn joints. Cells from five healthy Labradors were grown and pushed toward cartilage making.

Ovary-area fat cells showed stronger cartilage-forming ability and built a richer cartilage-like matrix than skin fat cells from the same dogs. Since this tissue is normally thrown away, the authors call it an ethical, ready supply for regenerative work. They aim at future cartilage repair for dogs with osteoarthritis.
pmc-13296601:
Michael J. Zachman and colleagues introduce an imaging method gentle enough to map atoms around single catalyst sites, in a 2026 paper. Single-atom catalysts promise cleaner energy chemistry, yet their activity likely depends on local structure that bulk measurements average away. Normal electron microscopes damage these fragile sites even at low voltage.

The team used electron ptychography at thirty kiloelectronvolts, well below the usual imaging energy. The approach recovered the lattice layout around individual metal atoms while essentially avoiding knock-on damage. Pairing such site-specific pictures with computation should clarify why some sites work better or last longer. Better structural knowledge could speed design of catalysts for hydrogen, carbon dioxide conversion, and storage.
pmc-13297001:
Alexander C Campbell and colleagues review, in 2026, how accurately billing and records codes capture real health conditions. Pooling 280 studies that checked diagnosis codes against a trusted standard, mostly hospital charts in rich countries, they summarise hit and miss rates across many conditions.

Codes were strong at ruling conditions out and moderate to strong at confirming them, but accuracy for catching true cases swung widely between studies and disease groups. Only two studies came from poorer countries. The authors urge ongoing accuracy checks, since such data now steer population health research and policy.
pmc-13297201:
Livia Stanga and colleagues chart drug-resistant kidney infections at a Romanian hospital and build a bedside risk score in a 2026 study. Records covered 129 adults with proven acute kidney infection over three years. Just over two fifths of the cases involved germs that resisted many drugs.

Recent antibiotic use was the strongest sign of resistance, ahead of repeat infection, a recent hospital stay, and weak kidneys on arrival. Resistant cases waited far longer for a drug that worked and stayed in hospital longer. The score built from these signs sorted resistant from treatable cases well in checks within the data. The authors offer it for local prescribing choices, pending tests elsewhere.
pmc-13297301:
Heba Elhaddad and a large team test whether gene data alone can sort acute myeloid leukaemia patients by risk and by likely response to first chemotherapy, in a 2026 study. Current risk checks for this blood cancer are complex and often imprecise. The team tried several data tools and datasets on targeted sequencing results taken at diagnosis.

Their tools improved risk sorting over current practice, the authors report, and better predicted who would respond to the opening drug course. Sharper sorting at diagnosis could spare patients judged resistant the toxic effects of drugs unlikely to help them. The approach points toward treatment plans set by a patient's own gene profile from the start.
pmc-13297901:
Zoe Leyva-Acosta, Eduardo Acuña Yeomans, and Francisco Hernández-Quiroz present a 2026 controlled comparison of two ways to estimate algorithmic complexity. One family squeezes strings through compression, while the other runs short programs, represented here by the Coding Theorem Method. Their framework uses the Block Decomposition Method to stretch program-based estimates onto longer strings.

A control estimator that keeps block structure but removes algorithmic information helps separate real agreement from effects driven by string length alone. Correlations between the two families proved weak and faded as model resolution fell. For long strings, apparent global agreement was largely explained by the control, suggesting each approach captures a different kind of structure.
pmc-13298001:
Honey pulled from the hive too soon sits in a gray zone in food law, and Anna Gajda and her team take that gray zone apart in a 2026 review. Some call such honey fake or low grade. The team finds the science and the rule books do not line up.

They read lab work on the microbes, make-up, and scent marks of honey. They also read world and EU food rules, from Codex Alimentarius to EU laws. Sugar-loving yeasts live in all honey, they note, so a yeast count alone should not fail a batch unless the honey is in fact souring. No rule sets a yeast cap today. Their fix is to judge ripe state by a set of signs at once, water level among them, and to test that set in many labs first.
pmc-13298201:
Ming-Jui Hung and co-authors develop artificial intelligence tools to predict coronary artery spasm without invasive testing, in a 2026 retrospective study. Patients lacked obstructive coronary disease yet underwent provocation testing across many years. A random forest model used routine clinical variables, later simplified to nine, while a deep learning model read raw electrocardiogram data.

The nine-variable score separated patients with spasm from those without it well in both the derivation group and an external validation group. Spasm became more common as risk factors accumulated. The electrocardiogram model caught most cases yet flagged many healthy patients, so the authors label it proof of concept needing refinement.
pmc-13298601:
A cheap wireless fetal monitor reads heart tracings nearly as well as the hospital machine, found Pajaree Ruenpeng and co-authors in a 2026 prospective study. Four hundred four pregnant women underwent simultaneous monitoring with mobile and conventional cardiotocography, and blinded physician groups scored the paired tracings.

Agreement on baseline heart rate was excellent, with correlation above 0.95, and readings of accelerations and decelerations also matched closely. Judgments of variability and contractions agreed only moderately, and reviewers gave the conventional device slightly higher quality and satisfaction scores. Even so, the authors back mobile monitoring as a workable option for low-resource settings, given its cost and portability.
pmc-13299101:
A gut molecule better known as a tumor suppressor may help obesity open the door to colon cancer, argue Sidharth Prasad Mishra and colleagues in a 2026 review. They trace how diet and gut microbes push the microRNA miR-101a into overdrive in the obese colon.

Ethanolamine from food and microbes raises miR-101a, which then dismantles the messenger for ZO-1, a protein that seals the gut lining. The leakier barrier admits bacterial products, feeding chronic inflammation, oxidative damage, and growth signals that favor tumors. Because miR-101a can be measured in tissue, blood, or stool, the authors propose it as an early warning marker and a target for diet or microbiome interventions.
pmc-13299601:
Luminita-Georgeta Confederat and colleagues weigh the benefits of a diabetes drug class against a dangerous side effect, in a 2026 concise review. SGLT2 inhibitors began as glucose-lowering agents yet now anchor care for heart failure, cardiovascular disease, and chronic kidney disease. Fear of side effects still limits prescribing, especially fear of ketoacidosis occurring at normal glucose levels.

That emergency arises through lower insulin and higher glucagon, which frees fatty acids for ketone production, usually alongside triggers like low carbohydrate intake, illness, surgery stress, or alcohol. The authors argue awareness of those triggers and symptoms lets clinicians avoid or manage the risk while keeping the cardio-renal benefits.
pmc-13299801:
Monika Mioduchowska leads a team asking whether tardigrades carry a distinctive microbiome during their dried survival state, in a 2026 study of two Paramacrobiotus species. Bacterial gene sequencing profiled eggs, active adults, dried tun-stage animals, specimens after short and long drying, dead specimens, and culture medium. Anhydrobiosis lets these animals survive near-total water loss.

Microbial communities varied strongly by life stage, showing high stage specificity rather than one fixed partnership. Several bacterial genera may assist survival through biofilm formation and support for stress proteins or trehalose production in eggs and tuns. The findings open a host-microbe angle on extreme stress survival.
pmc-13299901:
Jishna Vijayan and others map how two similar kinases, TLK1 and TLK2, are run by different phosphorylation networks, in a 2026 analysis drawing on thousands of human phosphoproteomic studies. The twin enzymes look alike yet behave in unlike ways across DNA replication, damage response, and chromatin layout. Main sites differed clearly between them.

TLK1's network centred on DNA damage signalling partners, while TLK2's centred on chromatin remodelling and replication partners, driven mainly by cell-cycle kinases. Downstream targets converged on genome stability with paralog-specific twists. The authors link TLK1 chiefly to checkpoint activation and TLK2 to replication-coupled chromatin care, with relevance to cancer resistance.
pmc-13300301:
D Debreceni and colleagues present a 2026 prospective comparison of two ablation methods for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. One arm used very high-power, short-duration radiofrequency energy, point by point. The other used a cryoballoon that freezes tissue around the pulmonary veins. The single-center study enrolled 164 patients in a row, 76 in the radiofrequency group and 88 in the cryoballoon group.

The high-power approach took about thirty-nine minutes on average, against fifty-five for the balloon. Every high-power case was done with no X-ray guidance at all, so patients got zero radiation, against a real dose in the balloon group. Rates of complications and one-year arrhythmia recurrence did not differ in a meaningful way between the two methods. The authors conclude that the newer radiofrequency style matches cryoballoon safety and rhythm control, while cutting procedure time and removing radiation exposure.
pmc-13300501:
Carmen Rajer and co-authors explore long-term care planning for Slovenia's Posavje region in a 2026 study linking user preferences, distance, and money. The team compared home care, institutional care, and community options such as sheltered housing and so-called silver villages. Their mixed methods combined interviews, a survey with 475 valid responses from just over a thousand people approached, spatial analysis, and cost estimates.

Preferences differed significantly by age group, and most people wanted care close to home, unwilling to move beyond ten kilometers and often preferring under five. Provider travel costs in rural areas proved substantial, in one municipality rivaling monthly housing costs in specialized community units. Cutting travel spending could therefore offset much of the housing expense. The authors argue that sustainable care systems need spatial coordination matched to what users actually want.
pmc-13300701:
Tiny fat bubbles secreted by cells can be turned into guided drug carriers, Sin Hye Park and colleagues demonstrate in a 2026 gastric cancer study. They fitted extracellular vesicles with the p51 peptide, which locks onto HER2, and loaded them with 17-DMAG, an HSP90-blocking drug. Tests ran in two cell lines and a mouse tumor model.

The guided vesicles entered HER2-positive cells far better than plain ones. Treated cells died by apoptosis, with cleaved PARP and caspase-3 up and growth signals such as c-Myc and VEGF down. In mice, the treatment slowed tumor growth without visible organ damage, marking the platform as a selective delivery route worth developing.
pmc-13301201:
S Hess and co-authors test whether atrial tachycardia ablation can be guided by maps made in ordinary sinus rhythm in a 2026 study. Finding the narrow slow corridor that sustains these rhythms usually means mapping during the tachycardia itself, a fiddly process. Thirty-seven patients had high density maps in both states, and the team checked whether the culprit sites, marked by long, fragmented, low voltage signals, announced themselves while the heart beat normally.

They did: sinus maps reliably showed the same slow zones that proved critical during tachycardia, with matching low voltages and drawn out signal durations. Burning those zones during sinus rhythm made the tachycardia non-inducible in every patient. About seventy-six percent stayed arrhythmia free over a mean follow-up near seven months. The authors argue the shortcut removes repeated induction and mapping rounds, simplifying a notoriously intricate procedure.
pmc-13302401:
Silencing four chitin-cutting genes could give farmers a greener weapon against the whitefly, Dejun Kong and colleagues report in a 2026 study of Bemisia tabaci. The pest drains plant sap and spreads viruses, and chemical sprays dominate current control. The team identified the whitefly's chitin deacetylase genes, which help build its cuticle and gut lining, then knocked them down with matching double-stranded RNA.

Two delivery routes worked: a nanomaterial carrier called SPc, and tomato plants engineered to produce the RNA themselves. Feeding whiteflies silenced the target genes in both cases. The authors present chitin deacetylases as promising targets for RNA-based pest control that leaves chemistry behind.
pmc-13302501:
A Keelani and co-authors evaluate, in a 2026 study, repeat ablation for atrial fibrillation using pinpoint pulsed field energy. Fibrillation often returns after a first ablation, and repeat work must close gaps while adding new lesions in thicker tissue. A focal system delivering short high-current applications through a force-sensing catheter was used.

The series held 180 consecutive redo patients, whose earlier treatments ranged from vein isolation alone to extensive line work. Most needed vein re-isolation or substrate changes, especially across the front and back walls of the upper chamber. Every target except two front-wall lines achieved block or isolation. Complications touched five percent of patients, including two coronary spasms that settled with medication and two temporary nerve palsies.
pmc-13302901:
Beatriz Rodrigues, Isabel M. Miranda, and Sofia Costa de Oliveira review, in a 2026 paper, gut microbe findings in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD. The gut-brain axis offers a plausible route from microbes to behaviour, yet single studies have clashed. The review searched three databases through the end of 2025 under standard reporting rules.

Twenty-three studies from 2015 to 2025 qualified, drawn from over five hundred screened. Overall microbe diversity inside each person rarely differed between ADHD and comparison groups. The mix of species, however, differed more consistently, with fewer butyrate-making Faecalibacterium and more Roseburia reported in ADHD. A few studies following children over time hinted that early patterns come before diagnosis. The authors blame uneven methods for much of the disagreement.
pmc-13303101:
Needling the spleen under ultrasound guidance cracked two diagnoses that safer routes could not, Zhuohang Zou and colleagues recount in a 2026 case report. Both patients arrived with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, a runaway inflammatory syndrome, driven by hidden B-cell lymphoma. Ravaged blood counts and clotting made standard biopsies too dangerous, and removing the spleen riskier still.

With disease centered in the spleen, the team sampled it percutaneously under imaging guidance. Both biopsies returned definitive lymphoma diagnoses and steered targeted therapy. The authors present the approach as a viable lifeline for carefully selected patients, provided a multidisciplinary team weighs the bleeding risk case by case.
pmc-13303301:
Guoliang Dou and co-authors feed ginseng compounds to rats for a month in a 2026 study of how the treatment changes gut microbes and its own absorption. Ginsenosides interact with intestinal bacteria, which convert them into absorbable forms. Whether long dosing helps or hinders that loop was unclear.

Twenty male rats split into a treated group and a water-only control group for thirty days. Treated rats showed richer, more diverse gut communities, with the Lactobacillus share climbing by roughly eighteen percentage points. Blood levels of a key converted ginsenoside ran significantly higher in treated animals, both at peak and overall. The authors conclude that chronic dosing improves the compounds' uptake by reshaping the gut community.
pmc-13303601:
Alin Gabriel Mihu and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, two imported cases of visceral leishmaniasis in western Romania, where the sandfly-borne disease is rare. Both men had travelled to eastern Spain, a region where the parasite circulates. Their presentations differed sharply from each other.

One patient showed the textbook pattern of fever, enlarged spleen, and low blood counts across the board. The other had only mild, vague symptoms with no organ enlargement at all. Bone marrow examination confirmed the parasite in both men. The authors stress that this potentially fatal infection belongs on the checklist for travellers returning from endemic areas, even when the picture looks atypical.
pmc-13304101:
Radivoje Jevtić and co-authors examine, in a 2026 field study, how shifting yellow rust races in Serbia hit wheat yield and grain quality differently by variety. The fungal disease is a worldwide wheat scourge, and symptom scores alone predict losses poorly. Trials ran across three seasons with differing rust pressure and a race change in the final year.

At mild to moderate infection, test weight fell in step with disease scores sooner than kernel weight did, making it an early warning trait. Kernel weight only gave way once a variety could no longer compensate for lost green tissue. Protein concentration rose under heavy infection, though its tie to yield loss stayed weak. Under severe pressure, varieties with equal visible disease diverged widely in damage, arguing for breeding on tolerance, not symptoms.
pmc-13305501:
Song Gao and co-authors chart global colorectal cancer patterns from 1990 to 2021 in a 2026 multi-part study. Burden figures span 204 countries, split by a development index, to show where the disease grows and who bears it most.

New cases reached into the millions worldwide by 2021 while death rates fell, a split credited to better screening and care in richer regions. Aging drove most of the global rise, while population growth dominated in poorer regions. Inequality between regions widened over the span. Forecasts see case rates edging up but deaths falling, and gene analysis tied body mass to higher risk.
pmc-13306201:
Gonca Vardar and colleagues present a 2026 newborn case that widened the known early brain picture of Fraccaro syndrome, a rare condition with four extra X chromosomes. Enlarged brain ventricles were spotted before birth. After delivery, doctors also found cleft palate, heart defects, undescended testes, and hearing problems.

Ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed enlarged ventricles at the back of the brain, plus an extra fluid space variant. Chromosome testing confirmed the 49,XXXXY pattern that defines the syndrome. The authors argue that enlarged ventricles can serve as an early clue prompting chromosome checks in newborns with several body anomalies. Early recognition, they note, allows timely monitoring across specialties and long-term hormone follow-up.
pmc-13307101:

pmc-13308801:

pmc-13310501:

pmc-13311101:

pmc-13311701:

pmc-13312001:

pmc-13313001:

pmc-13313301:

pmc-13313601:

pmc-13314201:

pmc-13314501:

pmc-13315001:

pmc-13315201:

pmc-13315501:

pmc-13316201:

pmc-13316701:

pmc-13317701:

pmc-13319501:

pmc-13321901:

pmc-13323601:

pmc-13327401:

pmc-13328401:

pmc-13335801:

pmc-13336501:

pmc-13336901:

pmc-13337401:

pmc-13340201:

pmc-13341501:

pmc-13341801:

pmc-13365401:
Qianqian Li and others showed that soluble TREM2 drives vascular permeability and bad ascites in ovarian cancer, in 2026. Ascites, a hallmark of advanced ovarian cancer, severely impairs quality of life and adds to care pushback, yet care remains largely palliative. The role of soluble TREM2 in vascular function and ascites making was poorly known.

Soluble TREM2 levels were elevated in bad ascites and correlated with ascites volume, and tests in vitro, in vivo, and ex vivo showed that it engages cell-surface nucleolin to increase vascular permeability. Blocking that link reduced ascites making. Oncologists gain a mechanistic target for a symptom that now has no disease-modifying care.
pmc-13366801:
Yuting Wu and Bin Li present MTRFU-Net, a net to cut lung nodules out of scans with more truth. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. True nodule cuts are key to early lung cancer finds, but nodules vary, blur at edges, and span sizes. Past deep nets still miss on those counts.

Their net pairs space traits with tone-band traits in a fused flow. A deep base pulls traits, a mid part mixes long links and multi-size views, and the tail weighs key traits on the fly. Tests on a known chest scan set gave top scores on two truth marks. The team says tone-band facts add real worth to this task.
pmc-13368601:
Ankit Sinha and co-workers map in 2026 the protein lay of hard artery lumps from neck artery cuts, split by cap depth. Lump burst drives most strokes, and thin caps mark weak lumps. The team reads 112 cut lumps by zone with a mass spec tool tied to flesh maps.

Thin and thick cap lumps part most in the dead core and cap zones. Marks of swell, fat work, and bone growth fill the gap. One fat clear protein runs top in thin caps, and stress tests make vessel cells shed more of it. Zone maps guide mark hunts.
pmc-13369101:
Jiajia Deng and co-workers sum up in 2026 two needle routes for neck root pain from worn neck discs. One route, plasma coblation, shrinks the disc core to ease press. The next, pulse waves at the root knot, tunes pain calls with no flesh burn. Both dodge open knife work.

Proof shows both give firm, long pain ease with good safe marks. The disc route can match knife care in picked cases, while pulse care beats shots lone. Pairs of the two, or adds like ozone, show joint gains. Case pick by scan and signs rules the odds.
pmc-13369201:
Hanjing Wang and twelve colleagues published a study in two thousand twenty-six on how people judge phone-based earthquake warnings. Android phones can warn of shaking seconds to a minute ahead. A strong quake near Istanbul in April two thousand twenty-five gave the system a real-world test.

The team used large language models to read over five hundred public posts about the alerts. They pulled out forty-two details about user experience and behaviour. Trust in the system tracked closely with how timely people found the warning. Users treated a fast alert as an accurate alert, whatever the engineering measures said. The authors draw lessons for alert design and public teaching in quake-prone regions.
pmc-13369701:
Yang Yang and colleagues build a computer tool to rank the risk of intravenous drug harm in hospital patients with heart failure in a 2026 study. The tool draws on records from 1,884 adults in seven large hospitals, with a separate group of 100 patients used to test it. Senior pharmacists classed each drug problem by type and by how serious it was.

The model sorts patients into risk levels from mild to more serious, so pharmacists can focus first on those most likely to be harmed. A web version lets care teams use the ranking at the bedside. The work aims to cut preventable drug harm in a group that often takes many strong drugs through a drip, where small errors can quickly become serious.
pmc-13371201:
Irene Msirikale and colleagues assess what intern doctors in Tanzania know about early warning signs of childhood cancer in a 2026 study. About 400,000 children are diagnosed each year worldwide, mostly in lower-income countries where cure rates lag far behind richer nations. Delayed diagnosis is a key driver, and interns are often the first clinicians to spot a suspect case.

The team surveyed 176 interns at Muhimbili National Hospital plus three regional referral hospitals in Dar es Salaam in 2025, testing knowledge alongside training exposure and attitudes. The study identifies which factors track with stronger knowledge, so training programmes can target gaps. Better warning-sign knowledge among interns could speed referral and give children a fairer chance at timely treatment.
pmc-13372201:
Baby Sharma and co-authors follow one man's long sugar disease turnaround in a 2026 case report from India. At age 61 he had new type 2 sugar disease, high weight, and poor blood fats. He joined a three-month plan of plant meals, daily exercise, yoga, and calm mind work.

In four months his weight fell by more than ten kilos and his blood sugar mark dropped to near normal, with no sugar drugs. At eight months he met the set bar for full remission. Yearly sugar drink tests stayed normal for nine years. One case cannot prove a cure, but it shows what steady habit change can hold.
pmc-13373601:
Madison Farnsworth and colleagues build machine learning tools to flag patients at risk after yellow fever vaccination in a 2026 study. The 17D vaccine prevents disease and usually gives lifelong immunity with few adverse events, yet rare reactions matter at scale. The team tested five algorithms, including random forest, gradient boosting, logistic regression, XGBoost, and naive Bayes, on cleaned electronic health records.

Performance was judged by precision, recall, F1 scores, accuracy, and area under the curve, with sampling used to reduce bias in clinical data. Feature ranking highlighted which history and demographic factors most shaped reaction predictions. The framework aims to help clinics spot higher-risk vaccine recipients in advance and watch them more closely after immunisation.
pmc-13373901:
Alexandria Smith Martin and Floyd Thompson review trauma stress in autistic youth in a 2026 paper. The search spanned three data banks and peer work in English from 2010 to 2025. Work on signs, tests, and care in autistic kids and teens was the core.

The review finds that trauma stress is often missed in this group. Signs can blur with autistic traits, speech gaps, sense strain, and the habit of staff to blame all on autism. Screens shaped for these youth, plus views from kin and teachers, help a lot. Fit care can then be built on a true read of the harm.
pmc-13374201:
He Cao and colleagues add a light transformer block to a liver tumour segmentation model in a 2026 validation study. Small, low-contrast liver tumours on contrast CT are hard to segment, partly because standard convolutional encoders miss long-range context. The team inserted a single lightweight Conv-Transformer block at encoder stage 3 of an otherwise unchanged 2D nnU-Net, with a progressive unfreezing schedule for stable tuning.

On an independent cohort of 42 patients, the hybrid scored a mean per-patient tumour Dice of 0.279 against 0.240 for the baseline, a paired gain near 0.039. Medium tumours from 10 to 50 millimetres were examined separately. The modest but pre-specified gain suggests that a small transformer addition, rather than a heavy redesign, can improve external performance for tricky liver lesions.
pmc-13374301:
Juanjuan Guo and others show how melatonin helps red raspberry cope with drought in a 2026 study. Drought cuts raspberry yield and fruit quality, and melatonin is known to aid plant stress toughness. The team tested added melatonin on raspberries at the squaring stage, tracking food-making, protective defences, leaf anatomy, gene activity, and hormone balance.

Drought lowered food-making, protective enzymes, and hormone balance and altered leaf structure. Melatonin, above all at 150 micromoles per litre, eased those harms: food-making and stomatal conductance rose, oxidative damage fell, and osmotic compounds built up. Treated leaves grew thicker with more compact spongy tissue. Gene and metabolite analyses point to coordinated shifts in food-making, carbohydrate, hormone, and amino acid pathways.
pmc-13375101:
Hadley Rahrig and co-authors argue for well-being in the act of research in a 2026 paper. Well-being is a top aim of much health work, yet those who do the work can fare poor. Rates of worry and sad mood run high in grad students and young fellows, the team notes.

Young staff bear much of the load of the science trade and feel that weight most. The paper sets key rules and hands-on steps to build well-being into lab life, not just lab aims. Steps span leads, work loads, and a tone that lets staff rest and speak. Care for staff, they hold, makes the science itself more sound.
pmc-13376101:
Zhenzhen Yang and others name copying factor C subunit 4 as a treatment target in gullet squamous cell cancer in a 2026 study. This cancer is highly lethal and aggressive, and new gene targets are urgently needed. Gene expression data from public GEO data sets were normalised, and in different ways made genes were screened with enrichment, network, and machine learning methods.

The analysis found 752 in different ways made genes, with upregulated DNA copying and mismatch repair pathways and downregulated autophagy. Hub genes AURKA, KIF4A, and RFC4 showed diagnostic areas under the curve from 0.976 to 0.983. Immune infiltration and tissue staining assessed medical relevance. The work presents RFC4 as a candidate for gene finding and aimed therapy in this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13376201:
Khodjaeva and colleagues charted chronic hepatitis D in Uzbekistan in 2026, using records from the national virology institute for 2023 to 2024. Hepatitis D only infects people already carrying hepatitis B, and it speeds liver damage, yet severity and treatment access in the country were poorly documented. The team reviewed all 1,393 hepatitis B patients who attended the institute in that year.

Coinfection with hepatitis D was the norm, found in about three of four patients. Those patients were younger yet far sicker: about 78 percent had cirrhosis, liver scarring, against about 44 percent in hepatitis B alone. Active hepatitis D virus was found in most of those tested, but only four patients had ever received treatment aimed at the virus. Cancer screening was thin in both groups. The authors call for wider access to hepatitis D therapy and screening.
pmc-13380201:
Muhammed Yusuf Afacan and a large team present a 2026 review of injuries to the ring of bones and joints that suspends the shoulder. Breaks at several points in that ring are uncommon and varied, and most published evidence comes from small case reports. That leaves surgeons with little guidance on when to operate.

The review builds a practical framework that starts with recognising the injury pattern, then steps through imaging, signs of instability, and the choice of treatment. Patient factors such as age, bone quality, other illnesses, and physical demands are weighed at each step. Illustrative cases from the authors' own institution show how the framework works in practice.
pmc-13380601:
Veronika Boichenko and colleagues present a 2026 review of small RNA molecules that help control scarring in the liver and the heart. Scarring, called fibrosis, stiffens both organs and drives long-term failure. It involves activated support cells, excess scaffolding material, and inflammation in each organ.

The review compares three families of non-coding RNAs, which regulate genes without building proteins. Some of them act alike in liver and heart, switching the same scarring pathways up or down. Others behave differently depending on the organ. Because these molecules also circulate in the blood inside tiny parcels, they may serve as low-burden test markers. The comparison highlights shared drug targets across both organs.
pmc-13380801:
Thomas Roosdorp, Michael Fridén, Daniel B Ibsen, and Fredrik Rosqvist published a 2026 methods study on how nutrition researchers model swapping one food for another. When studies adjust for total energy, they are in effect estimating substitution, and earlier simulations showed the modelling choice can flip the apparent effect. Few studies had tested the approaches on real data.

The authors compared strategies using milk, fermented and not, against death from any cause in a Swedish group of 1,063 older men. Models differed in which foods they adjusted for and whether intake was counted in grams, energy, or a mix. Eighteen model versions were run. The comparison shows how much conclusions depend on choices that are often left unstated.
pmc-13382301:
Qingyi Wu and a large team present a 2026 study on adding riboflavin, a B vitamin, to duck feed to improve breast meat quality. Pekin ducks are a major meat breed. Ninety-six young ducks were fed for 28 days with either no added riboflavin or a supplemented diet, in groups with several replicates.

Supplemented ducks had firmer breast meat and thicker muscle fibres. Gene studies showed higher activity in genes that drive muscle development and contraction, and in genes for building and burning fats. Chemical profiling of the meat showed more fat-burning related compounds. The combined evidence, gathered with several large-scale methods, explains how a cheap vitamin can change meat texture and composition.
pmc-13382701:
Jack E Thirkell and colleagues present a 2026 study of resting energy use in naked mole-rats, social mammals that live underground in colonies with a single breeding female. Resting metabolic rate shapes how energy is divided between survival, breeding, and long life. Its drivers inside such a structured society were unclear.

The team measured 76 animals from five colonies, testing body mass, sex, breeding status, age, rank, and colony stability. Body mass predicted energy use most strongly, though rates were far below those expected for mammals of that size, confirming a suppressed metabolism. Breeding females ran slightly higher than non-breeders, while age and rank had no effect once mass was allowed for.
pmc-13383401:
Giuseppe Giglia's team reports the first pituitary blastoma in a dog, in a 2026 animal case report. In people, this rare tumor of the front pituitary gland is tied to DICER1 syndrome and mostly affects children, with hormone excess and mass effects. The canine patient showed signs of ACTH-driven cortisol excess from a pituitary mass.

Histology revealed hallmark features matching the human tumor, including Rathke epithelium rosettes and primitive blastemal cells. Staining tests confirmed ACTH expression and nuclear TBX19, supporting a corticotroph origin. The case extends a human rare tumor entity into animal medicine and aids cross-species study of DICER1-related disease.
pmc-13383901:
Meixner and colleagues lay out a technique for revision repair of a ruptured quadriceps tendon, reinforced with a biocomposite scaffold, in a 2026 orthopedic technique paper. The quadriceps tendon, anchoring the thigh muscle to the kneecap, typically tears in middle-aged men, with systemic illness weakening the tissue. First-time repairs succeed. The method combines transosseous fixation, sutures passed through tunnels in the kneecap, with a cerclage, a reinforcing loop that shares load across it. Over the scaffold the surgeons lay BioBrace, a biocomposite implant to support healing biologically while adding strength. Meixner presents the sequence, from exposure and tissue preparation to closure and rehabilitation logic, as a reproducible recipe for a problem with no standard solution. It aims to give the tendon mechanical and biological help.
pmc-13384501:
Bhakti Banerjee and co-authors reply to readers about their study of tissue oxygen during heart surgery in a 2026 response letter. The original work tracked kidney and muscle oxygen with near-infrared sensors during bypass surgery. Readers had raised points about early creatinine shifts and what they truly signal.

The authors agree that small early creatinine changes do not always mean real kidney injury. They explain design choices, including a depth rule for sensor placement and using thumb muscle as a stand-in site. Both sides converge on the view that global blood flow targets alone cannot capture local tissue supply.
pmc-13384901:
Dania Al-Qasrawi and co-authors name an early driver of pancreatic cancer growth in 2026 research. The protein ECT2, known for roles in cell division, rises early in pancreatic ductal tumors and stays high as disease advances. High levels also track with poorer patient survival in the datasets studied.

Removing ECT2 slowed transformed growth, invasion, and tumor formation in animals, with little effect on cell division itself. Blocking its signaling also made cancer cells more sensitive to MEK-targeted drugs, which marks a possible paired treatment route.
pmc-13386501:
Yuxiang Zhao and colleagues track antibiotic resistance genes in Chinese soils across 14 years in 2026 work. Their set of 2,243 soil metagenomes spans 2009 to 2022 and feeds an open interactive map platform. The study tests whether the national action plan period left a mark on farm soils.

After 2016, total resistance gene abundance in croplands fell markedly compared with earlier samples, with high-risk genes dropping even more steeply. Cropland profiles worldwide also grew more alike under similar farm pressures, a homogenization the authors flag. They call for global coordination joining pollution control with better farm practice.
pmc-13386601:
Ryo Kanda and colleagues use guided talking-aloud to rebuild self-monitoring after stroke in a 2026 report of two cases. Both patients had executive problems that hurt daily life despite standard tabletop cognitive training. Therapists prompted each patient to voice their thinking, catch errors, and reflect during the tasks.

After the program, both patients completed trail-making tests they could not finish before. One also stopped making medication errors, and daily goal-directed behavior improved in both cases. The authors present guided verbalization as a feasible bridge from clinic tasks to real life, while noting two cases cannot prove cause.
pmc-13386701:
Maria Piedade Brandão and Beatriz Chaves studied digitalization and mental health among older primary care professionals in Portugal, in a 2026 mixed-methods case study. Digital tools transform primary care but add cognitive load and technostress, especially for workers aged 50 and older. The team surveyed 24 professionals aged 50-plus, 92 percent of eligible staff, in a northern Portuguese primary care unit.

Most recognized digitalization benefits for performance and efficiency at 91.7 percent, yet 62.5 percent reported more work stress and 33.4 percent worse work-life balance. Only 25.0 percent felt they had enough time to learn new technologies. Data protection confidence ran high, but only 26.1 percent reported adequate privacy training, flagging a training gap.
pmc-13386901:
Emre Aydin's team studied posterior air and gas migration after Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty, in a 2026 retrospective case series. After DMEK, air or gas placed to hold the graft can slip backward into the vitreous cavity, threatening graft attachment, especially when anterior-posterior segment integrity is compromised. Age, chamber depth, pressure, and visual acuity did not differ between groups, but pupils ran larger in the scleral-fixated group. Overall, 9 eyes, about 22 percent, developed backward migration, far more often with scleral-fixated lenses, about 64 percent versus about 7 percent. Larger pupils and prior retinal surgery also tracked with migration. The findings flag scleral-fixated lenses as a strong risk factor for graft detachment after DMEK.
pmc-13387401:
Priyanga Paranthaman's team pooled gene-activity data from five earlier studies to find immune-linked genes driving triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form that lacks three common treatment targets. They merged microarray and RNA gene reading results, mapped how the resulting proteins interact, and checked which genes sat at the centre of those networks.

KIF20A emerged as a promising but little-studied target, and the authors argue that reusing approved drugs against these hubs could speed up new treatment options.
pmc-13387601:
Cui and colleagues trace premature ovarian insufficiency, early loss of ovarian function, to a metabolic switch thrown by a missing enzyme regulator, in 2026 reproductive biology research. pmc-13389001:
Ezequiel Dantas's team ran a small randomised feasibility trial of a very-low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet in nineteen women with overweight or obesity and untreated endometrial cancer. People were assigned two-to-one to the diet or a standard diet for three to four weeks before treatment, with feasibility as the main goal.

Fifteen women finished, nearly all diet meals were eaten, weight fell about five percent, and no severe adverse events appeared. Fasting glucose and insulin dropped sharply while cholesterol rose modestly, and tumour samples showed more CD8 T cells at the margins. The authors call the diet feasible and well tolerated, not yet proven therapeutic.
pmc-13389501:
Chen-Xun Weng's team built and showed a fast relativistic zero-knowledge proof that stays secure even against quantum foes. Usual proofs rest on math guesses, and an earlier quantum-sound matched version needed so many rounds that real rollout was impractical.

Their one-sided protocol uses light-speed bit commitments and proves quantum soundness through the CHSH nonlocal game, with round count growing in line with the number of graph edges. A proof-of-principle run finished all live rounds in about 0.22 seconds at a random-bits cost near 431 megabytes, showing no-trust cryptography can lean on relativity as well as quantum theory.
pmc-13390201:
Sondra Turjeman's team tested whether having given birth before, and how births are spaced, shifts the mother germ mix in mice. Carrying young shifts gut germs in people, and earlier work hinted that changes might persist after birth, yet birth history's own effect stayed little-studied.

Mouse studies of carrying-young germs must account for age first, or they risk mistaking age effects for parity effects in both breeding and broader long-run designs.
pmc-13392201:
Donald R Royall and Raymond F Palmer test, in 2026, whether being afflicted by several dementia biomarkers at once adds up to worse dementia. Their view is that dementia has many causes at once. Alzheimer's-linked markers form just one set among them.

The team used tested scoring rules on nearly a thousand scan-positive people from a national imaging pool. Each person was classed as hit by, or holding firm against, three harms. The harms were brain amyloid, blood fat signals, and nerve cell loss. Dementia severity scores rose with the number of afflicting markers, in both demented and non-demented groups, and conversion risk was also tracked. pmc-13392501:
Milad Noei and colleagues measured two linked molecules in breast tissue: a small regulatory RNA called miR-326, known to restrain tumours, and NOB1, a gene needed to build the cell's protein-shredding proteasome. Earlier work showed the RNA targets NOB1 messages and lowers its output. The study compared cancer tissue, tissue beside the tumour, and healthy breast tissue.

Quantitative PCR testing covered forty-one cancers with matched nearby tissue plus eight healthy samples. The small RNA ran markedly lower in cancer than in either comparison group, while NOB1 ran higher, and the two moved in opposite directions within samples. Test accuracy figures were fair for both markers. The authors read the pattern as support for a control link that loosens in cancer, and float both molecules as possible markers for diagnosis or treatment research.
pmc-13393801:
Li and co-authors compare, in 2026, how resident physicians fare after intensive care unit night shifts versus night shifts on other wards. Sixty-one residents at one teaching hospital completed the questionnaire after a non-ICU night shift and after a second ICU night shift, so each doctor served as their own comparison. The survey captured duty length, sleep during the shift, overnight calls and awakenings, recovery, and well-being.

ICU nights brought longer duties, less sleep during the shift, and more work-related awakenings than ward nights. Emotional exhaustion ran higher after ICU shifts, with a mean paired difference of 3.39 points on the study scale. Life satisfaction also dropped, by 8.90 points on average in the paired comparison. The authors frame night-shift burden as more than a shift count, urging residency programs to target sleep opportunity, interruptions, and recovery time in scheduling.
pmc-13394901:
Patrick Swain and colleagues test, in 2026, jumping in fake Moon gravity with tight leg cuffs as space exercise. Fourteen healthy adults jumped while hung from a tilted frame that left them at one fifth of their weight. On one visit, cuffs partly blocked leg blood flow during two-minute jump rounds. The team tracked heart rate, breath gases, muscle oxygen, and felt effort.

With cuffs, hearts beat faster and muscles held less oxygen. Breath output and the burn marker lactate also rose. Leg force dropped about the same with or without cuffs after the sets. Effort and discomfort felt higher with cuffs. The authors say the cheap setup could help crews keep fit on the Moon.
pmc-13395401:
Aikta Sharma and co-authors film, in 2026, tiny strains inside mouse knees to catch arthritis at its start. Healthy joints pass loads smoothly across their parts. The team loaded knee bones while scanning them with bright X-rays, then computed strain in three dimensions. They compared normal mice with a strain prone to joint disease.

In disease-prone knees, hot spots of strain bunched in the bone plate under cartilage at ten weeks of age. That was before any cartilage wear showed. Healthy knees, young or old, sent strain away from the surface instead. Models blamed local flaws in bone texture. The authors name misaligned micro-structure as an early driver worth watching.
pmc-13396101:
Jiao Yang and others weigh crizotinib against vebreltinib in lung cancers with MET exon 14 skips in a 2026 real-world study. These gene faults hit 1 to 3 percent of non-small lung cancers, and drug spurn stays a snag.

Among 24 patients, middle time without growth hit 7.0 months in all, with crizotinib at 6.1 months and half worsening in three months, while vebreltinib held longer. Tumor defense maps and lab-grown tumor balls in dishes from three patients added response hints. Cancer doctors gain head-to-head data for picking between MET drugs with more sureness.
pmc-13396301:
Barbara Poletti and colleagues compared rival scoring rules for sorting ALS patients by their thinking and behavior profile, in a 2026 study. ALS, the motor neuron disease that weakens muscles, also affects the mind in many patients, and clinics need a shared way to name those changes.

Records came from 901 patients with no formal dementia diagnosis, each screened with the Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen plus a carer interview. The team applied several published algorithms, including those of Abrahams and of Poletti's own group, under the standard Strong criteria. Where the rules disagree on the same person, the study shows which choices drive the clash.
pmc-13396501:
Weiju Hao and others wake lattice oxygen in metal rust sheets for tough sea-water splitting in a 2026 study. Green sea-water splitting could mass-make green hydrogen, but plate rot and rival chlorine gas at high currents block the path.

Iron foam regrown into boron-laced cobalt-iron rust sheets bore oxygen gaps that eased water-split drag. The plate needed just 325 millivolts for 1.0 amp per square centimeter and shed under 2 percent punch after 600 hours in base sea water. Messy lattices freed a lattice-oxygen path past old caps. The paper moves factory green hydrogen a step near.
pmc-13397701:
Shuai Ren and Jun Wen review how sepsis can flip the immune system from overdrive into shutdown. Their 2026 survey covers the damage across both arms of immunity, from worn-out front-line cells to depleted T and B cells and a tangled signal network. Candidate treatments aim to wake the system back up, including IL-7, GM-CSF, checkpoint drugs and donated antibody preparations. The authors warn that none of these has yet proven itself in routine care, so careful trials remain the priority.
pmc-13398101:
Maria Grazia Cusi and co-authors report the first firm proof that Sindbis virus can invade the human brain and spinal cord. Family-tree analysis showed Clade D lineages circulating together in Italy, painting a tangled local picture. Sindbis, the authors conclude, should join the list of viruses doctors consider when the nervous system flares without a cause.
pmc-13398301:
Taylor C Johnson and co-authors test whether stronger local smoking bans bent cancer trends in Louisiana. Their 2026 study uses state tumour registry data from 2007 through 2022. Orleans Parish declined steadily at an annual pace near 3.02 percent per year in its trend line. Ouachita's line bent in 2016, and the paper weighs whether local laws, rather than background drift, explain the gaps.
pmc-13399101:

The journal's editor-in-chief, the Federation of European Biochemical Societies, and Wiley agreed readers should be alerted.

A third party posting on PubPeer pointed out a duplication. A STAT5 protein band in one figure also appears in a later paper by some of the same authors, shown there as different results. The editors confirmed the duplication. The authors supplied data to support their findings. Yet much of the underlying material, from work done in 2010 to 2012, no longer exists. Because a correction could not settle the matter, the journal flags the reporting as doubtful.
pmc-13399301:

The team set out to characterize these patients in a middle-income country during the months before vaccines arrived.

They included hospitalized adults who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 inside 14 days of stroke onset and had an imaging-confirmed event. pmc-13399401: The notice is a correction only. pmc-13399701:
Yukio Akasaki and colleagues describe a grafting trick that harvests bone from holes the surgeon has to drill anyway, in a 2026 technique paper. Their technique, abbreviated CATS, cores spongy bone out of the locking plate's proximal screw pilot holes in the tibia and packs it into the gap.

The authors call it a simple adjunct to plate fixation that delivers local graft with zero extra incisions.
pmc-13399801:
Taidhgin J. Keel and co-authors, including senior surgeon Robert F. LaPrade, describe a combined operation that fixes three related knee problems in one sitting, in a 2026 technique paper. Rebuilding the anterolateral ligament with the patient's own iliotibial band is meant to calm that rotation and protect both meniscus repairs.

The sequence starts by harvesting an 8 by 1 centimeter strip of iliotibial band, left attached at Gerdy's tubercle. Its free end is anchored at the ligament's tibial and femoral footprints. The authors argue that treating the rotational laxity and both tears together gives the meniscus its best chance to heal.
pmc-13400501:
Zhao and co-authors construct, in 2026, a signature for cutaneous melanoma from genes linking cuproptosis, a copper-driven form of cell death, with immune activity. Starting from cancer atlas data, they identified 474 cuproptosis-related immune genes by correlation, then found 194 of them dysregulated in melanoma against normal tissue. Cox and LASSO methods distilled the list into a twelve-gene model used to split patients into high- and low-risk groups.

The training cohort held 406 patients, and an independent cohort of 208 patients validated the model. High-risk patients survived worse, with tumors showing reduced immune infiltration, suppressed checkpoint levels, and lower mutational burden, an immunosuppressed microenvironment profile. Low-risk tumors looked immune-inflamed, with higher mutational burden and checkpoint gene levels, suggesting better candidacy for checkpoint blockade. Drug response analysis hinted high-risk patients might benefit from other agents, making the signature a tool for therapy selection.
pmc-13400601:
Blanca Sánchez-Moreno and co-authors compare, in 2026, where a language-linked gene factor called Foxp2 appears in the mouse, rat and macaque thalamus. Foxp2 is essential for building brain circuits for language. Its pattern in the cortex is well known, but the thalamus, a relay hub deep in the brain, was poorly mapped.

The protein appeared in most thalamic nuclei in all three species, but was consistently absent from two areas. Levels ran highest in midline and intralaminar nuclei. Macaques showed broader and stronger expression in associative regions such as the pulvinar. The authors read this as a conserved role in circuits for attention, memory and sensorimotor integration, expanded in primates alongside more complex wiring.
pmc-13400701:
Lingke Jiang, Robbie M Parks, Yoshira Ornelas Van Horne and Xiao Wu study, in 2026, how social vulnerability in United States communities evolves for years after tropical cyclones. Most research stops days or months after a storm. Long-term shifts in who lives in exposed places matter for recovery and fairness.

Using a synthetic control method, the team covered all United States cyclones from 2005 to 2018. Vulnerability rose in the year after a storm. It stayed elevated for at least five years. By twelve years, though, it fell slightly below what would be expected without a storm. That late reversal may reflect gentrification, where poorer residents are displaced and replaced by wealthier newcomers.
pmc-13401201:
Qi Zhou and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of the high-intensity zone and its place in disc degeneration. The zone is a bright spot in the outer ring of a lumbar disc on T2-weighted MRI scans. They frame the zone as a dynamic inflammatory hub rather than a passive imaging curiosity.

After a tear in the disc's outer ring, granulation tissue full of small blood vessels grows in, and new nerves grow with it. That sets up a self-feeding cycle of inflammation and matrix breakdown. Signals such as TNF-alpha and IL-1beta and enzymes such as MMPs and ADAMTS drive the cycle. The review also covers artificial intelligence and multimodal imaging for spotting the zone. Its diagnostic strength is high specificity for disc-related low back pain, though sensitivity is limited and false positives occur.
pmc-13401301:
Ahmed Abdellatif and colleagues ran a 2026 double-blinded randomized trial of computer-guided jaw fracture repair against the conventional plate method. The injury in question is a parasymphyseal mandibular fracture, a break near the chin, where standard open reduction and plate fixing depend heavily on surgeon experience and take considerable time.

Twenty-six patients with uncomplicated breaks of this type were randomized into two groups. The intervention group received a full virtual surgical planning protocol using a screw-holes locator guide and patient-specific custom plates. The comparison group had conventional plate osteosynthesis. The trial's central question is overall precision: whether the guided workflow reproduces the planned bone position more accurately and reproducibly than the experience-based routine, which the authors describe as labor-intensive and variable.
pmc-13401401:
Fuli Yan and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of stimuli-responsive biomimetic nanomedicines for ischemic stroke. These tiny drug carriers are dressed in biological material and release their cargo in response to conditions at the injury site. Stroke care has improved with clot removal and clot-busting drugs, yet getting medicine into the brain remains hard.

The blood-brain barrier, short treatment windows, varied lesion patterns, and secondary injury after blood flow returns all limit delivery. Carriers borrowing from cell membranes, extracellular vesicles, or natural targeting molecules can circulate longer, dodge the immune system, and home in on damaged tissue. The review weighs design principles and animal evidence against translation hurdles: safety and immune concerns, uncertain drug behaviour in the body, hard-to-scale manufacturing, and quality control. Regulation counts too, plus the trade-off between loading more drug and releasing it well.
pmc-13401701:
Mehdi Safarabadi and co-authors ran a 2026 randomized trial of progressive muscle relaxation for people with hypothyroidism whose fatigue and low mood persist despite standard hormone replacement. The Jacobson technique, tensing and releasing muscle groups in sequence, is a low-cost self-help candidate.

Sixty-eight adults at Fateme-Zahra Hospital in Khomain were split into relaxation training or routine care. The training group practised the technique twice daily for four weeks, and everyone completed tested fatigue and depression forms at the start and end. All 68 members stayed to the end, and the groups began largely alike. The control group showed no real change over the month. The relaxation group, by contrast, recorded clear drops in fatigue, and depression and quality-of-life results were also scored.
pmc-13402001:
Ravi Sharma and colleagues followed 282 adults after fracture surgery to test whether cheap blood markers can warn of early trouble. Patients were 18 to 65 years old and had fixation surgery at a large care center between December 2022 and June 2024. The team tracked ESR, C-reactive protein, D-dimer, and white cell counts from admission through day 14 after surgery.

Fifty patients, or 17.7 percent of the group, developed problems that included fracture-related infection, low oxygen, or low blood pressure needing support drugs. C-reactive protein gave the clearest warning for infection, especially when it stayed high near day 5 after surgery. High D-dimer flagged patients more likely to develop breathing or blood pressure problems. The authors suggest serial testing of both markers as a low-cost watch system where resources are tight.
pmc-13402101:
Samuel Novais and colleagues studied how beetles that live in dead wood, and the enemies that eat or parasitize them, answered the wreckage left by Hurricane Patricia. The category 5 storm flattened wide areas of tropical dry forest in Jalisco, Mexico, in October 2015. For two January seasons the team left 148 freshly cut branches in the field for 45 days, then trapped whatever insects emerged.

The first year brought more life: 133 species and 22,797 insects, against 82 species and 11,165 insects a year later. Fast-growing bark beetles and parasitoid wasps peaked early, while long-developing longhorn beetles and predatory beetles peaked in year two. The authors read the shift as a race set by life history: quick species feast first, then rivals and predators press them down as the wood ages.
pmc-13402301:
Heyi Wang and colleagues challenge a textbook strength rule by pulling layered crystals apart between their sheets. Frenkel classic model caps ideal elastic strain near 10 percent for strong solids, and ordinary materials obey it. Wang and the team stretched graphite and hexagonal boron nitride along the layer direction in place, pairing the tests with first-principles math.

Both crystals failed far early, by local splitting at roughly 3 percent strain for graphite and 2 percent for boron nitride, well below what flaws alone would explain. Other layered solids such as molybdenum disulfide and gallium selenide showed no such local split. The authors trace the failure to a flexural phonon instability, a bending vibration that runs away and opens repeating nanogaps to dump stored energy. The finding resets the true elastic limits of these layered solids and hints at strain tricks for tuning them.
pmc-13402501:
Mehmet Celegen writes a critical letter on a study of drug poisoning in emergency care by Oksuz and colleagues, arguing the work describes cases without measuring what matters for treatment. The study offered useful regional counts, yet it graded no severity. Hospital and intensive care admission rates, Celegen notes, reflect local practice and bed supply as much as poisoning depth, and no scores such as the Poisoning Severity Score were used.

Exposure detail also fell short. Broad drug classes stood in for dose and timing, and unidentified substances entered the case mix. Outcomes such as ventilator need, blood pressure drugs, or death went unreported. With 77 percent of cases tied to suicidal intent, the lack of any psychiatric or social variables wasted a chance to place findings inside self-harm care. Celegen asks future studies to record severity, dose, timing, and mental health context from the start.
pmc-13402801:
Sophie Seidel and colleagues present SciPhy, a Bayesian tool that rebuilds cell family trees from CRISPR lineage tracing records, using not only which edits happened but their order. Sequential editing stamps a running history into DNA, richer than a single snapshot. Built inside the BEAST 2 platform, SciPhy jointly estimates time-scaled trees and cell population growth numbers from those records.

On simulated data and on a real single-clone cell culture, SciPhy rebuilt trees more accurately than rival methods, and unlike simple clustering it reports uncertainty plus proliferation rates. A second test on mouse gastruloids, lab models of early embryos, showed it handling population sizes that change over time. The code is public. The authors pitch the framework as the quantitative backbone lineage tracing has lacked.
pmc-13403401:
Yao Xu and team modeled how tiny joint-line raises after partial knee replacement change knee mechanics. Their 2026 work uses a checked finite element model built from CT and MRI data. It simulates medial fixed-bearing partial knee replacement at native height, plus 1 millimeter, and plus 2 millimeters joint line height across four bend angles. Joint line elevation is common during surgery, but its biomechanical effects had been unexplored.

Effects depended strongly on bend angle and on induced alignment shifts. At full extension, elevation shifted alignment outward and raised outer compartment stress.
