One quirk emerged: GPP genetic correlations are directional, depending on which trait benchmarks the other.
pmc-13464101:
Mansoureh Barzegar and seven co-authors chart the small RNAs that guide human oligodendrocyte growth. These cells wrap nerve fibers in myelin, the fatty coat that speeds signals. Most prior maps came from rodents, leaving human steps poorly known.

The team grew the cells from human stem cells and fished out each stage with a built-in marker. Sequencing found stage-locked microRNAs, counting several never tied to this cell line before. Computer checks tied the new RNAs to target genes and to AKT and SMAD paths, both known growth routes. The atlas gives researchers fresh markers and candidate levers for myelin repair work.
pmc-13464401:
Hye-Jin Kang and eight co-authors craft two new stevia sweeteners with two enzymes in sequence. Rebaudioside M tastes closest to sugar among stevia compounds, yet plants hold little of it and it dissolves poorly in drinks. Their route starts from stevioside, a plentiful stevia compound.

A first enzyme added glucose units in one pattern, and a second enzyme finished the build, converting nearly all of the mid-product. The two analogs dissolved over one hundred times better than the natural compound in water. Both held up under heat and across wide acidity, and they kept their sweetness about three times longer in a tart store drink. Taste sensors rated one analog balanced and the other sweetness-forward with little bitterness.
pmc-13464801:

In healthy men with normal levels, a placebo-controlled trial found no real change in hormones or sperm. Gains seem to ride on better metabolic health rather than a direct hormone push. pmc-13465201:
Marcel Wehmann and four co-authors report a rare aorta cancer that masqueraded as graft infection after aneurysm repair. Infection markers ran only mildly high, and she had no fever.

PET imaging showed a hot mass hugging the aorta, a picture that fits bad infection or cancer alike. A fine needle biopsy settled the doubt by finding malignant cells. Surgeons removed the tumor wholesale, replaced the aorta section, and added chemotherapy with two drugs. Tissue study confirmed angiosarcoma, a vessel-wall cancer, which shows how biopsy can rescue a misleading case.
pmc-13465601:
Zengchen Liu and colleagues investigate why some virus-positive throat and mouth cancers still spread to neck lymph nodes, in a 2026 study of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Such cancers often end better than virus-negative ones, yet node spread still harms outlook and complicates care. The group worked with public single-cell and gene-activity data sets plus laboratory experiments.

They found a stem-like group of tumor cells tied to node spread. Early genes of the HPV16 virus seemed to lower levels of a protein called SERPINB3, and changes linked to the viral E7 gene connected with MYC pathway activity and stronger cell movement. The work offers one possible route by which the virus shapes how these tumors behave.
pmc-13466201:
Roepke and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the helper proteins that usher cargo through the type three secretion system. The rig is a needle germs use to inject attack proteins into host cells. It fires in order: needle parts, pore parts, then the attack set. Each cargo class has its own helper class. The review sets helper shapes and codes side by side.

Helpers guard cargo from firing too soon inside the germ. They hold loose cargo from clumping or rot, and walk it to the rig in rank order. pmc-13466301:
Dalal Al-Mutairi and colleagues report a gene fault behind heart and skin disease in an Arabian family with four affected sisters, in a 2026 case study. The sisters shared a heart muscle disorder, thickened skin on palms and soles, and woolly hair, a combination known as Carvajal syndrome. The two eldest died suddenly as children.

Mapping of shared inherited stretches pointed to the DSP gene on chromosome six. Sequencing found a stop-signal change present in two copies in the sisters, hitting only one of the gene's two message forms, the one that builds desmoplakin I. Both parents carried a single copy. Heart scans in the surviving sisters showed both ventricles involved.
pmc-13466801:
Yumin Wu and six colleagues published this 2026 review of stage-adapted cryotherapy, treatment by freezing, for oral mucosal melanoma, a rare cancer inside the mouth. The team reviewed 43 patients treated between 2016 and 2026. Earlier-stage patients received cryotherapy alone, while stage IV patients had freezing plus wide surgery. Estimated survival for the whole group was 93.0 percent at two years and 69.8 percent at five years after treatment started. Local recurrence struck 2 of 11 earlier-stage patients but 18 of 32 stage IV patients. Spread to lymph nodes was tied to worse survival, with a hazard ratio of 3.342 in their analysis. The authors stress the study was small and non-randomised.
pmc-13467001:

The process sparks a ceramic-like layer onto the metal in a chemical bath, guarding against corrosion. Simple fluoride additives were the old recipe; complex forms carrying zirconium, titanium, silicon, aluminum, or phosphorus now draw interest.

Most of these complexes break down in water depending on bath acidity and stabilizers. Stopping that breakdown is the key step, the authors argue, because intact complexes put more fluorine into the coating and improve its structure, phase makeup, and corrosion resistance. Bath chemistry thus decides the armor's quality.
pmc-13467501:

Simple comparisons of variant frequencies showed no clear differences between patients and controls. A fuller model that assumed two copies of a variant were needed did find significant links for one variant each in the MMP1 and MMP2 genes. Haplotype analysis, which looks at variants inherited together, also showed a significant overall pattern. The authors read the results as hints that tissue-remodeling genes shape risk in combination rather than alone.
pmc-13467801:
Katielle Vieira Avelino and colleagues explore in 2026 whether growing mushrooms together changes the useful chemistry of their fungal threads. Some single cultures led on antioxidant activity, while sun protection reached a factor of 39 in several single and paired systems. pmc-13468901:
Sabina Szymoniak and Mariusz Kubanek review in 2026 how distributed artificial intelligence can defend the Internet of Things, a web of billions of devices no central guardian can watch. Critical infrastructure gets special attention, because there a security failure threatens public safety and service continuity, not just privacy. The authors close with the research gaps: trust between cooperating agents, energy budgets, and standards. Their survey argues the defense of sprawling device networks must itself be sprawling and cooperative.
pmc-13469001:
Christoph Lange and four colleagues published this 2026 article on measuring the randomness of stochastic bit sequences. Standard test suites check whether bits behave as independent, identically distributed draws, but specialised checks are costly. The authors present a simpler gap-based approach. The authors offer it as a low-complexity complement to full randomness suites.
pmc-13469301:
Yuhan Gong and colleagues tested Saponin C in 2026, the main compound from Liriope muscari tubers, against influenza A and SARS-CoV-2. pmc-13469901:
Minseok Kim, Taekwon Kim, Kyungsub Song, Sang-hun Lee, and Jonghoon Yoo chart in 2026 where the burden of fall injuries falls across stages of care in Korea. Falls send older adults to hospitals in large numbers, but the stage at which harm concentrates differs by age. Emergency visit rates peaked in young children and in adults aged seventy five and older, at similar levels. From that point the paths split sharply. Admission after an emergency visit rose from under three percent in young children to about forty three percent in the oldest group. Hospitalization rates in the oldest adults ran about two and a half times those of adults aged sixty five to seventy four.
pmc-13470001:
Farhat and a large team report outcomes for a common leukemia subtype in this 2026 study from MD Anderson Cancer Center. The subtype is acute myeloid leukemia carrying a change in the NPM1 gene, which usually signals a better outlook, yet long-term results vary. The authors reviewed 396 newly diagnosed patients, who made up 18 percent of cases at the center, and compared treatments.

Patients given intensive chemotherapy lived a median of about 84.7 months, with just over half alive at five years. Those given a gentler drug pairing lived a median of about 23.3 months instead. Among intensively treated patients, older age, poor daily functioning, a FLT3-ITD gene change, or disease outside the marrow predicted worse survival. A cladribine-based lower-intensity regimen beat the gentler pairing in an age-matched comparison.
pmc-13470201:

pmc-13471201:

pmc-13471301:

Of those eight, two leftovers shrank, four stayed stable, and two grew and needed a second operation. No child with complete removal relapsed. pmc-13471401:
Kantha and co-authors compared leg muscle quality between older adults who had fallen in the past year and those who had not. Their 2026 cross-sectional study enrolled 120 community-dwelling adults, split evenly into 60 fallers and 60 non-fallers with median ages near 70.

Muscle quality was read from phase angle, an electrical measure from body-composition scans that reflects cell health. Overall phase angle did not differ between groups, but left-right asymmetry in the legs at the 5 kHz frequency was greater in fallers, with a statistical link of rs 0.29 to fall status. Prospective studies, they note, must still show whether the measure predicts future falls.
pmc-13471501:

The review weighs which therapies carry solid review-level evidence for the guideline panel.
pmc-13473101:

The authors frame ethical design, not raw security, as the bottleneck for connected transport.
pmc-13473301:
Panico and colleagues compared keyhole versus robotic surgery for ventral rectopexy, an operation that lifts a prolapsing rectum, in women treated at women's health centers. Their 2026 study of past cases included 102 women, 60 treated by keyhole surgery and 42 robotically, with functional scoring at a mean of 18 months.

Both approaches delivered large symptom relief. Constipation scores on the Wexner scale fell sharply with both methods: from 17.7 points to 2.5 after keyhole surgery, and from 15.2 points to 2.6 after robotic surgery. Incontinence scores dropped in step, from 11.6 points to 1.1 and from 10.7 points to 1.2 across the two methods, all highly significant. Posterior prolapse relapsed in just 1.0% of women, and no outcome significantly favored either technology. A combined front repair accompanied 70.6% of the operations.
pmc-13473501:
Salehi and co-authors compared the gene activity of nestin-expressing hair follicle cells, an accessible stem cell source, against bone marrow cells, dental pulp cells, astrocytes, and hypothalamic neurons. Their 2026 study measured growth-factor and neural-marker genes to judge the follicle cells' promise for nerve repair.

The follicle cells punched above their weight as growth-factor factories: their Gdnf expression ran 4.8-fold higher than in cortical astrocytes and 27-fold higher than in the hypothalamic cell line, with Bdnf comparable to bone marrow cells. Their Tubb3, a neuronal skeleton gene, ran 2.1-fold above bone marrow cells and 1.4-fold above dental pulp cells. Curiously, their own nestin marker sat lower, at 0.38-fold of dental pulp levels, hinting at readiness to mature into neurons.
pmc-13474001:
Isobel J Fetter, Veronica Haro Acosta, Sachin Parecadan and Shaheen S Sikandar published this 2026 study on how the protein LMO2 enables STAT3 in breast cancer cells. STAT3's activation drives tumour growth and spread, and the team had shown LMO2 helps STAT3 get phosphorylated, its activation mark. They asked whether an always-on version of STAT3 still needs LMO2 to produce metastases in mouse xenograft tumours.

It did. Forcing STAT3 into permanent activity was not enough to drive metastasis when LMO2 was knocked down in the cancer cells. Fractionation experiments showed why: LMO2 is required twice over, first for STAT3 phosphorylation in the cytoplasm and then for STAT3 to move into the nucleus, where it acts on genes. Without LMO2, the signal stalls outside the nucleus. The authors conclude that LMO2 controls the activation and the delivery of STAT3, making it a chokepoint in this metastasis pathway.
pmc-13474501:
Wang and co-authors fed cherry tomato seedlings a fertilizer made of beetle dung: the frass of Protaetia brevitarsis larvae, insects that efficiently digest crop straw into humus-rich droppings. Their 2026 pot experiments mixed the frass into growing substrate at 1, 2, 4, and 8% by weight and tracked plant growth alongside the substrate's microbial community.

The middle doses worked: 2% and 4% frass produced stockier, more robust plants with heavier stems and roots, while 8% proved too much and was dropped from sampling. Frass raised microbial diversity through two routes at once, importing its own microbes directly and waking up unknown resident microbes already in the substrate. The material's combined nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium content clears the 5% threshold in China's organic fertilizer standard, supporting its farm case.
pmc-13474801:
Zhaosashuang Tian and co-authors catalog a gene family in wheat in 2026 that may help plants handle drought and salt. Nine genes of the HB-PHD family were found across the wheat genome. Their traits, family ties, shapes, and control switches were charted in full. Tissue tests showed highest activity in roots and lowest in leaves.

Under drought, all nine genes turned down in a tolerant type yet turned up in a sensitive type. Under salt, two gene trios rose while a third trio barely moved. One gene form was named a drought-tough variant worth breeding for. Downstream targets include genes for RNA and protein marking, tying the family to broad stress control.
pmc-13474901:
Zheng and co-authors review neutrophil extracellular traps in liver cancer in 2026, focusing on how these web-like structures vary across a tumor and over time. The traps, called NETs, are strands of DNA and enzymes that white blood cells cast out, normally to catch germs. In hepatocellular carcinoma, the commonest liver cancer, the review argues these webs form a shifting barrier that helps tumors resist treatment.

The scale of the disease frames the review, since this cancer type makes up 75 to 85 percent of primary liver cancers worldwide. Hepatitis B and C infections account for about 80 percent of cases, and tumors return in up to 88 percent of patients even after curative treatment, the authors note. Response to immune checkpoint drugs stays under 20 percent, and the review links NET-driven immune-excluding zones to that resistance, then surveys drugs aimed at dismantling the traps.
pmc-13477101:
Rodolfo V. Rocha and eight colleagues reported in 2026 a twenty-five-year single-centre experience with aortic root replacement using a composite valve graft. They reviewed 1,332 adults operated on between 1990 and 2014, including many with prior surgery, infection, or combined procedures.

Death within 30 days ran 4.9 percent overall, but 8.6 percent with combined procedures against 2.5 percent for isolated grafts, while elective first-time isolated cases had under 1 percent death and stroke. Twenty-five-year survival reached 33.8 percent, worse than matched general population rates, especially in younger patients. Short-term results were excellent, but long-term excess death remains a challenge.
pmc-13478201:
Yinqiang Yu and six colleagues tested in 2026 whether foods' metaphorical hot or cold nature, rooted in Chinese food culture, steers food choices. Physical temperature had been studied before, but this cultural classification, independent of serving temperature, had been overlooked.

Across three studies, people imagining bodily cold chose hot-natured foods over cold-natured ones, seeing them as healthier in that state. The effect ran through perceived healthiness, not through actual temperature or calories. The findings show culture-based temperature thinking shapes how people judge foods and choose what to eat.
pmc-13478601:
Samaneh Safarpour and coauthors published a 2026 study on how radiation ages lymph vessel cells and worsens lymphedema, the incurable swelling that follows some cancer treatments. Radiation is a known risk factor, and it already suppresses a key growth receptor on lymphatic endothelial cells. What it does to cell aging in this system was unclear.

Irradiated lymphatic cells grew less and showed more aging signs, including higher activity of a standard senescence stain and raised p53, p21, and p16 proteins. In a mouse tail swelling model, radiation increased swelling after lymph vessel removal, and the swelling persisted at 30 days while shams recovered. Tissue from ablated, irradiated mice held more senescent and dying cells. The authors link radiation-driven aging to the stubborn course of this condition.
pmc-13479701:
Guoliang Chen and coauthors published a 2026 study of how two chemical marks on histones shift when wheat fights powdery mildew, a fungal disease that cuts yields worldwide. Gene activity data and mark mapping were combined in leaves infected with mixed races of the fungus. Transcription changed extensively after infection, including in genes that manage the marks themselves.

Both activating marks, H3K4me3 and H3K36me3, fell overall after infection. Their remaining distribution differed by location: the first mark concentrated near gene start sites, while the second enriched inside gene bodies. This redistribution suggests the plant retools its gene control landscape during defense rather than simply switching genes on. The authors provide a reference map for breeding or engineering mildew-resistant wheat.
pmc-13480701:
Alexander Oing and co-authors report a 2026 catalyst that turns carbon dioxide plus hydrogen into methanol with stubborn selectivity. Methanol from waste gas could close the carbon loop, yet heat favours a side product. Their zinc-hafnium oxide kept methanol share above seventy percent even when zinc rose to nearly the whole mix, a range where the rival zinc-zirconium oxide fades. Its per-site rate topped the rival as well.

Live spectroscopy plus modelling pinned the work to a zinc site beside a missing oxygen and a hafnium neighbour, running a formate-to-methoxy path. Such sites sat both inside mixed crystals and as lone hafnium clusters on zinc oxide patches at high zinc loads. Knowing the true site lets engineers build it on purpose rather than by luck.
pmc-13481401:
Kevisha Samlal and co-authors present a 2026 interview study of faith as a coping tool during the COVID years in Sandton, South Africa. Ten residents chosen for varied experience spoke at length about loss, grief, and fear under strict lockdown rules that barred gatherings and funerals in normal form.

Faith and spiritual practice sat at the centre of coping for most speakers. Prayer, home rituals, and framing loss within a larger meaning helped people steady their emotions when halls of worship stood shut. Speakers drew strength from belief even as they grieved at a distance from kin. The authors urge crisis mental health plans to weave in spiritual support rather than treat it as an extra. Small samples limit reach, yet the depth of the accounts carries weight for local services.
pmc-13482401:
Mohammadi and colleagues hunt for an early kidney warning in 2026 inside tiny blood-borne packets called exosomes, in septic patients heading into major non-cardiac surgery. Standard blood tests notice kidney injury late, only after the marker creatinine rises, so the team sampled blood before, during, and 24 hours after surgery in 120 adults at a Tabriz hospital. They measured microRNAs, small gene-regulating molecules that injured kidney cells shed into exosomes.

Patients who developed kidney injury showed distinct shifts in specific exosomal microRNAs across the surgical time points compared with patients whose kidneys stayed healthy after surgery. Several of the molecules separated the groups with measurable accuracy on standard diagnostic curves at particular sampling times, suggesting blood can carry injury signals before creatinine moves at all. The authors frame the markers as candidates for catching subclinical injury, kidney stress without test changes, and call for larger studies built for that endpoint.
pmc-13482601:
Lindsey G. Droz and co-authors report a 2026 review of a carbon-coated half-shoulder replacement for younger patients with shoulder arthritis. Full replacements wear fast in active people, so a hard pyrocarbon ball on the arm bone offers a middle path. Records covered 27 shoulders in 26 patients at one centre from 2015 to 2025, with average follow-up near three years.

Pain and function scores improved clearly, and arm lift plus rotation range grew. No breaks, dislocations, or infections appeared. Two patients needed conversion to a reverse replacement for cuff tendon trouble, not socket wear. Socket wear deepened in near half the group, and near half the implants sat slightly overfilled, a trait common in the wear group though angle measures did not separate them. The option stays viable for younger shoulders, with fit as the watch point.
pmc-13483201:
Fu and colleagues pooled trial evidence on internet-delivered acceptance and commitment therapy, a talking therapy that teaches people to accept hard thoughts and act on their values. Their 2026 review asked whether the online version improves sleep in adults. Eight randomized trials qualified, drawn from five databases, with smaller groups feeding the pooled sleep-quality and insomnia analyses.

Against passive comparison groups, the online therapy improved sleep quality by a clear margin in the pooled results reported. Insomnia symptoms also eased, though by a smaller amount than overall sleep quality did. Results varied a lot between trials, and the authors rate the overall certainty of evidence as low. Fu treats the findings as encouraging but preliminary, calling for bigger, better-matched trials before clinics lean on the approach.
pmc-13483601:
Evolène Fayolle and colleagues lay out a 2026 trial protocol testing tailored support against frailty in older people having bladder or kidney cancer surgery. Standard care often stops at surgery and short recovery, leaving long-term function to drift. The FRAGECO program instead offers a personal six-month pathway that starts before the operation.

Participants receive twice-weekly hour-long adapted activity sessions for a month on either side of surgery, mixing endurance, strength, and balance work. Optional education covers activity, food, treatment, and fatigue, followed by 12 weeks in local adapted activity services. Frailty at six months, judged by a six-minute walk test, is the main outcome. Strength, memory, mood, and quality of life are tracked as well.
pmc-13483901:
Tran and colleagues measured how much traumatic injuries cost Vietnamese patients in lost work after they leave hospital. Their 2026 analysis covered 253 patients treated at two hospitals in Hung Yen province, using a standard questionnaire that scores missed work and reduced performance while back on the job. Injury research in poorer countries rarely follows patients past discharge, so the team also priced the losses.

About 53 percent of patients had missed work in the week before the survey because of their injury. Far more, about 86 percent, reported working below their normal capacity while present at their jobs. Missed work cost an average of about 28 dollars per week, and reduced performance about 12 dollars weekly. Older age, worse health, and stronger trauma symptoms deepened the losses. Tran calls for rehabilitation that covers mental recovery, not just bones.
pmc-13488201:
Martin B. Rasmussen and colleagues test blood markers of tissue matrix in biliary tract cancer in a 2026 analysis of the CheckPAC trial. These cancers grow in the bile ducts, resist immune treatment, and sit in dense, collagen-rich tissue that can shut immune cells out. Sixty-one patients received focused radiation plus one or two immune drugs, and blood was sampled at entry and day sixty for fragments that reflect collagen building, breakdown, and killer cell activity.

High starting levels of two markers tracked with no benefit and shorter survival in the reported models, with one marker staying predictive after adjustment. A killer-cell marker rose by day sixty in every patient who gained benefit, and that rise linked with longer survival. The authors see a path to blood-based patient selection.
pmc-13490401:
Abdulaziz Alotaibi and colleagues predict accident risk at Saudi construction sites with machine learning in a 2026 modeling study. Building work carries high injury rates, and better foresight could target safety checks. Three model types were trained on a safety dataset and compared on prediction quality. The models were random forest, gradient boosting, and a neural network. Sensitivity analysis then probed how much each factor sways the predicted risk.

The neural network predicted best overall in the reported results, with gradient boosting close behind. Physical load and environmental strain, such as heat, ranked among the strongest risk drivers. Accident type and interruptions also contributed. Together, model scores and factor weights could guide site inspections and worker protection plans.
pmc-13490501:
SeyedShenava and team proposed a planning design for green energy areas that juggle power, heat, cooling, and hydrogen under uncertain green output. Cities usually plan transport, hydrogen, and storage separately, wasting synergies. Their 2026 robust tuning model coordinates energy hubs with hydrogen making, fuel cells, and carbon capture, while electric bus fleets double as mobile storage and carbon taxes plus trading steer decisions.

Case model runs showed the integrated design improved green use and cut emissions relative to fragmented planning in the cases examined. A welfare layer checked that affordability and fair access survived the tuning, not just savings. Demand-side running shifted flexible loads into green-rich hours in the modeled areas. SeyedShenava argues case-independent robust planning suits areas that cannot afford plans collapsing when the weather surprises them.
pmc-13491601:
Xinyi Zhang and nine co-authors review in 2026 how fat tissue around blood vessels may drive abdominal aortic aneurysm, a dangerous widening of the main artery in the belly. No drug has been proven to slow the widening, so surgery remains the only firm option. The review focuses on adipokines, signaling proteins released by the fat that hugs the aorta.

The authors sort adipokines into harmful ones that feed inflammation and weaken the vessel wall, and protective ones that calm inflammation and guard the tissue. Restoring balance between the two groups is presented as a promising treatment direction. Diabetes drugs such as metformin and GLP-1 agonists, plus new agents aimed at adipokine receptors, show early promise, though most evidence is still preclinical.
pmc-13491801:
Rabeet Tariq and five colleagues investigate in 2026 why surgical trainees quit before finishing residency at one institution in a low-middle-income country. Records spanning 2005 to 2024 covered 617 surgical residents, and the team also surveyed former trainees who had left about their reasons and later paths. Premature departure disrupts care teams and wastes scarce training capacity.

About thirty percent of residents left early, over half of them during the first year, with pediatric surgery and general surgery losing the most. Single residents quit significantly more often than married ones. Exit interviews blamed family commitments first, then personal reasons and better jobs, while survey answers added unprofessional behavior, toxic culture, and heavy workload. Most leavers joined another program, and most were glad they had gone, a verdict the authors say programs must answer.
pmc-13493401:
Handan Derebaşınlıoğlu and three colleagues investigate in 2026 whether the pain-relieving nerve blocks used in breast reduction surgery might carry a hidden cost in early complications. Pain control from regional blocks is well proven, yet nobody had checked their link with bleeding, wound opening, or infection after this operation. Records covered 144 consecutive patients at one center, sixty-four of whom received a block at the end of surgery.

About thirty-eight percent of all patients developed at least one early complication. The raw rate ran higher in the block group, near forty-seven percent against thirty-one, although the gap missed statistical significance and vanished after adjustment. Bleeding severe enough to need reoperation appeared only in block patients. How much tissue was removed was the sole independent predictor, and the authors demand prospective trials before blaming the blocks.
pmc-13494001:
Workisa Bacha Garuma leads an eleven-author team turning in 2026 two wastes, jimsonweed seeds and corncobs, into biodiesel and a reusable catalyst, then auditing the whole process environmentally. The corncobs became a sulfonated carbon acid catalyst in a single pot process, while the poisonous plant's seed oil supplied a feedstock nobody competes for as food. Reaction conditions were tuned experimentally.

The best recipe converted over ninety-one percent of the oil at modest temperature in under five hours. Life cycle analysis across eighteen impact categories blamed electricity and solvents, used in catalyst making and oil extraction, for most of the footprint. The optimized run paired high conversion with near-minimum emissions. Waste-derived catalysts, the authors conclude, can anchor a genuinely circular biodiesel route.
pmc-13495101:
Sofyan Jankowski and colleagues report a 2026 study asking patients, rather than experts, how ChatGPT answers stack up against official website answers on radiation imaging risks. Earlier expert reviews rated the chatbot's answers about on par with those from radiology bodies. No one had asked the patients who read such pages which source they liked and trusted more.

At hospitals in the United States, Switzerland, and Lebanon, 328 patients were each given one of five common risk questions. Without knowing the source, they rated both a chatbot answer and a human-written one for satisfaction, clarity, trust, and reassurance. The chatbot won on all four scales, and written comments leaned the same way, with far more praise and less complaint. The authors say the gap argues for patient-first writing, and that chatbot-style drafts under expert watch could lift the clarity of patient materials.
pmc-13495301:
Reza Zarezadeh and colleagues pool, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, studies of fatty acid makeup in women with polycystic ovary syndrome. The syndrome, a hormone disorder and a top cause of infertility, had never had its fat profile summed across blood and the fluid around the egg. The team searched four databases through early 2025 and weighed study quality and proof strength.

Twelve studies qualified. Women with the syndrome showed higher levels of several key fats, among them palmitoleic, oleic, linoleic, and arachidonic acids, spanning single- and multi-bond types. The pattern partly held when studies were split by sample type and fat fraction, and when weaker studies were dropped. The authors say the fat profile seems genuinely shifted in the syndrome, a clue that may one day feed into diet or drug strategies, though the pooled proof varies in strength.
pmc-13498601:
Ana Paola Yusti-Muñoz and co-authors study in 2026 whether livestock guardian dogs lower the risk of foxes killing sheep on ranches in Chilean Patagonia. Sheep losses drive conflict with wild carnivores and often lead to lethal control, so non-lethal protection matters for both farmers and wildlife. Earlier work rarely tested how dogs interact with habitat and prey levels, which this study set out to examine using 2017 to 2018 records.

Ninety-four fresh sheep carcasses from fox kills were compared across five ranches, two with dogs and three without. Kill density was lower where dogs worked, and modelled risk peaked on ranches without dogs. With dogs present, risk fell as open ground and hare numbers rose, while without dogs risk climbed sharply with hare numbers, suggesting the dogs blunt several risk pathways at once.
pmc-13498901:
Stenberg and colleagues compared dementia outcomes after weight-loss surgery in people with obesity and type 2 diabetes against matched patients who did not have surgery. They used Swedish nationwide registries in a 2026 study. Diabetes and obesity are major dementia risk factors, but earlier surgery results conflicted. Surgical patients were matched by statistical propensity scoring and followed for a mean of nine years.

Stenberg found surgery linked to a forty percent lower dementia risk, with the fifteen-year cumulative incidence about half again lower than in controls. Rates fell for Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia but rose for alcohol-related dementia, a fourfold relative increase, echoing known postoperative alcohol risks. The authors argue the combined long-term effects of surgery plausibly protect the brain, including sustained weight loss and remission of blood pressure and blood fat problems. The alcohol signal, they add, argues for vigilance in postoperative care and counseling.
pmc-13499401:
Published in 2026, an editorial in lipid research weighs new data on the cholesterol carried inside lipoprotein(a), a fatty particle in the blood. Its level is set largely by genetics and linked to heart disease. A gene segment repeated a variable number of times chiefly decides how much of the particle circulates, with fewer repeats tied to higher levels and higher risk. Measuring the particle's cholesterol content had given inconsistent results in older work, partly due to hard isolation methods.

A newer validated test now measures that cholesterol directly and relates it to particle size. Total cholesterol content rose with particle number and fell as particle size grew, matching known patterns. A surprise appeared in cholesterol per particle, which behaved differently than expected. The editorial discusses what clinicians and researchers should, and should not, do with that finding while drug trials targeting this particle continue.
pmc-13500501:
Erika T Camacho and colleagues model mathematically in 2026 how light-sensing cells of the retina die after separating from their supporting layer, an event behind vision loss in many retinal diseases. Detachment starves rods and cones of recycled parts and nutrients, including glucose, that the pigment layer normally supplies. Their model was built from published healthy-retina interactions and several datasets tracking rod and cone loss after detachment, then probed with sensitivity analysis to rank which factors drive survival at different times.

Factors that mattered most in the first week, the early intervention window, were not always those dominating at 150 days in the simulations. Some changes helped one cell type while hurting the other, and only raising nutrient availability and rod energy uptake efficiency avoided harming either population. The authors argue protection will need combined strategies timed to disease stage, testable in experimental models.
pmc-13500701:
Edina Rusen and colleagues explore in 2026 a copper-loaded porous crystal as a helper for controlled polymerisation, the chemistry that grows plastic chains to precise lengths. The crystal, a commercial metal-organic framework, acts as a co-catalyst that releases the active copper ions needed to start and regulate chain growth of methyl acrylate, a common acrylic building block. Activation came either from copper wire or from red light, and the team used chromatography, spectroscopy, and magnetic resonance to work out which reaction pathway actually ran.

Evidence pointed to one specific living polymerisation route in the reported analyses, with about a quarter of chains confirmed still living, meaning able to grow further on demand. Under red light the process also generated copper nanoparticles inside the mixture, and the same initiation scheme produced a stable emulsion directly. The work sketches a light-friendly, crystal-assisted route to well-defined acrylic polymers.
pmc-13501601:
Nasrin Rezaee leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 qualitative study of what parents need after an adolescent child has attempted suicide, set in Iran. Parents carry heavy distress after such an event, yet their own support needs are rarely mapped. The researchers purposively recruited parents whose adolescents had been admitted to psychiatric emergency wards after an attempt. They ran 24 semi-structured interviews, with 15 mothers and 9 fathers, continuing until no new themes appeared, and analysed the transcripts with conventional content analysis.

Parents' needs grouped into two broad categories. The first covered practical knowledge: how attempts might be prevented, how to manage a crisis, and how to care for an adolescent who survived an attempt. The second covered outside support, namely reaching mental health professionals and remedying cultural and societal attitudes that surround suicide. The authors direct the findings at policymakers, health administrators, and clinicians planning family support services.
pmc-13501801:
Yağmur Yıldız and Ayşe Nur Kahve report a 2026 randomized trial of suspension training and gut comfort in young competitive swimmers. Thirty-two prepubertal boys aged nine to thirteen, all trained swimmers, were split between an eight-week TRX programme of bodyweight exercises hanging from straps, and a control group. Bowel habits were scored with the Bristol Stool Scale and a defecation questionnaire before and after the programme.

The share of boys who habitually postponed defecation fell in the training group, while among controls it rose. Stool form itself showed no clear shift between groups. A repeated-measures analysis found a significant group-by-time interaction for total gastrointestinal symptom scores, F of 13.73 and partial eta squared of 0.314. The authors suggest TRX work is a safe way to ease gut symptoms in young athletes, while the small, single-sex sample tempers the claim.
pmc-13503901:
Elżbieta Szostak leads a team that used spider webs to trap and study airborne microplastics in a Polish city, in a 2026 study. Tiny plastic bits drift in city air, yet catching them for lab work is awkward. Webs of funnel-weaver spiders act as ready-made sticky nets.

Two lab methods probed the catch. One read the organic compounds clinging to the webs, and the other read polymer signs in the solid residue. Every web held polymer-linked compounds, and rubber signals showed at all sites from center to suburbs, with no clear gap between them. Residue checks found tire-linked material in all samples, plus nylon, polypropylene, and other plastics in shares of the webs. The authors back webs as cheap passive samplers.
pmc-13504001:
Miao-xia Chen leads a team reporting a rare lymphoma that starts in the bile duct, in a 2026 case report. The cancer is often mistaken for the far more common bile duct cancer on scans, which can lead to needless surgery. Chemotherapy, not surgery, is the main treatment.

Their patient was an older man with upper belly pain, first thought to have bile duct cancer. Tissue tests showed a B-cell lymphoma instead. His past care for a throat cancer and a long hepatitis B infection, with a lingering virus known to drive lymphoma, may have played a part. He was frail and hit by acute problems, so he got only two days of a standard drug mix before dying of sepsis. The authors share scan traits that may flag this rare cancer sooner.
pmc-13507101:
Shabnam Kumari, Zinnu Rain, Pradyot Prakash, Ragini Tilak, and Ashish Kumar Singh report a 2026 study of Candida yeast bloodstream infections at a hospital in northern India. Their three-year watch from 2022 to 2025 covered 357 distinct isolates. Tests named each species, checked harm traits such as biofilm growth, and measured drug response by standard methods.

Species other than Candida albicans made up more than three quarters of cases, led by Candida tropicalis. Harm genes were common, and trait tests matched gene results well. One species, Candidozyma auris, resisted many drugs, while a drug class called echinocandins stayed potent overall. Joint tracking of harm traits and drug response can improve care.
pmc-13507201:
Xin Shen, Xiaomei Liu, Rahmat Hidayat, and Yali Xu present a two thousand twenty-six kinematic comparison of futsal instep shots between trained and novice players. Twenty trained athletes and twenty novices performed standardized shots filmed at high speed. Joint angles, angular speeds, torso posture, and ball velocity were extracted frame by frame. Trained players showed more efficient knee positioning, steadier torsos, and better arm placement. Knee angular velocity predicted ball speed most strongly, giving coaches a concrete technical target.
pmc-13507301:
Danting Sun leads a 2026 team that ties the RNA-reading protein IGF2BP3 to epithelial ovarian cancer growth through fat building.
