Silencing either partner reversed the malignant traits in dishes and animals. The fat-blocking drug orlistat also undid the effect. The chain offers both a biomarker and a drug pairing.
pmc-13508201:
Dheyaa Al-Najafi leads a fourteen-author trial comparing exam questions written by AI with questions written by senior students, in 2026 work. Writing good multiple-choice questions for medical exams takes much staff time. First-year medical students were assigned at random to sit a 112-question mock exam built one way or the other. Both sets followed the same course goals. The AI set came from a two-model process, with one system drafting and another checking.

A total of 258 students took part, split almost evenly between the two exam forms. Making questions with AI help proved 5.6 times faster per item than student authorship. Students rated both exams much the same on clarity, difficulty, relevance, and learning value. Score patterns and consistency were also compared under a standard test-quality framework. The authors see AI drafting, with human checks, as a way to ease a heavy chore in medical schools.
pmc-13508301:
Kristi Ho and Phillip Hwang ask whether having a wide circle of social ties helps the brain resist damage in later life, in 2026 work. Bigger networks may build a reserve that keeps thinking sharp despite brain wear. Data came from the long-running Framingham Heart Study and covered 1,602 adults. Participants rated their social networks on a standard index, had a blood marker of nerve damage measured, and took thinking tests covering memory, language, and executive skills. Resilience was scored by how much better a person performed than the damage marker predicted.

People with large networks showed greater resilience in memory than those with small networks. No clear link appeared for language or executive function. Adjustments covered schooling, genes, activity, smoking, and mood. The authors read the result as support for social connection as one piece of brain health in aging, strongest for memory.
pmc-13508401:
Luis Carmona-Rosado and five co-authors ask whether unhealthy food shops around the home change the link between neighborhood wealth and child weight in Madrid, in 2026 work. Data came from a city-wide survey of 3,505 children aged three to twelve. Home areas were graded for wealth using census data. Height and weight gave overweight and obesity rates. Mapping software counted unhealthy food retailers within a short walk of each home, and models split results by that exposure and by sex.

About one in four children had overweight and about one in six had obesity. Children in the poorest areas carried far more of both than children in the richest areas, with obesity more than twice as common. The wealth gap in weight persisted even where unhealthy shops were scarce. The study frames child weight inequality as rooted in neighborhood conditions wider than food retail alone.
pmc-13508501:
Solomon Getachew Alem leads a ten-author pilot study asking whether group pregnancy care can work at Ethiopia's smallest health posts, in 2026 work. Group antenatal care blends checkups with shared learning and peer support among women at similar pregnancy stages. The pilot placed a six-meeting model in five health posts in two zones of the Amhara region. Fifty-four pregnant women under twenty weeks joined. After the second meeting, researchers ran in-depth and key informant interviews, then coded the transcripts for themes.

Enough women were found early in pregnancy to form groups without trouble. Women joined willingly and said they wanted to keep attending later meetings. Health extension workers ran the sessions well, showing the facilitation side is realistic at this level. Existing community structures helped recruitment. The authors judge the model feasible at health post level and ready for wider testing.
pmc-13511701:
Ian Hoyin Cheng, Jibrin Sammani Usman, and Shamay Sheung-Mei Ng review in 2026 whether pairing two electrical stimulation therapies helps stroke patients recover arm and hand use. One therapy applies a weak current to the scalp; the other stimulates nerves in the arm itself.

Pooling twelve trials with four hundred forty-nine participants, they found no clear extra gain for the pairing over either therapy alone on standard arm scores. A few single-study results hinted at better hand scores and daily activity when both were added to usual rehabilitation. The certainty of that evidence was rated very low. The authors call for factorial trials that test each part separately before clinics adopt the combination.
pmc-13513001:
Xinyu Cai, Shuxuan Jing, Yanan Zhu, Jiaxing Huang, Qiaoxia Shang, and Guiling Ding track how two pheromone glands develop in virgin queens of the Asian honeybee, in 2026 work. The queens were followed across their first ten days of adult life. A queen holds colony order through chemical signals from several glands, yet gland growth in young queens was poorly mapped. The team measured jaw size and the mandibular and tergal glands from emergence to day ten.

Jaw size barely moved with age. The mandibular glands, seated in the head, grew to their largest around day seven. The tergal glands, along the back, reached a stable plateau between days five and seven. The first week after emergence thus looks like the key window for signal gland maturation. The authors say the timeline can guide queen quality checks and later work on colony management.
pmc-13513701:
Yasemin Behram Kandemir and six co-authors compare blood organic acid profiles in people with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, a weakened heart muscle not caused by blocked arteries, against matched controls, in 2026 work. The study enrolled 160 people, eighty patients and eighty controls of similar age and sex. A targeted mass spectrometry panel measured circulating organic acids, with strict correction for many simultaneous tests.

Sixteen metabolites differed after correction. The largest rise sat in a marker tied to branched-chain amino acid breakdown, followed by two acids from core energy pathways. Several energy cycle acids also ran high, while one acid fell. The pattern points to disturbed mitochondrial fuel handling. The authors caution that kidney function, blood sugar, other illness, and medication differed between groups, so the profile marks association rather than a clean disease signature.
pmc-13514301:
Aysun Benli and co-authors compare cryptococcal fungal infections in patients with and without HIV across several centers in a middle-income country, in 2026 work. Records covered adults diagnosed between 2013 and 2025 and followed for one year. The cohort held 92 patients with an average age in the mid-forties, just over half living with HIV, and nearly nine in ten with weakened immunity from some cause.

Infection of the central nervous system was the most common form, at about two thirds of cases. Overall, close to half the patients died within a year of diagnosis. Altered consciousness at presentation stood out as a strong independent predictor of death in the adjusted model, with further factors detailed in the full report. Splitting results by HIV status shaped the rest of the analysis. The authors call for earlier recognition of brain involvement in both groups.
pmc-13515001:
Mara Klibus leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 pilot study on steadier anaesthesia induction. Blood pressure often sags when propofol puts a patient to sleep and a breathing tube goes in. The team therefore tested whether adding low-dose ketamine and intravenous lidocaine, while halving the fentanyl dose, would smooth that phase. Thirty adults having elective surgery were split between the standard propofol-fentanyl regimen and the adjunct mix, with pressure and a finger-based perfusion index recorded at set points.

Average pressures did not differ significantly between the groups at any point. Within the standard group, though, mean arterial pressure fell sharply after induction and stayed down, while the adjunct group showed no significant internal drop. The perfusion index climbed higher in the adjunct group at both later time points, and those patients reported less sore throat and weaker cough reflexes afterward.
pmc-13517901:
Yayun Zhang leads a nine-author study of a little-watched water contaminant in mice in a 2026 paper. Chlorinated drinking water spawns disinfection byproducts, and the nitrogen-bearing branch, here 2-chlorophenylacetonitrile, worries toxicologists more than the regulated classics. Mice drank low-dose water for six months while the team inspected gut tissue and sequenced spleen genes.

The exposed mice gained far less weight and their guts suffered visibly: inflamed stomach lining, blunted intestinal villi, scrambled crypts, and a leaky barrier wall. With the gate breached, gut alarm signals seemingly reached the spleen, whose white pulp shrank and whose tidy zones dissolved toward scarring. Gene readouts split two ways: stress and chemokine machinery surged, including heat-shock proteins up tenfold, while cell-division genes collapsed across every checkpoint. Zhang's team calls it a gut-spleen toxicity axis and urges long-term organ endpoints into byproduct risk rules.
pmc-13518101:
Mirza Muflihul Haque and five colleagues recount a pregnancy seizure case that was not what it seemed in a 2026 report. A thirty-one-year-old woman at thirty-six weeks arrived convulsing, deeply unconscious, with high blood pressure. Eclampsia was the working call, and an emergency caesarean followed. The seizures and poor recovery continued after delivery, which broke the script.

A brain scan found a large bleed with heavy pressure shift, drained in emergency surgery. When progress still lagged, vessel imaging exposed the true cause: a tangled arteriovenous malformation fed by the middle cerebral artery. Catheter treatment closed about eighty-five percent of the tangle. The woman left hospital fully alert and seizure-free, later walking on her own with no new events. Haque's team warns that failed recovery after correct eclampsia care demands brain imaging fast, above all where resources make the first label stick.
pmc-13518801:
Shengwei Feng leads a nine-author team unveiling in 2026 a security tag that pairs glowing patterns with fingerprints no copier can reproduce. Fake goods and documents remain a worldwide problem. Uniform printed labels are easy to copy, while most unclonable tags need costly making or special readers.

Their porous polymer skeletons are printed without masks, then coated with iridium complexes and fluorescent dyes that amplify and mix light signals under one excitation color. Peeling the tag with tape fractures each pixel in a random microscopic way, creating a unique fingerprint while the visible pattern survives. A handheld flashlight and a smartphone suffice for checking, making field authentication practical.
pmc-13518901:
Baomin Wang and seven colleagues overturn a common assumption in 2026. TMAO, a compound made from gut microbe products and often blamed for metabolic harm, is also made inside pancreatic beta cells, where it protects them. Beta cells release insulin, and their failure under aging and diabetes drives high blood sugar. The enzyme FMO3 makes TMAO locally, yet that machinery fades in diabetic and aged tissue.

Deleting FMO3 only in mouse beta cells drained internal TMAO, triggering cell aging, inflammation, and faulty insulin release through the NF-kB pathway. TMAO normally grips a brake protein that keeps NF-kB out of the nucleus. Restoring FMO3 calmed aged human islets, pointing to a protective local role.
pmc-13519001:
Chuyang Liu leads a nine-author team solving an impurity problem in 2026 for high-entropy M-type ferrites meant to absorb millimeter waves. Such absorbers matter as 5G and radar crowd the 35 gigahertz atmospheric window, yet stray phases kept ruining performance because the material's disorder was not quite high enough.

Deliberately starving the recipe of iron raised the configurational entropy, wiped out impurities, and loosened the local structure. Added zirconium ions widened the magnetic loss range by shifting natural resonance. The final single-phase ferrite absorbed across 12.18 gigahertz of bandwidth at a matching thickness under 1 millimeter. Liu and colleagues frame iron deficiency as a general tuning lever for stealth and pollution shielding.
pmc-13519801:
Jung Hyun Park and colleagues measured how brain stiffness changes with age and sex in healthy adults. Published in 2026, the study reviewed 96 adults aged thirty-one to eighty who had MRI scans during routine checkups, using a virtual elastography method built from diffusion imaging. Brain stiffness reflects tissue makeup and can shift in tumors and diseases such as Alzheimer disease and multiple sclerosis.

Deep structures like the thalamus and basal ganglia ran stiffer than the outer lobes, with the occipital lobe stiffest among lobes and the temporal lobe softest. Stiffness eased slightly with age overall, most sharply in cerebral gray matter, while the hippocampus softened markedly after age fifty. Sex gaps appeared only in the parietal lobe and basal ganglia. The work supplies a healthy baseline against which disease-related softening can be judged.
pmc-13519901:
Caravello and Blidy propose a 2026 hypothesis linking aging, cancer, and chronic infection through one shared failure in dendritic cells, the immune cells that instruct other defenders. In all three settings, a key dendritic cell type stops producing IL-12p70, a signal needed to launch strong immune attacks.

The authors lay out a four-step chain. Inflammatory signals from aging cells switch on a protein called STAT3 in blood cell precursors. STAT3 then recruits two silencing enzymes to the IRF8 gene, locking it off with chemical marks. With IRF8 silenced, IL-12 output and dendritic cell instruction collapse. As a correction, they propose giving patients lab-made polarized dendritic cells grown outside this suppressive environment, and they list testable predictions and ways the idea could be proven wrong.
pmc-13520301:
Evan Weldon and colleagues report in 2026 on training mid-level health workers in rural Nepal to find forearm fractures with portable ultrasound. X-ray units are scarce in that setting, so the study asks whether short training can work in daily practice at Bayalpata Hospital.

Seventeen health assistants and auxiliary workers who finished a two-day course took part in interviews. They described using ultrasound often, feeling more confident, and relying less on X-ray referrals. Language and duty-time pressures still caused difficulty. Support for wider rollout was strong. Readers see practical evidence that a brief, hands-on course can change fracture care where imaging is limited.
pmc-13521001:
Yan Pan and colleagues track in 2026 how lutein-enriched eggs hold quality during a month of fridge or room storage. Feeding hens marigold-derived lutein deepens yolk colour and nutrition, yet storage losses were poorly defined.

Before storage, enriched yolks held roughly triple the lutein of control eggs, confirming diet transfer. Temperature and time drove most freshness decline, covering weight loss, white thinning and firmness changes, while egg type mattered little there. Enriched eggs kept a clear colour edge at both temperatures, although lutein fell after thirty days, especially at room temperature. Cooked texture depended mainly on storage conditions.
pmc-13521901:
Thanh Nguyen and colleagues demonstrate in 2026 an ultrafast X-ray method that films heat flow inside gallium nitride thin films used in power electronics. Crowded devices overheat easily, while defects and interfaces that trap heat are hard to measure with contact tools.

Laser pulses strained the crystal lattice, with X-ray snapshots tracking how strain spread sideways over time. Reconstructions yielded sideways heat conductivity and interface conductance near a wrinkle defect. Conductivity near the wrinkle fell fourfold, while interface transfer dropped by one quarter, with clear asymmetry across the flaw. The contact-free method suits layered films where buried interfaces govern reliability.
pmc-13522001:
Takeshi Murata and colleagues ask in 2026 if progesterone receptor status predicts survival after local breast cancer return. Data came from a Japanese national base for 2004 to 2015. All cases were hormone-sensitive and HER2-negative at first care. The set held 1,625 patients with local or regional return only.

Patients whose return tumour lacked the receptor fared worse. Gaps showed in both overall and cancer-specific survival. That held no matter what the first tumour showed. Node spread, short disease-free gap and low oestrogen levels also marked worse outlook. No surgery on the return marked worse outlook as well. Retesting receptors at return thus holds real value for advice.
pmc-13522501:
Woo and colleagues used in 2026 a systematic evolution experiment to teach a soil bacterium to use plant sugars more fully. Pseudomonas putida had been engineered to eat xylose and arabinose, two sugars from plant fibre, alongside glucose, but such added pathways can be unstable. With an automated evolution platform, the team grew the strain under single-sugar and mixed-sugar pressures that varied in amount and timing.

Woo found the environments split the bacteria into specialists and generalists. When xylose use was not rewarded, the ability to eat it was often lost. Carbon-poor mixed-sugar settings instead kept all pathways and tuned them together, improving growth and sugar use. Gene, protein, and chemistry checks showed each pathway's fitness cost set its stability. One generalist clone also made more of a blue pigment product from mixed sugars than its parent, a sign of wider value for bioconversion.
pmc-13522601:
Zixing Yan, Xinyun Xie, and Ziming Wang link a new metal-exposure index to chronic lung disease in a 2026 analysis of United States survey data. The index combines mixed heavy metal exposure with low-grade body inflammation. More than eleven thousand participants from 2005 to 2018 were studied, including five hundred fifty people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term breathing disorder.

Higher index values were tied to much higher odds of the lung disease, and a waist-based obesity measure partly explained the link. Higher index values also predicted greater overall death rates in people with and without the disease, though no link appeared for cardiovascular death specifically. The authors suggest body weight plays a small part in how metal mixtures relate to lung health.
pmc-13523201:
Laura-María Compañ-Gabucio leads a team studying ultra-processed food intake in Spanish children in a 2026 analysis of a birth cohort. Diet was assessed with validated questionnaires in more than fifteen hundred mother-child pairs at age eight and a smaller group at age twelve. Foods were classified by processing level, and intake was split into thirds to find factors tied to the highest group.

At age eight, high intake linked to lower maternal social class, higher maternal ultra-processed intake during pregnancy, male sex, and heavy television viewing. At age twelve, pregnancy intake and television time still mattered, while university education in mothers and high physical activity in children linked to lower intake. The authors highlight family habits formed before birth as lasting influences on children's diets.
pmc-13523301:
Öznur Erbay Dalli surveys knowledge gaps about skin injury among intensive care nurses in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Two hundred eighty-three nurses completed three validated surveys covering pressure injuries, device-related pressure injuries, and skin tears. Critically ill patients face high risk of all three, and nurses lead prevention, yet combined knowledge across the three areas had rarely been measured.

Scores varied by topic, and stopping harm was the weakest domain throughout all three surveys. Nurses with more experience, advanced education, or prior skin tear care experience scored higher. The author recommends targeted education to strengthen prevention knowledge across skin integrity care, while cautioning that social media sign-up may have biased the sample and that no deeper analysis was performed.
pmc-13525001:
Zeinab M. Awwad reports, in a 2026 rat study, that the diabetes drug dapagliflozin eased Alzheimer's-like disease induced by scopolamine. In Alzheimer's, the renin-angiotensin system, a hormone network, runs too hot on its harmful arm, which drives amyloid damage, while a helpful arm with ACE2 and a small peptide counters it. The drug was meant to reset the balance between the arms.

Treated rats showed lower ACE, angiotensin II, and its harmful receptor in the hippocampus, with higher ACE2, the helpful peptide, and its receptor, plus boosted signaling through a survival pathway. Death and inflammation markers fell, tissue damage eased, and scores improved in object and maze alternation tests of learning and memory. Awwad presents the results as first findings for this helpful mechanism against cognitive deficits.
pmc-13525501:
Mia Panlilio and co-authors present a narrative review, published in 2026. It covers microdosing of GLP-1 receptor agonists. These diabetes and obesity drugs copy a gut hormone. The hormone lowers blood sugar and body weight. Shortages and high costs have pushed clinicians toward smaller doses. The review gathers evidence on what such low doses can still do.

The drugs' benefits span several systems. They cover metabolism, the heart, and the kidneys. Keeping some drug activity may preserve meaningful effects. This may hold for some patients. The authors favour gradual, individualised dosing. They oppose rapid escalation to the highest tolerated dose. Long-term microdosing evidence remains limited, they note.
pmc-13526401:
Nakano and fellow doctors in Japan ran in 2026 a phase 3 trial of ensitrelvir in children with COVID-19. Ensitrelvir is a once daily pill that blocks a key virus enzyme. Kids under twelve had few drug choices, since most pills were cleared by age or weight. The trial enrolled 117 children aged six to eleven with mild to moderate illness. They got five days of drug or placebo, dosed by body weight.

The drug was well borne, with no new safety flags. Blood levels matched adult levels across all three weight bands used. By day four, viral RNA in nose samples had dropped by about one log step more with the drug than with placebo. Time to clear the main symptoms, a blocked or runny nose, cough, and fever, was much the same in both groups.
pmc-13526701:
Chen and co-authors collapse a vibration bistability by tuning internal resonance mismatch. Coupled micro oscillators can lock into two stable swing states. Past control of that collapse was stuck with fixed damping. The team tuned a second mode near a 1:2 resonance ratio. That opened a path for energy to drain from the driven mode.

Inside a set mismatch window, the high swing branch collapsed. Jump frequency dropped sharply at the same point. Stored vibration energy fell by about 80 percent. Phase reads showed the second mode split two phase zones. Models tied the collapse to fast growth of resonance-driven damping.
pmc-13528001:
Mohammad Vesal Bideshki and seven colleagues update a pooled review of synbiotic supplements and oxidative stress in adults for 2026. Synbiotics mix live gut microbes with the fibers that feed them. Oxidative stress means harm from reactive oxygen molecules outpacing the body's defenses. The team pooled trials in adults lasting at least three weeks. Retracted or suspect trials were left out.

Eighteen trials entered the final pool. Supplements lowered a marker of cell damage and total oxidant levels. Several defenses rose, including the enzymes SOD and GPx. Certainty ratings ranged from very low to moderate across outcomes. The authors warn that some markers rest on few studies. They call for bigger, better trials to confirm the effects.
pmc-13528101:
Liwen Zhang, Yu Xia, and Weidi Wang use genetics to test causes of pregnancy complications in a 2026 study. Everyday studies tangle cause with coincidence. Mendelian randomization uses gene variants as natural experiments instead. Traits studied included schooling, income, heavy physical work, and ages at first sex and first birth. Eight complications were checked, from miscarriage to gestational diabetes.

Later first birth slightly cut the odds of postpartum depression. Earlier first sex raised risks for several outcomes, including miscarriage and diabetes. More schooling and income looked protective across many outcomes. Physically demanding work raised the odds of postpartum depression and pre-eclampsia. Combined models kept the key links standing. The authors note limits in the genetic data. Still, they argue social and timing factors shape pregnancy risk in causal ways.
pmc-13528601:
Stefan Fattinger and twelve co-authors study why one immune signal makes tuberculosis worse, in this twenty twenty-six paper. The TB germ kills more than a million people a year, yet most infected people never fall ill. A family of alarm signals, the type I interferons, has emerged as a driver of severe disease.

Working in infected immune cells, the team found the alarm signal blunts a second, protective signal inside the same cell. Only cells bathed in strong, lasting alarm levels lost the protective reply. Removing a booster of the alarm erased that harmful state. The work names a target for future TB treatments.
pmc-13529801:
Siew Bee Aw, Pau Chung Leng, and Yaik Wah Lim build a smarter way to pick weather files for daylight design in the tropics in a 2026 study. Designers often borrow the nearest weather file, which can mislead sunlight simulations. The team compressed many weather traits into four main components. Those four explained about eighty-nine percent of file differences. Tropical files were then clustered by climate character.

A similarity index based on the components was tested against a Malaysian benchmark city. The new pick gave a seventy-eight percent chance of matching daylight scores within ten percent. Pure distance picks did worse. Across world class A files the protocol reached about eighty-seven percent selection accuracy. The authors say matching sky character beats matching map distance. The method helps sites that lack their own weather station.
pmc-13530201:
Po-Kai Yang and colleagues validated a deep learning tool that scores freezing of gait from wearable sensors. Published in 2026, the multicenter study built a model on a local cohort of 85 participants and tested it across six outside cohorts with 256 participants. Freezing of gait, the sudden failure to step forward despite intent, afflicts many people with Parkinson disease, yet video scoring is slow and laborious.

Local agreement between model and experts was strong, but outside cohorts proved harder, with agreement falling markedly. Fine-tuning on just fifty minutes of outside-cohort data lifted agreement close to the range seen between two human video raters. The authors propose a human-in-the-loop workflow with a web platform for tuning and expert review as a practical bridge. Readers get a validated sensor tool with honest limits on generalization.
pmc-13531801:
Austen El-Osta leads a 2026 evaluation of a tabletop role-playing program meant to keep at-risk pupils engaged in London schools. Young Dragons adapts a fantasy game to build emotional control, teamwork, and belonging. Ten schools ran weekly hour-long sessions for six to eight weeks with small steady groups.

Surveys from matched pupils showed no firm average change, with paths splitting: many gained mood, calm, and confidence, while a few withdrew further. School records hinted suspensions fell to zero after the program. Staff praised engagement and safety when groups stayed stable and facilitation stayed skilled.
pmc-13532001:
Hui Xu, Xiaodong Li, and Yong Liu hunt in 2026 for predictors of artery re-narrowing after catheter treatment of leg artery disease. Records covered 1,005 treated lesions in 917 patients at one center from 2019 to 2024, with ultrasound checks over three years. Models weighed clinical, anatomical, and procedural factors, then added two blood indexes.

By two years about 31 percent of lesions had re-narrowed past halfway. Advanced disease stage, long lesions, leftover narrowing, kidney disease, and severe symptoms raised risk, while good downstream flow protected. Adding a fat-based index and an inflammation index sharpened prediction clearly.
pmc-13532201:
Yong Wang and co-authors map day by day in 2026 how a cattle herpesvirus moves from nose surfaces to the nerve hub where it hides for life. Calves received virus through nose and eyes, with daily shedding swabs and tissue checks at days four and fourteen. Gene reading in the nerve hub tracked host response over time.

Shedding peaked around days three to six, highest from the nose. Tonsils carried the most virus early, while the nerve hub held low yet persistent levels by day fourteen. A nuclear defense protein restricted early viral growth until a viral protein dismantled its hubs.
pmc-13536201:
Scott Griffiths and colleagues set self-rated TikTok use beside logged TikTok data in eating disorder research. Published in 2026, the study took in 103 people, including 42 known to have eating disorders, pairing past-month how-often self-ratings with TikTok data files. Self-ratings are handy, yet how well they match logged use was not yet tested in this field.

Self-ratings lined up fairly to strongly with videos sent, videos liked, sessions, and binge-scroll sessions. Yet logged use varied hugely within each self-rating group: among self-called sometimes users, one got 99 videos while another got over 19,000, a nearly two-hundred-fold gap. Illness type and symptom strength did not alter the match. The authors urge careful reading of self-ratings when how much is seen matters for care.
pmc-13536701:
Ilan Hudson Gomes de Santana and colleagues review botulinum toxin type A for jaw muscle pain disorders in a 2026 systematic review. The toxin briefly weakens overactive muscles by blocking nerve signals. Ten randomized trials were gathered from five databases and checked for bias. Because trial methods differed widely, the authors combined results in words rather than in a single pooled number.

Pain eased over time in both toxin and comparison groups, including saltwater injections and standard care. Toxin did not beat saltwater injections in a steady way, though larger pain drops appeared in hard-to-treat muscle pain cases. Jaw function also improved in both groups, and benefits generally lasted from 8 to 24 weeks. Side effects were mostly mild and short-lived. The review advises against routine first-line use.
pmc-13538301:
Amjad Islam Amjad and colleagues model student mental health after the pandemic in a 2026 cross-sectional survey of 388 university students. Academic stress tied to heavy technology use may harm mental health through digital fatigue, with loneliness shaping the strength of that path. Students completed an online wellbeing scale built for the post-pandemic setting. Models tested direct links, a middle step through fatigue, and a loneliness interaction.

Academic stress linked strongly to mental health problems on its own. Digital fatigue carried part of that link, supporting a partial middle-step role. Loneliness also interacted with stress, strengthening the harmful pattern when loneliness ran high. The authors suggest smarter use of digital tools and more chances for students to socialize as practical responses for universities.
pmc-13538401:
Chen and colleagues published a 2026 study on hidden protein shape changes in liver cancer. Proteins can misbehave by changing shape even when their amounts stay normal. The team paired two mass-scan methods to read shape and amount together. Samples covered tumor, near-edge, and far-edge tissue from liver cancer patients.

Hundreds of proteins changed shape between tumor and edge tissue zones. Many shape changes came with no change in protein amount at all. Four proteins stood out, rising in both shape signal and amount. Those four also tracked with poorer survival in patient data. Shape reading adds a layer that amount-only studies miss entirely. Hub proteins from the maps offer leads for drug hunting next.
pmc-13538601:
Tailiang Lu and colleagues compare eye measurements between the two eyes of children with uneven focus in a 2026 school-based study. Uneven focus, called anisometropia, means the eyes differ by at least one diopter. Among 765 screened children, 91 aged 6 to 16 years met the definition and received full eye exams with relaxed-focus measurements. Lens power was computed from a standard formula, and eye-pair gaps were modeled against focus gaps.

The more short-sighted eye ran longer, with a deeper front chamber, thinner lens, and deeper rear chamber than its partner. Cornea traits and lens power showed no overall pair gap, though one focus pattern subgroup differed. Focus gaps tied mainly to length gaps, age, and lens power gaps in adjusted models. The authors describe lens compensation as varying by uneven-focus type.
pmc-13540201:
Hugo Swenson leads a team on methylation marks in ovarian cancer. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with epithelial ovarian cancer types. The disease is often found late with high death rates.

No reliable screening tests exist for it today. DNA methylation marks are robust and easy to reach. Early stage samples were read with non parametric methods. Promoter regions that differ by tumor type were mapped. Results were set against existing analysis programs. A CpG panel was built to sort the types. It held up in outside data cohorts.
pmc-13540401:
Maud Hermans and eight colleagues explore, in a 2026 study, whether mast cells in bone marrow explain the severe itching that troubles some people with slow-growing blood cancers called myeloproliferative neoplasms. Mast cells release histamine, a classic itch signal.

Thirty-two untreated patients gave marrow and blood samples and completed a symptom questionnaire covering essential thrombocythemia, polycythemia vera, and primary myelofibrosis. Eleven reported significant itching, and their marrow held notably more mast cells, both as a raw count and as a share of marrow cells. Mast cell appearance and blood levels of related markers did not track with itch. Whether the cells cause the itching or merely accompany it stays open.
pmc-13540901:
Zaixing Zheng and six colleagues compare, in a 2026 meta-analysis, two flavours of digital home rehabilitation for heart failure: programs guided by wearable devices and programs guided by interactive contact. Rehabilitation at home suits patients who cannot travel, yet nobody had sorted which digital style does what.

Twenty randomised trials with 4,652 patients were pooled. Digital rehabilitation improved walking distance, peak oxygen uptake, and quality of life over usual care. Wearable-guided programs won on walking distance and quality of life, while interaction-guided programs led on oxygen uptake. The authors label the split preliminary and ask for direct head-to-head trials sorted by patient type.
pmc-13541901:
Jiwon Han, Hyokee Kim, and Wan Joon Kim gauged how fast a surgeon learns robotic liver surgery, in a study from twenty twenty-six. They drew on one surgeon's cases at a single center from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-five. They used a running-sum method adjusted for how hard each case was. Fifty-five robotic cases and one hundred forty-nine keyhole cases were weighed.

The curve bent at case eleven for robotic surgery, against case fifty for keyhole surgery. Time per case fell from two hundred fifteen minutes to one hundred forty-five. Blood loss fell by more than half. No case switched to open surgery, and safety held steady. The authors say deep keyhole skill helps a surgeon shift to the robot fast, since hard cases came from the start.
pmc-13543301:
Jing Liang and six co-authors study a virus-like gene built into human DNA, in work on brain cancer cells from twenty twenty-six. The gene came from an ancient virus and now sits in our own genome. It seems to help keep DNA stable, but its role in glioblastoma, a harsh brain cancer, was unknown.

The team turned the gene down in lab-grown tumor cells and watched growth, cell death, and DNA breaks. They also checked two master switches of DNA repair. How the cells changed may show whether this old viral gene guards the tumor or the patient. The work hints at new treatment angles for a cancer that resists care.
pmc-13543601:
Fatıma Yaman's team tested in 2026 a detailed occupational-therapy cognitive assessment in older people with Parkinson's disease. The usual quick screening test misses executive and visuospatial problems that Parkinson's causes early. Ninety people over sixty-five took part: thirty patients with cognitive impairment, thirty without, and thirty healthy peers. All took both the brief screen and the dynamic geriatric assessment, which watches how a person performs thinking tasks.

The in-depth tool split the groups on nearly every subscale, including awareness and visuomotor construction, where even unimpaired patients scored below healthy peers, a gap the brief screen would miss. Scores from the two tests moved together strongly where their domains matched. A task-based assessment, the authors argue, catches the quiet cognitive erosion of Parkinson's soon enough to plan therapy around it.
pmc-13545201:
Wu and colleagues study what happens inside couples when a colorectal cancer patient and their caregiver disagree about how bad the patient's symptoms are. Such incongruence is common and corrosive, yet rarely measured dyadically, as a property of the pair. Their 2026 analysis surveyed 271 patient-caregiver pairs on pain, fatigue, and sleep disturbance, plus mood, relationship quality, and quality of life, then modelled how mismatched perceptions in one partner ripple to both.

Sleep disturbance was where perceptions genuinely diverged, with a statistically clear gap between patients' and caregivers' ratings, while pain and fatigue ratings aligned better. Education in both partners shrank the sleep gap, as did longer time since diagnosis, while the pair's gender mix and relationship type widened it in the regression results. The authors advise clinicians to ask caregivers separately, not assume the patient's report is shared.
pmc-13545301:
Jie Xu and colleagues reported in 2026 on feeding Chinese mitten crabs diets fermented with lactic acid bacteria taken from crabs themselves. Three hundred crabs were split into five feeding groups for twelve weeks, comparing plain feed, feed fermented without bacteria, and feeds fermented with one or both bacterial strains. Growth, gut microbes, and liver and intestine health were measured at the end.

Crabs on the single-strain and mixed fermented feeds showed stronger digestive and antioxidant enzyme activity plus higher activity in immune and gut barrier genes. Their gut communities shifted toward helpful bacteria and away from likely pathogens. In a separate inflammation challenge, fermented feeds calmed the response and helped restore the gut lining.
pmc-13546201:
Minsong Xue and nine co-authors gauge how three dose plans of a weak eye drop touch the eye's face in children with near sight. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, is a fresh read of a past trial.

The children, aged six to fourteen, were split by lot: drops once a day, twice a week, or once a week. One hundred thirty finished the checks. The team read the tear film's break time, its pool's height, its fat coat's depth, blink gaps, and redness of the eye's white coat. A self-score of eye strain was taken too. Checks ran at the start, at two weeks, and at a year.
pmc-13547901:
Hicham I Cheikh Hassan and colleagues tested whether a back-up fistula helps belly dialysis patients. Published in 2026, the look-back cohort study covered 115 Australian belly dialysis patients from 2017 to 2023. A back-up fistula aims to dodge blood dialysis through a central line, yet no prior study weighed its deaths or harms.

Fifty patients had a back-up fistula, and 31 of those matured for use. Death risk and overall blood-dialysis transfer risk did not differ between groups, but transfer with a central line ran lower with a back-up fistula. Problem rates looked similar at 28 percent versus 14 percent. The authors present back-up fistulas as a line-sparing option, not a life gain.
pmc-13548601:
Könül Umudova and Ömer Demir ask whether leftover urine after voiding explains how bothered postmenopausal women feel by urinary symptoms, in a 2026 exploratory study from a Turkish university clinic. Residual volume is checked routinely when women have incontinence or prolapse, yet its meaning without those conditions is unclear. Seventy women without either problem gave flow measurements, ultrasound residual readings, and answers on a quality-of-life questionnaire about urinary impact.

pmc-13548701:

pmc-13549101:
Gürel Neşşar and colleagues showed a simple stitch fix for rectal prolapse in frail patients. The Thiersch stitch narrows a lax anus with a ring suture, suiting elders unfit for major surgery.

The authors pitch the stitch as cheap, repeat-friendly, and mixable, while warning germ and return rates run high.
pmc-13550401:
Chenye Zhang proposes a control system for AI-generated photography aimed at new media artists, in a 2026 study of diffusion models. Semantic guidance comes from a vision and language model. Spatial layout mapping supplies structure, and style loss tuning sets the look. Attention and consistency mechanisms hold the image together.

pmc-13551801:
Ferhat Yakup Suçeken, Ayşe Nur İhvan, Aydan Arslan, and Hakan Keski published a 2026 case report of a rare adrenal lymphoma that imaging first mistook for adrenal cancer. pmc-13552601:

Stay, age, and weight did not differ between the high-flow and CPAP groups.
pmc-13553701:

pmc-13554201:
Yikai Guo leads a six-author team building a quantum-flavoured detector for faults in factory sensor streams in a 2026 study. Energy per check fell by about a fifth as well. Speed also improved, reaching hundreds of windows each second, suiting live factory watch.
pmc-13555001:
Alexandra Pollitt leads a large team pricing the hidden cost of applying for research grants in a 2026 study. Writing, reviewing, and judging proposals eats time across universities and funding bodies. The authors argue that cutting waste means reforming university habits as much as funder forms, since most of the burden sits with applicants.
pmc-13556001:
Natalie Jones and seven colleagues described in 2026 how they co-designed a hospital breakfast group for stroke survivors who struggle to eat and drink. Five core parts were agreed, covering team involvement, physical rehabilitation, and food preparation with real choice. pmc-13556301:
Wenting Wang and six colleagues argued in a 2026 letter that wind energy should reach into the high sky, past the classic limit on turbine efficiency. Conventional turbines can capture at most about fifty-nine percent of the wind's energy, a ceiling set by the Betz limit, and land limits plus slow, costly offshore building constrain growth. High-altitude systems fly tethered devices where winds run stronger and steadier.

It maps wind power density over East Asia at several heights and sketches ground and airspace systems that could work together. Application scenarios close the piece. The authors present high-altitude wind as a serious route toward deep cuts in carbon emissions rather than a curiosity.
pmc-13556801:
Li and colleagues studied how much energy the brain needs to hold its large-scale states in children with ADHD. The brain shifts between joined-up states and split states across the day. Most scan studies treat brain activity as steady and never price those shifts. The team used brain control theory to price them.

Basic measures of time spent in each state showed no clear group gap. In controls, children spent more time in the joined-up state than in the split state. That pattern was missing in the ADHD group. pmc-13557001:
Xiaoyan Si and colleagues reviewed in two thousand twenty-six anemia caused by inflammation in patients with solid tumors. The review gathers what is known on frequency, symptoms, causes, diagnosis, and newer treatments.

One immune signal sits at the center, driving a chain that traps iron in storage. Newer therapies aim at that chain directly. Teaching material for cancer doctors and nurses is woven in, covering recognition and day-to-day management. Busy clinics gain one practical guide linking lab science to bedside care.
pmc-13558501:
Silverberg and a large team analyze real-world eczema data in this 2026 study. The topic is minimal disease activity. Data came from the MEASURE-AD study of adults with moderate-to-severe disease across 28 countries.

Those missing the target averaged 3.8 to nearly 9.8 flares in the same data. Long flares over seven days struck only about a tenth to an eighth of achievers, versus up to half of non-achievers. pmc-13558601:
Ana Rožić, Mija Marinković, and Ivana Novak reviewed in 2026 the family of receptors that tag worn-out mitochondria for disposal, a cleanup process called mitophagy. These receptors weave together energy control, stress response, and cell fate, and their malfunction shows up across many diseases. In heart and brain disorders, too little or too much receptor activity both damage tissue. In cancer, receptors suppress tumours early yet later help them adapt, persist, and resist therapy. Precision targeting, tuned to tissue and disease stage, is the authors' prescription.
pmc-13560001:
Cao and colleagues map where allergy-causing plants grow in China and where risk will rise. Pollen allergy has climbed worldwide, and the authors take an ecological view of why.

Allergy risk correlated significantly with socioeconomic and environmental factors, and regions southeast of the Heihe-Tengchong line, China's famous population divide, were especially vulnerable. Under future climate scenarios, natural allergenic plants expand substantially by 2100, enlarging high-risk areas. Monitoring linked warmer temperatures to longer flowering and higher pollen counts. The authors urge adaptive public health planning in response.
pmc-13560201:
Congyue Zhang, Chao Sun, and Yuemin Nan review FSP1, a protein that shields cancer cells from ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death caused by fat oxidation in membranes. Their 2026 article explains how FSP1 works in parallel with the better-known GPX4 defense. It restrains lipid peroxidation mainly by recycling coenzyme Q10 using cellular reducing power.

Layers of regulation, from gene control to protein stability, decide how much protection a tumor gets. High FSP1 helps cancers resist therapy and adapt under stress. Preclinical efforts to block it include small-molecule inhibitors, rational drug combinations, and candidate biomarkers for picking responsive tumors. The authors flag translational hurdles while positioning FSP1 as a priority target.
pmc-13560401:
Yilong Yang and colleagues engineer a ferritin particle with a positive charge that cloaks adenovirus vaccine vectors against pre-existing immunity. Their 2026 study tackles a known weakness: many people already carry antibodies to adenovirus type 5, which blunt vaccines built on it. pmc-13560801:

Automated annotation identified 47,051 protein-coding genes in the coral's chromosomes. From the same specimen's microbial reads, the team recovered two binned bacterial genomes. They were assigned to the Bacteroidota phylum. The data note deposits the assembly and its notes openly. It adds a scleractinian genome to the comparative toolkit for coral biology.
pmc-13563901:

pmc-13564701:

pmc-13567901:

pmc-13571701:

Each muscle held a distinct set of abundant metabolites, in the dozens. Core pathways behind the variation were uncovered. Such maps can guide breeding and handling to raise the quality of lower value cuts.
pmc-13571801:

pmc-13572401:

pmc-13572501:

pmc-13573401:

pmc-13575201:

pmc-13575501:

pmc-13578401:

pmc-13578701:

Hotspot maps point to where heat stress bites hardest.
pmc-13580001:

pmc-13580101:

pmc-13582701:

Last, a coping shell forms, and cynicism is its visible crust. The path loops rather than running straight, the authors stress. pmc-13583001:

pmc-13592301:

Such sites could serve catalysis and molecular electronics.
pmc-13592501:

pmc-13593701:

pmc-13596801:

pmc-13597601:

pmc-13598201:

pmc-13600201:

pmc-13601501:

pmc-13604201:

That group showed clearly lower nutrition scores than the rest, along with weaker lung test results. Their blood protein and lymphocyte counts were lower too. pmc-13604701:
Ugur Ozkerim and colleagues published a 2026 study of third-round treatment choices for advanced colorectal cancer that has spread. The team reviewed records of one hundred twenty-two patients treated at one center over several years.

All patients shared a similar cancer type and treatment history, which made the comparison fairer. Statistical weighting balanced the groups further. pmc-13607601:
Lamorna Coyle and six colleagues review what can go wrong after mastectomy with immediate breast reconstruction. Rebuilding the breast in the same operation has grown common, with implant-based, tissue-based, and hybrid options multiplying. Each pairing of mastectomy style and rebuild type carries its own complication pattern, and patient factors such as other illnesses, cancer treatment, and personal goals shift the balance.

The review sorts complications by technique and by patient, aiming to sharpen care around surgery and one-to-one planning. Clinical photographs show how the same complication can present differently across approaches and bodies. The broader setting matters too: breast cancer is the world's most diagnosed cancer, bilateral rates have risen, and up to half of patients choose reconstruction. The authors build a framework for judging candidacy and risk, so counseling rests on the specific combination a patient faces, not pooled averages.
pmc-13608001:
Yujun Jiang leads a seven-author team solving how a bacterial protease keeps biofilm slime in check. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a hospital pathogen, persists in chronic infections by building biofilms rich in the sugar alginate. The protease MucD was known to influence alginate output, but its direct targets were a mystery. Mass spectrometry and sequence analysis caught MucD cutting two alginate-handling proteins, AlgX and AlgK.

A cryo-EM structure of MucD gripping an AlgK-derived peptide revealed how the enzyme assembles and chooses substrates. Guided mutations and biochemical tests showed activity flips with assembly state: MucD rests as a twelve-unit complex and works as a three-unit one. Cutting AlgX and AlgK means MucD restrains alginate production at the protein level too. This two-layer control and unusual activation switch, the authors say, sharpen understanding of the HtrA family and may suggest points of attack against biofilms.
pmc-13611101:
Fabila and coauthors build a camera system that spots pain in children. Pain checks in children rest on staff judgment and can miss shifts. A camera tool could watch pain signs nonstop at the bedside. The team used face point tracks from video clips.

They filmed 125 children aged 6 to 17 around planned surgery. An app on a phone took front face videos. Software mapped near 500 face points in each frame. Depth checks cleaned the point tracks for fair contrast. A smart network then learned pain patterns over time. The goal is fast, fair pain flags for care teams.
pmc-13611401:
Gibble and five co-authors describe poisoned sea birds in California in work from twenty twenty-six. In twenty seventeen, a large bloom of algae made a toxin called domoic acid. Many live and dead marine birds washed up at the same time.

Loons were the most hit species. A rescue center took in more than a hundred live loons with signs of poisoning. Many that lived through the first days soon looked well again. More than half, though, died or could not be released due to odd behavior or injury. The team examined dead and euthanized birds to detail how the toxin harms the bird brain and body.
pmc-13613001:
Aravind P. Gandhi and colleagues set out a protocol for a planned review of when to start thyroid hormone therapy for subclinical hypothyroidism. This is a mild form of underactive thyroid, where hormone levels still look near normal. The condition affects roughly 4 to 20 percent of people and has been linked with poor outcomes in pregnancy. For clear thyroid failure the choice to treat is easy, yet for this mild form the right timing is still debated.

The review will gather only randomized controlled trials from databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE, following the PRISMA-P reporting guide. It will compare starting treatment early against watchful waiting, delayed treatment, or no treatment. Outcomes include progress to full thyroid failure and related harms. As a protocol, the work promises a careful answer later rather than giving one now.
pmc-13613501:
Derjung Tarn and colleagues use a community translation method to make Medicare's Annual Wellness Visit understandable and attractive to older adults. The free annual visit was created to increase preventive care uptake, yet many patients are unaware of it and uptake in primary care has stayed low. Boot Camp Translation is an evidence-based method for converting medical jargon into patient-facing messages and materials.

A national advisory council of primary care clinicians and Medicare-eligible patients worked over seven months, through a kickoff meeting, calls, and video conferences. Thirteen patient partners, four clinicians, and two staff developed the messages. They emphasized prevention, staying healthy, more time with primary care clinicians, and the chance to keep doing liked activities for more years. Messages also noted the visit is usually free and can benefit the practice financially.
pmc-13614001:
Rita Forde leads a large team reviewing in 2026 how diabetes affects women's mental and social well-being across their lives, a side of the disease they say is overlooked. Diabetes touches fertility, pregnancy, and sexual health, yet care tends to focus on blood sugar numbers alone. The review gathers studies on four stages: monthly periods, pregnancy, the change of life, and sexual functioning.

Hormone swings during periods made blood sugar harder to steady and raised distress, often with little guidance from clinics. Pregnancy with any type of diabetes brought anxiety, stigma, and guilt, while support for those feelings stayed thin. Similar burdens showed up around menopause and in sexual life. The authors map clear gaps where research and routine care both fail women, giving clinics a direct agenda for change.
pmc-13615201:
S. I. M. M. Raton Mondol and Sangmin Lee present a 2026 method for teaching computers to read emotion from speech while keeping the process open to inspection. Emotion systems often swallow hundreds of sound features at once, which makes them slow, prone to overfitting, and hard to explain. Their approach ranks features two ways, by a game-theory style credit score called SHAP and by how much performance drops when a feature is scrambled, then merges the ranks.

A penalty for features that echo each other keeps the final set lean without throwing away sounds that carry real feeling. Tests ran on four well-known emotional speech collections and three kinds of classifier. Trimming to features that truly matter could make emotion software lighter and more trustworthy in settings like call centres and mental health tools.
pmc-13615601:
Zahra Hooshanginezhad, Houshang Bavandpour Karvane, Babak Mohammadi, and Sepehr Nemati study in 2026 how taking many medicines at once affects survival in people with heart failure who attend a clinic in Spain. The data covered 1,375 outpatients treated between 2006 and 2016. Patients were split into low and high medicine groups at a line of five heart drugs, and a machine-learning survival model adjusted for other traits.

Survival clearly worsened as the drug count rose, with the steepest risk in people taking seven or more heart medicines. Patients in the high group also did worse on adjusted analysis. The link does not prove the pills themselves harm, since sicker patients collect more prescriptions. Still, the study argues for regular medicine reviews in heart failure care, trimming what no longer earns its place.
pmc-13616001:
Linus Hesse and Linus Haberbosch review in 2026 how functional imaging helps find pituitary tumours that standard MRI scans miss or leave in doubt. High-detail MRI locates most of these small hormone-making growths at the base of the brain. Two groups stay hard: tiny tumours that drive Cushing's disease, and leftover tumour after surgery, where scar, gland, and growth look alike.

The authors propose an MRI-first ladder, adding PET scans, which light up active tissue, only when the plain scan is unclear. They walk through five tracer options and how to pick among them by the hormone pattern, past treatment, and the plan for surgery or focused radiation. Read this way, functional imaging becomes a problem-solving tool that protects the healthy gland while hunting the last piece of tumour.
pmc-13616301:
Yuan Zhang and colleagues engineer a wound treatment for diabetic foot ulcers that releases its healing protein only where tissue-chewing enzymes run too high. Such ulcers heal slowly and return often, largely because an enzyme called MMP-9 chews up new tissue faster than it forms, outrunning its natural blocker, TIMP1. Their system anchors the blocker to the surface of the patient's own cells through a link that MMP-9 itself can cut.

Where the enzyme is overactive, it snips the link and frees the blocker exactly on target; where levels are normal, the blocker stays parked. Lab tests confirmed the triggered release. Static dressings dose the whole wound evenly, yet this design answers a wound that changes day by day, matching drug release to the local level of harm.
pmc-13616601:
Yongjin Qiu leads a team mapping in 2026 the Rickettsia bacteria carried by ticks across eight provinces of Zambia. They draw on 1,587 ticks collected from plants and farm animals between 2016 and 2018. These bacteria include spotted fever agents that threaten people and animals, yet Zambia's picture was patchy. Ticks were named by shape, then screened with a test for a shared bacterial gene, and positives were read more deeply across five further genes.

In all, 204 ticks, or 12.9 percent, tested positive, with finds in every province. Gene reading found 26 variants, 25 in the spotted fever group. Several matched known or suspected disease agents, including the African tick bite fever germ. A province-by-province map gives health and veterinary services a starting grid for warning farmers and clinics where risk concentrates.
pmc-13617801:
Daniel B. Ibsen and four colleagues write a debate article answering a three-part Lancet series that blamed ultra-processed foods for displacing traditional diets and driving chronic disease worldwide. The respondents agree diet quality is a major health problem, yet they argue the data tying harm to processing itself, rather than to known nutritional risks. That evidence, they argue, carries deep uncertainties that policy should acknowledge.

Three questions structure their case. The Nova classification lumps together nutritionally diverse foods unlikely to share one biological effect, which muddies causal claims. Most proposed mechanisms are not unique to ultra-processing and could operate in less processed foods too. Studies usually pit ultra-processed against minimally processed foods, while pitting processed against ultra-processed items would isolate the processing effect better. They propose splitting the category into parts and traits, so risks can be pinned down clearly and responses aimed well.
pmc-13619301:
Dulce Maria E Ovalle Sanchez and three colleagues report a quality improvement project that raised interpreter use in pediatric heart units. Families whose home language is not English often get less clear communication in hospital, even though services exist. The team worked in an acute care cardiology unit and a cardiothoracic intensive care unit, using baseline data from 2022 through 2024.

Their changes made interpreters easier to reach, taught staff to use them, and added translated documents. Interpreter encounters more than doubled per hundred patient-days, and average minutes per patient rose from ten to well over twenty. Use during emergencies climbed from under a third of cases to nearly all cases. The authors say direct, practical fixes standardized care for these families and improved engagement with the care team.
pmc-13620401:
Jeallyza Muthia Azra and three colleagues turned young coconut drink into a yogurt-style fermented beverage and tuned the recipe. The drink blends coconut water with young coconut flesh, offering natural sugars and minerals for fermentation. They tested two starter doses and two fermentation times using the two classic yogurt bacteria, watching microbe counts, acidity, texture, nutrition, and taste.

Every version kept lactic acid bacteria well above the viability mark that defines a live fermented product. Starter dose shaped the results more than time did, driving acidity, thickness, nutrient use, and taster approval. The batch with the higher dose and the longer, ten-hour ferment balanced all measures best. Its fats leaned on medium-chain types, led by lauric acid, and lab digestion freed most of its potassium, magnesium, and iron for absorption. The authors see a workable local plant-based yogurt, with room to improve nutrition and flavor.
pmc-13621201:
Mingtian Ding and twelve colleagues found a chemical tag that lets brain tumor stem cells dodge a copper-based death. Glioblastoma is notorious for returning after treatment, driven by stem-like cells that resist therapy. Cuproptosis, a death route where copper makes mitochondrial proteins clump, should threaten such cells, yet they survive it. Profiling their protein tags pointed to one enzyme carrying a lactate-based mark.

One protein adds the mark using lactate, and another removes it. The mark leaves the enzyme's machinery intact but throttles a partner complex, cutting the fatty tags copper needs to trigger clumping. Erasing the mark restored the tags and made the cells sensitive to a copper-carrying drug again. Blocking lactate production, boosting the removing protein, or aiming a peptide at the marked spot all strengthened the drug in patient-derived and mouse brain tumor models. The authors name the axis a druggable target.
pmc-13621401:
Surthi M Ravedar and seven colleagues reviewed animal studies on whether plant extracts can shield the liver from tuberculosis drugs. First-line TB medicines cure the infection but injure the liver often enough to limit treatment. Following standard review practice, the team searched three databases for live-animal studies of herbal protection and scored their quality with an animal-research bias tool.

Sixty-eight studies made the cut. Protection varied widely by plant and study, yet three species stood out for cutting liver enzyme leaks and bilirubin while restoring antioxidant defenses in the tested animals. Those three were a ridged gourd, henna, and a wild melon relative. The reviewers think antioxidant and cell-protective chemistry explains the benefit, though exact mechanisms stay murky. They call for careful dosing and safety work, and eventually human trials, before any extract joins TB treatment.
pmc-13621601:
Annika Walter led a large team probing how Staphylococcus aureus behaves once it hides inside human cells, and why outcomes differ by strain. This common pathogen survives inside cells, beyond the easy reach of antibiotics and antibodies. The team infected human cells with four isolates, imaged where the bacteria settled, and read the host's gene activity.

Every isolate turned up in digestion compartments and free cytosol, often close to the nucleus. Infected monocytes switched on a shared stress program, yet each also drove its own distinctive pattern across inflammation, metabolism, and cell-fate genes. One chronic-infection isolate provoked a muted response. Cell death pathways fired differently by strain and cell type. Removing the TNF receptor, a key immune signaling dock, delayed death early but worsened it later, in a tissue-specific way. The authors caution that strain variety and this signaling axis should shape future host-directed therapies.
pmc-13622401:
Ben McFarlane, Zoey Robinson, David Curran, and Stephanie Burns gather what research says about the stigma faced by parents who have intellectual disabilities. Their review and synthesis was published in twenty twenty-six. Past reviews focused on support needs and services; this one centers on stigma itself.

The team searched four databases and kept twenty-three studies that met their rules. From them they drew five themes. Parents were cast as unfit, watched and controlled, and harmed by systems through force and family split. Stigma also shaped how parents saw themselves and felt. Yet parents pushed back, using support and their own agency. The authors call for services that start from parents' strengths and are easy to access, rather than from assumed deficits.
pmc-13623101:
Juhong Xie and colleagues uncover a fish-specific protein that helps a deadly carp virus switch off the fish immune system. Grass carp farming in China suffers heavy losses from grass carp reovirus, which causes bleeding disease. The team studied a gene called nhre3, already tied to disease risk, using rare minnows as a model fish.

Fish bred without the gene resisted the virus far better. The protein it makes, named NHRE3, works as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, an enzyme that tags other proteins for shredding. Lab work showed it tags ISG15, an antiviral defender, with a chain that sends it to the cell's disposal machinery. Without that attack, ISG15 partners with another immune protein and boosts downstream defences. The authors say the mechanism differs from mammal tricks against the same defender, and they point to resistant fish breeding as a practical use.
pmc-13623201:
Luisa Vargas Braz and colleagues look for factors that predict trouble eating by mouth in patients having surgery for primary brain tumours in Santa Catarina, Brazil. Eating ability was graded on the Functional Oral Intake Scale, which runs from tube feeding only to a normal diet. Tumour position, size, and type can disturb swallowing after an operation.

The team reviewed records of sixty-eight patients treated between January 2021 and March 2023. Women made up most patients, and meningioma, a tumour of the brain's coverings, was the most common type, often in the left half of the brain. Patients with tumours in the posterior fossa, the lower back part of the skull, showed the biggest drop in eating level right after surgery. Two patients needed tube feeding but climbed back to near-normal diets by discharge with speech therapy help. No factor besides tumour location predicted worse eating in this group.
pmc-13623401:
Grace El Nabbout, John J Kowalczyk, and Kelly J Manahan present a case of splenogonadal fusion in an adult. In this rare birth defect, spleen tissue fuses with the testicle and imitates cancer. Fewer than two hundred cases have been reported. No scan or test can rule it in or out with confidence before surgery, making it a diagnostic blind spot.

The patient was a twenty-nine-year-old man with a painful left testicular lump. Imaging looked suspicious for a tumour, and standard checks could not clear the mass, so surgeons removed the testicle through a groin incision, the cancer operation. Tissue examination afterward told a different story: the lump was misplaced spleen tissue, with no germ cell tumour or cancer. The authors use the case to warn that rare benign look-alikes can cost young men an organ, and they urge awareness of the defect.
pmc-13623901:
Chenghao Xiao and colleagues published a 2026 study on scrubbing personal details from medical free text in many languages at once. Clinical notes hold rich detail for research, yet names and other identifiers must come out first. Older tools need hand-labelled training data and work in one field or language, which makes them hard to scale.

The team's framework trains a generative language model on synthetic text, text made up for the purpose, tuned with instructions rather than human-labelled records. Tested on synthetic sets and on real patient requests sent to a digital triage service, the models beat strong existing systems across several medical fields. They removed sensitive details accurately while leaving the clinical meaning of the rest nearly untouched. Small training sets still worked, the models coped with medical fields they had never seen, and they anonymised other languages without extra training data.
pmc-13624101:
Xiaoming Huang, Changjuan Lei, Wei Xiao, and Heli He study how anxiety, sleep, and life quality hang together in a gut ill. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The ill is functional dyspepsia, a long-term upset of the upper gut with no clear cause in the tissue. Anxiety is common in these patients and can drag down daily life.

They review past cases and score each trait with set scales. More anxiety tracks with worse sleep and with lower life quality. Worse sleep also tracks with lower life quality. A path model shows sleep carries part of the anxiety effect: anxiety harms life in part by harming sleep. Care for sleep may thus lift life quality.
pmc-13624201:
Jinheng Gan, Yang Chen, and Lin Xin review MFSD2A, a transport protein that ferries fatty building blocks into the brain and other guarded tissues. The protein carries a fat molecule called DHA, vital for brain growth, across the blood-brain barrier while also keeping that barrier sealed. The review weighs evidence link by link, from transport chemistry to disease.

The firmest ground covers how the transporter grabs its cargo with sodium's help and how brain blood vessels use it during development. Children born with two broken copies develop small brains and severe developmental problems, the strongest human evidence of its role. Evidence from the eye, placenta, lung, kidney, and skin points to local jobs rather than one universal pathway. Hopes for cancer prediction or drug delivery through the barrier remain mostly associations so far. The authors map what is proven, what is tissue-specific, and what is still guesswork.
pmc-13624301:
Xuanyu Zhu leads a materials study building crystals that keep glowing long after the light switches off, and wiring that glow into a device that behaves like a synapse. Lasting glow can store information optically, yet classic glow materials form poor films and conduct electricity badly, which keeps them out of practical electronics. The team turned to a layered perovskite crystal that can be printed from solution.

By adjusting the number of inorganic layers in the crystal and adding antimony, the researchers tuned the internal defects, called traps, that catch and slowly release charge. The best films glowed for well over five thousand seconds and shone efficiently. Paired with carbon nanotube wiring, the chosen crystal formed a light-sensitive synapse that remembered ultraviolet flashes, strengthened with paired pulses, and held a visual pattern. The authors pitch the platform for combined sensing and memory in brain-inspired hardware.
pmc-13625201:
Ayumu Kocha and colleagues present a woman in her fifties whose severe depression arrived together with Graves' disease, an overactive thyroid. She believed she was guilty and poisoned, refused food and medicine, and stayed highly agitated, which blocked the thyroid care she needed. A standard calming injection given into a vein barely helped her settle.

After checks ruled out a thyroid crisis and confirmed her heart was stable, the team used modified electroconvulsive therapy, planned with hormone and anesthesia specialists. Agitation fell sharply after one session, restraints came off, and she could swallow pills, so thyroid treatment began. Her depression score fell from deep severity to near zero by day thirty-six, and calm held through two months of clinic visits.
pmc-13625501:
Débora M Morais and four colleagues, publishing in 2026, test whether a urine marker of nitrate intake tracks with muscle strength. Nitrate, plentiful in leafy greens and beetroot, helps blood vessels and muscles work. Intake is hard to measure, though. So the team used urine levels from the national NHANES survey of 2011 and 2012. Their group held 1,301 adults, split at age sixty, and strength was the sum of both hands' grip.

Among the 399 older adults, higher urine nitrate went with modestly stronger grip, by two ways of scaling the urine measure. No such link appeared in younger or middle-aged adults, nor in the whole group pooled. The effect was small, so the authors ask for follow-up studies over time before anyone prescribes nitrate for aging muscle.
pmc-13625601:
Tcheishvili and coauthors report a cancer case that mimicked a grave blood illness. A 77-year-old woman had breast cancer spread to bone. She came in with nausea, fast pulse, weakness, and brief nerve signs. Blood tests showed severe anemia and low platelets.

Shattered red cells on a blood smear pointed to one rare illness. That illness needs urgent plasma exchange to save life. Wide cancer spread can cause near the same pattern, though. Plasma exchange helps that cancer form far less well. Cancer control is the true fix in such cases. The case warns teams to check for cancer first.
pmc-13626601:
Marius Stoeckle, Kersten S Rabe, and Christof M Niemeyer present a bench workflow that sniffs out hydrogen-handling enzymes in bacteria without purifying anything. Hydrogenases, which split or make hydrogen gas, are prized for green energy ideas, yet testing them usually demands clean protein and genetic tinkering. Their method runs crude cell membrane and lysate fractions through gas chromatography, watching hydrogen rise or fall directly in the messy native mix.

Across a panel of unrelated bacteria, two species clearly oxidized hydrogen, and one relative-rich genus lit up again and again. One standout kept working for long stretches, tolerated some oxygen, and stayed active when hot, all rare and useful traits. A strain with no annotated hydrogenase gene still showed weak activity, proof that activity-first screening finds what gene hunting misses.
pmc-13629801:
Ann-Louise Ljungblad and Lisa Hellström present a shared concept for well-being work in schools. They call it pedagogical health. Health work in schools often splits between professions that lack a common language. The pair drew on material spanning preschool to upper secondary school. They frame well-being through four bases: mental, physical, social, and inner-life health.

The study's main yield is 52 candidate signs. These observable signs turn broad bases into daily practice. They give teachers, nurses, and counsellors a concrete base for joint talk and action. The authors supply teaching-based definitions for each base. They link the approach to global goals for health and schooling. Weaving well-being into teaching itself, they argue, strengthens school health work. It also makes that work last.
pmc-13629901:
Riccardo Stefanelli and thirty-nine colleagues tested a psychosis risk score in a large fresh sample. The score totals a person's life exposures linked to psychosis risk. The data came from a global programme. It held 1,642 people at high clinical risk for psychosis, plus 519 community controls.

The first score split the high-risk group from controls well. After recalibration it predicted accurately too. The team then refined it. They added loneliness and neighbourhood quality. They sharpened current predictors such as childhood trauma and parental mental illness. The refined version split groups notably better under cross-checks. It stayed well calibrated. The authors propose the score as a scalable first step. Stepped assessment paths could start with it.
pmc-13630501:
M. Al Fatly and seven colleagues used the Rotterdam Study to chart what drives immunoglobulin E levels in middle-aged and older adults. Published in 2026, their letter analyses blood samples from 8,679 residents, measuring total IgE and IgE specific to inhaled allergens, with a smaller group measured again years later.

Age, sex, smoking, body mass, season, and steroid creams or inhalers emerged as determinants of one or both measures. Total IgE traced a U-shape across age, falling until about seventy and rising thereafter, while allergen-specific IgE declined steadily with age, fastest in the younger participants. The authors note that IgE is increasingly tied to chronic diseases beyond allergy, making its ordinary drivers worth mapping in ageing populations.
pmc-13630801:
Carolina Coli Zuliani and seven colleagues compared two sources of human stem cells for growing new cartilage. The cells grew inside porous scaffolds. Cells from amniotic fluid and from fat were both coaxed toward cartilage with a growth factor. The work addresses a real gap. Joint cartilage barely repairs itself, and arthritis treatments rarely restore it.

Both cell types stuck to the scaffolds and multiplied. They laid down matrix rich in the sugars and fibres cartilage needs. The signature type II collagen and aggrecan showed up in staining and imaging. The amniotic fluid cells integrated more fully. They also assembled richer matrix. The authors back them as the stronger candidate for cartilage engineering.
pmc-13631401:
Mikaela Sundberg and one colleague ask how much a doctor needs to know before certifying why a patient died. Death certificates feed national statistics and prevention policy. Yet the person signing one faces a judgement call about sufficient knowledge. Official guidance barely addresses it. The authors use the case to build a broader idea. They call it knowledge-producing responsibility.

The pair interviewed 35 physicians. Certifiers draw on the medical record, on colleagues, and on family accounts. They also draw on their own sense of whether a death was expected. That distinction shapes how hard they push to investigate. It also shapes when they judge an autopsy necessary. The authors argue that mortality statistics cannot be split from these daily professional judgements.
pmc-13634301:
Gurisch and co-authors compare how nurse-linked scores are used in German and U.S. wards. Such scores track care traits that nurses sway most, like falls or sores. In a learn-health frame, those scores can flag where care can grow. The team ran 17 talks with 19 nurses from June to late 2025. Nine came from four German wards in the Magnet4Europe study. Ten came from four U.S. Magnet wards.

U.S. nurses said their score range was more broad and their logs more sound. U.S. wards also shared scores in a more open, set way. Staff roles for score checks and set talks spanned all ranks there. German wards had less of that shared frame in the talks. Three themes and eight sub-themes came from the talk texts.
pmc-13635601:
