Freeman W Chabala and colleagues, working through an African hepatitis B research network, measured fatty liver in people living with chronic hepatitis B across six countries. Fatty liver disease is rising worldwide, yet its overlap with hepatitis B in Africa was barely documented. The team scanned over sixteen hundred participants with a device estimating liver fat and stiffness. They tested which factors tracked with fat, and whether fat tracked with scarring.

About one participant in four had fatty liver, and half of those had the severe form. Older age, male sex, and overweight raised the odds, while living with HIV lowered them. Only severe fat, not milder grades, tied independently to liver scarring. Deaths over the short follow-up were too few to link to fat. Ultrasound missed most fatty liver despite naming it accurately when positive. The authors support screening for metabolic problems inside hepatitis B care.
pmc-13635801:
Pingping Huang and six colleagues asked whether electrical signals from leg muscles can reveal frailty in older heart patients. Frailty forecasts poor outcomes in cardiovascular disease and intertwines with muscle and nerve decline. The team studied one hundred fifty older adults, half frail by the standard checklist and half not. Wireless sensors on four leg muscles recorded activity while each person walked a short measured course.

Frail participants walked far slower and scored worse on a balance and mobility test. Their muscle signals differed in telling ways: stronger activity in one back-thigh muscle, a shifted order of muscle firing, and higher signal frequencies in several muscles. A few signal features predicted frailty independently alongside age and mobility scores. A model mixing signals with age identified frailty with strong accuracy. The authors present walking muscle signals as a practical window into frailty a clinic could capture in minutes.
pmc-13636101:
Felix von Krogh and four colleagues surveyed satisfaction with video consultations in dermatology, in a study written in German. Video visits are growing inside skin care, yet rollout still stumbles. Over one year, the team ran a questionnaire study at one center, asking both patients and doctors about their experience. They used a home-grown questionnaire plus a validated satisfaction scale adapted into German.

Of two hundred fifty planned consultations, nearly nine in ten took place successfully. One hundred twenty-eight patients and thirteen doctors answered. Overwhelming majorities on both sides said they would recommend video visits. Patients praised ease of use and the overall experience; doctors rated scheduling almost perfectly. Judgments on connection stability and how reliably skin findings could be judged varied widely. Doctors unhappy with skin assessment recommended video visits far less. The authors see strong acceptance, with image quality as the gap to close.
pmc-13637401:
How gender and race or skin colour intersect in Brazilian teenagers' eating habits is analysed by Rosa and two colleagues. Adolescent diets in Brazil feature heavy intake of ultra-processed food and low intake of fresh food, yet most studies treat gender and race separately rather than together. The team used the 2019 National Student Health Survey, covering more than 155,000 students, and built ten groups from gender crossed with white, Asian, Black, brown, and Indigenous identity.

Regular fruit and vegetable intake was highest among white boys. Black, brown, and Indigenous girls fared worse than white boys on beans, vegetables, and sweet treats alike. Black boys reported less regular vegetable intake and more sweet treats, while brown, Asian, and Indigenous boys reported more regular bean intake. Rosa and colleagues read the pattern as evidence that racial and gender inequality together shape adolescent diets. Black and Indigenous girls faced the greatest vulnerability.
pmc-13637601: Systematic Biology published this correction to a 2022 article by Cuong Cao Dang and colleagues. The article introduced nQMaker, software that estimates amino acid substitution models not reversible in time. The authors found a coding slip in one analysis: a matrix step used the wrong kind of multiplication. The error distorted one figure and one linked claim. The corrected figure places each nonreversible model beside its reversible counterpart rather than apart in their own cluster. The results and the article's conclusions stand unchanged.
pmc-13638701:
Yasuyoshi Morita, Yukie Tsuji, Tomoharu Yasukawa, and Kinuko Mitani report a post market watch study in Japan of darbepoetin alfa for anemia in myelodysplastic syndromes, bone marrow ills that cut blood counts. The watch ran for years after the drug's launch. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Near two thousand patients, most of them old, were tracked for five years from care start. Risk groups were mostly low or mid low. Side effects were told in three fourths of patients, with lung infection most common and shift to acute leukemia next. Blood counts rose past a key line within a year. Over half cut their transfusion need by half or more.
pmc-13644801:
Claudia Nieto and six colleagues present a 2026 content analysis of food and drink marketing on Mexican websites of International Food and Beverage Alliance members during Covid-19 lockdown. The alliance pledges restraint in marketing to children, and Mexico faces very high child obesity.

Across 269 websites, nearly all linked to social media, three quarters used charitable responsibility themes, and sixty percent appealed directly to children. Twenty-eight percent used the pandemic itself as a hook. Judged by Mexico's nutrient model, eighty-nine percent of marketed products were unhealthy. The authors say the practice contradicts the industry's own rules and call for binding regulation.
pmc-13645401:
Sara Moeini and six colleagues present a 2026 retrospective study of bone-anchored fixtures that hold silicone ear, nose, and eye prostheses at a large London teaching hospital. Data for Southern-brand fixtures were scarce compared with implants generally.

Sixteen patients received fifty-eight implants between 2013 and 2024, followed for an average of about four and a half years. About eighty-three percent of implants stayed integrated, with failures concentrated in bone previously treated with radiotherapy. Eight of ten surveyed patients wore a prosthesis daily, and satisfaction scores sat near the top of the scale. Problems were mostly minor and manageable.
pmc-13645601:
Yuxin Ma and four colleagues report the case of a seventeen-year-old boy with ameloblastic carcinoma, a rare cancer that grows from tooth-forming tissue in the jaw. His tumor sat in the upper jaw and was first taken for a returning benign growth. Surgery removed part of the upper jaw, and tissue tests confirmed the cancer. The team also reviewed past literature on this disease.

Eight months later a lump on the boy's cheek grew fast, and scans plus tissue tests showed the cancer had spread to a lymph node above the jaw. A second operation, followed by radiation and drug therapy, left him free of visible disease at six months. The authors say this is the first reported spread of its kind, and they urge careful scans of nearby nodes before surgery.
pmc-13645701:
Bayu Satria Wiratama and seven colleagues map research on the biological, psychological, and social factors that shape tuberculosis care and outcomes. Tuberculosis remains a leading infectious killer, with millions of new cases each year. Their scoping review searched three databases through January 21, 2026, and added a bibliometric analysis of publication patterns. Eligible work had to examine body, mind, or social factors tied to care or treatment results.

The review gathered 124 studies naming seventy-eight factors spread across the three domains. HIV infection, diabetes, poor nutrition, smoking, and alcohol use appeared often, alongside stigma, low disease knowledge, poverty, and hard-to-reach care. Publication output in this area has grown steadily and widened from body-focused topics toward mental health and social questions. The authors offer the map as a base for care programs that treat the whole situation of the patient, not only the infection.
pmc-13646001:
Lauris Kaldjian, Kristján Kristjánsson, and Shane McLoughlin published a philosophy paper in two thousand twenty-six defending practical wisdom in medicine. Some thinkers call the ancient virtue of phronesis redundant. The authors argue it is the master virtue that steers all the others.

Practical wisdom, as they define it, joins clear goals, sharp reading of context, moral virtues, careful deliberation, guided emotion, and motivation. In medicine it means patient-centred judgment aimed at health and flourishing. The paper answers the redundancy charge with arguments, reports from practitioners, and survey data from American and British adults. The authors note the concept has survived over two thousand years. They expect it to endure because moral problems demand it.
pmc-13647101:
Fin J E van Uum and ten colleagues use a parent-child trio design to separate how genes reach children's behavior directly from how parental genes shape the home, in a 2026 study. The data cover 3,270 families from a Dutch population study. Genetic scores captured broad neurodevelopmental liability and specific risks for ADHD, autism, and depression. Brain structure was measured at age nine and behavior problems at fourteen.

Most genetic influence traveled the direct route, through genes the child actually inherited. One indirect path stood out: mothers' genetic liability to depression related to children's behavior problems across domains, beyond the child's own genes, while fathers' did not. That maternal path was partly tied to who reported the behavior, though attention problems showed it in every report. Brain size measures explained none of the paths. The authors highlight mothers' mental health environment as a real channel of risk.
pmc-13648401:
Vinod Jaskula-Ranga and three colleagues study a quiet manufacturing problem in gene therapy: the end sequences of adeno-associated virus vectors, called inverted terminal repeats, often mutate while their plasmids grow in bacteria. These repeats are essential for packaging the therapy into virus particles, so hidden deletions can undermine quality.

Sequencing several plasmids and surveying more than seven thousand archived ones, the team found damage concentrated in whichever repeat sat nearest the plasmid's origin of replication, including one widespread short deletion. Guided by that pattern, they built a new vector whose repeats stayed intact and packaged a large gene-editing cassette. The work frames repeat damage as a preventable design flaw.
pmc-13650701:
Severin D H Irl and eight colleagues compare plant sizes on quartz islands in South Africa's Richtersveld desert, patches of pale rock that sit like islands in a darker landscape. Habitat islands promise clean tests of how environment shapes species, yet plant size on land-based islands had never been examined this way.

The team measured height and leaf traits for 67 species from the three dominant families. The species sorted into quartz specialists, generalists living both on and off the islands, and species found only in the surrounding matrix. Specialists proved shorter and consistently more variable in size, while their leaves matched the others in size and succulence, meaning whole-plant stature moved independently of leaf design. Harsh filtering by scarce resources and fierce sun on the quartz, the authors argue, favors compact dwarf succulents as an evolutionary specialization.
pmc-13662901:
Kelsey North and six co-workers pinned down where the steroid pregnenolone acts to shut potassium paths in brain blood tubes. BK paths help rule tube width, and many steroids tune them. This steroid was odd, since it worked with no help from the extra parts that peer steroids need. The team guessed the path's own pore protein holds a spot that grasps the steroid. They tested the grasp with a heat based gauge tool.

The steroid bound to the path protein at dose levels that block the path and squeeze brain tubes. A model on a known path shape named three amino acid spots as touch points. Bonds with ring groups seemed to hold the steroid in place. To know the spot counts, since BK paths sway blood force and brain blood flow. The 2026 finds open a path to drugs aimed at this nook.
pmc-13680501:
Hyun Sik Yoo and eleven colleagues raised the power of a protonic ceramic fuel cell by improving how its layers touch. Such cells promise clean power and hydrogen production, but resistance at the layer boundary limits them, most of all at low heat. The team sprayed a thin, dense film onto the electrolyte with a cheap spray method that can scale up. The film covered about ninety-three percent of the contact area. Impedance tests confirmed that both ohmic and polarization resistance fell as coverage rose.

The finished cell gave a peak power density just over one watt per square centimeter at five hundred degrees. In electrolysis mode it drew high current at modest voltage. The layer joint also survived harsh heat cycling without peeling apart. This twenty twenty-six study puts a number on a simple lesson: in ceramic energy devices, how well layers touch is performance.
pmc-1664601:
Mathers and Loncar project world deaths and disease burden from 2002 to 2030. Earlier projections from the Global Burden of Disease project, based on data from 1990, were still widely quoted years later. Fresh forecasts were needed as populations aged and disease patterns shifted.

The authors update those outlooks by cause, for the world and its regions. Their projections weigh trends such as rising chronic disease and falling infections in many places. Governments and health agencies use such forecasts to plan hospitals, training, and prevention long before needs arrive.  Readers can see which causes drive the totals in each region.
pmc-2245901:
Zhang presents the I-TASSER server for predicting the three-dimensional shape of proteins from their sequences. Guessing shape from the amino acid chain alone is one of the hardest problems in computational biology. Shared contests had been set up to judge prediction methods fairly and openly.

The server threads a new sequence through known shapes, then assembles a best model of its fold. Shape hints at function, so a good model can guide drug work and basic experiments. Making the method a free server let any lab obtain careful predictions without owning specialist software.
pmc-2777001:
Hruz, Laule, Szabo, and co-authors present Genevestigator V3, a reference database for gene expression across many studies. Their web tool lets biologists explore how genes behave across a wide range of biological settings. Early versions, though, were limited by how well the system could scale.

Version three rebuilds storage and architecture to handle data from multiple organisms and growing transcriptome collections. Pooling many experiments lets users compare a gene's activity across tissues, diseases, and treatments at once. A shared reference of this kind saves each lab from rebuilding the same costly archive.
pmc-3965101:
Overbeek, Olson, Pusch, and their colleagues described the SEED and RAST systems in 2014. The SEED, started in 2004, was built to give steady, accurate labels for genes across many thousands of genomes. RAST is its rapid annotation service for microbial genomes, meaning it names genes and their roles.

The SEED links genome data with expert knowledge of cell pathways, grouped as subsystems. RAST uses that base to label a new microbe genome quickly and in a form other tools can use. Together they help labs move from raw DNA reads to a first clear map of what a microbe can do.
pmc-4993001:
Li, Severson, Pignon, and their team studied tumor immunity in 2016. A tumor does not grow alone; immune cells move in and act on it. How those two sides interact shapes how the disease will go and how drugs will work.

The team used new computing methods to count the immune cells inside tumors from gene data. They also mapped how the mix of cells forms and shifts over time. A sound count can flag which patients may gain from immunotherapy, drugs that free the immune system to attack the tumor. It can also hint at why some tumors resist drugs, and guide new cures.
pmc-535701:
Taheri, Lin, Austin, and their team studied sleep length and body weight in 2004. Short sleep had been linked to a higher body mass index in large groups of people. The team asked whether hormones that control hunger might explain that link.

They measured two hormones: leptin, which signals fullness, and ghrelin, which sparks hunger. People who slept less had lower leptin, higher ghrelin, and a higher body mass index. That hormone mix would be expected to raise appetite and drive weight gain. The study gave a clear, testable path from poor sleep to extra weight, and it is still widely cited.
pmc-5388101:
Shu and McCauley recounted GISAID in 2017, the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data. Influenza viruses change constantly, so tracking them depends on laboratories worldwide sharing virus data quickly. GISAID was created as the platform for that sharing, and the paper traces it from vision to reality.

Under GISAID, labs deposit influenza sequences and related data in a shared database with credit to the data producers. That credit system was designed to encourage sharing that pride and politics had slowed before. Fast, open virus data let scientists spot new strains and update vaccines in time. The initiative became a model for pathogen data sharing.
pmc-5908901:
Nicola Sproston and Jason Ashworth reviewed C-reactive protein at sites of inflammation and infection in 2018. This protein rises sharply in the blood when tissue is infected or inflamed. Doctors already use it as a general marker of trouble.

The review explains the protein's two forms and how the second form acts right at damaged sites. There it helps clear dead cells and can also stir further inflammation. That dual role shapes debates about whether the protein is a helper, a harm, or both. Readers get the biology behind a very common blood test.
popular-pastimes-for-amusement-and-instr:
Henry Davenport Northrop compiled Popular Pastimes for Amusement and Instruction, a fat standard work on games. Plays, magic, and natural phenomena suitable for all occasions, issued by the National Publishing Company of Philadelphia. The title page promises a treasury for the home, public schools, lodges, social gatherings, and Sunday schools: parlor games. Charming tableaux, tricks of magic, charades, conundrums, and curious puzzles, with phrenology, mind reading, and palmistry on the side.

Humorous and pathetic recitations and dialogues fill out the program, and a section teaches the delightful art of entertaining itself. Northrop was a professional maker of home cyclopedias, and the book is built to be used to pieces. Any family or society with a winter evening to fill could find its entertainment here, from a card trick to a full charade, with instructions plain enough for amateurs.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-159-19:
Punch for September 1, 1920, in volume 159, leads with Charivaria, its column of brief comic notes. Miners and strikes hang over the page, as they did over Britain that autumn.

A Newcastle miner said to earn a pound a day is fined ten pounds for neglecting his children, and the column wonders why he did not wait for Mr. Smillie to neglect them. Smillie's hobby is given as collecting strikes. Amundsen is in no hurry to return to civilisation. The Poet Laureate has written no ode to British weather, and a Tube traveller of twenty years' standing is pitied and offered a seat.
queen-victoria-story-of-her-life-and-rei:
Queen Victoria: Story of Her Life and Reign, 1819-1901, is a brief life of the Queen. Verses from Tennyson head it. A tribute from Norman Macleod heads it too. The tribute praises her courage, patience, and endurance. No author is named on the pages shown.

The preface promises the salient features of the reign. It promises its domestic and public life. It gives a glance at the progress of the country across half a century. All of this comes in short compass. It asks readers to mark how freedom broadened, and how knowledge, wealth, and well-being spread wider than in any earlier age, under what it calls the golden reign.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: Volume one of The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte carries nothing before it here but a publisher's header in the old plain-text style. That header gives the title, names Constant as author, and states that the text is in English. No preface, contents list, or opening chapter follows it in these pages. A reader can learn the book's name, its writer, and its place as first part of a long set. Nothing is shown of what Constant tells of Napoleon in this part.
rhys-celtic-folklore-1901:
John Rhys, the Oxford Celtic scholar, gathered this two part set of Welsh and Manx folk lore, printed in 1901. He drew on tales told to him and on notes sent from Wales and the Isle of Man. His aim was to save folk belief before it faded.

The pages hold fairy tales, ghost lore, well rites, and tales of folk heroes. Rhys traced marks of the old Celtic faith in what the folk still did and said. The set is a rich store for any reader drawn to Wales and Man.
richard-carvel-volume-01:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel opens its first volume with seven chapters, though the front pages print the contents of the complete book. Lionel Carvel of Carvel Hall gives the first its name. Some Memories of Childhood and Caught by the Tide follow, in Richard's own telling of his early years.

Grafton would heal an old breach in the fourth chapter, and a song title, If Ladies be but Young and Fair, heads the fifth. Richard first suffers for the Cause in the sixth, and Grafton has his chance in the seventh. The wider contents printed here map five more volumes of the Carvel family's story beyond this first part.
rob-roy-volume-01:
Sir Walter Scott's Rob Roy begins its first volume with the advertisement to the first edition, in which its editor pleads guilty to breaking a promise. On publishing The Antiquary some two years before, he had announced that he was intruding on the public for the last time in that capacity. He shelters under the plea that an anonymous writer is a phantom.

His better apology, he says, is Benedict's: when he vowed to die a bachelor, he never meant to live long enough to marry. Papers holding the outlines of the narrative had reached him through his publishers, he claims, with a request to give them to the public. The first volume proper follows that playful frame.
royce-world-individual-vol-2-1901:
Josiah Royce published The World and the Individual, Volume 2, in 1901, completing his Gifford Lectures. This volume turns from metaphysics to nature, man, and the moral order. Royce studies how the Absolute expresses itself in the natural world. He also treats evil, individuality, and the hope of immortality.

Nature, for Royce, is the outer sign of an inner spiritual order. Human selves matter as unique members of a divine community. The supplementary essay on the one, the many, and the infinite is a technical high point. Together the two volumes state his system whole. They remain a peak of American idealist thought.
scheible-das-kloster-vol01:
Johann Scheible, a Stuttgart publisher, began Das Kloster in 1845 as a vast storehouse of older German print. The title means the cloister, worldly and spiritual, and band one holds the first four cells, or Zelle, of the set. Scheible reprinted rare and half-lost texts whole, rather than in scraps.

Readers find grimoires, Faust books, and the stern spell books called Höllenzwänge side by side with folk charms. Cheap chapbooks and popular tales fill out the shelf. Few readers of the day could have found these works at all without Scheible's press. The set grew into the central source book for the German grimoire world.
schiller-maid-of-orleans-1801:
Schiller's Maid of Orleans, his tragedy of Joan of Arc, appeared in 1801 in Anna Swanwick's English translation. Joan, a shepherd girl, hears voices calling her to save France from English invasion. Schiller makes her a figure of pure faith and martial fire.

Crowned by her victory at Orleans, Joan falters when love and doubt touch her mission. Schiller departs from history, giving her a death in battle rather than at the stake. The play fixed Joan's image for much of the nineteenth century. Verdi and Tchaikovsky both later drew operas from Schiller's version. Its verse and pageantry show Schiller's Romantic side at full stretch.
sebillot-folk-lore-pecheurs-1901:
Paul Sebillot, a French hoarder of folk lore, wrote this book on the lore of fishermen in French in 1901. He spent years on the coasts of Brittany and Normandy, where he heard the tales at first hand. No book of his day knew the French sea folk so well.

Sirens, morgans, and the freaks of the sea fill his pages from the tales of the coast. He tells how fish folk read winds, wrecks, saints, and strange lights on the waves. In French, the book is the lead word on the sea lore of France.
serapis-volume-01:
Georg Ebers wrote this historical novel of Alexandria, here in English by Clara Bell; volume one opens the tale. Night has hushed the town's turmoil in chapter one, with moon and stars on watch. Yet barred shops and armed patrols show a city braced against harm, not at rest.

Weeks of fevered strain hang over the streets near the harbor called Kibotus. An old man creeps close to the houses while monks' cries and Roman orders break the quiet. This first volume sets the stage: a rich port in the year 391, torn between old gods and new faith, awaiting a storm.
serge-panine-volume-01: Georges Ohnet, a French novelist, stands as author of Serge Panine. The pages at hand belong to volume one of the tale's English issue. That issue forms part of a series of French romances crowned by the French Academy. Only the publisher's header appears in these pages. It gives the title, the author's name, and the series note. No opening scene or cast list is shown. Which chapters this first volume holds stays unstated here.
serviss-other-worlds-1901:
Garrett P. Serviss made star science a joy for the plain reader in the United States. His Other Worlds came out in 1901. The full title deals with the nature and chances of life on the planets. Serviss tests each world with the best facts then known.

The Moon, Mars, Venus, and the far gas worlds each get a test. He weighs air, heat, and water, and asks who might live there. Serviss writes with warmth and a clear love of the sky. The book was the States' match to Proctor's famed work on the worlds.
shiel-purple-cloud-1901:
One man wakes to a dead world in M. P. Shiel's novel The Purple Cloud, from 1901. A strange cloud from a burst peak has killed all life on earth. He sails and walks through still towns. Grief and pride warp his mind year by year.

For much of the tale he is the last man alive. Then a sign of hope tests all he has built. Shiel set the mold for last-man tales. His rich prose makes ruin feel grand, sad, and oddly bright. He burns dead towns, mints coins, and builds a vast tomb for the world. Those mad acts show pride and grief at war in one soul.
sidonia-the-sorceress-the-supposed-destr:
Lady Wilde translated this German tale of Sidonia von Bork; volume two appeared in 1894 and carries Book Three onward. Contents pick up Sidonia's life inside the convent at Marienfliess and run until her execution on August 19, 1620. Chapter heads grow grim and strange in turn.

Sidonia talks Dorothea Stettin out of office, wounds Ambrosia von Guntersberg with an axe over a planned marriage, and prays the convent porter to death, the heads allege. The chaplain refuses her shriving and denounces her from the altar. A sorcery tale built on a real trial reaches its scaffold close.
sketches-by-seymour-volume-01:
Robert Seymour's comic plates open this first part of his sketches, issued in various forms about 1836 from a Thomas Fry printing in London. An editor's note counts ninety plates in the full set, many engraved by H. Wallis. Five small volumes merged into the whole, with order muddled by the printer, the editor suspects.

Everyday scenes lead: a sleeping fisherman, an early morning lark, and Sally passing word to her mistress. The editor frankly rates the pictures above the brief, punning text. Part one gives readers the first taste of Seymour's sporting and street humor in plate and verse.
spr-proceedings-vol15-1900-1901:
Volume fifteen gathers parts thirty six through forty, spanning 1900 and 1901. Five parts in one volume mark a burst of society business. The new century finds the SPR testing telepathy with card and drawing trials. Apparition reports continue, now sorted by standards set in the census years.

Trance mediumship holds the center, with Piper sittings reported in detail. Physical phenomena surface now and then, handled with visible caution. The journal of record keeps its promise: print the evidence, print the doubts. Volume fifteen bridges the society's Victorian and Edwardian phases. Its cases entered the standard literature of the field. It is a rich year book of psychical research.
spr-proceedings-vol16-1901:
Part forty one alone forms volume sixteen of the Proceedings, dated 1901. A single part can still run long when the Society for Psychical Research has much to report. Telepathy experiments and their statistics take a leading place. The society by now weighs chance results with practiced care.

Sittings with trance mediums supply the human drama of the volume. Named sitters, verbatim notes, and cross references fill the reports. Apparitions and kindred experiences arrive in smaller, well checked batches. Volume sixteen shows the enterprise in its mature routine. The evidential debate of 1882 to 1930 rests on files like these. Readers get method and mystery in equal share.
strindberg-easter-1901:
August Strindberg wrote Easter in 1901, a three-act drama, here in Edith and Warner Oland's translation. The Easter drama of guilt and forgiveness marks the turning point toward reconciliation in Strindberg's art after Inferno. Its quiet close shocked readers who knew only the Strindberg of the battle of the sexes plays.

The Heyst family waits in dread for a creditor who holds their father's fraud over their heads. Elis, the son, nurses grievances against the world, his fiancée, and the asylum-kept daughter's strange return home. Lindkvist, the feared creditor, arrives and proves gentle, forgiving the debt in the spirit of the season. Maundy Thursday to Easter Saturday frames a slow thaw from resentment toward a chastened, communal grace in the house. The Olands' translation brought this gentler Strindberg to English readers who had missed the turn.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Joconde leads off Volume 1 of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels in English verse. A life of the author and a preface come first. The tale itself treats a king, a queen, and a handsome courtier. It sets the book's tone at once. The table continues with The Cudgelled and Contented Cuckold and The Husband Confessor.

The Cobbler and The Peasant and His Angry Lord follow. The Muleteer and The Servant Girl Justified come next. Then stand The Three Gossips' Wager and The Old Man's Calendar. The Jealous Husband and The Gascon Punished close that run. Further on stand The Magick Cup, The Falcon, The Ephesian Matron, Belphegor, and imitations of Anacreon. This first volume already holds the heart of La Fontaine's art: old Italian and French stories reborn as nimble, smiling verse.
tales-from-the-arabic-volume-01:
John Payne's Tales from the Arabic begins with Volume the First. A Delhi edition carries the printing, dated 1901. The tales come from the Breslau and Calcutta texts of the Thousand Nights and One Night. Those texts are dated 1814 to 1818. The tales are missing from the other printed versions.

Its contents open on Asleep and Awake. The lackpenny and the cook stand inside that tale. The Khalif Omar Ben Abdulaziz and the poets follow. El Hejjaj and the three young men come next. Haroun Er Reshid and the woman of the Barmecides close the run. Then The Ten Viziers frames King Azadbekht and his son. Inset tales branch off from that frame. One tells of the unlucky merchant. One tells of Abou Sabir and the advantages of patience. One tells of Prince Bihzad and the ill effects of rushing in. Payne kept the tales' frame-and-inset build intact.
tesla-talking-planets-1901:
Nikola Tesla told Collier's Weekly in February 1901 that he had caught signs from Mars. The piece, Talking with Planets, set out his claim in his own words. Tesla said odd beats in his gear in Colorado matched no earthly source. He thought wise beings on Mars might be at work.

He goes on to muse on how men might hail other worlds one day. Plans for vast power and clear signs fill the last pages. No proof came, and most star men doubt the claim. The piece stays the most famed tale of its kind from the dawn of radio.
the-adventures-of-ferdinand-count-fathom: Tobias Smollett wrote The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom, and this first volume holds Part One of the two-part novel, with the author's preface and an opening essay by G. H. Maynadier of Harvard University. Chapter heads run from Fathom's infancy and army start through a rich jeweller's house, where he lodges by fraud and is at last exposed.
the-antiquary-volume-01: Volume One of Sir Walter Scott's The Antiquary is present only as cover, spine, and contents matter. A title page and frontispiece are named but not shown. The contents list an introduction and an editor's introduction, then chapters counted in words from first through thirteenth and onward. Nothing of the novel's people, place, or plot can be read from these pages.
the-arabian-nights-entertainments-volume: Volume one of an 1813 two-volume set has a full title page. It tells how a sultaness of the Indies told one thousand and one stories. Her aim was to turn a sultan from a bloody vow. He had sworn to wed a lady each day and have her killed the next morning. The set also promises an account of eastern ways and faith. Contents begin with fables of the ass, the ox, and the labourer. The merchant and genius and the fisherman follow.
the-attache-or-sam-slick-in-england-volu: Volume one of Thomas Chandler Haliburton's The Attaché, or Sam Slick in England, opens with the same matter as the complete edition. It has a Greek proverb motto and Sam Slick's warning about having his talk printed. It also has the author's letter from London, dated July 3, 1843. The letter sends the attaché ahead to Edmund Hopkinson at Edgeworth, Gloucestershire, asking kind reception for his quirks, quaint sayings, and queer views of England. The volume's contents begin with Uncorking a Bottle and A Juicy Day in the Country.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-01:
Volume 1 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers and translated from the German by Clara Bell, opens with the same preface as the complete form of the tale. Ebers tells the student reader that the Bride needs no preface, then makes two scholarly points. The word Mukaukas, he holds with de Goeje, is a title and not a name. Arab writers use it of the Byzantine Emperor's men in Egypt, set against the Moslem power.

The long point deals with Horapollo, author of the Hieroglyphica. Ebers would place him in the seventh century, not under Theodosius. Suidas lists the other Horapollo's works, those of a scholar on Greek poetry, with no word of the Hieroglyphica at all. No chapter of the tale is shown in these pages.
the-burgomaster-s-wife-volume-01:
Volume 1 of The Burgomaster's Wife, by Georg Ebers and translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, opens with the same dedication and first chapter as the complete form of the tale. The dedication goes to Baroness Sophie von Brandenstein, née Ebers. Ebers writes from Leipsic on October 30, 1881. He recalls working, as her guest seventeen years earlier, on the facts at the book's base.

His profession kept him from his favorite study, the history of Holland, his mother's home, and his aunt never tired of reminding him of the fallow material. At last he gave it its just dues. Holland's glorious history is the espalier, he says, for the tendrils of his tale. The first chapter sets spring in the Netherlands in 1574, come early that year. Gnats dance in sunshine, butterflies settle on yellow blooms, and a stork by a ditch snaps up a frog.
the-captives-pg3601: This copy of The Captives, by Hugh Walpole, carries the same dedication to Arnold Bennett and the same long epigraph from William James as its sibling, but its contents run further. Part II, The Chariot of Fire, continues through Mr. Crashaw and The Choice, and the listing reaches Part VII with The Prophet in His Own Home and The Outside World. Only the front pages and the table of contents are shown.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton, Lord Lytton, opens The Caxtons here with Part I and his preface. The book is billed as a family picture, and the preface sets honest terms for readers. Its plot is slight, its events are few, and most of them match ordinary life.

Only the fate of Vivian brings sharper stakes to the tale. Lytton notes that humor here serves kind people rather than satire. Man appears at rest by his own hearth, not in action abroad. The hero tells his own life story, which links the whole cast together. That story is meant to show how home shapes a young man's conduct and career. This first part thus sets up a quiet novel where household love holds the foreground.
the-celebrity-volume-01:
Volume 1 of Winston Churchill's novel opens with Chapter I and a narrator who has known its hero since boyhood. The hero is the man later known as the Celebrity, Mr. Charles Wrexell Allen. In the days when he wore kilts, fame had not yet touched him.

The narrator recalls that the boy showed no mark of genius to his plain, unwatching mind. No manuscripts were read aloud, and none of the odd habits of later fame had appeared. He grants that his own lack of sight may share the blame. This first volume sets up the contrast the whole tale turns on: the plain boy of memory against the famed figure society will pursue at Asquith.
the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bierce-vo:
Ambrose Bierce's collected works open with this first volume, dated 1909. The contents begin with Ashes of the Beacon, then a run of invented histories and far lands: the land beyond the blow, sons of the fair star, and an interview with Gnarmag-Zote. Civil War pieces close the list, among them What I Saw of Shiloh and Four Days in Dixie.

Ashes of the Beacon bills itself as an historical monograph written in the year 4930, a future vantage for Bierce's satire. Other titles promise the Tamtonians, a dog in Gangewag, a conflagration in Ghargarioo, and an execution in Batrugia. The war writings shift the key: a little of Chickamauga, the crime at Pickett's Mill, and what occurred at Franklin. The volume shows both Bierces at once, the fabulist of invented kingdoms and the veteran who wrote war from inside it.
the-complete-works-of-brann-the-iconocla: Volume 1 of the complete works of Brann the Iconoclast, by William Cowper Brann, was issued as a Project Gutenberg text in June 1996, etext number 567. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, which notes that the set runs to twelve volumes and that volumes 1, 10, and 12 were then in progress. This first volume opens the series.Its contents rest on the strength of the title page alone.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book I of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume I of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. An introduction by S. W. Orson opens the volume and sets the work's rank at once.

Orson reckons the Confessions among the notable books of later times, and indeed of all time. The book deals, he says, with leading people and events of a momentous epoch. In that age absolutism and feudalism were rallying for a last struggle against the modern spirit. Voltaire, the Encyclopedists, and Rousseau himself chiefly stood for that spirit. After fierce quarrels and bloody wars across Europe and America, more tolerant and rational principles prevailed. Book I then begins Rousseau's own account, the start of an autobiography that retells a whole life without flattery or hiding.
the-crisis-volume-01: Volume 1 of Winston Churchill's novel The Crisis is shown here only by the contents of the entire set, the same set-wide list carried in the complete edition. Book I begins with chapters on origins, The Mole, Black Cattle, and Silas Whipple, then runs through Bellegarde, a quiet Sunday in Locust Street, and The Party. Book II adds Abraham Lincoln, Glencoe, and signs of the times. Only that contents list is present here, so this volume's own chapters do not appear.
the-disowned-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's novel The Disowned opens in this first volume with a quiet May evening in the English countryside. A young man walks down a green lane at dusk, singing snatches of an old song as he goes. Soon a second, older traveller catches up with him, and their chance meeting sets the tale in motion.

Later parts of the volume follow Clarence, a young man cut off from his father's house and name. He lodges with the comic Copperas family and moves among proud lords and kind friends. The story turns on lost rights, hidden guilt, and a young man's fight to rise by his own worth.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-h:
Part one of Hell, in Dante Alighieri's Vision of Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise, holds cantos one and two in the verse rendering by the Rev. H. F. Cary. Lost midway through life, Dante wakes in a dark wood and climbs toward a sunlit hill. Fear eases when a guide appears and offers to lead him through the realms of the dead.

These first cantos set up the whole journey. Dante doubts his strength, and his guide answers with the story of the aid sent from heaven. The part forms a calm gate into a grim road.
the-emperor-volume-01:
Volume one of Georg Ebers's The Emperor, in Clara Bell's rendering, carries his full preface. He planned the tale, he says, from lectures on Roman Egypt, then let science claim fourteen years. The book crowns his Egypt series, joining Uarda, An Egyptian Princess, The Sisters, and Homo Sum in one sweep from Pharaohs to monks.

The tale starts at Alexandria as the city readies for Hadrian's visit. Builders rush to fix the palace at Lochias. Young sculptor Pollux, the steward Keraunus, and his daughters step forth. Ebers builds a whole city in words.
the-great-events-by-famous-historians-vo: Rossiter Johnson was editor-in-chief of The Great Events by Famous Historians. Charles F. Horne and John Rudd were associate editors. This record is Volume I. The National Alumni published the set. Its copyright is dated 1905. Only front matter is present here: the title page and the start of a contents list. The title page states the plan: great events told as full narratives, in the words of eminent historians. The set is non-sectarian, non-partisan, and non-sectional. The contents open with a general introduction.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part: John Ormsby translated this stretch of Cervantes' Don Quixote, Volume 1, Part 01. An editor's note explains that the cover and pictures come from the 1880 J. W. Clark edition, with engravings by Gustave Dore, while the text is Ormsby's; the same note stands at the front of the complete Volume I record. The contents list Part I chapters on the pursuits of Don Quixote and his first sally. Only the editor's note and contents are present here.
the-innocents-abroad-volume-01: Part 1 of Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad opens a six-part split. The text comes from the 1869 first edition. Only the title page and contents are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The summaries cover the voyage out. Popular talk of the excursion comes first. Grand preparations and the assembling of the clans follow. The patriarchs suffer tribulation at sea. Horse-billiards and mock trials pass the days. Landfall in the Azores ends the stretch. Spain, Africa, and Gibraltar come into view.
the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-01: Volume 1 of Winston Churchill's The Inside of the Cup carries the same full table of contents as the complete record in this set, listing every chapter of all eight volumes. Only that contents listing is present here, so the narrative itself does not appear. The four chapters assigned to this first volume are The Waring Problems, Mr. Langmaid's Mission, The Primrose Path, and Some Riddles of the Twentieth Century, opening the story of a rector and his fashionable parish that the later volumes carry through crisis, arraignment, and retribution.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-01:
Edward Bulwer Lytton opens this record with the same dedicatory epistle found in the complete record of his historical novel. He defends fiction built from real records, arguing that a tale can supply habit, motive, and feeling that a chronicle leaves cold. The letter also admits the field of English historical romance was already crowded.

This record presents the opening portion of the novel of Edward IV and Earl Warwick. Readers should note its first pages duplicate the complete record exactly. The story then moves toward court life, private love, and the baron power behind the throne.
the-letters-of-wolfgang-amadeus-mozart-v:
Ludwig Nohl collected Mozart letters from 1769 to 1791, and Lady Wallace translated volume one for a New York and Philadelphia edition in 1866. A preface argues that earlier biographies quoted the letters in broken pieces. Quoting, the editor says, destroyed the familiar and confidential mood that gives them charm.

Contents divide the volume by place and date, from Italy and Vienna through Mannheim and Paris to the Idomeneo months in Munich. Readers meet Mozart living, working, enjoying, and suffering in his own vivid words. Family money worries, patrons, and new music fill letters home.
the-life-of-marie-de-medicis-queen-of-fr: Julia Pardoe wrote her life of Marie de Medicis in three volumes issued in 1890, and a note at the front of this record states plainly that it holds volume three. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, opening book three on Marie as exile with a chapter dated 1618. De Luynes moves to keep the queen mother at Blois, and Richelieu treachery raises her suspicions. The biography itself is absent from this record.
the-magus-or-celestial-intelligencer-bei: Only library stamps and a garbled title page are present here, so the work itself does not appear. The stamps place a copy in Glasgow's Ferguson Collection, dated 1921. What can be read names The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer, a system of occult philosophy in three books, printed by Knight and Compton of Cloth Fair, London. Its title promises the ancient and modern practice of the cabalistic art, natural and celestial magic. It promises wonderful effects worked through knowledge of celestial influences and the occult properties of metals, herbs, and stones.
the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volume-01: Volume 1 of Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont was edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott. Only its title information and contents appear here, so the memoir text itself does not appear. Its contents are the same listing carried by the complete edition: a biographical sketch of Hamilton, then ten chapters. They run from the Chevalier Grammont at the siege of Trino to Turin, banishment from France, the English court, and his falling in love with Miss Hamilton.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 271 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, September 1, 1827, describes Norwich's new prison. The old gaol, insecure and too small for classifying prisoners under the new act, drove the magistrates to build outside the city near St. Giles's gates. Designs were invited in competition through the Norwich papers. The plan of Mr. Brown of Wells Street, London, won and was carried into execution.

The foundation stone was laid in 1824, and the building finished in 1827, the year of the article. It holds 120 prisoners besides turnkeys and servants, and cost the city 23,000 pounds. Its quadrangular boundary wall runs 1,220 feet, cut at the angles by bastions, enclosing nearly an acre and three quarters. The entrance bastion packs porter's room, baths, and an oven for purifying foul linen below the drop room.

Volume 19, No. 528, dated January 7, 1832, opens at the Surrey Zoological Gardens. Engravings show two entrance lodges, a rustic building not yet assigned a use, and a glazed round building meant as a refreshment room. Tropical birds occupied that round room for the present.

The grounds covered about fifteen acres and promised a delightful promenade near London. Mr. Loudon, editor of the Gardeners' Magazine, is quoted with mixed praise. He admired the gardens overall, yet found their scenes lacking unity, since each view competed for attention instead of leading visitors on step by step. He also credited Mr. Cross with building faster, and with grander structures, than the older gardens in Regent's Park.
the-parisians-volume-01:
Volume 1 of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's novel The Parisians opens with a prefatory note by the author's son. The same note opens the record of the complete novel, word for word. The son says The Parisians and Kenelm Chillingly share one central idea with The Coming Race, and that the three late fictions warn against certain social and political theories of the day.

He calls The Parisians a work of dramatized observation, not romance. Where Chillingly follows one man's inner life, this novel follows a whole community. Parisian society of imperial and democratic France is itself the hero, shown through many figures drawn with equal care on a large, crowded canvas.
the-prince-of-india-or-why-constantinopl: Volume I of Lew. Wallace's The Prince of India, or Why Constantinople Fell, opens with verses from Longfellow calling the shapes and shadows of the past to rise. The pages shown give the title page and contents, so the novel itself is not on view. Book I lists The Nameless Bay, The Midnight Landing, and The Hidden Treasure. Book II, named for the Prince of India, moves through A Messenger from Cipango and The Pilgrim at El Katif. It reaches The Prince and the Emir and The Arrival in Constantinople.
the-red-lily-volume-01: Anatole France is named as author on the electronic edition header, which labels the text volume one and gives an April 2003 release. Here only that edition header and its general notices are present, so no part of the novel itself appears and nothing about its story can be told from these pages. A companion complete record in the set carries a biographical preface instead.
the-right-of-way-volume-01: Gilbert Parker opens the first of six volumes here. Eight chapters fill this opening volume. A road to a verdict leads the list. The trial's outcome and five years of change follow. Charley makes a discovery in the middle chapters. A woman in heliotrope appears there too. Wind, a shorn lamb, and troubled peace come next. The cost of an ornament closes the volume. Later volumes are listed in full as well. Only those contents lists are present here. The narrative itself does not appear on these pages.
the-science-of-palmistry-and-its-relatio: Irene Smith wrote The Science of Palmistry and Its Relations to Astrology and Phrenology. She published it herself from a post office box in Tacoma, Washington. The copyright entry is dated 1901, in the author's name. The printing is badly garbled in the copy shown, with letters scrambled throughout. Even so, the title, author, place, and date can be read. Nothing beyond the copyright and title pages is present. No palmistry instruction, charts, or arguments appear, so the book's teaching cannot be described from these pages.
the-story-of-my-life-volume-01: Volume one of Georg Ebers's autobiography, in Mary J. Safford's translation from the German, opens with the same dedicatory poem To My Sons that heads the complete edition in a companion record. Only that poem is present here. Ebers stands near the end of life's journey. He bids his sons search the harvest of the vanished years. He tells them to steer their life bark by one star. That star lit his own pathway. The first volume's narrative does not appear.
the-thirty-years-war-volume-01:
Volume one of Frederick Schiller's History of the Thirty Years' War reaches English readers through a collected edition of his works, introduced here by a preface to the sixth edition. The publishers call theirs the best collected Schiller available in English. They praise Schiller as a historian formed to excel in every department of literature, citing his lucidity of style and impartial judgment. His historical writings, they say, will always recommend themselves as popular expositions.

The preface also sorts out the translators, noting that the Rev. A. J. W. Morrison ably translated the Thirty Years' War itself. Coleridge's versions of the Wallenstein plays are mentioned among the collection's treasures. Readers meet Schiller the historian through his publishers' confidence that a dramatist's clarity made his history endure.
the-wandering-jew-volume-01:
Volume one of Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew opens with the same author note printed in the library's complete edition of the novel, and that shared front matter is stated here plainly. The note follows Sue from medicine and six years in the French Navy to inheritance, first success, and fame through The Mysteries of Paris. Exile after Napoleon III's coup and death in banishment close the sketch.

What follows in this record is a contents list for book one only, part first, The Transgression. A prologue at the lands end of the world precedes chapters on Morok, the travellers, Dagobert, Rose and Blanche, a secret, and extracts from General Simon's diary. The novel's text itself does not appear in the pages preserved here.
thomasius-de-crimine-magia-latin-1701:
Christian Thomasius, professor at Halle, defended his theses on the crime of magic in 1701. The Latin dissertation is a juridical demolition of witchcraft prosecution. Thomasius argues that the crime, as the courts defined it, rests on a pact no evidence can prove and no law should punish.

With this work the Enlightenment enters the courtroom in robes and wig. Thomasius traces the trials to torture, bad metaphysics, and borrowed Roman law. His students carried the argument across German courts. Within a generation, prosecutions withered in the lands his influence reached. The dissertation is brief, dry, and devastating. Reason here performs the executioner's last service, ending the trials for good.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-01:
Charles Thomson, secretary of the Continental Congress, spent his retirement translating the Greek Septuagint into English. His version, printed at Philadelphia in 1808, was the first English Bible translation published in America. This first volume runs from Genesis through the second book of Samuel.

Thomson worked straight from the Greek, not from the Hebrew or the Latin, so his Old Testament often reads fresh against the King James text. The volume gives the creation, the patriarchs, the exodus, and the rise of Israel's kings. Jane Aitken, the printer, was the first woman to print a Bible in America. The work is a landmark of the young republic.
tob-0101:
Five books of Solomonic magic make up the Lemegeton, called the Lesser Key of Solomon. Mathers edited the famous English text. Its first book, the Goetia, lists seventy-two demons with their ranks, seals, and powers, and tells the magician how to call and bind them.

Later books cover spirits of the air, planetary angels, and the Ars Notoria, prayers said to grant learning and memory. The set reads like a court directory for an unseen world. No grimoire name is better known to modern occultists. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10501:
Three classic English renderings of the Quran stand side by side here, verse by verse: those of Abdullah Yusuf Ali, Marmaduke Pickthall, and Mohammad Habib Shakir. A compiled edition like this serves comparison rather than devotion alone. Readers can watch three translators handle the same Arabic line in real time.

Where the three agree, the sense is likely clear; where they differ, readers see genuine choices about tone, theology, and English idiom. Yusuf Ali's poetic notes, Pickthall's plain formality, and Shakir's directness contrast sharply at times. For students without Arabic, parallel translation is an invaluable tool for reading the Quran carefully and honestly.
tob-10801:
Matthew Arnold delivered the lectures published as On the Study of Celtic Literature in 1867, asking what Welsh and Irish poetry in translation contributed to English letters. Arnold was a poet and critic concerned with the cultural balance of Britain. The Celts, he argued, supplied qualities the Saxon temper lacked.

In Celtic writing he finds natural magic, melancholy, and a joyful wildness, set against English steadiness and common sense. Part literary criticism and part cultural politics, the lectures helped invent the modern idea of Celticism. Scholars now question his racial categories, but the essays remain a landmark in how English readers learned to value Celtic literature.
tob-9101:
Griffith translated the Atharva Veda, the fourth and most earthly of the Vedas, in the edition verified from the 1919 scan. Where the Rig Veda soars, the Atharva works at ground level: spells against fever and worms, charms to win love, keep a king safe, or curse a rival.

Healers, lovers, and householders speak in its verses more than priests at great sacrifices do. Hymns to time, breath, and the earth show its reach upward as well. Scholars call it the everyday religion of ancient India, and the description fits. Griffith's flowing English keeps the charms brisk, strange, and very human.
tolstoy-anna-karenina-garnett-1901:
Leo Tolstoy wrote Anna Karenina in Russian, and Constance Garnett made it English in 1901. Garnett's was the first major English version, and it made Tolstoy's novel an English classic. The book pairs a doomed love affair with a search for faith and meaningful work.

Anna leaves her cold husband Karenin for Count Vronsky and loses her son and rank. Levin, the other lead, seeks truth in farming, marriage, and God on his estate. Anna's passion curdles into jealousy and despair as society shuts its doors to her. Her death under a train closes one of fiction's most famous arcs of love. Tolstoy renders balls, races, harvests, and inner thought with equal, unmatched vivid force.
travels-in-the-interior-of-africa-volume:
Mungo Park's first African journey fills volume one of the 1893 Cassell edition of his Travels in the Interior of Africa. An introduction traces his life before the voyage. Park was born near Selkirk in 1771, studied medicine at Edinburgh, and sailed as a ship's surgeon.

The African Society chose him to replace Major Houghton, who had died in the field. Park sailed for Senegal in May 1795 and came home shortly before Christmas 1797. The introduction also tells the grim sequel: a second expedition in 1805, ending with Park killed at Boussa on the Niger. Readers meet the man before they follow his route.
uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-volume-:
Georg Ebers's Uarda, a romance of ancient Egypt, opens its first volume with a dedication in verse and a preface. The English translation is Clara Bell's, from the German. Ebers explains that the book grew from a winter spent in 1873 among the tombs of Thebes, studying the monuments of the city of the dead.

Long rides in the silent desert developed the story's germ, and a long illness gave him leisure to write. He dropped his first plan of heavy endnotes, since his earlier Egyptian Princess had covered that ground. The notes, he says, had guaranteed his care with archaeological detail drawn from monuments and classic authors.
ueber-kunst-und-kunstler-1901: Ueber Kunst und Künstler, 1901. The art essay. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
un-ga-res-63-301:
A coup in Honduras in the summer of 2009 drew swift rebuke in Resolution 63/301 of the General Assembly. Troops had seized President Jose Manuel Zelaya Rosales on 28 June 2009 and forced him from the land. The text voices deep worry at the break in the state's lawful and free order. It also faults acts of force against envoys and their staffs, in breach of the 1961 Vienna pact on such ties.

The coup is condemned in plain words. It broke the free and lawful order of Honduras and cut short the rule of a president the people had picked. The Assembly demands the instant and full return of the lawful state, headed by Zelaya. The record's catalog year of 1961 is wrong; the vote is of 2009.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 63/301 responds to the military coup of 28 June 2009 in Honduras. In that coup, the elected president was detained and expelled, and a de facto government installed. Adopted at the sixty-third session, the text treats the overthrow as a serious attack on democratic order and constitutional rule.

The resolution condemns the coup and the detention and expulsion of President Manuel Zelaya Rosales. It demands his immediate and unconditional restoration, together with the government he headed. It calls on all states to recognize no Honduran government other than his. It backs regional efforts under the United Nations Charter to settle the crisis. It asks the Secretary-General to report as the situation develops. The vote signaled that the Assembly would not treat a military takeover as a fait accompli.
un-sc-res-101:
An Israeli raid on the Jordanian village of Qibya brought the Council's strongest censure in 1953. Armed Israeli forces had attacked the village on the night of 14 October. Dozens of civilians died in the assault. Truce officials reported on the attack twice that autumn. On 24 November 1953 the Council found the raid broke the ceasefire rules of 1948. It also broke the armistice duties both sides owed.

The Council expressed its strongest censure of the action. Such raids, it said, hurt the chances of the peace both parties had to seek. Israel had to take real steps to stop them for good. Jordan, for its part, had to keep blocking armed crossings of the line. The Qibya case became a byword for reprisal raids.
un-sc-res-1301:
Morocco and the Polisario Front remained deadlocked over Western Sahara in 2000. On 31 May 2000 the Security Council extended MINURSO for two months. The mission's task was to run a referendum on self-determination. The Secretary-General's envoy had just toured the region. His report saw the same old split over the Settlement Plan's main terms.

The mandate now ran until 31 July 2000. In that time the parties were expected to bring the envoy concrete proposals. The Council wanted ideas that both sides could accept. It hoped that would open a path to an early and lasting settlement. A fresh assessment had to reach the Council before the term expired.
un-sc-res-1401: Numbered 1401 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 2001 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1501: Crossing into the 1500s sequence, Resolution 1501 was adopted by the Security Council in 2003. The text here follows the official record as transcribed on English Wikisource. Readers will find the Council speaking in its two registers: weighing language in the preamble, and direct orders, authorizations, or demands in the paragraphs that follow.
un-sc-res-1601:
Haiti's stabilization mission received a short bridge in May 2005. On 31 May 2005 the Security Council extended MINUSTAH until 24 June 2005. The Council said it meant to renew the mission for further periods. A Council team had visited Haiti in April. Its report, and the Secretary-General's May report, informed the decision. The situation still threatened peace in the region. The mission acted under Chapter VII of the Charter.

The brief term covered the gap before a fuller renewal. Haiti's transitional government was preparing elections for that year. The mission guarded security while the vote was organized. The Council stayed seized of the matter. A longer extension followed within the month.
un-sc-res-1701:
Resolution 1701 ended the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon. After a month of fighting, the Council adopted the text in August 2006, with both sides accepting a halt. It remains the basic settlement document for southern Lebanon.

The text calls for a full stop to attacks, Israel's withdrawal as a strengthened UNIFIL deploys, and no armed groups south of the Litani River except Lebanon's army and UN troops. It also demands respect for the Blue Line border. Nearly every later crisis on that border has been argued in this resolution's language.
un-sc-res-1901:
Rwanda tribunal judges gained room to finish their trials on 16 December 2009. The tribunal's president had written in October and November about the bench. Its completion strategy report admitted that not all work could end in 2010, as the Council had ordered. Terms of judges had already been extended to the end of 2010.

The Council said it meant to extend the appeals judges' terms by 30 June 2010, in light of progress. To let the tribunal finish trials already running, it raised the number of ad litem judges who may serve at one time. Judge Erik Møse was allowed to complete the Setako case, which he had begun before his term ran out. Judgment in that trial was expected by February 2010. The Council stayed seized of the matter, as the tribunal's slow wind-down became a standing item on its agenda.
un-sc-res-2001:
Resolution 2001 extended the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq once more in 2011. American forces were preparing to leave the country by year's end. The Council kept UNAMI in place to advise Iraq's government through the transition.

Its tasks in the text include election support, help with disputed internal borders such as Kirkuk, and work on refugees and human rights. The Secretary-General is asked to report every few months. The resolution shows the UN becoming the main outside presence in Iraq just as the military chapter closed. It stands in a long series of yearly UNAMI renewals preserved in this record.
un-sc-res-201:
The military situation in Cyprus stayed mostly quiet in the first months of 1965, and the Secretary-General credited the peacekeeping force for much of that calm. His report recommended keeping the force in place. Cyprus's government wanted it to stay beyond 26 March 1965. Resolution 201 was adopted unanimously on 19 March 1965.

The Council thanked the states that supplied troops, police, supplies, and money. The parties were told to show restraint and to cooperate with the force. The earlier Cyprus resolutions were reaffirmed. The force's stationing was extended for three months, ending on 26 June 1965. The renewal was routine in form, but it rested on a clear judgment. Without the force on the ground, the quiet on the island might not have held.
un-sc-res-301:
With Resolution 301, adopted on 20 October 1971, the Council turned to Namibia. South Africa ruled the territory in defiance of the United Nations, which claimed direct duty for it. France and the United Kingdom abstained, while thirteen members voted in favor.

The Council backs the World Court's advisory opinion of 21 June 1971 in full. That opinion held South Africa's presence in Namibia to be illegal. South Africa must pull its administration out at once. Member states must treat the occupation as unlawful and give it no support. The text also condemns South Africa's plan to split Namibia into tribal Bantustans.
un-sc-res-401:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was extended once more on 14 December 1976. The Secretary-General's report of 9 December held that the force's presence remained essential. It kept quiet on the island and supported the search for a settlement. The force's freedom of movement in the north was still restricted, though talks on its stationing were moving. Both communities had agreed to the extension.

The Council restated resolution 186 (1964), which had created the force. It also restated its backing of the General Assembly's call for a settlement respecting Cyprus's sovereignty and unity. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint and avoid any act that could spoil the talks. The stationing of the force in Cyprus was extended for six months, to 15 June 1977. The Secretary-General would continue his good offices mission and keep the Council informed of progress.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A night raid on a Jordanian town shocked the world in 1953. Israeli troops hit Qibya on 14 and 15 October. Homes fell. Scores of folk died. Truce staff sent word on 27 October and 9 November. Both Jordan and Israel spoke their case. Resolution 101 passed on 24 November 1953 by nine votes to none. Lebanon and the Soviet team held back.

The raid was found to break the 1948 ceasefire text. It broke the armistice pact with Jordan as well. The Council gave the act its strongest blame. Israel had to bar all such raids to come. Jordan, in turn, had to firm its watch on wild crossings of the line. Those crossings fed the cycle of raid and counter-raid. More staff for the truce team were pledged. Its chief owed a report in three months.

Two months, and a pointed wish, mark this Sahara text of 2000. On 31 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1301. The Secretary-General's May report lay before it. His Personal Envoy's mission won the Council's backing. The vote mission, MINURSO, had been blocked for years. The parties read the vote plan's core rules in opposed ways.

The text extends the mandate just to 31 July 2000. It sets a clear hope for those two months. The parties should bring the envoy firm, concrete offers that both can accept. All paths to an early, lasting deal should be tried. The Secretary-General must assess the state of play before the term ends. The deadline kept pressure on both sides.

A new United Nations mission for Afghanistan, UNAMA, is created on 28 March 2002. The Bonn Agreement had set the country's interim path, and an Afghan Interim Authority had taken office in December 2001. The Secretary-General's report of 18 March 2002 laid out the new mission's shape.

UNAMA is set up for an initial 12 months, with the tasks and structure the report proposed. Its work covers political support for the Bonn process, human rights, relief, and recovery across the country. All Afghan parties are called on to cooperate with the mission and protect its staff, and progress reports are due every four months.

Bunia, in Congo's Ituri district, changes hands in this text of 26 August 2003. A French-led Interim Emergency Multinational Force had stabilized the town. Its authority was to pass to the United Nations mission, MONUC, on 1 September, and the Council wanted no security gap in between.

States in the departing force are authorized to help the MONUC contingent in and around Bunia if the mission asks and exceptional circumstances require it. That backup applies only to force elements still present before 1 September and only during the pullout, which was to end by 15 September at the latest. The aim was a smooth transfer.

Haiti's peace force won a stay of just three weeks in 2005. The force, MINUSTAH, had run the land's guard since 2004. A Council team had toured Haiti in mid-April. Its tale, plus the chief's report, sat on the table. Resolution 1601 passed on 31 May 2005.

The mandate ran to 24 June 2005, and no more for now. The text says the Council means to renew it for more terms. The short span let members weigh the state of play first. Haiti's strife was named a risk to peace in the area. The force drew its teeth from a 2004 text. That text let it act with force to keep the peace. Brief stays like this one marked the Council's watchful, month-to-month grip on Haiti.

The 2006 war between Israel and Hizbollah in Lebanon is ended by this text of 11 August 2006. A month of fighting had killed and injured hundreds on both sides, wrecked much civilian infrastructure, and displaced hundreds of thousands. A full cessation of hostilities and the release of the abducted Israeli soldiers are called for.

A permanent ceasefire is backed, built on Hizbollah ending all attacks and Israel ending offensive operations, followed by Israel's withdrawal as a strengthened UNIFIL deployed. UNIFIL is greatly expanded, up to 15,000 troops, with a stronger mandate to help Lebanon's army hold the south. An arms embargo on weapons to Lebanon outside state authority is also called for, along with urgent world aid for Lebanon's recovery.

Resolution 1901, adopted on 16 December 2009, extends the terms of the Rwanda tribunal's judges. Letters from the Secretary-General in November passed on the tribunal president's requests. The completion strategy report for 2009 conceded the tribunal would not finish all work in 2010 as once ordered. A July resolution had already stretched trial judges' terms to the end of 2010.

The Council extended the terms of the permanent and temporary judges sitting in the trial chambers to 31 December 2010, or until their assigned cases finished, if sooner. It also signaled it would review the appeals judges' extensions before mid-2010. The genocide trials' slow tail, not new policy, is what this administrative text protects.

Iraq's security had improved after years of war, but attacks and sectarian violence continued. On 28 July 2011 the Council adopted Resolution 2001. It extended the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, known as UNAMI. National unity in Iraq remained fragile at the time.

The Council extended UNAMI's mandate for twelve more months. The mission advises and assists Iraq's government and people. Its work covers elected bodies, broad political talks, and national unity. It also helps with regional dialogue and talks on disputed internal borders. Aid for refugees and displaced people is part of the job, along with human rights work and reform of the courts and laws. The Council said it would review the mandate again in a year.

Spring 1965 brought another Cyprus renewal in New York. On 19 March, the Council adopted Resolution 201 without dissent. The Secretary-General advised keeping the peace force three more months. The Cyprus government said it wanted the force past its March end date.

His report noted a mostly quiet island. The force itself deserved much of the credit. Yet the calm stayed uneasy in several spots. A fresh round of fighting was a real danger there. Such a clash would bring harsh results. The Council renewed the mission and thanked its backers again. The text shows why the force stayed: few trusted the calm to hold without it.

Namibia's illegal occupation by South Africa is condemned in Resolution 301, adopted on 20 October 1971 by 13 votes to none, with France and the United Kingdom abstaining. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966, making the UN responsible for the territory. The International Court of Justice advised in June 1971 that the presence was illegal.

The Council agrees with the Court: South Africa must withdraw its administration now. Member states must treat the presence as illegal, South Africa's acts for Namibia as invalid, and give it no support. It condemns moves to destroy Namibia's unity, such as the Bantustans, and calls again on South Africa to leave. States must not sign treaties with South Africa for Namibia, send consular agents there, or strike economic deals that entrench its rule. Contracts granted by South Africa after 1966 get no protection against a lawful Namibian government.

Resolution 401, adopted on 14 December 1976 by thirteen votes to none, renews the Cyprus peacekeeping force for six months. The Secretary-General's report of 9 December said the force was essential both to keep the island quiet and to help the search for a settlement. Talks between the two communities' representatives offered the best hope, he judged, if both sides showed flexibility.

The Council extended UNFICYP's stationing to June 1977. It noted that the force's freedom of movement, and that of its civilian police, was still restricted in the north, though talks on deployment were inching forward. Concern was voiced about actions raising tension between the communities, and the parties were reminded to honor the agreements reached in earlier rounds of talks.

Czechoslovakia split in two at midnight on New Year's Day 1993. The Czech Republic and Slovakia parted without violence. Both needed fresh UN seats, since the old federation's membership lapsed. Resolution 801, adopted without a vote on 8 January 1993, handled the Czech application, filed as document S/25045.

The Council recommended the Czech Republic's admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly acted on 19 January. Prague's diplomats took their places within weeks of independence. The speed showed how orderly the divorce had been. Unlike Yugoslavia's violent breakup, this split needed no peacekeepers. The resolution is a brief, calm record of a negotiated separation entering international law.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1301:
Section 1301 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets out definitions for its chapter. It sits in Chapter 24 of that title, the Congressional Accountability Act, in its general subchapter. Part (a) states that the terms that follow carry the senses given, except as the chapter otherwise provides in a specific place. The first term defined is Board.

Board means the Board of Directors of the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights. Chair means the Chair of that Board. Covered employee is defined by a list of employing offices. The list as shown names the House of Representatives, the Senate, and the Office of Congressional Accessibility Services. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1501:
Section 1501 of Title 2 of the United States Code states the purposes of its chapter. It sits in Chapter 25 of that title, on unfunded mandates reform. The first purpose named is to strengthen the partnership between the federal government and state, local, and tribal governments. The second is to end a named practice by Congress.

That practice is the laying of federal mandates on those governments without full thought by Congress and without fit federal funds. Such mandates may push aside other key needs of those governments. The third purpose is to help Congress in its thought on bills that set up such duties, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
