uslaw-usc-t2-s2001:
Section 2001 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the House Office Building and its care. It sits in Chapter 30 of that title, on the operation of the Capitol complex, in the House part. The building is to bear the name House Office Building from then on. Its control, oversight, and care are assigned by the section.

The staff hired for the service of the building, other than the Capitol Police, fall under the same control. Such staff are those Congress funds for the guard, care, and use of the building. Control rests with the Architect of the Capitol, subject to a further term stated in the text. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4301:
Section 4301 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the staffs of committees. It sits in Chapter 43, on committees of Congress, in a general part of the chapter. Each standing committee of the Senate, save the Committee on Appropriations, may name a set of skilled staff. That set is in aid of the staff of clerks. No more than six such staff may be named by a committee. The naming is by a vote of the most of the committee.

Those skilled staff are to be set to work for the chair and for the head of the minority of the committee. The committee is to fix that set-out as it sees fit. One guard is set for the claims of the minority.
uslaw-usc-t2-s501:
Section 501 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets up a named body of the House. It sits in Chapter 16, on the marks for mail sent by Congress. The body set up is a special commission of the House of Representatives. Its name is the House Communications Standards Commission. A second clause deals with the make-up of that body. The Commission is to be made of six Members of the House.

The Speaker of the House is to name those six Members. Three are to come from the party with the most seats in the House. Three are to come from the party with the fewer seats. The Speaker is also to name the chair of the Commission. That chair must be a member of the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service who sits on the Commission.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5101:
Section 5101 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the hire of aids for the heads of the House. It sits in Chapter 51, on the heads of the House, in a general part of the chapter. The Speaker, the head of the majority, and the head of the minority are each given a grant. Each of them may hire an aid for the work of the office. The aid is to be paid at a base rate that may not top $8,000 a year.

A second clause deals with the funds for those pays. Sums of need are let through for the pay of such aids. The funds are to be granted by the law that sets the money for the House. The rule is thus a short one on staff for three named posts.
uslaw-usc-t2-s901:
Section 901 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the force of caps on set kinds of spend. It sits in Chapter 20, on powers for times of need to cut budget gaps. The part deals with the wiping out of gaps past a top sum. A first rule sets a cut by force of law, called a sequestration. In 15 days past the end of a session of Congress, such a cut is to be made. Its aim is to wipe out a breach for the year of the budget in any class of spend.

A second rule sets how a breach is wiped out. Each account that is not let out of the cut, in the class in view, is to be cut by a set sum.
voltaire-philosophical-dictionary-flemin:
Voltaire built an arsenal in dictionary form, and William F. Fleming's 1901 translation gives the Philosophical Dictionary complete in ten volumes merged. Entries run from angels to zeal, each a small essay with a sting. Superstition and intolerance take the blows, in the cool voice of a man who trusts reason.

Short pieces suit quoting, which made the dictionary the Enlightenment's most handy reference of dissent. Some entries argue, some mock, some simply define a word until its misuse shows. Readers can open anywhere and find Voltaire thinking aloud, the eighteenth century's sharpest pen at work on faith and power.
voyages-of-samuel-de-champlain-volume-01: Volume one of the Voyages of Samuel de Champlain came from the French in Charles Pomeroy Otis's rendering. Historical notes and a memoir by the Rev. Edmund F. Slafter go with it. A transcriber's word on spelling opens the book. The old footnotes have been moved to the end of each chapter. The tall letter s of the original gives way to the modern form. Pages present here hold those notes and the start of the title page only, so Champlain's narrative itself is not shown.
wells-first-men-in-the-moon-1901:
H. G. Wells sent two men to the Moon in The First Men in the Moon in 1901. A broke man of trade, Bedford, meets a sage, Cavor, with a great find. Cavor has made a stuff, cavorite, that shuts off the pull of Earth. They seal it in a sphere and ride it to the Moon.

In the Moon they find air in deep caves and a race of ant-like Selenites. Chains, strange beasts, and a vast brain at the core fill their tale. Bedford wins back to Earth, while Cavor's fate comes by faint signs. The book is a key text of the first space age tales.
weston-legend-sir-lancelot-du-lac-1901:
Jessie Weston, the scholar who translated Parzival and retold Gawain, turned to Lancelot in this study of 1901. She asked who the famous knight was before the great French romances made him the queen's lover. Her book traces the character across centuries of story.

Weston follows Lancelot from early folk tale roots through the poems of Chrétien de Troyes. She ends with Malory, who gave the knight his lasting English shape. Her work was bold research for its day and still reads well. Anyone who loves the Arthur tales will find here the life story of a legend in the making.
what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-01:
Volume one of Lord Lytton's What Will He Do With It? opens at a summer fair in Surrey. Lytton wrote under the name Pisistratus Caxton. Booths crowd the main street with toys, bright crockery, ribbons, and gilded gingerbread. On the green, shows offer a mermaid, a Norfolk giant, and a two-headed calf.

A high stage promises a play called The Remorseless Baron and the Bandit's Child. Drums, fifes, and penny whistles sound on all sides. This record shares its opening pages with the record named as the complete work. The fair sets a lively stage for the long tale of Lionel Haughton, Waife, and his grandchild Sophy.
works-of-john-bunyan-volume-01:
George Offor edited this first volume of John Bunyan's works, covering experimental, doctrinal, and practical writings. The contents list opens with a memoir, then Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners. It also names Bunyan's account of his imprisonment. Treatises follow on the soul, prayer, grace, and the fear of God. Each work gets an introduction and notes from Offor.

The memoir's first section traces Bunyan from poverty to soldiering and marriage. His wife's small dowry of religious books changed his path. Readers get the core of Bunyan's teaching in one volume. Conversion and assurance are its driving themes.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol01:
Sermons preached in Utah's first settlements fill Volume I of the Journal of Discourses, printed at Liverpool in 1854. Reporters took down the talks in shorthand as Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve Apostles spoke. The result is a running doctrinal record of the Latter-day Saints in their founding decades.

Doctrine, counsel, and daily building orders share these pages, since the speakers led both church and colony. Historians read the Journal to hear early Mormon teaching in the speakers' own words, unedited by later hands. Volume I opens a set that would run to twenty-six volumes.
zicci-a-tale-volume-01: No author's name is printed in the pages present here for this first book of the tale. Its opening matches the complete record for the same title, stated plainly here. In Naples gardens, young Glyndon turns pale among friends drinking sherbet. A grave stranger explains the shudder as a known visitation. Cold awe, bristling hair, and a sense of something unearthly mark the sign, he says. This record holds book one only.
